units.la: QUod in publicum commodum hic meditatus sum, id inprimis grati animi existere volui erga Te indicium pro iis, quæ tam ubertim in meconferre dignatus es, meritis. Nec dubitare me sinit Tuum liberale in iis collocandis ingenium, quin candido id accepturus sis animo, quamvis vilis sit nimium eorundem hæc mea recognitio. Res est utique omnium Christianorum benevolentia digna, quippe ea, quam hic offero, Prophetia, peculiari modo nobis suggerit mirandam illam Spiritus Sancti effusionem, exactamque gratiarum ac donorum ejus collationem; quæ temporibus Christi futura erat, atque a S. Petro allegatur in ejus adventus promissorumque a Deo præstitorum argumentum. Nonpaucis hic Propheta difficultatum implicitus est nodis, quos uti resolvere omni nisu contendi, ita, ut conatus meos qualescunque habeas acceptos, veniaque, si quid cespitatum fuerit, digneris summo peto opere,
units.tr: That I have pondered this for the public benefit, I wished above all to show as a token of a grateful mind towards you, for the favours which you have deigned to bestow on me so generously. Your generous nature in bestowing such favours does not allow me to doubt that you will receive this with a kindly spirit, although my acknowledgement of them is altogether too slight. This is indeed a matter worthy of the goodwill of all Christians, since the Prophecy which I offer here presents to us in a particular way that wonderful outpouring of the Holy Spirit and the abundant bestowal of his graces and gifts, which was to come in the times of Christ, and which St Peter cites as proof of his coming and of the promises made by God. The Prophet here is entangled in not a few knotty difficulties, which I have striven with every effort to unravel; and I earnestly ask that you would graciously accept my efforts, whatever their worth, and pardon any stumbling on my part.

units.la: {*}Omnem curam laboremque nostrum, quem annotationibus hisce impendimus, ad hunc collineare scopum nemini non vel leviter inspicienti apertum esse poterit, ut textus, quantum potest, genuinum ac literalem erueremus sensum. Postquam enim multiplici mihi deprehensum est observatione, eum ab interpretibus pro suo cujusvis judicio secus plane reddi, quam habemus in Anglicis nostris Bibliis, easque ipsa non paucis in locis scatere interpretationum varietate, quæ ad marginem sunt notatæ, omnem meam operam in id collocandam ratus sum, ut, quænam earum, quæ ad meam pervenerant cognitionem, sit veritati maxime congrua, rite inquirerem, & ad textum Hebraicum examinarem, qui uti unica est regula a divina benignitate per Prophetas ac sanctos viros divino Spiritu agitatos nobis tradita; ita exinde ab ejusdem miranda providentia incorrupta ac integra servata.
units.tr: Anyone who looks at this work even briefly will see that all the care and labour I have devoted to these notes aims at one thing: to bring out, as far as possible, the genuine and literal sense of the text. I have often observed that the interpreters, each according to his own judgement, render it quite differently from what we have in our English Bibles, and that these Bibles, in not a few places, abound in variant renderings, which are noted in the margin. I therefore thought my whole effort should go into examining properly which of the renderings known to me comes closest to the truth, and testing it against the Hebrew text. That text is the only rule that divine goodness handed down to us through the Prophets and holy men moved by the divine Spirit, and it has been preserved uncorrupted and whole by the wonderful providence of the same God.

units.la: Haud enim injuria ex iis quæri posset, qui secus sentiunt, quo tempore is fuisset corruptus, num ante vel post Christi Salvatoris nostri adventum? Si ante Christi tempora id factum fuisse afferant, atque argumenti loco adducere velint interpretationem Græcam, quæ antiquitate cæteras longe post se relinquat, atque adeo a Textu Hebraico differat, ut non obscure liqueat multa alio modo extitisse in eo, quo usi sunt illi Authores, codice, quam hodierno, nihil ea nos plane movere possunt, nisi hæc tria nobis prius dent comprobata. 1. Istud apographum, quo usi sunt, accuratius fuisse iis, quæ postea a Judæis sunt conservata atque ab illis ad nos derivata. 2. Illos interpretes stricte ac præcise literam illius apographi esse secutos, atque nunquam aulos suam, quam cujusdam putabant loci, interponere sententiam, aut laxius aut diversis verbis expressisse, vel non habuisse quasdam verborum significationes, quæ nobis usu adeo non sunt cognitæ. 3. Versionis illorum exemplaria esse tam genuina ac incorrupta, uti ab eis sunt conscripta sine mixtura & alteratione. Quæ certe nunquam satis fuere probata, nec unquam a quoquam probari posse utique persuasum habeo.
units.tr: Those who think otherwise might fairly ask: at what time was this text corrupted, before or after the coming of our Saviour Christ? If they say it was corrupted before the time of Christ, and wish to use as evidence the Greek version, which by its antiquity far outdistances all others and therefore differs from the Hebrew text, so clearly that the codex used by those authors plainly contained many things differently from the present one, then these arguments cannot move us at all unless they first establish three points for us. (1) That the copy they used was more accurate than those which the Jews afterwards preserved and handed down to us. (2) That those translators followed the letter of that copy strictly and precisely, never inserting their own opinion, as they thought some passage required, nor expressing it more loosely or in different words, nor lacking certain meanings of words that are now so little known to us. (3) That the copies of their version are as genuine and uncorrupted as they were written by the translators, without admixture or alteration. These points have certainly never been adequately proved, and I am fully persuaded that they never can be proved by anyone.

units.la: Præterea nullum est dubium, si Christi tempora præcessisset hujusmodi corruptio textus, quin ejus rei aliqualem injecisset mentionem; Vero enim non absimile est, eum qui Judæos ob perversas interpretationes traditionumque glossemata toties reprehendit, non magis fuisse reprehensurum, si ipsum textum corrumpere ausi fuissent.
units.tr: Moreover, there is no doubt that if such a corruption of the text had existed before the time of Christ, he would have made some mention of it. For it is not unlikely that the one who so often rebuked the Jews for their perverse interpretations and the glosses of their traditions would not have rebuked them any less if they had dared to corrupt the text itself.

units.la: Quod si ejus tempora hanc alterationem vel corruptionem dixeris secutam esse, in id facinus ad unum omnes conspirasse malitiose Judæos, ut omnia etiam corrumperent exemplaria concedes, nisi conatus tuos vanos esse velis. Atqui jam constat, multos extot myriadibus fuisse conversos ad Christum, nec paucos inter eos extitisse, opinamur, similes Apollo, qui potens dicitur in S. literis (Act. 18,24.) in quorum manibus genuina versabantur apographa, ex quibus facile vel minimam eorum adulterationem potuissent detegere. Unde ad alios Christianos redundasse eadem, haud sine ratione colligi potest ex eo, quod lingua Hebraica Veteris Testamenti libri inveniamus in Ecclesia inter eos lectos multis annis post Christum. Id enim apud Syros in usu fuisse, ex erudito aliquo ejus gentis a Viro didicimus, qui in libro quodam Arabice exarato de diversis Christianæ Religionis capitibus, cum de ratione legendi Scripturam in Ecclesia verba facit, inquit: كان في الكنيسة الديرية بالعبرية ومنع عن ذلك حتى اذ يهود
units.tr: But if you say that this alteration or corruption followed in his time, you must concede that the Jews of that age all conspired maliciously in such a crime, so that they corrupted even all the copies, unless you wish your efforts to be in vain. Yet it is now established that many thousands were converted to Christ, and we suppose that not a few among them were like Apollos, who is said to be mighty in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24), and who had the genuine copies in their hands, from which they could easily have detected even the slightest falsification. From this it can reasonably be gathered that the same texts passed to other Christians, since we find the Hebrew books of the Old Testament read in the Church among them many years after Christ. We learned this about the Syrians from a certain learned man of that nation, who, in a certain book written in Arabic on the various heads of the Christian religion, when he speaks of the manner of reading Scripture in the Church, says: "kāna fī al-kanīsa al-dayriyya bi-al-cibriyya wa-muni'a 'an dhālika ḥattā idh yahūd" (it was in the monastery church in Hebrew, and this was forbidden until the Jews...).

units.la: i.e. Antiquis temporibus Veteris Testamenti libri legebantur hebraica lingua, donec id S. Ephraim prohiberet.
units.tr: That is: In ancient times the books of the Old Testament were read in the Hebrew language, until S. Ephraim forbade it.

units.la: Quod nulla alia de causa factum esse patet, quam quod genuinum magis ac authenticum putarent Textum hebraicum, quam ullam ejus translationem in linguam genti peculiarem, non autem ex interpretationum ullo defectu, quod plus quam probabile esse exemplo comprobatum dabimus.
units.tr: It is clear that this was done for no other reason than that they thought the Hebrew text more genuine and authoritative than any translation of it into a language peculiar to a people; not from any defect in the interpretations, which we will show by example is more than probable.

units.la: His
units.tr: With these

units.la: a) Al Tacriti c. 29.
units.tr: a) Al Tacriti, ch. 29.

units.la: His atque aliis rationibus expensis, quibus etiam merito accensenda ipsorum Judæorum, quæ omnibus est probe cognita, cura, quam in iis accurate describendis semper tam religiose adhibebant, ut permagni salutis ipsorum interesse id putarent, non video qua saltem rationis specie in dubium vocari posset textus integritas. Quin imo doctus quidam b) vir ex eis, qui textus Hebraici corruptionem adstruere conati sunt, lubens id nobis concedit, eadem fuisse olim autographa hebraica tempore Christi & Jonathanis Paraphrastis cum illis, quibus hodie utimur. Quid ergo de hac re ulterius sumus solliciti? Etenim non poterat non hujus notæ fuisse & codex, quem legendi causa pervolvebat Salvator noster in Synagoga, atque per eundem Spiritum exponebat, a quo hæc antea erant dictata Luc. 4,16. 17. &c. & quod legimus, quo eum comprobat, responsum legisperito datum, cum interrogaret, quid faciendum esset, ut vitam posside ret æternam; Quomodo scriptum est in lege? Quomodo legis tu? Luc. 10,26. & Scripturæ, quas Judæos jubet scrutari, in quibus videbantur vitam æternam habere, & quæ testabantur de eo, Joh. 5, 39. & lex quam dicit non venisse ut dissolveret, sed implereret, & ex qua, usque dum præterierit cælum & terra, ne unum jota aut apicem esse periturum, donec omnia facta fuerint, Matt. 5,17.18. quamque toties citat & ad eam Judæos ablegat, cujusque impletionem rerum gestarum ac passionum suarum constituebat regulam. Plus igitur haud immerito
units.tr: When these and other reasons are weighed, including the care which the Jews themselves took in copying the text, which is well known to all, and which they always applied so scrupulously, judging it of the greatest importance to their salvation, I do not see by what plausible reasoning the integrity of the text could be called in doubt. Indeed, a certain learned man b) from among those who have tried to maintain the corruption of the Hebrew text willingly concedes to us that the Hebrew autographs were the same in the time of Christ and of the paraphrast Jonathan as those we use today. Why, then, should we be further anxious about this matter? Surely the copy which our Saviour unrolled in the synagogue to read, and expounded by the same Spirit by whom these things had been dictated before (Luke 4:16, 17, etc.), could not have been of any other kind. And this is confirmed by what we read: the answer given to the lawyer, when he asked what must be done to possess eternal life, was: What is written in the law? How do you read? (Luke 10:26). Also the Scriptures, which he bids the Jews search, in which they thought they had eternal life, and which bear witness of him (John 5:39). And the law, which he says he came not to dissolve but to fulfil, and from which, until heaven and earth pass away, not one jot or tittle shall perish until all things are done (Matt. 5:17, 18), and which he so often cites and sends the Jews back to, and whose fulfilment in his deeds and sufferings he made the rule. Therefore, not undeservedly, the testimony of this one man, given at that time concerning the integrity of the text, by which he approves it without any objection to the copies, ought to count for more than the doubts of men raised from the varying readings of this or that interpretation, which are linked to it.

units.la: {b} Lud. Capel. in Crit. defenf. p. 572. rito ejus unius de integritate Textus tunc temporis testimonium, quo sine contestatione codicum eum approbat, valere debet, quam hominum ex diversa hujus vel illius interpretationis lectione, quod nectitur, dubium. Quomodocunque autem hæc argumenta ab iis eludi possint, qui contentiosi esse volunt; hujus tamen ponderis esse ea nemo non videt, ut evincant neque ante, neque post Christi adventum codices Hebraeos esse corruptos, regulamque idcirco nostram esse oportere indubiam.
units.tr: {b} Lud. Capel., in Crit. defens., p. 572. However those arguments may be evaded by those who wish to be contentious, no one fails to see that they are of such weight as to prove that the Hebrew copies were corrupted neither before nor after the coming of Christ, and that for this reason our rule must be unquestioned.

units.la: Idem, quem jam citavimus, c) Author, versiones censet examinandas esse ad textum Originalem, si ullum ejus apographum sit incorruptum, non hoc ad illas. Atque hinc est, cum ejus characteris illos esse codices, quos habemus, nulli dubitemus, quod id facere nos aggressi sumus, ad eam saltem versionem, quam sequimur, (idque merito, cum tam accurate cum Originali concordet, ut præ cæteris eligi digna sit, quamvis nostra non esset, aut authoritate inter nos publica stabilita) vel tuendam vel ejus rationem reddendam, quod fieri equidem non potuit, quin cum aliis etiam comparetur, omnesque ad textum originalem referantur tanquam ad lapidem Lydium, quo prædicato hactenus fuit insignitus atque insignitur adhuc dum, quia tali divino charactere gaudet, qui contra quoscunque contra nitentes jus suum atque authoritatem tuebitur.
units.tr: The same author we have already cited c) thinks that versions are to be examined by the original text, if any copy of it is uncorrupted, and not the reverse. And hence, since we do not doubt that the copies we have are of that character, we have undertaken this, at least to defend the version we follow (and rightly so, since it agrees so accurately with the original that it deserves to be chosen above others, even if it were not our own, or established by public authority among us), or to give an account of it. This could not be done without also comparing it with others and referring them all to the original text, as to a touchstone. It has been marked with this quality up to now and is still so marked, because it possesses such a divine character that it will defend its right and authority against all who strive against it.

units.la: Hunc in finem haud semel necessitate coacti sumus in significationem vocum ejus linguæ inquirere, sensusque
units.tr: To this end we have more than once been compelled by necessity to inquire into the meaning of the words of that language, and to bring out the various senses they can bear,

units.la: c) Id. p. 625. que diversos,quos ferre possunt, eruere, ut probe liqueret, quænam earum a diversis interpretibus suggestarum & loco, ubi occurrit,& constructioni, in qua ulurpatur,optime conveniat. Etenim sola earum diversa acceptio causa est tantæ inter interpretes discrepantiæ, cujus ratio reddi non potest. Nec est quod interdum conciliari inter se posse credas, aut omnes discrepantes interpretationes ex uno eodemque fonte,aut saltem ex una eademque lectione prodire tibi persuadeas. Quinimo rite attendenti contrarium patebit, quod ex lectionum varietate non oriantur, sed ex diversis alicujus vocis significationibus, quarum alii hanc, alii aliam pro diverso suo judicio elegerunt,certo interim persuasi in eo se sequi textum originalem,nec suam interpretationem inconvenientiæ ullius arguiposse. Qua ratione quædam in Novo Testamento loca ex Veteri citata, quæ nonnihil differentiæ videntur præ se ferre juxta vulgares interpretationes , nihil plane differre in aprico est,si ad aliam respicias significationem, quam vox varians æque admittit ac eam, quam recentiores ei tribuunt, eorumque sequaces nullam ejus aliam esse sibi constanter persuadent. E. G. Hebr.8,9. Et ego sprevi eos ait Dominus, qui locus apud Jerem.31,32. juxta nostrat. aliorumque translationes ita habet: quamvis essem conjugio junctus eis ,ait Dominus. Hanc diversitatem quis putaret prodire ex eadem Textus Hebraici lectione? attamen si cumpiam in vocem hebraic. בעלתי baalti scrutari volupe fuerit, is reperiet utraque eam significatione gaudere,& conjugio jungi & spernere, contemnere, nulloque loco
units.tr: c) The same author, p. 625. so that it might be clear which of the meanings suggested by the different interpreters best fits the place where the word occurs and the construction in which it is used. For the sole cause of so great a discrepancy among the interpreters is the diverse acceptance of the words, and this cause cannot be explained away. Nor should you think that the discrepancies can sometimes be reconciled, or believe that all the differing interpretations arise from one and the same source, or at least from one and the same reading. Indeed, to one who attends carefully the opposite will be evident: they do not arise from variety of readings but from the different meanings of some word, one interpreter choosing this meaning and another that according to his own judgement, each being certain that he follows the original text and that his interpretation involves no inconsistency. In this way, certain passages of the Old Testament quoted in the New, which seem to show some difference from the common interpretations, plainly differ in nothing, if you look to the other meaning which the variable word equally admits, besides the one which recent writers assign to it, and which their followers constantly persuade themselves is the only one. For example, Heb. 8:9, And I regarded them not, saith the Lord; this passage in Jeremiah 31:32, according to our translation and those of others, reads: though I was a husband unto them, saith the Lord. Who would think this difference arises from the same reading of the Hebrew text? Yet if one wishes to examine the Hebrew word baalti [בעלתי] carefully, he will find that it has both meanings: to be joined in marriage, and to despise, to scorn, and in no place to hold as

units.la: b loco habere. Idem fit, ut alia exempla non adducam, in tritissimo illo Prophetiæ loco apud Mich. 5, 2. qui citatur hunc in modum Matt. 2, 6. Tu Bethlehem Ephrata non es minima inter Principes Juda, ubi non eadem cum Evangelista legisse videtur Propheta ita hodie reddita, At tu Bethlehem minima ut fis inter mille Juda, donec sedula inquisitione adhibita, invenerimus, vocem יצר Tsair, a Propheta usurpatam pariter significare magnum & excelsum, ac parvum esse. Atque tum non nisi interpretum culpa hanc oriri differentiam constat, quibusdam hac, aliis alia significatione vocem accipientibus, eumque locum eodem modo in Veteri Testamento reddi debere, ac est in Novo, Quare non statim damnanda est ea interpretatio, eo quod ab alia differt, sed utraque est examinanda ad Textum Originalem; cui cum utraque videris congruentem, neque tum alterutra statim rejicienda, sed rite expendendum, quænam loco subjecto quam maxime sit conveniens, quod utique interdum adeo anceps est ac dubium, ut & viris acerrimo judicio præstantibus aqua hæreat, neque in alterutram partem quicquam temere determinare audeant.
units.tr: no loco habere. The same happens, to give no other examples, in that most familiar prophecy of Micah 5:2, which is cited by Matthew 2:6 in this way: And thou Bethlehem Ephratah, art not the least among the princes of Judah. Here the prophet seems not to have read what the Evangelist read, which today is rendered But thou Bethlehem, though least, art among the thousands of Judah. Yet after diligent inquiry we have found that the word יצר [tsair], used by the prophet, can equally mean great and exalted as well as small. It is clear that this difference arises only from the fault of the translators, some taking the word in one sense and others in another, and that the passage ought to be rendered in the Old Testament in the same way as it is in the New. Therefore that interpretation should not be condemned at once merely because it differs from another. Both must be examined against the original text. When each is found to agree with it, neither should be rejected at once. Instead one must weigh carefully which fits the subject passage best. This is sometimes so doubtful and uncertain that even men of the keenest judgment hesitate and dare not rashly settle on either side.

units.la: Cujus rei cum rationem habuerunt interpretes nostri, summa, uti videmus, modestia & ingenuitate ad marginem rejecerunt diversas lectiones & interpretationes Bibliorum nostrorum, ubi dubitabant quas aliis præferrent, & in prudentis Lectoris arbitrium eligendique placitum injurii esse nolebant, cum non minus hæc quam illa (ut Judæi loqui amant tali in casu) viventis Dei sint verba, utrinque vera & verbis hebraicis ac analogiæ fidei pariter congruentia. Qua modestia, quicunque Scripturas S. explicare aggrediuntur, eos nihil prius nihilque antiquius habere oportet, quippe qua vix credibile est, quot præcidantur ansæ litigandi, quo non tantum veritas præpostere defensa amittitur, sed etiam ille, qui ad eam inveniendam omne studium curamque convertit, nec ab ea fortean vel latum unguem aberrat, censura rigida veritatis habetur abnegator.
units.tr: Our translators, mindful of this, with great modesty and candour, as we see, placed in the margin the different readings and interpretations of our Bibles where they doubted which to prefer. They were unwilling to impose their own judgment on the prudent reader's choice, since these readings are no less (as the Jews love to say in such cases) words of the living God than those in the text. Both are true, and both agree equally with the Hebrew words and with the analogy of faith. Whoever undertakes to explain the Holy Scriptures ought to have nothing more important or prior to this modesty. It is hard to believe how many occasions of quarrelling are cut off by it. Not only is truth lost when it is defended in a perverse way, but also the man who devotes all his zeal and care to finding it, and who perhaps does not stray from it by the breadth of a fingernail, is regarded by the stern judgment of the truth-deniers.

units.la: Quocirca ut vocis alicujus dubiæ vel difficilis unam vel plures invenirem significationes, illamque cum primis, quæ loco subjecto ejusque scopo ac contextui apprime effet conveniens, omnia pro mea facultate, adhibui adminicula, eaque non unius generis. Primo omnia ea loca inter se contuli, in quibus eandem vocem vel phrasin in S. literis extare memineram. Secundo nullum in præcipuis interpretum maxime celebrium translationibus evolvendis subterfugi laborem. Tertio in consilium adhibui non tantum eos libros, qui nobis singulorum duntaxat vocabulorum recludunt significationes, ut sunt Dictionaria &c. verum etiam, qui ad sensum eorum, quatenus cum aliis sunt conjuncta, nos intromittunt, uti Commentatores & Expositores. Quod ad translationes attinet, quas hic præcipue lustrare libuit, illæ sunt vel antiquæ, vel recentiores. Exantiquissimis sunt (quæ plerumque τῶν LXX. vocatur) & latina (quam communiter nuncupant Vulgatam) & Syriaca & Arabica. Nec incognitæ sunt a multis annis in hac occidentali Mundi plaga, Græca & latina; tina,quin imo a quamplurimis tam accurate earum pertexta est ratio & feries, ut supervacaneum fore arbitremur amplius quid addere velle. Alia vero est ratio Syriacæ & Arabicæ,quæ uti perquam familiares fuerunt tantum in orientalibus istis oris ; ita nullam earum unquam notitiam habuerunt noftrat. donec ultima excellentissima excusa sint Biblia Parifienfia & Londinenfia Polyglotta. Quare ab instituto nostro haud alienum remur,ut earum originem ac Historiam, quam poterit fieri, brevissime his præexamus. Manifesta res est,Syros olim habuisse translationem S. Scripturæ propria lingua, eamque, fi quæ illis ipsis fides habenda, antiquitate contendere cum Græca. Verum enim vero,ut rem paulo enucleatius demus, obfervandum est,eos habere duas translationes, quarum altera concinnata est ex Hebraeo, altera ex Græco. Habemus referente Gregorio Abul Pharajio (cujus historia impressa est Oxoniæ Arabice & Latine) Græcam versionem opera τῶν LXXII. tempore Ptolomei Philadelphi factam, receptam quidem fuisse & Græcis & plurimis Christianorum sectis;minime vero gentium Syris,iisque potissimum, qui magis ad orientem habitabant. Eos enim perhibet habuisse versionem quandam,quam vocabant simplicem five planam, quia interpretes in ea non studebant verborum phaleris, sed quæ conspirabat cum codicibus Judæorum. Qui vero magis habitabant ad occidentem, eos ait duas habuisse versiones; aliam simplicem, quæ ex Hebraeo in Syriacam linguam erat translata post Christi adventum tempore Addæi (vel Thaddæi) Apostoli; vel ut aliis liis placet, tempore Salomonis Davidis Filii, & Hierami: aliamque multo concinniorem, quæ ex Græca τῶν LXX. erat facta longo post incarnationem Salvatoris nostri intervallo. Porro ut mentem ejus probe teneamus, opinionemque harum gentium recte capiamus, attendendum velim, quod prolatum est a quodam Soaded Episcopo olim Hadethensi, qui citatur a doctissimo Sionita in præfatione Editionis ejus Psalmorum Syriace & Latine. Is enim dicit libros sacros, scilicet Deuteronomion, Josuam, Judices, Ruth, Samuelem, Davidem (sive Psalmos) Proverbia, Ecclesiasten, Canticum Canticorum & Jobum translatos esse tempore Salomonis rogatu Hierami regis Tyri amici ejus. Cæteros vero tum Veteris, tum Novi Testamenti tempore Abagaris regis Syriæ Thaddæi aliorumque Apostolorum cura. Quandoquidem autem posterioris ævi aliam habeamus, eam a Thoma Heracleensi concinnatam esse haud injuria mihi persuadeo. Id enim reperio in MS. quodam Syriaco (de quo nonnihil dictum est in præfatione posterioris Epistolæ S.Petri Syriace, Græce & Latine impressæ Lugduni 1630.) ubi inter antiquam & recentiorem Thomæ Heracleensis probe distinguitur. Pari ratione versioni historiæ Susannæ V.T.in codice quodam Syriaco MS. præfixum invenio, eam esse ܡܥܕܐ ܕܫܘܫܢ ܐܝܬܝ ex versione Heracleensis. Binæ enim sunt hujus historiæ in eo codice versiones, quarum tamen neutram antiquam eam esse simplicem putandum. Nec verofimile est, ullum Apocryphorum librorum simplici eo stylo inveniri, quippe quibusdam eorum expresse præfigitur, uti primo libro Esdræ, eum conformatum esse ad versionem τῶν LXXII, & sub finem ejus, eum non reperiri in versione simplici, quod idem repetitur ante Tobiæ librum. Quo autem tempore Thomas Heracleensis vixerit, nondum mihi ex quoquam certò lcire contigit. Id tamen silentio nequaquam prætereundum est, quod inter sanctos eum repererim notatum in Calendario quodam Syriaco, cujus in memoriam cum aliis dies 26. Hariran vel Junii erat consecratus, unde haud improbabile est eum sequioris fuisse ævi. Quod etiam non parum confirmatur, si idem sit, quod equidem puto, cujus mentionem facit Schultingius in sua Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica tom.3.pag. 106. sub nomine Thamæ Harchalani, qui ejus memoriam ex catalogo Miffalium ab Ignatio Patriarcha Antioch. factorum producit, ubi ex Græca in Chaldaicam (ita vocant Syriacam) transtulisse dicitur Miffalia Johannis Evangelistæ & Clementis, quadringentis & septem circiter annis post Christum. Cum vero contendant Syri de antiquitate suæ interpretationis, de altera illa antiquiore id accipiendum esse patet. Quod autem de antiquitate cujusdam Syriacæ versionis dicant, quam nimis fortean videantur jactare, id idem habemus non tantum testimonio Patrum Græcorum, sed & omnium codicum τῶν LXXII. fide comprobatum. Quotcunque enim τῶν LXXII. editiones extant, sive juxta vetustissimum ex Bibliotheca Regis exemplar, sive juxta alia quaecunque, solis Complutenfibus exceptis, expressæ, ad unum omnes sub finem libri Jobi habent hæc verba, ἔτος ἐρμηνεύεται ἐν τῆς Συριακῆς
units.tr: Therefore, so that I might find one or more meanings of some doubtful or difficult word, and especially the one best suited to the subject passage, its purpose and its context, I used every aid within my power, and these were of more than one kind. First, I compared with one another all the passages in which I remembered that the same word or phrase occurs in Holy Scripture. Second, I shrank from no labour in going through the principal translations of the most celebrated interpreters. Third, I took counsel not only from those books which unlock for us the meanings of single words, such as Dictionaries etc., but also from those which introduce us to their sense as they are joined with other words, such as commentators and expositors. As for the translations, which I particularly wished to survey here, some are very old and some more recent. The most ancient are the Greek (commonly called the Septuagint), the Latin (commonly called the Vulgate), and the Syriac and Arabic. The Greek and Latin have not been unknown for many years in this western part of the world. Indeed their history and sequence have been so thoroughly worked out by many that I think it superfluous to add anything more. The case of the Syriac and Arabic is different. As these were very familiar only in those eastern regions, our people had no knowledge of them until the recent, most excellent, printed Paris and London Polyglot Bibles. Therefore I think it not foreign to my plan to examine their origin and history here, as briefly as I can. It is plain that the Syrians once had a translation of Holy Scripture in their own language, and, if their own claims are to be believed, one that rivals the Greek in antiquity. But, to explain the matter a little more clearly, it must be observed that they have two translations, one made from the Hebrew and the other from the Greek. Following Gregory Abul Pharajius (whose history was printed at Oxford in Arabic and Latin), we have the Greek version made by the labour of the Seventy-Two at the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus. This was indeed received by the Greeks and by many Christian sects, but not by the Syrian peoples, especially those who dwelt further east. For he says they had a certain version which they called simple or plain, because the translators in it did not strive for ornament of words, but kept to the agreement of Jewish manuscripts. Those who lived further west, he says, had two versions: one simple, translated from the Hebrew into the Syriac language after the coming of Christ, in the time of the Apostle Addaeus (or Thaddaeus), or, as others prefer, in the time of Solomon, son of David, and Hiram; and another, much more polished, made from the Greek of the Seventy at a long interval after the incarnation of our Saviour. Furthermore, that we may properly grasp his mind and rightly understand the opinion of these peoples, I would have it noted what was stated by a certain Bishop Soaded, once of Hadeth, who is cited by the most learned Sionita in the preface to his edition of the Psalms in Syriac and Latin. For he says that the sacred books, namely Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Samuel, David (that is, the Psalms), Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs and Job, were translated in the time of Solomon, at the request of Hiram, king of Tyre, his friend. The rest of the Old and New Testament were done under the care of Thaddaeus and the other Apostles, in the time of Abgar, king of Syria. Since we have another, later version, I am fairly persuaded that it was produced by Thomas of Heraclea. For I find this in a certain Syriac manuscript (of which something was said in the preface to the later Epistle of St Peter printed in Syriac, Greek and Latin at Leiden in 1630), where a clear distinction is made between the ancient version and the more recent one of Thomas of Heraclea. In the same way I find, prefixed to the version of the history of Susanna from the Old Testament in a certain Syriac manuscript, that it is the version (transliterated: ma'da d-Shushan ithai) from the version of Heraclea. For there are two versions of this history in that codex, and neither should be thought to be the ancient simple one. Nor is it likely that any of the apocryphal books is found in that simple style, since some of them are expressly said to have been conformed to the version of the Seventy-Two, as at the end of the first book of Esdras, and at the end of it, that it is not found in the simple version, which is repeated before the book of Tobit. At what time Thomas of Heraclea lived I have not yet been able to learn with certainty from anyone. Yet this must by no means be passed over in silence: I have found him noted among the saints in a certain Syriac calendar, in which, along with others, the 26th day of Hariran or June was dedicated to his memory. Hence it is not improbable that he belonged to a later age. This is not a little confirmed if he is the same person (as I think) whom Schultingius mentions in his Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica, vol. 3, p. 106, under the name Thamas Harchalanus. He gives this man's memory from the catalogue of Missals made by Ignatius, Patriarch of Antioch, where it is said that he translated the Missals of the Evangelist John and of Clement from Greek into Chaldaic (as they call Syriac), about four hundred and seven years after Christ. But since the Syrians contend about the antiquity of their translation, it is plain that this must be understood of the other, older version. As for their claim to the antiquity of a certain Syriac version, which they may seem to boast of too much, we have the same confirmed not only by the testimony of the Greek Fathers, but also by the agreement of all the manuscripts of the Seventy-Two. For however many editions of the Seventy-Two exist, whether according to the very ancient copy in the King's Library or according to any other, all of them, printed without exception except the Complutensian, end with these words at the end of the book of Job: It is translated [ἔτος ἐρμηνεύεται ἐν τῆς Συριακῆς]

units.la: ϱιακῆς ϱιαϰὴς BΙΒΛΩ, &c. Hic translatus est ex quodam sive (illo, Syriaco libro i.e. Bibliis; ex alio enim libro constat illos non petiisse verba Textus authentica. Quod indicio est haud indubio, librum quendam Syriacum (vel versionem) fuisse Syriacum longe antiquiorem quovis Græcorum. Et quamvis in aliis non parum discrepent inter se codices ab antiquioribus illis, quibus id erat adscriptum, descripti, in eo tamen omnes insigniter concordant. Quare ne antiquam valde censeamus versionem Syriacam, vix a nobis impetrare possumus. Atque id ipsum est quod jam affirmamus, quodque simul argumenti loco esse potest, fuisse ante tempora S. Ephraimi (quod supra innuebamus) talem versionem, qua potuissent uti, nisi textum hebraicum magis censuissent authenticum tantique habuissent, ut non nisi eum solum in publicum Ecclesiarum suarum adhibuissent usum. Quod si autem tunc temporis nullam velimus extitisse versionem privatos suisse eos omnino usu S. literarum V. Testamenti, si textus hebraici usus illis etiam interdictus fuisset, manifestum est; quod equidem ita accipiendum non est, quippe ejus mens alia nostra opinione non fuit, quam ut illi legerentur vulgari lingua, qua in eos etiam scripsisse perhibetur Commentarios.
units.tr: ϱιακῆς [ϱιαϰὴς] BΙΒΛΩ, &c. This is translated from a certain Syriac book (that is, the Bibles); for it is clear from another book that they did not seek the authentic words of the Text. This is no doubtful indication that there was a certain Syriac book (or version), a Syriac one far older than any Greek. And although the manuscripts copied from those ancient ones, in which this was written, differ not a little among themselves in other respects, in this they all agree remarkably. Hence we can scarcely bring ourselves to think the Syriac version very ancient. And this is precisely what we affirm, and what can at the same time serve as an argument: that before the time of St. Ephraem (whom we hinted at above) there was such a version which they could have used, had they not judged the Hebrew text to be more authentic and held it in such esteem that they used it alone in the public worship of their churches. But if we were to suppose that no version existed at that time, and that the private persons had no use at all of the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, it is plain that the Hebrew text would have been forbidden them too; which, indeed, is not to be so understood, since his intention, in our opinion, was nothing other than that they should read them in the vernacular tongue, in which he is said to have written commentaries for them as well.

units.la: Hæc in rem nostram quamvis sufficere videantur, ulterius tamen, postquam in hanc materiam delapsi sumus, in eandem inquirere abs re esse non arbitramur etiam atque etiam rogantes, ut transeant Lectores ea, quæ fortean minoris videbuntur ponderis.
units.tr: Although these things seem sufficient for our purpose, we nonetheless think it not out of place to inquire further into this matter, now that we have fallen into it, asking again and again that readers pass over those things which may seem of less weight.

units.la: PRÆFATIO GENERALIS.
units.tr: GENERAL PREFACE.

units.la: Quicunque ultimum inspexerit caput Jobi in Textu Hebraico, iisque in Versionibus, quæ ad illum sunt concinnatæ, deprehendet eum finiri verlu 17. in hæc verba: Ita mortuus est Jobus senex & fatur dierum. Secus vero habet in Græca, quæ vocatur Septuagintaviralis. Ibi enim additi sunt quidam versus, idque a tam longo temporis intervallo, ut Græci quidam Patres simili ratione in eas commentati sint ac in Textum authenticum. d) Olympiodorus statuit eos esse traditos ab ipsis Apostolis; & Polychronius, perinde eos haberi a Patribus. Primo additum est: Scriptura est eum resurrecturum cum illis quos Dominus excitabit. Deinde sequitur, quod diximus, Is (vel hic vir) translatus est ex libro Syriaco, habitans (vel qui habitabat) in terra Ausitis (vel Uz) infinibus Idumeæ & Arabiæ: ejus nomen erat Jobab, cum aliis multis quæ spectant ad ejus uxorem & filium, uti & ad genealogiam ejus, e.g. quod effet fatus posteritate Efavi atque ab Abrahamo quintus, & quod rerum potiretur in Edom post Balac &c. pari modo quæ pertinent ad amicos ejus, qui veniebant illum visitatum. Quæ omnia in exemplari impresso juxta antiquissimum illud M.S. quod in Bibliotheca Regis servatur, rursus excipit brevior de ipsius Jobi vita narratio, cui iterum id est præfixum, Is translatus est ex libro Syriaco; verum id idem in aliis codicibus non extat. Quod quem habeat usum, ex sequentibus dilucide patebit. Præterea res est testimonio non minus veterum quam recentiorum confirmata, Aquilam & Symmachum, quorum uterque
units.tr: Whoever examines the last chapter of Job in the Hebrew text, and in the versions made from it, will find that it ends at verse 17 with these words: So Job died, an old man and full of days. It is otherwise in the Greek, which is called the Septuagint. For certain verses have been added there, and at so great an interval of time that some Greek Fathers have commented on them in the same way as on the authentic text. d) Olympiodorus holds that they were handed down by the Apostles themselves, and Polychronius that the Fathers likewise regard them so. First is added: Scripture says that he will rise again with those whom the Lord will raise up. Then follows what we have mentioned: He (or this man) was translated from a Syriac book, dwelling (or who dwelt) in the land of Ausitis (or Uz) on the borders of Idumaea and Arabia; his name was Jobab, together with many other things concerning his wife and son, and also his genealogy, for example that he was descended from the posterity of Esau and was the fifth from Abraham, and that he ruled in Edom after Balac, and so on; likewise things relating to his friends who came to visit him. All these things, in the printed copy following that most ancient manuscript which is kept in the King's Library, are again taken up by a shorter account of Job's own life, to which again this is prefixed: He was translated from a Syriac book; but this same thing is not found in other codices. What use this has will become clear from what follows. Moreover, the matter is confirmed by the testimony of ancient and recent writers alike: Aquila and Symmachus, each of whom

units.la: d) Proœmio in Catenam Jobi Londini 1637. terque ex Hebræa in Græcam linguam transtulit Vetus Testamentum, eodem modo finem impositurum huic Libro atque Textum Hebræum; Theodotionem autem, qui idem fecit & circa 180. annum post Christum floruit, non secus eum finivisse ac LXX. cum additione ex versione Syriaca.
units.tr: d) From the Proem to the Catena on Job, London 1637. translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Greek, would likewise end this Book in the same way as the Hebrew text; but Theodotion, who also did the same and flourished about the year 180 after Christ, ended it no differently from the Seventy, with an addition from the Syriac version.

units.la: Hic vero contra illud, quod ex hisce de antiquitate Versionis Syriacæ elici potest argumentum, excipi posse id, quod Græcorum nonnulli dicunt, per Syriacam, quæ in his Additionibus Jobi nominatur, intelligi linguam Hebraicam, quo facit, quod a quodam anonymo Græco Autore (cujus verba mecum communicavit Reverendus ac Doctissimus Vir D. Thomas Marshall) asseritur, in M.S. quodam Johanni Melalæ præfixa, hanc fuisse opinionem Origenis. At cujus is Autor sit authoritatis nescio, vero saltem simile non est Origenem ita sensisse aut locutum esse. Eo enim in Commentario, qui sub ejus nomine circumfertur, expresse habetur, hunc librum initio scriptum Syriace, atque deinde in hebraicam linguam translatum & a Mose politum & persectum. Quod si ita est, diversæ ipsi sine controversia habentur lingua Syriaca & Hebraica. Verum in dubium vocatur ejus libri authoritas, unde nullo suffulcimento nititur hæc opinio. Quod porro de ea re statuit Origenes, facile poterit colligi ex ejus epistola ad Africanum, cujus pars præfixa est libro Jobi a Doctissimo Patricio Junio, juxta MS. in regia Bibliotheca edito, ubi expresse habet, ea verba, quæ post 17. versum capitis ultimi
units.tr: Here, however, it can be objected against the argument for the antiquity of the Syriac Version that can be drawn from these things, that some of the Greeks say that by the Syriac, which is named in these additions to Job, is meant the Hebrew language. To this favours what is asserted by an anonymous Greek author (whose words the Reverend and most learned Mr Thomas Marshall communicated to me), prefixed in a certain manuscript to Johannes Malalas, that this was the opinion of Origen. But what authority that author has I do not know; it is at least not likely that Origen thought or said so. For in the commentary which circulates under his name it is expressly stated that this book was first written in Syriac, and then translated into the Hebrew language and polished and perfected by Moses. If that is so, Syriac and Hebrew are without controversy regarded as different languages. But the authority of that book is called in question, so this opinion rests on no support. What Origen further determined on this matter can easily be gathered from his letter to Africanus, part of which is prefixed to the book of Job by the most learned Patrick Junius, published from a manuscript in the royal library, where he expressly says that the words which follow the 17th verse of the last chapter in the Greek version are not found in the Hebrew, and therefore not in Aquila, but in the Seventy and Theodotion.

units.la: c mi sequuntur in Græca versione, non reperiri in Hebraico, atque ex eo nec in Aquila, sed in τοῖς LXXII. & Theodotione. Quodsi ei persuasum fuisset per Syriacam, ex qua expresse dicitur versio facta, intelligendam esse Hebraicam, equidem non dixisset in Hebraicis codicibus ea defuisse. Utcunque fit, aliis nihilominus sic visum est. Ita enim Nobilius refert in variantibus suis lectionibus versionis Græcæ, Græcum Scholiasten dicere se dialectum Hebraicam vocare Syriacam, propter affinitatem, quæ illis intercedit, quod probare conatur. At quid de hoc Græco Scholiaste referam, aliunde nihil habeo quam abeo. Idem autem ab Olympiodoro in Catena Jobi expresse affirmatur, qui, postquam observavit Aquilam & Symmachum eodem modo claudere hunc librum ac Textum Hebræum, Theodotionem vero easdem habere additiones quas LXXII. ita mentem suam declarat, quod hoc loco dialectum hebraicam vocet Syriacam; quam postea confirmat his ficulneis & nil ad rem facientibus argumentis; quia multum affinitatis habet Syriaca lingua cum Hebræa, utraque eodem literarum numero (scil. 22.) gaudente; & quia Judæa comprehenditur sub nomine Syriæ.
units.tr: ...which follow in the Greek version are not found in the Hebrew, and therefore not in Aquila, but in the Seventy and Theodotion. Were he persuaded that the Syriac, from which the version is expressly said to have been made, must be understood as Hebrew, I would not have said that these words were absent from the Hebrew codices. However it is, others nevertheless have thought so. For thus Nobilius reports, in his variant readings of the Greek version, that the Greek Scholiast says he calls the Hebrew dialect Syriac on account of the affinity between them, which he tries to prove. But what I may say of this Greek Scholiast, I have nothing to go on except what he himself says. The same is expressly affirmed by Olympiodorus in the Catena on Job, who, after observing that Aquila and Symmachus close this book in the same way as the Hebrew text, while Theodotion has the same additions as the LXX, declares his mind thus: that in this place he calls the Hebrew dialect Syriac; which he afterwards confirms with these flimsy arguments that have nothing to do with the matter: because the Syriac language has much affinity with Hebrew, both having the same number of letters (namely 22); and because Judaea is comprehended under the name of Syria.

units.la: Quod quamvis ei aliisq;, qui has linguas forsitan su-perficiarie & summis labris tantum attigere, tam serio fit persuasum, nos tamen eo adduci non facile patiemur, ut hisce quicquam moveamur. Præterquam enim quod hæc verba nullibi inveniantur in quodam Codice Hebræo, quod ipse fatetur, atque ita suo ipsius gladio sibi jugulum petit,non est eadem omnium Patrum consensu recepta opinio,fi eadem est Syriaca lingua cum Hebraica. Quidam enim eorum dilucide prædicant Hebraicam & Syriacam linguam inter fe differre, nec confundendas esse alia pro alia accepta. Utramque citat & Syriacam & Hebraeam, tanquam diversas lectiones in versum quendam 48. Pfalm. juxta Græcorum divisionem, S. Chryfoftomus, qui Antiochiæ in Syria vixit, & cui, quid Syriacæ linguæ nomine tunc veniret, non potuit non incognitum esse. Idem facit Theodoretus in Pfal. 115. & Jon. 3, 4. ut jam præteream Origenem supra citatum, aliaque non pauca testimonia, quarum quædam reperiuntur inScholiafte Græco, & Nobilii in eum notis.
units.tr: Although this is so seriously persuaded to him and to others who perhaps touched these languages only superficially and on the surface, we will not easily allow ourselves to be moved by these things. For besides the fact that these words are not found anywhere in a certain Hebrew codex, which he himself admits, and so he seeks his own throat with his own sword, it is not the common opinion received by the consensus of all the Fathers that the Syriac language is the same as Hebrew. For some of them plainly declare that the Hebrew and Syriac languages differ from each other, and that the one must not be confused with the other. Chrysostom, who lived at Antioch in Syria, and to whom it cannot have been unknown what was then meant by the name of the Syriac language, cites both Syriac and Hebrew as different readings for a certain verse of Psalm 48 according to the Greek division. Theodoret does the same on Psalm 115 and Jon. 3, 4, not to mention Origen cited above and many other testimonies, some of which are found in the Greek Scholiast and in Nobilius's notes on him.

units.la: Quodsi alii, eodem Nobilio notante, dicant per Syriacam intelligi Chaldaicam, nihil dicunt. Idem enim est ac fi dicerent,per Syriacam intelligi Syriacam, Hæ namque unius tantum linguæ sunt duæ dialecti, quamvis Chaldaica præcipue vocata fit, quam retinuerant Judæi reversi ex Babylone, ubi eam didicerant, propriæque linguæ multum perdiderant, quæ tamen maximam partem ad regulas Hebraicæ est conformata, uti cuivis cognitionem ejus rei majorem cupienti patebit ex erudita præfatione Grammaticæ Linguarum Orientalium Ludovici de Dieu. Quo tempore multi Syri fe ipsi vocabant Chaldæos, suamque linguam Chaldaicam, quamque nos vocamus linguam Chaldaicam, Judæi nuncupabant Arami Syriacam. Quod cum illis lubens porrigamus, quid aliud inde inferri potest, quam librum Jobi aut fuisse scriptum dialecto Chaldaica ; aut quandam ejus libri fuisse tra- lationem, in qua tanquam verba authentica scripta erant hæ additiones, cujus authoritatem secuti sunt LXX. in Græcam linguam eum transferentes. At neutrum horum a quoquam concessum iri puto. Nam præterquam quod Paraphraftes Chaldæus, quem habemus, hujusmodi additiones non agnoscit, fine controversia is multo recétior est temporibus Ptolomæi Philadelphi,nec ullo argumento probari potest, aliam hac dialecto tunc temporis extitisse versionem, quæ periit, nec facile aliquis Christianorum in eam sententiam adducetur, licet quidam e) Judæi id nobis persuadere conentur, Septuaginta que non ex genuino quodam Hebraico Codice,sed ex ea suam versionem concinnaffe contendant, quæ certe tanta est,ut vix illis possit affricari macula. Nihil itaque huc usque promotum est, nisi per Syriacam velint intelligi hebraicam, & quis quæso ita sentiret ? Septuaginta nequaquam, certum habeo; qui cum unanimi omnium consensu dicantur Judæi, linguam suam sanctam (sicuti omnes eam κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocant atque ita ab aliis & quidem præcipue a * Syriaca distinguunt) eo usque non putandi sunt profanaffe, ut eam hoc nomine indigitarent,vel pro authenticis verbis habuisse ea, quæ in textu non inveniebant; quid ! quod nec ipse Theodoti- on,
units.tr: If others, as Nobilius notes, say that by Syriac is meant Chaldaic, they say nothing. For it amounts to the same as if they said per Syriacam intelligi Syriacam, "by Syriac is meant Syriac." These are two dialects of one language only, although the one is especially called Chaldaic, which the Jews who returned from Babylon retained, having learned it there, while losing much of their own language; yet it is for the most part conformed to the rules of Hebrew, as will be clear to anyone who wishes for fuller knowledge of this matter from the learned preface of Ludovici de Dieu's Grammar of the Oriental Languages. At that time many Syrians called themselves Chaldeans, and the Jews called the Syriac language, which we call the Chaldaic language, Aramaic. Since we gladly grant them this, what else can be inferred from it than that the book of Job was either written in the Chaldaic dialect, or that there was some translation of this book in which these additions were written as authentic words, whose authority the Seventy followed in translating it into Greek? But I think neither of these will be granted by anyone. For besides the fact that the Chaldee paraphrast we have does not acknowledge such additions, he is without controversy much more recent than the times of Ptolemy Philadelphus, nor can it be proved by any argument that another version in this dialect existed at that time which has since perished. Nor will any Christian easily be brought to that view, although some Jews try to persuade us of it, and contend that the Seventy made their version not from a genuine Hebrew codex but from that one, which is certainly of such standing that scarcely any stain can be fixed upon it. So nothing has been advanced so far, unless they wish by Syriac to mean Hebrew; and who, I ask, would think so? The Seventy certainly would not, I am sure. They are said, by the unanimous agreement of all, to be Jews, and they did not profane their holy language (as all call it par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν] and distinguish it from others, and especially from Syriac) to such an extent that they would designate it by this name, or would have held as authentic words those things which they did not find in the text. What! Not even Theodotion himself,

units.la: {e} R. Ararias. Vid. Buxt. de punct. antiquitate part. 1. c. p. 128. &c. & R. Gedaliah ab Hotting. citatus Phil. Sac. p. 205.
units.tr: {e} R. Ararias. See Buxt. de punct. antiquitate, part 1, c. p. 128 etc., and R. Gedaliah ab Hotting, cited in Phil. Sac. p. 205.

units.la: {*} Corari l. 2, c. 68. on, qui tanto temporis intervallo post eos vixit, hæc nomina, quamcunque etiam linguæ hebrææ notitiam habuerit, confuderit, nec ullus alius Græcorum priscorum, qui tanta literarum cognitione pollebat, ut versionem in se recipere potuisset.
units.tr: {*} Corari, bk. 2, ch. 68. ...on, who lived so long after them, confused these names, however much knowledge of the Hebrew language he may have had. Nor was there any other of the earlier Greeks who was so accomplished in letters that he could undertake the translation.

units.la: At, uti jam notatum est antea, postquam redierant Judæi ex captivitate Babylonica, adeo erat illorum lingua chaldaica, vel Syriaca, mixta, ut pari ferme jure mereretur Syriacæ nomen ac Hebraicæ. Verum enim vero etiam tunc temporis vocata est potius Hebraica, quam Syriaca, ut ex Novo Testamento apparet. Quod vero ad propriam illam vetustam hebraicam attinet, de qua jam verba facimus, quivis facile videt, qui harum linguarum aliquem gustum habet, eam non ita appellari posse nisi certo quodam respectu. Quare qui per Syriacam intelligi cupiunt hebraicam, ii sunt quidam Græci aut harum linguarum omnino expertes, aut nimis invidi Syriacæ versionis laudi, qua antiquitate Græcam videretur vincere. Pari facilitate nobis suggerere possent, Jacobum locutum esse Syriace, quando eundem cumulum vocat Galeed, quem Laban appellabat f) Jegar Sabadutha. Quod si autem illis largiamur, Græcos Syriaca innuisse linguam hebraicam, qua ratione nobis expedient, quare illud, quod juxta eorum sententiam olim constituebat hebraici Textus partem, atque idcirco etiam in græcam linguam translatum, hodie in omnibus hebraicæ linguæ codicibus omnino defit, atque olim etiam
units.tr: But, as has already been noted above, after the Jews had returned from the Babylonian captivity, their language was so mixed with Chaldean or Syriac that it deserved the name Syriac almost as much as the name Hebrew. Indeed, even at that time it was called Hebrew rather than Syriac, as appears from the New Testament. As for that ancient Hebrew language proper, which is what we are now discussing, anyone who has some taste for these languages easily sees that it cannot be called by that name except in a certain sense. Therefore those who want "Syriac" to mean Hebrew are either Greeks or men wholly ignorant of these languages, or men too jealous of the praise of the Syriac version, which would seem to surpass the Greek in antiquity. With equal ease they could suggest to us that Jacob spoke Syriac when he called the heap Galeed, which Laban called Jegar Sahadutha [f]. But even if we grant them that the Greeks meant by "Syriac" the Hebrew language, how will they explain why that part which, in their opinion, once formed part of the Hebrew text, and was therefore also translated into Greek, is now wholly missing from all copies of the Hebrew language, and why Aquila and Symmachus, who undertook to write out the whole authentic text in Greek, once transmitted it too?

units.la: f) Gen. 31, 47. iam transmitteretur ab Aquila & Symmacho, qui totum textum authenticum græca lingua describere adorti erant? In vado hærent, certo scio, nec ulla rationabili responsione se extricare poterunt. Nobis autem in eare nil est negotii, qui per Syriacam nullam aliam intelligimus linguam, quam quæ proprie ita appellatur. Facilis enim est & expedita nostra responsio quærentibus, unde in græcam versionem se insinuaverint hujusmodi additiones, quas Hebraicus sermo non agnoscit, sed ex Syriaco libro fluxisse perhibent. Nimirum morem fuisse olim constat quibusdam Syris, talem, ut codicibus suis adderent vel inferrent notas vel Scholia, cujus specimina quædam cognita exhibentur collecta a varia eruditione instructo Viro M. Thorndikio in Bibliis Polyglottis, in variantibus Syriacæ versionis lectionibus. Ex quo factum est, ut quidam explicationis causa libro Jobi alicubi eorum, quæ vel extra ditione, vel ex quodam ejus temporis historico de persona Jobi acceperat, adjecerit summaria, quorum non absimile quid, quamvis non fit idem, prænixum invenimus illis duobus ejusdem linguæ codicibus, quibus usi sunt in excudendis Bibliis Polyglottis, quorum alterum ab altero nil quicquam differt, aliudque alio brevius est, ut inspicienti varias ejus versionis lectiones in prædictis Bibliis luculenter patebit. Quæ cum invenerint olim in quibusdam Syriacis Exemplaribus librarii versionem τῶν LXX. & Theodotionis describentes (ipsos enim Authores id fecisse, non dixerim facile, priores inprimis, si fuerint vere illi Septuaginta, quorum plerumque hæc versio præfert nomen) digna habuerunt quæ & in linguam græcam transferrent, & suis apographis suffigerent. (Ita tamen, ut, cum diversa hujusmodi in diversis codicibus occurrerent summaria, & illorum haberent rationem, ut id ex codice vetustissimo M. S. in Bibliotheca Regis apparet, veluti notavimus.) Quod idem deinde secuti sunt librarii, donec in genuini textus partem tandem temporis decursu cooptata sunt, quæ ante alium in finem erant addita, summa quidem imprudentia, cum satis clare viderent, appendicem, ut in Græca Editione Francof. bene notatum est, non redolere stylum Canonis. Quibus omnibus rite observatis illorum verborum ita fluit sensus: Hic (i. e. Job, ejus persona, non liber, ut author Commentarii, qui Origeni inscribitur, videtur sentire) translatus est, i. e. ejus vitæ ratio hic redditur in sequentibus verbis ex Syriaco libro (vel Versione.) Ejusdem enim hæc exprimendi forma significationis est, atque vox ἐφμηνεύεσθαι & μεθερμηνεύεσθαι &c. (transferri) in Novo Testamento & aliis Authoribus, & usitatum est valde orientalibus eosque inter cum primis Arabibus, ut Genealogiæ, nominis & Historiæ alicujus traditionem vocent ـــــــــــــــ Tarjamatoho, ejus interpretationem, quod non uno in loco apparet in celeberrimo Authore vitarum Ebn Chalican, & aliis, Nec ratione vacat in Syriaco libro scriptum fuisse Hu Methtargam, Isita est translatus, i. e. ejus vita ratio ita est tradita.
units.tr: [f] Gen. 31:47. They are stuck in the mud, I am certain, and they will never be able to extricate themselves by any reasonable answer. But for us there is no difficulty in this matter, since by "Syriac" we understand no other language than the one properly so called. Our answer is easy and ready for those who ask how such additions, which the Hebrew text does not acknowledge and which they claim flowed from a Syriac book, found their way into the Greek version. It is certain that it was once the custom among some Syrians to insert or add marginal notes or scholia into their copies. Some specimens of these, gathered by the learned Mr. Thorndike, are shown in the Polyglot Bibles among the variant readings of the Syriac version. As a result, some, to explain the book of Job, added in certain places summaries of things either drawn from their own conjecture or taken from some historian of that time about the person of Job. We find something not unlike these, though not the same, written in the two copies of the same language used in printing the Polyglot Bibles, of which one differs in nothing from the other, and one is shorter than the other, as anyone who examines the various readings of that version in the said Bibles will clearly see. When the copyists who wrote out the version of the Seventy and of Theodotion found these in some Syriac manuscripts, they thought them worth translating into Greek and attaching to their own copies. (Yet they did so in such a way that, since different summaries of this kind occurred in different manuscripts, they took account of them, as appears from the very old manuscript in the King's Library, as we have noted.) Later copyists followed the same practice, until in the course of time these additions, which had been inserted at the end for another purpose, were at last incorporated into the body of the genuine text. This was done with great imprudence, since they clearly saw that the appendix, as was well noted in the Greek edition of Frankfurt, did not smack of the style of the canon. When all these things are rightly observed, the sense of those words flows thus: "Here (that is, Job, his person, not the book, as the author of the commentary which is ascribed to Origen seems to think) was translated, that is, the account of his life is given here in the following words from a Syriac book (or version)." For this form of expression has the same meaning as the words ἐφμηνεύεσθαι and μεθερμηνεύεσθαι [to be interpreted, to be translated] in the New Testament and other authors, and it is very customary among Orientals, and above all among the Arabs, to call the tradition of a genealogy, name or history "tarjamatoho", that is, its interpretation. This appears in more than one place in the famous author of biographies, Ibn Khallikan, and in others. Nor without reason is it written in the Syriac book "Hu Methtargam", that is, "it is thus translated", that is, "the account of his life is thus handed down."

units.la: Hæc conjectura ex eo abunde confirmatur, quod apud prædictum Polychronium scriptum legimus, qui ingenue fatetur, has additiones in Jobum ab aliis esse rejectas, quamvis a non paucis reciperentur in textum, eorumque opinio sibi ipsi arrideret ob Patrum authoritatem. Rejiciunt, inquit, Genealogiam suffixam, quia „non est in Hebraeo, & liber in hæc verba definit. Et „Job moriebatur senex & satur dierum, dicuntque nominis similitudinem in Genealogia Esavi, quæ est in „Genesi, ubi cujusdam Jobabi mentio fit, dedisse occasionem errandi quibusdam, ut hoc Scholion vel notam „apponerent, quodque initio margini erat adscriptum, „aut alibi notatum, postea temporis tractu ab aliis alcitum in verba Textus.
units.tr: This conjecture is amply confirmed by the fact that we read in the aforementioned Polychronius that he frankly admits these additions to Job were rejected by others, although they were received into the text by not a few, and their opinion pleased themselves because of the authority of the Fathers. "They reject," he says, "the genealogy appended, because it is not in the Hebrew, and the book ends with these words: 'And Job died an old man, full of days.' And they say that the similarity of the name in the genealogy of Esau, which is in Genesis, where mention is made of a certain Jobab, gave some people occasion to err, so that they added this scholion or note, and that what was at first written in the margin, or noted elsewhere, was afterwards taken up by others into the words of the text."

units.la: Quomodocunque autem hæc se habeant, id saltem in aprico est ex eis, quæ hactenus sunt dicta atque ultimo pro causa nostra allata, Syriacam Versionem esse perquam antiquam. Priscum enim sit necesse est, quod in vetustissimis exemplaribus extat τῶν LXX. & Theodotionis, quibus utebantur ac videbant Patres Græci, quodque tanti habebatur, ut rationem ejus haberent describentes, tantæque authoritatis esset, ut non minus fere censerent authenticum quam Textum ipsum. Equidem dem non arbitror fore, qui hæc eludat dicendo, solum Jobum Syriace tunc esse translatum, non autem simul omnes alios Scripturæ libros. Id enim non tantum contrarium esset omnium Syriacorum Authorum aliorumque testimonio, quod non facile contemnendum est, verum & omni rationi.
units.tr: However these things stand, this at least is clear from what has been said so far and from what was finally brought forward for our cause: the Syriac version is very ancient. For it must be of early date, since it is found in the most ancient manuscripts of the Seventy and of Theodotion, which the Greek Fathers used and looked at, and which were held in such regard that those who copied them took account of it, and it was of such authority that they judged it almost no less authentic than the text itself. Indeed, I do not think there will be anyone who will mock this by saying that only Job was then translated into Syriac, and not at the same time all the other books of Scripture. For this would be contrary not only to the testimony of all Syriac authors and others, which is not easily to be despised, but also to all reason.

units.la: Huc etiam facit, quod colligi potest ex fine Libri Job in Arabica versione impressa, in qua ille versus, quem Græci constituunt 18. Scriptum est eum furrecturum &c. non invenitur, neque id quod sequitur, Ille translatus est ex libro Syriaco, cum cætera fere omnia, interjecta distinctionis nota, adsint & parum a Græcis verbis abeant. Nam cum in Græcis extet, eum fuisse quintum ab Abrahamo, Arabica eum dicit sextum, ut alias in ipsa Arabica differentias transeam, quæ maximam partem sunt factæ Latini Interpretis culpa, ut cuilibet id inspicienti obvium erit. Exempli loco sit, quod pro Asom, quod loci proprium est, substituat nomen, quia eadem habet literas id nominis atque illud. Cum autem ad finem perveniat, adjicit, Authorem autographi illius, ex quo suam describebat, dicere, hunc librum translatum esse ex Syriaco in Arabicum. Quod an de toto libro sit intelligendum vel de additionibus tantum, dubium est, quod & de quibusdam aliis dicendum, quæ, nisi hoc M. S. inspecto ulterius determinari non possunt. Utcunque vero hæc sint, satis superque inde constat, Syriacæ versioni magnam olim fuisse authoritatem, venerationemque. Longe in ea digressus sum, fateor, quod utique factum non est,ut plusei versioni tribuam, quam ex æ-quo & justo sibi postulat, sed ut eam vindicem suæ, quæ jure merito illi competit,antiquitati. Quare ut inde redeamus, telamque inchoatam pertexamus.
units.tr: This also supports the point, which can be gathered from the end of the book of Job in the printed Arabic version, where that verse which the Greeks put as 18, Scriptum est eum furrecturum, etc., is not found, nor is what follows, Ille translatus est ex libro Syriaco, although almost everything else is present, with a mark of punctuation inserted, and differs little from the Greek words. For while the Greek has that he was the fifth from Abraham, the Arabic says he was the sixth, to pass over other differences in the Arabic itself, which for the most part are due to the fault of the Latin translator, as will be obvious to anyone who inspects it. By way of example, he substitutes nomen for Asom, which is the proper place-name, because nomen has the same letters as that name. When he comes to the end, he adds that the author of the autograph from which he copied his own says that this book was translated from Syriac into Arabic. Whether this is to be understood of the whole book or only of the additions is doubtful, and the same must be said of certain other points, which cannot be determined further unless this manuscript is inspected. However these things are, it is clear enough and more than enough from this that the Syriac version once had great authority and reverence. I confess I have digressed at length here, not in order to give the version more than is fairly and justly its due, which was in fact not done, but in order to vindicate for it the antiquity that rightly belongs to it. Let us therefore return from this and weave on the thread we began.

units.la: Sciendum est, inter veteres versiones etiam haberi Arabicam, priori multo recentiorem. Ea autem lingua variæ sunt versiones, quarum quædam sunt concinnatæ ex Hebraeo, quædam ex Græco, quædam ex Syriaco,quædam,& ni fallor, ex Vulgata latina, fequiore ævo facta & Romæ impressa; id enim quodam ejus Ecclesiæ assecla referente habeo, quam dicebat illos moliri; contigit etiam mihi quædam ejus fpecimina videre ; sed plane ignoro, num ad finem ea unquam fit perducta. At, quicquid de ea fit statutum vel factum, manifestum est, eam in censum nostrum non posse venire. Quæ instituto nostro inservire possunt, duæ sunt, quarum altera extat in Bibliis Polyglottis, quæ quo tempore, vel a quonam fit facta, incertum est. Quod ad Prophetas minores, in illis maxime ea congruit versioni Græcæ. Biblia enim tota non videntur unius contexturæ, quippe in quibusdam magis videtur accedere ad Hebraeum (uti in Pentateucho) in aliis ad Syriacum, in aliis ad Græcum, sicuti perscrutanti id dilucide patebit. Altera est Manufcriptum quoddam,cujus usus mihi suppeditatus ex penu omnigena eruditione conspicui & amicitia intima mihi conjuncti Viri M. Roberti Hugingtonii. At neque in eo authoris nomen alicubi expressum invenio. Num is sit R. Saadiah Haggaon (Judæus, cujus fama insignis est tum ex aliis operibus, tum ex versione, quam fecit librorum Vet. Testamenti ex Hebræa in Arabicam linguam) haud immerito dubito, quia, quam in eodem volumine reperio Esaiæ prophetiæ versionem, ab ea differt quam in alio codice invenio ejus nomen præferentem. Certum etiam est, alios fuisse Judæos præter illum, qui S. literas (vel quandam illarum partem) in eam linguam transtulere, quare, sicubi a nobis extra hunc locum citaretur, sciat benignus Lector, me id non positive affirmare, imo magis etiam propendere in partem negantem. Alicujus tamen vetustatis eam esse, non est denique quod diffitear, quippe Judæorum consuetudo Arabice scribendi non recens est, ut in præfatione Portæ Mosis ostensum est. Quorsum porro referendus sit Jonathan, qui in Prophetas Paraphrasin scripsit, inter interpretesne an Expositores, utique hæreo, quia, cum Paraphrastæ utatur libertate, in id verius incumbit, ut verborum tradat sensum, quam eorum peculiarem significationem, quod præcisi interpretis est, quamvis quilibet hujusmodi interpres non injuria possit haberi expositor sive Commentator. Magnæ authoritatis est ejus paraphrasis inter Judæos, constansque omnium opinio longe ante Christi tempora eam esse concinnatam, nec scio cur id ab aliquo in dubium vocari possit. Quod enim contra eam allegatur ex Paraphrasi Leonis, quæ sub nomine Jonathanis circumfertur, & præter stili differentiam, in multis aliis novitate redolet, nullius momenti est, quippe quod uno omnes ore confiteantur id opus ad Jonathanem nihil pertinere, multoque igitur minoris (si modo ullius) esse authoritatis cæteras Paraphrases in alios libros, quam Onkelos in legem, vel veri Jonathanis in Prophetas.
units.tr: It must be noted that among the old versions the Arabic is also reckoned, though it is much more recent than the Syriac. There are various versions in that language: some were put together from the Hebrew, some from the Greek, some from the Syriac, and some, unless I am mistaken, from the Vulgate Latin, made in a later age and printed at Rome. I have this on the report of a certain adherent of that Church, who said that they were engaged in this work; I have also happened to see some specimens of it, but I do not know at all whether it was ever brought to completion. Whatever has been decided or done about it, it is plain that it cannot come into our reckoning. Two versions that can serve our purpose remain. One is found in the Polyglot Bibles; when or by whom it was made is uncertain. As regards the Minor Prophets, it agrees especially with the Greek version in them. For the whole Bible does not seem to be of one texture: in some books it comes closer to the Hebrew (as in the Pentateuch), in others to the Syriac, in others to the Greek, as anyone who examines it closely will clearly see. The other is a certain manuscript, the use of which was granted to me from the store of his many-sided learning, by Mr. Robert Huntington, a man outstanding in learning and joined to me by close friendship. Yet I find no author's name expressed anywhere in it. I have serious doubts whether he is R. Saadiah Haggaon (a Jew whose fame is distinguished both from his other works and from the version which he made of the books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew into the Arabic language), because the version of the prophecies of Isaiah which I find in the same volume differs from that which I find in another codex bearing his name. It is also certain that there were other Jews besides him who translated the Sacred Letters (or some part of them) into that language; so, wherever we cite it outside this place, let the kind reader know that I do not affirm it positively, and indeed I lean rather to the side of denial. Yet I do not, finally, deny that it is of some antiquity, since the custom of the Jews of writing in Arabic is not recent, as was shown in the preface to the Porta Mosis. Further, whether Jonathan, who wrote a paraphrase on the Prophets, should be reckoned among the translators or the expositors, I hesitate greatly; for since he uses the freedom of a paraphrast, he aims more at conveying the sense of the words than their particular meaning, which is the mark of a strict translator, although any such translator may not unjustly be regarded as an expositor or commentator. His paraphrase is of great authority among the Jews, and the constant opinion of all is that it was composed long before the time of Christ; nor do I know why anyone can call this into doubt. For what is alleged against it from the Paraphrase of Leo, which circulates under the name of Jonathan, and which, apart from its difference of style, smells of novelty in many other respects, is of no weight, since all confess with one voice that that work has nothing to do with Jonathan; and therefore the other paraphrases on the other books are of much less authority (if of any at all) than Onkelos on the Law, or the true Jonathan on the Prophets.

units.la: Operæ etiam pretium duximus alias, præter antiquas illas, consulere versiones recentiores, quales sunt Pagnini, Tigurin. Munsteri, Castalionis, Junii & Tremellii latinas, & Diodat. Italicam &c. quas interdum allegatas invenies. Quæ cum sæpe differant & inter se ipsæ, & a veteribus & a nostratibus,ansam nobis præbuere & verba hebraica examinandi, & in originem hujus diversitatis accuratius inquirendi, & quid Textus originalis ferat perscrutandi, ut inter eas rite nostrum interponeremus judicium, quod ardui interdum negotii est, necessitatemque nonnunquam imponit libero lectoris judicio quædam judicanda ac præferenda relinquendi, quæ pro diverso usu ac significatione vocis occurrentis, multiplicem, eumque bonum inveni parere sensum. Cum se occasio obtulerit Latinam vulgatam allegandi, id plerumque feci ex Duacensium versione Anglicana, quia plus forsan habitura est authoritatis, quam mea propria. In communi nostra Anglicana elim Lectorem æque oculos habeat fixos in lectiones marginales, quam in ipsum Textum.
units.tr: We have also thought it worth while to consult, besides those ancient versions, more recent ones, such as the Latin versions of Pagninus, the Tigurine, Münster, Castalio, Junius and Tremellius, and the Italian of Diodati, etc., which you will sometimes find cited. Since these often differ both among themselves and from the ancients and from our own countrymen, they gave us occasion both to examine the Hebrew words, to inquire more carefully into the origin of this diversity, and to search out what the original text bears, so that we might properly interpose our own judgment among them. This is sometimes a matter of some difficulty, and it sometimes forces the necessity of leaving certain points to the free judgment of the reader, to be judged and preferred; for I have found that, according to the different use and meaning of the word occurring, these yield a manifold, and a good, sense. When the occasion has offered itself of citing the Latin Vulgate, I have for the most part done so from the English version of the Douai translators, because it will perhaps have more authority than my own. For in our common English version the reader should keep his eyes fixed as much on the marginal readings as on the Text itself.

units.la: Jam quod attinet adminicula vocum hebraicarum inveniendi significata, citatas reperiet interdum, præter cognita ac usitata Dictionaria, R. Davidis Kimchi Radices, Lexicon Hebraicum abeo compilatum, quæ voces explicat in S. literis usitatas, undeque Lexicographi nostri non pauca mutuati sunt, ut & Abu VValid, ætate longe majorem eo quem allegat ut plurimum nomine Rabbi Jonab, veluti Aben Ezra nomine R. Marini, cujus nomen pluribus est Abu VValid Marun Ebn Jannahi Cordubensis, virum certe masculè doctum ac tantæ inter eos authoritatis, ut Grammaticorum Princeps appelletur, qui de re Grammatica diversos scripsit Tractatus, cujus ultimus fœtus fuit Radicum liber sive Dictionarium, quo Hebraica exponit Arabicè, qua lingua omnes suos libros exaravit. Non est quicquam, quod sciam, ex ejus operibus subjectum prelo atque publici juris factum; qua igitur citantur, ex M.S. ejus cuncta petita sunt. His accedit etiam aliud Dictionarium Authore R. Tanchum elaboratum, quod studiis nostris quoque inservivit, licet non præcipue in eo exponantur voces Sacrarum literarum, sed tantum quæ occurrunt in Misnajoth (sive in textu Talmud) aliudque pervetustum HebræoArabicum Glossarium. Quibus etiam addidimus capitula Concordantiarum Hebraicarum a R. Nathan compilata, quæ latina lingua sunt descripta ab Antonio Reuchlino, ut & a doctissimo viro M. Nicolao Fullero, cujus versio nunquam in lucem edita est, sed in Bibliotheca Bodlejana propria ipsius manu exarata servatur. Hunc in censum venere etiam quædam Arabica Lexica, quæ in usum nostrum adhibere necesse fuit, ut quarundam hebraicarum vocum eliceremus significationem ex comparatione ejusdem radicis cum simili in lingua Arabica. Quod facere perquam necessarium duxi, quia ea lingua est admodum copiosa, ejusque usus latius patet quam Hebraicæ, (unde Arabica originem duxit tantamque affinitatem cum ea habet, ut quidam ) Judæorum doctissimorum magis eam habeant ejus dialectum, quam separatam ab ea linguam) eaque propter genuinas nobis non raro suppeditat diversarum radicum significationes, quas Hebræi perdiderunt, earumque vocum, quæ raro in Textu Originali occurrunt (alium enim librum pure hebraicum præter eum non habemus, cujus ambitus tam arctus est, ut omnia vocabula capere non possit,) ut perquam difficile foret, hoc adminiculo posthabito, verum earum sensum invenire. Atque hinc est quod Rabinorum etiam doctissimi eas inde petant atque nos in vicinam eam linguam ablegent, qua significatio interdum familiarior est, & ex usu communi sensus ejus magis elucescit.
