Quod idem etiam dictum velim de lingua Syriaca & Chaldaica, quia & hæ una cum Hebraica sunt ejusdem familiæ, ut mea faciam verba Aben Ezra, excepto quod tam usitatæ ac tritæ non sint quam est prædicta Arabica.
units.tr: As for aids for finding the meanings of Hebrew words, you will sometimes find cited, besides the known and usual dictionaries, the Radices of R. David Kimchi, a Hebrew lexicon compiled by him, which explains the words in use in the Sacred Letters, from which our lexicographers have borrowed not a few things; and also Abu Walid, who was far older than the one he usually cites by the name Rabbi Jonah, just as Aben Ezra cites R. Marinus, whose full name is Abu Walid Marwan ibn Janah of Cordoba, a man certainly manly in learning and of such authority among them that he is called the Prince of Grammarians. He wrote various treatises on grammar, and the last fruit of his labour was a book of roots or a dictionary, in which he explains the Hebrew in Arabic, the language in which he wrote all his books. As far as I know, nothing from his works has been put to the press and made public property; so whatever is cited from him has all been taken from his manuscripts. To these is added also another dictionary, composed by R. Tanchum, which has also served our studies, although in it the words of the Sacred Letters are not chiefly explained, but only those which occur in the Mishnayoth (or in the text of the Talmud), and another very ancient Hebrew-Arabic glossary. To these we have also added the chapters of the Hebrew Concordance compiled by R. Nathan, which were described in the Latin language by Antonius Reuchlin, as well as by the most learned man Mr. Nicholas Fuller, whose version was never published, but is preserved in the Bodleian Library, written out in his own hand. Among these also have come some Arabic lexicons, which it was necessary to use for our purpose, in order to elicit the meaning of certain Hebrew words from the comparison of the same root with a similar one in the Arabic language. I thought this very necessary to do, because that language is very copious, and its use extends more widely than Hebrew (whence Arabic took its origin and has such affinity with it that some of the most learned Jews regard it as a dialect of it rather than a separate language), and therefore it not infrequently supplies us with genuine meanings of various roots which the Hebrews have lost, and of those words which rarely occur in the original Text (for we have no other purely Hebrew book besides that, whose compass is so narrow that it cannot contain all the vocabulary), so that it would be very difficult, with this aid set aside, to find their true sense. And hence it is that even the most learned of the Rabbis seek them from there and send us into that neighbouring language, in which the meaning is sometimes more familiar and its sense shines forth more clearly from common usage. I would wish the same to be said of the Syriac and Chaldee language, since these also, together with the Hebrew, are of the same family, to use the words of Aben Ezra, except that they are not so common and worn as the aforesaid Arabic.

units.la: Hisce adminiculis ad singularum vocum significationem eruendam, ex qua earum sensus quam maxime dependet rite adhibitis, officii mei deinceps esse putavi, ut expositores & commentatores, qui facere poterant ad earum cum aliis conjunctarum sensum eliciendum, assidue con-
units.tr: Having used these aids rightly to elicit the meaning of each word, on which their sense very largely depends, I thought it my next duty to consult assiduously the expositors and commentators who could help in eliciting the sense of these words in connection with others, and that among them not only Christians but also Jews. These last, though they have so far lost the use of the Hebrew language that it is no longer their vernacular, yet acquire it with equal zeal and industry...

units.la: *) Vid. Notas miscell. ad Portam Mosis c.1. p. 5. consulerem eosque inter non tantum Christianos; verum & Judæos. Qui postremi etsi hebraicæ linguæ usum eatenus perdiderint, ut illis non amplius vernacula sit, sed pari studio ac industria eam acquirere debeant, qui ejus discendæ sunt cupidi, ac cæteri; ii tamen, qui ad eruditionem quandam adspirant, huic linguæ a teneris etiam annis tantam impendunt operam, ut supra vulgus non mediocriter assurgant, majoremque sibi plerumque cognitionem sensus literalis in S. literis comparant, quam alii quicunque. Eo saltem tempore ita fecerunt, quo in vivis fuere illi, quibuscum nobis negotium hic intercedet. Ita ut maximo adjumento eorum commentaria habeantur habitaque sint omni tempore ad sensum literalem rite erundum, iis locis exceptis, quæ prophetias de Christo complectuntur, & ad Christianam religionem tuendam adversus eos adducuntur, in quibus cum traditionibus Patrum authoritate acceptis mordicus adhæreant, ac cum illis unanimiter contra Christum conspirent, secus certe non fieri potest, quin ea quam longissime a vero sensu detorqueant. Verum enim vero neque tum a nobis plane transmittuntur, quin potius eorum opiniones accurate scrutemur, ut, si cubi ullum hujusmodi locum glossis suis perverterint, eum pro virili vindicemus atque ex eorum unguibus recuperemus, ne habeant quo sibi de patrocinio S. literarum adversus nos gratulentur. Atque non exigua certe hic fuit hujusmodi in locis mea industria, quam tam uberem non nunquam collocavi, ut, ne taedium lectoribus creare voluisse videar, valde timeam.
units.tr: *) See the miscellaneous notes on the Gate of Moses, ch. 1, p. 5. I would consult them, and among them not only Christians but also Jews. Although the latter have so lost the use of the Hebrew language that it is no longer their mother tongue, and those who wish to learn it must acquire it with the same zeal and effort as everyone else, still those who aspire to some learning devote so much effort to this language from their earliest years that they rise considerably above the common people, and they generally gain a better knowledge of the literal sense of Holy Scripture than anyone else. At least they did so in the time when those men were alive with whom we have to deal here. Their commentaries are therefore held to be of the greatest help for explaining the literal sense correctly at all times, except in those passages that contain prophecies about Christ, or that they bring forward against the Christian religion. In these passages they cling stubbornly to the traditions of the Fathers, which they accept as authoritative, and they unanimously conspire with those traditions against Christ. In such cases it is certainly inevitable that they twist the meaning as far as possible from the true sense. Yet we do not therefore neglect them altogether; rather we examine their opinions carefully, so that if they have ever perverted any such passage with their glosses, we may vindicate it as far as we can and snatch it from their claws, lest they have anything to boast of in the support of Scripture against us. Certainly my diligence in such passages has not been small, and I have sometimes spent so much of it that I greatly fear I may seem to have wished to weary the readers.

units.la: Quippe eorum sententias refellere non potui, quin eodem tempore etiam eorum causam producerem, argumentaque, quibus eam defendant, iis præberem.
units.tr: Indeed, I could not refute their opinions without at the same time setting out their case and providing the arguments by which they defend it.

units.la: In consilium itaque cum primis adhibitus est Rabbi Salomo Jarchi, R. Abraham Ezra, R. David Kimchi, & Isaac Abarbinel, (quem alii vocant, Abrabaniel,) quorum nomina tum ex libris eorum impressis, tum ex recensione Buxtorfii aliorumque probe cognita sunt. Quod ad eorum expositiones, haudquaquam gravatus sum eas & fideliter & prolixe, ubi in rem nostram id videbatur necessarium, adducere, ut, si ad veritatem inveniendam non ubique directe quicquam facere potuerint, saltem pateat, quomodo ab ea deflexerint, quo erroribus illorum detectis magis magisque incitaremur ad eam sedulo quærendum ac ambabus, ut dicitur, ulnis amplectendü. Reperiet præterea benignus lector quendam allegatum nomine R. Tanchum Hierosolymitanum, qui minus hactenus innotuit, quia nihil unquam ex ejus scriptis est vulgatum, licet non minus ea digna sint quæ edantur, quam quorumvis aliorum, quia in multis locis plus auxilii fert ad Textum intelligendum, quam ullus alius. Notas scripsit Arabica lingua in Totum Vetus Instrumentum (ipso declarante,) quamvis eas mihi non contigerit videre nisi in quosdam libros, quippe tantum ea, quæ in Prophetas, Esaia excepto, scripsit, in manibus meis versantur. Quo tempore vixerit, me prorsus latet, id tantum apparet post Mosen Maimonidem scripsisse, quem sæpe citat ac in plurimis sequitur. Cui accensere velim Talkut, quod libri nomen est, in quo variæ expositiones S. literarum Allegoricæ colliguntur. Cæteros vero vulgatos hebraicos libros ut in specie recenseam haud necessarium reor, quoniam eorum rationem quivis facile petere potest ex Buxtorffii Bibliotheca Rabinica, aliisque. Eadem ratio est Christianorum, vel aliorum Græcorum, Latinorum &c. Authorum, quos studio noftro inservire voluimus, omnibus illi æque noti sunt, qui huic rei operam navant, nec potest quicquam alicui occultum esse eorum operum ac præfixi scopi, qui eos ipsos aut præfationes eorum inspicere haud detrectant. Nil etiam omnino refert, quod non sint omnes ejusdem prosessionis. Omnis enim rei cardo in eo tantum vertitur, quantum possint conferre ad genuinum Textus sensum eruendum, non autem quibus peculiaribus opinionibus sint dediti, quo tempore inprimis videndum non quis dicat, sed quid dictum sit, veritasque fine ullo alicujus perfonæ aut authoritatis respectu amplectenda. Eo enim ipso, quod in diversa abeant commentantes, adduci debemus, ut textum accuratius scrutemur, & quid ferat, quidque eorum maxime congruat ei, quod omnium est præcipuum, omni cura circumspiciamus. Nec est quod eorum varietatem valde mireris, modo in mentem revoces, quanta interdum fit explicationis rerum planis etiam vocibus imo linguis vulgaribus phrasibusque noftro tempore tritis expositarum diversitas. Quanto igitur major erit, cum Originalis linguæ usus, quæ hic in censum venit, tam longo abhinc tempore desierit multæque loquendi formæ, quæ tum temporis nil ambigui habebant quin imo etiam vulgo familiares erant, nobis videantur meræ ænigmata, Historiæque ac consuetudines pleræq; illius temporis prorsus in oblivionem venerint? Imo quod magis est, cum etiam eo tempore quædam in Scriptis Propheticis viderentur abstrusa, ut apparet ex Ezech. 20, 49. Domine, ipsi dicunt de me, nonne loquitur parabolas? Adeo ut ad illa declaranda, quamvis adhibeamus omnia, quæ possumus, adjumenta, ea tamen sunt perquam exigua, ne dicam insufficientia. Præstat quidem alterum altero, nihil autem tam perfectum est, quod posterorum cura non potuit reddi perfectius. Quare mirandum non est, alios post tot commentarios erudite exaratos, conaturos adhuc planiora quædam, clarioraque reddere suo labore, adminiculoque fortasse alio adhibito, quo præcedentium nemo antea usus est. Campus semper hic erit amplus, quamdiu terrarum orbis perstiterit, donec eum in locum pervenerimus, ubi eadem, quæ nunc eo usque perdita est lingua, omnibus, quorundam judicio, erit universalis.
units.tr: Accordingly, the first men I took into counsel were Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, R. Abraham Ezra, R. David Kimchi, and Isaac Abarbinel (whom others call Abrabaniel). Their names are well known both from their printed books and from the list of Buxtorf and others. As for their expositions, I have not been reluctant to cite them faithfully and at length where this seemed necessary for our purpose, so that, if they could not always contribute directly to finding the truth, it may at least be clear how far they have departed from it. By detecting their errors, the kind reader will be more and more stirred to seek the truth eagerly and to embrace it with both arms, as they say. The reader will also find a certain man cited under the name R. Tanchum of Jerusalem, who has so far been less known, because nothing of his writings has ever been published, although they are no less worthy of publication than those of any others, since in many places he gives more help for understanding the text than any other. He wrote notes in the Arabic language on the whole Old Testament (as he himself declares), although I have not been able to see them except in certain books, since only those he wrote on the Prophets, except Isaiah, are in my hands. When he lived I am quite unaware; it only appears that he wrote after Moses Maimonides, whom he often cites and follows in very many points. To these I would add the Talkut, the title of a book in which various allegorical expositions of Holy Scripture are collected. As for the other printed Hebrew books, I think it unnecessary to list them individually, since anyone can easily get an account of them from Buxtorf's Bibliotheca Rabbinica and other works. The same is true of the Christian authors, or other Greek, Latin and so on, whom we have wished to serve in our study. All of them are equally well known to those who are engaged in this work, and nothing of the purpose of their works and of the aim set before them can be hidden from anyone who does not shrink from looking at the works themselves or their prefaces. It also matters not at all that they are not all of the same profession. For the whole hinge of the matter turns only on how far they can contribute to bringing out the genuine sense of the text, not on what particular opinions they are devoted to. In this matter we must consider above all not who says a thing, but what is said, and embrace the truth without any regard to the person or authority of anyone. For the very fact that commentators go in different directions ought to lead us to scrutinize the text more carefully, and with every care to look around for what it says and what agrees most closely with that which is above all the principal thing. Nor should you be greatly surprised at their variety, if you recall how great, at times, is the diversity of explanations even of plain matters, expressed in plain words, indeed in vernacular languages and in phrases worn smooth in our own time. How much greater, then, will it be when the use of the original language, which is in question here, has ceased so long ago, and many forms of speech which at that time had nothing ambiguous about them, indeed were familiar even to the common people, seem to us to be mere riddles, and most of the histories and customs of that age have quite passed into oblivion? Indeed, what is more, even at that time some things in the prophetic writings seemed obscure, as appears from Ezech. 20, 49. Ah Lord God, they say of me, doth he not speak in parables? So that, although we use all the aids we can to explain those things, they are nevertheless exceedingly small, not to say insufficient. Certainly one thing is better than another, but nothing is so perfect that the care of posterity cannot make it more perfect. Therefore it is not to be wondered at if others, after so many learned commentaries have been written, will still try by their labour to make some things plainer and clearer, perhaps with some other aid applied which none of their predecessors used. This field will always be wide, as long as the world endures, until we come to that place where the language which is now lost to us will, in the judgment of some, be universal to all.

units.la: Cæterum quod præsens hoc opus spectat, animus initio erat sensum verborum marginalibus quibusdam notulis reddere. At satius multo duximus animo iterum hæc revolventes, verborum prolixiorem tradere expositionem, qua res discutiantur atque in ambiguis locis interpretationum discrepantium rationes exponantur, ne in iis, quæ cæteroquin erant positive affirmanda, nimium viderer imperiosus. Ea enim absoluta, facile breviores (fi ita ferret occasio, notas exinde confici, atque ad largiores in earum vindicationem Lectorem posse remitti mihi persuadebam. Religio præterea nobis fuit, quod cuiquam palam fiet, quibusdam in locis alteram alteri expositioni præferre, vel quicquam in aliquam partem decernere, rectius multo putantibus, id arbitrio lectoris judicandum relinquere atque quodvis eo accipiendum modo prout oportunitas sese obtulerit, cum quid magis videatur accedere verbis & analogiæ fidei, sensumque bonum constituat.
units.tr: As for the present work, my intention at the beginning was to give the sense of the words in certain marginal notes. But on turning these matters over again in my mind, I thought it much better to give a fuller exposition of the words, in which the matters are discussed and, in ambiguous passages, the reasons for differing interpretations are set out, so that I might not seem too domineering in those matters which otherwise had to be affirmed positively. For once these were done, I persuaded myself that brief notes could easily be drawn from them, if the occasion so required, and that the reader could be referred to fuller discussions in their defence. Moreover, I have scrupled to say plainly, in certain places, that I prefer one exposition to another, or to decide anything on one side, thinking it far better to leave it to the judgment of the reader, and to let each thing be taken in whatever way the opportunity offers, as it seems to agree more with the words and the analogy of faith and to yield a sound sense.

units.la: Conclusiones tandem ac consequentias ex verbis inferre ferio me cohibui, ratus id ejus duntaxat esse, qui opinionis suæ habet fixum ac immobile fundamentum, quo fine corruant necesse est ædificiorum instar fundamento destitutorum. Quicquid vero fecerim, Lectoris erit judicare, a quo etiam magnopere peto, ut candide mihi impertire ne gravetur, fi quando vel aberraverim, vel nimis concise quid tractaverim, vel fupervacanea quædam adjecerim, quæ nullum usum habeant, quod in tanta diversorum Commentatorum varietate, quorum expositiones erant inspiciendæ, earumque ratio habenda, factum fuisse vix ac ne vix quidem dubitare possim. Denique fi quid hoc meo opere, quantulumcunque etiam fit, ad gloriam Dei ac incrementum Ecclefiæ promovero, erit quod votorum meorum apicem me attigisse gaudeam, Deoque foli humillimas agam gratias, quod me huic rei obeundæ idoneum reddere voluerit.
units.tr: Finally, I have restrained myself from drawing conclusions and consequences from the words, thinking this belongs only to one who has a fixed and immovable foundation for his opinion, since otherwise, like buildings without foundations, they must collapse. Whatever I have done, it will be for the reader to judge, and from him I earnestly ask that he be willing to grant me a candid hearing if at any point I have gone astray, or treated something too briefly, or added some superfluous matter which serves no purpose. Given the great variety of the various commentators, whose expositions had to be examined and taken into account, I can hardly doubt, and indeed scarcely doubt at all, that this has happened. Lastly, if by this work of mine, however small it may be, I shall have advanced the glory of God and the growth of the Church, I shall rejoice that I have reached the summit of my wishes, and I shall give the most humble thanks to God alone, who has been pleased to make me fit for undertaking this task.

units.la: Quod vero in specie ad Joelem pertinet, sufficiet vel tribus verbis Lectores admonuisse, ut ab hoc legendo non sinant se terreri Hebraicæ ac Arabicæ linguæ imperiti, quando hujusmodi authorum verba vel opiniones sua cuiusque lingua viderint citari, quoniam non mediocris fuit, quam huic operi adhibuimus, cura, ut vernacula omnia rite exprimerentur, quæ ad rem atque nostrum consilium videbantur aliquatenus spectare. Qui vero harum linguarum sunt optime gnari, sciant velim, nos in citandis Arabicis interpretibus, Commentariis vel Lexicis non eandem ubique servasse rationem. Quædam enim eorum loca iisdem proferuntur characteribus, quibus lingua ea communiter ac proprie solet exarari; alia characteribus citantur hebraicis, quibus Judæi plerumq; utebantur, qui inter Arabes Mahometanos atq; illis in locis degebant, ubi lingua Arabica, quæ est omnium orientaliū eruditissima, & literatis & vulgo erat perquam familiaris ac trita. Nec difficile est hujus rei divinare rationem, quam haud injuria dixeris fuisse, ne a Mahometanis suæ religionis hostibus juratis legerentur libri religionis mysteria tractantes; unde quoque factum, quod Syriacis Syri emittebant in vulgus literis ea, quæ ipsis erant concinnata Arabicis. Nec quicquam, opinor, hujus operæ pœnitebit lectorem, qui harum linguarum est peritus & Arabica hebraicis literis intelligere assuefit, quippe incredibilem sibi sic comparabit facultatem ac promptitudinem in eis scriptis legendis, quæ non pauca hacce ratione inveniuntur exarata.
units.tr: As for what concerns Joel in particular, it will be enough to warn the readers in a few words that those unskilled in the Hebrew and Arabic languages should not be frightened from reading this work when they see the words or opinions of such authors cited in their own language. For we took no small care in this work that all the vernacular material which seemed in some way relevant to the subject and our purpose should be correctly rendered. Those who are thoroughly versed in these languages should know that in citing Arabic interpreters, commentaries and lexicons we did not follow one method throughout. Some of their passages are given in the same characters in which that language is commonly and properly written; others are cited in Hebrew characters, which the Jews for the most part used, living among the Mahometan Arabs in places where the Arabic language, the most learned of all the Eastern tongues, was very familiar and common to both the learned and the people. The reason for this is not hard to guess. It may not unfairly be said that it was so that books treating the mysteries of their religion would not be read by the Mahometans, their sworn enemies. Hence it also happened that the Syrians published in Syriac letters what had been composed for them in Arabic. I think that no reader who knows these languages, and who is accustomed to read Arabic in Hebrew letters, will regret this labour, since by this method he will acquire for himself an incredible facility and readiness in reading those writings, of which not a few are written in this way.

units.la: Præcipuum vero, quod hic monendum reor, de
units.tr: Now the chief thing which I think should be noted here concerns

units.la: iconographia est, vel schemate areæ templi ejusque partium diversarum, quod æri incidi ac hic inseri sedulo curavi. Commendavi illud cap.2. v.17. p.118. quod in quodam inveni vetusto M.S. Maimonidis, quod ejus continebat Commentarium in Misnajoth, vel textum Judaici Talmudis, in tractatu qui inscribitur Middoth. Ex eo, quod haud sine gravi adductus causa censeo ejusdem cum ipso Autore ætatis, illud apponere placuit, quia horum nihil in exemplaribus impressis ac interpretationibus hebraicis mihi occurrit, præterquam quod in quadā editione prisca spatium pro eo sit relictum, ubi & loco cœterorum schematum non nisi charta pura, cum hæc inscriptione: Et hæc est [illegible, ~3 letters] Tsurah sive figura. De hoc autem schemate & Hebraice & Arabice dicitur, esse eam generalem iconographicam, quam diversis in locis in Commentar. promiserat; eamque omnia ea comprehendere quorum antea fecerat mentionem. Unde liquido constat tale schema fuisse in autographo Autoris, quo attentum lectorem ad majorem harum rerum notitiam ducere voluit. Simile schema extat etiam in alio quodam M.S. quod versatur in manibus honoratissimi amici mei D. Hungintoni & titulum gerit Tad Chasaka summamque doctrinæ Talmudicæ complectitur, quod tamen tam vetustum non arbitror quam illud prius. Huic instripserat eruditus quidam Judæus, qui ejus possessor fuerat illud a se esse emendatum juxta autographum Autoris. Notandum tamen in impressis ejusdem libri exemplaribus id non reperiri. Quibus omnibus rite expensis id communicandi cum lectoribus ribus tanquam ipsius proprium nullam viam duxi commodiorem quam ut ea ratione æri curarem incidi, qua ab eo erat concinnatum. Multa sunt ejusdem rei alia schemata ab aliis Authoribus tradita, quæ cum hoc possunt comparari, quod propter suam & antiquitatem & Authoris authoritatem non potuimus non exhibere. Duo equidem sunt, haud diffiteor, hujus Autoris diversa schemata, quorum alterum est in Commentario in Misnajoth, alterum in M.S. ejus Tad, verum prius eligere maluimus, quod alterum & antiquitate & elegantia longe post se videbatur relinquere. Et quamvis neutrum illorum exactitudine linearum cum mensura spatiorum diversorum convenientium adæquet quædam recentiora, non multum tamen interest, quia mensura cujusvis spatii suo loco verbis adjecta est, ubi eas facilius lector curiosus cognoscere potest quam ex lineis ipsis. Quæ verba in M.S. etsi ipsi schemati erant inscripta, e regione tamen a nobis constitui necesse erat, quia spatium iconographiæ ea capere non poterat.
units.tr: the iconography, or the plan of the court of the temple and its various parts, which I have carefully had engraved in copper and inserted here. I drew attention to it at chapter 2, verse 17, page 118. I found it in an old manuscript of Maimonides, which contained his commentary on the Mishnayoth, or the text of the Jewish Talmud, in the tractate entitled Middoth. I thought it fitting to add this, not without a serious reason, since I believe it to be of the same age as the author himself. None of these things had come to my notice in the printed copies or the Hebrew translations, except that in one early edition a space was left for it, where, in place of the other diagrams, there is only blank paper, with this inscription: "And this is" [illegible, about three letters] Tsurah, that is, "figure." Now concerning this diagram both in Hebrew and in Arabic it is said that it is "the general iconography which he had promised in various places in the Commentary," and that it "comprehends all those things of which he had previously made mention." Whence it is clear that such a diagram was in the author's own autograph, by which he wished to lead the attentive reader to a fuller knowledge of these matters. A similar diagram also exists in another manuscript, which is in the hands of my most honoured friend Mr. Huntington, and bears the title Tad Chasaka, and comprises the sum of Talmudic teaching. I do not think this one is as old as the former. A learned Jew, who had been its owner, wrote on it that it had been corrected by him according to the author's autograph. It should be noted, however, that this is not found in the printed copies of the same book. With all these things duly weighed, I judged that there was no more convenient way of communicating it to the readers, as if it were the author's own, than to have it engraved in the same form in which he had drawn it. There are many other diagrams of the same matter handed down by other authors which could be compared with this one, but because of both its antiquity and the authority of its author, we could not but present it. I admit that there are indeed two diagrams of this author, differing from each other: one is in the Commentary on the Mishnayoth, the other in his manuscript Tad. But we preferred to choose the former, since the other seemed by far to fall short of it in both antiquity and elegance. And although neither of them, in the exactness of its lines, matches the measurements of the various spaces as some more recent ones do, this matters little, because the measure of each space has been added in words in its proper place, where the curious reader can more easily learn them than from the lines themselves. These words, although in the manuscript they were written upon the diagram itself, nevertheless had to be placed by us alongside it, because the space of the iconography could not contain them.

units.la: ADMONITIO AUCTORIS.
units.tr: ADMONITION OF THE AUTHOR.

units.la: Spero equidem nullum eorum locorum, quæ a nobis sunt citata atque versione donata ex variis Auctoribus variaque lingua, aut falso esse allegatum aut perperam redditum. Quod si tamen præter opinionem id contigisset, ejus ut me admoneat eruditus lector etiam atque etiam peto. Id quod hic subjiciendum putavi partim, quod ne hujusmodi errores alii observent assidui harum rerum scrutatores, timeam; partim, quod me magis cautum reddit, quod hujus notæ errorem mihi objecerit vir eruditissimus Iobus Ludolphus, quem licet in alio opere notaverit, hic tamen ejus mentionem facere allubuit, cum alia mihi hactenus, ex quo ad cognitionem meam pervenit ejus correctio, non fuerit unquam commodior opportunitas. Res autem ita se habet. In Historia Arabica, quæ mea versione donata sub titulo Gregorii Abul-Pharajii Historia Dynastiarum in lucem est edita de Samaritanis p.116. arabice dicitur ܣܡܪܝܐ quod latine est redditum pag. 74. sumed, idem corporeitatis (in Deo) assertores. Hic mendum latere ratus pro ܣܡܪܝܐ corporeitatis assertores, legendum censet machmufato, quod significat quinquepartitum, adeoque referendum ad alturato legem, cujus ante fit mentio, non autem ad Samaritanos dictos, ad quos hic hoc esset referendum, dicendum fuisse Abulpharajio Wahon & illi numero plurali, non autem Wahi, & illa, numero singulari ac fœminino genere. Quæ conjectura satis videtur expedita, nec sine præmeditato consilio mihi posthabita, utpote cui assentiri non poteram, quia duo optimæ notæ codices, quibus doctissimi quidam viri in eis mundi partibus, ubi exarati sunt, usi erant (saltem eorum unus, qui non mediocrem spirabat vetustatem) quosque consului conveniunt in ܣܡܪܝܐ, unde si convertendum in ܣܡܪܝܐ obvium est, literas debere & mutari & transponi & augeri, quod utique sine quadam auctoritate fieri non potest. Quod porro pro conjectura sua confirmanda adfert, quod nostra lectione retenta pronomen debeat esse illi non autem illa, nullius omnino momenti est, quia illud commode referri potest ad secta, quo etiam deducimur præcedenti voce septima. Quodsi autem huic rei ita insistere velit, scito, unum ex his codicibus habere illi, atque id conn ectere cum Samaritani. Ita ut novam hujus libri editionem adornantibus nequaquam auctor sim alicujus in Arabico immutationis. Quod autem ad versionem Latinam, omitti vellem hæc verba in Deo, quæ Arabice non habentur, adeo ut sensus sit, interpretantur res corporaliter i.e. divinas promissiones ac comminationes, non tribuunt quidem stricte Deo corpus, sed interpretantur dicta ac promissa divina corporaliter atque eum in modum, ac si ad hanc vitam tantum spectarent. Maresitanus & Abulpheda referunt quosdam e secta Dosithaeorum affirmasse, ان الثواب والعقاب في الدنيا praemia & poenas divinas tantum ad hanc vitam pertinere, quamvis alii eorum ea etiam ad futura extenderint. Hujusmodi quid de iis inaudivisse vel fando Abulpharagium haud vero absimile est. Alio enim modo ea, quae expressi, legere prohibet duorum codicum diversis temporibus & diversis locis (ni fallor) exaratorum auctoritas.
units.tr: I hope indeed that none of the passages I have cited and given in translation from various authors and in various languages has been either wrongly cited or wrongly rendered. But if this has happened contrary to my expectation, I earnestly ask the learned reader to point it out to me. I have thought it right to add this here, partly because I fear that other diligent investigators of these matters might notice such errors, and partly because the very learned Job Ludolf has made me more careful. He has charged me with this kind of error, and although he noted it in another work, he was pleased to mention it here too. Until now I have never had a more suitable opportunity, since his correction only came to my knowledge recently. The matter stands as follows. In the Arabic history published in my translation under the title Gregorii Abul-Pharajii Historia Dynastiarum, concerning the Samaritans on p. 116, the Arabic reads [Samraya], which on p. 74 of the Latin is rendered sumed, idem corporeitatis (in Deo) assertores. Ludolf thinks there is an error here, and that instead of [Samraya] meaning "assertors of corporeity," one should read machmufato, which means "quinquepartite" and so refers to the "law of the alturato," mentioned earlier, and not to the Samaritans named here. He also holds that Abulpharajius should have said Wahon and that plural, not Wahi and that singular feminine. This conjecture seems quite plausible, and I have not set it aside without deliberate thought. But I could not agree with it, because two very good manuscripts, which certain learned men used in the parts of the world where they were written (at least one of them, which has no small antiquity), and which I consulted, agree in the reading [Samraya]. So if one wished to change it to the reading Ludolf proposes, the letters would have to be altered, transposed and added, which cannot be done without some authority. As for his further argument to confirm his conjecture, that with our reading retained the pronoun ought to be illi and not illa, it has no weight at all. It can conveniently refer to secta, which is also suggested by the preceding word septima. But if he wishes to insist on this point, know that one of these manuscripts has illi and joins it with Samaritani. So I would by no means advise anyone preparing a new edition of this book to make any change in the Arabic. As for the Latin version, I would wish the words in Deo omitted, since they are not in the Arabic. The sense is then: they interpret things corporaliter, that is, the divine promises and threats. They do not indeed ascribe a body strictly to God, but they interpret the divine sayings and promises in a bodily way, as if they pertained only to this life. Maresitanus and Abulfeda report that some of the sect of the Dositheans affirmed that rewards and punishments [inna al-thawab wa-al-'iqab fi al-dunya] pertain only to this world, although others of them extended them to the future as well. That Abulpharagius heard something of this kind about them, even by report, is not at all unlikely. For otherwise the authority of two manuscripts, written at different times and in different places (unless I am mistaken), forbids reading the words as I have rendered them.

units.la: Hisce responsionis loco adjectis silentio praetereundum non est, quod alium Arabicum Historicum mecum postea communicavit omni cultus ac amoris genere mihi suspiciendus D. Bernhardus, cujus possessor est Venerandus D. Huntingtonus. Auctor quidem hujus libri in eo non est expressus, apparet tamen, illum opus suum compilasse ex nostro Gregorio aliisque, qui hanc rem tractarunt, Arabicis Scriptoribus. Eadem autem verba in hoc codice extant de Samaritanis, quae in nostra editione sunt exhibita, scilicet سامريين, unde constat hanc genuinam esse ejus lectionem, nullo autem modo per errorem positam pro سامريين. Vale.
units.tr: Having added these remarks by way of reply, I must not pass over in silence that another Arabic historian was later communicated to me by Mr. Bernhard, a man worthy of every kind of respect and affection, whose copy belongs to the venerable Mr. Huntington. The author of this book is not named in it, but it is clear that he compiled his work from our Gregory and other Arabic writers who treated this matter. In this manuscript the same words about the Samaritans appear as are given in our edition, namely [Arabic: Samariyyin]. This shows that this is the genuine reading and was in no way put there by mistake for something else. Farewell.
