units.la: COMMENTARIUS in PROPHETIAM JOELIS.
units.tr: COMMENTARY on the PROPHECY OF JOEL.

units.la: Cap. I.
units.tr: Chapter I.

units.la: Vers. 1. Verbum Domini, quod venit ad Joëlem, filium Pethuelis.
units.tr: Verse 1. The word of the Lord that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel.

units.la: [Od] se omnium primo quasi sua sponte hic offert inquirendum, eo scilicet tendit, quisnam Joel Paterque ejus fuerit, ubinam vixerit, quoque seculo demum suam prophetiam protulerit. Attamen cum nulla horum mentio in sacris literis neque hic neque alibi facta sit expresse, unde ea certo cognosci possient; manifestum est, quæcunque ab interpretibus recentioribus de iis sunt prolata, conjecturas esse, nec quicquam certi in se continere. Plures equidem Joeles (a quibus hic Propheta adjecto patris Pethuelis nomine distinguitur) Scripturæ lectio nobis suggerit: at Pethuelem, excepto hoc Joelis loco, reperias nusquam. Hinc Judæorum nonnulli (innixi, ut puto, incertæ suæ regulæ, quod ubique una cum propheta nominetur ejus pater, hic non vir tantum bonus, sed & propheta fuerit,) Pethuelem Samuelemque pro uno eodemque habuere. Habet sane a) Samuel filium qui vocabatur Joel; at uti neque tempus, quo hic vixit, admittere videtur, ut cum Nostro eundem esse opineris; ita nec id, quod de Joële Samuelide memoriæ proditum novimus, vero esse simile, prophetam fuisse hunc hominem pessimæ vitæ & morum insimulatum b): quin nec ulla praeterea possit dari ratio, cur Pethuel iste Samuel esse existimetur. Illa enim quam affert Rabbi Salomon ratio nullius momenti esse videtur, nempe quod sic appellatus sit, quia בהפירתו לא ... persuadebat vel flectebat Deum precibus suis. Nam ea ratione quilibet Propheta, vel alius vir probus non minus atque Samuel sic nominari pos-
units.tr: The first thing that presents itself for inquiry is who Joel and his father were, where he lived, and in what age he finally delivered his prophecy. Yet since Scripture nowhere expressly records any of these things, here or elsewhere, from which they could be known with certainty, it is clear that whatever the more recent interpreters have offered on these points are conjectures and contain nothing certain. Reading Scripture does indeed suggest several men named Joel (from whom this prophet is distinguished by the addition of his father's name, Pethuel), but apart from this passage in Joel you will nowhere find Pethuel. Hence some Jews, relying (as I think) on the uncertain rule that a prophet is always named together with his father, and that the father here was not only a good man but also a prophet, have taken Pethuel and Samuel to be one and the same. Samuel did indeed have a son called Joel; but just as the time in which this man lived does not seem to allow that he be the same as our Joel, so what we know to have been handed down in memory about Joel the son of Samuel, that he was a prophet, is not likely to be true, since he was accused of a very wicked life and corrupt morals. Indeed no other reason can be given why this Pethuel should be thought to be Samuel. The reason brought forward by Rabbi Solomon seems to be of no weight, namely that he was so called because [Hebrew: בהפירתו לא ... ] "he persuaded or bent God by his prayers." For by that reasoning any prophet, or any other upright man, could be called so no less than Samuel.

units.la: a) 1. Sam. 8, 2. b) ibid. v. 3. posset. Cum itaque meliori auctoritate id ipsum firmari nequeat, e contrario nobis dicere licet פתואל אינו שמואל Pethuel non est c) Samuel, proinde nec Joel filius Samuelis, sed alterius cujusdam. Quo tempore vixerit & prophetaverit, (cum Sacra Scriptura profusus hac de re sileat,) æque incertum est, neque sine ratione Aben-Ezra ait: אין ידך לרעת הרוח הפשט אינן בן שמואל nullam tam esse ad cognoscendum ejus statem & absque figura loquendo, eum non fuisse filium Samuelis. Quin imo nequaquam probabile est, tantumdem illum esse. (סיף רבר לא ביאר הכתוב ואנחנו לא נרע יואל הנביא מאיה שכט היה ובאיז ז דור היר.) hoc est, In summa: Scriptura non declaravit, & nos non possumus cognoscere de Propheta Joele, qua ex e) tribu fuerit, quove seculo vixerit. Hinc tantopere a se invicem dissentiunt interpretes circa tempus, quo prophetia hæc edita est. Taceo, quæ de sententia Rab. Salomonis supra monui. Sunt, f) qui Joelem floruisse ferunt regnante Joramo filio Ahabi, cum septem annis ingens in terra Israel fames g) esset, de qua hunc prophetam loqui opinantur. Alii faciunt eum coætaneum Hoseæ, qui ante eum collocari solet, regulæ huic, quam h) incertissimam, quin plane falsam judico, innixi: i) Quando tempus Prophetæ non exprimitur, reputandus est eodem tempore prophetasse, quo proximo loco eum præcedens prophetavit. Alii censent edidisse prophetiam suam sub Manasse, quæ est opinio quorundam Judæorum, quam ex k) Chronico aliquo hauserunt, magnæ inter eos auctoritatis. l) Alii tempore Josiæ regis. Judæ, quodque dictum est ab ipso (ut putant) de fame, ad eandem referunt, de qua loquitur Jeremias 14, 1. 2.
units.tr: a) 1. Sam. 8, 2. b) ibid. v. 3. Since therefore a better authority cannot confirm this, we may on the contrary say, Pethuel is not c) Samuel [פתואל אינו שמואל], and so Joel was not the son of Samuel but of some other man. When he lived and prophesied is equally uncertain, since Holy Scripture is silent on this matter at length. Not without reason Aben-Ezra says [אין ידך לרעת הרוח הפשט אינן בן שמואל]: there is no means of knowing his time, and, to speak plainly, he was not the son of Samuel. Indeed it is by no means probable that he was the same man. [סיף רבר לא ביאר הכתוב ואנחנו לא נרע יואל הנביא מאיה שכט היה ובאיז ז דור היר] That is, in short: Scripture has not declared, and we cannot know, from which e) tribe the prophet Joel was, or in what age he lived. This is why the interpreters differ so widely from one another about the time when this prophecy was published. I say nothing of what I have already noted about the opinion of Rab. Salomon. Some say that Joel flourished in the reign of Joram, son of Ahab, when there was a great famine in the land of Israel for seven years, and they think the prophet speaks of that famine. Others make him a contemporary of Hosea, who is usually placed before him, relying on this rule, which I judge most uncertain, indeed plainly false: When the time of a prophet is not stated, he is to be regarded as having prophesied at the same time as the prophet who immediately precedes him in the order of the book. Others think he published his prophecy under Manasseh; this is the opinion of certain Jews, who drew it from some chronicle and hold it in great authority. Others refer it to the time of Josiah, king of Judah, and they relate the famine he speaks of, as they suppose, to the one mentioned in Jeremiah 14, 1. 2.

units.la: Qui existimant, quod sub recentioribus Regibus floruerit, exinde argumenti vim petunt, quod, cum nulla decem tribuum fiat mentio in hac prophetia, sed duarum duntaxat, quibus omnia congruant, quæ ab eo prolata sunt, consequens sit, non nisi decem tribubus in captivitatem abductis eum prophetasse. Satis igitur opinionum hæc varietas ostendit, quam incerta sit ejus rei ratio, cujus cum sacræ literæ
units.tr: Those who think he flourished under the later kings derive the force of their argument from this: since no mention is made of the ten tribes in this prophecy, but only of the two, with which everything he uttered agrees, it follows that he prophesied only after the ten tribes had been carried into captivity. This variety of opinions therefore shows well enough how uncertain the reckoning of this matter is, about which the sacred letters...

units.la: e) Abarbanel. d) Abar. e) Epiphanius ex tribu Ruben fuisse adserit, sed qua ratione nitatur, non patet. f) Kimchi. g) 2. Reg. 8. 1. h) Tarnov. i) Hieron. in præf. in 12. Proph. k) Seder. Olam. l) Dancus. ræ quoque nullum indicium faciant, evidenter patet, quam parum debeamus esse foliciti circa tales minutias. Suffecerit nosse, Joelem fuisse Bethuelis filium, quo cognomine ab aliis distinguitur ejusdem nominis, eo tempore, quo vixit; ex iis fuisse, quem Deus idoneum & censuit & reddidit, ut munere legationis ad populum rite fungens suo nomine loqueretur, quod iis innuitur verbis aperte, verbum Domini esse, quod ad Joelem fuit, & in hac prophetia continetur, significantibus. Atque hisce auctoritatem verbo comparavit, quod scilicet sit verbum Domini, non verbum Joelis. Quod cum indubiæ veritatis sit, auctoritatemque in se habeat, factum est, ut in Canonem sacrarum literarum receptum & inter eos libros relatum sit, qui, quantumvis hujus vel illius ætatis homines, apud quos verba fuerant prolata, specialius spectaverint, constans tamen ac firma debent esse regula cunctis generationibus futuri temporis, ut eas exemplo suo in voluntate Dei instruant, m) utilesque fiant ad doctrinam, redargutionem, correctionem, & disciplinam in justitia.
units.tr: e) Abarbanel. d) Abar. e) Epiphanius asserts that he was of the tribe of Reuben, but on what reasoning this rests is not clear. f) Kimchi. g) 2 Reg. 8. 1. h) Tarnov. i) Jerome, in the preface to the Twelve Prophets. k) Seder Olam. l) Dancus. Nor do the Scriptures give any indication on this point, which clearly shows how little we ought to be anxious about such trifles. It is enough to know that Joel was the son of Bethuel, a surname by which he is distinguished from others of the same name who lived at the same time. He was one of those whom God judged fit and made fit to discharge the office of an envoy to the people properly, speaking in his own name, as is clearly indicated by the words saying that it is the word of the Lord that came to Joel and is contained in this prophecy. By this, the word gained its authority, namely that it is the word of the Lord and not the word of Joel. Since this is of indubitable truth and carries authority in itself, it came about that it was received into the canon of sacred Scripture and reckoned among those books which, however much they look especially to the people of that age to whom the words were spoken, must nevertheless be a constant and firm rule for all future generations, so that they may instruct them by example in the will of God, and be useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and discipline in righteousnessm).

units.la: Quodque ejus verbum non illud tantum concernat seculum, sed & futurum, aperte testatur S. Petrus, qui illud citat tanquam prædictionem eorum, quæ erant futura tempore Christi (Act. 2,17. &c.) id quod tam evidenter præstat, ut Judæi ipsi non potuerint non illud confiteri.
units.tr: That his word concerns not only that age but also the future, St Peter clearly testifies, who cites it as a prediction of what was to happen in the time of Christ (Acts 2.17 etc.); and he does this so evidently that the Jews themselves could not but acknowledge it.

units.la: Confitetur certe Kimchius, Prophetam primo prophetare de locutis, quæ ventura essent super terram Israelis propter peccata, & non multo post eandem exponit prophetiam עתידים לימות המשיח [?] ut quæ eventum habitura sit diebus Messiæ, de quibus Petrus ibidem ait, hoc est, quod dictum est a Propheta Joele, quæ idcirco etiam suo loco reservanda sunt, ubi data ulteriori occasione speciatim in hæc inquiremus. Sufficiant in præsentiarum, quæ præfationis loco adduximus: jam quid contineat hoc verbum Domini, quod fuit ad Joelem, suo ordine exposituri sumus.
units.tr: Kimchi certainly admits that the prophet first prophesied of things that [were] to come upon the land of Israel [on account of sins], and not long after he expounds the same prophecy as [Hebrew: עתידים לימות המשיח] "destined to come to pass in the days of the Messiah," of which Peter says in the same place, "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." These things are therefore to be reserved for their proper place, where, on a further occasion, we shall inquire into them particularly. For the present let what we have adduced by way of preface suffice; now we shall set out in order what this word of the Lord that came to Joel contains.

units.la: 2. Audite hoc, o Seniores, & auribus percipite omnes habitatores hujus terræ: an fuit hoc temporibus vestris, aut etiam diebus majorum vestrorum?
units.tr: 2. Hear this, O elders, and give ear, all you inhabitants of this land: has this happened in your days, or even in the days of your fathers?

units.la: 3. De hoc filiis vestris narrate, & filii vestri filiis suis, & filii illorum generationi vestrae.
units.tr: 3. Tell this to your sons, and let your sons tell it to their sons, and their sons to the following generation.

units.la: Propheta hic a Deo missus, & verba habens ori suo imposita, ut stupidos illos peccatores, ad quos ablegatus erat, eo perduceret, ut peccata sua agnoscerent, matureque ac serio resipiscerent, quo tristissima Dei averterent judicia, quae suis istis peccatis (quibus adhuc inhaerebant) in se provocaverant, initium facit a designatione magnitudinis & natura illorum judiciorum, ut cum ad ea rite attenderent, facilius perciperent, ea nequaquam ejus generis esse, qualia, ut se communiter res habent in mundo, contingebant hominibus. Quocirca necesse erat, ita stylum ac linguam informare, ut extraordinariam Dei manum ac virtutem in iis sentirent, atque palam fieret, quam atrociter & quam graviter iram divinam irritassent, quodque minime sibi possent persuadere, neque sperare, se ab ipsis jam liberos & immunes esse, antequam pacem iniissent poenitentia seria cum eo, qui, sicuti solus ea immiserat, ita & solus ea avertere, & quae damna inde illata erant, compensare posset. Quod magnitudinem ac gravitatem attinet, tantam fore eam describit, quantam nec ullus antea oculus, nec ulla unquam vel fando percepisset auris, quantamque generationes secuturae, quum ad ipsorum noticiam perventura esset, non secus consideraturi essent, ac rem plane inauditam nulliq; antea aetati cognitā. Haec comprehenduntur v.2. & 3. ubi per interrogationem propriae ipsorum menti omniumq; inter eos ordinum hominibus expendendum proponit, annon hujus rei veritatem ipsos oporteret confiteri. Audite hoc, o Seniores, & auribus percipite omnes habitatores terrae.) Audite, quae dicturus sum, o seniores. Cognitione imprimis pollebant rerum, quas tum ex propria experientia, tum ex relatione aliorum gestas longo annorum retro spatio certo sciebant hincque tanto magis idonei erant ad judicandum de iis, quae erant jam dicenda, annon haec descriptio sit gravioris tristiorisque longe judicii, quam antea meminerint factum aut relatum esse; vos, inquit, una cum omnibus habitatoribus terrae (vel ut aliis placet, totus terrarum orbis, & uniuscujusque regionis) percipite auribus, scrutamini & considerate, an ullo prorsus tempore pore vel loco tale quicquam videre vel audire sive ipsismet vobis sive majoribus vestris contigerit; quod si minus, quid magis jam necessarium, quam operis hujus tam insoliti inquirere causam, minimeque eam negligere, veluti rem, quae saepe usu venire solet, sed qualis a tas praeterita nec viderit & secutura vix visura sit. Excitatis hoc modo ad attentionem animis, progreditur ad descriptionem illius judicii, quod juxta quosdam jamjam dicit immissum, juxta alios tam certo futurum, ac si jamjam adesset.
units.tr: The prophet, sent by God and having the words put in his mouth, begins by describing the magnitude and nature of those judgments. He does this so that these stupid sinners, to whom he was sent, may be brought to recognise their sins and to repent seriously and in good time, and so turn away the most dreadful judgments of God, which they had provoked upon themselves by these very sins, to which they still clung. If they rightly considered these judgments, they would more easily perceive that they were of no ordinary kind, such as commonly befall men in the world. For this reason he had to shape his style and language so that they would feel the extraordinary hand and power of God in them, and it would be made plain how atrociously and how grievously they had provoked the divine wrath. Thus they could not persuade themselves or hope that they were already free and exempt from these things, unless they first made peace through earnest repentance with him who, as he alone had sent them, so he alone could avert them and make good the losses they had caused. As to their magnitude and gravity, he describes them as greater than any eye had seen or any ear had ever heard, and such that future generations, when they came to know of them, would consider them no less than a thing wholly unheard of and unknown to any age before. These things are contained in verses 2 and 3, where by a question he sets before the minds of each one of them, and of men of every rank among them, the matter to be weighed: whether they ought not to confess the truth of this thing. Hear this, O ye elders, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land. Hear what I am about to say, O elders. They excelled above all in knowledge of things, which, both from their own experience and from the accounts of others, they knew for certain over a long span of past years; and therefore they were all the more fit to judge whether this description was of a far heavier and sadder judgment than they remembered anything to have happened or been reported. "You," he says, "together with all the inhabitants of the land (or, as others prefer, the whole world, and of each region), perceive with your ears, search out and consider whether at any time or place anything of this kind has ever been seen or heard, either by yourselves or by your fathers. And if not, what could be more necessary now than to inquire into the cause of so unusual a work, and not to neglect it as a thing that often happens, but as one of a kind which past ages have neither seen nor future ages are likely to see." Having thus roused their minds to attention, he goes on to describe the judgment which, according to some, he is already declaring to be about to fall, and according to others, is as certain to come as if it were already present.

units.la: 4. Quod reliquit eruca, comedit locusta; & quod reli- quit locusta, comedit melolontha ac; quod reliquit melolontha, comedit bruchus.
units.tr: 4. What the cankerworm has left, the locust has eaten; and what the locust has left, the palmerworm has eaten; and what the palmerworm has left, the caterpillar has eaten.

units.la: Quod reliquit eruca. Interpretes nostri notant in margine, quod in hebraeo sit reliduum eruca, ut verba יתר הגזם אכלה הארבה Yether hagazam acal haarbeh, ad literam sonant. Cur vero hac ratione illa reddiderint, eam causam subesse reor, quod ambiguitatem evitare voluerint, cui literalis sensus videtur subjectus, sed vellet, quae vermes superant, a locustis sunt comesta. Idem observatum est Rabbi Tanchum, ... Intelligit per Yether hagazam reliquum eruca, quod reliquerunt ex plantis terrae, non reliquias ipsarum et ucarum. Et si tali modo reddatur, ut factum est in posteriori nostra translatione, multo est clarius quam in Genevensi, quae habet, quod reliquum est eruca. Infectorum vel creaturarum noxiarum recensentur hic species quatuor, quarum alia alii succedit, & ubi posteriori cedit, quod a priore relictum est, donec quaecunque fructuum terrae erant comestibilia, absumta sint omnia; & illae quidem in medium producuntur velut executores gravium judiciorum, quae Deus immissurus erat Judaeis. Prima est Gazam, quae nostris interpretibus eruca vocatur tum hoc in loco, tum Amos 4, 9. cujus denominatio descendit a radere, tecare, evellere, & litera in fine addita; vel alias a Gazam, quae vox quamvis in sacris literis non extet, eandem tamen significationem in hebraeo habere conjicimus, quam
units.tr: What the cankerworm has left. Our translators note in the margin that the Hebrew reads the remainder of the cankerworm, the words יתר הגזם אכלה הארבה [yether hagazam acal haarbeh] sounding literally thus. I believe the reason they rendered it in this way is that they wished to avoid an ambiguity, to which the literal sense seems open: namely, that the worms that survived were eaten by the locusts. The same point was noted by Rabbi Tanchum: He understands by yether hagazam the remainder of the cankerworm, that is, what they left of the plants of the earth, not the remains of the worms themselves. And if it is rendered in this way, as was done in our later translation, it is much clearer than in the Geneva version, which has that which is left of the cankerworm. Four kinds of insects or noxious creatures are listed here, each succeeding the other, and where the later one leaves off, what was left by the earlier is consumed, until everything that could be eaten of the fruits of the earth has been devoured. These creatures are brought forward as the executors of the grave judgments which God was about to send upon the Jews. The first is Gazam, which our translators call the cankerworm, both here and in Amos 4:9. Its name is derived from shaving, cutting or tearing up, with a letter added at the end. Or else, from Gazam, a word which, although it does not occur in the sacred writings, we suppose has the same meaning in Hebrew that it has among the rabbis.

units.la: a) Ab. Ezra. R. Tauch. Fuller. Cap. Concord. quam habet apud Rabbinos. Pari modo & Arabicum ۔ۦ→ significationem eandem admittit, quod indicio est exinde ipsi nomen ortum שניז ארת התביאר quia detondet frumenta ut Kimchi habet. Secunda est ארבה Arbeh, quae vox nostratibus eadem vocula hic reddita est, qua Exod. 10,4. At aliis in locis jam locusta, jam cicada redditur. Videtur nomen suum traxisse a רבר multum esse vel multiplicari, quod hujus speciei magnæ sit copia. Occurrit hujus vocis radix & nomen Jer. 46,23. רבו מארבה rabbu mearbeh, quod nostrates interpretantur, plures sunt (arbores) quam locustæ. Sic & Jud. 6,5. occurrit cum alio quidem nomine conjunctum, at non alia significatione, כרי ארבה לרב sicut locustæ præ multitudine. Tertia est ילק yelek, quæ hic non secus ac Jer. 51,14. per volvocem transfertur, at Nah. 3,15. per erucam. Verum si usitatæ derivationi accurate attenderis, idem significare comperies ac lincorem, quippe ad radicem ... kak, lingere, eam reducendam esse, interpretum unanimis est ... ntia שהוא לוקק ולוחך ארת העשב quia agit ac si herbæ lambendo essent absumtæ, ut Kimchi loquitur, easque tali modo devorat. Quarta est חסיל Chafil, quam ubique per volvocem reddunt, cujus denominatio videtur designare exesorem, confumtorem, a verbo חסל Chafal, quod, (quamvis p) a nomine magis videatur deductum) significat consumere, eaque significatione nostratibus usitatum, Deut. 28,38. יחסילנו הארבה yachsilenu haarbeh, locusta illud absumet. Græcis interpretibus reddita est hic ἐςυσίβη, & Vulgatæ q) rubigo, (quam Duacensis interpretatur flamen) alicubi tamen eandem Græci exprimunt nomine alicujus noxiæ creaturæ, ut βρῦχος, bruchus, 2. Chron. 28. & ἀκρίς locusta, Esa. 33,4. Quo in loco utroque Vulgata etiam habet vocem bruchi. Quantumvis igitur nulli refragemur, quin significationem eam vox admittat, quam ipsi tribuere r) quibusdam placuit, prætereaque non improprium valde sit rubigini, noxam inferre & viridantibus frumentis & aliis quibuscunque rebus; id tamen certo affirmare habeo, quod magis convenire huic loco videatur, si de vivente creatura accipiatur, quippe reliquæ tres priores ejus-
units.tr: a) Abraham Ezra, Rabbi Tanchum, Fuller, Cap. Concord., as they have it among the rabbis. In the same way the Arabic word also admits the same meaning, which is an indication that the name itself came from this, because it shears the crops, as Kimchi has it. The second is arbeh (ארבה), which our translators render here with the same word they use at Exodus 10:4, though in other places it is rendered sometimes locust, sometimes cicada. It seems to have taken its name from רבה [rabah], to be many or to multiply, because there is a great abundance of this kind. The root and noun of this word occur at Jeremiah 46:23, רבו מארבה [rabbu mearbeh], which our translators render, they are more (trees) than locusts. So also at Judges 6:5 it occurs joined with another noun, but not in another sense: כרי ארבה לרב [kiri arbeh lerob], as locusts for multitude. The third is yelek (ילק), which here, as at Jeremiah 51:14, is rendered by caterpillar, but at Nahum 3:15 by cankerworm. Yet if you attend carefully to the usual derivation, you will find that it means the same as the lapping creature, since it is agreed by all the interpreters that it is to be traced back to the root לקק [laqaq], to lick. Kimchi says that it works as if the grass were consumed by licking and lapping, שהוא לוקק ולוחך את העשב [shehu loqeq velocheakh et haeseb], and so devours it in this way. The fourth is chafil (חסיל), which they everywhere render by palmerworm. Its name seems to signify a devourer or consumer, from the verb חסל [chasal], which (although it seems more derived from a noun) means to consume, and in this sense it is used by our translators at Deuteronomy 28:38, יחסילנו הארבה [yachsilenu haarbeh], the locust shall consume it. The Greek translators render it here by ἐρυσίβη [erysibē], and the Vulgate by mildew (which the Douai version renders blast); yet elsewhere the Greeks use the same word for the name of some noxious creature, as βρῦχος [brychos], caterpillar, at 2 Chronicles 28, and ἀκρίς [akris], locust, at Isaiah 33:4. In that place the Vulgate also has the word bruchus. Therefore, although we do not deny that the word admits the meaning which some have preferred to give it, and although it is not improper to say that mildew does harm both to green crops and to all other things, I nonetheless affirm with confidence that it seems to fit this place better if it is taken of a living creature, since the three earlier ones are

units.la: o) Ita & Aben Ezra. p) R. Tanch. q) Sic etiam Tigurini & Munsterus. r) Ribera. Pet. a Fig. Chr. a Castro. ejusdem procul dubio sunt speciei, singulæque posteriores comedise dicantur, quod a prioribus fuerat relictum, cui rationi quoque pondus accedit, cum proprie comedisse eos statuatur, eo nimirum modo, qui conveniens est creaturis vita præditis. Difficultas tamen non levis hinc urget s) quosdam singularis quoque eruditionis viros, si pro quadam animalium specie sumunt, quæ hic dicuntur comedisse, quo scilicet nomine Latine proprie sint efferendæ. Id quod in aliis linguis quoque locum habere putant, quum non minus ac latina vocibus sint destitutæ, quibus probe ab invicem distingui queant. Arabica sola distinctis ac propriis referta est vocibus, quibus absque ulla ambiguitate reddi possunt; at quomodo hic ea sint applicanda, ut prophetæ mentem protinus exhauriant, hoc opus, hic labor. Quin imo difficulter, ne dicam, prorsus non ad cognitionem illarum perventuri famus, nec qua sint forma, quæque earum proprietates sint, cognoscemus, nisi quis regionem illam ingressus oculis eas perspexerit, nomenque cuiusvis auribus perceperit. Hinc factâ, ut interpretum nonnulli in quibusdam illarum t) Hebraica nomina maluerint retinere quam interpretari. Quare sufficiat nobis, ut cum u) Judæo quodam erudito dicamus هذه الاسما تكلها تد تكون لاصناف من الجر ... Hæc nomina omnia continent certas locustarum species, & sunt Synonyma, vel distincta ejusdem creaturæ nomina, cujus diversæ species esse ex eo apparet, quod dictum est in lege Levit. 11, 22. הארבה למינו Haarbeh lemino, locustam secundum speciem suam. Quam hic invenimus positam vocem Arbeh, ac si unius speciei nomen esset, eandem habemus ibi quasi sub se varias species comprehendentem, unde jure merito conjecceris, aliquando admodum generaliter, aliquando specialiter nimis voculam hanc esse positam وهي يطلق الواحد منها على الجميع ... positionius speciei nomine (ut ille loquitur) pro omnibus. Quatuor autem harum hic distincte satis introducuntur, quæ appellationes, quasgerunt, a diversa lædendi ratione obtinuisse videntur; quæ in eo tamen conveniunt, quod omnes damnum inferant, ac frumenta terræque
units.tr: So also Aben Ezra. p) R. Tanchum. q) So also the Tigurines and Munster. r) Ribera. Pet. a Fig. Chr. a Castro. They are without doubt of the same kind, and each of the later ones is said to have eaten what the earlier ones had left. This reasoning also carries weight, since they are held to have eaten in the proper sense, in the way that suits creatures endowed with life. Yet a difficulty not slight presses here, from some men of singular learning as well, if they take these as a certain kind of animal said here to have eaten, and so ask what name they should properly be given in Latin. They think this holds also in other languages, since they are no less lacking than Latin in words by which they can be properly distinguished from one another. Arabic alone is full of distinct and proper words, by which they can be rendered without any ambiguity; but how these are to be applied here so as to exhaust at once the mind of the prophet, that is the work, that is the labour. Indeed, we shall with difficulty, not to say not at all, come to know them, nor shall we know what form they have or what their properties are, unless someone who has entered that region has seen them with his own eyes and heard the name of each with his ears. Hence it has come about that some of the interpreters preferred to retain the Hebrew names for some of them rather than translate them. So it is enough for us to say, with a certain learned Jew: "These names all may be for kinds of locusts, and they are synonyms, or distinct names of the same creature, whose different species is evident from what is said in the law, Lev. 11:22, hā'arbeh lemino [הארבה למינו], 'the locust after its kind.'" Where we find the word Arbeh put here, as if it were the name of one species, we have it there as if comprehending several species under it; whence you may rightly conjecture that this word is sometimes used very generally, sometimes too specially. "And one of them is applied to all of them ... as the name of a single species (as he puts it) is used for all." Now four of these are introduced here quite distinctly, and the names they bear seem to have arisen from their different ways of doing harm; yet they agree in this, that all of them inflict damage and devour the grain and the produce of the land.

units.la: s) Ar. Montanus. Bochart. t) Pag. Interlin. u) Rab. Tanchum. que proventus exedant atque consumant. Recte itaque nostros fecille interpretes arbitror, quod talia substituerint creaturarum nomina, quæ & notissima sunt & pariter nova, quamvis ratione admodum diversa, qua nimirum, quod reliquit altera, altera sibi vendicat, donec omnia prorsus absumta sunt ac devorata. Quandoquidem igitur facis jam patet, ejusmodi noxia animalcula innui hisce nominibus, quærendum venit, an quæ de ipsis dicta sunt, proprie etiam de ipsis sint intelligenda, & si hoc sit, quidve damni inferant, ut habent verba prophetæ; an potius de hostibus quibusdam sint exaudienda, qui cum illis comparentur, quarumque sub nomine & figura hujusmodi destructio ac desolatio proponatur, quam illæ faciunt sibi invicem succedentes, nihilque illæsum relinquentes. Quæstio hæc jam olim mota, tam magna opinionum super eandem diversitate, ut nec nunc quidem neque inter Judæos, neque inter Christianos Auctoribus conveniat. Mentionem quidem ejus rei facit S. Hieronymus, at fluctuare in hoc negotio valde videtur, magis tamen in eorum sententiam propenedns, qui id de hostibus, regionem Judæam invadentibus, interpretantur, quo sensu & Judæorum nonnullos ante se accepisse affirmat, (etsi minime constet, quosnam indigitaverit); ita ut prima vox respiciat Assyrios, Babylonios & Chaldæos; secunda Medos & Persas; tertia Græcos, Alexandrum & ejus successores, eosque inter imprimis Antiochum Epiphanem, quo regnante gesta sunt Maccabæorum bella: quarta Romanos. Qui populi omnes diversis temporibus Judæorum regionem invaserant, eamque desolatam utplurimum reddiderant. Attamen alios etiam fuisse Judæos affirmat, qui tempore Joelis tantam locustarum copiam invasisse terram Judæam statuerint, ut omnia implerent, neq; frumenta tantum devorarent, verum etiam vites arborumque cortices & ramos exederent. Verum enim vero qvum nulla hujus rei verisimilitudo sit, neq; in historia profana neq; in Sacra appareat ejus vel exile vestigium, quod sit tamen, cum regionem fames aliquando afflixit; mirum nobis videri non potest, quod in dubium hanc sententiam vocet, quin potius rejiciendam esse arguat. Hinc demum ambiguis quantumvis verbis pedem figit, dum invasionem hostium, quos ante memoravimus, sub figura locustarum stanum innui ait, & quia ex mente & intentione Prophetæ collegisse videtur, quod scilicet hostium improbitatem vel crudelitatem sub figura locustarum ipse velit depingere, locustasque ita describere, ac si imaginem illarum gererent hostes, ut cum locustas legeris, hostes cognos, cum hostes cognatione seducas ad locustas. Atque ita locus iste dubitatur per ipsum exponitur. Pari ratione & Cyrillus de illis hostibus verba intellexisse patet, qui Judæos diversis temporibus aggressi sunt, quos inter postremi imprimis erant Salmanasser, Nabuchadnezzar, Antiochus & Romani, qui tamen nihilominus ad vers. 14. rursus dicit, quod quæ dixerat, æque vera sint, si vel maxime de locustis aliisque creaturis noxiis intelligerentur. Theodoretus aliquorum tropice ea intelligentium mentionem facit, quosdam de Regibus, videlicet Assyriæ, ut sunt Tiglath Pilefer, Salmanasser, Senacherib & Nebuchadnez-zar secundum etiam sententiæ tanquam veræ adstipulari non verentur, subjiciens tandem, κατα τὰ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν νοούμενα τῷ ὄντως γεγενέσθαι, quæ sic sensum litteralem sensum intelliguntur, revera facta esse. Alt Rufinus planissime persuasus est, non tantum hæc de animalibus illis dictis secundum literam esse capienda, verum & eos refutandos, qui de hostibus Judæorum sumenda esse arguunt. Atque exinde cuique liquere arbitror, quam varię sententiæ & Latinis & Græcis interpretibus ævi antiquioris hac de re fuerint. Sed minus obvium est, quinam sint illi Doctores Hebræorum veteres, quorum mentionem injecit Hieronymus. Retinet plerumque, ut alibi ita & hic, Chaldæus literam, quæque hic extant voces, vocibus eis in sua lingua responden-dibus quam maxime reddit. Cum vero eundem, quamvis inverso ordine, cap. 2,25. fit repetitio, alio modo visum fuit ipsi agere, quippe sensum earum, quem habere sibi persuadet, potius exprimit, quam literam, quando illarum in locum substituit עמים אומים ולשנים ומלכים פרנסים Nationes, populi, linguæ, principes & reges. Quod diversitatem interpretationum illius temporis immane quantum confirmat. Idem inter recentiores Judæos post Hieronymi tempora obtinuit. R. Sal. Aben-Ezra & David Kimchi, celebriores suæ gentis interpretes, proprie hæc verba exponunt de locustis & hujusmodi noxiis vermibus, qui fructus terræ absumebant,
units.tr: s) Ar. Montanus. Bochart. t) Pag. Interlin. u) Rab. Tanchum. They devour and consume the produce. I therefore think our translators did well to substitute such names of creatures, names that are both very well known and at the same time unfamiliar, although they differ greatly in their manner of harm: one kind takes what the other has left, and the next claims what remains, until everything has been wholly consumed and devoured. Since it is now clear from what has been said that these hurtful little creatures are meant by these names, the question arises whether what is said of them should be understood literally, and if so, what damage they inflict, as the words of the prophet have it, or whether instead it should be taken as referring to certain enemies with whom they are compared, and whose destruction and desolation is set forth under the name and figure of these creatures, which, succeeding one another, leave nothing unharmed. This question was raised long ago and has provoked such great disagreement that today neither the Jewish nor the Christian authors agree. St Jerome does indeed mention this matter, but he seems to waver greatly in it, though he inclines more to the opinion of those who interpret it of enemies invading the land of Judea. In this sense he also asserts that some Jews before him had taken it, although it is by no means certain whom he had in mind. So the first word refers to the Assyrians, Babylonians and Chaldeans; the second to the Medes and Persians; the third to the Greeks, Alexander and his successors, and especially Antiochus Epiphanes, in whose reign the wars of the Maccabees were fought; the fourth to the Romans. All these peoples had at various times invaded the land of the Jews and had mostly left it desolate. Yet he also affirms that there were other Jews who judged that at the time of Joel so great a swarm of locusts had invaded the land of Judea that they filled everything, devouring not only the grain but also the vines, the bark and the branches of the trees. But since there is no likelihood of this, and not even a faint trace of it appears either in profane or in sacred history, though a famine has at times afflicted the region, it cannot seem strange to us that he calls this opinion into doubt, or rather argues that it should be rejected. At last he takes his stand, however ambiguous the words, saying that the invasion of the enemies we mentioned above is hinted at under the figure of locusts. He seems to have inferred from the mind and intention of the prophet that he wishes to portray the wickedness or cruelty of the enemies under the figure of locusts, and to describe the locusts in such a way as if the enemies bore their likeness: so that when you read of locusts, you recognise enemies, and when you consider enemies, you are led to locusts. And so this passage is explained by him in doubtful terms. In the same way it is clear that Cyril also understood these words of those enemies who attacked the Jews at various times, among whom the last were especially Shalmaneser, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus and the Romans; yet nonetheless, at verse 14, he says again that what he had said is equally true even if it is understood chiefly of locusts and other harmful creatures. Theodoret mentions some who understand these things tropically, namely some who refer them to the kings of Assyria, such as Tiglath-Pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib and Nebuchadnezzar, and he does not hesitate to agree with this view as if it were true, adding at last: κατα τὰ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν νοούμενα τῷ ὄντως γεγενέσθαι [kata ta kata to rheton nooumena tō ontōs gegenesthai], that is, these things, understood according to the literal sense, are shown to have really happened. But Rufinus was most clearly persuaded that these things are to be taken according to the letter of those animals, and that those must be refuted who argue that they are to be referred to the enemies of the Jews. From this, I think, it will be plain to anyone how varied were the opinions on this matter among the Latin and Greek interpreters of earlier times. But it is less obvious who those ancient teachers of the Hebrews were whom Jerome mentions. The Chaldee paraphrast, here as elsewhere, for the most part keeps to the letter and renders the words that stand here as closely as possible by the corresponding words of his own language. But since the same words recur, though in reverse order, at chapter 2, verse 25, he chose to do otherwise there, for he expresses the sense that he believes they have, rather than the letter, when in their place he substitutes nations, peoples, tongues, princes and kings [עמים אומים ולשנים ומלכים פרנסים, ammim umaim velishenim umelakhim parnasim]. This confirms beyond measure the variety of interpretations of that time. The same view prevailed among the later Jews after the time of Jerome. R. Saadia Ibn Ezra and David Kimchi, the most celebrated interpreters of their nation, expound these words properly of locusts and such harmful worms, which consumed the fruits of the earth,

units.la: Beoque causam præbebant ingentis famis, reique frumentariæ inopiæ, quæ regioni incubuit. R. Tanchum non tantum de locustis creaturisque his similibus ea exponit verba, quæ hic extant, sed & quæ sequuntur versu 6. Gens enim ascendit super terram meam, ita tamen ut confiteatur non absurdum esse dicere, quascunque memorantur de natura locustarum, earumque actionibus, parabolicam esse expressionem de invasione inimicorum, eorumque multitudine & devastatione regionis cujusque corruptione. Idque ex aliis loquendi modis, quæ sequuntur, conatur confirmare, præsertim ex illo terrore, quo afficiebantur in cuitu harum locustarum. Nec non ex eo, quod nulla littera dicatur, nisi in residue, quos Jehova vocaverit, cap 2,32. unde difficile est creditu, tantam valuisse locustarum immiſsionem: Eo quoque tendunt, quæ adjunguntur de sumenda vindicta de hostibus, quando hic infit cap. 3,7. Congregabo omnes gentes &c. Dispergabo eos pro populo meo & possessione mea &c. Et quid mihi vobis mecum Tyre & Sidon &c. Festinanter & velociſsime reddam retributionem vestram in caput vestrum. Et quamvis inquit interpretes & expositores tantum de locustis sermonem hic esse autumant, quæ terræ Israelis ingredere, magis tamen convenire videtur, ut antea dixi.
units.tr: and so caused a great famine and the scarcity of grain that lay upon the land. R. Tanchum expounds the words that stand here not only of locusts and creatures like them, but also the words that follow at verse 6: For a nation has come up upon my land; yet he confesses that it is not absurd to say that whatever is recorded of the nature of locusts and their actions is a figurative expression of the invasion of enemies, of their multitude, and of the devastation and corruption of each region. He tries to confirm this from other turns of expression that follow, especially from that terror with which people were struck at the sight of these locusts. He also argues from the fact that no remnant is mentioned except among the survivors whom the LORD shall call (chap. 2, verse 32), so that it is hard to believe that so great a swarm of locusts could have prevailed. He also points to what is added about taking vengeance on the enemies, where it begins at chapter 3, verse 7: I will gather all the nations, etc.; I will scatter them among my people and my heritage, etc.; and what is this to me and to you, Tyre and Sidon, etc.; I will swiftly and speedily return your recompense upon your own head. And, he says, although the interpreters and expositors think that the discourse here is only about locusts entering the land of Israel, it seems more fitting, as I said before.

units.la: Ex quibus jam videre est, eum non protinus abhorrere ab expositione, quæ respicit eos, illisque similes creaturas noxias, ut tamen usque adeo illam recingat, ut nonnisi nomina ab his sumantur libus mutuo esse sumpta fatuat, quibus inimicos Judæorum jurant. Propheta vult indignare. Recentior hic est Abarbanel, sibique non constans in sua expositione, quum in illam sententiam totus ruat, quod his verbis caeteraque alias exprimendi formis Propheta non loquitur de locustis ... Procul a me, ut id credam, ... quatuor de hostibus illi qui diruebant eius civitatem, populumque suum expugnabant. Eos vero hostes statuit quatuor regna, id est licet Babylonicorum, Persarum, Graecorum & Romanorum, cui expositio eden tar ere & congruere credit dicendi quae sequuntur, formulas, ut vel quam induci possit ad credendum, de locu- atque hujusmodi novus vermiculis hic esse sermonem.
units.tr: From these things it can now be seen that he did not at once shrink from the explanation which refers to them and to harmful creatures like them; yet he so far curbs it that he admits only names taken from these creatures, names which are borrowed from one another, by which the enemies of the Jews are called. The prophet wishes to shame them. The more recent writer here is Abarbanel, who is not consistent with himself in his exposition, since he falls wholly into that opinion, namely that by these words and by other forms of expression the prophet does not speak of locusts ... Far be it from me to believe it ... but of four enemies who destroyed his city and overthrew his people. These enemies he holds to be the four kingdoms, namely the Babylonians, Persians, Greeks and Romans, with which he believes the exposition agrees and harmonises, and the words which follow, so that one may be led to believe that there is here a discourse about locusts and about such new little worms.

units.la: Quod si etiam volupe est recentiores Christianorum inspicere interpretamenta, credas velim, te eandem varietatem sententiarum cognoscere quam. Quare nonnisi earundem rerum opus et regerendi ... lactenus appositumus. Quidam eorum praeferunt opinionem, qui non secundum literam verba exponunt de locused de inimicis, qui eo nomine innuuntur, quorumque Judaeis ruina est illata. In eo tamen minus conveniunt, quod per inimicos istos sint intelligendi. Alii proprie ea sumunt de Judaeis, damnumque regioni illatum primario ac proprie illis tributum putant, quos inter doctissimus est Bochartus, qui se aperte fatentur Abarbinelis Judaei, quam postremo recensuimus, oppositione & per consequens omnibus aliis, qui huic in eo concinunt, quod non praedictae befliolae, sed inimici terram invasuri inprimis respiciantur. Alii utrumque fuisse designatum contendunt, alteros alterum exstitisse praecursores. Hinc praecelisse locu- inimicorumque invasionem pertendisse x) aliis observatum est. Verum enim vero ne nos intermisceamus ulterius hilce controversiis, eam putamus viam ad id extricandum esse planam maxime & securam, quae est simplicissima. Huc autem institutum esse nos, nemo iniciasire poterit, si inhaerens verbis, prout sonant, quippe cum denique fas esse cuique patet pro libitu suo huic vel illi rei ea applicare. Quod ad expressiones attinet, ex quibus nonnulli contrariam sententiam confirmant, cum suo ordine nobis sese offerent, earum quoque vim diligenter tunc expendere non obliviscemur. At aliae expressiones insuper ... rite explicatas adhuc urae hi historiae, operae pretium omnino judicamus eas exacte resolvere. Exempli causa, primum, quomodo quae hic dicuntur de noxiis animalibus eorumque damno illato, an sint hoc tempore venturi, ut erunt temporibus majorum vestrorum? cum iis pollint conciliari, quae
units.tr: If you also wish to look at the more recent interpretations of the Christians, I would have you know that you will find the same variety of opinions. Therefore I shall say no more here about these matters than is enough for our purpose. Some of them prefer the opinion of those who do not expound the words according to the letter of locusts, but of the enemies who are signified by that name, and by whom the ruin was brought upon the Jews. In this, however, they agree less, as to who these enemies are to be understood to be. Others take the words properly of the Jews, and think that the damage done to the region is attributed primarily and properly to them; among these the most learned is Bochart, who plainly confesses that he is opposed to the Jewish Abarbanel, whom we last mentioned, and consequently to all the others who agree with him in this, that it is not the aforesaid little beasts but the enemies about to invade the land that are chiefly in view. Others contend that both were meant, one being the forerunner of the other. From this it has been noted by others that the locusts went before, and the invasion of the enemies followed. But, in truth, lest we become entangled further in these controversies, we think the road to the resolution of the matter is most plain and safe, and it is the simplest. No one will be able to object that we have turned aside to this, if we keep to the words as they sound, since it is clear that in the end it is lawful for each to apply them to this or that matter at his own pleasure. As for the expressions by which some confirm the contrary opinion, when they present themselves in their order we shall not forget to weigh carefully their force then. But since other expressions too ... have been rightly explained up to now in this history, we judge it well worth the effort to resolve them exactly. For example, first, how the things said here about harmful animals and the damage they inflicted can be reconciled with those things which are they to come this time, as they were in the times of your fathers?

units.la: quæ dicuntur de locustis, quas immisit Deus terræ Ægyptiorum Exod. 10, 14. quod fuerint valde graves, ante quas non fuissent sic locustæ pares istis, & post quas non essent futuræ sic? Alii aliter hunc nodum conantur solvere. Sunt, qui rem optime expediri statuunt, dicendo: Primo 1) de magnitudine locustarum ibi, de multitudine hic term onem esse, veritatemque utrique loco constare, quod nec unquam visæ essent tam magnæ, quam ibi, nec tam multæ, quam hic. Secundo in Ægypto 2) unius generis tantam fuisse multitudinem, quanta unquam fuerat nec unquam futura erat; hic vero multitudinem variorum generum, quorum nusquam fuerat vel hic vel alibi tam numerosa turba. Ad hæc vero objici potest, quod quamvis in lege non nisi locustarum mentio facta sit, id tamen minime impedire quo minus & alia genera earum eo nomine indicentur, ut constat ex Auctore Psalmi 78, 46 qui ad hanc historiam respexisse putandus est, quando dicit: Et dedit brucho proventum eorum, ac laborem eorum locustæ. Et Psalm. 105, 34. quod simul locustæ & melolonthæ advenerint exque innumeræ. Quam objectionem tamen ex eo solvere conatur Kimchi, quod locustæ solum præcipuæ fuerint earum, de quibus in lege relatum est. Tertio in Exodo omnium locustarum in alionem non nisi 3) unius diei vel paucorum dierum fuisse; hic vero successivam innui irreptionem, & unius quidem generis post alterum. Quod tamen num eo pacto factum sit, ulteriori probatione ac indagine indiget. Quarto, clarior responsio esse videtur, si dicamus, ad Ægyptum tantum respicere, quod in Exodo contigisse legimus; e contrario vero Judæam, quod hic memoratur, unde utrumque veritati congruere, ratione scilicet loci, quo contigit. Sed adversus hæc excipit Abarbanel, quod [Hebrew] dictum sit, quod in Exodo legimus de qualitate & quantitate earum locustarum, nullo modo referendum ad regionem Ægyptiorum, sicut quod paulo ante extat de grandine Exod. 9, 18 de qua expresse dicitur, quod sit futura tanta, cui par nec existura sit, nec in regione Ægypti unquam talis extiterit, qualis v. 24 fuisse narratur. Idque ipsum eum etiam videtur movere, ut de innumeris hæc verba potius intelligere cupiat, quam proprie de locustis, quippe minus tunc hos duos locos sibi invicem contrariari persuasum habet. At nonne licebit conjicere, eandem restrictionem grandinis ad Ægyptum locum quoque habere in cæteris plagis, si locustæ ad eam regionem restringerentur, & quod erant facturæ, peculiariter ad eandem pertinere intelligendum sit? Quicquid demum ad reconciliationem horum locorum, qui sibi invicem directe non sunt contrarii, affertur, manifestum est, quemlibet horum continere descriptionem insignis & infinitæ plagæ, ex qua certo scire poterant, Deum quam maxime esse offensum, serioque pœnitentia opus esse, de rebus iis, quibus ad iram provocatum esse, ignorare ipsimet prorsus non poterant.
units.tr: What is said of the locusts that God sent upon the land of the Egyptians, Exod. 10:14, namely that they were so grievous that before them there had not been locusts like these, and after them there would not be such? Others try to untie this knot in different ways. Some hold that the matter is settled very well by saying: first, that the passage in Exodus concerns the size of the locusts and this passage concerns their number, and that the truth of both holds, since they had never been seen so large as there, nor so numerous as here. Second, that in Egypt there was a multitude of one kind as great as had ever been or ever would be, whereas here there is a multitude of various kinds, of which nowhere, either here or elsewhere, had there been so numerous a swarm. Against these, however, it can be objected that although the Law mentions only locusts, this does not in any way prevent other kinds from being indicated under that name, as is clear from the author of Psalm 78:46, who must be thought to have had this history in view when he says: And he gave their produce to the caterpillar, and their labour to the locust. And Psalm 105:34, that locusts and melolonthae came together, and innumerable ones. Kimchi, however, tries to answer this objection by saying that only the chief locusts were those reported in the Law. Third, that in Exodus all the locusts came into the land for only one day or a few days, whereas here a successive invasion is implied, one kind after another. Whether this happened in that way, however, needs further proof and inquiry. Fourth, a clearer answer seems to be this: if we say that what we read in Exodus refers only to Egypt, while what is mentioned here refers to Judea, then both agree with the truth, namely by reason of the place where it happened. But against these, Abarbanel objects that the words [Hebrew] said in Exodus about the quality and quantity of the locusts cannot be referred to the region of Egypt, as what stands a little earlier about the hail, Exod. 9:18, can be; of that it is expressly said that it would be of such a kind that none like it would exist, nor had there ever existed in the land of Egypt one such as is said in v. 24 to have been. This same thing seems also to move him to prefer to understand these words of innumerable things rather than properly of locusts, since he is persuaded that these two passages are then less opposed to each other. But may we not conjecture that the same restriction of the hail to Egypt also holds in the other plagues, if the locusts were restricted to that region, and that what they were going to do is to be understood as pertaining peculiarly to the same? Whatever at last is brought forward for reconciling these passages, which are not directly contrary to each other, it is clear that each of them contains a description of a remarkable and immense plague, from which they could know for certain that God was very greatly offended and that repentance was seriously needed; nor could they themselves be utterly ignorant of the things by which they had provoked him to anger.

units.la: Secundo quæritur, quo tempore id sit factum, quod a Propheta hic futurum prædicitur. Quemadmodum vero sacræ literæ omnino silentio involvere ætatem vel tempus, quo Propheta noster vixerit & prophetiam suam protulerit; sic quoque nullibi hujusmodi vel famis extat memoria, quæ hic prædicitur. Quidam famem fuisse putant, de qua Elisha loquitur 2. Reg. 8,1. Quia autem septennium usque perdurasse in proclivi est, nec ejusdem temporis raro constare potest, nisi annorum numerus utrinque par constituatur, eo suam sententiam tueri conantur, quod quatuor annorum famem ex quatuor noxis animalibus, frumenta terræ exedentibus, traxisse originem, reliquam vero trium annorum ex defectu pluviæ, velint. At quoniam nil præterea est, unde vel certo vel probabiliter poslit erui, Prophetam eo tempore spatio floruisse, quo Jehorammo, nec eam septennii fuisse famem aut ullam aliam in Sacra Scriptura memoratam, aliis videtur improbatum, quod nil certi de ea habeatur, & Abarbanel defuncto inde argumentum, quod quamquam ejusmodi sit intelligenda, quæ originem suam animalculis hisce voracibus debeat, sed potius invalionis vis quæ ab inimicis truculentis his nominibus desectus facta sit. Alii rursum nullius putant momenti illud argumentum, quod ex Scriptura nullam hujus rei alibi mentionem faciat, cum bene multa eaque valde ioi gnia accidisse perhibeant.
units.tr: Second, it is asked at what time this was done, which the Prophet foretells here as future. Just as the sacred letters entirely veil in silence the age or time in which our Prophet lived and uttered his prophecy, so nowhere does any memory of such a famine as is foretold here exist. Some think it was the famine of which Elisha speaks in 2 Kings 8:1. But since it is obvious that it lasted seven years, and nothing certain can be established about the time unless the number of years is made equal on both sides, they try to defend their opinion by saying that the famine of four years arose from four harmful animals eating the fruits of the earth, and that the remaining three years' famine came from lack of rain. But since there is nothing else from which it could be drawn, either with certainty or with probability, that the Prophet flourished at the time of Jehoram, nor that there was that seven-year famine or any other mentioned in Holy Scripture, others think this view is refuted, and Abarbanel, having died, draws an argument from it that, although it must be understood as of this kind, which owes its origin to these voracious little animals, it is rather the violence of an invasion made by truculent enemies under these names. Others again think that argument of no weight, that Scripture nowhere else makes mention of this matter, since they maintain that very many and very remarkable events occurred.

units.la: b) Rab. Salom. & David Kimchi. c) Pet. a Fig. Merc. habeantur, quæ tamen nullibi in sacris literis expressis habeantur termi-nis, quo in numero dicunt esse terræ motum, qui tanquam maxime notus & insignis describitur Amos. 1,1. & Zach. 14,5. Nec id proprie Sacræ Scripturæ intentum, ut harum rerum accuratam reddat rationem; quod ex aliis etiam d) familibus constat, quæ non idcirco solum referuntur, ut earum cognitionem habeamus, sed ut illustria reddantur magis alia, quæ tunc temporis sunt gesta. Hinc quæ Abrahami temporibus extitit fames, eam ob causam memoriæ proditam esse censent, ut ratio constaret peregrinationis ejus in Ægyptum, Gen. 12, 10. Quæ temporibus Isaaci, ut cognitum esset, quo pacto se contulerit ad Abimelecum regem Philistæorum, Gen. 26,1. Quæ septennalis temporibus Iosephi, ut occasio redderetur omnes insignes exhibendi historias de Iosepho, ejusque fratribus, de filiorum Israelis servitute in Ægypto & mira inde eorum ereptione, Gen. 41. Quæ temporibus Ruth, ut ostenderetur, quâ occasione regnum Moab intravërit Abimelech, cum tamen altum ejus sit silentium in libris Judicum, quorum tempore eam evenisse in aprico est. Quæ temporibus Sau-lis, quam Gibeonitarum cædes intulerat, quæque non nisi suspensione septem filiorum ejus restingui poterat, ut appareret, qua ratione stabilitum esset regnum David is. Quæ temporibus Eliæ Prophetæ 1. Reg. 18,2. & Elisæ 2. Reg. 4,32. ut palam fierent, quæ fecerat eo tempore miracula. Nec prorsus ratione caret, plures tanto annorum spatio extitisse alias fames, verum oblivioni traditas esse compertum habemus. Cumque relatarum alia de causa fiat mentio, ut nobis observatum est cum doctissimo Bochart o, qui eandem famis rationem & in Novo Testamento locum habere asserit, mirum prosecto esse non potest, quam hic refert Propheta Joel famem, in aliis historiis insuper haberi & omitti plane esse. Interim vero extitisse talem Ioelo plagam, famemque per eas factam, eamdem disseri poterit, quanquam nullibi temporis ratio exacte designetur. Quod si autem necessarium adeo fuisset atque utile ad instructionem nostram, utique e) Spiritus S. Sanctus dixisset. Interea nobis quoque dictum esse, quod hac historia ab eo intenditur, omnino perfi-ciendam habead) Bochart. e) Oecol. habeamus; quare in nostrum quoque ut deducamus usum, etiam atque etiam monendi sumus. Quod autem ad quæstionem illam attinet, ad quod nimirum tempus referenda sint verba a Propheta priuata, determinatum certe non est, nec quoad ætatem quam impleta sunt, nec quoad circumstantias temporis quo prolata sunt, num scilicet famem prædixerit, antequam extiterit; an vero designatio iam iam præteritam, aut immunerit præsentem? Eo autem fundamento hæc mittitur quæstio, quod verba hic præteriti sint temporis, & indicare videntur ipsam aut revera jam contigisse, aut nunc demum incipere & inoræscentiarum savire. Id namque perquam similiare est Prophetis ut præterito tempore utantur loco futuri, quo significare volunt, tam certe ea futura esse, quæ Deus constituit facere, ac jam essent præterita. Atque hinc magna iterum expositionum loquitur loci est diversitas. Quidam de prædictione accipiunt verba, quæ eos admonere voluerit, ut respiscentia amoliri ingruentia mala solo darent operam. Alii descriptionem ejus esse putant, quod eam est ictum, quo animos istorum excitaret Propheta, ut ea qua par erat attentione id adverterent, & ad Deum reverterentur, quodque ipsis tum est numissum, eum in finem factum esse putarent, ut sentirent, quam graviter Deum provocassent, quantaque opus esset moveri eum sedulitate, ut, quodcunque adversi immorigeris obvenirs s s s bemaniter velit ire compensatum. Rab. Salomon, ut & Aben-Ezra & Rad. David, qui verba proprie & juxta literam de creaturis noxiis sunt, (nam si de inimicis ac hostibus intelligerent diversis s ventur, quod alios dixerunt paulo ante notavimus, quas ioni non esset locus, dicunt eum prædixisse שיבאו יבאו באותן הימים ... ) s s s elleent futurae, quoque sis diebus congrue venirent s s immittit a Deo in terram illorum propter sua peccata. Huic opinioni nonnulli & h) Christianorum interpretum succinunt dicentes: de satiris loquitur in præterito propheticō more. Ast sunt alii, quibus de præteritis dixisse visum est. Calvinus eos dicit errare & errorem s s Prophetas sensum, qui ea pro denunciatione poenæ in ss s ss s s s s s s accipiunt, quippe Prophetæ intentionem esse reprehend-e s ssupi-
units.tr: Rabbi Solomon and David Kimchi ... Pet. a Fig., Mercer. These things, however, are nowhere in the sacred letters stated in express terms, though they say that an earthquake is among them, which is described as most well known and remarkable, Amos 1:1 and Zech. 14:5. Nor is this properly the purpose of Holy Scripture, to give an exact account of these matters; this is clear from other famines also, which are recorded not for this reason only, that we may have knowledge of them, but so that other things that were done at that time may be made more illustrious. Hence the famine that occurred in the times of Abraham, they think, was recorded so that the reason for his journey into Egypt might be known, Gen. 12:10. That in the times of Isaac, so that it might be known how he went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, Gen. 26:1. That seven-year famine in the times of Joseph, so that an occasion might be given for narrating all the remarkable histories of Joseph and his brothers, of the servitude of the sons of Israel in Egypt and of their marvellous deliverance from it, Gen. 41. That in the times of Ruth, so that it might be shown on what occasion Abimelech entered the kingdom of Moab, although his silence in the books of Judges, in whose time it is clear it happened, is deep. That in the times of Saul, which the slaughter of the Gibeonites had brought on, and which could be quenched only by the hanging of seven of his sons, so that it might appear by what means the kingdom of David was established. That in the times of the prophet Elijah, 1 Kings 18:2, and of Elisha, 2 Kings 4:32, so that the miracles they performed at that time might be made plain. Nor is it wholly without reason that we know that several other famines occurred in so long a span of years, but have been handed over to oblivion. And since mention of the famines related is made for other reasons, as we have observed with the most learned Bochart, who asserts that this same reason for a famine also has a place in the New Testament, it certainly cannot be surprising that the famine which the Prophet Joel here recounts should be passed over and omitted in other histories. Meanwhile, that such a plague, and the famine made through it, existed in Joel's time can be argued, although the reckoning of the time is nowhere exactly designated. But if it had been necessary and useful in the highest degree for our instruction, the Holy Spirit would surely have said so. Meanwhile we are to be reminded, again and again, that what this history aims at must be entirely carried into effect in us, so that we may also bring it into our own use. As for that question, namely to what time the words spoken by the Prophet are to be referred, it is certainly not determined, neither as to the age in which they were fulfilled nor as to the circumstances of the time in which they were uttered: whether, that is, he foretold the famine before it came, or whether it is a designation of what has already happened, or still is present? This question arises on this ground, that the verbs here are in the past tense, and seem to indicate that the thing had either already truly happened, or was only now beginning and raging as a devastation. For it is quite common for the Prophets to use the past tense in place of the future, by which they wish to signify that those things which God has determined to do are as certain to be as if they were already past. And hence again there is great diversity of interpretation of this passage. Some understand the words as a prediction, which he wished to warn them to avert the impending evils by repentance alone. Others think it is a description of what has already happened, which the Prophet struck so as to stir up their minds, that they might give heed to it with the attention it deserved and return to God; and that the thing, which had then been sent upon them, was thought to have been done for this end, that they might perceive how grievously they had provoked God, and how great diligence was needed to move him, so that whatever adversity came upon the disobedient he might be pleased to make good. Rabbi Solomon, as well as Aben Ezra and Radak, who take the words properly and according to the letter as about noxious creatures (for if they understood them of enemies and hostiles, as we noted a little earlier that others have said, there would be no place for this), say that he foretold that [Hebrew: "they will come, they will come in those days..."] would be future, and that they would come duly in those days, sent by God into their land on account of their sins. Some Christian interpreters also agree with this opinion, saying: he speaks of the satyrs in the prophetic past tense. But there are others to whom it seemed right to speak of things past. Calvin says that these err, and that they err in their sense of the Prophet, who take these words as a denunciation of punishment, since the Prophet's intention is to rebuke the stupidity of the people, by which they understood less what plagues they had been struck with by God, nor did they understand that they were to be overwhelmed by them on account of their sins.

units.la: {f} R. Sal. {g} Kimchi. Mercer. {h} Mercer. Vet. a Fig. Bocharti. stupiditatem populi,qua minus sentiebant,quibus a Deo correpti essent plagis, nec,quod propter peccata sua iisdem obruerentur,intelligebant. Atqui ad eas cum nequaquam essent attenti, l) ideo praeteritas proponit calamitates,docens esse poenitendum peccatorum. Quantumvis igitur hæ sententiæ sibi invicem videantur contrariæ, nihil tamen meo judicio impedit, quo minus ambæ hoc loco jungantur, quippe veri quid utrique inesse arbitror. Nullus enim dubitationi hic locus est, quin, quæ hic describuntur plagæ,per aliquot annos duraverint, quodque nondum ab iis prorsus fuerint immunes,cum diceretur cap.2, 2s. Et repetendam vobis annos illos, quos absumsit locusta,&c. Unde dicta ea esse,cum jam plagæ immitterentur, non difficile conjecteris. Quin & aliquamdiu jam durasse constat diutius vero duraturas pronunciat Propheta, si in peccatis suis essent perseveraturi. Nondum enim finis illis impositus erat,nondum resini, quos adhuc dum absumserat locusta, nondum famés ... Hinc alii nonnulli malunt descriptionem poenæ, k) qualis & tamen parte sententiæ batur, & magis adhuc percipienda erat. Et alius, l) quod huc usque passi & quid præterea passuri sint, commemorat. Porro quæritur de tempore & ordine, quo noxiæ illæ bestiolæ venerint,scilicet successerintne sibi invicem diversis annis eo ordine, quo sunt consignatæ, an omnes eodem anno venerint? D. David Kimchi successisse sibi invicem diversis annis statuit,adeo ut anno primo venerit Gazam vel eruca, & comedesit, secundo anno & absumserit, quod prior reliquerat, & sic deinceps. Nam, s quatuor genera venerunt eodem anno, sed unum post alind diversis annis, prout posset dici. Et repetendam vobis annos illos, quos absumsit locusta, melelontha, bruchusque & eruca. At sunt qui consentiunt sententiæ, nimirum quod eodem anno omnia eorum genera venerint,idque ex eo probatum eunt,quod dicatur reliquum vel reliquum erucæ &c. Quia, quod reliquerat erucæ, eodem anno a sequenti animalculorum specie absumtum fuisse nam, postposset vocari יתר yether, residuum vel reliquum ejus, quod eodem anno reliquerat vermis præcedens, quippe cum potius alterius anni fit productum & incrementum antea prorsus intactum. Unde tam absurdum non fit, quin potius necessarium, ea sic accipere, quod fimul venerint unum post aliud eodem anno, ita ut ab alio fit devoratum, quod ab altero fuerat relictum, eaque ratione ad interitum usque ab illis abfumta, quæcunque terra produxerat. Quod autem ad annos attinet, quorum hic ratio habetur, absit cuique locustarum speciei unum destinemus, cum nihil aliud significari hic manifestum fit, quam quod depastionem illam quotannis sint repetituræ. Nec obscure id indicat diversa nominum istarum creaturarum proferendi ratio, qua quæ priora hujus loci, posteriora sunt in sequenti capite; argumento certe non levi, quod simul omnes fuerint, alteraque in alterius locum successerit. Ac illa quidem tot generum locustarum invasione, uno eodemque anno in terræ nascentia facta, pœnam fuisse redditam tanto mirabiliorem gravioremque, auctor est m) Hieronymus.
units.tr: {f} R. Sal. {g} Kimchi. Mercer. {h} Mercer. Vet. a Fig. Bocharti. The stupidity of the people, by which they understood less the blows with which they had been chastised by God, nor did they perceive that they were being overwhelmed by them on account of their sins. But since they were in no way attentive to them, l) therefore he sets forth past calamities, teaching that sins must be repented of. However much these opinions may seem contrary to each other, nothing in my judgment prevents both from being joined here, since I believe something true is contained in each. For there is no doubt here that the plagues described here lasted for some years, and that they had not yet been wholly removed from them, since it was said in chap. 2, 25. And I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten, etc. From this you may easily conjecture that these things were said when the plagues were already being sent. Indeed it is evident that they had already lasted for some time; the Prophet declares that they would last longer if they persisted in their sins. For no end had yet been set to them, no remnants yet of what the locust had hitherto consumed, no famine yet... Hence some others prefer to take it as a description of the punishment, k) of what sort it was, and yet it was in part a matter of the sentence, and was still to be perceived more fully. And another, l) that they have suffered up to this point, and what they are yet to suffer, recalls it. Further, a question is raised about the time and order in which those harmful little creatures came, namely whether they succeeded one another in different years in the order in which they are listed, or whether all came in the same year. D. David Kimchi holds that they succeeded one another in different years, so that in the first year the caterpillar came to Gaza and ate, and in the second year consumed what the former had left, and so on from then on. For the four kinds came in the same year, but one after another in different years, as might be said. And I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten, the bruchus, the palmerworm and the caterpillar. But there are those who agree with the opinion that all their kinds came in the same year, and they prove this from the fact that it is said "the remnant of the caterpillar" etc. For what the caterpillar had left was consumed in the same year by the following kind of little creature; for it could be called the Hebrew word yether [יתר], its remainder or residue, that is, what the preceding worm had left in the same year, since it is rather the produce and growth of another year, previously quite untouched. Hence it is not so absurd, but rather necessary, to take them thus: that they came together, one after another, in the same year, so that what one had left was devoured by another, and in this way everything the earth had produced was consumed by them down to its destruction. As for the years, which are taken into account here, let us not assign one to each kind of locust, since it is made plain here that nothing else is signified than that they would return to that devastation year by year. The different manner of naming these creatures also indicates this clearly, in that those which are first in this passage are last in the following chapter; certainly a argument of no slight weight that they all came together, and one succeeded the other in its place. And that the punishment was rendered all the more wonderful and grievous by the invasion of so many kinds of locusts, all arising at one time in the same year upon the growing crops, is asserted by m) Jerome.

units.la: Sed tanti forsitan vix cuipiam videantur nonnullæ harum quæstionum, in quibus enucleandis tantum temporis consumatur, quippe nec ad doctrinam, nec ad redargutionem, correctionem aut inftructionem in justitia, nec ad ullum alium, quorsum Scriptura Sacra potissimum spectat, finem utiles? At multum conducunt eadem ad eruendum totius versus perspicuum verborum sensum, qui quam proficuus fit, nemini obscurum esse potest, fi modo singulare illud, quod hic exhibetur, divinæ justitiæ ac severitatis, qua in peccata ab universis perpetrata universaliter animadvertit, exemplum paulo accuratius confiderat. Quo sane nil aliud innui videtur, nisi ut intelligamus, quam promte advolent ad perficiendam Dei fui voluntatem, quotiescunque supplicium exigere constituit, creaturæ omnes ac singulæ, indomitæ licet alias regique nesciæ, adeo ut ne tenuissimi quidem viliffimiique vermiculi imperium ejus detrectare valeant, fatis idonei habiti, qui elatam hominis mentem nimiamque fui confidenden-
units.tr: But perhaps some of these questions, on the clearing up of which so much time is spent, seem to few people worth so much effort, since they are useful neither for doctrine, nor for refutation, correction, or instruction in righteousness, nor for any other end to which Holy Scripture chiefly looks? Yet these matters contribute much to bringing out the plain sense of the words of the whole verse; how profitable this is no one can fail to see, if only one considers a little more carefully that singular example here presented of the divine justice and severity, by which it universally punishes sins committed by all. Indeed nothing else seems to be hinted at here, except that we should understand how promptly all creatures, each and every one, however otherwise untamed and ignorant of rule, hasten to carry out the will of God whenever he resolves to exact punishment, so that not even the tiniest and most worthless little worms can refuse his command, being considered quite fit to lower and utterly cast down the exalted mind of man and his excessive confidence.

units.la: m) Hieronymus in hæc verba: Ut quæ singula raro ebeniunt, omnia simul fuffa memorentur, & ideo mirabilia sint. dentiam deprimere ac penitus dejicere queant. Præterea versus hic fundamentum est totius sermonis Prophetæ, unde eum amplificat, atque ex eo infert, quicquid inculcandum habet. Ut adeo ad propositum ejus rite eruendum dictaque bene intelligenda nil magis convenire putem, quam ut omnia ejus verba & circumstantiæ ea, qua decet, dexteritate & opera exponantur.
units.tr: m) Jerome on these words: So that things which rarely happen singly are all recorded together, and therefore are wonderful. Moreover, this verse is the foundation of the whole discourse of the Prophet, from which he enlarges upon it and infers from it whatever he has to impress. Hence I think nothing is more fitting for rightly drawing out his purpose and understanding his words well than that all his words and circumstances be expounded with the care and skill they deserve.

units.la: ꝟ. Expergiscimini ebriosi, ac flete, ac ejulate omnes vini potores, propter mustum, quod excisum sit ex ore vestro.
units.tr: Verse 5. Awake, you drunkards, and weep and wail, all you wine-drinkers, because of the must, which has been cut off from your mouth.

units.la: Debebat eos equidem e somno peccatorum suorum expergefacere gravissima, quæ hic describitur, pœna, eaque ex parte jamjam illata, vel a Deo intentata, adeoque inevitabiliter ipsis imminens parataque ad occupandum ipsos, nisi plane fuerint stupidi ac mentis impotes, atque adeo impellere, ut obviam irent Deo suo, eumque intuerentur, cujus brachium adversus eos jam erat extensum in percutiendo ægre desiturum. At tanta eos invaserat stupiditas, ut conditionis suæ miseriam minime sentirent, quod vel ex alloquio & clamore magno apparet, quo eos Propheta ad expergiscendum incitat, & quid illis faciendum sit, ut salvarentur, præscribit. Verba ipsa videntur adhortationem ad pœnitentiam continere, quemadmodum eos etiam paulo post ad illam serio adhortatur; eaque explicatio suos adinvenit defensores. At vero si diligentius expendantur, ex iis rationeque addita, cur agere debeant quod jubet, magis apparebit, exprobrationem ea continere, quod non citius id adverterint, quasi diceret: Tempus nunc quidem præterlapsum est satis diuturnum, quo vestra ipsius sponte abstinuisse debebatis; at jam in eo est, ut non amplius res vestri sit arbitrii, velitis an nolitis, quippe nec materia nec occasio indulgendis iis est relicta, necessario vobis abstinendum ebrietate vestra & excessu, cum nil vini, nil grati liquoris mentem dementantis superfit, quo animus obrui atque in altum soporem conjici ulterius queat. Atque ita declaratur, quamquam sub forma exhortationis, quem nimirum effectum habitura sit pœna descripta,
units.tr: Indeed, the most grievous punishment described here ought to have roused them from the sleep of their sins. It was already partly inflicted, or at least threatened by God, and so it hung over them inevitably and was ready to seize them, unless they were utterly dull and senseless. It ought therefore to have driven them to go out to meet their God and look upon him, whose arm was already stretched out against them, and which would not cease to strike until it was done. But such stupidity had overtaken them that they did not feel the misery of their condition at all. This appears from the address and the loud cry by which the prophet urges them to wake up, and from what he prescribes for them to do in order to be saved. The words themselves seem to contain an exhortation to repentance, just as he earnestly exhorts them to it a little later, and this interpretation has found its defenders. But if they are weighed more carefully, together with the reason added for why they must do what he commands, it will appear more clearly that they contain a rebuke, that they had not noticed this sooner. It is as if he were saying: The time that has now passed is quite long enough, during which you ought to have abstained of your own accord. But now the matter is no longer within your power, whether you are willing or not. Neither the material nor the opportunity for indulging is left to you, so you must necessarily abstain from your drunkenness and excess, since no wine and no pleasant liquor that dulls the mind remains, by which the soul could be further buried and cast into deep sleep.
