And so it is declared, though under the form of an exhortation, what effect the punishment described will have, namely that they, who are drowsy, stupid and drunken, and otherwise the last to judge of any matter, will be compelled to recognize and feel it.

units.la: n) Vid. Cyril. Tarnov. o) Mercer. p) Diodat. in Analysi. pta, ut ita & somnolenti,& stupidi & ebriosi, postremi alioquin rerum omnium æstimatores,eam agnoscere ac sentire cogantur.
units.tr: n) See Cyrillus of Tarnov. o) Mercer. p) Diodati in his Analysis. ...so that in this way both the drowsy, the stupid and the drunken, who otherwise are the worst judges of all things, are compelled to acknowledge and feel it.

units.la: Expergiscimini ebriosi.) Huic vitio videntur homines istius ætatis imprimis indulsisse, stupidi&sque ac fatuos, ut ebriosi solent & somnolenti, eo effectos fuisse,tantumque inde contraxisse soporem, ut non solum operum Dei nullam habuerint rationem, sed & sui ipsius salutem prorsus neglexerint. Quare & in specie ad hos orationem suam accommodat, cum pessimo hoc vitio præsentem poenam sibi suisque terris contraxissent. Accommode igitur vox הקיצו hakitzu, expergiscimini, de illis usurpatur, quippe quæ proprie dirigitur adversus hujus vitii stuporem, moremque ac consuetudinem illorum,qui ei sunt dediti,complectitur. Ita ebriosis tanquam contraria stupori hujusmodi malorum, quæ inde originem ducunt, applicatur Prov. 23,35. Alias adhibetur ad exprimendum excitationem hominis ipsius a securitate in aliis peccatis, ut Rom. 13,11. & Ephes. 5,14. Verba reliqua quæ his addita sunt, videlicet ובכו והילילו Ubecu vehelilu, ac flete & ejulate, explicant magnitudinem calamitatis, quæ non tantum ex quieto somno illos sit excitatura,verum etiam eo usque provocatura, ut quam profunde miseriæ hujus sensu tangerentur, sive ex mœrore propter peccata sua, quibus hæc commeriti erant, sive ex impatientia perpessionis, gravioris fortasse (ut supra annotatum) quam videretur, significationem ederent haud obscuram. Hanc vero calamitatis descriptionem excipit demum adhortatio ad veram resipiscentiam cum debita conditionis suæ consideratione conjunctam, verf. 13. Qua in re autem consistat hæc ipsorum calamitas, apparet tum ex personarum hic designatarum descriptione, ebriosorum videlicet & vini potorum; tum ex declaratione ejus quod factum aut futurum erat,his verbis: propter musllum, quod excisum sit ex ore vestro, h. e. quod eo deberent carere, in quo omnes delicias summamque animi voluptatem collocabant, & sine quo nullum amplius vitæ ipsius solatium restare sibi videbantur. Vox quæ a nostratibus vertitur vinum novum, est עסיס asis, quæ juxta radicis significationem videtur innuere liquorem, qui premendo & calcando ex uvis aut aliis fructibus exprimitur. Quemadmodum & ipsa etiam
units.tr: Awake, you drunkards.) It seems that the men of that age especially indulged in this vice. Just as drunkards and sleepers commonly become dull and foolish, so they became such, and they drew from it such a sleep that they not only took no account of the works of God but utterly neglected their own salvation. Therefore he also addresses his speech specifically to these men, since by this most wicked vice they had brought upon themselves and their lands the present punishment. The word הקיצו [hakitzu], awake, is therefore fittingly applied to them, since it is properly directed against the stupor of this vice and takes in the custom and habit of those who are given over to it. Thus it is applied to drunkards as the opposite of the stupor of such evils, which arise from it, Prov. 23:35. Elsewhere it is used to express the rousing of a man from security in other sins, as in Rom. 13:11 and Eph. 5:14. The remaining words added to this, namely ובכו והילילו [ubecu vehelilu], and weep and wail, explain the greatness of the calamity, which will rouse them not merely from quiet sleep but will even provoke them so far that they make clear how deeply they were touched by the sense of this misery, whether from grief over the sins for which they had deserved these things, or from impatience at the suffering, which was perhaps graver than it seemed (as noted above). Finally, this description of the calamity is followed by an exhortation to true repentance, joined with due consideration of their condition, v. 13. In what this calamity of theirs consists appears both from the description of the persons designated here, namely drunkards and wine-drinkers, and from the statement of what had happened or was about to happen, in these words: on account of the must, which has been cut off from your mouth, that is, because they were to be deprived of that in which they placed all their pleasures and their greatest enjoyment of mind, and without which no further comfort of life seemed left to them. The word which our people render new wine is עסיס [asis], which, according to the meaning of its root, seems to indicate the liquor which is squeezed out of grapes or other fruits by pressing and treading. Just as the same word is also used for tread in Mal. 4:3, ועסותים רשעים [veassotem reshaim], and you shall tread down the wicked.

units.la: pro calcare usurpatur Mal. 4, 3. ועסותים רשעים veaffotem reshaim, & conculcabitis improbos. Atque hoc nomine עסיס asis ideo denotatur vinum, لكونه يداس حين العصر quia calcatur, quando conficitur. Kimchi transfert id nomen ad כל משקה שיצא ורירכות quemvis potum vel liquorem, qui producitur tundendo (aut premendo) & calcando. Exemplum hujus, ut opinor, extat Cant. 8, 2. מעסים רמני Measis rimoni, quod interlinearis interpretatur de vino dulci mali granati mei, noftrates vero de succo mali granati mei; sed minus valebit hoc exemplum, fi interpretationem R. Tanchum sequamur, qui illud q) exponit de vino coloris rubri instar mali granati, ita ut ex ejus sententia vinum fit intelligendum, quod ejusdem coloris est cum malo granato, non autem vinum quod ex malis granatis exprimitur. An vero de aliis quoque liquoribus fit accipiendum, instituti nostri ratio non permittit ut inquiramus. Illud vero non obscure liquet, imprimis hic respici vinum, vel vini productum, nec male noftratibus redditum novum vinum, aliis muflum, cum plerumque id significet; quamvis ambigue magis reddere velint r) propter succum expressum, vel s) propter laborem. Chaldæus habet חמר מרוח purum vinum; Rab. Sal. המיב יין bonum vinum. Drufius proprie significare ait vinum dulce & recens expressum. LXX. reddunt עיס al asis, quia novum vinum est t) εἰς μέθην ad ebrietatem, quos impressa etiam sequitur Arabica; Vulgatus latinus in dulcedine. Equidem non arbitror ullum horum alio fignificatu vocem Asis accepisse, ac ab aliis factum, ut antea vidimus, per eam nimirum non significari proprie ebrietatem, sed vinum robustum ad dementandum atque inebriandum aptum; non dulcedinem in abstracto, sed dulce atque gratum vinum. Quod vero nonnulli ista verba aliter interpretati sunt, ex eo factum esse constat, quod diversa ratione ea distinxerint atque construxerint, præpositionemque עי ab, quæ præponitur voci asis, notione diversa sumserint non pro de, ob vel propter,
units.tr: used for to tread, in Mal. 4, 3. וַעֲסוֹתֶם רְשָׁעִים veaffotem reshaim, "and you shall tread down the wicked." For this reason the word עסיס asis denotes wine, because it is trodden when it is made, as the Arabic has it: lakawnihi yudas hina al-'asr. Kimchi applies the name to any drink or liquid that is produced by pounding (or pressing) and treading. An example of this, I think, is Cant. 8, 2. מְעַסִּים רִמּוֹנִי Measis rimoni, which the interlinear gloss renders of the sweet wine of my pomegranate, but our people of the juice of my pomegranate. This example carries less weight, however, if we follow the interpretation of R. Tanchum, who explains it as wine of a red colour like a pomegranate, so that on his view the wine meant is that which has the same colour as the pomegranate, not wine pressed out of pomegranates. Whether it should also be taken of other liquids, the plan of our work does not allow us to inquire. It is clear, however, that the wine itself, or the product of wine, is chiefly meant here, and our people have rendered it fairly as new wine, others as must, since it generally signifies that; though some prefer to render it more ambiguously, r) on account of the juice pressed out, or s) on account of the labour. The Chaldee has חֲמַר מְרוֹחַ khamar merokh, pure wine; Rab. Sal. has הַמֵּיטִיב יַיִן hameitiv yayin, good wine. Drusius says it properly means sweet wine freshly pressed. The Seventy render עַל עָסִיס al asis t) εἰς μέθην, to drunkenness, because new wine is such, and the printed Arabic follows them; the Latin Vulgate has in sweetness. For my part I do not think any of these has taken the word asis in another sense than that given by others, as we saw earlier: it does not properly mean drunkenness, but strong wine fit for making men senseless and drunk; not sweetness in the abstract, but sweet and pleasant wine. That some have interpreted these words otherwise is due to their dividing and construing them differently, and taking the preposition ab prefixed to asis in a different sense, not as of, on account of or because of,

units.la: q) R. Tanchum in Lexico (uo. r) Tigur. s) Caftal. t) Vetus latina: in ebrietate. propter, sed pro eis ad vel in,super vel cum. Noftrates cum aliis tam recentioribus, quam antiquis, Chaldaeo nimirum & Syro, verba al afis (quae Chaldaeus reddit עַל חִבְר מָרִיר ob vel propter mcrum (vel novum) vinum, Syrus ܥܠ ܚܡܪܐ ob vinum) eo referentes verba, ut idem comma efficiant cum praecedentibus, flete & ejulate, quasi causam hujus fletus & ejulatus declarantia; alteram vocis significationem eligere maluerunt, qua innuatur videlicet, quinam fleturi sint ac ejulaturi, ebriosi nimirum & vini potores, quorum ratio bibendi vinum robustum describitur, nempe ad ebrietatem usque, ut sumunt LXX. vel cum dulcedine, ut vulgatus accipit. Ac verbis hunc in modum conjunctis & retentis, prout ad literam sonant flete vini potatores, cum vel super Afis, vino robusto, vel novo grato vino, palam fiet, quam sententiam quisque foveat. Tum vero in conclusione hujus versiculi, quod excisum sit ex ore vestro, necesse est ut aut eadem vox, aut huic aequivalens alia subintelligatur. Atque hac ratione Vulgatus accepisse videtur. At LXX. u) juxta codices usitatos supplent ἰυφεσυ̇ν καὶ χαρᾶ, quia gaudium & hilaritas ab ore illorum erant detracta. Planior nihilo secius apparet prior altera distinguendi ratio atque constructio verborum, quam non tantum recentiores interpretes secuti sunt, verum & antiquiores, Chaldaeus & Syrus; Quin idem suggerit manuscriptum Arabicum, cujus verba cum praelo nunquam sint publicata, digna sunt ut subjiciantur, استبيشتوا يا سكاري وابكوا وولولوا يا كل شاربي الخمر على العصير ان انقطع من فيكم Quae transferri aliter opus non habent, quam factum est Anglis ex Hebraeo, praeterquam quod ultima habeant verba: videntes quod excisum sit ex ore vestro. Atque hinc Afis vel vinum novum non erat, quod bibebant cum voluptate & ultra satietatem, sed Afis erat subjectum, cujus causa flebant & ejulabant, quod non haberent quod biberent, quia excisum erat ex ore illorum, protinusque abstractum, adeo ut non haberent quod summis etiam labiis libarent vel attingerent, locustis omnes prorsus devastantibus w) uvas, ex quibus
units.tr: q) R. Tanchum in the Lexicon, under the word. r) Tigurine. s) Castalio. t) Old Latin: in drunkenness. but as to, unto, or in, upon, or with. Our people, together with others both recent and ancient, namely the Chaldee and the Syriac, refer the words al asis (which the Chaldee renders עַל חֲמַר מְרִירָא al khamar merira, on account of bitter wine or new wine, and the Syriac 'al khamra, on account of the wine) to the preceding words, so that they form one clause with them, wail and howl, as if they stated the cause of this weeping and howling. The others preferred to take the other meaning of the word, namely that it indicates who shall weep and howl, that is drunkards and wine-drinkers, whose manner of drinking is described as strong wine, even to drunkenness, as the Seventy take it, or with sweetness, as the Vulgate understands it. If the words are joined and kept in this way, reading literally, wail, you wine-drinkers, over the asis, strong wine, or new pleasant wine, it will be plain which view each man favours. Then at the end of this verse, that it is cut off from your mouth, either the same word or some equivalent must be understood. In this way the Vulgate seems to have understood it. But the Seventy, following the usual copies, supply εὐφροσύνην καὶ χαράν, joy and gladness, because joy and merriment were taken from their mouths. Nonetheless the first way of dividing and construing the words appears no less plain, and it is followed not only by recent interpreters but also by the older ones, the Chaldee and the Syriac. Indeed the Arabic manuscript suggests the same, whose words, since they have never been published in print, are worth setting out: istabshiruu ya sakari wa-ibkuu wa-wawiluu ya kull shaaribi l-khamr 'ala l-'asir in inqata' min fikum. These need no other rendering than the English has from the Hebrew, except that they end with the words seeing that it is cut off from your mouth. Hence asis was not the new wine which they drank with pleasure and beyond satiety; asis was the subject for which they wept and wailed, because they had nothing to drink, since it was cut off from their mouths, and at once removed, so that they had nothing even to sip or touch with the very tips of their lips, the locusts laying waste all the w) grapes, from which

units.la: u) Nam deest in eo quem Hieronymus sequitur, & in quibusdam aliis. Vid. Conject. Drusii, §§). Kimchi. bus illud exurgeret. Eandem construendi rationem & horum nonnulli secuti sunt, qui per ea instrumenta, quibus illorum vinum excidendum erat, non proprie intelligunt locustas & hujusmodi vermiculos, sed inimicos sub hoc nomine latitantes. Ita hunc versum satis perspicue etiam explicat Abarbenel: Expergiscimini ebriosi & flete &c. hoc est: Vos omnes, qui vanitatibus mundi atque deliciis abdominis semper estis profunde immersi, nullamque rationem operum divinorum habetis, expergiscimini ab ebrietate vestra, ac flete & ejulate propter destructionem regionis vestræ. Vinum enim & mustum, quæ fructuum terræ sunt delicatissima, quibusque vescebamini & quæ bibebatis, sunt excisa ex ore vestro pro appulsibus inimicorum ad omnia late diripienda.
units.tr: u) For it is lacking in the text that Jerome follows, and in some others. See Drusius's Conjectures, §§. Kimchi ... would arise from it. Some of these also followed the same way of construing, and by those instruments with which their wine was to be cut off they understand not properly locusts and such little worms, but enemies hiding under this name. Abarbanel also explains this verse quite clearly: Awake, you drunkards, and weep, etc. that is: You all, who are always deeply immersed in the vanities of the world and the pleasures of the belly, and have no regard for the works of God, awake from your drunkenness, and weep and wail for the destruction of your land. For wine and must, which are the most delicate products of the earth, which you eat and drink, have been cut off from your mouth by the approach of enemies who will plunder everything far and wide.

units.la: 6. Gens enim ascendit super terram meam, robusta & innumera, cujus dentes dentes sunt leonis, cui mo- lares immanis leonis sunt.
units.tr: 6. For a nation has come up against my land, strong and innumerable, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and whose molars are those of a fierce lion.

units.la: In hoc & sequenti versiculo describuntur porro executores plagarum divinarum, quæ recensentur v. 4. atque pressius paulo persequitur modum & media, quibus efficiebatur, vel efficiendum erat malum, cujus auctores esse vel fore dicuntur. Hæc vero divinæ vindictæ instrumenta non multo ante dicta, eruca, locusta, melolontha & bruchus vocantur hic habita conditionis suæ ratione Gens robusta & innumera, cujus dentes similes sunt dentibus Leonis &c. Quæ denominatio quibusdam argumento est, quod non proprie noxii illi vermiculi, qui hujusmodi nominibus plerumque gaudent, sint intelligendi, sed tales homines, qui non secus atque in agris contingit locustis, terram Judaicam jussu Dei essent late direpturi. Ita enim Abarbenel
units.tr: In this and the following verse, the executors of the divine plagues are further described, those listed in v. 4, and he follows more closely the manner and the means by which the evil was brought about, or was to be brought about, of which they are said to be the authors or will be. These instruments of divine vengeance, not long before named eruca, locusta, melolontha & bruchus, are here called, with regard to their condition, a strong and innumerable nation, whose teeth are like the teeth of a lion, etc. This designation is an argument for some that those harmful little worms, which mostly enjoy such names, are not to be understood properly, but rather men who, just as happens with locusts in the fields, were by God's command to lay waste the Jewish land far and wide. For so Abarbanel says,

units.la: להשחיתה h.e. Propheta hoc non revera dicit de locustis; quomodo enim eas vocaret gentem & multitudinem gentium? Sed dicit hoc de illis hostibus, qui venicbant terram depopulatum. Verum nullius momenti hanc argumentandi esse rationem, ex impositione hujus nomi-nis nis defumtam, ex eo liquet, quod, quamvis istud nomen, (fortasse etiam proprie & usitate) hominum congregationi ac multitudini tribuatur, commodum nihilominus fatis fit, ut aliis etiam imponatur creaturis non minus atque עם am populus, quod constat ex Prov. 30, 25. &c. nec non ex sequenti capite v. 2. Quare sine ratione forsitan non est, quod observavit Kimchi גוי קבוץ מן החי יקראֵ congregationem quamvis vel multitudinem creaturarum vivarum appellari גוי Goi, Gentem. Est etiam illud in omni fermelingua usitatum valde, ut gentis vel populi denominatio & aliis praeter homines imponatur creaturis; gentis inprimis illis applicari, quae hic vocantur locustae, exempla probant diversorum Auctorum a doctissimo Bocharto allata, eorumque quod lingua Arabica Ommaton gens, sit usitatum pro collectione creaturarum vivarum, & praecipue pro locustis, prout ex dicto, quod Mahumedi adscribitur, patet, quo Deus creasse dicitur mille gentes, quarum sexcentae sunt in mari, quadringentae in terra & quod أول prima, quae interitura est ex his gentibus, (sic enim vertenda esse haec verba arbitror, non prima pestis, ut putat Bochartus) sint locustae, quibus interemtis reliquae suo ordine secuturae sint. Unde concinne admodum a Rab. Tanchum (quamvis alia ratione ipsi) de hac voce dictum, quod sit استعارة metaphorica expressio locustarum respectu habito ad earum multitudinem & praedam ingentem cui inhiant. Nec ulla praeterea inest vis huic ratiocinio: Vocantur hic locustae gentes, ergo de locustis non sunt accipienda quae traduntur versu praecedenti, quod Abarbenel vult. Nec approbanda x) aliorum placita, quod alii hic innuantur, quibus appellationis ratio magis proprie conveniat, nimirum inimici quantumvis in praecedentibus de locustis sermo fuerit. Nec simpliciter eas appellari nationem apparet, sed additione hujusmodi epithetorum, quae eam ut eminentem prae cateris, ita terribilem etiam reddunt aliis gentibus, eo quod gens sit robusta & innumera, cujus dentes similes sunt dentibus leonis. Robusta. Licet hae creaturae natura sunt imbelles admodum & despicatissimae,
units.tr: to destroy it [להשחיתה], that is: The prophet does not really say this of locusts; for how would he call them a nation and a multitude of nations? But he says this of those enemies who came to lay waste the land. But this line of argument, drawn from the application of this name, is of no weight at all. This is clear from the fact that, although this name (perhaps also properly and commonly) is given to a gathering and multitude of men, it may nonetheless well be applied to other creatures no less than the Hebrew am [עם], people, as is evident from Prov. 30, 25, etc. and also from the following chapter, v. 2. Hence perhaps not without reason Kimchi observed that a gathering or multitude of living creatures is called goi [גוי קבוץ מן החי יקרא גוי], nation. It is also very common in almost every language that the name of gens or people is applied to creatures other than men; that gentis especially applies to those here called locusts is proved by examples from various authors brought forward by the most learned Bochart, and by the fact that the Arabic word Ommaton, nation, is in use for a collection of living creatures, and especially for locusts, as is clear from a saying ascribed to Muhammad, in which God is said to have created a thousand nations, six hundred of them in the sea and four hundred on land; and that the first (awwal) of these nations, which is to perish, (for I think these words should be rendered thus, and not as "the first plague", as Bochart thinks) are locusts, and when these have been destroyed the rest will follow in their order. Whence Rabbi Tanchum has said very neatly of this word (although for another reason, of his own) that it is isti'ara, a metaphorical expression for locusts, with regard to their multitude and the huge prey they gape after. Nor is there any force in this reasoning: "Locusts are here called nations, therefore what is handed down in the preceding verse is not to be taken of locusts," which Abarbanel maintains. Nor is the view of others to be approved, that others are hinted at here, to whom the name would more properly apply, namely enemies, although the discussion in what precedes has been of locusts. Nor does it appear that they are called simply a nation, but by the addition of such epithets, which make them stand out above the rest and also make them terrible to other nations, namely that the nation is strong and innumerable, whose teeth are like the teeth of a lion. Strong. Although these creatures are by nature quite unwarlike and most contemptible,

units.la: x) Calvin. pretantur dentes maxillares, hoc observandum est, quod alias quoque inveniatur transpositis literis מלתעות Maltaoth, ut Psal. 58,6. vocula לביא Labi nostratibus redditur immanis leonis, at aliter apud alios. Paraphrastes Chaldaicus habet כבר־אריה ut catuli leonis, sic & Græca, Vulgata, Syriaca atque impressa Arabica. Quippe omnes habent catulum leonis. Cujus translationis proprietatem b) quidam explodere conantur exemplo validissimo, quod extat Job. 4,11. ubi legitur כני לביא bene Labi, quod nostrates reddunt audacis leonis catulorum, ubi aperte distinguuntur & qui appellatur Labi, & qui nominantur catuli, tanquam senior & juniores. c) Alii vertunt, petuli leonis, qui tamen objectionibus obrui possunt, quia vetus leo d) non habet dentes validos, cum tamen ad validitatem quam maxime hic videatur alludi. Alii reddunt e) Lexnæ, (quod & Vulgato aliis in locis frequens) quam translationem duo recentioris ævi viri illustrissimi, Hugo Grotius & f) Bochartus, aliis præferre videntur, eamque probare nituntur ex usu vocis ﻟﺒﻮﺍﺕ Labwat, quæ non aliter ac ﻟﺒﺄ Labah & ﻟﺒﻴﺔ Labiyah, & similia lingua Arabica, de fœmina dicuntur, non de mare. Prorisus vero ignoro, num validum sit satis ad probandum, quod vox לביא labi linguæ hebraicæ ac generis masculini, ea de causa fœminino applicari possit, quia ea nomina lingua Arabica fœminini generis sunt, etsi nullum ejus radicis derivatum masculino genere usitatum sit. Id tamen affirmare habeo, quod masculinum æq; ac fœmininum hac in lingua possit discerni, quantumvis usu adeo frequens non sit. Hoc enim ex manuscriptis Arabicæ translationis apparet, qui reddunt ואניאב אללבי לה & literis Arabicis لا واليان ﻟﻠﺒﻮ Waanyah allabu labo, quod significat longos dentes Labii, & cur non debemus vertere leonis, cum sit masculini generis sine ulla terminationis nota, qua fœmininum a masculino distinguitur? At sensum nullo modo infringere potis est generis ambiguitas, quippe cum lœna non minus sit ferox atq; leo, neque adeo ad sexum ea alludatur expressione, quam ad fortitudinem. Celeberrimus Grammaticus Hebræus Abu Walid ait, g) לבו labuo plerumque
units.tr: x) Calvin [takes them as the grinding teeth]. It is to be noted that elsewhere too, with the letters transposed, one finds מלתעות Maltaoth, as in Ps. 58:6. The little word לביא Labi is rendered by our people a fierce lion, but otherwise by others. The Chaldee paraphrast has כבר־אריה [kevar-aryeh] as the whelp of a lion, and so also the Greek, the Vulgate, the Syriac and the printed Arabic. Indeed all have the whelp of a lion. Some try to overthrow the propriety of this rendering by a very strong example, found in Job 4:11, where we read bene Labi [כני לביא], which our people render of the bold lion's whelps, where both the one called Labi and those named whelps are clearly distinguished, as senior and juniors. Others render it young lion, which, however, can be refuted by objections, because the old lion does not have strong teeth, although strength seems to be alluded to here above all. Others render it lioness, which is also frequent in the Vulgate elsewhere. Two very illustrious men of more recent times, Hugo Grotius and Bochart, seem to prefer this translation to the others, and they strive to prove it from the usage of the word Labwat, which, like Labah and Labiyah and similar words in Arabic, is said of a female, not a male. Truly I do not know whether it is strong enough to prove that the Hebrew word לביא labi, which is of masculine gender, can for this reason be applied to the feminine, because those nouns in Arabic are of feminine gender, even though no derivative of that root is used in the masculine. I can, however, affirm this, that the masculine as well as the feminine can be distinguished in this language, although the usage is not so frequent. For this appears from the manuscripts of the Arabic translation, which render it Waanyah allabu labo, which means the long teeth of the Labi. And why should we not render it lion, since it is of masculine gender without any mark of termination by which the feminine is distinguished from the masculine? But the ambiguity of gender can in no way impair the sense, since the lioness is no less fierce than the lion, nor does the expression allude to sex so much as to strength. The most celebrated Hebrew grammarian Abu Walid says that לבו labuo is mostly

units.la: b) Livel. Drus. c) Castal. & Trem. citati a Drufio. d) Drufius. e) Tigur. f) De animal. part. 1. p. 719. g) Ultima litera ubique fere est extrita, aliam tamen non posse esse ex spatio colligo; eodem etiam redit, si N Substituamus, quamvis vix eam admittit spatii angustia.
units.tr: b) Livel. Drus. c) Castal. and Trem., cited by Drusius. d) Drusius. e) Tigur. f) De animal. part. 1, p. 719. g) The last letter is almost everywhere worn away; but I gather from the space that it cannot be any other; it also comes to the same if we substitute N, although the narrowness of the space scarcely admits it.

units.la: que lingua Arabica etiam dici leonem, neque tamen id se legisse unquam in ullo libro authentico, cujus autoritate posset niti. Utcunque sit, sive in Arabica lingua ea vox tantum sit usitata foeminino genere pro leaena, sive masculino etiam genere pro Leone, hoc tamen validum argumentum non est, eam masculino genere sermone hebraico esse positam ad significandum tantum sexum foemininum. Meo quidem ipsius judicio majori nititur ratione, quod dicit Kimchi, masculinum Lab eo loco denotare leonem, cum formam foemininam eadem vox producat, quae occurrit Ezech. 19,2. לביא, quae quamvis iisdem scripta sit literis atque Lab, aliis tamen gaudet vocalibus, videlicet Lebiya. Attamen magis in usu est לביאה Lebiah secundum Aben Walid & Kimchi. Quare non video, cur a doctissimo Bocharto connexus tradictum sit, at suspicor initio sic fuisse lectam eaque forma foemininum constituisse, unde in omnibus aliis locis, ubi legitur Lab, magis videtur congruere masculino, ut a praedictis Hebraeis grammaticis aliisque in genere annotatum est. Quid? quod hanc quoque sententiam stabiliat plurale masculinum לבאים Lebaim ab una, & foemininum לבאות Lebaoth ab altera deductum. Sed, ut jam dixi mus, non hic ulla ratio habetur sexus, sed fortitudinis tantum, quae antecellit aliis generosa bestia. Atque ideo maxime inter commentatores convenit, eam vocem tantummodo respicere Leonem justae magnitudinis ac fortitudinis, non catulum, qui haec nondum est assecutus, neque vetulum, qui ea jam perdidit, unde commode satis ea videtur expressa & a nostratibus & aliis per Leonem vel magnum, quantumvis aliis in locis simpliciter eam reddant per leonem, ut Hos. 13,8. a Kimchi observatum est, quod sit majoris efficaciae, quam vox Arieh paulo ante posita, quod generalius leonis nomen est, necessario refert, quippe quod ideo adhibeatur, evidentior evadit comparatio, & dentium harum rami inter creaturarum, cum dentibus tam immanium bestiarum, & inferendi rerum perniciem, utpote quarum dentes non exlex tantum ut dentes communis leonis, sed ut illius, qui ad eam pervenit tatem atque fortitudinem, ut possit vocari Libi. Si per hæc infecta locusta &c. antea nominatæ literaliter, ut interpretati sumus, sint intelligendæ, dentes etiam ac molares de talibus, quos habent, proprie sumendos esse ipsa res loquitur; E contrario si per hæc verba illi Judæorum inimici, quos Abarbinel & alii volunt, intelligendi sint, oportet certe quid aliud in iis per dentes & molares significari, quod ei maxime accedat in quo vis atque potentia nocendi præcipue sit est. k) Quare Arias Montanus his putat denotari illorum arma, alia quidem propter aciem, ut enses, hastæ & sagittæ; alia propter ingentem efficaciam, ut afflictes pro munimentis &c. Hieronymus in eo acquiescere videtur, ut generaliter capiantur ad de notandum ferocitatem & crudelitatem; & Abarbinel, ut sit expressio significans illorum vim & fortitudinem. Grotius: Rapiditas hic significatur.
units.tr: also said of a lion in Arabic, yet he says he has never read this in any authoritative book on which it could rest. However that may be, whether in Arabic this word is used only in the feminine for lioness, or also in the masculine for lion, this is nonetheless not a strong argument that it was placed in the masculine gender in Hebrew to signify only the female sex. In my own judgment it rests on a stronger reason, that Kimchi says the masculine Lab there denotes a lion, since the same word produces a feminine form, which occurs in Ezek. 19:2, לביא, which, although it is written with the same letters as Lab, has nonetheless other vowels, namely Lebiya. Yet according to Abu Walid and Kimchi the form לביאה [Lebiah] is more in use. Wherefore I do not see why the connection was handed down by the most learned Bochart; but I suspect that it was first read thus, and the feminine form was constituted from it, whence in all other places where Lab is read it seems rather to agree with the masculine, as noted by the aforementioned Hebrew grammarians and others in this regard. What more? The masculine plural לבאים [Lebaim], derived from one form, and the feminine plural לבאות [Lebaoth], derived from the other, also strengthen this view. But, as I have said, no account is taken here of sex, but only of strength, which surpasses other noble beasts. And so the commentators are most agreed that this word refers only to a lion of proper size and strength, not to a whelp, which has not yet attained this, nor to an old one, which has now lost it; whence it seems to be expressed well enough by ours and others as lion or great, although elsewhere they simply render it lion, as in Hos. 13:8, which Kimchi has observed. It has greater force, which is necessarily conveyed by the more general name of lion, Arieh, placed just before; for it is used for this reason, and the comparison becomes more evident, and the mention of these teeth among creatures, with the teeth of such huge beasts, and of inflicting ruin, since their teeth are not merely like those of the common lion, but like those of one who has reached that age and strength that he can be called Libi. If by these, the locusts etc. named before, are to be understood literally, as we have interpreted, the thing itself makes clear that the teeth and molars are to be taken properly, as those which they have. On the contrary, if by these words are to be understood those enemies of the Jews whom Abarbanel and others mean, then certainly something else must be signified by teeth and molars, which should most closely correspond to that in which the power and force of harming especially lies. k) Wherefore Arias Montanus thinks that their weapons are denoted by these, some indeed on account of their edge, such as swords, spears and arrows; others on account of their great efficacy, such as the siege-engines against fortifications, etc. Jerome seems to rest content with this, that they are taken generally to denote ferocity and cruelty; and Abarbanel, that it is an expression signifying their force and strength. Grotius: Speed is signified here.

units.la: Tradita vero executorum vindictæ divinæ exacta quoad qualitatem & conditionem, vim atque potentiam nocendi descriptione, modum exequendi Propheta etiam notare haud negligit, quando hisce verbis infit: ascendit super terram meam, posuit meam vineam in desertum &c. Tanto scilicet furore aggressa est ea gens regionem, ut nec repellere nec resistere, imo ne prohibere quidem valuerint, quin faciat quæ fecisse dicitur. Super regionem meam, inquit, (quisquis tandem hic intelligatur loqui) degebat, & posuit vineam meam in desertum & ficum meam decorticavit. Hic quæstio oritur ex pronomine affixo primæ personæ, quo non simpliciter Propheta dicit, regio, vinea, &c. sed ac si ejus esset potestas, mea regio. Quis nimirum hæc omnia sibi vindicet, atque ita horum verborum auctor concipi queat? Kimchi constructionis ambiguitatem advertens ait: כל הכנויים הם דברי יושב הארץ או הנבאים omnia hæc prenomina ostendunt verba esse aut habitatoris terræ, aut Prophetæ. l) Alii membrum addunt, quod verba possint esse vel verba Dei vel Prophetæ, vel ipsius etiam populi. Ita Drusius: Deus loquitur, aut Propheta, aut quilibet e populo dicet. Quin divino mandato prophetaverit Propheta, nemo unquam dubius hæsit; at in eo versatur
units.tr: Having set out the nature and character of the agents of divine vengeance, and their power and capacity to harm, the Prophet also takes care to note the manner of their advance, when he begins with these words: He has come up upon my land, he has laid my vine waste, etc. Clearly that nation attacked the region with such fury that the inhabitants could neither repel nor resist them, nor even prevent them from doing what they are said to have done. "Over my land," he says, (whoever is supposed to be speaking here) "he lived, and laid my vine in waste and stripped my fig tree bare." Here a question arises from the first-person possessive pronoun, by which the Prophet does not simply say "land," "vine," etc., but as though they belonged to him: my land. Who, then, could claim all these things for himself, and so who could be imagined as the speaker of these words? Kimchi, noticing the ambiguity of the construction, says: כל הכנויים הם דברי יושב הארץ או הנבאים [kol hakinuyim hem devarei yoshev ha'aretz o hanevi'im], "all these pronouns show the words to be either those of the inhabitant of the land or of the prophets." l) Others add a further possibility, that the words could be the words of God, or of the Prophet, or even of the people themselves. So Drusius: God speaks, or the Prophet, or some one of the people will say. That the Prophet spoke by divine command no one has ever doubted; but the question lies elsewhere,

units.la: k) Et Tirinus. l) Pet, a Fig. fatur quæstio, num Dei an ipsius populi hic gerat vicem, cum quisque illorum posset dicere, mea regio, reliquaque omnia tanquam sua sibi vindicare. Si DEum hic introducit loquentem, ejusque verba recenset, manifestum est, complecti ea declarationem eorum, quæ vel immiserat, vel immittere regioni constituerat, quam cum iis omnibus, quæ continebat, peculiari jure tanquam suam ac sua sibi asserit; unde curæ sibi esse eam etiam peculiariter, quamvis non mediocriter potuisset colligi ex eo quod Moses dicit: Jugiter oculi Jehovæ Dei tui intenti sunt in eam, a principio anni usque ad finem ejus, Deut. 11, 12. eam tamen propter impietatem incolarum tradidisse in destructionem atque desertum abunde patet. Id si rite atque debita ratione ad mentem revocassent, certo scio, nisi m) somno fuissent alto sepulti, eoque sensibus prorsus privati, non potuissent non expergisci ac conditionis suæ miserimæ sensu tangi, quam sibi ipsis provocaverant irritando atque offendendo tamdiu Numen benignum, ut quam hactenus eorum summam gesserat curam, plane abjicere coactus fuerit; eaque ratione impelli, ut, quo repentina resipiscentia cum eo in gratiam redirent, omnem locarent operam, quorsum quidem præcipue hanc prophetiæ partem spectare perspicuum habeo.
units.tr: k) And Tirinus. l) Pet. a Fig. whether here he takes the place of God or of the people themselves, since each of them could say my land and claim for himself all the rest as his own. If he introduces God as speaking and recounts his words, it is plain that they embrace a declaration of what he had either sent upon the land or had determined to send upon it, which God asserts as his own, with peculiar right, together with all that it contained; whence it can be gathered that the land was an object of his special care, as Moses says, though it could be inferred no less clearly: The eyes of Jehovah your God are continually upon it, from the beginning of the year even to its end, Deut. 11:12. Yet that he handed it over to destruction and desolation because of the impiety of its inhabitants is abundantly clear. If they had called this rightly and duly to mind, I am certain that, unless m) they had been buried in deep sleep and so utterly deprived of their senses, they could not have failed to wake and be moved by a sense of their most wretched condition, which they had brought upon themselves by provoking and offending the gracious Deity for so long, so that he was compelled to abandon altogether the great care he had hitherto shown them; and by that consideration they would be driven to devote every effort to returning into favour with him through a sudden repentance. This, I clearly hold, is what this part of the prophecy chiefly looks to.

units.la: Si ipsius Prophetæ verba hic sunt, pronunciasse ea, quæ a DEO ipsi erant injuncta ut populo indicaret, dicendus est, quo mentem ac animum adhiberent ad eas calamitates, quarum ipsi fuerant Auctores, quasque tantopere lugebant. Si populi nomine, vel alicujus ex populo proferuntur, lamentationem indidisse ejus ori putandus est, qua possent vel deberent calamitates suas deplorare, ac quæ horrenda ipsis accidebant, quorum non nisi lacrymis procidentibus possent meminisse, & enumerando exponere. n) Ita Mercerus, qui lamentationis formulam a verbis, expergisceimini ebrufi &c. ordiri statuit. At eodem res redit, ad quamcunque demum harum personarum pronomen retuleris. Nimirum Regio significat regionem Judæorum arboresque arbores in ea virentes. Regio illa erat Jehovæ Hos. 9, 3. simulque Prophetæ & populi, quia in ea erant nati ejusque adhuc dum
units.tr: If these are the Prophet's own words, he must be taken to have uttered what God had enjoined upon him to tell the people, so that they might attend and consider the calamities of which they had themselves been the authors, and which they so greatly lamented. If they are uttered in the name of the people, or of some one of the people, we must suppose that a lament has been put into their mouths, by which they could and should bewail their calamities, and recall and set forth in enumeration the dreadful things that were befalling them, and of which they could speak only with tears streaming down. n) So Mercerus, who holds that the form of lamentation begins with the words Awake, drunkards, etc. But the matter comes to the same thing, whichever of these persons you refer the pronoun to. For the land signifies the land of the Jews and the trees that flourish in it. That land was Jehovah's, Hos. 9:3, and at the same time both the Prophet's and the people's, because they were born in it and were still living in it,

units.la: m) Vide Calvin. n) Sic Tarnov. ait, hæc verba ori cujusque Judæorum indita, quibus quæstus suos ederent tot malis obruti. dum incolæ. Hinc pari horum quisque gaudebat jure eam vocandi suam, cæteraque omnia, in ea virentia sibi tribuendi tanquam sua.
units.tr: m) See Calvin. n) Thus Tarnov. says these words were placed in the mouth of each Jew, by which they might pour out their complaints, overwhelmed by so many evils. while they dwelt there. Hence each of them had an equal right to call it his own, and to claim for himself all the things flourishing in it as his own.

units.la: Quid vero huic regioni, rebusque in ea existentibus factum fit vel faciendum esset ab ea natione, quæ descendisse hic dicitur, id omne sequentibus verbis declaratur.
units.tr: What was done, or was to be done, by that nation which is said here to have come down upon this land and the things existing in it, all this is declared in the following words.

units.la: 7. Posuit vitem meam desertam, & decorticavit fi- cum meam, nudans spoliavit eam & projecit, ra- mí ejus albi facti sunt.
units.tr: 7. He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree; he has made it bare and cast it away; its branches are made white.

units.la: Posuit vitem meam desertam &c.) vel depopulata est vitem meam; usque adeo eam exedendo, arrodendo, vel aliis mediis perdidit, ut amplius non fit proficua, nec alius porro usus, quam ut solum tegat. Vulgatus habet: Posuit vineam meam in desertum, quem Duacenses sequuti sunt. Quod tamen Drusius minus recte factum arguit, quum Gephen magis proprie significet vitem, quam Cerem, vineam; at non constat Vulgatum ejus fuisse sententiæ, cum utrumque significet hæc vox & vineam & vitem. Et cum vinea non nisi plurium vitium sit congregatio, rei nulla est differentia. Qui etiam vitem hic proprie spectari censent, numero plurali vocem vertunt, o) vites meas, quasi p) collective nomen capiendum sit, non pro una particulari ac simplici vite, sed pro pluribus vel omnibus hujus generis, quas noxia illa vermiculorum gens depopulata erat. Pari ratione & sequentem vocem non denotare q) contendunt ficum, sed ficus, quibus, ut manifestum esset, quid detrimenti inferrent vel illaturi essent vermiculi, inquit, & ficum meam decorticavit, vel ut in margine est vocum hebraicarum exactior expressio, Uteenati Likrsapha, posuit ficum meam pro excoriatione. Non abludit hinc Vulgata, & ficum meam decorticavit, quæ eadem sunt ac nostrates habent (sed a Duacensibus ita expressa: & decorticavit corticem a mea ficu.) Eandem translationem approbant & alii recentiores interpretes reddendo, & ficum meam in decortationem,
units.tr: He has laid my vine waste, etc.) Or: he has ravaged my vine; he has so eaten it away, gnawed it, or destroyed it by other means, that it is no longer profitable, nor of any further use except to cover the ground. The Vulgate has: He has laid my vine in desolation, which the Douai translators followed. Drusius, however, argues that this was done less correctly, since Gephen signifies more properly a vine than Cerem, a vineyard; but it is not established that the Vulgate held this view, since this word signifies both vineyard and vine. And since a vineyard is only a gathering of many vines, there is no real difference. Those who think that a single vine is properly meant here render the word in the plural, o) my vines, as though the term were to be taken collectively, not for one particular and single vine but for several or all of that kind, which that harmful race of little worms had ravaged. By the same reasoning q) they maintain that the following word does not mean the fig tree but fig trees, so that it might be clear what harm the worms were inflicting or were about to inflict: and he has stripped my fig tree, or, as the margin of our Bibles gives a more exact rendering of the Hebrew words, Utenati Likrsapha, "he has set my fig tree for stripping." The Vulgate does not differ much from this, and and has stripped my fig tree is the same as our translators have (but the Douai translators expressed it thus: and has stripped the bark from my fig tree). Other more recent interpreters also approve this rendering, translating and my fig tree for stripping,

units.la: o) Jun. & Tremel. p) Mercer. q) Drus. nem, quæ in nostris Bibliis in marginem sunt rejecta. Nec secus facit Kimchi,cum quorundam sententiam esse referat, quod קצפה Ketsipha, coincidat significatione cum קליפה Keliphah,decortatio, quando Ketfeph corticem arboris Hof. 10,7. significare posse affirmat,ac in libro radicum idem statuit addita hujus sententiæ causa שנקרפה מרוב היובש quia decorticata est præ nimia siccitate. Sic & Vatablus,præ nimia siccitate siccitate & ariditate,vel quod locusta decorticavit & comedit eam. Verum enim vero non desunt, qui diversas alias hujus vocis significationes & priscis & hodiernis temporibus notant. R. Tanchum reddit per תשוביט והחרפות adustionem & concremationem, & ante illum Abu Walid שובת והחרפה adustit vel concremavit eam. Quodque conveniat hæc significatio voci, probat R. Tanchum tum ex frequenti sacrarum literarum usu, tum ex radice & formis quæ inde deducuntur,ad notandum adustionem vel ebullientem ex furore & calorem. Congruit etiam rei, fi voci congruat, significatio,quippe naturalium rerum r) fcrutatoribus hæc quoque locustarum proprietas notatur, multa contactu adurere, ita ut arbores s) ejus contactu pereant & exarescant. Hujus significationis, qua vox denotat calorem vel ustionem ex ira, illi quoque habuerunt rationem,qui eam reddunt, ut t) M. S. Arabicum ira; vel ut Kimchi לקצף ולמארור in iram & indignationem & maledictionem, hoc est, ut Mercerus vult, in talem statum, qui provocat poffeffloris incundiam & mærorem non tolerandum, vel qui possit considerari ut u) divinæ vindictæ signum, aut maledictio vel ipsius ficus,vel qui eam possidet,qua eandem conditionis fortem subiisse conjiciendum effet, atque w) illa, cui Salvator noster maledixerat. Significat hæc vox etiam fpumationem, quam x) nonnulli primariam ejus ducunt significationem, cui altera suam originem debeat; at non una ratione interpretantur,qui id innunt. Vatablus notat, in y) spumam quibusdam Judæo-
units.tr: o) Jun. and Tremel. p) Mercer. q) Drus. which in our Bibles has been put in the margin. Kimchi does the same, when he reports the opinion of some that קצפה [ketsipha] agrees in meaning with קליפה [keliphah], peeling, stripping, and when he affirms that Ketseph can signify the bark of a tree, Hos. 10:7, and in his book of roots he states the same, adding the reason for this opinion: שנקרפה מרוב היובש [shenikrafah merov hayyovesh], because it has been stripped by excessive dryness. So also Vatablus: by excessive dryness, and aridity, or because the locust has stripped and eaten it. But there are not lacking those who note various other meanings of this word, both in ancient and in modern times. R. Tanchum renders it by תשוביט והחרפות [teshuviṭ veha-ḥaraphot], burning and scorching, and before him Abu Walid gives שובת והחרפה [shovet vehaharafah], he burned or scorched it. R. Tanchum proves that this meaning suits the word both from the frequent usage of Holy Letters and from the root and forms derived from it, to denote burning or a heat boiling up from fury. The meaning also agrees with the thing, if it agrees with the word, since natural scientists note this property of locusts too, that they burn many things by contact, so that trees perish and dry up at their touch. Those also took account of this sense, by which the word denotes heat or burning from anger, who render it as the Arabic manuscript has anger, which he prefers to the view of those who render Gamo as grief; or as Kimchi renders it, לקצף ולמארור [lik'tsef ulme'arur], into wrath and indignation and cursing, that is, as Mercerus wishes, into such a state as provokes the possessor's discomfort and sorrow, not to be endured; or which may be considered as a sign of divine vengeance, or a curse either upon the fig tree itself or upon its owner, by which it is to be conjectured that it had undergone the same lot, and that which our Saviour had cursed. This word also signifies foaming, which x) some hold to be its primary meaning, from which the other derives its origin; but those who suggest this do not interpret it in one way. Vatablus notes that it was rendered into foam by some Jews.

units.la: r) Plin. vid. Bochart. s) Bochart. t) quod præferendum censet interpretationi illorum, qui reddunt Gamo dolor. u) Pet. a Fig. w) Matth. 11,19. x) Nic. Ful in Concord. y) Bux. Lex. Tarnov. Judæorum esse redditam. A quibus non longe abeunt, qui vertunt m z) clavum vel fungum, in fungum, vel quod idem est, spumæ productum, vel humiditatem, quæ se non rite per omnes arboris partes diffundit siccitate vel aliqua alia re impedita, sed quæ ad radices arboris expullulascit in hujusmodi effervescentias, quæ vel ex spuma constant aut eam referunt. Hinc Grotius: Hebræa vox spumam significat, & sic videntur per similitudinem appellari clavi arborum. Huc etiam referri videtur expositio Aben-Ezræ, qui ejusdem significationis hanc vocem vult cum קצף Kutseph Hos.10,7. quam nostrates reddunt, spumam, quamque sic explicat, quod fit res שאין כי משׁ cui nil subsistantia solida sit, res nihili, ut Buxtorfius eam interpretatur in Dictionario suo minori, quo, a) eodem referente, etiam Paraphrastes Chaldæus collineasse videtur, qui habet b) למפחת נשׁ exhalationem animæ, ut Mercerus, aut ut alii, exhalationem animæ, quod juxta quosdam, quæ ejusdem Auctoris nota est, nihil aliud significat quam vel levissimum quod anhelitu diffla-tur. Nos tamen, pergit idem, pro exhalatione animæ accipimus, quasi dictum esset, is marorem, qno anima tandem effla-tur, hoc est, in mœstam suspirationem, in quam erumpebant tantæ rerum *) jacturæ memores. Atque hac ratione voce accepta magis eum probasse, in aperto est, priorem significationem talis ac ira quæ non minus, ac mœror, ponit anhelitus, sufflationes & suspirationes, inprimis cum simul sint juncta cademque causa prognata, sicuti hic loci, ubi tanta rerum erat destructio, ut utrique locum fuisse jure merito dicendum sit. Diverse tamen etiam a LXX redditur, ἀφ' ὧν τῆς ουκάς μυ εἰς ε) ἀγχλαςμον, & sicus meas in confusionem, quibus cum & Syro convenit ܠܚܫܘܒܟܐ Lephushocho (quæ latine redduntur ad distributionem) & Arabicæ impressæ le'taphsih للتفسيح ad disoerptionem, quam significationem maxime propriam esse Bochartus statuit,
units.tr: Pliny, see Bochart. Bochart, who judges this reading preferable to the interpretation of those who render it "Gamo dolor." Pet. a Fig. Matthew 11:19. Nic. Ful in Concord. Bux. Lex. Tarnov. It was rendered by the Jews in one of these ways. Not far from these are those who translate knob or fungus, meaning a fungus, or what is the same, a growth produced from foam, or moisture that does not properly spread through all the parts of the tree because it is hindered by dryness or some other cause, but which sprouts up at the roots of the tree into such effervescences, which either consist of foam or resemble it. Hence Grotius: The Hebrew word signifies foam, and so the knobs of trees seem to be called by analogy. To this also seems to refer the explanation of Aben Ezra, who holds that this word has the same meaning as קצף [Kutseph] in Hos. 10:7, which our people render foam, and which he explains as a thing שאין כי משׁ [a thing to which there is no solid substance, a thing of nothing,] as Buxtorf interprets it in his smaller Dictionary. By the same author's account, the Chaldee paraphrast also seems to have aimed at this, who has למפחת נשׁ [lemafchat nash], exhalation of the soul, as Mercer has it, or as others, exhalation of the soul, which according to some (as is a note of the same author) signifies nothing else than the very slightest thing that is blown away by breath. We, however, the same author continues, take it as exhalation of the soul, as if it had been said a grief by which the soul is at last breathed out, that is, into sad sighing, into which they burst, mindful of so great a loss of things. And by this reasoning, having taken the word in this way, it is plain that he prefers it to the former meaning, such as anger, which, no less than grief, produces panting, blowing and sighing, especially since they are joined together and born of the same cause, as here, where there was such great destruction that it may rightly be said that both had their place. Yet it is also rendered differently by the LXX: ἀφ' ὧν τῆς συκάς μου εἰς ἀγχλασμόν [from which, of my fig-tree, into strangling], and with them agrees the Syriac Lephushocho (which in Latin is rendered into distribution) and the printed Arabic le'taphsih, into tearing apart, which meaning Bochart holds to be the most proper,

units.la: a) Jon. Tr. Gros. Tarn. a) in Dictionario suo majori. b) Vide hæc verba hebr. Job. 3, 10 c) In d... Fer. 21 g-in celat... Tarnov. c) Bibl. Polyglott. Alii enim aliter legunt, videlicet γλυκεσμον, ac perperam judice Drusio.
units.tr: a) Jon. Tr. Gros. Tarn. a) in his larger Dictionary. b) See these words in Hebrew, Job 3:10. c) In d... Fer. 21 g-in celat... Tarnov. c) Bibl. Polyglott. Others read it differently, namely γλυκεσμόν [glykesmon], which, in Drusius's judgement, is wrongly so read.

units.la: tuit, cujus confirmandi argumentum ex usu petit, quem obtinet in Arabica lingua, in qua ﮐﺴﻔﻪ Kasapha significat frangere (quocirca proprie ramus arboris fractus dicatur ﮐﺴﻔ Kasph) ac si innueretur, locustas exedendo & arrodendo ficuum ramos in frusta esse fracturas. Et in eo non longe relinquunt interpretationem, quam nostrates secuti sunt, vertendo decorticare. Id solum interest, quod τὸ frangere non solum videatur respicere corticem, sed etiam lignum; cum corticem tantum τὸ decorticare spectet. Attamen utrobique fractio interveniat necesse est, quare translationi adhaerere fas esse censeo, quam tot aliis posthabitis interpretes nostri elegerunt, qua arrodendo d) ramos tenues fuisse fractos innuunt, quod locustis aeque convenire, ac aliis, nemini dubium esse potest. Exinde e) quidam argumentum deducit contra literalem sensum, quod durum admodum sit, statuere, locustarum attactu ficum fuisse laesam, morsuque folia, quin & corticem exesum, quia praeterquam, quod aspersit omnino, habeat etiam insipidum & amarum succum; unde multo probabilius esse cum Hieronymo sentire, quod non proprie sit accipiendum de locustis, sed de damno a Babyloniis illorum & regionis hostibus intentato; vel si proprie accipiendum de locustis, tantam fuisse ipsorum voracitatem, arguere, ut neque foliis neque cortici ficus pepercerint. At explosa est ab f) aliis protinus haec difficultas, qui ex eo, quod experientia est suffultum & rerum naturalium scriptoribus observatum, plane affirmant, ideo vitis & ficus mentionem fieri, quia bruchi & locustae utrique infesti sunt. Quod elucescit ex descriptione damni ab illis illati, Nudavit eam prorsus & projecit &c. (Eam) Affixum cum sequatur immediate nomen ficus, necessario ad eam etiam referendum est; sed, ut Kimchi arbitratur, non ad eam solam, sed & ad aliud nomen, praecedentem scilicet vineam, ita ut, quod illatum est, g) utrique illatum esse intelligatur, quare a b) quibusdam etiam vertitur eas, vel, vitem juxta ac ficum חשיף ושיף Casaph casaph, nec non MSS. Arabicum תקשיר קשרהא Nudando illa (scilicet natio vel gens) nudavit, id est, ut habent nostrates, plane eam.
units.tr: which he confirms by argument from the usage it has in the Arabic language, in which kasapha means to break (so a branch of a tree that has been broken off is properly called kasph), as if it were implied that the locusts, by eating and gnawing away the fig branches, break them into pieces. In this they do not stray far from the interpretation our people followed, rendering it to strip the bark. The only difference is that to break seems to regard not only the bark but also the wood, whereas to strip the bark regards the bark alone. Yet in either case breaking must necessarily occur, so I think it right to adhere to the translation that our interpreters chose, passing over so many others, by which they imply that the thin branches were broken off by gnawing, which fits locusts as well as anything else, as no one can doubt. Hence some derive an argument against the literal sense, saying it is too harsh to state that the fig was harmed by the touch of locusts, its leaves gnawed and even its bark eaten away, since, apart from the fact that this is wholly unlikely, the fig also has an insipid and bitter juice. Whence it is much more probable to agree with Jerome that the passage should not be taken literally of locusts, but of the damage threatened by the Babylonians and the other enemies of that region; or, if taken literally of locusts, it argues such great voracity in them that they spared neither the leaves nor the bark of the fig. But this difficulty was at once set aside by others, who, supported by experience and by what writers on natural things have observed, plainly affirm that the vine and the fig are mentioned because caterpillars and locusts are hostile to both. This is clear from the description of the damage done by them: He has stripped it bare and cast it away, etc. Since the attached pronoun it immediately follows the noun fig, it must necessarily be referred to it; but, as Kimchi thinks, not to it alone, but also to the other noun, namely the preceding vine, so that what was done is understood to have been done to both. Hence it is rendered by some as them, or the vine as well as the fig, חשיף ושיף [Casaph casaph], and likewise in the Arabic manuscript, taqshir qasharha, stripping them (namely the nation or people) has stripped, that is, as our people have it, plainly it.

units.la: Hanc sequitur והשליך Vehiscblic, & projecit. Noftrates adduni id, quod putant subintelligendum id scilicet, quod arroserunt & manducaverunt de foliis, fructu vel cortice, decidere finentes, quæ non devoraverunt, cum absumerent humiditatem, quæ est inter corticem & arborè, cujus folia (inquit Kimchi referendo id ad vitem) postquam exederant, uvam projecerunt in terram, quo facto הלבינו שריגיה Hilbinu Sharigeha, rami illius (vitis vel ficus) albi facti sunt. Quanquam hoc verbum plerumque transitivum sit, tamen intransitive hoc loco sumitur. Dicuntur autem albi facti, vel quod cortice ac omni viridi exeso, nudum lignum apparebat, quod album est, ut quibusdam placet; vel ut aliis, quod ipse k) cortex vel folia & germina contrectatu & fuctu horum tam noxiorum vermiculorum corrupta
units.tr: This is followed by והשליך [vehishlich], and cast away. Our people add it, which they think should be understood, namely, that which they had gnawed and eaten of the leaves, fruit or bark, letting fall what they did not devour, since they consumed the moisture that lies between the bark and the tree; and Kimchi says (referring it to the vine) that, after they had eaten its leaves, they cast the grape to the ground, and by this act הלבינו שריגיה [hilbinu sharigeha], its branches (of the vine or fig) became white. Although this verb is usually transitive, here it is taken intransitively. They are said to have become white either because, when the bark and all the green had been eaten away, the bare wood appeared, which is white, as some think; or, as others think, because the bark itself, or the leaves and shoots, being touched and gnawed by these most harmful little worms, were corrupted,

units.la: i) Merc. Druf. k) Bochart. part.2. pag. 469. rupta & putrefacta, amittebant viriditatem atque alba evadebant. Utrumque valet, cum hac voce illa indigitetur tabes ac interitus, quem induxerant pernitiosæ bestiolæ arboribus, in quascunque etiam incidebant. Æquum enim censeo, quod contigisse hic vitiac ficui dicitur, ad omnes arbores referre, quarum non paucæ hanc fere ob causam v. 12. recenseri putandæ sunt, quia cæteris præstant plurimo usu ac emolumento, unde ex illarum etiam corruptione accrevisse magis calamitatem conjiciendum est, quam quod aliæ male erant constitutæ. Alii tamen hanc rationem subesse putant, quod in dulcedine horum fructuum ebriosis, quorum mentio fit v. 5, plus delectamenti situm fuerit, quam in cæteris, unde citius etiam mentem adhibere ac sentire poterant, quam hujus rei gravem fecissent jacturam.
units.tr: Mercer, Drusius. Bochart, part 2, p. 469. rotted and putrefied, and lost their greenness and became white. Both are valid, since this word denotes the wasting and destruction which those deadly little creatures brought upon the trees on which they fell. For I think it fair to refer what is said here of the vine and the fig to all the trees, of which, for nearly this same reason, not a few are thought to be listed in verse 12, because they surpass the rest in very great use and profit; whence it must be conjectured that the calamity was increased by their corruption more than by others which were badly situated. Others, however, think that this reason lies behind it: that in the sweetness of these fruits, which are mentioned in verse 5 as belonging to the drunkards, there was more pleasure than in the rest, so that they could also more quickly give heed and perceive how grave a loss they had suffered.

units.la: Vox שריגים Sharigim nostratibus æque ac Vulgato rami, quibus alii non pauci accedunt. Verum Junius & Tremellius habent, botri illarum, scilicet vires illarum uvæ, quæ succo destitutæ pallidæ albæque redduntur. Censoria tamen virgula eos propterea notat Piscator, tum quod ad vitem eam vocem referant, quam ad ficum magis spectare persuasum habet, tum quod botros uvarum viridium interpretentur, quum magis proprie ea vox significet palmites. Ipse vero reddit, albæ evaserunt frondes earum, quam vocem, quamvis magis ejus sententia palmites notet, molli tamen metaphora translatam ad notandum frondes ficus, de qua hic peculiariter sermonem esse, atq; ad eam pronomen præcipue referendum nullus ambigit. Abu Walid comparat hanc vocem cum radice ṣrn Saran linguæ Arabicæ, quæ usurpatur pro frondibus & ramis cum se ipsos extendant. l) Præcipuus Arabum Lexicographus ait nomen ṣrn Sarno significare تضيب الكرم teneros ramusculos vitis primi anni vel تضيب رطب كل aliquam madidam (aut viridem) virgam. Idem nobis refert, ṣrg الشرج arfargo conjunctam cum ṣ g, (quæ sono ab hebraica non admodum differt) esse تضيب الكرم virgam (vel ramum) vitis.
units.tr: The word שריגים (Sharigim) is rendered "branches" by our translators, as by the Vulgate, and many others agree. Junius and Tremellius, however, have "the clusters of them," meaning the strength of those grapes, which are made pale and white by the loss of their juice. Piscator nevertheless marks them with a critical stroke, both because they refer the word to the vine, which he is persuaded looks rather to the fig tree, and because they translate it "clusters of green grapes," whereas the word more properly means "shoots." He himself renders it "their leaves have become white." Although his sense more properly denotes "shoots," this word, by a gentle metaphor, is taken to mean the leaves of the fig tree, which is the tree especially under discussion here, and no one doubts that the pronoun refers chiefly to it. Abu Walid compares this word with the Arabic root ṣrn, saran, which is used for leaves and branches "when they stretch themselves out." The chief Arabic lexicographer says that the noun ṣrn, sarno, means tadhīb al-karm, "the tender young shoots of a vine in its first year," or tadhīb raṭb kull, "any moist (or green) rod." The same writer tells us that ṣrġ, arfargo, which is joined with ṣ g (a sound not very different from the Hebrew), means tadhīb al-karm, "a rod (or branch) of the vine."

units.la: {l} Auctor Kamus. vitis. Qui accuratius introspiciunt radicem hebraicam, volunt ea denotari **) tales ramos, qui sunt quasi intertexti atque alii aliis implicati, ut ramis contingit vitis; attamen in genere pro ramis usurpari.
units.tr: {l} The author of the *Kamus*: "vine." Those who examine the Hebrew root more carefully want it to denote such branches as are, as it were, interwoven and entangled with one another, as happens with the branches of a vine; but in general it is used of branches.

units.la: Ita vero haec verba explicavimus propriamque eorum significationem eruimus, ut, retento sensu literali hujus versus, prout etiam factum in praecedenti, declarationem continere statuamus detrimenti, quod afferebant vel allaturi erant vermiculi arboribus ac fructibus terrae infestissimi. Atqui eo sensu a non paucis sunt accepta. Verum qui praecedentia allegorico sensu accipiunt, eundem hic ita continuant, ut per vitem, vel vineam & ficum intelligant populum Judaicum (de quo dictum est Jef. 5, 7. Vinea Jehovae exercituum domus Israelis, & viri Juda sunt planta deliciarum ejus) & per vitem desertam redditam ficumque decorticatam (vel factam indignationem aut maledictionem) quarum utraque nudata, abjecta earumque rami facti sunt albi a locustis & aliis vermiculis, destructionem populo ab inimicis illatam, qua privati sunt omni honore & omnibus rebus quibus insigniter gaudebant, ipsique redditi captivi, atque pauperes & moesti. Sic inter Judaeos Abarbinel & inter Christianos **) diversi.
units.tr: We have explained these words in this way and drawn out their proper meaning, so that, keeping the literal sense of this verse, as we did in the preceding one, we may hold that it contains a description of the harm which the grubs, most destructive to trees and the fruits of the earth, were causing or were about to cause. Indeed, many have understood it in that sense. But those who take the preceding verses in an allegorical sense carry the same sense on here, so that by the vine or vineyard and the fig tree they understand the Jewish people (of whom it was said at Isaiah 5:7, "The vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant plant"), and by the vine made desolate and the fig tree stripped bare (or made an object of indignation or curse), both of which, stripped and cast down, had their branches made white by locusts and other grubs, they understand the destruction inflicted on the people by their enemies, by which they were deprived of all honour and of all the things in which they took special delight, and were themselves made captives, poor and sorrowful. So among the Jews Abarbanel, and among the Christians ** various writers.

units.la: 8. Plange, ut virgo accincta sacco propter maritum adolescentiae suae.
units.tr: 8. Lament, like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.

units.la: Subest sane ratio, quare inprimis compellentur, qui nominantur ebriosi ac vini potores, qui luxuriae ac abdominis toti se dederant, ad flendum & ejulandum; quippe qui iis privabantur fructibus, ex quibus omne deliciarum genus sibi hactenus profluxerat. At malum non tantum in ipsos, sed etiam in longe sobriores ac prudentiores redundabat. Et calamitas, qua premebantur, inprimis eas tangebat res, quae ipsis maximam afferebant voluptatem, maximeque erant necessariae; hoc est, non tantum eas, quae humana ac terrestria concernebant bona, ac delitias, sed & quae ad cultum DEI praestandum
units.tr: There is certainly a reason why those are especially summoned to weep and wail who are called drunkards and wine-bibbers, who have given themselves wholly to luxury and gluttony; for they are deprived of those fruits from which every kind of delight had hitherto flowed for them. But the evil spread not only to them but also to those far more sober and prudent. And the calamity which pressed upon them touched especially those things which afforded them the greatest pleasure and were most necessary, that is, not only those goods and delights which concern human and earthly life, but also those things which were required for the worship of God.

units.la: **) Ramus tortilis atque implexus. Etenim Radix haec proprie sonat perplecti, implicari, contorqueri. Nic. Fuller. Cap. Concord. **) Ar. Mont. Christ. a Castro. Brent. standum requirebantur. Atque ideo ad illos pariter atque ad universum populum jam dirigit Propheta sermonem, ut attentos eos faciat ad considerandum, quid ipsis accidisset, quaque animi sedulitate id sit expendendum; Plange, ut virgo &c.) Quæ extant v. s. sunt numeri pluralis, pariterque nomina, ad quæ verba sunt referenda; sed hic singularis numeri ac fœminini generis, quæ cum ejusdem rationis nomen requirant, quod non extat, per se patet, illud subintelligendum esse. Quod Kimchi cum Paraphrasta Chaldæo haud sine ratione supponit esse כנסרת ישראל congregationem Israelis. Aben-Ezra putat illud esse vel ארמיה regionem, vel נפשי Naphshi animam meam. R. Tanchum ברת ציון o filia Zionis, vel aliquid huic simile. Ut innotescat quantum mereatur planctum calamitas ingressa vel ingressura, quantumve sit extortura, exprimit id per ἀνξησιν desumpta comparatione ab eo, quod in eo genere maxime sit frequens, scilicet ut plangat, non sicut persona vulgaris ordinaria occasione, sed sicut virgo accincta sacco propter maritum adolescentiæ suæ, i. e. sicut quæ vix dum gustata nuptiarum suavitate, sponsique blanditiis, immaturo mariti recentis interitu vidua non potest non gravem exinde concipere dolorem, atque evidentibus externis indiciis, (quæ illis temporibus usu veniebant, ut exempla multa atque formulæ S. literarum loquendi probant) sacci scilicet induitione ac planctibus lugubribus prodere.
units.tr: ** A twisted and intertwined branch. For this root properly means to be entwined, to be entangled, to be twisted. Nic. Fuller, *Cap. Concord.* ** Ar. Mont., Christ. a Castro, Brent. Therefore the Prophet now directs his speech both to them and to the whole people, so as to make them attentive to considering what had befallen them and with what earnestness of mind this ought to be weighed: "Lament, like a virgin," etc. The words that follow, *v. s.*, are in the plural number, and are likewise nouns to which the verbs are to be referred; but here the singular number and feminine gender occur, which, since they require a noun of the same kind, and none is found, it is plain in itself that one must be understood. Kimchi, with the Chaldee paraphrast, reasonably supplies *congregation of Israel* (כנסרת ישראל). Aben Ezra thinks it is either *land* (ארמיה) or *my soul* (נפשי, *Naphshi*). R. Tanchum (*bat Tsiyyon*) "O daughter of Zion," or something similar. To make known how greatly the calamity that has come, or is about to come, deserves lamentation, and how greatly it is about to wrench (them), he expresses it by an amplification, taking a comparison from what is most frequent in that kind of thing: that one should *lament*, not as an ordinary person on any ordinary occasion, but *like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth*; that is, as a woman who, having scarcely yet tasted the sweetness of marriage and the caresses of her spouse, cannot help but conceive a grievous sorrow at the untimely death of her newly wed husband and show it by the evident outward signs (which were customary in those times, as the many examples and formulas of the Holy Scriptures' manner of speaking prove), namely by putting on sackcloth and mournful lamentations.

units.la: Quod omnia, quæ huc extant, בתולה Betulah & בעל Baal, virgo & maritus translata proprie hanc significationem ferant, a nemine, quod sciam, unquam in dubium vocatum est. Verum ut horum alterum non tam stricte sumatur, ut fas esset, sensus videtur exposcere. Quomodo enim virgo dici potest proprie, quæ habebat maritum, cuique ipso loquendi genere libatus videtur esse pudor a marito? Hinc eit ut alii alterum, alterum alii conentur infringere; vel quod primum non stricte significet virginem, sed o) novam nuptam,
units.tr: That all the words found here, בתולה (Betulah) and בעל (Baal), "virgin" and "husband," properly carry this meaning when translated, has, so far as I know, never been called into doubt by anyone. But the sense seems to demand that the one of these two not be taken so strictly as would be permissible. For how can one properly be called a virgin who had a husband, and to whom, in the very manner of speaking, a loss of virginity by her husband seems to have been inflicted? Hence some try to overturn the one, and others the other: either because the first does not strictly signify a virgin, but o) a newly married woman,

units.la: {o} Atque vocem בתולה hujusmodi denotare quidem ex eo probant, quod, cum de Rebrkab sermo fit, immediate subjiciatur Gen. 24, 16. quam vir non cognovit, verum si nuda vox stricte sumta talem significat, quam vir non cognovit, cur hoc adjecit, si Betbula non est etiam juvenca? Drus. ptam, quæ nunc primum nupserat; vel quod alterum non solum denotet virum, qui revera duxerat uxorem, sed qui desponsatam habebat nondum geniali pompa celebrata. Qui priori expositioni sec mancipant, eorum non postremus est Kimchi, qui verba sic explanat: Hæc dicit ad congregationem Israelis, Plange propter illud malum luctumque age gravem, sicuti virgo, quæ nupsit adolescenti, qui mortem subit, dum illa adhuc est puella, quia tunc p) utriusque lætitia maxime viget, unde ea, cum moritur, graviter dolet locoque suorum cuiuscliorum atque ornamentorum induit se sacco: Hancque explanandi rationem tanquam maxime planam q) diversi sequuntur. Alii tamen accipiunt hoc nomen sensu strictissimo & maluntamplificare alterum, adeo, ut non stricte pro r) marito sit sumendum, sed pro quodam, qui mulierem deperit eamque sibi desponsatam habet, quacum tamen non consuevit. Sic intelligendus per maritum, inquit Piscator, is, qui uxorem virginem sibi despondit quidem, sed nondum cum ea consuevit, quippe mortuus ante consuetudinem conjugalem. Eandem videtur sententiam fovere Autor versionis Arabicæ MS. non adeo transferendo nomen posterius, quod vertit maritus, quam prius vertendo quod significat puellam matrimonio aptam, at nondum a parentibus separatam ad commorandum cum præstituto marito Jauhari. Est & aliud in Piscatore observatione dignum, quod scilicet, quæ nostratibus & aliis redduntur maritum adolescentia sua, quod idem est ac si dicas, cui nupserat in adolescentia sua, ille secundum literam denotare velit, maritum juvenem suum, adeo ut ætatis maritii hic rationem haberi, non sponsæ, ducat. Atque in eo videtur ipsi quoque accedere Grotius, cum explanationi verborum adjiciat, solent enim mariti a fœminis magis amari, quibus adolescentulis adhuc nuptæ sunt.
units.tr: {o} Indeed they prove that the word בתולה has this sense from the fact that, when the discussion concerns Rebekah, there immediately follows Genesis 24:16, "whom no man had known"; but if the bare word, taken strictly, means one whom no man has known, why did he add this, if Betulah is not also a young heifer? (Drusius.) — who had only now first married; or because the second denotes not only a husband who had in fact taken a wife, but one who had betrothed her and not yet celebrated the marriage with nuptial pomp. Among those who adhere to the former explanation, Kimchi is not the least, who explains the words thus: "He says this to the congregation of Israel: Lament over that evil and mourn gravely, as a virgin does who has married a young man who dies while she is still a girl, because then the joy of both is at its height; wherefore she, when he dies, grieves greatly, and in place of her ornaments and finery clothes herself in sackcloth." This way of explaining is followed by various writers as the plainest of all. Others, however, take this word in its strictest sense and wish to make the second term broader, so that husband is not to be taken strictly, but for someone who loves a woman and has her betrothed to him, though he has not yet lived with her as her husband. Thus, says Piscator, husband is to be understood as "one who indeed has betrothed to himself a virgin wife, but has not yet lived with her, since he died before the conjugal union." The author of the Arabic manuscript version seems to favour the same opinion, not so much in translating the latter word, which he renders husband, as in translating the former by what signifies a girl fit for marriage but not yet separated from her parents to dwell with the appointed husband (Jauhari). There is also another point in Piscator worth noting: what our people and others render "the husband of her youth" is the same as if you said "the one to whom she had married in her youth"; he, taking the words literally, wishes them to denote "her young husband," so that the age of the husband, not of the bride, is taken into account here. And in this Grotius seems also to agree with him, when he adds to his explanation of the words: "for husbands are wont to be loved more by women to whom they were married while they were still young men."

units.la: p) Ita Aben-Ezra in diebus lætitiæ ejus. q) Betulah ætatis hoc non integritatis nomen. r) Non videtur sibi constare Mercerus, cum in prioribus suis notis in hunc versum dicat Baal proprie significare Amasium, non maritum. In posterioribus autem non Amasium, sed maritum qui jus habet in uxorem. Rursus in prioribus notis Hos. 2,18. dicit Baal utrumque denotare, Dominum & Amasium; & in posterioribus falsum esse, quod quidam statuant, Baal hebraice denotare Amasium.
units.tr: p) So Aben-Ezra: "in the days of her joy." q) Betulah is a name of age, not of integrity. r) Mercer does not seem consistent with himself. In his earlier notes on this verse he says that Baal properly means Amasius, not maritum. In his later notes, however, it means not Amasium but maritum qui jus habet in uxorem. Again, in his earlier notes on Hos. 2.18 he says that Baal denotes both Dominum & Amasium, and in the later notes he says it is false, as some maintain, that Baal in Hebrew denotes Amasium.

units.la: Sed hujus constructionis quanquam exempla, quæ adducantur, non desint, tamen rigidam esse magis, quam priorem, certum est. Nec novi satis, utra magis vel æque multum rei subjectæ conveniat, quia moeroris illius vis exprimitur, qui potissimum locum invenit apud tales, qualis hic nobis sistitur virgo (desponsata vel juvencula) recens conjugata, quæ immatura morte amiserat (sponsum) vel maritum suum. Nec alienum est conjicere, florem suæ ipsius ætatis æque auxisse vim moeroris, atque adolescentiam mariti; hinc utrumque hic notari non obscure liquet, & juvenculam fuisse recens nuptam, & juvenem, quem tam impense amaverat, cujusque manes adeo copiose deplorabat, atque omnia doloris insignia edebat, ita ut ab ejus conditione apta defumta sit comparatio ad gravissimum luctum argumendum.
units.tr: But although examples of this construction are not lacking, it is certainly stricter than the earlier one. Nor do I know well enough which of the two suits the subject better, or equally well, since the force of that grief is expressed, the grief which finds its strongest place among such a person as the virgin here set before us, a young bride recently married, who had lost by an untimely death her betrothed or husband. Nor is it out of place to conjecture that the flower of her own age increased the force of her grief just as much as the youth of her husband did.
