Hence it is clear enough that both are indicated here: that the young woman had recently been married, and that the young man, whom she had loved so deeply and whose shade she mourned so abundantly, displaying every sign of sorrow, was the one from whose fitting condition the comparison was drawn to express the most grievous mourning.

units.la: Græca, quamvis ab aliis discrepare paululum videatur verbis, sensu tamen convenit, cum habeat, Θρήνησον πρὸς με ὑπὲρ νύμφην περιεζωσμένην σάκκον, ἐπὶ τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς τὸν παρθενικόν. Quam Arabica impressa sequitur: نوحي علي اكثر من عروس اتزرت بالسوح علي رجلها العذروي Quæ sic vertit Vetus eorum latinus Interpres: Plange ad me super sponsum accinctum cilicio, super virum suum virgineum; quod anglice deberet reddi: Lament to me above (or more then) a bride (or nevv married vvoman) girded vvith sackcloth, for her virgin husband; qua in versione additur πρὸς με, ad me, quod textus Hebraicus non agnoscit, cujus causam Drusius divinat fuisse hanc, quod duplici ratione posset reddi vox אלי, Eli, quæ cum sic legatur, notet plange, sed iisdem literis Elui, ad me, quarum utraque antiquis quibusdam scriptoribus inveniatur conjuncta; ita ut ad conciliandum id cum textu hebraico supponat posteriorem significationem esse protinus extrudendam. Pari modo supponit ὑπὲρ νύμφην, quæ deberent verti supra vel plus quam novam nuptam, initio scriptum fuisse ὥσπερ, sicut, quod congruit voci hebraicæ כבתולה Cibtulah, erroreque amanuensis vel librarii mutatum in ὑπὲρ: Per ἀνδρα αὐτῆς τὸν παρθενικόν, virgineum sunm maritum intelligit Hieronymus
units.tr: The Greek, though it seems to differ slightly from the others in wording, agrees in sense, since it reads: "Lament to me over a bride girded with sackcloth, over her virgin husband" [Θρήνησον πρὸς με ὑπὲρ νύμφην περιεζωσμένην σάκκον, ἐπὶ τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς τὸν παρθενικόν]. The printed Arabic follows it: "nawḥī ʿalā akthar min ʿarūs ittazarat bi-s-sawḥ ʿalā rijlihā al-ʿudhrawī". Their old Latin translator renders this thus: Lament to me over the bridegroom girded with sackcloth, over her virgin husband; which in English ought to be rendered: Lament to me above (or more than) a bride (or new married woman) girded with sackcloth, for her virgin husband; In this version the words "to me" are added, [πρὸς με, ad me], which the Hebrew text does not have. Drusius conjectures the reason for this: the word אלי [Eli] can be read in two ways. Read thus, it means lament; but with the same letters it reads Elui, "to me", and both readings are found joined together in certain ancient writers. So, to reconcile this with the Hebrew text, he supposes that the second meaning must be dropped at once. In the same way he supposes that ὑπὲρ νύμφην, which ought to be translated above or more than a new bride, was originally written ὥσπερ, as, which corresponds to the Hebrew word כבתולה [Cibtulah], and that by an error of a copyist or scribe it was changed to ὑπὲρ. As for "her virgin husband" [ἀνδρα αὐτῆς τὸν παρθενικόν], Jerome understands it as her virgin husband,

units.la: u) Liveley. hymnus juxta cum aliis, primum ejus maritum, qui eam ducebat cum adhuc esset virgo, qui eo nomine indigitetur, quod primus flores virginitatis abstulerit.
units.tr: u) Liveley, with others, takes hymnus [the hymn] to mean her first husband, who led her while she was still a virgin, and who is so called because he first took away the flowers of her virginity.

units.la: Quorsum alludi censeat Abarbinel, ab hujusmodi virginis conditione hanc comparationem desumendo, ex ea verborum paraphrasi apparet; Plange o congregatio Israelis, quae cras olim sicut virgo, quatenus nulla unquam gens tibi dominata fuit, & accinge te cilicio propter maritum adolescentia, qui Deus est (benedictus in aeternum) quia augusta ejus praesentia desessit a te. Quod ab Hieronymo accepisse videtur qui eandem ferme tuetur sententiam.
units.tr: From what this comparison, drawn from the condition of such a virgin, is meant to allude to, Abarbanel makes clear in his paraphrase of the words: "Lament, O congregation of Israel, who was yesterday like a virgin, inasmuch as no nation ever ruled over you; and gird yourself with sackcloth on account of the husband of your youth, who is God (blessed for ever), because his august presence has departed from you." This seems to be what he received from Jerome, who holds nearly the same opinion.

units.la: 9. Succisum est sacrificium & libamen a domo Jehovae, lugent sacerdotes ministri Jehovae.
units.tr: 9. The meal offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of Jehovah; the ministers of Jehovah mourn.

units.la: Si ad literam haec verba sumenda sunt, declaratur, quare praedicta ratione ipsis sit lugendum totiusque praeterea illorum coetui. Respici tamen adhuc in specie supra memoratos ebriosos, Autor est Aben-Ezra, qui ea verba confirmationis loco habet, cujus antea mentio injecta erat, quod nimirum excideretur vinum ex ore illorum, ac si diceret: unde vobis vinum suppetet, quo tam copiose & ad excessum usque uti solebatis, quando sacrificium & libamen, necessarium officium atque totius coetus oblatio, quod, siulla tantum praestandi sese offerret occasio, nequaquam omitti debet, succisum est a domo Jehovae (nulla re amplius ad sacrificium exsistente) ut Sacerdotes ministri Jehovae lugere cogantur. illorum tam misere laborantes defectu? Verum magis placet, ad totum coetum iterum direxisse haec verba Prophetam, quibus haud obscure docet, quare plorandum sit non tantum ebriosis, quibus & necessariis non fit satis, verum & iis, qui nihil amplius expectebant, quam necessarius usus exigebat, cum vel id ipsum, quo sine vota Deo persolvere pares non erant, cujusque rationem majorem habere tenebantur, quam aliarum rerum, sive ad prium commodum sive ad voluptates spectantium, succisum esset ab illis. Hoc sacrificium & libamen, inquit, est succisum, quia, secundum
units.tr: If these words are taken literally, it is made clear why they must mourn for the reason given, and the whole assembly with them. Yet, according to Aben-Ezra, who is the author of this view, the words still look specifically at the drunkards mentioned above, and he takes them as confirmation of what had been said earlier, namely that the wine would be cut off from their mouths. It is as if he said: where will you get the wine with which you were accustomed to indulge so copiously and to excess, when the sacrifice and drink offering, a necessary duty and the offering of the whole assembly, which ought never to be omitted if there is any opportunity of performing it, has been cut off from the house of Jehovah (no longer any thing existing for the sacrifice), so that the priests, the ministers of Jehovah, are compelled to mourn for their defect, they who labour so wretchedly? But it pleases me more that the prophet directed these words again to the whole assembly, by which he shows quite plainly why they must mourn, not only the drunkards, who did not even have what was necessary, but also those who expected nothing beyond what necessary use required, since they were bound to take greater account of this very thing, without which they were not able to render their vows to God, than of other things, whether they related to profit or to pleasures, when it had been cut off from them. This sacrifice and drink offering, he says, has been cut off, because, according to

units.la: At Cyrillus exponit id per παρθενικος τε και εὐηβον νυμφιον, ac ἢ denotatur aetatem viri integram, ut apud alios videre est. x) Vide Ar. Mont. cundum literalem sensum verborum praecedentium, vermiculi isti pernitiosi Ꝁ.4. omnes terrae fructus populati erant, unde ea conficiebantur. Qua in re consistat, undeque conficietur מנחה minchah sacrificium, consignatum extat Levit. 2, 1. &c. & 6, 14. &c. Num. 15, 4. &c. & 28, 5. &c. Vox ea quidem generaliter alibi accipitur pro quovis dono vel oblatione, at praecipue sacrificio attribuitur in lege, cujus praecipua pars y) erat similia. Libamen appellatur נסך Nesec & fiebat ex vino, ut eodem capite describitur Num. 15, 5. & 28, 7. 14. Tritico vero & vino, ex quibus ea conficiuntur, ab erucis, locustis, & aliis harum similibus creaturis noxiis adeo vitiato, ut amplius fructum nihil expectandum esset, necesse erat, ut succideretur similia & vinum. Cumque adeo invalesceret illarum rerum defectus, ut non amplius restaret, quo rem sacram in domo Dei sacrificiis & libaminibus rite administrarent, certum est tantam fuisse penuriam, ut ad plangendum eo, quo describitur, modo non potuerit non excitare, & totum populum, qui ea perpessus est, quemque hic ad plorandum provocat Propheta, & praecipue Sacerdotes, qui rerum sacrarum in domo Dei curam gerebant, atque eas, quamdiu earum suppetebat copia, indesinenter, prout officii eorum ratio exigebat, offerebant. Hinc cum totum coetum acerbissimos jubet edere luctus & gemitus, lugere jamjam eos affirmat. LXX. quidem hanc legunt vocem אבלו, quam alii praesentis vel praeteriti temporis volunt, lugent vel luxerunt, modo imperativo, πενθήσατε lugete, coque non adeo praecedentibus verbis eam conjungunt, quam consequentibus, quibus simili modo indicatur quare ipsis sit lugendum, atque iis, quae ad populum antea dicta sunt. Quae quantumvis non adeo cum reliquis constructione conveniant, sensum tamen non multum immutant, quippe eandem tantum lugendi causam ipsis injungunt. Quare autem sacerdotes cumprimis hic in considerationem veniant, a) duplici ex ratione factum esse probabile est. Quarum una est, quod magno amore atque zelo flagrarent erga cultum divinum, qui illo tempore absque
units.tr: But Cyril explains it by παρθενικος τε και εὐηβον νυμφιον [παρθενικὸς τε καὶ εὔηβον νυμφίον] [a virgin and a youthful bridegroom], where it is denoted that the husband's age is complete, as may be seen in others. x) See Ar. Mont. According to the literal sense of the preceding words, those pernicious little worms (Joel 1.4) had ravaged all the fruits of the earth from which these offerings were made. What the minchah [מנחה] sacrifice consists of, and from what it is made, is set down in Lev. 2.1 etc., and 6.14 etc., Num. 15.4 etc., and 28.5 etc. This word is indeed used elsewhere in general for any gift or offering, but in the law it is especially assigned to the sacrifice, the chief part of which was y) similia. The drink offering is called nesec [נסך], and was made from wine, as is described in the same chapter, Num. 15.5 and 28.7, 14. But since the wheat and wine from which these offerings are made had been so spoiled by caterpillars, locusts, and other noxious creatures of this kind that no further fruit could be expected, it was necessary for the sacrifice and the drink offering to be cut off. And since the lack of those things grew so severe that there no longer remained anything with which they might duly administer the sacred rite in the house of God by means of sacrifices and drink offerings, it is certain that the scarcity was so great that it could not fail to provoke the mourning in the manner described, both in the whole people, who suffered it, and whom the prophet here calls to mourn, and especially in the priests, who had charge of the sacred things in the house of God and who offered them incessantly, as long as their supply lasted, as the rule of their office required. Hence, when he bids the whole assembly to utter the most bitter lamentations and groans, he affirms that they are to mourn at once. The Seventy indeed read the word abelu [אבלו], which others take as present or past tense, they mourn or they mourned, in the imperative mood, πενθήσατε [penthēsate, mourn ye], and they join it not so much with the preceding words as with the following ones, in which the reason why they must mourn is similarly indicated, and with what was said before to the people. Although these do not agree so well with the rest in construction, they do not change the sense much, since they only impose the same reason for mourning on them. Why the priests are especially brought into consideration here, a) it is probable that this happened for a twofold reason. One is that they burned with great love and zeal for the divine worship, which at that time, without these sacrifices, which had necessarily to be joined with the others, could not in any way be performed as it should be; the other is that they were deprived of their domestic resources, which God had assigned to them from the sacred ministries among the other tribes, so that they had no other possession in their land, nor a share...

units.la: y) Cum Minchah sit foemininì generis, MS. Arabicum praefigit Korban, quasi subintelligatur, ut expressè habetur Levit. 2, 5. quia verbum מנחה masculini gen. est. a) Hieronymus.
units.tr: y) Since minchah is of the feminine gender, the Arabic manuscript prefixes Korban, as if it were understood, as is expressly stated in Lev. 2.5, because the word מנחה [minchah] is of the masculine gender. a) Jerome.

units.la: absque-his sacrificiis, quæ cum aliis necessario erant conjungenda, nequaquam ea, qua par erat, ratione poterat præstari; Altera,quod domesticis sumtibus privarentur, quos Deus ex sacrorum ministeriis inter alias tribus iis designaverat,ita ut in terra illorum nullam aliam haberent possessionem, neque partem inter eos, Num. 18,§.9. & 20. Syrus inter lugentes etiam, quamvis, qua ratione nitatur, prorsus ignoro,recenset reges,cum ea verba reddat: [Arabic] Simila (sacrificium) & ad-spersio (vel libamen) abiit (vel decessit) a domo Jehovæ, Reges sedent (vel sederunt) in mœrore, & sacerdotes ministri Jehovæ. Non est translatio, quarum quidem cognitio huc usque ad nos pervenit,quæ vocem Reges agnoscit,nec in Textu Hebraico aliquid invenitur,quod huic voci respondeat, quove verisimiliter saltem posset niti,præterquam quod duplici ratione vox Cohanim reddita censeri posset,quasi æque notet reges atque sacerdotes, quarum utramque significationem forsitan autor voluerit retinere,quia utrosque hic innui ratus sit. Id adfirmare certe habeo, quod in Glossario Hebræo-Arabico quodam [Arabic] Moltan regem reddi non minus, quam sacerdotem reperericm, atque tum præcipue locum habere, cum dicitur, Tu es Cohen in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedec. Ulitatum est quoque alibi pro Principe vel magnate; verum non constat dilucide,num ejus rationem habuerit Syrus nec ne: at nulla plane est ratio, cur eum in eo sequamur. Quæ adduntur,ut constare possit, quinam intelligendi sint,videlicet verbi ministri, vel qui res sacras Deo administrant, evidenter vocem restringunt ad Sacerdotes, quibus prædicta ex causa plorandum erat.
units.tr: Without these sacrifices, which had to be joined with the others, they could in no way be performed as they ought to be. The second reason is that they would be deprived of household provision, which God had assigned to that tribe from the ministries of the sacred things, among the other tribes, so that they had no other possession in their land and no share among the others (Num. 18, §9 and 20). Among the mourners, the Syriac also, though I am utterly ignorant of what reasoning supports it, lists the kings, rendering the words: "The meal offering (sacrifice) and the drink offering (or libation) have departed (or ceased) from the house of Jehovah. The kings sit (or sat) in mourning, and the priests, the ministers of Jehovah." No translation known to us up to now recognises the word "kings", and nothing in the Hebrew text corresponds to this word or could plausibly support it, except that the word Cohanim could be taken in a twofold way, as if it signified both kings and priests equally. The author perhaps wished to keep both meanings, because he thought both were implied here. I must certainly affirm that in a certain Hebrew-Arabic glossary Moltan is rendered king no less than priest is, and that this applies especially where it is said, "Thou art Cohen for ever after the order of Melchizedek." It is also used elsewhere for a prince or magnate. But it is not clear whether the Syriac took this into account or not, and there is plainly no reason why we should follow him in this. What is added, so that it may be clear who is meant, namely "ministers of the Word" or those who administer sacred things to God, clearly restricts the word to the priests, for whom mourning was to be made for the reason stated.

units.la: Qui allegorico sensu per noxias creaturas indigitari censent hoftes Judæorum, horum alii per decisionem sacrificiorum & libamitum a domo Jehovæ intelligunt b) depopulationem regioni illam ab illis hostibus, qui fructus terræ delebant; c) alii vias simul impervias ab iis redditas, quo minus ex aliis locis transferrentur,quæ ad templi ministeria pertinebant. Abarbinel alia ratione procedit, cum
units.tr: Those who, in an allegorical sense, take the noxious creatures to indicate the enemies of the Jews, some of them understand by the cutting off of the sacrifices and libations from the house of Jehovah b) the depopulation of that region by those enemies who destroyed the fruits of the land; c) others understand the roads made impassable by them at the same time, so that the things pertaining to the ministries of the temple could not be brought in from other places. Abarbinel proceeds by another method, when

units.la: {b} Ribera, Menochius. {c} Gvalt. cum destructionem templi, ut fit ꝟ. 10, hic notari statuat, ita ut quæ sacrificanda erant non adeo dicantur succisa propter illorum defectum, ex quibus fiebant, quam quod d) locus, ubi more solenni osserebantur, esset destructus. Verum ex ipsis verbis e) contrarium elucescit, quippe calamitas erat plaga, quæ immittebatur integro adhuc templo. Non dicitur, domus succidetur a sacrificiis, sed sacrificia a domo, & quomodo dici possunt ab ea succisa, quæ non amplius erant in rerum natura?
units.tr: {b} Ribera, Menochius. {c} Gualther holds that the destruction of the temple is noted here, as in v. 10, so that the things to be sacrificed are not said to be cut off because of the lack of those things from which they were made, but rather because the place where they were offered in the solemn manner was destroyed. But the contrary is clear from the words themselves: the calamity was a blow inflicted while the temple was still intact. It is not said, "the house will be cut off from the sacrifices," but "the sacrifices from the house." And how can things be said to be cut off from it which no longer existed in nature?

units.la: 10. Vastatus est ager, luget terra, quia vastatur fru- mentum: Mustum exarescit, languet oleum.
units.tr: 10. The field is laid waste, the land mourns, because the grain is wasted; the new wine dries up, the oil languishes.

units.la: Pergit in descriptione hujus calamitatis, quæ jamjam venerat, vel certo ventura erat, atque particulatim jam exhibet, quibus in rebus potissimum sese sint exsertura tristissima fata. Hæcque tam accurata omnium descriptio, crebraque ejusdem pluribus verbis repetitio, quod pancioribus potuisset capi, indicium videtur nonnullis ingentis f) stupiditatis incolarum, qua, licet tanta malorum serie premerentur, ut quam maxime eam debuissent sentire & subista suspirare, non tamen curabant, ita, ut considerarent causam mali, & respexissent ad illum, qui id propter detestanda ipsorum peccata immiserat, & ad pœnitentiam commoti fuissent. In specie vero dicit: Schuddad Sadeh, Vastatus est ager. Id scilicet verbum notat vastare, destruere, spoliare & diripere. Chaldæus habet agri sunt spoliati, nec non Syrus & MS. Arabicum ager est vastatus, vel spoliatus, literali sensu retento, a locustis &c. quæ absumebant, quicquid in eo vernabat. Græci habent τεταλαιπωρημένη, vel in aliis apographis τεταλαιπωρημένης, quæ vox cum bis in hoc versu occurrat, ab interprete latino altero commutate reddita est, desolati sunt campi, altero, afflictum est triticum, id est, male habet, in pessimo statu est. Vulgatus, depopulata est regio, cujus vestigiis insistunt Duacenses: Alii recen-
units.tr: He goes on describing this calamity, which was already coming or was certain to come, and now sets out particularly in which things the most dreadful fates will chiefly show themselves. This so careful description of all things, and the frequent repetition of the same thing in several words, which could have been taken in fewer, seems to some to indicate a great f) stupidity of the inhabitants, who, although they were pressed by such a series of evils that they ought most of all to have felt them and groaned under them, nevertheless did not care, so that they did not consider the cause of the evil, nor look to him who had sent it because of their detestable sins, and were moved to repentance. Specifically he says: "Schuddad Sadeh, The field is laid waste." That word, of course, signifies to lay waste, to destroy, to despoil and to plunder. The Chaldean has "the fields are despoiled," and the Syriac and the Arabic manuscript likewise "the field is laid waste" or despoiled, retaining the literal sense, by the locusts etc. which devoured whatever was growing in it. The Greeks have τεταλαιπωρημένη [tetalaipōrēmenē], or in other copies τεταλαιπωρημένης; since this word occurs twice in this verse, the Latin translator rendered it differently: once "the plains are made desolate," and the other time "the wheat is afflicted," that is, it is in a bad way, in the worst condition. The Vulgate has "the region is laid waste," in whose footsteps the Douay translators follow. Other more recent ones

units.la: d) Ita Interpretes Duacenses in suis notis: Hierosolyma superata, & templo Babyloniorum irruptione devastato, sacrificia ex mente hujus & aliorum Prophetarum cessabant. e) Bochart. f) Calvin. recentiores, ϸass.tus est, ut & nostrates, privatus est g) omni suo fructu & incremento. Luget terra ארמ״ית אבל״ית Abelah adamah, luxit terra, Vulgatus, luxit humus; præteriti temporis revera est verbum hebraicum, ita ut Syrus ܐܒܠܬ ܐܕܡܐ & terra fedit in mœrore, & MS. Arabicum الأرض حزنت terra fiut tristis vel mœrore gemens. At non est, quod acute interpretationes has rimentur, utrum præterito, an præsenti, vel futuro accommodatius verba sint reddenda, cum horum cuilibet forma præteriti temporis possit accommodari. LXX. vero, licet verba præcedentia præterito perfecto, quo cum præcedentibus etiam conjungantur, reddiderint, imperativo tamen modo ea hic vertunt, ϖϵνθϵτω ἡ γῆ, quos sequitur Arabica impressa الارض تحزن lugeto terra, vel esto tristis, quantumvis ex usu hebraicæ formæ non sit, quo eos fuisse b) nixos appareat. Nos igitur eo collineantes quoque expressum hic esse, statuere possemus tam lugubrem rerum statum, ut & creaturas sentire nescias, imo ipsam terram ad lugendum provocare & impellere valeat.
units.tr: d) So the Douay interpreters in their notes: Jerusalem having been overcome and the temple devastated by the Babylonian invasion, the sacrifices ceased in the mind of this prophet and the others. e) Bochart. f) Calvin. Recent ones, as also our own people, have "is stripped" g) of all its fruit and increase. "Luget terra," Abelah adamah [ʾābelâ ʾădāmâ], "the land mourned"; the Vulgate has "the ground mourned." In fact it is a Hebrew verb in the past tense, so that the Syriac has "the land mourned" and the Arabic manuscript "the land became sad" or groaned in mourning. But there is no need to strain over whether these interpretations should be rendered in the past, present or future, since any of these may fit the form of the past tense. The Septuagint, indeed, although they rendered the preceding verbs in the perfect past, with which they are joined, here translate these in the imperative mood: ϖϵνθϵτω ἡ γῆ [pentheto hē gē], "let the land mourn," and the printed Arabic follows them, "let the land mourn," or be sad; although it does not agree with the usage of the Hebrew form, which shows that they had relied on b) it. We therefore, aiming at this too, could hold that what is expressed here is so mournful a state of things that even the creatures are made to feel it, indeed that the land itself is driven and compelled to mourn.

units.la: אבל״ית ארמ״ית Adamah Terra (luget) i. e. inquit Aben-Ezra incolæ ejus lugent, atque ita etiam Hieronymus ante eum, qui persantur in humo, vel quæ vivunt in ea animantia, atque de illis magis proprie dici videtur, quam de iis, qui damnum sentiebant. Aliis tamen ἐμΦατικώτερον videtur, id referri ad ipsam terram, cum & in aliis locis ad eandem & suam in ea contentarum rerum faciem exprimendam eodem modo adhibeatur, ut Esa. 24, 4. Terra luget & languet, & Jer. 4, 28. Ad hæc lugebit Terra, & 12, 4. Quousque lugebit terra? ut i) reliqua dicta jam non adducam. E contrario, quando spirant arva croceis vestita floribus forteque placida utuntur, colles dicuntur exultare, vallesque plaudere, ut canit Psal. 65, 12, 13. Nec inusitata est aliis linguis hæc figura, quippe prata dicuntur etiam illis ridere, & lætus ager, quando campi vernant & floribus numerosis sese conspiciendos præbent; sicut contra, cum sunt desolati ac omnibus
units.tr: Adamah [ʾădāmâ], "land," (mourns), that is, as Aben Ezra says, "its inhabitants mourn," and so Jerome before him, "who dwell in the ground," or the living creatures that live in it; and this seems to be said more properly of them than of those who suffered the loss. To others, however, it seems more emphatic that it refers to the land itself, since in other places too the same figure is used to express the appearance of the same land and of the things contained in it: Isaiah 24:4, "The land mourns and languishes," and Jeremiah 4:28, "For this the land shall mourn," and 12:4, "How long shall the land mourn?" as i) I will not now cite the other sayings. On the contrary, when the fields breathe, clothed with saffron flowers and enjoying a calm and gentle wind, the hills are said to exult and the valleys to clap their hands, as the psalm sings (Psalm 65:12, 13). Nor is this figure unusual in other languages: meadows are also said to smile in them, and a joyful field, when the plains grow green and show themselves to be looked at with abundant flowers; and conversely, when they are desolate and

units.la: g) Vatab. b) Merc. i) Ita Lam. 2, 8. Et luctum affert præmunitioni & muro pariter lan-guefcentibus. bus his prorsus destituti, lugere, tristes esse, mœsta facie ac lugubri habitu dicuntur. Paraphrastes Chaldæus magis rationem habet subjecti, de quo sermo est, quam vocis proprietatis, ideoque reddit: חרובר ארנא regio vel terra est k) desolata. Interea manifestum est, qua ratione ad incolas spectet quod de terra dictum est. Si enim luget ut desolata & proventibus orbata, necessario lugebunt, qui ex proventuum ubertate vitam ducunt & absque iis subsistere vix possunt. Quare vero terræ lugendi causa sit, ex verbis sequentibus apparet, quibus tropologico iterum sermone tristem earum rerum faciem depingit, quibus bene se habentibus exultare solebant & cristam erigere incolæ. Scilicet quia שרד רנן Schuddad dagan, frumentum devastatur, vel ut Genevensis, destruitur. Eadem vox est atque antecedens, eodemque modo a nostratibus expressa. Quod etiam fecit Græca, Syriaca & MS. Arabicum. Sed differt Chaldæus non adeo quidem sensu, quam voce, quia, quod ibi reddit per Embezitu, spoliantur, hic exprimit per סף Saph, consumitur, destituitur. Sic & Vulgatus priori loco habet depopulari, posteriori devastari. Id nimirum, quod omnium maxime fructuum terræ præstat, quo vita mortalium sustentatur, quod hominis corroborat vires atque unde petebatur substantia minchah vel sacrificii, quod Deo immolabatur, id, inquam, deest illis, vel a l) noxiis ante memoratis vermiculis corruptum vel absumtum: vel ut m) quidam ex sequentibus colligunt, per nimium æstum solis. Porro eundem statum alia ratione depingit הובש תירוש Hobisch Tirosh, Mustum exarescit, ita textus nostep; verum in margine, pudefit: cujus diversitatis ratio est ambigua significatio vocis הובש Hobisch in textu originali, quæ interdum ordinariam retinet significationem verbi יבש Jabasch exarescere; interdum vero verbi בוש Bosh, quod notat pudefieri. Cumque harum radicum n) formæ atque hinc etiam notationes multifariam plerumque misceantur & confundantur, factum est ut interpretes hic sibi non constent, quod de antiquis quoque affirmare habeo, quippe LXX. reddunt ἐξηράνθη exaruit, & Chal-
units.tr: g) Vatablus. b) Mercerus. i) So in Lam. 2:8: "and brings mourning on the rampart and the wall, which languish together." Stripped of all these things, they are said to mourn, to be sad, and to have a sorrowful face and dismal dress. The Chaldean paraphrast pays more attention to the subject under discussion than to the proper force of the word, and therefore renders: "the region or land is k) desolate." Meanwhile it is plain in what way what is said of the land pertains to the inhabitants. For if it mourns as desolate and deprived of its produce, then necessarily those will mourn who live on the abundance of the produce and can hardly subsist without it. Why the land has cause to mourn appears from the following words, in which, again in a tropological manner, he depicts the sad face of those things with which the inhabitants used to exult and raise their heads when all was well: namely, because Schuddad dagan [shuddad dāgān], "the grain is laid waste," or, as the Geneva version has, "is destroyed." It is the same word as the preceding one, and it is expressed by our people in the same way. The Greek, Syriac and Arabic manuscript also do so. But the Chaldean differs, not so much in sense as in wording, because what there he renders by Embezitu ("they are despoiled"), here he expresses by Saph ("is consumed, is destitute"). Thus the Vulgate too has "to be laid waste" in the first place and "to be wasted" in the second. That, of course, which most of all supplies the fruits of the earth by which the life of mortals is sustained, which strengthens the power of man and from which the substance of the minchah [minḥâ], that is, of the sacrifice that was offered to God, was drawn, that, I say, is lacking to them, or corrupted or consumed by the noxious little worms mentioned before; or, as some gather from what follows, by the excessive heat of the sun. Further, he depicts the same state in another way: Hobisch Tirosh [hôbîš tîrôš], "the new wine dries up," so our text; but in the margin, "is ashamed." The reason for this difference is the ambiguous meaning of the word Hobisch in the original text, which sometimes keeps the ordinary sense of the verb Jabasch, "to dry up," and sometimes that of the verb Bosh, which means "to be ashamed." Since the forms of these roots, and hence also their meanings, are for the most part mixed and confused in many ways, it has come about that the interpreters here do not agree with one another, which I must also affirm of the ancients: for the Septuagint render ἐξηράνθη [exēranthē], "it dried up," and the Chaldean

units.la: k) Et quidam alii, desolata est terra. Pag. l) Cyrill. m) Pisc. Dan. Tarnov. per nimium æstum & infecta vapia. n) Buxt. Lex. in יבש & ibid. Schindl.
units.tr: k) And some others: the land is laid waste. Pag. l) Cyrill. m) Pisc. Dan. Tarnov., through excessive heat and a spoiled vintage. n) Buxt. Lex. under יבש, and ibid. Schindl.

units.la: Chaldæus vites aruerunt; sic & Syrus & Arabica impressa,cum non paucis aliis recentioris ævi; sed Vulgatus: o) confusum est vinum, quo convenit MS. Arabicum: כצי אר מסתאר mustum est pudefactum. Nec hodiernis admodum in eo convenit & sunt Rabbinorum Hebraicorum nonnulli,qui utrique significationum congruere statuunt; sic p) R. Tanchum שיון ני ארבי ניו ... [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters]
units.tr: The Chaldee paraphrase has the vines have withered; so also the Syriac and the printed Arabic, with not a few others of more recent date. But the Vulgate has the wine is confounded, in agreement with the Arabic manuscript: kaṣī ar mustaʾār [כצי אר מסתאר], the must is put to shame. Nor do the modern writers agree among themselves on this point, and some of the Hebrew rabbis hold that the word fits both meanings; thus R. Tanchum [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible].

units.la: i. e. sicri potest, ut significet pudorem & confusionem, & sic metaphorica expressio est defectus illorum; & fiers potest, ut significet siccitatem & tabem, ut in Hobushta Neburoth Eiton, exsiccas potentes fluvios Ps. 79,15. qua ratione accipitur ut intransitivum, quantumvis sit conjugationis Hiphil, in qua verba plerumque sunt transitiva.
units.tr: That is, it can signify shame and confusion, and so the expression is a metaphorical defect of those things; and it can signify dryness and wasting, as in Hobushta Neburoth Eiton [הובשתה נהרות איתון], you dried up the mighty rivers, Ps. 79,15. By this reasoning it is taken intransitively, although it is in the Hiphil conjugation, in which verbs are for the most part transitive.

units.la: Et hæc est vocis notatio,quæ cum utrique significationi accommodari possit, diversas in sententias traxit interpretes,quorum quisque eam seligit quæ scopo suo maxime videtur convenire: Quam nostrates alteri præferant, ex textu illorum apparet; Verum ne lectori judicandi atque eligendi præriperent facultatem, margini apposuerunt quoque alteram, quam viri quidam eruditi præhabent,ut vidimus, utpote qui accommode hic autumant describi frustrationem vini, & voluptatis, quam ex eo capiebant,ita ut per metaphoram q) affici dicatur, sicut homines, qui erubescunt ac pudore suffunduntur,quotiescunque earum rerum spe excidunt, quas vel r) expectare erant jussi,vel ipsimet expectabant. Quod porro vocis notatio, quantumvis s) hominibus duntaxat ac sensu & vita præditis creaturis proprie congruat, etiam sensu destitutis per figuram apte possit applicari, manifestum reddunt t) nonnulli ex eo,quod eadem significatione usurpetur Jef.33,9. ubi הִחְאֵי Hecbephir, quæ solummodo
units.tr: And this is the notation of the word. Since it can be applied to either meaning, it has drawn interpreters into different opinions, and each chooses the sense that seems best to suit his purpose. Which sense our countrymen prefer appears from their text. But so that they would not take away the reader's freedom to judge and choose, they placed the other rendering in the margin. Certain learned men hold this in higher regard, as we have seen, since they judge that the frustration of the wine, and of the pleasure men got from it, is fittingly described here. By metaphor, the wine is said to be affected as men are who blush and are suffused with shame whenever they fall from hope of those things which they were either bidden to expect or were themselves expecting. Moreover, although the notation of the word fits properly only to men and to creatures endowed with sense and life, some make it plain that it can also be aptly applied by figure to creatures devoid of sense, since in the same sense it is used at Isaiah 33:9, where הִחְאֵי Hecbephir, which properly means only "to be ashamed," is said of Lebanon, "Lebanon is ashamed."

units.la: r) Et Duacenses. p) Et Kimchi. q) Tanta cultores frustratione deceptæ, ut mendacium suum videantur erubescere. Ruff. Vide sis Kimchi & Druf. r) Lively. s) Sic hoc lo-co accipit Pet. a Fignr. scil. pro causa pudoris,quo suffundebantur illi, qui spe sua excidebant. t) Livel. Bochart. modo notet, pudere, nunquam vero exarescere, dicitur de Lib.mo, Libanum pudet. Verum enim vero, licet quoad sonum illarum significationum quædam sit differentia, quoad sensum tamen aut exilis aut nulla est, quippe vinum pudefactum est, succo uvarum siccatione adeo destituto, ut cultoris expectationem, qua majorem sibi sperabat, quam accipiebat, copiam, protinus explere non potuerit: quocunque igitur sensu id lector acceperit, sive proprio sive improprio, cum utrumque vox ferre non recusat, rei diversitas nulla erit. Caftalio habet, fœdatum vinum, ita scilicet ut exinde pudorem contraherent cultores. אמלל יצהר, Umlal ytshar, Oleum languet, u) vox ea notat الضعف والوهن infirmitatem & languorem ut Abu Walid; vel ut David Kimchi הולשרים וכהתורים infirmitatem & excisionem. Græcus reddit ὠλιγώθη, diminutum esl quantitate, ut & Arabica impressa Chaldæus olivæ deciderunt. Sic etiam w) Buxtorffius. Alii x) defluxerunt olivæ, vel y) Oles, & Mercerus, foliis spoliatæ sunt olivæ; vel ut in notis suis super hunc locum, defluxerunt (foliis scilicet,) oleæ, Vulgatus, elanguit oleum. Syrus olea amputata sunt vel destructa, MS. Arabicum אנקף אלרהן, quod z) præsuppono legendum Enkaffal dohn, ac transferendum, oleum exsiccatum est. Diverse diversi recentiores translatores habent, ut fracuit oleum, excisum est, exterminatum est, infirmatum est, a) deformatum est, b) perit, languit, & elanguit. Paucis, olei c) corruptio indigitari videtur, cujus nec integritas nec quantitas tanta erat, ut pro more usui esset aut fieret vel in sacrificiis, quæ immolabantur Deo, vel in sua ipsorum ratione vivendi. Hæc tria, frumentum, vinum & oleum, cum tanti inter eos essent, ut sine iis nec ea persolvere possent sacrificia, quæ lege erant sancita, & necessario ex iisdem constituebantur; nec vitam agere jucundam, quippe quæ, ut Kimchi ait, רוב חיי האדם maxima pars humanæ vitæ; panis scilicet ad animum corroborandum, u) Vid. Hof. 4, 3. §6) Lex Chald. x) Bib. Polyglot. y) Pet. a Fig. z) Vel potius انقف ut v. 11. infirmatum. a) Drus. b) Fig. a Cast. c) Parum provenit morbo & erubigine corruptis oleis. Pet. a Figuiero. dum, vinum ad exhilarandum, & oleum ad reddendum gratum adspectum, cumque iis privarentur tam misere, non poterat non maxima enascı occasio lugendi, non tantum sacerdotibus & ministris Dei, verum & omnium ordinum inter eos hominibus: Quare eorum conditione hac in re rite proposita, etiam caeterorum mobis statum condocefacit. Ad eos enim suam orationem sequenti commate dirigit, qui rerum illarum cura maxime tanguntur, & in illis praecipue, qui laborem suum iis locant, adjuncta etiam mentione defectus rerum aliarum, quae ad rationem jucunde vivendi summe necessariae sunt.
units.tr: r) The Douai (Duacenses) version too. p) Kimchi too. q) The cultivators are so frustrated and deceived that they seem to be ashamed of their own lie. Ruff. See Kimchi and Drusius. r) Lively. s) Pet. a Figueiredo takes the word in this sense here, namely as the cause of the shame with which those were suffused who fell from their hope. t) Lively, Bochart. The verb to be ashamed is used only of shame, never of to wither, as when Lebanon is ashamed. Yet, although there is some difference between these meanings in sound, in sense it is slight or none. The wine was put to shame, dried up of its juice to such an extent that it could not at once fill the cultivator's expectation, since he hoped for a greater quantity than he received. Therefore, in whatever sense the reader takes it, proper or figurative, since the word admits both, there will be no difference in the matter. Castalio has the wine was defiled, so that the cultivators would thereby incur shame. The Hebrew אמלל יצהר, Umlal ytshar, the oil languishes... The word means, as Abu Walid says, weakness and languor; or, as David Kimchi says, weakness and cutting off. The Greek renders it ὠλιγώθη, it was diminished in quantity, and the printed Arabic and the Chaldean paraphrast the olives fell off. So too Buxtorf. Others the olives dropped off, or the olive trees, and Mercerus the olives were stripped of their leaves; or, as in his notes on this passage, the olive trees dropped off (their leaves, of course); the Vulgate, the oil has languished. The Syriac, the olive trees were cut off or destroyed. The Arabic manuscript has אנקף אלרהן, which I suppose should be read Enkaffal dohn and translated the oil has dried up. Various recent translators have, for example, the oil is broken, cut off, exterminated, weakened, deformed, perished, languished, and has languished. In brief, the corruption of the oil seems to be indicated, neither whole nor so great in quantity that it could be customarily used either in the sacrifices offered to God or in their own manner of living. These three things, grain, wine and oil, were of such importance to them that without them they could neither perform those sacrifices which were ordained by the law and necessarily made from these very things, nor lead a pleasant life, since, as Kimchi says, they are רוב חיי האדם the greater part of human life: bread, namely, to strengthen the heart, wine to gladden, and oil to give a pleasing appearance. And since they were so miserably deprived of these, there could not but arise the greatest occasion for mourning, not only for the priests and ministers of God, but also for men of all ranks among them. Therefore, having properly set out their condition in this matter, he also teaches us the state of the rest. For in the following verse he directs his speech to those who are most affected by the care of these things, and especially to those who let out their labour for them, adding also mention of the lack of other things which are most necessary for living pleasantly.

units.la: 11. Erubescite, agricolae, ejulate, vinitores, propter triticum & propter bordeum: quia messis agri periit.
units.tr: 11. Be ashamed, O farmers; howl, O vinedressers, for the wheat and for the barley: because the harvest of the field has perished.

units.la: 12. Vitis exaruit, & ficus elanguit, malus punica etiam, palma & malus, omnes arbores agri arent, quia gaudium exaruit a filiis hominum.
units.tr: 12. The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languishes; the pomegranate also, the palm tree and the apple tree, all the trees of the field are withered, because joy has dried up from the sons of men.

units.la: {g} Kimchi. {h} Polyglot. {i} Pet. a Fig. {k} Pagn. Tigur. Munst. fit, nulla prorsus est ratio. Probabile quidem videtur eos Coremim pro Ceremim accepisse, verum quod κλήματα sit legendum, non κτήματα, evidens certe non est, cum id autoritate apographorum ullorum notorum non nitatur, imo iisdem potius omnibus, ut & veteri latinæ versioni τῶν LXX. apud Hieronymum contrarietar, qui illud vertit possessiones: id quod ex Arabica quoque manifestum fit, quæ habet, cattel, quod possessionis notione venit, (quantumvis non talem, qualem græca videtur innuere) non vitium propaginum. Præterea eadem vox כרם Cerem, alias quoque vertitur per κτῆμα, ut communiter legunt, quæ græca habemus, apographa. Ita Prov. 31,16. quod in hebræo est כרם נטעה Nateah Cerem, plantat vineam, Græca reddit κατεφύτευσε κτῆμα, plantavit possessionem. Et Hos. 2,15. ubi est כרמיו Carmela, redditum est τὰ κτήματα αὐτῆς, quo in loco legendum putat Drusius κλήματα, vitium propagines, ut hic Mercerus; sed quæ ibi mutandi ratio fuerit, ibi vidimus, & minorem hic esse præsupponimus, quia κτήματα, possessiones, quamvis non simpliciter notent vineas, melius eas exprimit quam ea vox, quæ non nisi plantas ac ramos significat, lecto Cerimim vineas pro Coremim vinitores: Verum cum ita legatur (scil. κτήματα) vel aliter, quæstio oritur, quomodo ea vox sumenda sit? Nimirum utrum regat verbum, an a verbo regatur? Primo modo sumitur, lectione usitata retenta, ejulate o possessiones, sed Cyrillus alia distinctionis ratione adhibita, aliam etiam videtur sequi rationem interpretandi, lugete possessiones, ut hoc ex explicatione ejus clucet, qua procul dubio illum rerum in agris interitum in mærorem injecturum esse eos indicat qui terram colunt. Hujusmodi difficultates ac scrupuli oriuntur ex versione, at evanescunt, si plana reineatur lectio textus hebraici atque eorum interpretatio, qui ei adhærent, ut sunt nostrates & alii.
units.tr: {g} Kimchi. {h} Polyglot. {i} Pet. a Fig. {k} Pagn. Tigur. Munst. It is indeed probable that they read Coremim for Ceremim, but that κλήματα rather than κτήματα should be read is certainly not evident, since it rests on the authority of no known manuscript. Indeed all of them, like the old Latin version of the Seventy that Jerome cites, contradict it. Jerome renders it possessions. This is clear also from the Arabic, which has cattle. That word carries the sense of possession, though not in the way the Greek seems to suggest, and it does not mean vine shoots. Moreover, the same word כרם [kerem] is elsewhere also rendered by κτῆμα [ktēma], as the Greek copies commonly read. Thus at Prov. 31:16, where the Hebrew has נטע כרם [nata kerem], he plants a vineyard, the Greek renders it κατεφύτευσε κτῆμα, he planted a possession. And at Hos. 2:15, where the Hebrew has כרמיו [karmav], it is rendered τὰ κτήματα αὐτῆς [ta ktēmata autēs]. Drusius thinks κλήματα, vine shoots, should be read in that place, as Mercerus does here. But what reason there was for changing it there we have already seen, and we assume the reason is smaller here. For κτήματα, possessions, though it does not simply mean vineyards, expresses them better than that word, which signifies only plants and branches. If one reads Cerimim, vineyards, for Coremim, vinedressers, the matter is different. But however it is read, whether as κτήματα or otherwise, a question arises: how is that word to be taken? Namely, does it govern the verb, or is it governed by the verb? In the first way, keeping the usual reading, it is wail, O possessions. But Cyril, adopting another way of dividing the words, also seems to follow another way of interpreting, mourn, possessions. This is clear from his explanation, in which he indicates that the destruction of the crops in the fields will undoubtedly cast grief upon those who till the land. Difficulties and scruples of this kind arise from the version, but they vanish if the plain reading of the Hebrew text and the interpretation of those who adhere to it are retained, as our own people and others do.

units.la: Qui jubentur ejulare, sunt Coremim, vinitores, quorum possessiones ac emolumenta erant vineæ, in quarum ubere fructuum segete ac incremento omnis erat collocata voluptas ac commodum cuiusque ipsius, tum aliorum, qui una cum ipsis inhabitabant terram ac laborum suorum fructibus gaudebant. Nec deest hic ulterior legendi ratio in sequenti versu, quanquam in præcedentibus plus satis sit exposita, praefigitur tamen, cur praedicti agricolae jubeantur pudeficeri, in hoc versu, videlicet propter triticum & propter hordeum &c. frumentis praecipuis hominum usui destinatis, in quorum cultura agricolarum cura consistit, & ex quorum grato incremento spes omnis & patrimonium dependet, adeo devastatis (ut retineamus sensum literalem praedictum) l) a locustis & aliis noxiis creaturis supra recenfitis (vel ut alii ab hostibus) ut nulla omnino fructuum colligendorum messis fit expectanda, gravis nascitur causa, ut pudore fuffundantur ac confundantur, qui talibus omnibus perditis spe sua frustrati sunt, etsi ad totum etiam regionis populum ea respicere nullus dubitaverit, qui jacturam omnium rerum ad vitam necessariarum confiderraverit, ita ut gravem ac generalem hic depingat calamitatem, qua omnes eo redigere vult, ut eam advertant, tanquam signum irae divinae, quam sibi accersiverant, praesertim cum & aliorum fructuum, quorum jacturam vel corruptionem vinitores jubentur dolere, in sequentibus mentio fiat. Latet interea prorsus, quam ob rationem LXX. haec verba קצִיר שְׂדֵה Ketfir Sadeh, messis agri per vindemiam reddiderint τρυγητος εκ αγρου. Et Arabica impressa الغطّاى vindemia periit ex agro. Quamvis enim generalis fit messis significatio & ad collectionem omnium fructuum, ut uvarum &c. extendi patiatur, magis tamen proprie ac ftrictius, quod apparet, hic sumitur pro collectione & meffione tritici & hordei, circa quae אכָּרִים Iccarim vel agricolae inprimis sunt occupati atque ideo in specie jubentur pudefieri ἐπὶ πυρῶν καὶ κριθῆς, ut Graeca versio habet, propter triticum & hordeum. Prorsus enim persuasum habeo, non bene intellexisse haec verba Arabem qui LXX. sequitur, cum sensu omnino corrupto legat plus quam triticum & hordeum; Perspicuum magis est, atque cum textu hebraico plus convenientiae habet in his omnibus MS. Arabicum propter triticum & hordeum, videntes messem agri periisse: ita ut haec ver-
units.tr: Those who are bidden to wail are the Coremim, "vinedressers," whose possessions and gains were their vineyards. In the abundance of their fruit and the growth of the vines lay all their pleasure and profit, and also the welfare of others who lived with them in the land and rejoiced in the fruits of their labours. Here too there is a further reason for the reading in the following verse, although enough has been said of the preceding verses. It is set out, however, why these farmers are bidden to be ashamed in this verse, namely "because of the wheat and because of the barley," etc., the principal grains destined for human use, in whose cultivation the farmers' care consists, and on whose welcome growth all their hope and livelihood depend. These have been so devastated (to keep to the literal sense stated above) by locusts and other harmful creatures mentioned above (or, as others say, by enemies) that no harvest of fruit at all is to be expected. This brings about a grave cause for them to be covered with shame and confounded, since they have been disappointed in their hope by the loss of all these things. Yet no one doubts that he also has in view the whole population of the region, all who consider the loss of everything necessary to life. So he depicts a grave and general calamity, to which he wishes to bring them all, so that they may take notice of it as a sign of the divine anger which they had brought upon themselves. This is especially so because mention is made in what follows of other fruits, the loss or spoiling of which the vinedressers are bidden to lament. Meanwhile it is entirely hidden why the Seventy rendered the words קצִיר שְׂדֵה (Ketfir Sadeh), "the harvest of the field," as τρυγητος εκ αγρου [trygētos ek agrou], "the vintage from the field." And the printed Arabic has, "the vintage has perished from the field." For although the general meaning of harvest is allowed to extend to the gathering of all fruits, such as grapes, it is here taken more properly and strictly, as is evident, for the gathering and reaping of wheat and barley, with which the farmers in particular are occupied; therefore they are especially bidden to be ashamed, ἐπὶ πυρῶν καὶ κριθῆς [epi pyrōn kai krithēs], "because of the wheat and barley," as the Greek version has it. For I am fully persuaded that the Arab who follows the Seventy did not understand these words well, since he reads "more than wheat and barley," which gives an entirely corrupt sense. The Arabic manuscript, "because of the wheat and barley, seeing the harvest of the field perished," is clearer and agrees more with the Hebrew text in all these respects. So these words...

units.la: l) Druc. Dan.
units.tr: l) Druc. Dan.

units.la: verba proprie respiciant agricolas, vel terræ cultores; vinitores vero sequentia, nempe vitis exaruit, ubi idem rursus occurrit verbum, quod non ita multum ante, videlicet הובִיש Hobifch, quod v. 10. translatum est notione exarescendi, & in margine erubescendi, quæ ultima significatio etiam retinetur v. 11. eandemque hic ferre posse, quam ibi, annotat R. Tanchum juxta cum aliis. Nihil tamen prohibet ejus decisio, quin diverse diversis transferatur. Noftratibus placet, exaruit, m) aliis pudefactla est. Ita Vulgatus: n) vinea confusa est: Sic MS. Arabicum vitis erubuit: & recentiorum Drufius: vitem pudet, nam, inquit, succo suo & fructu spoliatæ vites quasi erubescunt, ut homines solent, cum illis mali aliquid præter opinionem accidit; vel cum spe sua, qua aluntur, excidunt. Quod etiam sic accipi posset, ut pudorem o) injecisse diceretur culturibus suis, qui sua, quam de ea conceperant, fructrati sunt spe & expectatione. Nil interim patitur damni, in injuriæ sensus, quamcunque significationem elegeris, sive erubescendi metaphoricam, sive propriam exarescendi, quippe nil nisi defectus fructuum innuitur, cum vitis exarescens liquore suo proficuo privatur, atque exinde suboritur pudor. Et ficus אמללה Umlalah, languet; eadem itērum vox, quæ ante v. 10. noftratibusque non secus atque antea reddita. Quomodo ab aliis alii differant ibi probe observavimus, quibus insuper addendum, quod eodem modo hic reddant interpretes, quo reddiderunt ibi. Sic faciunt LXX. Arabica impressa, Syrus, Vulgatus, & Chaldæus utroque in loco eadem voce utitur, quod & recentioribus nonnullis proprium, ut verbum mutent; p) alii immutata sensus integritate. MS. Arabicum habet Encafaphat (quod interpreteris, debilis est vel fractla) atque sic arbitror oportuisse scriptum extare etiam v. 10. etli in eo apographo, quo utor, deest una litera in Enkaffa. Expedit explicationem adducere, quam tradit horum verborum Drufius; præsertim cum optime congruat vocis notationi: Succo ficus omni exsuctlo ficus ipsa elanguet, m) Ita LXX. Chaldæus, Syr. Arab. impref. & diversi recentiores. Merc. Dagn. n) Duac. o) Pet. a Fig. Confidit, & pudefecit eos, & eorum spes frustrata est. p) Ita Pagninus v. 10. exsiccatum est oleum, v. 12. ficus desolata est, v. 12. ficulnea encrbata est. guet, i. e. debilis ac infirma relicta est, nec amplius usum fui praebet. Sic vitis languere dicitur Jesa. 24,7. & terra 33,9. Hiisce subjunguntur ad indicandum instans malum, diversae aliae arbores, quarum fructus etsi ad sustentandum adeo necessarii non sunt, q) delectamento tamen ac commodo hominibus esse constat, nempe malus punica, etiam palma & malus, nec non arbores agri arent. Harum destructio tanquam causa adducitur, quare vinitoribus lugendum sit, quia illorum s) curae ac inspectioni erant demandatae una cum vineis harum omnium praestantissimis, earumque fructibus, quos & in suum & omnium hujus terrae incolarum colligebant ac dispensabant usum. De his omnibus dicit יבשו Jabeshu, quod exaruerint, torruerint, defloruerint, juxta sententiam quorundam pernitie assectae, quae a t) locustis & aliis noxiis animalculis illis inferebatur. Abarbanel hinc sumit argumentum contra eos, qui hoc & cetera mala ab animalculis supra dictis illata fuisse putant, quia verum non sit, totas illas exedere arbores, etsi foliis infensae sint atque fructibus. Doctissimus autem Bochartus exprobrat ipsi horum animalculorum naturae ac mali ignorantiam, quod inferre posse aliis observatum est. Cujus generis inter plures citat auctorem Arabem Al-Damiri, cujus verba, juxta ejus apographum, de locustis haec sunt: لعابه سم ناقع ولا يقع علي شي منه الا اهلكه admodum validum quod earum sputum, vel humor, venenum fit plantis & arboribus & non ingrediatur illarum quandam, quin eas destruat (meum apographum tantum habet لعابه سم ناقع ولا يقع علي شي الا اهلكه sputum est venenum admodum validum, quod nihil contingit quin id destruat) Quorum confirmationem ex Pisida petit, qui eodem modo affirmat, quod arbores juxta ac fructus reddant marcescentes acaridos, nec sibi aliter visum esse innuit, quam de ea noxa hic sermonem esse, quam fructibus terrae ac arboribus illae beltiolae intulerant. Utcunque vero haec sint, quaecunque demum instrumenta, tanta hinc calamitate superfusa erat tota terra, ut pudoris
units.tr: The words properly refer to the farmers, or cultivators of the land; but the following words, the vine is dried up, refer to the vinedressers. Here the same word occurs again that was used not long before, namely Hobifch, which at v. 10 is rendered in the sense of drying up, and in the margin being ashamed. This latter meaning is also kept at v. 11. R. Tanchum notes, together with others, that it can bear here the same meaning it has there. Nothing, however, prevents its being rendered differently in different places. Our people prefer dried up, others was put to shame. So the Vulgate: the vine is confounded. So the Arabic manuscript: the vine blushed. Among recent writers Drusius has: the vine is ashamed; for, he says, vines stripped of their sap and fruit blush, as men do when some misfortune befalls them contrary to expectation, or when they fall from the hope by which they were sustained. This could also be understood to mean that shame was cast upon its cultivators, who were cheated of the hope and expectation they had conceived of it. In the meantime no harm is done in the sense of injury, whichever meaning you choose, whether the metaphorical being ashamed or the literal drying up; for only the lack of fruit is signified, since a withering vine is deprived of its useful liquor, and shame arises from this. And the fig tree umlalah languishes: the same word again, rendered by our people no differently than before at v. 10. We have carefully observed above how others differ from one another there; to these must be added that the interpreters here render it in the same way they rendered it there. So the Seventy do; the printed Arabic, the Syriac, the Vulgate, and the Chaldee use the same word in both places, which some recent writers also do, changing the word, while others keep the sense intact. The Arabic manuscript has Encafaphat (which you may render is weak or broken), and I think that in the copy I use, where one letter is missing in Enkaffa, it ought to have been written so at v. 10 as well. It is useful to adduce the explanation Drusius gives of these words, especially since it agrees very well with the meaning of the word: with the juice of the fig completely drawn out, the fig itself languishes. So the Seventy, the Chaldee, the printed Syriac and Arabic, and various recent writers. Mercerus, Dagnaeus, Duaceni, Pet. a Fig.: it is confident, and has put them to shame, and its hopes have been frustrated. Pagninus at v. 10: the oil has been dried up; at v. 12: the fig is desolate; at v. 12: the fig tree has withered. Languishes, that is, is left weak and infirm, and no longer offers its use. So the vine is said to languish at Isaiah 24:7, and the land at 33:9. To these are added, to indicate the impending evil, other kinds of trees, whose fruits, though not so necessary for sustenance, are known to be a delight and benefit to men: namely the pomegranate, also the palm and the apple, and likewise the trees of the field, which are dried up. Their destruction is adduced as the cause why the vinedressers must mourn, because the care and oversight of all these, especially the vines and their fruits, had been entrusted to them, which they gathered and distributed for their own use and that of all the inhabitants of this land. Of all these it is said Jabeshu, that they have dried up, scorched, lost their bloom, according to the opinion of some, in the ruin that was brought on them by locusts and other harmful little creatures. Abarbanel takes from this an argument against those who think this and the other evils were inflicted by the little creatures mentioned above, because it is not true that they eat up those trees entirely, although they are hostile to the leaves and fruit. But the most learned Bochart reproaches him for his ignorance of the nature and harm of these creatures, which has been observed to be a fault in others too. Among several of this kind he cites the Arabic author Al-Damiri, whose words about locusts, according to his copy, are these: [Arabic] the spittle of it is a very strong poison, and it does not fall upon anything of it without destroying it. (My copy has only [Arabic] its spittle is a very strong poison, which does not fall upon anything without destroying it.) He seeks confirmation of this from Pisida, who in the same way affirms that trees as well as fruits are rendered withering and mildewed, and he indicates that it seemed to him that the harm spoken of here is the harm those little beasts inflicted on the fruits of the land and the trees. However these things may be, and whatever the instruments were, the whole land was so overwhelmed by this great calamity that the cause of shame and sorrow clearly pertains

units.la: q) Tarnov. s) Ar. Mont. Per. a Fig. t) Sic Hieronymus hunc locum accipit. u) Impressum est in exemplari suo لبابان at perperam mea sententia. ris ac mœroris causam non tantum ad agricolas & vinitores,qui hic inprimis nominantur, cum eos immediate concernat illarum cura, spectare manifestum fit,sed ad incolas, quotquot erant hujus terrae ad unum omnes, quia, inquit, gaudium exaruit a filiis hominum. Particula כי noftratibus & w) aliis redditur quia,aliis x) imo , y) aliis sane, certe , z) aliis ideo, Münstero,ut scilicet arescat gaudium &c. Quae cum has ac similes notiones particula recipiat,quamcunque denique selegeris, perparum diversitatis adferet & connexioni horum verborum cum praecedentibus, & rationi qua praecedentia inferuntur; omnes vero in eo conveniunt dictae calamitatis gravitatem notari, qua omne genus populorum in ea terra erat obruendum,causamque innui gravissimam, cur acerbissimo affici deberent luctu,five intueare duntaxat praecedentia verba, quibus ad luctum monentur agricolae & vinitores, five quae v.3. extant, ubi in genere jubentur ejulare propter ea mala, quae & antea jamjam erant descripta, & aliis porro intermixta, & de novo jam repetita. Quod attinet ad ea verba, gaudium exaruit, eadem hic occurrit nobis ambigua vox, quae antea, nimirum הבִּישׁ Hobbish: quare locum etiam hic habet, quod R. Tanchum ante notaverat eam a) posse sumi notatione الخرى Chazyio, pudoris vel pudore suffundi, atque inde notare الانقطاع وا لسعم defectum & privationem, vel aliter, nimirum significatione الجفاف exarescendi, quod variarum in variis versionibus translationum dedit occasionem. Vetus latina videtur eam accepisse priori significatione,cum reddat, b) confusum est gaudium a filiis hominum. Eadem ante eam sumunt illam LXX, sed diversa constructione, χαρὰ χαρὰν οἱ υἱοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, (quos sequitur Arabica impressa الإنسان الذي quia filii hominis pudore affecerunt gaudium (vel posuerunt in pudorem) qua in translatione Mercerus putat Hobifch forma passiva acceptum. Atque tum ita accipiendum esse arbitror,ac si verba hebraica haberent,gaudium positum est in pudorem a vel per filios hominum, qua
units.tr: q) Tarnov. s) Ar. Mont. Per. a Fig. t) So Jerome takes this passage. u) It is printed in his copy as lababan, but wrongly, in my opinion. The cause of shame and sorrow is clearly not limited to the farmers and vinedressers, who are named first because the care of those crops concerns them directly, but extends to the inhabitants, all of them without exception throughout the land: because, he says, joy has dried up among the sons of men. Our translators render the particle ki [כי] as because; others as indeed, surely, certainly; others as therefore; Münster as so that, namely, joy may wither, and so on. Whichever of these senses and similar ones the particle receives, and whichever you choose, it makes little difference to the connection of these words with what precedes and to the reasoning by which the preceding words are supported. All of them agree, however, that they note the gravity of the said calamity, by which every class of people in that land was to be overwhelmed, and they indicate the most serious cause why they ought to be struck with the bitterest grief. This holds whether you look only at the preceding words, in which the farmers and vinedressers are urged to mourn, or at what follows in verse 3, where in general they are ordered to wail over those evils which have already been described and mixed with others, and are now repeated anew. As for the words joy has dried up, the same ambiguous word meets us here as before, namely הבִּישׁ Hobbish. Hence it also applies here what R. Tanchum had earlier noted, that it can be taken in the sense of al-khazy, to be covered with shame or to blush, and from this mean al-inqita' and wa-l-sam', defect and privation; or otherwise, namely in the sense of al-jafaf, to dry up, which has given occasion for various renderings in various translations. The old Latin seems to have taken it in the former sense, since it renders b) the joy has been confounded by the sons of men. The Seventy took it in the same way beforehand, but with a different construction, χαρὰ χαρὰν οἱ υἱοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων [joy, joy, the sons of men], which the printed Arabic follows: because the sons of man have put joy to shame (or have brought it to shame), a translation in which Mercerus thinks Hobbish was taken in the passive form. I think it should then be understood as if the Hebrew words read: joy has been put to shame by, or through, the sons of men, in which way also the Latin Vulgate may be construed.

units.la: {b} Vulg. Lat. Jun. Chal. Syr. MS. Arab. ܐܠܐ ecce quando. x) Pisc. Tarnov. y) Merc.
units.tr: {b} Vulgate, Old Latin, Junius, Chaldee, Syriac, MS, Arabic. The Syriac word 'ala, meaning behold, when. x) Pisc. Tarnov. y) Merc.

units.la: * z) Grot. a) Et sic Kimchi. b) Ita & Duacenses. qua ratione & Latinus Vulgatus possit construi. Ab alijs tamen plerumque alio modo accipitur, prout mox sumus tradituři; obiter autem annotasse juvabit aliam viam, quam ingreditur Ludovicus Capellus ad componendum LXX. cum Hebraeo. Supponit enim eos pro הבישׁ Hobish (a יבש jebash) in singulari numero, legisse הבישו hobishu, quasi a ביש Bosh, & in plurali numero, atque in sequentibus, מן בני אדם Min bene Adam, a filiis hominum, praetermisisse praepositionem מן min a; sed planior videtur conciliandi ratio prior, quippe quae non exigit tam enervem ac firmi parum habentem legendi differentiam, quam haec, in qua irregularis tantum est usus verbi הבישׁ Hobish, quo forma passiva exprimitur, cum aliis intransitive accipiatur, sicut R. Tanchum observat hic esse דאתי Dhati intransitivum, nec alia ratione acceptum Vulgato vulgo advertitur, cum consusum est nihil aliud latine significet quam pudet vel pudefit, & in filiis hominum reddatur, a filiis hominum, non per filios hominum. d) Horum vero interpretum, qui hanc interpretationem approbant, eo redit sententia, gaudium insueta rerum bonarum jactura, ut hordei ac vini aliorumque fructuum terrae, quorum ubere proventu soliti erant gaudere atque jam expectabant, ut gaudio exinde perfunderentur, esse quasi pudefactum ut sese illis offerret vel recipi ab eis expectaret. In eandem sententiam vergunt & caeterae talium tum antiquiorum, tum recentiorum interpretum versiones, ut est MS. Arabici quandoquidem gaudium pudefactum est a filiis hominum, quae eandem vocabuli significationem retinent; & Drusii, Puduit gaudium a filiis hominum. Eadem notione habet etiam Caftalio: foedata humani generis voluptate, i. e. quo antea erant gavisi, eo jam erant pudefacti. At qui recentissimi sunt interpretum, alteram cum nostratibus praeferunt significationem, scilicet, e) exarserunt; exarescentibus etenim hordeo, vitibus, olivis & aliis fructiferis arboribus, totoque denique campo, ut scriptum extat, commodedici
units.tr: * z) Grotius. a) So also Kimchi. b) So also the Douai translators, by which reasoning the Latin Vulgate too could be construed. Others, however, mostly take it in another way, as we shall presently set out; but it will be helpful to note in passing the other route that Louis Cappel takes in order to reconcile the Seventy with the Hebrew. For he supposes that they, for הבישׁ Hobish (from יבש jebash) in the singular, read הבישׁו hobishu, as if from ביש Bosh, in the plural, and in what follows, מן בני אדם Min bene Adam, from the sons of men, that they omitted the preposition מן min, from. But the former explanation seems the plainer way of reconciling them, since it does not require so weak a difference of reading, one that has little support, as this one, in which there is only an irregular use of the verb הבישׁ Hobish, which expresses the passive form, while it is taken by others intransitively, just as R. Tanchum observes that here דאתי Dhati is intransitive. Nor is it taken in any other way by the common Vulgate reading, since confusum est means nothing else in Latin than is ashamed or is put to shame, and in filiis hominum is rendered from the sons of men, not through the sons of men. d) Now the sense that those interpreters who approve this rendering arrive at is this: joy, through the unaccustomed loss of good things, such as barley and wine and the other fruits of the earth, in whose rich yield they were accustomed to rejoice and which they were now expecting so that they would be filled with joy from them, has been put to shame, as though it presented itself or awaited to be received by them. To the same effect also incline the other versions of such interpreters, both older and more recent, such as the Arabic manuscript, since joy has been put to shame by the sons of men, which retain the same meaning of the word; and Drusius, joy has been ashamed by the sons of men. Castalio also has the same sense: the pleasure of the human race being spoiled, that is, those by whom they had formerly been gladdened were now put to shame. But the most recent interpreters prefer, with our people, the other meaning, namely e) have been scorched; for with the barley, vines, olives and other fruit-bearing trees withering, and indeed the whole field, as is written, it is fitting to say

units.la: {e} Ouomvis ex eo, quod ante a nobis dictum est, luculenter appareat eodem redire ac minus difficultatis ac immutationis habere, si retineatur Hobuhu, cum ceteri sensu utuntur, atque Hebuhu. &) Mercer. pudet audium conspectus hemiaum. Ita Ribera, Menach, Tigurus, Tarnov. e) Pag. Munst. Tig. dici potest gaudium, f) quod ex florenti illorum statu capiebant, g) exaruisse ab illis. Quomodocunque autem sumseris eam vocem ex sua literali ac propria significatione, quod ad sensum attinet, eo spectare utramque ejus significationem patet,ut cessaturum illud gaudium indicet, quo plerumque perfundebantur,imo cui jamjam inhiabant, fi rerum fuisset ordinarius status & Deus faustos esse juffifset & illos & illorum regionem. Ita & Paraphraftes Chaldæus [Syriac/Hebrew text] &c. quia gaudium cessavit (vel) defecit a filiis hominum; ipseque Hieronymus, qui habet confusum est, idem tamen esse quoad sensum,quam auferri, putat.
units.tr: {e} Although it is clear from what I said earlier that the sense comes to the same thing, and that there is less difficulty and less need to change the text if we keep Hobuhu in the sense the others use, as well as Hebuhu, &) Mercer: "the joy has been put to shame at the sight of the people." So Ribera, Menach, Tigurinus and Tarnovius. e) Pagninus, Münster, Tigurinus: the joy may be called f) that which they drew from their flourishing state, g) which has dried up from them. However you take the word from its literal and proper meaning, as far as the sense goes it is plain that both of its meanings point to a joy that will cease, which they were used to feel in great measure, indeed one they were already yearning for, if the course of things had been normal and God had made both them and their country prosperous. So also the Chaldee paraphrast: [Syriac/Hebrew text], "because the joy has ceased (or) has failed from the sons of men." Jerome, who has "has been confounded," nevertheless thinks this amounts in sense to the same as "has been taken away."

units.la: Per filios hominis hic h) quidam intelligunt incolas hujus regionis, quæ ea calamitate atque mœrore superfundebatur. Verum generaliter hoc trahi posse ad omnia nil est,quod vetat; causa etenim universali existente atque ad quovis genus omnium terræ partium spectante, effectus etiam nonnisi universalis esse potest,quo omnia gaudio esse privata dicenda sint. Abarbinel vero,qui ab inimicis hæc omnia esse illata statuit,nationem per illos intelligit,quæ adducebatur in captivitatem [Hebrew text], derelicta &i) dolens spiritu.
units.tr: Some here understand by sons of man h) the inhabitants of this region, which was overwhelmed by this calamity and grief. But nothing forbids that this be applied generally to all things; for if the cause is universal and bears on every part of the earth, the effect too can only be universal, so that all may be said to be deprived of joy. Abarbanel, however, who holds that all these things were brought on them by enemies, understands by these the nation that was led into captivity [Hebrew text], forsaken and i) grieving in spirit.

units.la: 13. Accingite vos & plangite sacerdotes, ejulate miniftri altaris: ingredimini, pernoctate in sacco, miniftri Dei mei: quoniam interiit sacrificium & libatio de Domo Dei vestri.
units.tr: 13. Gird yourselves and lament, ye priests; howl, ye ministers of the altar: come, lie all night in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God: for the meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of your God.

units.la: Quanquam in præcedentibus,excepto quod hic versus cum 5, 8, & 12. contineat adhortationem,non adeo admonitionis ad pœnitentiam habeatur ratio,quam quidem k) farcafticæ cujusdam exprobrationis atque declarationis, quem lugubrem in statum incidissent vel reservarentur, quid jam sufferrent vel sufferendum iis in posterum effet, quodque nulla amplius superesset spes emendandi ac excitandi eos ex gravi stupiditatis somno; extra omnem controversiam tamen positum
units.tr: Although in what precedes, apart from the fact that this verse with 5, 8 and 12 contains an exhortation, no great account is taken of admonition to repentance; indeed there is a certain sarcastic rebuke and declaration of the grievous state into which they had fallen or were reserved, what they would now have to suffer or what was to be their lot in future, and that no hope remained of their amending and rousing themselves from the heavy sleep of stupidity. Yet, beyond all controversy, k)

units.la: f) Pfal. 4,7. Jer. 9,3. 16,10. & Jer. 48,33. g) Gaudium μετουυμιχῶς pro illis rebus ponitur, ex quibus gaudium capiebatur, Livel. h) Bifc. i) Jef. 54,6. k) Mercer. in v. 5. positum arbitror,feriam hic sisti eorum hortationem,ut de remediis in tempore sibi prospicerent,quibus averterent mala,quæ iis aut impendebant, aut jamjam eos invaserant.
units.tr: f) Ps. 4:7; Jer. 9:3; 16:10; Jer. 48:33. g) Joy is here put metonymically for the things from which joy was drawn; Livel. h) Bisc. i) Isa. 54:6. k) Mercer on v. 5. I think it settled that their exhortation should stop here, so that they might take thought in time for remedies with which to avert the evils that either hung over them or had already all but overtaken them.

units.la: Accingite vos ipsos) i. e. ut ait R. Tanchum,cui suffragantur non tantum Judæorum nonnulli, sed & alii l) simili modo, שקיים faccis, vel amicite vos ipsos saccis, quæ vox supplenda videatur ex v.8: הגורת שש Cherugah fak, accinctiacco, vel ex sequentibus hujus versus, quia expressum est in לינו בשקיים linu befackum, pernoctate in sacco; quamvis aliis sensus appareat integer fine ullo supplemento, nimirum m) Festinate,scilicet ad id faciendum quod in proximis verbis exprimitur, n) vel parate vos ad planctum, fatis accommodate ad eum sensum, quo fe ipsos accingere fæpiufcule dicuntur quialiquam rem aggrediuntur; licet nullum idoneum vocis sic usitatæ exemplum in ea materia prostare o) alii contendant. Verum enim vero,planiorem plerique statuunt esse priorem interpretandi modum; quid? quod sint ex recentioribus non minus ac ex antiquioribus interpretibus,qui expresse adjiciunt vocem sacco, tanquam necessario in Hebræo fubintelligendam. Ita Syrus ... facerdotes, accinginmini saccis. MS. Arabicum ... circumcingite vos saccis; & Munfterus: accingimini saccis: is nimirum erat olim habitus lugentibus atque pœnitentibus,ut ex sacræ scripturæ formulis multiplicibus non obscure colligitur,ita,ut præfixam eis ipse cingendi admonitionem immediate sequatur excitatio ad planegendum & ejulandum, non secus atque Jerem. 4,8. ubi pari ratione duo actus conjunguntur שקיים Sakkim, quæ hic vox folummodo fubintelligitur. Admonentur vero idcirco eorum,quia sunt insignia externa interni doloris, externusque hominis habitus,posthabitis omnibus aliis incitamentis, inservit producendis atque inflammandis cordis, ubi gignuntur primo,affectibus & ad humilitatem plurimum conducit, qua fine omnes certe istæ externæ actiones nihil valent. Quos hic vocat ad pœnitentiæ signa edendum,sunt Sacerdotes,vel aliis verbis in eandem sententiam, ministri altaris, qui scilicet altari infer-
units.tr: Gird yourselves) That is, as R. Tanchum says, l) whom not only some Jews but others also support in a similar way: שקיים sakkim, wrap yourselves in sackcloth, which word seems to be supplied from v. 8: הגורת שק chagurah saq, girded with sackcloth, or from what follows in this verse, since it is expressed in לינו בשקים linu bassakim, lie all night in sackcloth; although to others the sense appears complete without any supplement, namely m) Hasten, that is, to do what is expressed in the following words, n) or prepare yourselves for lamentation, quite suitable to the sense in which people are said to gird themselves when they undertake something; although others maintain that no suitable example of the word used in this way is to be found in such a context. Yet most hold the former way of interpreting to be the plainer. Why, there are among the more recent interpreters, no less than among the older ones, those who expressly add the word sackcloth, as if it must be understood in the Hebrew. So the Syriac: "Priests, gird yourselves with sackcloth." The Arabic manuscript: "gird yourselves with sackcloth"; and Münster: "gird yourselves with sackcloth." This was clearly the dress of mourners and penitents of old, as is not obscurely gathered from the many formulas of Holy Scripture. So the admonition to gird themselves is immediately followed by the call to lament and howl, just as in Jer. 4:8, where for the same reason two acts are joined, שקים sakkim, which word here is only to be understood. They are admonished of this, however, because these are the outward marks of inward grief, and an outward habit of the man, which, all other incitements set aside, serves to produce and kindle the affections of the heart, where they are first engendered, and contributes much to humility, without which all those outward actions are certainly worth nothing. Those whom he here calls to show the signs of repentance are priests, or in other words to the same effect, ministers of the altar, who, that is, served at the altar

units.la: l) Aben-Ezra,Kimchi. m) Calvin. n) Druf. o) Tarnov.
units.tr: l) Ibn Ezra, Kimchi. m) Calvin. n) Drusius. o) Tarnovius.

units.la: inservicbant {p} (1 Cor. 9,13.) atque ibi sacrorum curam gerebant; quorum officium in eo consistebat, ut sacrificia immolarent iisque omnibus rite fungerentur, quæ lege erant sancita atque ad cultum Dei præstandum in unctâ iis, qui sacerdotes erant; quos pariter in sequentibus nuncupat Ministros Dei sui, vos ministri Dei mei, illius Dei; cui non sicut c: teri fucata sed bona fide Propheta serviebat; fuique Dei, a quo p) missus ad illos erat hoc nuncio; vel q) Dei mei, apud quem ego pro vobis intercedam. LXX. omittunt hic præfixum mei. Illorum erat r) victimas offerre pro peccatis propriis æque ac populi, ac pro illis intercedere; atque hinc est quod exemplo præire pœnitentiæ signis jubeantur. Illi enim, ut sequacem haberent populum, debebant se accingere, plangere, & ejulare, quod ne perfunctorie ac leviter, sed ex animo atque serio agerent, compellat eos porro in sequentibus: Ingredimini, pernoctate in sacco ministri Dei mei. בֹּאוּ Bou Venite. Hoc verbum nonnullis non minus ac aliis exhortationis particula videtur, qua s) excitantur illi ad id probe efficiendum, quod jubentur communate proximo. Alii proprie reddunt verbo veniendi vel intrandi nimirum t) in atrium templi, ut ibi hoc, tanquam in loco huic rei proprie dicato, peragerent. hoc est, ut ibi pernoctarent in sacco, non vero abicerent eum vel desinerent lugere, Kimchi, Druf.
