Accommodutis erat hic locus suis affectibus serio & infucate indulgendis, quippe Deus peculiari ratione ibi adesse pollicitus fuerat, nec aliud habitus lugubris aliquantum continuatus & stabilis indicare poterat, quam quod serio & omni fuco posthabito ad animam vocabant mala quæ peccatis suis meruerant.
units.tr: served (1 Cor. 9:13) and there had charge of the sacred things. Their office consisted in offering sacrifices and duly performing all those duties which the law had enjoined and which were committed to those who were priests in order to render worship to God. These the Prophet likewise names in what follows: ministers of his God, you ministers of my God, that God, to whom the Prophet did not serve with feigned devotion as others did, but in good faith; and of his God, by whom he was sent to them with this message; or of my God, before whom I intercede for you. The LXX omit the prefixed my here. It was their task to offer victims for their own sins as well as for the people's, and to intercede for them; and hence it is that they are ordered to lead the way by the signs of repentance. For in order to have a people following them, they had to gird themselves, lament and howl; and that they might do this not perfunctorily and lightly, but from the heart and in earnest, he goes on in what follows to address them: Come, lie all night in sackcloth, ministers of my God. בֹּאוּ bo'u, come. This word seems to some no less than another particle of exhortation, by which they are roused to carry out thoroughly what they are commanded to do together. Others take the word properly as coming or entering, namely t) into the court of the temple, so that they might carry this out there, as in a place specially dedicated to the purpose; that is, so that they might lie there all night in sackcloth, and not cast it off or cease to mourn; Kimchi, Drusius. This place was suited to indulging their feelings seriously and without pretence, since God had promised especially to be present there; nor could a mourning habit, kept up somewhat continuously and steadily, indicate anything else than that they were calling upon the evils their sins had deserved, in earnest and with all pretence set aside.

units.la: Quam gravis illis causa esset ita actiones suas intendendi & inpœnitentiæ signis aliquandiu perseverandi, prout jubentur accingendi se, plangendi, ejulandi, & pernoctandi in sacco phrasibus, quæ sequuntur, optime declarant. Nimirum calamitatis gravitas erat, quam sibi accerciverant peccando, nam interiit sacrificium & libatio de domo Dei nostri. Eandem fere expressionem habemus v. 9. id tantum interest, quod hic dicatur intercidisse, יִכְרְתוּ Nimna, quod ibi הכרית Hocrat succi-
units.tr: How grave the cause was for them to direct their actions this way and to persist for some time in the signs of repentance, the phrases that follow, in which they are commanded to gird themselves, lament, howl, and lie all night in sackcloth, make very clear. Namely, the gravity of the calamity they had brought on themselves by sinning: for the meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of your God. We have almost the same expression in v. 9. The only difference is that here it is said to be cut off, יִכְרְתוּ yikhretu, which there is הכרית hokrit

units.la: p) Calvin. Tarnov. q) Merc. Tarnov. r) Heb. 7,27. s) Merc. Druf. t) Iatra בית in domum Dei, scil. in atrium templi, ut ibi Deum invocetis. Pisc. succisum esse,eadem utrobique sententia eodemque designandi illorum defectum fine; quodque hic addatur affixum Dei Vestri,quod minus ibi; quæ hic adjecisse ulteriori verborum explicatione nos exsolvet,quæ satis luculenter ibi tradita est. Quando se Deum illorum vocat, in mentem illis revocare videtur relationem,quæ cum illis sibi intercesserat propinquior, qua ad se ipsum eos traxerat ex omni populo peculiariter sibi eligens,ut servirent aræ suæ atque omnia curarent,quæ ad suum cultum rite præstandum pertinebant,fruerentur queiis peractis,quæ in ara fuerant oblata. Ita ut expressa his verbis calamitas, nam interiit sacrificium & libatio de domo Dei Vestri, præcipue eos videatur spectare, causaque lugendi orta tum ex zelo, quo flagrandum illis erat pro cultu divino,qui hac ratione interturbabatur,tum quod neque ipsis templi sacrorumque ministeria suggererent ad domesticos sumtus necessaria, quæ pro locato servitio a Deo illis erant hastenus delegata ac concessa. Quomodo hæc sacrificia interierint de domo Dei illorum, luculenter ante vidimus,eorum scilicet fructuum absumtione id factum esse,ex quibus conficiuntur, & annonæ caritate per dicta animalcula voracia facta, cujus hæc verba descriptionem ulteriorem tradere jure merito dixeris. Abarbinel vero ea, quam introspeximus, ratione, templi,domus Dei destructionem hic minatum esse Prophetam putat,quo destructo omnia sacrificia simul succidi ac cessare necesse sit,quod debebant lugere ולא תורה זאת באמרו כי אכם בחרכן הבירית ובית העבירה, & hoc (inquit) non revera fiebat; sed per destructionem domus Dei,& cessationem necessariam cultus ejus. Sed,ut jam ante ad v. 9. annotavimus atque Bocharto observatum est, videntur hæc verba potius contrarium innuere, quippe factum erat aut futurum, (ν) præterito pro futuro sumto) quod hic dicitur, cum domus Dei, in qua hæc sacrificia pro cultu divino erant immolanda,adhuc consisteret integra; & quoniam gravi ex penuria ac defectu rerum ad ea necessariarum destituebantur immolandis Sacerdotes, quorum erat ea offerre; nil sacrificii,nil libationis habentes, x) se ipsos ut immolarent, admonentur, utque sese sistant altari tanquam sacrificium
units.tr: p) Calvin, Tarnovius. q) Mercer, Tarnovius. r) Heb. 7:27. s) Mercer, Drusius. t) Some read בית, into the house of God, that is into the court of the temple, that there you may call upon God. Piscator. cut off; in both places the same sense and the same end is intended, the defect of those things. And here is added the suffix your God, which is absent there; what we have added here will release us from a further explanation of the words, which is set out there quite clearly. When he calls it their God, he seems to recall to their minds the relationship that had come about between them and him, which was closer, by which he had drawn them to himself, choosing them specially out of all the people, so that they might serve his altar and attend to all the things that belong to duly rendering his worship, and enjoy the things that were offered on the altar once these were done. So the calamity expressed in these words, for the meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of your God, seems chiefly to concern them, and the cause of mourning arose partly from the zeal they had to feel for divine worship, which was disturbed in this way, and partly because the temple and the ministries of the sacred things no longer supplied them with what was needed for domestic expenses, which had hitherto been granted and assigned to them by God as wages for their service. How these sacrifices had been cut off from the house of their God, we have seen clearly before: namely that it came about through the consumption of the fruits from which they are made, and through the dearth of grain caused by the voracious little creatures; a description of which these words may rightly be said to give further. Abarbanel, however, by the way we have examined, thinks the Prophet here threatens the destruction of the temple, the house of God, and once it is destroyed all sacrifices must of necessity be cut off and cease together, which they ought to mourn: ולא תורה זאת באמרו כי אכם בחרכן הבירית ובית העבירה, and this (he says) was not really happening; but through the destruction of the house of God and the necessary cessation of his worship. But, as we noted before at v. 9 and as has been observed by Bochart, these words seem rather to imply the contrary, since what is said here is done or about to be done (the past being used for the future), while the house of God, in which these sacrifices were to be offered for divine worship, still stood whole; and since the priests, who were to offer them, were deprived of what was necessary for them through grievous scarcity and lack of things, having no sacrifice and no libation, they are admonished to offer themselves, and to present themselves at the altar as a sacrifice

units.la: *) Sic & Arias Mont. & Duacens. nor. in v. 9. ff) Vide sis Theodoret. x) Mercer. ficium acceptum, suas animas humiles & corda contrita precibus, lachrymis ac obtestationibus, quod unum medium erat super ad removendam calamitatem (vel rei frumentariæ annonam) qua erant obruti, & ad obtinendum rursus eorum largam copiam, ut iterum esset integrum immolare sacrificia in domo Dei, quæ nunc temporis ab eo peccatis lacessito ex ea erant sublata. Atque eo hic spectat illorum appellatio, ut seipsos Deo tradant, & sicuti his verbis singuli pro se ipsis, tanquam privati, suis fungi officiis, gregique tale exemplum præbere admonentur: ita regimine suo ac mandatis, quibus toti cœtui inserviebant, ut idem facerent, sequentium verborum scopus est.
units.tr: *) So also Arias Montanus and the Douai version, on verse 9. ff) See Theodoret. x) Mercerus. The sacrifice was accepted, and the humble souls and contrite hearts of the people were offered with prayers, tears and entreaties. This was the one remaining means of removing the calamity that had overwhelmed them, namely the scarcity of grain, and of obtaining its abundant supply again, so that the sacrifices could once more be offered whole in the house of God, which had now been taken away from them because they had provoked him by their sins. Hence the force of this appeal: the priests are told to give themselves up to God, and, as they do this individually for themselves, acting as private persons and fulfilling their own duties, so they are to set this example before the flock. The purpose of the words that follow is that the same ministers, by their rule and commands, which they exercised over the whole assembly, should lead everyone to do the same.

units.la: 14. Sanctificate jejunium, proclamate solennem cœtum, congregate seniores, & omnes habitatores terræ in domum Domini Dei vestri, clamate ad Dominum.
units.tr: 14. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the LORD your God, and cry unto the LORD.

units.la: Sanctificate jejunium &c.) קדשו צום Kaddeshu Tsum. Ita LXX. ἁγιάσατε νηστείαν, Syrus ܩܕܫܘ ܨܘܡܐ: Arabica impressa قدسوا الصوم Kaddesu Al-saum; Vulgatus: sanctificate jejunium, ut & nonnulli recentiores; hinc dubio procul hanc literalem verbi esse significationem colligas, cum & in eandem sententiam reddat Chaldæus Gazaru, decernite jejunium; MS. Arabicum עדו צום præparate jejunium, qua ratione & Rabbi Tanchum id explicat praparate (vel sancite) dies pro jejunio, & R. Solomo הכינו צום & Abcn-Ezra alia voce, sed non alio sensu præparate jejunium, & Kimchi: הכינו העם להעניה præparate populum ad jejunium; quo collineant etiam, qui sunt hujus seculi, reddendo z) præparate, a) indicite. Drusius hebraismum hic notat, sanctificate pro indicite jejunium, quod idem erat ac si sacerdotibus indixerit, curate ut plebs ad jejunium parata sit. Itaque bene translata sit hæc vox multiplicique usu alibi confirmata in Sacris literis, cum exprimitur: præparate, indicite, vel constituite jejunium, dedicate vel separate diem vel dies pro jejunio; at majoris emphaseos videtur, si propriè retineatur vocis notatio sanctificandi, quæ ut alteram includit, itaque præterea innuere videtur, qua ratione populus, cui jejunium indicitur,
units.tr: Sanctify the fast, etc.) קדשו צום Kaddeshu Tsum. So the LXX, sanctify a fast [ἁγιάσατε νηστείαν]; the Syriac, qaddishu tsawma; the printed Arabic, qaddesu al-saum; the Vulgate, sanctificate jejunium, as do some more recent translators. Hence you may doubtless conclude that this is the literal meaning of the word, since the Chaldee paraphrast Gazaru likewise renders it to the same sense, decree a fast. A Arabic manuscript has prepare a fast [עדו צום], and on this basis Rabbi Tanchum explains it as prepare (or consecrate) a day for fasting; R. Solomo has prepare a fast [הכינו צום], and Aben-Ezra, with a different word but not a different sense, prepare a fast; and Kimchi, prepare the people for fasting [הכינו העם להעניה]. To this view also incline those of our own age who render it prepare (z) or appoint (a). Drusius notes a Hebraism here, sanctify for appoint a fast, which would be the same as if he had commanded it to the priests, see that the people are made ready for the fast. Thus this word is rightly translated and is confirmed by its frequent use elsewhere in Sacred Scripture when it is rendered prepare, appoint, or establish a fast, dedicate or set apart a day or days for fasting. Yet it seems to carry greater emphasis if the proper meaning of the word to sanctify is retained, since it includes the other meanings; and so it seems also to hint at the manner in which the people to whom the fast is appointed ought to prepare themselves for it, and order and conduct themselves: clearly an extraordinary holiness was required, which did not consist merely in abstaining from food and drink, which is what is ordinarily meant by fasting, but also in abstaining from sin.

units.la: z) Pag. a) Munst. Cast. Jun. Tr. tur, sese debeat ad id præparare, illudque ordinare ac sese gerere: nimirum extraordinaria opus erat sanctitate, qua non sufficiebat, abstinere a cibo ac potu, quod alias jejunii venit nomine, sed insuper a peccato & impietate, quod ad sanctum & religiosum jejunium requiritur, quod & officium & signum est pœnitentis demissi, unicumque, in quo Deo beneplacitum, & jejunanti reconciliatio est; quod si secus fiat, certo futurum scimus, ut Deus illud respicere nullo modo dignetur. Hujus generis est de quo loquitur stomachabundus Jef. 58, 5. An hujusmodi est jejunium, quod eligo? ubi simul declaratur, quonam revera delectetur. Ut Ezech. 7, 5. Quando jejunabitis & ejulabitis, an omnino jejunabitis propter me? Quare jejunium sanctum est, quod sacerdotes debebant indicere, cum sibi ipsis, tum populo, cui erant præpositi, ut ipsorum exemplo, exhortatione & instructionibus impulsus eo rite fungeretur; unde fit, ut non tantum eos alloquatur, quasi ad illos solummodo id negotii spectet, sed jubeantur proclamare cœtum solennem. Universalibus peccatis, universalique calamitate imversi impelluntur ad pœnitentiam, ut veniam petant plagasque propter peccata sua illatas avertant. Proclamate, inquit, solennem cœtum; in margine extat: vel diem restrictionis. Ita & in aliis locis usitatum est nostratibus, ut eadem voce Atsarah occurrente, in textu ponant cœtum solennem, & in margine, ceu differentem vel potius indifferentem translationem, diem interdicti, ut Levit. 23, 36. cœtus solennis est, in textu; in margine vero dies restrictionis; qua utrumque innuitur, videlicet dies, quo populus ab aliis usitatis expeditionibus repressus, publico cœtu colligebatur, extraordinaria id jubente occasione. Verbum Atsar, unde hoc nomen derivatur, præcipue tunc significat restringere, continere, precludere, prohibere, retinere, impedire vel compellere, unde de interpretatione nominis sententiam ferre licet, quam nostrates habent in textu & in margine, ut vidimus, & alii nonnihil ab eis differentes, quanquam quoad sensum idem fere omnes intendant. Vulgatus habet cœtum, atque sic a Judæorum nonnullis exponitur; & Paraphrastes Chaldæus Cenusha, Syrus Cenushyo; ita & R. Solomo Asipha, & in eundem sensensum b) R. Japhet קלוּלּ Kehalah, congregationem vel confortium, (quo sensu trahitur Jer.9,2. עצרת בוגדים, consortium impiorum) cujus c) denominationis ratio est לפי שנעצרים ומתעכבים במקום אסיפתם quia detinentur & morantur in eo loco, ubi una sunt congregati; nec omnino abhorrent ab ea significatione Scriptores nostri temporis. Aliter alii eam reddunt, ita ut non tantum coetum denotet hominum congregatorum, vel unà degentium; verum & praeterea insinuet rationem & occasionem congregationis modumque ibi vivendi. Sic MS. Arabicum נאזרו بالاعتكاف, & iisdem ferme verbis R. Tanchum proclamate retentionem vel commorationem ad devotionem vel expectationem Dei; & accommodè Kimchi in hunc locum, ut populus cohibeatur מסאכתם ויאספו להתלהר ולבקשו d) ab opere suo & congregetur ad preces & supplicationes. Huc accedit interpretatio Christianorum: e) proclamate ferias, hoc est, diem cessationis ab opere & diem interdicti, quod & nostratium est in margine. Neque quicquam hic differunt sensu hi omnes, quin potius in eo insigniter conveniunt universi, solennem innui coetum ad officia praestanda, quae occasionis ratio requirebat, vel sanctitatis quaeque, ut alias eorum admonentur, vel jejunii & poenitentiae, uti hoc loco, additis humilitatis infucatae coram Deo signis, ut gravia ab ipsis rursus retrahat supplicia. Ambigue & hic & cap.2,25. ubi eadem verba occurrunt, LXX. Κηεύξατε Θεραπείαν, juxta antiquam latinam translationem, praedicate f) curationem. Quod Hieronymus intelligit de emendatione peccatorum suorum poenitentia, in quo Theodoretus ipsi adstipulatur. Vocque hebraea עצרת non minus videtur curationis notationem admittere, quam radix עצר Atsar, significationem claudendi & constringendi. g) Vulnera enim conflrictione curantur, atque ita ad vulnerum animae curationem applicari posse haud absonum videtur. Hac significatione reddunt eam per ἰδοὺ LXX. Jer.33,1. At alias praeterea habet vox graeca Θεραπεία h) signib) In Aben-Ezra. c) Kimchi Rad. d) Ira & Aben-Ezra. e) Calt. Druf. f) Ita citantur a Tertull. & Cyprian. g) Pet.a Fig. h) Steph.Lex.
units.tr: z) Pag. a) Munst. Cast. Jun. Tr. must prepare itself for this, and order and conduct itself accordingly. Clearly an extraordinary holiness was required, which did not consist merely in abstaining from food and drink, as the name of fasting usually implies, but also in abstaining from sin and impiety. A holy and religious fast requires this, and it is both the duty and the sign of a penitent who is humbled, and it is the only thing in which God takes pleasure and the fasting person is reconciled. If it is done otherwise, we know for certain that God will in no way deign to look upon it. Of this kind is the passage where the indignant prophet says, Isa. 58, 5. Is it such a fast that I choose? where it is also declared what truly delights him. Likewise Ezek. 7, 5. When you fast and mourn, did you at all fast for me? Therefore the holy fast was one that the priests were bound to proclaim, both to themselves and to the people over whom they were set, so that, moved by their example, exhortation and instruction, the people might perform it properly. Hence it is that the prophet does not address only them, as if the matter concerned them alone, but orders them to proclaim a solemn assembly. Because of universal sins and a universal calamity, all are driven to repentance, so that they may seek pardon and turn away the plagues inflicted for their sins. Proclaim, he says, a solemn assembly; in the margin stands: or a day of restraint. Our countrymen have also customarily done this in other places: when the same word Atsarah occurs, they put a solemn assembly in the text, and in the margin, as a differing or rather indifferent translation, a day of prohibition. For example, Lev. 23, 36. It is a solemn assembly, in the text; but in the margin a day of restraint. By both is meant a day on which the people, held back from their usual activities, were gathered into a public assembly, on an occasion that required it. The verb Atsar, from which this noun derives, especially means to restrain, contain, shut up, prohibit, retain, hinder or compel. From this one may judge the meaning of the name, which our countrymen give in the text and in the margin, as we have seen, and others give somewhat differently, although almost all intend the same sense. The Vulgate has assembly, and so it is explained by some of the Jews. The Chaldee paraphrast has Cenusha, the Syriac Cenushyo; so too R. Solomon has Asipha, and to the same effect b) R. Japhet has קהלה Kehalah, a congregation or company (in this sense Jer. 9, 2 is rendered עצרת בוגדים, a company of traitors). The reason for this name is לפי שנעצרים ומתעכבים במקום אסיפתם [lifi shene'etzarim umit'akavim bamakom asifatam], because they are detained and delayed in the place where they have gathered together. Nor do the writers of our own time altogether shrink from this sense. Others render it differently, so that it signifies not only an assembly of people gathered together or living together, but also suggests the reason and occasion of the gathering and the manner of living there. Thus the Arabic manuscript has ne'uzru bi-al-i'tikaf, and in nearly the same words R. Tanchum: proclaim a retention or a staying for devotion or for waiting upon God; and Kimchi fittingly on this passage: so that the people may be restrained מסאכתם [from their work] and gathered to pray and to seek him. To this is added the interpretation of the Christians: proclaim a holiday, that is, a day of cessation from work and a day of prohibition, which is also what our countrymen give in the margin. Yet all these differ in sense not at all; rather they agree remarkably in this, that a solemn assembly is meant for the performance of duties which the occasion required, whether of holiness generally, as they are elsewhere admonished, or of fasting and repentance, as here, with the added signs of unfeigned humility before God, so that he may withdraw from them the grievous punishments. Both here and at Joel 2, 25, where the same words occur, the Septuagint is ambiguous: Κήρυξατε Θεραπείαν [Kēryxate therapeian], according to the old Latin translation, proclaim a cure f). Jerome understands this of the amendment of their sins by repentance, and Theodoret agrees with him. The Hebrew word עצרת also seems to admit the meaning of healing no less than the root עצר Atsar admits the sense of shutting up and binding. g) For wounds are cured by binding, and so it seems not at all absurd that it may be applied to the healing of the wound of the soul. In this sense the Septuagint renders it by ἴασιν [iasin] in Jer. 33, 1. But the Greek word θεραπεία has other meanings besides, h) which others here prefer as more suited to this place, such as divine worship, service, ministry. By this sense, impressed on both passages, the Arabic renders it as proclaim ministry, that is, admonish them to come together at once to serve God. b) In Aben-Ezra. c) Kimchi Rad. d) Ira & Aben-Ezra. e) Calt. Druf. f) Ita citantur a Tertull. & Cyprian. g) Pet.a Fig. h) Steph.Lex.

units.la: significationes, quas alii hic anteferunt tanquam huic loco magis convenientes, ut sunt, i) cultus divinus, famulatus, ministerium, qua notione Arabica impressa in utroque loco eam reddit ﻟﻮﺍ ﺍﻟﺴﻮﺍ proclamate ministerium, hoc est, admonete eos ut simul accedant ad serviendum Deo. Secus factum est caeteris graecis interpretibus, ut ex illorum fragmentis videre est. Symmachus habet συνοδον, Synodum; Aquila, ἡμέραν συλλογῆς, diem congregationis. Omnes vero has significationes exhaurire videtur Cyrillus, cum eam exponat τὴν τῶν θείων θελημάτων ἐκτλήρωσιν, executionem eorum quae Deus exigit. Cunctos denique idem intendere in propatulo est, scilicet diem coetus solennis, quem debebant secernere a caeteris, ut una congregarentur jejunandi, resipiscendi, ac supplicandi gratia, & quae reliquae erant cultus divini partes rite exequendi: Ad quae ut eos adduceret eo citius, addit porro: congregate seniores & inhabitatores terrae &c. זקנים zekenim, seniores. Eandem vocem supra habuimus v.2. verum illius loci non congruit interpretatio cum praesenti, quippe anglico sermone ibi non vocantur seniores, sed senes, quod nonnihil diversitatis sensui alterutrius loci inferre posse non nemini posset videri, quin imo a quibusdam aliter verba sumta sunt, quamvis eadem sit vox utriusque loci, puta senes. Quorsum vero alii respexerint, ex Drusii verbis apparet: Hic, inquit, senes accipiunt alio sensu quam supra, nam ibi aetatis erat, hic est officii nomen, hoc est, magistratuum, vel qui sunt constituti in quodam dignitatis officio, auctoritate praeditorum, imperatorum, consiliariorum, quorum prudentia & auctoritate alii reguntur. Probe enim liquet, etiamsi primario k) haec vox denotet viros aetate provectos, alteram quoque sustinere posse significationem; quippe aetatis provectioris viri plerumque his muneribus magis pares sunt, communiterque ad ea subeunda eliguntur. Sunt tamen nihilominus qui priorem notionem retinent, qua monenturii, quorum anni sunt provecti, ne in aetatis infirmitate surripiendi sese a consortio caeterorum officia praestantium praetextum quaerant, eidem potius viae insistentes, l) licet tremebundi & suis baculis innixi, ut canorum auctoritate juvenes ad poenitentiam moveant. Quos
units.tr: meanings which others prefer here as more suited to this place, such as divine worship, service, ministry. In this sense the printed Arabic renders it in both places as lawa al-sawa, "proclaim the ministry," that is, admonish them to come together to serve God. The other Greek translators did otherwise, as may be seen from their fragments. Symmachus has συνοδον [synodon], a synod; Aquila has ἡμέραν συλλογῆς [hēmeran syllogēs], a day of gathering. Cyril seems to comprehend all these senses when he explains it as τὴν τῶν θείων θελημάτων ἐκτλήρωσιν [tēn tōn theiōn thelēmatōn ekplērōsin], the carrying out of the things that God requires. Finally, it is plain that all intend the same thing, namely a day of solemn assembly, which they were to set apart from others, so that they might gather together for fasting, repentance and supplication, and duly perform the remaining parts of divine worship. To lead them to these the more quickly, he adds further: gather the elders and the inhabitants of the land, etc. זקנים [zekenim, elders]. We had the same word above at v. 2, but the interpretation of that place does not agree with the present one, for in the English there they are not called "elders" but "old men," which might seem to some to introduce a certain difference in the sense of one place or the other; indeed some have taken the words differently, though the word is the same in both places, namely "old men." What others had in view appears from the words of Drusius: "Here," he says, "the old men are taken in another sense than above, for there it is a name of age, here it is a name of office," that is, of magistrates, or those who are appointed to some office of dignity, endowed with authority, commanders, counsellors, by whose wisdom and authority others are governed. For it is quite clear that, although this word primarily denotes men advanced in years, it can also bear the other meaning, since men of more advanced age are for the most part better fitted for these offices and are commonly chosen to undertake them. Nevertheless there are those who keep the former notion, by which they are reminded that, since their years are advanced, they should not seek, under cover of the weakness of age, to withdraw from the company of others who perform their duties; rather, following the same path, though trembling and leaning on their staves, they should by the authority of their grey hairs move the young to repentance. Whom

units.la: i) Merc. Druf. k) Schindl. Lex. l) Pet. a Fig.
units.tr: i) Mercerus, Drusius. k) Schindler, Lexicon. l) Pet. a Figueroa.

units.la: Quos inter & Hieronymus censendus est, qui eam quoque sumit pro senibus, quorum ætas vicina morti, maturæque sententiæ, magis timorem & cultum Dei suscipit. Alii vero latissime eam accipiunt utraque significatione cum pro eis, qui ætate provecti, tum pro illis, qui dignitate seniorum nomen adepti fuerant; quos utrosque ad pœnitentiam agendum citari quidam hic putant præcipue, ætate quidem provectiores, eo quod magis Deum offendissent, illorumque reatus esset gravior, autoritate vero eminentes, quod eorum exemplo alii ad peccata illecti essent populusque horum culpa plerumque ita dissolute viveret. Nec est, quod alterutros, strictiori hujus vocis usu hoc loco retento, ab officio, ad quod monentur, excludi putaveris, cum in sequentibus expresse adjiciatur, & omnes inhabitatores, ubi conjunctio &, quæ in Hebræo non est, à nostratibus vero & nonnullis aliis suppletur, clare arguit, & hos & illos simili modo vocatos esse, videlicet الشيوخ مع سكان الارض seniores (vel senes) cum omnibus inhabitatoribus terræ, ut MS. Arabicum habet; ita, ut utrumque nomen, quod regitur a verbo congregate, ad eundem nominativum referendum sit, quo præcedentia, scilicet ad sacerdotes; atq; adeo omnium ordinum homines, quibus tunc Judæorum natio discernebatur, ad conjunctim hic solennem cœtum constituendum, scilicet sacerdotes eum convocantes, seniores & plebeji, (qui terræ inhabitatores vocantur, & a principibus & sacerdotibus æque ista denominatione distinguuntur ac Jer. 1,18.) accersantur. Hæc regularis est constructio, planissimusque verborum sensus & a plerisque fere approbatus; verum cum & alia ratione possint construi, non desunt etiam, qui nominativum ex præcedentibus non accersendum, sed in ipsis verbis contineri reputantes reddunt vel, o vos seniores congregate omnes inhabitatores &c. vel, o vos omnes inhabitatores terræ congregate seniores in domum Domini. Alteram interpretandi rationem adprobat Aben-Ezra, congregate הזקנים vos seniores omnes inhabitatores terræ Israelis; cui accedere videtur Arias Montanus. Altera fide quorundam LXX. apographorum suffulta est,
units.tr: Among these Jerome is to be counted, who also takes the word for old men, whose age is near death and whose judgment is mature, who take up more the fear and worship of God. Others, however, understand the word very broadly in both senses, both for those advanced in years and for those who had obtained the name and rank of elders. Some think that both groups are summoned here to repent: those advanced in age, because they had offended God more and their guilt was greater, and those eminent in authority, because others had been enticed to sin by their example, and the people for the most part lived so dissolutely because of their fault. Nor should you think that either group is excluded from the duty to which they are summoned, by keeping the narrower use of the word here, since the following words expressly add and all the inhabitants. Here the conjunction "and", which is not in the Hebrew but is supplied by our people and some others, clearly shows that both groups were called in the same way: namely, al-shuyūkh maʿa sukkān al-arḍ (the elders together with all the inhabitants of the land), as the Arabic manuscript has it. So the two nouns, governed by the verb congregate, are to be referred to the same nominative as the preceding words, namely priests. Thus men of every order by which the Jewish nation was then distinguished are gathered together to form a single solemn assembly: the priests summon it, and the elders and common people (who are called inhabitants of the land, and are distinguished from the princes and priests by this same name, as in Jer. 1,18.) are brought together. This is the regular construction and the plainest sense of the words, and it has been approved by almost everyone. But since the words can also be construed in another way, there are some who think the nominative is not to be drawn from the preceding words but is contained in the verb itself, and they render it either o you elders, gather together all the inhabitants &c. or o you all inhabitants of the land, gather the elders into the house of the Lord. Aben Ezra approves the second way of interpreting, congregate [הזקנים] you elders, all the inhabitants of the land of Israel, and Arias Montanus seems to agree with him. The other reading is supported by the authority of some manuscripts of the Septuagint,

units.la: m) Sic Calv. Tarnov. n) Tig. Mun. Jun. Trem. elt, συναγαγετε προσβυτέρος παντες οι κατοικουντες την γην, congregate seniores vos, omnes inhabitatores terrae; & ex recentioribus Castalio: convocate senes o omnes incolæ &c. Adversus quos excipit Mercerus, nomen esse accusativi, non nominativi casus, cum sacerdotum esset, non populi, alios congregare ad hujusmodi obeunda officia. Ab omnibus vero deflectit Syrus, eo quod passive sumat verbum, quod alii active congregamini seniores & omnes inhabitatores terrae. Has in aliis differentias annotare allubuit, at non sunt tanti momenti, ut hinc moveamus scrupulos, vel nostram translationem relinquamus. At quacunque demum constructione acceperis, hoc omnium maxime elucet, fieri hic adhortationem ad omnis generis ac conditionis homines, ut solenni & nationali cœtu congregati vindictam Dei deprecentur, quam nationalibus sibi accersiverant peccatis, calamitatesque amoveant, quibus idcirco erant obnoxii. Locus, in quo debebant congregare, est templum, quod nuncupatur domus Domini Dei illorum; ipse illud vocat domum suam, & domum orationis omnibus populis, Ef. 56, 7. Eo tendebant o) Salomonis preces, quas fundebat primo cum illud Deo dicaret, si fames foret in terra, pestis, uredo, rubigo, locusta vel bruchus, vel si inimicus eorum angeret illos in terra civitatum illorum, vel quæcunque futura esset plaga, quæcunque ægritudo, ut omnem orationem, omnem deprecationem, quæ fieret a quocunque homine, vel a toto populo, quum agnoscentes quisque plagam animi sui expandissent manus suas versus domum hanc (vel in hac domo, ut vertitur, 2.Chron.6,29.) exaudiret Deus in cœlis vel ex cœlis, statione habitationis ejus & condonaret & daret &c. & in p) sequenti capite Deus ipsi dicit, se audivisse orationem ejus & confecrasse domum illam, quam ædificaverat, & collocasse nomen suum in æternum, oculosque ejus & animum ibi fore omnibus diebus. Atque ita rebus Judæorum constitutis, quorum in regione istud templum erat, ut ingenti famis calamitate a locustis & bruchis terræ fructus absumentibus (vel ut alii volunt ab invasione inimicorum) illata premerentur, eo confugiendum esse ipsis, ubi folen-
units.tr: m) So Calvin, Tarnovius. n) Tigurine, Munster, Junius, Tremellius: "elt" [Greek: συναγαγετε προσβυτέρος παντες οι κατοικουντες την γην], gather together, you elders, all the inhabitants of the land; and among the more recent, Castalio: convocate the old men, O all the inhabitants, etc. Against these Mercerus objects that the word is an accusative, not a nominative, since it was for the priests, not the people, to gather others to perform duties of this kind. The Syriac departs from them all, because it takes as passive the verb which the others take as active: be gathered together, you elders and all the inhabitants of the land. I have been pleased to note these differences among the others, but they are not so important that we should be troubled by them or abandon our translation. However, whatever construction you adopt, this above all is clear: here there is an exhortation to men of every kind and condition to gather together in a solemn and national assembly, and to entreat God's vengeance, which they had brought upon themselves by national sins, and to avert the calamities to which they were therefore exposed. The place where they were to gather is the temple, which is called the house of the Lord their God; he himself calls it my house, and a house of prayer for all peoples, Is. 56, 7. To this point the prayers of Solomon tended, which he poured out at the first, when he dedicated the temple to God: if there is famine in the land, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust or caterpillar, or if their enemy besieges them in the land of their cities, or whatever plague or sickness there is, whatever prayer and supplication is made by any man or by the whole people, when each one, acknowledging the plague of his own heart, spreads out his hands toward this house (or, as it is translated, in this house, 2 Chron. 6, 29.), may God hear in heaven or from heaven, the place of his dwelling, and forgive and give, etc. And in the p) following chapter God says to him that he has heard his prayer and has consecrated that house which he had built, and has set his name there forever, and that his eyes and heart will be there all days. And so, with the affairs of the Jews standing thus, since this temple was in their country, and since they were oppressed by a great famine caused by locusts and caterpillars devouring the fruits of the land (or, as others will have it, by the invasion of enemies), it is ordered that they must take refuge there, where a solemn

units.la: o) 1. Reg. 8,37. &c. p) Ibid. c. 9,3. folennis colligebatur cœtus, nec privatis precibus singulos debere acquiescere in privatis conclavibus, edicitur. Occasio etenim exigebat tum eorum congregationem in hoc loco, qui, uti vocatur domus Domini ipsorum, non nisi eorum animis reverentiam indere poterat ac in mentem revocare Dei præsentiam; quodque propterea agendum esset ibi, ut agerent tanquam in conspectu Dei summa animi sinceritate atque tam accurate, ut acceptum esset in ejus oculis atque benigne respiceretur ab eo, qui est cordium scrutator & inspector omnium illorum cogitationum. Et ut eos ita excitet, ut dicto sint obedientes animumque illis addat, q) emphasis notanda est in pronomine affixo nomini Dei, nimirum Dei vestri, quo illis asseverare videtur, in Deo nil impedimenti esse, quo minus in gratiam cum illis redeat, pro suis agnoscat & benignum se præbeat, modo illum debito modo & ex intimis visceribus quærerent, quo sequentia spectant verba, quibus & vocantur ad salutem suam & instruuntur, quomodo sit inveniendus; & clamate ad Dominum, h. e. fundite ardentissimo desiderio & maximis interioris mœroris lignis vestras preces ad Deum. Ad quam officii rationem expediendam ut rite præparentur, sacco indui, jejunii rationem habere, atque in domo Dei congregari jubentur, utpote quibus susque deque habitis parum proficerent, cum plurimum e contrario conduceret precum concinna dispositio, quæ quando ad Deum ab hominibus diriguntur animo humili ac omni affectu, multum revera valent ad removendum publicas calamitates. Hujusmodi ad preces invitat eos vox ꝓ זעקו zaaku, clamate, etsi ea alias significet vocis elevationem; manifestum tamen est hic, ut & alibi in S. literis, deucere atque exigere ardentem affectum animi, quo afficit atque movet linguam & labia ad tales exercendum assectus in precibus ad Deum. Quare ad illum clamandum esset, eo tendit, ut removeat ab iis gravem plagam, quam & in præcedentibus & in sequentibus verbis habemus consignatam. Hoc vero totum "(verba sunt Kimchi) ut faciant, jubet Propheta, cum locusta in eos" veniet; aut ut redeant per pœnitentiam ante adventum ejus, ut ita" Deus propter miserationes suas revocet decretum hoc. Qui ab" inva-
units.tr: o) 1 Kings 8, 37, etc. p) Ibid. ch. 9, 3. a solemn assembly was gathered, and that they should not rest content with private prayers in their private chambers. The occasion indeed required their gathering in this place, which, as it is called the house of their Lord, could alone instil reverence in their minds and recall to their memory the presence of God; and therefore they ought to act there as in the sight of God, with the utmost sincerity of mind and with such care that they might be accepted in his eyes and kindly regarded by him who is the searcher of hearts and the inspector of all their thoughts. And so that he may thus rouse them, make them obedient, and encourage their minds, the emphasis is to be noted in the pronoun attached to the name of God, namely your God, by which he seems to assure them that nothing in God stands in the way of his being reconciled to them, acknowledging them as his own and showing himself kind, provided they seek him in the proper manner and from the depths of their hearts. To this the following words refer, by which they are both called to their salvation and instructed how he is to be found: and cry out to the Lord, that is, pour out your prayers to God with the most ardent desire and the greatest groanings of inward sorrow. That they may be duly prepared for this duty, they are commanded to put on sackcloth, to observe a fast, and to gather in the house of God; for if they treated these things lightly they would accomplish little, whereas a well-ordered arrangement of prayers would greatly help. When such prayers are directed to God by men with a humble mind and every feeling, they indeed have great power to remove public calamities. The word zaaku [זעקו] (cry out), ꝓ, invites them to such prayer, although elsewhere it means the raising of the voice. It is clear, however, here as elsewhere in Holy Scripture, that it signifies to kindle and drive forth the ardent feeling of the mind, which stirs and moves the tongue and lips to such emotions in prayers to God. Therefore to cry out to him tends to this, that he may remove from them the grave plague which we find set down both in the preceding and in the following words. But (these are the words of Kimchi) the Prophet commands them to do all this, "when the locust comes upon them; or that they should return by repentance before its coming, so that God, because of his mercies, may revoke this decree." Those who think that this evil arose from an invasion of enemies

units.la: q) Oecolamp. Merc. Tarnov. invasione hostium hoc malum ortum esse putant, contra eosdem preces debuisse dirigi statuunt. Clamare jubentur ad Deum, quem peccatis suis provocarant, qui minatus fuerat vel revera immiserat has poenas, cujusque unius erat eas removere. Quam gravis etiam mediis hisce utendi adsit causa, partim ex jam dictis Prophetæ apparet,partim ex dicendis, quibus harum plagarum depingit terrorem.
units.tr: q) Oecolampadius, Mercerus, Tarnovius. decree that prayers ought to have been directed against those same enemies. They are commanded to cry out to God, whom they had provoked by their sins, who had threatened or indeed inflicted these punishments, and whose alone it was to remove them. How serious the reason for using these means is appears partly from what the Prophet has already said, and partly from what he is about to say, by which he depicts the terror of these plagues.

units.la: 15. Ebeu diei isti; nam propinquus est dies Jehovæ & sicut vastatio ab Omnipotente adveniet.
units.tr: 15. Alas for that day! For the day of Jehovah is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.

units.la: Ut hæc verba cum præcedentibus connectantur, interpretes inferuerunt quidam aut suppleverunt vel in fine præcedentis, vel ab initio hujus versus, dicentes,vel, & dicite, scilicet אבה Abah, Eheu &c. ita Syrus ܐܘܝ & MS. Arabicum & dicite; Kimchi quoque אמרו אבה dicite, Ebeu, &c. quasi a Propheta illis injungeretur, quid clamandum vel dicendum effet. Ita Hieronymus hoc habet pro voce Sacerdotum & populi ad Deum clamantis; ita r) recentiores quidam supplent, dicentes vel dicendo. At alii nil opus esse supplendi ratione autumant, quin Prophetam sub s) sua ipsius persona ac lingua pathetica lugubrem impoenitentis populi lugere conditionem, & gravitatem supplicii prædicti describere, sibi persuadent. Verum idem est literalis verborum sensus, quocunque modo sumtum fuerit. Vocem hebraicam t) אבה Abah, exclamandi propter u) dolorem vel metum vel utrumque particulam esse, ex hoc loco non minus atque ex aliis apparet היאה קריאה כך עור הצער והאנחה Exclamatio est, inquit Kimchi, propter angorem & folicitudinem. Quare ab interpretibus hujusmodi vocibus exprimitur, quæ talem assectum indicant, ut w) Ebeu, Heu, Hui, Hei, Ah, Abah, o! LXX. habent οἴμοι, væ mihi! At speciem præ fe ferunt sententiæ, unam vo-
units.tr: So that these words may be joined to the preceding ones, some interpreters have supplied, either at the end of the previous verse or at the beginning of this one, the word "saying" (dicentes) or "and say" (dicite), namely Abah, "Alas," and so on. So the Syriac and the Arabic manuscript read "and say," and Kimchi too has "say, Abah, Alas," as if the Prophet were enjoining on them what they should cry out or say. Jerome takes it as the voice of the priests and people crying out to God, and some recent writers supply "saying" or "by saying." Others, however, think nothing needs to be supplied, and are persuaded that the Prophet himself, speaking in his own person and in a pathetic tone, laments the wretched condition of the unrepentant people and describes the gravity of the punishment foretold. Yet the literal sense of the words is the same however they are taken. That the Hebrew word Abah is an exclamation of pain or fear, or of both, appears from this passage no less than from others. "It is an exclamation," says Kimchi, "born of anguish and anxiety." Therefore the interpreters render it with words that express such feeling: Alas, Woe, Ah, Hui, Hei, Oh! The LXX have "oimoi," woe is me! Yet these present the appearance of a sentence, and one word does not seem enough to express the gravity of the suffering by which the speaker's mind appears to be moved.

Sunt z) autem qui literas contrahendas esse statuunt tanquam unam syllabam,easque separatas scribarum a) lapsu, qui scribere debebant aha. Simili ratione Syrus bis repetit, σιο] σιο] uh, uh, quod est particula اسفاه الى exclamandi ad Deum pro auxilio; atque eo sensu videtur etiam accepisse hebraea MS. Arabicum, dicens الغوث الي الله من جهة هذا اليوم clamo ad Deum, ut auxilio sit in hoc die, vel adversus hunc diem; nec longe hinc abit Chaldaeus Paraphrasta, quanquam hic vertat ܘ vae, cum in quibusdam aliis locis eam deprecandi ac supplicandi habeat particulam קבר בעותי יי אלהים Exaudi orationem meam o Domine Deus, ut Jer. 1,6. & 4,10--14. 13. --32. 17. Ezech. 4,14. 9,8. --11. 13. -20. 49. (quam Graeca etiam Jos. 7,7. reddit διόμαι, oro.) Id vero propter vel adversus quod suam lamentationem instituit,quodque tam lugubri declamatione persequitur, & idcirco auxilium divinum implorat, non alio hic venit nomine quam diei, qui acerbitate & calamitate, quam inferebat, ab aliis distinguitur atque dignoscitur. Ex eo fit ut Munsterus translatione sua praeter simplicem literam hebraici textus inserat, O calamitatem c) diei illius! & Mercerus, Hei qualis dies! in verbis proxime sequentibus vocat illum diem Domini; quod vene-
units.tr: r) Jun. Tr. Merc. Oecolamp. etc. s) Pet. a Fig. Pisc. & Merc. t) It is also written without the letter aleph at the beginning, הי [hi]. u) "... is a particle of pain," says Abu Walid, "... fear," says Aben Ezra. w) 1. Jun. Tr. 2. Drus. 3. Calv. 4. Merc. Gua. 5. Oecolamp. 6. Pag. 7. Tig. Munst. Hence, besides adding ἐκτενῶς [ektenōs], vehemently, after the preceding verb "cry out," they repeat the particle thrice: οἴμοι, οἴμοι, οἴμοι [oimoi, oimoi, oimoi], just as the printed Arabic has al-wayl li al-wayl li, "woe to me! woe to me! woe to me!" And perhaps the Vulgate translator should be thought to have been moved by the same reason, repeating the letter a three times, saying "a, a, a," if each of these is read distinctly. Hence the conjecture of those who want to draw some other mystery out of these is to be regarded as vain. Some, however, decide that the letters are to be contracted and read as one syllable, and that they were separated through the error of the scribes, who ought to have written "aha." In a similar way the Syriac repeats "uh, uh" twice, which is a particle of exclaiming to God for help, and the Arabic manuscript seems to have understood the Hebrew in this sense as well, saying: "I cry out to God for help in this day, or against this day." Nor does the Chaldee paraphrast differ much from this, although here he renders it with the Chaldee "vai" (woe), since in certain other places he has the particle of entreaty and supplication, [קבל בעותי] "Hear my prayer, O Lord God," as in Jer. 1,6; 4,10–14; 13,22–32; 17; Ezech. 4,14; 9,8–11; 13,20; 49 (which the Greek also renders at Jos. 7,7 as δέομαι [deomai], I pray). But the reason for which, or against which, he institutes his lamentation, and which he pursues with so mournful a declamation, and therefore implores divine help, is here designated by no other name than "day," which is distinguished and recognised from others by the bitterness and calamity it brings. Hence Munster, in his translation, besides the plain letter of the Hebrew text, inserts "O the calamity of that day!" and Mercer, "Alas, what a day!" and in the words immediately following he calls it "the day of the Lord," which comes...

units.la: x) Etsi in quibusdam editionibus praeter ἐxτευῶς nihil extet, quam idcirco Kircherus pro vocis significatione accepit. y) Hieron. quia offendeTant Trinitatem. z) Ribera: Modo ut unam dictionem proferamus. a) Pet. a Fig. Ribera,cum nihilominus alibi ita inveniatur,ut Jer. 1,8. c) Diem moestum,calamitosum, lugubrem & miseriarum plenum diem Ar. Mont. Et Pet. a Fig. idem innui putat ac si diceretur, Ea dominibus in illa die. venerandum nomen epitheti loco plerumque adjicitur, cum magnum quid atque communem rerum fortem excedens denotatur. Hic quidem talem diem significare videtur, hujusmodique tempus, quale Deus judiciis illis, quibus animadvertere volebat in populum pro culpae admissione, notabile atque illustre cupiebat. Ipsa etiam diei vox, ut d) quidam observant, pro judicio sumitur (sicuti Apostoli hominis dies accipitur quibusdam pro hominis judicio, quomodo & nostratibus redditum 1. Cor. 4, 3.) quia judicium pronuntiatur statuto hunc in finem die, ita ut sensus sit hic: dies judicii Domini. Quam gravia autem forent ea judicia, praecedentia judicant ut & quae proponuntur v. 25. Hinc per diem Domini intelligi diem e) graviorum malorum, quae Deus immittere comminatus erat, nisi poenitentia repentina reverterentur, non levis est quae nobis persuadet ratio. Non autem diserte exprimitur, quibus mediantibus ea judicia erant exequenda, quorum invasionis initium dies nominatur; quippe qui supra nominetenus sunt traditi v. 4. nimirum, eruca, locusta, melolontha, & bruchus, animalcula noxia devorantia, quorum frequens invasio annonae caritatem ciere potis est. Haec communiter pro hujusmodi animalculis juxta literam sumuntur, ratione, quae nobis videtur planissima; verum per figuram aliis allubet denotare illos hostes, qui terram invasuri essent, obvia quaeque, prout illis usu venit, devastantes. Atque eodem modo hic differunt interpretes, quippe qui literaliter id accipiunt de animalculis, per diem illud tempus intelligunt, quo Deus illa immittebat vel immissurus erat tanta copia, quae antea nemini unquam erat visa, ut fructus terrae absumerent & gravem inferrent regioni famem. Ita Drusius: Dies quo locustae venient, quia his mediantibus Deus exequebatur judicia sua super Judaeos, atque propter male admissa in eos graviter animadvertebat. Eadem ratione & Doctissimus Bochartus illum vocari diem Domini statuit, quo erat se stituros tanquam judex, ut in Judaeos animadvertat, locustarum agmine in eos immissio. Alii tamen ambigui haerent nec definire audent, num de invasione horum animalculorum proprie, vel de hostium ingressu figurate accipien-
units.tr: x) Although in some editions nothing appears besides ἐκτενῶς, Kircher therefore took it for the meaning of the word. y) Jerome: because they offended the Trinity. z) Ribera: Provided that we pronounce one word. a) Peter à Figueroa, Ribera, though elsewhere it is found in this way, as Jer. 1:8. c) Mournful, calamitous, grievous day, full of miseries. Arias Montanus. Peter à Figueroa thinks the same is hinted as if it were said, such things in that day. The venerable name is often added in place of an epithet, when something great and a fate beyond the common run of things is signified. Here it seems to signify such a day, and such a time, as God, in those judgments by which he wished to punish the people for their sin, desired to be notable and illustrious. The word day itself, as some observe, is also taken for judgment (just as the Apostle's day of man is understood by some as man's judgment, as it is rendered for us in 1 Cor. 4:3), because judgment is pronounced on a day appointed for this purpose. So the sense here is: the day of the judgment of the Lord. How grave those judgments would be, the preceding ones show, as do those set forth in v. 25. Hence the reason that persuades us is not slight: by the day of the Lord is understood the day of the more grievous evils that God had threatened to bring, unless the people turned back by sudden repentance. It is not expressly stated, however, by what means those judgments were to be carried out, whose invasion is named the day. Clearly those named above in v. 4 are meant, namely the locust, the cankerworm, the palmerworm, and the caterpillar, harmful little creatures that devour, whose frequent invasion is able to stir up dearth of food. These are commonly taken literally as such small creatures, for a reason that seems to us most plain. But others choose to signify figuratively those enemies who were about to invade the land and lay waste everything they met, as they happened to do. In the same way the interpreters differ here. Those who take it literally of the small creatures understand by the day that time when God sent, or was about to send, those creatures in such numbers as had never before been seen, to consume the fruits of the earth and bring a grievous famine on the region. So Drusius: the day when the locusts will come, because by these means God carried out his judgments upon the Jews and punished them severely for their evil deeds. On the same ground the most learned Bochart also holds that it is called the day of the Lord, on which he would stand as judge to punish the Jews, by the sending of the swarm of locusts against them. Others, however, hesitate in doubt and do not dare to decide whether it should be understood properly of the invasion of these small creatures, or figuratively of the entry of enemies.

units.la: d) Druf. Bochart. e) Livel. piendum fit. Ita Cyrillus: Diem Domini vocat, qua iræ ejus satisfieri oportet, aut locusta ipsis immissa & fruges in terra devastante, & famis atque penuriæ horrorem incutiente, ipsumque mortis pavorem inferente; aut Babyloniis omnia vastantibus &c. f) Alii utrumque hic innui putant, ac si alii aliorum invasionem prævenerint Prophetæque mens esset, declarare Domini decretum de venturis locustis & Chaldæis omnia vastatum is. Alii vero & locustarum cæterarumque dictarum creaturarum nullam volunt habere rationem, cum de inimicis Chaldæis duntaxat sermonem esse illorum animo inhæreat, a quibus Abarbinel stat. Hinc per diem intelligi asserit nonum diem mensis Ab, qui ex g) mente ejus Judæis fatalis erat, quippe quo eversum erat templum; unde illis etiam notabilis, tanquam dies mœroris ac lamentationis clamationisque ad Deum, in ejus rei memoriam. At non est causa ulla prægnans, cur prior sententia eaque planissima abjiciatur, qua, quamvis jamjam prædicta mala toleraverant, gravior tamen fames expectanda iis statuitur, nisi pœnitentia præpropera præveniretur. Verbo, in proclivi est exhortari eos hac pathetica exclamatione ac provocare ad hujusmodi resipiscentiam, cujus ut rationem haberent justam, eumque in finem hæc tendere adverterent, duplex adjicitur ratio, quarum alteram sumit a propinquitate diei, alteram ab ejus terrore, quodque nullo alio medio posset evitari. Primum, Nam dies Domini propinquus est; subito erat venturus, hinc subito erant adhibenda media, quibus præverti posset; nullum morandi tempus in hoc casu, quo etenim veniente, frustra foret, quicquid contra molirentur. Adveniet enim ut destructio ab omnipotente, cujus potentia non potest frangi: Quod unum superesset, remedium prius eum effugiendi, quam veniret, repentina erat resipiscentia; cum vero veniret, actum foret de omnibus, etsi fortissimis resistere audentibus, cum sit ab omnipotente. Eandem expressionem habemus Jes. 13, 6. Ejulate, nam dies Domini propinquus est, veniet ut vastatio ab Omnipotente. Verba hebraea habent וכשד משדי יבוא uceshod mishaddai yabu, quibus video exacte con-
units.tr: d) Drusius, Bochart. e) Liveleus. Thus Cyril: he calls it the day of the Lord on which his wrath must be satisfied, either by locusts sent against them, devastating the crops in the land and striking the terror of famine and want, and bringing the dread of death itself; or by the Babylonians laying everything waste, etc. f) Others think both are hinted here, as if the one invasion had gone before the other, and the Prophet's mind were to declare the Lord's decree concerning the locusts to come and the Chaldeans laying all waste. Others, however, want no account taken of the locusts and the other creatures named, since their minds are fixed on the Chaldeans as the enemy alone, against whom Abarbanel stands. He asserts that by the day is meant the ninth day of the month Av, which by his judgment was fateful for the Jews, since on it the temple was overthrown; hence it was also for them a notable day, a day of mourning and lamentation and cries to God, in memory of that event. But there is no weighty reason why the former view, which is quite plain, should be rejected, namely that although they had already endured the evils foretold, a graver famine was still to be expected for them unless a premature repentance forestalled it. In short, it is easy to see that they are exhorted by this pathetic exclamation and provoked to such repentance; and that they might have a just reason for it and might note that these things tended to this end, a twofold reason is added. One is taken from the nearness of the day, the other from its terror, and from the fact that it could be avoided by no other means. First: For the day of the Lord is near; it was to come suddenly, so the means by which it could be forestalled had to be applied suddenly. In this case there was no time for delay, since when it came, whatever they attempted against it would be in vain. For it will come as destruction from the Almighty, whose power cannot be broken. The one remedy left was to escape him before he came, by sudden repentance; but once he came, all would be over for everyone, even for those who dared to resist most bravely, since it is from the Almighty. We have the same expression in Isa. 13:6: Wail, for the day of the Lord is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty. The Hebrew words are וכשד משדי יבוא [uceshod mishaddai yabu], with which I see the words agree exactly

units.la: f) Pet. a Fig. g) In hunc locum; at largius multo in Jer. 2,14. & Hof. 5,7. ubi diversa quædam recenset mala quæ Judæis hoc die evenerant. congruere nostram translationem Anglicam; quod autem impedimento nobis non erit, quo minus aliorum placita de horum verborum vel alicujus illorum partis expositione inspecturi simus. Quod attinet ad particulam ב Ce, in ucesbod, quæ vertitur ut, etiamsi ipse auctor MS. Arabici quoque eam reddat ut, omissa conjunctione ו, quæ illam antecedit, notat tamen ab aliis respici ceu ܫܒܚ *) redundantem, adeo ut sensum constituat solum שׁוד Shod, Vastatio veniat a Schaddai; Hinc Syro insuper habetur, & spoliatio veniet a Deo. Abarbinel quidem non putat eam redundare, alia tamen ratione debere accipi, quam alii fecerunt, asserit, non quidem pro particula comparationis vel similitudinis, sed b) temporis denotati (הומן כף) prout interdum usu venit, ita ut verborum ea sit mens; Nam dies Domini propinquus est, vindictæ sumendæ; & quandoquidem vastatio ab Omnipotente est, veniet eo die, qui ab eo inferendis malis constitutus est. Atque huic viæ insistere videtur, quia expositioni dici optime congruit, qua diem pro nono die mensis Ab sumit, ut supra retulimus. At non adeo convenit cum ea ratione, quam nos pariter & alii sequimur, qua observata, certum est, particulam ut, non carere sua emphasi, quippe qua mala ventura significantur, nec fore ex accidenti, nec ex rerum solitarum numero, nec ab alia ordinaria potestate, cui resisti non posset, sed tam lugubria, quemadmodum infligi constitutum erat, quæque infligerentur forsitan expectatione citius a tanta potestate, cui resistere nemini foret integrum, utpote a Deo profecta, eoque, quo solent, modo in usum deducenda.
units.tr: f) Pet. a Fig. g) On this passage; but at much greater length on Jer. 2:14 and Hos. 5:7, where he recounts various evils that befell the Jews on this day. Our English translation agrees, which will not stop us from looking at the opinions of others on the explanation of these words or of some part of them. As for the particle *ce* (ב) in *ucesbod*, which is rendered "as", even though the author of the Arabic manuscript also renders it "as", omitting the conjunction *ve* (ו) that precedes it, others nevertheless regard it as redundant, as *shbh*, so that the sense is made up only of *shod*: "destruction will come from Shaddai". Hence the Syriac additionally has "and spoiling will come from God". Abarbanel indeed does not think it is redundant, but asserts that it must be taken in another way than others have taken it: not as a particle of comparison or similarity, but of denoted time (*ke* as "when"), as sometimes happens in usage, so that the meaning of the words is: "For the day of the Lord is near, the day of taking vengeance; and since destruction is from the Almighty, it will come on that day which he has appointed for inflicting evils." He seems to follow this line because it agrees very well with the exposition which takes the day to be the ninth day of the month Ab, as we related above. But it does not agree so well with that reasoning which we and others likewise follow. By this reasoning, it is certain that the particle "as" does not lack its emphasis, since by it evils to come are signified: that they will not happen by accident, nor belong to the number of ordinary events, nor come from some other ordinary power that could not be resisted, but will be as grievous as it was determined they should be inflicted, and will perhaps be inflicted more quickly than expected by so great a power, to which no one would be free to resist, as it proceeds from God, and is to be brought into effect in the way such things usually are.

units.la: Quod attinet ad vocem שׁוד Shod, vastatio & שׁדי Schaddai, Omnipotens, non tantum est alius ad aliam allusio ac literarum convenientia, sed & radicis affinitas, quamvis sensu immane quantum ab invicem diffent. Vox שׁוד Shod, descendit a radice שׁדד Shadad, vastavit, ac proprie significat, ut versa est, vastationem. Ab eadem radice derivatur etiam vox שׁדי Schaddai, qua Deus hic nominatur, hinc proprie significare vastatorem videri posset. Quanquam igitur a quampluri-
units.tr: As for the word shod, "destruction", and Shaddai, "Almighty", there is not merely an allusion of one to the other and an agreement of letters, but also an affinity of root, although in meaning they differ enormously from each other. The word shod descends from the root shadad, "he laid waste", and properly signifies, as it is translated, "destruction". From the same root is also derived the word Shaddai, by which God is named here; hence it might seem to signify properly "the destroyer". Although, therefore, by very many

units.la: *) Sic etiam capit Joel 7,* in כשׁלשׁים. b) Ita & Ar. Montanus.
units.tr: *) Thus also Joel 7,* takes *keshelashim* (כשׁלשׁים). b) So also Arias Montanus.

units.la: plurimis Judæis,ut sunt Abu Walid, Aben-Ezra, & Kimchi, hoc Dei nomen,quo seipsum nominat (Gen. 17,1. Exod. 6,3.) ac in S. literis ita nominatur,regulariter ab hac radice deducitur ; Abarbinel nihilominus contra eam excipit, quod a voce derivetur,quæ violentiam,injuriæ ac damni illationem, oppressionemque denotare videtur,unde Deo attribui nequeat. Qui gloriosum Deum S. Scriptura nominaret vel describeret בתיאר מנוחה אשר כוחי epitheto ac tam praeclara significationis nomine, quam hoc? Nec illi satis fit, quod a simili radice aliis derivatur מנצח Menatseach, Victor, etsi nec Deus cum hominibus, nec homines cum Deo bellum gerant ; cum attributa Potentis, Dominatoris, Ducis, Præfecti magis Deo convenire possint quam Schoded vel Menatseach. Quo fit ut præferat,quam aliunde voci attignaverat,derivationem, qua non multum abscedere videtur ab opinione R. Saadiah, k) qui tantum eam valere putat ac si diceretur מי שאמר לעולם יי ille qui dicit mundo, satis vel sufficiens. Quod tametsi vix intellexisse Aben-Ezra sibi videatur, eo tamen ejus sententiam redire patet, quod libera voluntate ac beneplacito, quo omni necessitate remota DEus cuncta creabat,mensuram atque modum omnibus constituerit, quem ultra citraque vel excedere vel recedere haud concessum, eumque servantibus dicat: satis est (sistite, ultra procedere non datur.) Ratum etiam habet quod alii dicunt, significare eum, qui est sufficiens, vel omnisufficiens in se ipso, sui ipsius causa, & a nemine alio essentiam recipiens, sicuti cum aliis eam interpretatur ; vel ut alii, qui est sufficiens ad producenda omnia, vel qui l) in se habet quod sufficiens est pro omnibus creaturis, vel qui supplendis omnibus illorum defectibus. Hanc derivationem a די sufficiens, adjecta litera Schin, Maimonides præferre videtur Moreh p.1. c.63. qua ratione etiam apparet ab auctore MS. Arabici esse acceptum, qui reddit, m) שדי כן אלהאי sicut sholum a sufficienti vel ab omnisufficienti. Quæ superfunt derivationes, tanti ipsi non sunt,ut iis examinandis operam suam
units.tr: Jews, such as Abu Walid, Aben-Ezra, and Kimchi, this name of God, by which he names himself (Gen. 17,1; Exod. 6,3.) and by which he is so named in the Holy Scriptures, is regularly derived from this root. Abarbanel nevertheless objects against this that it is derived from a word which seems to denote violence, injury, the infliction of harm and oppression, and so cannot be attributed to God. Who, if Holy Scripture wished to name or describe the glorious God by an epithet and a name of such splendid meaning as this? He is not satisfied even by the fact that others derive it from a similar root, menatseach, Victor, although neither God makes war with men, nor men with God; since the attributes of the Mighty, the Lord, the Leader, the Commander can apply to God more than Shoded or Menatseach. Hence he prefers the derivation which he had previously attached to the word, a derivation that does not seem to differ much from the opinion of R. Saadiah, k) who thinks it has the same force as if it were said: he who says to the world, enough or sufficient. Although Aben-Ezra himself seems scarcely to have understood this, it is evident that his view comes back to this: that by free will and good pleasure, by which God created all things with all necessity removed, he set a measure and limit for all things, which it is not permitted to exceed or fall short of, and he says to those who keep it: enough (stop, it is not given to go further). He also holds to what others say, that it signifies him who is sufficient, or all-sufficient in himself, being his own cause, and receiving his being from no one else, as he interprets it together with others; or, as others say, he who is sufficient to produce all things, or who has in himself what is sufficient for all creatures, or who supplies all their defects. Maimonides seems to prefer this derivation from dai, sufficient, with the letter shin added, in Moreh part 1, chapter 63; by this reasoning it also appears to have been understood by the author of the Arabic manuscript, who renders it as the sufficient one or from the all-sufficient. The remaining derivations are not so important that I should devote my effort to them,

units.la: i) In Exod. 6,3. Vide Buxt. de nomin. Dei. k) Quod aliis etiam antea observatum in Tam. Buxt. l) R. Sal. Gen. 17,1. m) Legendum esse puto אלהי sicut Isa. 13,6. Ita enim scriptum significat pro latorem. suam collocet, in quo etiam nos ei accedimus, quales inprimis sunt, quod hæc vox sit derivata a שד Schad pectus vel mamma (& שריים Schadaim mammæ) quasi ex sua ubertate, qualis est mammillarum, omnia replerentur benignitate, cunctaque nutrirentur. Alii rursus, quod sit a שרא Schada (quæ vox Chaldaica respondet hebraeo אשר ashad) effundere, ac si denotaret largam effusionem benignitatis in omnes creaturas, omniumque illorum procurationem, quæ sunt ad vitam spiritumque ducendum perquam necessaria. Verum hæ omnes quamvis sensum adeo non infringant, quin potius in eundem singula insigniter conspirent, nulla tamen adeo conveniens est, quam quæ primo loco adducta est, qua scilicet vox refertur ad שדי Schadad: quare etiam a Judæis haud infimæ fortis eo relatam supra vidimus, nec, quod contra objicitur ab Abarbinel, nulla ratione firma niti videtur. In eo enim, ut diximus, omnem contrariæ sententiæ vim collocat, quod ea radix nonnisi violentiam ac destructionem, quin & injuriæ illationem inferat, eoque vox hæc ratione hic sumta denotaret צודי ... כעורי latronem perversum vel injuriosum, oppressorem; quod DEO inconveniens omnino putat. At solus est, qui huic voci tam duram imponit significationem, atque eo & auctoritati aliorum, qui eam ad radicem hanc referunt, & rationi, qua eam defendunt, sese opponit. Observant etenim designare o) عزيز جبار potentem, magnum p) תקיף מנצח potentem, expugnantem, vincentem (non quod hæc vox, quod ipsi arridet, tantum denotet victorem in praelio, sed eum qui vincit & supprimit) & מתגבר Mithgabber, prævalentem, q) ארקאר prædominantem (ut non nemo illorum habet) Arabice. Hujus vero interpretationis causam ex usu Arabicae linguae petunt, in qua radix شدّ Schaddah significat valere, firmum esse, (non autem devastare vel destruere ut in Hebraeo) unde اشد Aşaddo robur vel robustissima pars aetatis hominis & شديد Schadid, (quod congruit hebraico שדי) fortis, firmus, qua denotatione inter attributa DEI referri a quodam Scriptore r) Orientali legisse meminimus. Syriace redditur لعزيز & s) Arabice non differt a عزيز potens. Exinde
units.tr: i) On Exod. 6,3. See Buxt. de nomin. Dei. k) This was also observed earlier by others in Tam. Buxt. l) R. Sal. on Gen. 17,1. m) I think one should read Elohi, as in Isa. 13,6; for so the written text means, as a bearer. ...in which I too side with him, such as are especially these: that this word is derived from shad, "breast" or "teat" (and shadaim, "breasts"), as if all things were filled with benignity from his abundance, like that of the breasts, and everything were nourished. Others again, that it comes from shada (which Chaldean word corresponds to the Hebrew ashad), "to pour out", as if it denoted a large outpouring of goodness upon all creatures and the provision for all those things which are extremely necessary for leading life and breath. But all these, although they do not so much break the sense, rather agree in the same meaning, none of them is so suitable as the one first brought forward, namely that the word is referred to Shaddai. Therefore, as we have seen above, the Jews also referred it to this with no small force; nor does what Abarbanel objects against it seem to rest on any firm reason. For he places the whole force of the contrary opinion in this, that this root brings only violence and destruction, indeed even the infliction of injury, and so this word, taken in this sense here, would denote tsodi ... ka'ori, a perverse or injurious robber, an oppressor; which he thinks wholly unfitting for God. But he alone gives this word so harsh a meaning, and in doing so sets himself against both the authority of others, who refer it to this root, and the reasoning by which they defend it. For they observe that it signifies in Arabic 'aziz jabbar, "mighty, great", taqif menatseach, "powerful, conquering, victorious" (not that this word, which pleases him, signifies only "victor in battle", but one who conquers and suppresses), and mithgabber, "prevailing", and arqar, "predominant" (as one of them has it) in Arabic. But they seek the reason for this interpretation in the usage of the Arabic language, in which the root shaddah signifies "to be strong, to be firm" (not, however, "to lay waste" or "to destroy" as in Hebrew), whence ashadd, "strength" or "the most robust part of a man's age", and shadid (which agrees with the Hebrew Shaddai), "strong, firm", a meaning which I remember having read a certain Oriental writer count among the attributes of God. In Syriac it is rendered la'aziz, and in Arabic it does not differ from 'aziz, "mighty". Hence
