units.la: Exinde non leve opinioni accedit pondus, cum hebraicæ linguæ suus adhuc constaret honos, cumque late pateret ac communis esset loquentibus, דור non tantum denotasse devastare & destruere, verum & valere, firmum ac potentem esse, prout Arabibus hodie adhuc quoque familiaris est; priorem tamen, scil. valere potentia & robore in genere, primariam esse significationem; hinc, cum robore opus est destruenti, sensim ad eam denotationem deflexisse, quæ idcirco sola esse nequit; de DEO vero quando usurpatur, omnem illam potentiam designare, qua valet quæque creandi & destruendi; at cum præter DEum aliis attribuatur, talem denotare, cujus potentia magna frangique difficilis. Quod ultimo adjeci, huc in finem factum scias, quod sint qui hanc vocis פוך robustus, & potens vel valens, significationem cum nostratibus & non paucis aliis non tanquam propriam applicandam putant Omnipotenti, sed & alicui alii, qui potentia magna valet. Nec obscuri nominis est inter Judæos, qui ab Abenezra & Kimchi allegatur הגדיד Hannaggid (Princeps) dicens בַּמָּךְ הוא הרחיק אינו שאין הגבור non esse nomen gloriosi Dei, sed adjectivum aliis quoque commune, atque sic arguere destructionem inevitabilem a talibus illatum, quorum potentiæ effugiendi locus non sit. De quo Ab. Ez. testatur ישר אמר pulchre dixisse; & inter Latinos de tali destructione hanc vocem accipit Ruffinus, quam potentissimus quisque ultor inveheret. Non est dubium quin bono sensu hæc omnia sumi possint; at prævalet cæteris multumque efficaciæ habet ea, qua nostratibus & plerisque aliis consentientibus pro attributo ac nomine DEI accipitur adeo, ut DEI omnipotentiam & virtutem, cui resisti nequit, ea vox der otet illosque commonefaciat, illatam destructionem tantos editurum revera effectus, ut nequaquam relinquere, vel effugere integrum fuerit cuiquam. Et ut omnis tollatur vocis ambiguitas, quam æque ad alium referri posse constat, Chaldæus cum ea conjungit nomen ידוה (Jehovah) & Syrus simpliciter vertit per nomen Dei ܐܠܗܐ ܕܡܪܝܐ ܘܗܝ ܥܠܝܐ ܕܝܢܐ ܬܒܪܐ... & destructio veniet a Deo. Cæ te-
units.tr: Hence the opinion gains no small weight. While the Hebrew language still kept its honour, and while the word דור was widely current and in common use among speakers, it meant not only "to lay waste" and "to destroy" but also "to prevail, to be firm and powerful," as it is still familiar to the Arabs today. The former sense, namely "to prevail in power and strength" in general, is nevertheless the primary meaning. Hence, when strength is needed for destroying, the word gradually bent to that sense, which therefore cannot be its only sense. When it is used of God, it designates all that power by which he is able to create and to destroy. But since it is ascribed to others besides God, it denotes one whose power is great and hard to break. I have added this last point for a particular purpose, so that you may know: there are some who, along with our people and not a few others, think that this sense of the word, "robust" and "powerful" or "prevailing," is not to be applied to the Almighty as its proper meaning, but also to someone else who prevails by great power. Nor is the term obscure among the Jews. Abenezra and Kimchi cite Hannaggid (Prince), who says that it is "not the name of the glorious God," but an adjective common to others also, and so argues that the destruction brought by such persons is inevitable, since there is no way of escaping their power. Abenezra testifies that he "said it beautifully" (ישר אמר). Among the Latins, Rufinus takes this word of such destruction as that which "the most powerful avenger might bring." There is no doubt that all these things can be taken in a good sense. But the sense that prevails over the others and carries the most force is that in which the word is taken, as our people and most others agree, as an attribute and name of God. That word reminds them of God's omnipotence and power, which cannot be resisted, and that the destruction brought will produce such effects that it would be impossible for anyone to remain untouched or to escape. And so that all ambiguity of the word is removed, since it is clear that it can equally be referred to another, the Chaldee joins with it the name יהוה (Jehovah), and the Syriac simply renders it by the name of God, "Alaha d-Maryā ... wa-hi ʿalāyā dînā tabrā ..., and destruction will come from God." The rest-

units.la: {t} Vid. Tarnov. qui ex Mahana, vastitas a potente, non ab omnipotente, quia non loquitur de Deo, sed viro potenti, cujus vastationi nemo resistat; quæ demum rejicit.
units.tr: {t} See Tarnov., who from Mahana reads "devastation by the mighty," not "by the Almighty," because the passage does not speak of God but of a powerful man, whose devastation no one resists. He finally rejects this reading.

units.la: Caeterum quos hactenus adduximus omnes legisse patet שדי Schaddai; at ita interpretantur eam LXX, ut aliter plane illos legisse haud immerito opinentur nonnulli, quum reddant ὡς ταλαιπωρία ἐκ ταλαιπωρίας ἥξει, veniet sicut miseria ex miseria (quorum vestigiis etiam insistit Arabica imprella (كبتل شقوة من شقوة ياتي) Unde Capello conjectura nascitur, eos non legisse secundo loco cum alias שדי Schaddai, sed solummodo שד Schad, sicuti primo loco sine litera י jod, atque exinde eadem etiam significatione accepisse. At crebra observatione perspectum est, quando eadem vox in Hebraeo occurrit Esa.13,6. Cesbod Mishaddai yabo, ratione plane diversa ab illis ibi reddi, quae aliorum interpretationi magis accedit; nimirum, και συντριβη παρα τα Θεα ηξει (sicuti etiam وألانكسار ياتي من قبل الله) & contritio veniet a Deo, quod argumento esse videtur non esse translatos hos duos libros ab iisdem personis. Qua occasione vero tint permoti ita, ut factum est, hanc interpretandi vocem, non est quod nos sollicitos habeat, cum constans caeterorum omnium sit lectio eademque vera.
units.tr: Moreover, it is clear that all those whom we have cited so far read שדי (Shaddai). But the Seventy translate it in such a way that some not unreasonably think they read it quite differently, since they render ὡς ταλαιπωρία ἐκ ταλαιπωρίας ἥξει, "it will come as misery from misery." The printed Arabic version also follows their footsteps (kabtal shaqwa min shaqwa yātī). From this arises Capellus's conjecture that they did not read the second word as Shaddai, but only as שד (Shad), just as in the first place they read it without the letter yod, and that they therefore took it in the same sense. But by frequent observation it has been seen that when the same word occurs in Hebrew at Isa. 13:6, "Cesbod Mishaddai yabo," it is rendered there in an entirely different way, which comes closer to the interpretation of others: καὶ συντριβὴ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἥξει, "and destruction will come from God" (as also the Arabic wa-l-inkisār yātī min qibal Allāh). This seems to be evidence that these two books were not translated by the same persons. But as to what moved them to translate in this way, there is no reason for us to be concerned, since the reading of all the others is constant, the same, and true.

units.la: 16. Nonne cibus exscisus est coram oculis vestris, imo; e domo Dei nostri laetitia & exsultatio.
units.tr: 16. Is not the food cut off before your eyes? Yea, joy and exultation from the house of our God?

units.la: Posteaquam annunciaverat, propinquum esse diem Domini eumque omnino terribilem, ne stupiditati summae immersi procul abesse putarent relipiscentiamque, qua una ab eo, caeterisque exinde provenientibus malis possent immunes reddi, laxius debito prorogarent, exaggerat porro plagam eo, quod jamjam initia sua sumebat, describitque ejus naturam & conditionem in modum, ut jure merito ea jam debuissent affici, additis pejorum, quae erant futura, minis. Attollant modo oculos, & dubium non est, quin eam percipiant. Quid autem factum dicit? Nonne cibus, inquit, coram oculis vestris exscisus est? imo &c. Verba interrogandi forma prolata evidentius validiusque affirmant & rerum dictarum veritatem probant ita, ut emphasi sua non carere dicenda sit particula הלא halo, numquid non, vel nonne, vel annon? Attamen omittitur hic a LXX. qui affirmandi formam simpliciter habent, κατέναντι τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὑμῶν βρω-μάτα ἐξωλοθρεύθη, coram oculis vestris cibi excisi sunt. Eodem modo emphasin hanc negligit Arabicæ impressæ versionis Auctor. In Syriaco vero ut ejus vis exhibeatur, mutata est particula in demonstrativam לא hoˌecce cibi coram oculis vestris sunt excisi. Duo vero ex mente nostratium eorumque interpunctione affirmantur defectus,scilicet tum alimentorum,quorum usus ad vitam alendam domi opus erat; tum rerum, quæ erant offerendæ in domo Domini,quorum utriusque copia ex fructibus terræ superfundi folenne erat,quæque adeo ab invicem dependebant, ut priori deficiente nulla posterioris spes superesset. Ut autem hi ab invicem distinguantur,visum est nostratibus interserere particulam imo,quæ cum in Hebræo non extet, aliis placuit ita reddere, ac si utraque expressione idem innueretur, nimirum per cibum primo loco positum nihil aliud denotari autumant, quam sacrificia, quæ quoniam nominantur lætitia & exsultatio domus Dei, quibus ea erant conjuncta, innui loco secundo censent. Ita MS. Arabicum אליס הרי אעינינא אנקטע אלקרבן מן בירת אלאהנא מע אלפרח ואלטרב nonne coram oculis vestris excisum est sacrificium ex domo Dei vestri, cum lætitia & exsultatione? Et ut mentem ejus haud difficulter assequeremur, notam adjicit, idcirca vocare sacrificium אכיל Ocel cibum, quia illud est מאכיל אלאר quod comeditur (vel devoratur) ab igne. Huc quoque vergunt vetba Vulgati: nunquid non coram oculis vestris alimenta perierunt de domo Dei nostri, lætitia & exultatio? Quæ Duacenses hunc in modum vertunt: why, are not the victuals perished before your eyes, joy and exultation out of the house of our God. Nec abhorrent ab hac interpretatione quidam alii, quia per alimenta &c. id genus sacrificiorum x) intelligunt,quod in domo DEI oblatum sustentationi sacerdotum tributum erat,unde mutuum solebat oriri gaudium, tam offerentium quam sacerdotum. Sunt tamen alii, qui diversas res hic innui volunt,per cibum scilicet omnia ea in genere, ν) quæ ad victum necessaria fuerunt, & per lætitiam & exsultationem, quæ ad lætitiam & celebritatem pertinebant. Ita ut,quod ꝳ) quidam in eandem
units.tr: After he had announced that the day of the Lord was near and altogether terrible, he further magnifies the plague, lest men sunk in the deepest stupidity should think it far off and postpone repentance, by which alone they could be made immune from it and from the other evils that follow, too loosely beyond what is due. He describes its nature and condition in such a way that they ought rightly to have been moved already, and adds threats of worse things still to come. Let them only lift their eyes, and there is no doubt they will perceive it. What, then, does he say has happened? "Is not the food, he says, cut off before your eyes? Yea, etc." Words put in the form of a question affirm more clearly and forcefully, and prove the truth of what is said. So the particle הלא (halo, "surely not?" or "is not?") should be said not to lack its emphasis. Yet the LXX omit it here, and simply have the affirmative form, "the foods were destroyed before your eyes." The author of the printed Arabic version likewise neglects this emphasis. In the Syriac, however, so that its force is shown, the particle is changed to a demonstrative: "these foods before your eyes are cut off." According to our people and their punctuation, two defects are affirmed: first, of foodstuffs, whose use was necessary at home to sustain life; second, of the things that were to be offered in the house of the Lord. It was customary for an abundance of both to be poured out from the fruits of the land, and they were so dependent on each other that if the former failed, no hope of the latter remained. In order to distinguish these from each other, our people thought fit to insert the particle "yea." Since it does not stand in the Hebrew, others preferred to render it so that both expressions seem to indicate the same thing. They think that by food, placed first, nothing else is denoted than sacrifices. Since these are called the joy and exultation of the house of God, to which they were joined, they consider that these are implied in the second place. So the Arabic manuscript: "Is it not that before your eyes the sacrifice has been cut off from the house of our God, with joy and exultation?" (alīs hāḏā aʿyunanā ankaṭaʿa al-qurbān min bayt ilāhinā maʿa al-faraḥ wa-l-ṭarab). And so that we may grasp his mind without difficulty, he adds a note that he calls the sacrifice maʾkil (food) because it is "what is eaten, or devoured, by fire" (maʾkil al-nār). The words of the Vulgate also tend this way: "Has not food perished before your eyes from the house of our God, joy and exultation?" The Douay translators render it thus: "why, are not the victuals perished before your eyes, joy and exultation out of the house of our God." Certain others also do not shrink from this interpretation, since by food, etc., they understand that kind of sacrifice which, offered in the house of God, was assigned to the support of the priests, whence joy was wont to arise on both sides, both of the offerers and of the priests. There are, however, others who wish different things to be indicated here: by food, all those things in general that were necessary for sustenance, and by joy and exultation, those that pertained to gladness and festivity. Certain writers incline to the same opinion as this, which is not obscurely noted by these words, that God had removed not only those things by which we live (for the prophet joins himself to these) but also those which he had commanded to be offered to him from the fruits of the land.

units.la: κ) Sic Kimchi. ꝯ) Ar. Mont. ꝳ) Targ. dem sententiam proclivis non obscure notat, his verbis declaretur, DEum non eas tantum exscidisse res,ex quibus vivamus, (Propheta enim sese his adjungit) sed & quæ sibi a nobis offerri jussit ex terræ fructibus, ut cum eo lætaremur. Eodem spectare LXX. Cyrilli sententia est, intelligendos scilicet esse per cibum fructus terræ jam maturos, frumentum messi aptum, uvasque calcari idoneas, quibus coram oculis eorum existentibus atque tantum non in manu versantibus in illorum lætitiam, subitaque locustarum invasione abfumtis, inquit, cibum illorum esse excisum coram oculis eorum, hoc est, quasi ex ore illorum ereptum, cum accincti effent jam atque parati ad colligendum eum atque comedendum; per lætitiam vero & exultationem, quas dicit excisas ex domo Dei illorum, intelligendas oblationes vel sacrificia, quæ offerebant læti ex earum rerum copia, quas campi uberes præbebant, tanquam χαρισήμα, id est, oblationes, quibus gratiæ aguntur ei pro benigna, qua fruebantur, largitione. Pari ratione inter Judæos ea verba distinguit Kimchi, atque ita explicat, ut per alterum comma, Nonne cibus coram oculis vestris excisus est? intelligat, fupervenifle fructibus terræ maturis existentibus locustas, eosque devoraffe; per alterum vero, lætitiam atque exultationem, cibo succiso, succisam quoque esse de domo Dei illorum, quia facrificia juxta statutum tempore messis offerebant & lætitiæ indulgebant, quæ quanta fuerit, ex eo patet quod dicitur Esa. 9,3. Iætati sunt coram te quasi lætitia, quæ agitatur in messe. Aben-Ezra ut clausulas vel membra hujus versus distinguat, hæc putat verba הלא נכרת נוֹנָה nonne excisus est, ad priora æque spectare atque ad posteriora, ante quæ repetenda ea censet hunc in modum: Nonne lætitia & exultatio exisse sunt ex domo DEI vestri? In quo ɣ) nonnullos etiam alios asseclas habet, quin ipse Paraphraftes Chaldæus non prorsus alienus ab eo videatur, cum duas voces ejusdem significationis apponat, quarum prior prius membrum claudit, posterior posterius inchoat, reddens alterum הלא עור ואנחנו חין עברים פְּסַח מְבִיא Nonne frumentum, adhuc spectantibus nobis, defit? alterum פסח מביא מקרשא דאלהנא חרוב ובית Nonne (hoc enim necessario subintelligitur) defecit a domo sanctuarii DEI nostri lætitia & exultatio? R. Tanchum ambiguus hærere videtur, quomodo hæc verba sint distinguenda, quæque harum duarum rationum fit maxime approbanda. Interdum necessario fubintelligendam ac supplendam supponit conjunctionem &; at tum iterum ambigit, quonam fit referenda, num ad שמחה lætitiam, ita ut verba sonarent: Nonne cibus excifus est coram oculis vestris ex domo DEI vestri & lætitia & exultatio? (quam viam etiam Syrus ingreditur; & ecce coram oculis vestris ceciderunt cibi ex domo DEI vestri ... & lætitia & exultatio?) an ad verba בית אלהינו domus Dei vestri, hac ratione: Nonne cibus excisus est coram oculis vestris & a domo DEI nostri lætitia & exultatio? Et hæc est ratio, quam Angli nostri sequuntur, & paulo exactius Genevensis, quæ non habet imo, sed, & lætitia & exultatio a domo DEI nostri. Eatenus autem differunt hæ inter fe, quod in altera per cibum tales oblationes præcipue intelligantur, quæ in templo in lætitia offerebantur, in altera vero magis generaliter ea, quæ ad victus rationem necessaria erant, atque tum per lætitiam & exultationem ea, quæ afferebantur ad offerendum DEO in templo & in suftentationem sacerdotum, ordinata erant. Nec multum intererit, quamcunque harum approbaveris, quippe utraque declaratur, magnam fuisse rerum necessariarum penuriam. Ni fructibus terræ effent privati, nec rerum ad victum sibi necessariarum, nec lætitiæ defectus extitisset, quia sacrificia a DEO jubebantur offerri ac comedi in templo suo juxta mandatum Deuteronom. 11, 7. & 16, 11. Utrumque igitur defectus ab una eademque causa nascitur, alterque alterum infert, quippe lætitiæ defectus nonnisi ex earum rerum defectu existit, quæ illam debuissent excitare. Ita ut bene hæc conveniant cum dictis v. 9. &c. Sacrificium & libamen succisum est a domo Domini: v. 7. cohibitum est a domo DEI vestri. Aben-Ezra vini penuriam in specie innui asserit, quod dicitur exhilarare DEum & homines, Jud. 9, 13. At hæc expressionis ratio minime probat, eam hic tantummodo describi lætitiam, quæ ex vino vel libaminibus oriebatur; quippe sacrificia quævis, ut ex Kimchi ante audivimus, (imprimis tempore messis) ingenti cum lætitia conjuncta fuisse feruntur,
units.tr: Thus Kimchi. Arias Montanus. The Targum. Its meaning is plainly inclined in this direction, and it is expressed in these words: that God has cut off not only the things by which we live (for the prophet includes himself), but also the things he commanded to be offered to him from the fruits of the earth, so that we might rejoice with him. The Septuagint, according to Cyril's view, also looks in this direction, namely that by food we are to understand the fruits of the earth already ripe, grain fit for harvest and grapes fit for the winepress, which were before their eyes and almost in their hands, to their joy. When the sudden invasion of locusts consumed them, he says, their food was cut off before their eyes, that is, snatched as it were from their mouths, when they were already girded and ready to gather and eat it. By joy and exultation, which he says were cut off from the house of their God, we are to understand the offerings or sacrifices which they used to bring in joy from the abundance of those things which the fertile fields provided, as charisema [χαρισήμα], that is, offerings by which thanks are rendered to him for the kind bounty they enjoyed. In the same way Kimchi distinguishes these words among the Jews and explains them so that, by the first clause, Is not the food cut off before your eyes?, he understands that locusts had come upon the ripening fruits of the earth and devoured them; and by the second, that when the food was cut off, the joy and exultation were also cut off from the house of their God, because according to the appointed time of harvest they used to offer sacrifices and indulge in joy. How great that joy was is clear from what is said in Isaiah 9:3: They rejoiced before you as with joy in harvest. Aben Ezra, in order to divide the clauses or members of this verse, thinks that the words Is it not cut off? [הלא נכרת] refer equally to what goes before and what follows, and he judges that they should be repeated before them in this way: Have not joy and exultation gone out from the house of your God? He has several other followers in this, and indeed the Chaldee paraphrast himself does not seem wholly alien to this view, since he adds two words of the same meaning, the first of which closes the first member and the second begins the second, rendering the one Is not the grain, while we are still looking on, lacking? [halo ʿawar waʾanachnan chayyin ʿibrayya PSaḤ MEBI'] and the other Is not (for this must necessarily be understood) joy and exultation lacking from the house of the sanctuary of our God? Rabbi Tanchum seems uncertain how these words should be divided, and which of these two explanations is most to be approved. Sometimes he supposes that the conjunction and must necessarily be understood and supplied; but then again he hesitates as to which word it should be referred to: whether to שמחה, joy, so that the words would read Is not food cut off before your eyes from the house of your God, and joy and exultation? (a way the Syriac also follows: And behold, before your eyes the foods have fallen from the house of your God … and joy and exultation?), or to the words בית אלהינו, the house of our God, in this way: Is not food cut off before your eyes, and joy and exultation from the house of our God? And this is the reading our English translators follow, and the Geneva version more exactly, which does not have Nay, but and joy and exultation from the house of our God. These readings differ from one another only in this: in the one, by food such offerings are chiefly understood as were offered in the temple with joy; in the other, more generally, those things which were necessary for the sustenance of life, and then by joy and exultation those things which were brought to be offered to God in the temple and for the support of the priests were meant. Nor will it matter much which of these you approve, since both explain that there was a great want of necessary things. If they had not been deprived of the fruits of the earth, there would have been neither a lack of the things necessary for their living nor a lack of joy, because God commanded that sacrifices be offered and eaten in his temple according to the commandment in Deuteronomy 11:7 and 16:11. Both the lack and its cause therefore arise from one and the same source, and the one brings about the other, for a lack of joy comes only from a lack of those things which ought to have aroused it. Thus these readings agree well with what is said in verses 9 etc.: The meat offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the LORD; verse 7: It has been laid bare from the house of your God. Aben Ezra asserts that a lack of wine is meant in particular, from what is said, that wine cheers God and men (Judges 9:13). But this manner of expression does not prove that only that joy which arose from wine or drink offerings is described here; for, as we heard earlier from Kimchi, all sacrifices (especially at harvest time) are said to have been joined with great joy.

units.la: ip e juc ipsque DEus illis adeo z) delectatus dicitur, ut in a) odorem gratum ipsi fuerint juxta sacrarum literarum usitatam exprimendi rationem. Praeterea in eo omnibus convenit, a quibus haec praedicta, cibus aeque ac laetitia & exultatio, sint excisa vel porro adhuc essent b) exscindenda. Eadem nempe hic intercedit illis differentia, quae a nobis antea est notata. c) Sunt, quibus, ab inimicis haec facta suisse, placet, quorum invasione totam destructam illorum regionem, d) Alii locustis ea adscribunt caeterisque animalculis noxiis, quae supra nominatim exhibita sunt. e) Non nemini tamen adeo dubium est, ut dicat: dum locusta vel loftis iis fructibus nos privavit, quorum uberem jam sperabamus messem; nec deest f) qui de locustis intelligendam rem planissimam judicat, quid? quod argumenti haud levis loco g) quidam habet dicens: Hic locus facere videtur pro illis, qui veras locustas venisse intelligunt. Neque Doctissimus Bochartus hinc argumentum contra Abarbinel petere desistit, qui calamitates has accidisse putat templo vel destructo, vel jam pene destruendo a Chaldaeis, quo probat talia hic describi mala, quae stante adhuc templo erant ingressura; quippe id solitis sacrificiis frequentare atque celebrare non amplius erat integrum, locustis haec omnia devastantibus, quibus quam apte addenda sit intempestiva licitas atque ariditas, sequentia manifestum reddent.
units.tr: And God himself is said to have been so pleased with them that they were a sweet savour to him, according to the customary manner of expression in the sacred letters. Moreover, in this all agree: that by whomever these things, food as well as joy and exultation, were cut off, or are yet to be cut off, the same difference is found as we noted before. Some are pleased to think these things were done by enemies, by whose invasion their whole region was destroyed. Others ascribe them to locusts and to the other noxious creatures that have already been named above. Yet some doubt it so much that they say: while the locust or the caterpillar has deprived us of those fruits whose abundant harvest we had hoped for … ; and there is no lack of those who judge that the matter is most plainly to be understood of locusts. What is more, a certain writer of no little authority says: This passage seems to favour those who understand that real locusts came. Nor does the most learned Bochart cease to draw an argument against Abarbanel from this, who thinks these calamities happened when the temple was either already destroyed or almost destroyed by the Chaldeans; by this he proves that such evils are described here as were going to enter while the temple still stood. For it was no longer possible to frequent and celebrate the customary sacrifices there, with the locusts devastating all these things; and how aptly untimely drought and dryness are to be added to this, the following verses will make clear.

units.la: 17. Satum (vel uti in margine grana) est (vel sunt) fa- ctum (facta) mucidum (a) sub glebis suis, horrea sunt desolata, granaria destructa; Nam frumen- tum exaruit.
units.tr: 17. The seed is rotted (or, as the margin reads, the grains are rotted) under its clods; the barns are desolate, the granaries destroyed, for the grain has dried up.

units.la: Verba haec, quorum interpretationem maxime textui originali convenire & recor & comprobatum dabo postea, nil aliud continent, quam ulteriorem calamitatis praedictae descriptionem, qua non tantum terrae fructus virescentes atque laetitiae non vulgaris speciem praebentes ex ore illorum eripiebantur imprasentiarum; verum ad futu-
units.tr: These words, whose interpretation I will later show to agree most closely with the original text and confirm, contain nothing other than a further description of the calamity already foretold. Not only were the green crops of the land, which gave a appearance of unusual joy, being snatched from their mouths for the present, but as regards the future, no change for the better was to be hoped for in the future as well.

units.la: z) Merc. a) Levit. 23,13. b) Ita de futuro tempore quidam capiunt. c) Abarb. Ar. Mqnr. Ribera. d) Hieron.Cyrill. Kimchi. e) Merc. f) Sanct. g) Pet.a Fig. futurum tempus quod attinebat, nulla etiam conditionis h) immutatio speranda erat: Illud enim fatum, quod progerminare debebat in sequentis anni messem, mucidum erat factum vel marcidum sub glebis terræ, sui simile igitur producere non capax; ita ut ratione præsentium habita pagi redditi essent desolati, granaria destructa, ruitura, nullius usui porro futura, nihil jamjam capientia, nec verosimiliter captura in posterum. Verum ut hanc interpretationem probatam sistamus contra alias, quas plures ac diversas ab ea esse nemo ignorat, e re nostra esse arbitror, verborum singulorum prius eruere significationem, cui rei ut nobis viam præparemus, non ingratum fore autumo lectoris oculis primo loco subjicere diversas, quas diximus, a nostra interpretationes, eas inprimis quæ ponderis ac auctoritatis nonnihil sibi vindicare videntur, ab antiquitatis gloria nimirum.
units.tr: z) Merc. a) Lev. 23:13. b) Some take it this way of the future time. c) Abarb., Ar., Mont., Ribera. d) Jerome, Cyril, Kimchi. e) Merc. f) Sanct. g) Pet. a Fig. For that seed, which was to sprout into the harvest of the following year, had become rotten or withered under the clods of the earth, and so was incapable of producing anything like itself. Thus, considering the present state of things, the villages were made desolate, the granaries destroyed and about to fall, of no use henceforth, holding nothing now and likely to hold nothing in the future. But that we may set this interpretation against the others, which everyone knows are many and differ from it, I think it fitting for my purpose first to draw out the meaning of the individual words. To prepare the way for this, I think it will not be unwelcome to put before the reader's eyes, first of all, the various interpretations that differ from ours, as I said, especially those which seem to claim some weight and authority, that is, from the glory of antiquity.

units.la: 1. Chaldæi Paraphrastæ, qui primam partem hujus commatis reddit אתמסיו גרבי חמר תחורת מגיפתהן quod ita i) translatum in Bibliis Polyglottis: Computruerunt k) dolia vini sub operculis suis; & Mercero: Soluta sunt sub suis operculis dolia vinaria; (quod idem esse duco, ac, disjuncta sunt) quod ita explicat Abu Walid حجتت دنان الخمر وعفنت من طول مكثها فاسدة dolia vinaria fiant vel rancida & mucida redduntur, quod tamdiu vacua maneant.
units.tr: 1. The Chaldee paraphrast, who renders the first part of this verse [אתמסיו גרבי חמר תחורת מגיפתהן] thus, as translated in the Polyglot Bibles: "The jars of wine have rotted under their lids"; and Mercerus: "The wine casks have been loosened under their lids" (which I take to mean the same as "have been separated"). Abu Walid explains it thus: "the wine jars have become spoiled and mouldy from long standing, so that the casks are made rancid and mouldy, since they have remained empty for so long."

units.la: 2. LXX. qui habent εσκίρτησαν δαμάλεις επὶ ταῖς Φάτναις αὐτῶν. Saltaverunt jumenta in suis stabulis. Quibus convenit Arabica impressa.
units.tr: 2. The Seventy, who have ἐσκίρτησαν δαμάλεις ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [eskirtēsan damaleis epi tais phatnais autōn], "the heifers leapt upon their mangers." The printed Arabic agrees with them.

units.la: 3. Syri ܩܠܘܝ ܪܥܝܢܐ oquæ interpres Latinus reddit, incænatæ manserunt juvencæ super præsepibus suis (etsi planior mihi videatur vocis significatio, cum vertitur tostæ, quam incænatæ, ita ut commode reddi posset, torrefactæ sunt vel siccitate adustæ.)
units.tr: 3. The Syriac [qalwi ra'ina], which the Latin translator renders "the heifers remained unfed over their mangers" (although the meaning of the word seems plainer to me when it is rendered "roasted" rather than "unfed", so that it could fittingly be rendered "have been scorched" or "burnt up by dryness").

units.tr: 4. The Vulgate.

units.la: Vulgati: Computruerunt jumenta in stercore suo. Atque iste sunt, quæ omnium longissime abeunt a noftratibus, quibus Judæorum pleriq; accedunt, nec non recentiores Christianorum. Tria potissimum sunt in hoc commune vocabula, quæ adeo in diversum trahunt interpretes, quæ cum alias in S. literis non extent, fit, ut conjectura eorum significationem eruant, prout sensui hujus loci quàm maxime quadrare putant. Prima harum vocum præeunte textu hebraico est עַפְשׁ, quæ noftratibus redditur, saeclum est mucidum (vel facta sunt mucida) cujus vice cognata in S. literis adhibetur אַפְשְׁ Aphehu, quæ etiam Rabbinis in usu est, nec quicquam radices illarum discernit, quam commutatio literæ ב,b, in פ,p, l) quod & in aliis vocibus fieri observatum est. Hinc eadem significatione venire illam cum hac ultima, Judæorum Doctores m) diversi notant, scilicet, mucefcere, mucidum fieri, putrescere. Verum antiquus ille eruditus Grammaticus n) Abu Walid conatur significationem ejus eruere comparando eam cum voce Arabica Abefa, quatenus idem significat quam Tabefa exarescere, quod optime huic loco arbitratur convenire, eo, quod damnum hic descriptum magis videatur illatum liccitate, quam humiditate, prout mox fumus subjecturi. Auctor MS. Arabici exprimit eam per עתרת Orbhat, qua denotari suspicor, vermibus arrosum est, (Arabes enim utuntur ea pro arrofione vermium vel blattarum, & Athatho, ab eadem radice pro corruptione) non esse in hebraica lingua innuens, unde ea vox derivetur, quare illis exprimi עבשו Abeshu per Abthu sicut locus videtur flagitare. Hi vero, quorum interpretationem hactenus inspeximus, in eo universi conveniunt, talem hac exprimendi formula hic designari rerum dictarum corruptionem, qua usui ac fini non respondebant, qui alioqui communiter inde expectari possit; cui sensui adstipulantur interpretes plerique latina vel aliis linguis reddentes, computruerunt (ut Vulgatus) vel alia ratione non absimili. Idem quoad vocis significationem suggerit Chaldæus. Ad Græcos vero quod attinet, sane non liquet ex
units.tr: The Vulgate: "The beasts have rotted in their dung." These are the renderings that differ most widely from ours, and most of the Jews and some recent Christians agree with them. Three words in particular are common to this verse, and since they do not occur elsewhere in Holy Scripture, the interpreters pull them in very different directions; they try to work out their meaning by conjecture, each according to what he thinks best fits the sense of this place. The first of these words, following the Hebrew text, is [עַפְשׁ], which our people render "the seed is mouldy" (or "have become mouldy"). A cognate of it used in Holy Scripture is [אַפְשְׁ, Aphehu], which is also in use among the rabbis; nor does anything distinguish their roots except the interchange of the letter ב, b, with פ, p, which has been observed in other words too. From this, various Jewish teachers note that it has the same meaning as the last word, namely "to grow mouldy, become mouldy, rot." But the ancient learned grammarian Abu Walid tries to work out its meaning by comparing it with the Arabic word ['abifa], insofar as it means the same as ['tabifa], "to dry up", which he thinks fits this place best, because the damage described here seems to have been done more by dryness than by moisture, as we shall presently show. The author of the Arabic manuscript expresses it by [עתרת, Orbhat], which I suspect denotes "gnawed by worms" (for the Arabs use it of the gnawing of worms or beetles, and ['athatha], from the same root, for "corruption"), while noting that there is no Hebrew word from which it could be derived; hence he would have [עבשו, Abeshu] expressed by "Abthu", as the place seems to require. Yet those whose interpretations we have so far examined all agree that this expression here designates a corruption of the said things by which they no longer served their use and purpose, which they could ordinarily be expected to serve; to this sense the majority of interpreters who render it into Latin or other languages agree, saying "have rotted" (as the Vulgate does) or in some other not dissimilar way. The Chaldee suggests the same as regards the meaning of the word. As for the Greek, it is certainly not clear from
