units.la: ex verbis hebraicis, prout hodie leguntur, qua ratione eam reddide‑ rint per ισχιρτησαν. De Arabica voce Abesa, quæ luminis nonnihil huic affudisse interpretationi videri posset, Capellus observat, opponi eam græcæ voci σκιρτᾶω, saltare, exultare, eoque denotare mœrere, vel trifari; quamvis evenire sæpius dicat, ut vox ex alia in aliam linguam translata, contrariam ibi accipiat significationem, quam habebat antea; unde ejus opinio, suspicor, nata, vocem Abesa, quæ denotat Arabice dolere vel mœrere, posse deduci ab עבש Abasb, quæ hebraice significat saltare vel exultare præ lætitia. Sed aliunde hujus opinionis argumentum non petit, quam quod eam Græci reddiderint ισχ ρτησαν. Verum feliciori fortean conatu comparasset cum Abetha, mutata litera ש sch in ש, quod inusitatum non est in his linguis, quæ significat ludere. Eam autem potiorem judicat rationem interpretationis hujusmodi, quod aliter olim legerint in codice hebraico, quam hodie, videlicet non עבשו Abeshu, sed בעט Bathu a verbo quod significat o) calcitrare, petulantem esse. At adeo differunt sono & scriptione hæ voces, ut aliam pro alia in ullo accurato apographo poni vix ac ne vix quidem verisimile sit. Græcorum translationem excipit Syriaca, cujus vox Tabai, si ad mentem Latini interpretis sit exprimenda, succensatus, manserunt; non satis mihi constat, cui denotationi, cum duplex vocis hebrææ עבשו haud multum ante a quodam tradita est, potissimum sit vindicanda. Si ulsitationi significatione sit sumenda, qua, ut dictum est, redditur, torrefacta sint vel adusta, eo reducenda videtur, quo Abu Walid visum fuit proprie spectare, nimirum ad τὸ arcere, qua notatione etiam prædicta vox Arabice Abesa venit. Jam ordo postulat, ut & nos aliquid adjiciamus de his interpretationibus, earumque sensu ab interpretibus assignato; sed id consultius duco tamdiu differre, donec introspectum fuerit accurate, quid intelligant per sequentem vocem, quacum præcedens construitur, פרודות Perudoth, quæ a nostratibus reddita est fatum; in quo consentientes habent plerosque tum Judæos, tum recentes Christianos, qui
units.tr: the Hebrew words, as they are read today, how they came to render it ἐσκίρτησαν [eskirtēsan]. Concerning the Arabic word ʿabisa, which might seem to have shed some light on this interpretation, Capellus observes that it is set against the Greek word σκιρτάω [skirtaō], "to leap, to exult," and so denotes "to mourn or grieve"; although he says it often happens that a word carried from one language into another takes on a meaning contrary to what it had before. Whence, I suspect, arose the opinion that the word ʿabisa, which in Arabic means "to grieve" or mourn, can be derived from עבש [ʿabash], which in Hebrew means "to leap" or "exult for joy." But he does not draw the argument for this opinion from elsewhere than that the Greeks rendered it ἐσκίρτησαν. Yet perhaps with a more fortunate effort he would have compared it with ʿabitha, the letter ש [sh] being changed to ש [s], which is not unusual in these languages, and which means "to play." He judges this a stronger reason for such an interpretation: that in the Hebrew manuscript they once read differently from today, namely not עבשו [ʿabeshu] but בעט [bāʿaṭ], from a verb meaning "to kick," to be wanton. But these words differ so much in sound and spelling that it is scarcely even probable that one should be put for the other in any accurate copy. The Syriac translation follows the Greek, whose word tabai, if it is to be rendered according to the mind of the Latin translator, means "they were inflamed, they remained." It is not sufficiently clear to me which meaning should especially be claimed for it, since the double sense of the Hebrew word עבשו was given not long before by a certain person. If it is to be taken in the sense of scorching, by which, as has been said, it is rendered "they have been burnt or scorched," it seems to be referred to what Abu Walid thought properly to look at, namely to τὸ ἀρκεῖν [to arkein], "to suffice, to hold off," a meaning from which the aforesaid Arabic word ʿabisa also comes. Now the order requires that we too add something about these interpretations and the sense assigned to them by the interpreters; but I think it wiser to defer this until it has been examined carefully what they understand by the following word, with which the preceding one is construed, פְּרוּדוֹת [perudoth], which our translators render "the seed." In this matter most of both the Jews and the recent Christians agree with them, who

units.la: *) Deut. 32, 15. qui eadem significatione eam accipiunt impulsi & a radicis hebraeae significationibus,& dialectis,quae illi convenientes sunt,& formis quae inde more hebraico deducuntur. A Radice פרר P.rad, quae Hebraeis, Chaldaeis & Arabibus significat separare vel separatum esse, possunt deduci nomina, quae denotant quid singulare, & separatum vel divisum ab aliis, ut frumenti granula & semen, quod seminatur ac terrae mandatur. Atque eo sensu & hic accipi posse nomen hebraicum,absurdum non est,quamvis formae admodum peculiaris sit, cum p) nominis substantivi loco in S. literis nullibi usurpetur, nec ulla ejus occurrat occasio; sicut q) Syriaci ࡦ Pheredro, quod in N. T. versione occurrit ea significatione grani vel satis,& in plurali granorum vel satorum: unde apparet haud sine praegnanti ratione sic esse redditam & a quibusdam r) Judaeorum explanatam grana tritici & bordei, vel &c. s) grana feminis,quae seminantur,separantur & dissipantur per solum; vel ut Abu Walid Arabice or grana disjecta seminando,& R. Tanchum grana praeparata ad seminandum, ita dicta quia spargentur per solum. MS. Arabici auctor eandem ei tribuit denotationem, atque ab eadem radice deducit reddendo Atmotapharredatu (quod ad literam sonat separatum) ubi peculiari nota exponit se intelligere semen tritici, quod est triticum separatum, cui non est immixtum lolium quia mos hominibus est seminare praecipuum (vel exquisitum) tritici. Ita quidem & Abarbinel accipit, sed aliam significationis adducit causam, scilicet, non quod alterum ab altero sit separatum & distinctum, vel a lolio sejunctum, sed quod separatum sit (vel sebductum) ab oculis hominum atque occultum.
units.tr: *) Deut. 32, 15. who take it in the same sense, being moved both by the meanings of the Hebrew root and by the dialects that agree with it, and by the forms that are derived from it in the Hebrew manner. From the root [פרר, P.R.R.], which in Hebrew, Chaldee and Arabic means "to separate, or to be separated", there can be derived nouns denoting "something single and set apart or divided from others, such as grains of corn and seed that is sown and committed to the earth." And it is not absurd that the Hebrew word may be taken in this sense here, although its form is quite peculiar, since it is nowhere used in Holy Scripture as a substantive noun, nor does any occasion for it occur; likewise the Syriac [Pheredro], which occurs in the version of the New Testament, in the sense of "grain" or "seed", and in the plural "of grains" or "of seeds". Whence it appears that it has been rendered thus, and explained by some Jews, not without a weighty reason, as "grains of wheat and barley", or, etc., "grains of seed, which are sown, separated and scattered over the ground"; or, as Abu Walid says in Arabic, "grains scattered in sowing", and R. Tanchum says "grains prepared for sowing", so called "because they are scattered over the ground." The author of the Arabic manuscript attributes the same meaning to it, and derives it from the same root, rendering it [Atmotapharredatu] (which literally sounds like "separated"), where with a special note he explains that he understands "the seed of wheat", that is, wheat set apart, with no darnel mixed in, "because it is the custom of men to sow the choicest (or most exquisite) wheat." Abarbinel too takes it in this way, but adduces another reason for the meaning: not that one thing is separated and distinct from another, or set apart from the darnel, but that it is separated (or withdrawn) from men's eyes and hidden.

units.la: p) Usurpatur participii loco Ezech. 1, 10. q) Et פרר apud Rabb. r) Ab. Ezra. s) Kim. chi Rad. & Net. in latebris soli semen. Atque sic omnibus his hactenus convenit in eadem significatione eademque nominis radice, utut in derivationis ratione nonnihil vacillent; eaque notatio tam probabilis est vocique tam propria, ut recentiores inter Christianos interpretes plerumque exponant per femina, grana, fata, t) femina dispersa, u) grana feminum. Quod vero cæteras interpretationes interpretum antiquorum allegatorum concernit, non æque liquet, lubens fateor, cur Chaldæus Paraphrasta reddiderit vocem per dolia vini; non est certe ulla alia ejus rei ratio, quam nuda ejus auctoritas, & prorsus latet, quo usu venerit hæc vox suo ævo. Quod ad Græcorum δαμάλεως (quorum vestigia Syrus & Arabs prementes similem incurrunt censuram) vitulos, extra omnem controversiam est, non esse hanc significationem vocis בררות Perudoth; hinc w) quidam conjectant illos aliter legisse, videlicet פרות (sine litera ד d.) Paroth, quæ hoc valet. Idem x) statuendum de Vulgato Latino, qui vertit, jumenta, quamvis y) quibusdam videatur iisdem consonantibus legisse vocem, at non iisdem vocalibus; ac si numerum pluralem formasset a פרדה Pirdah, quod genus fœmininum est nominis רד Perid mulus: uno bestiarum genere expresso, quo cæteræ similis naturæ comprehenduntur bestiæ vel catuli in genere. At lubrica est omnino confugiendi ratio ad variarum lectionum conjecturas: Probandum erat prius ita eos legisse, atque ratio suppeditanda, quare ita legendum sit, quando lectio, a qua variant, tam bonum vel meliorem sensum præbeat, quam quæ subistituitur, ut hic apparet. Tertia vox, qua hic utitur Propheta, quæque in S. literis alibi non extat, atque idcirco interpretationis variæ fortem non minus subit, quam præcedentes, est מגרפתיהם Magrephotehem, nostratibus, glebæ suæ. Atque in eo antecessores habent non tantum Judæos, sed & recentiores interpretum, qui plerumque eam sic exponunt; licet interdum quoad exprimendi rationem, non quoad sensum, paululum (si modo paululum) iis intercedat diversitatis. z) Abu Walid, quem eorum, quos habemus Grammati-
units.tr: p) Used in place of a participle, Ezek. 1, 10. q) And among the rabbis, פרר [parar]. r) Ibn Ezra. s) Kimchi, Radak and Nethanel: "in the hiding-places of the soil, seed." So far all of these agree on the same meaning and the same root of the noun, though they waver somewhat over the reasoning of its derivation. This sense is so probable and so proper to the word that more recent Christian interpreters mostly explain it as "seeds," "grains," "crops," t) "scattered seeds," u) "grains of seed." As for the other interpretations of the ancient interpreters I have cited, I gladly admit the matter is not equally clear. Why the Chaldee paraphrast rendered the word as "casks of wine" I cannot say. There is certainly no reason for it except his bare authority, and it is quite unknown in what usage this word had in his day. As for the Greek δαμάλεως [damaleōs], "calves" (which the Syriac and Arabic versions, following in their footsteps, also incur a similar criticism), it is beyond all controversy that this is not the meaning of the word בררות [Perudoth]. Hence w) some conjecture that they read something else, namely פרות [Paroth], without the letter ד (d), which means this. The same must be said of the Latin Vulgate, which translates "beasts of burden." Some think they read the same consonants but not the same vowels, as if he had formed the plural from פרדה [Pirdah], the feminine of the noun רד [Perid], "mule," so that one kind of animal is named and the other beasts of a similar nature, or the young, are included under it. But it is altogether a slippery recourse to take refuge in conjectures about variant readings. It had first to be proved that they read it so, and a reason had to be given why it should be read so, when the reading from which they differ gives as good a sense as the one substituted, or a better one, as is clear here. The third word the Prophet uses here, which is found nowhere else in Holy Scripture and therefore undergoes no less varied interpretation than the preceding ones, is מגרפתיהם [Magrephotehem], which our translators render "their clods." In this they have as predecessors not only the Jews but also more recent interpreters, who mostly explain it thus, though sometimes there is a slight difference between them, if only a slight one, in the manner of expression rather than in the sense. Abu Walid, whom we judge the most ancient of the Jewish grammarians we have...

units.la: f) Tigur. u) Munst. §§) Merc. Capell. x) Grotius. y) Ribera, Chr. a Castr. z) In Rad. גרף. maticos inter Judæos, censemus antiquissimum, habet حطوطها ... כטיטוט Catuteba fulci illorum, quibus intelligit الخطوط quos agricola dentali suo ducit, postquam a) frumentum fatum est, qui sunt, addit, sicuti خدوش في الأرض scalptura in fundo. Et in eandem sententiam alio loco b) rursus ait, sic nominari بالخدوش propter similitudinem scalpturarum vel vulnerum, quæ fiunt in cute alicujus unguibus, quæ sunt fractura cutis. Eadem voce tantum non utitur c) R. Tanchum, adeo, ut & illi תחת מגרפותיהם tachath magrephotehem (sit תחרת חרושהם) sub scalpturis illorum, i.e. تحت الخطوط التي تحفرها أحراث التي كانها كسوم في fulcis, (lineis) quos aratrum fodit, qui sunt tanquam lirae in terra, quomodo & alibi (Psal. 65, 10.) eadem fere ratione vocantur גרוורים Gedudim, incisiones (noltr. fulci) a גרד Gedad, incidere. Huic significationi fulcrum quærunt ex voce אגריף Egroph, quæ reperitur Exod. 21, 25. & noltratibus aliisque tum Judæis, tum Christianis redditur pugnus, sed illis شانح حكاسر aliquid quod vulnerat vel facit d) incisuram بك شيء يجرح او يشدخ. Interim apparet his lineis vel scalpturis (ut eas vocant) non intelligendos sulcos excavatos & apertos, sed terra obtectos, qui aratro vel occa ducuntur per eam, quippe vox תחרת tachath, sub, ei adjuncta hoc necessario requirit; atque ideo Aben-Ezra exponit eam per העפר pulverem vel terram, & Kimchi per תחיבורת העפר fragmenta vel particulas pulveris (vel terræ); hinc nostrates reddunt glebas cum recentioribus interpretibus plerisque. Quod c) quidam confirmare conantur ex lingua a) Quod agro sulcato tradi solet, hinc occasionem intelligendas esse suspicor. b) In Rad. פרך. c) Qui in Dict. suo ita reddit verba عقرن الحب البنوم ... frumentum rancidum redditum est (vel putrefactum) sub feriebus terræ accumulatum. d) Abu V Val. גרף. e) Bochart.
units.tr: f) The Tigurine version. u) Münster. §§) Mercerus, Cappellus. x) Grotius. y) Ribera, Christophorus a Castro. z) In the root גרף [garaph]. Of the Jewish grammarians, the oldest we have, Abu Walid, has khututaha ... katuteba, "the furrows of them," which he understands as the lines that the ploughman draws with his share after the grain has been sown; these, he adds, are like khudush fi al-ard, "scratches in the ground." To the same effect, in another place he says again that they are called bi-al-khudush, "by analogy with the scratches or wounds that fingernails make in a person's skin, which are a breaking of the skin." R. Tanchum uses almost the same word, so that for him too tachath magrephotehem (read tachareth charushehem), "under their furrows," means taḥt al-khuṭūṭ allatī taḥfiruhā aḥrāth, "under the furrows which the ploughs dig, which are like lines in the earth." In the same way, elsewhere (Ps. 65:10) furrows are called by almost the same figure gedudim, "incisions" (in our language "furrows"), from gadad, to cut. For this meaning they seek support in the word egroph (Exod. 21:25), which is found there and which our people, together with other Jews and Christians, render "fist," but which the Arabic renders as "something that wounds or makes an incision." Meanwhile it is clear that by these lines or scratches (as they call them) are not to be understood open and excavated furrows, but furrows covered with earth, which are drawn through it by plough or harrow; for the word tachath, "under," joined to it necessarily requires this. So Aben Ezra explains it as "dust" or earth, and Kimchi as "fragments" or particles of dust (or earth). Hence our people, with most of the more recent interpreters, render it "clods." Some try to confirm this from the language a) which is customarily applied to a ploughed field; I suspect this is the occasion for the meaning. b) In the root פרך. c) Who in his Dictionary renders the words ... "the rancid grain is returned (or rotted), accumulated under the clods of earth." d) Abu Walid, root גרף. e) Bochart.

units.la: Arabica, qua جرف Jarph significare perhibetur glebam terræ, quam aqua convolvit vel secum abducit, ita ut pro quavis gleba possit usurpari. A radice hujus vocis hebraica גרף g.arph & Arabica جرف quæ significat f) & convolvere & abducere vel dispergere, non incommode forsitan posset deduci nomen, quod denotet terram fractam, superfusam, convolutam vel projectam super frumentum aratro vel occa; gleba denotatione confirmata a جرف significante frustum panis fracti, atque ita fortean quædam fragmenta vel frusta fracta alius rei, sicuti glebæ terræ. Restat interpretationis vocis alia ratio, cujus meminit auctor MS. Arabici, (etsi ipsa hebraica voce exprimat [?]) nimirum [?] quæ designat vel granaria vel acervos frumenti in granarijs [?] a quibus triticum (vel semen) remotum est (vel aversum, vel ablatum) & delatum in campum, ut terræ demandaretur, ita ut eandem notionem habeat hæc radix, quam præcedens, nimirum demendi vel auferendi. Hac ratione etiam accepisse nonnullos refert Grotius, qui habent acervos, ac si semina vel grana fuissent corrupta atque ad seminandum inidonea reddita jam in acervis suis, quo congesta erant. Quamvis igitur non una ratione differant, quos adduximus hactenus; in eo tamen sibi minus contrariantur, plagam hic traditam corruptionem esse fatorum, quæ eo usque se extendere deberet, ut futuræ messis nil spei reliquum foret. Quemadmodum vero prædicti antiquiores interpretes longe diffident in verbis prioribus exponendis, sic & in posterioribus, accommodantes singuli ea ei sensui, quem putant commodissime posse ferre. Chaldæus habet מגופתהון Meguphathon sub operculis suis, scilicet doliorum vini. LXX. & cum illis Syrus & Arabica impressa ἐπὶ ταῖς Φάτναις αὐτῶν in stabulis suis (vel ad præsepia sua) Vulgatus in stercore suo. Quorum utramque versionem Mercerus putat quam maxime
units.tr: Arabic, in which jarph is said to mean "a clod of earth that water rolls over" or carries off, so that it can be used of any clod. From the root of this Hebrew word garaph and the Arabic jarf, which means both to roll over and to carry off or scatter, a name might not unfittingly be derived that denotes earth broken up, poured over, rolled or thrown upon the grain by plough or harrow; the sense "clod" is confirmed by jarf, which means a broken piece of bread, and so perhaps some fragments or broken pieces of another thing, such as clods of earth. There remains another explanation of the word, which the author of the Arabic manuscript mentions (though he expresses the Hebrew word itself as [?]), namely [?], which denotes either "granaries" or "heaps of grain in the granaries [?], from which the wheat (or seed) has been removed" (or turned aside, or carried away) "and taken out into the field, to be committed to the earth." So this root has the same meaning as the previous one, namely "removing" or "carrying away." Grotius reports that some have understood it in this way too, who render it "heaps," as if the seeds or grains had been spoiled and made unfit for sowing while still in the heaps where they had been gathered. Although the explanations we have so far cited differ in more than one way, they are at least in agreement on this point, that the blow described here is the corruption of the seed, which would extend so far that no hope of a future harvest would remain. Just as the earlier interpreters mentioned differ widely in explaining the first words, so they do in the latter, each fitting them to the sense he thinks can best be borne. The Chaldee has Meguphathon [מגופתהון], "under their lids," namely of the wine casks. The Seventy, and with them the Syriac and the printed Arabic, have "in their stalls" [ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν] (or "at their mangers"); the Vulgate has "in their dung." Mercerus thinks that both of these versions are most strongly supported by a derivation of the word from the root garaph, insofar as it means "to turn aside," just as dung is turned aside from beneath cattle or out of their stalls.

units.la: {f} Hinc מירבר dialecto Rabb. & Chald. & Arab. جرف ligo vel talc instrumentum fimo ejiciendo vel pulveri extergendo aptum. xime niti derivatione vocis a radice גרף Garaph, quatenus denotat avertere, sicuti stercus avertitur sub pecudibus vel ex illorum stabulis. At aliam & pleniorem & aptiorem vocis hujus significationem non novi, quam quæ primo loco a nobis est adducta, quamque sequuntur cum nostratibus nonnulli alii, quare ad eam retinendam magnis adducimur rationibus. Sed tum hic quæstio exoritur, quam diverse solvunt, qui hanc interpretationis rationem amplectuntur, nimirum quo pacto satum in terra sit corruptum, ut hic innuitur? g) Alii causam petunt ab abundantia humiditatis, vel pluviæ ingenti copia. Alii a magna siccitate vel inopia pluviæ, cum nemini dubium sit, utramque perniciosam esse ac destruere satum in terra, alteram putredine, alteram marcore & tabe vel siccitate, ut non possit crescere vel expullulare. Inter eos, qui abundantiæ pluviæ eam tribuunt, recenset doctissimus b) Bochartus Kimchi, cujus verba, prout ab eo citantur, sunt hæc ... interprete eodem Bocharto, putrescunt grana feminis propter pluvias. At vel ipse hic hallucinatur, vel exemplar est corruptum, quod sequitur. In exemplaribus enim omnibus quæ mihi videre contigit impressa & MS. alia adduntur citatis verba, quæ perfectum sensum conficiunt & contrariam ejus mentem adaperiunt, in quibus post verba מפני הגשמים propter pluvias, adduntur ... quæ non descendent super eas, quia futura est magna siccitas (vel pluviæ defectus) eo tempore. Nec secus actum cum Deodati, quem ejusdem sententiæ asseclam citat. Verum equidem est, verba ejus citata extare in i) quadam editione, scilicet grana esse corrupta du foverchie piogge per niniam pluviam; sed inveniuntur in k) posteriori editione, quam interpres Anglicanus sequitur, verba, quæ omnino contrarium indicant, videlicet non potuisse progerminare per lestreme joccita propter summam siccitatem, ac si ambiguus hæreret cum aliis, num hæc vel illa illata sit noxa, l) vel pluviarum frequentia, vel raritate nimia, vel, ut placet m) quibusdam utramque conjungere. post diuturnos imbres,
units.tr: {f} Hence mirbar in the Rabbinic, Chaldee and Arabic dialects, jarf, is a hoe or a tool suited to throwing out dung or scraping away dust. But I know of no fuller or more suitable meaning of this word than the one first cited by us, which some others follow along with our people, and so we are strongly drawn to retain it. But here the question arises, which those who embrace this interpretation resolve in different ways: in what manner the seed in the ground was spoiled, as is hinted here? g) Some seek the cause in an abundance of moisture, or a great quantity of rain. Others in great drought or lack of rain. Since no one doubts that each is harmful and destroys the seed in the ground, the one by rot, the other by withering, decay and drying up, so that it cannot grow or sprout. Among those who attribute it to abundance of rain, the very learned b) Bochart lists Kimchi, whose words, as he cites them, are these: "... by the same interpreter, Bochart, the grains of seed rot because of the rains." But either he himself is mistaken here, or the copy that follows is corrupt. For in all the printed and manuscript copies of the cited words that I have happened to see, words are added which complete the sense and reveal its opposite meaning; after the words "because of the rains" (mippenei hageshamim) there are added "... which will not come down upon them, because there will be great drought (or lack of rain) at that time." Nor is it otherwise with Diodati, whom he cites as a follower of the same opinion. It is true that the words he cites do appear in i) a certain edition (namely the 4to Geneva of 1607), saying that the grains were spoiled "from too much rain" (du foverchie piogge); but in k) a later edition (Geneva, 1641, in folio), which the English interpreter follows, there are words that indicate the exact opposite, namely that they could not sprout "through extreme dryness" (per lestreme joccita) because of the great drought, as if he were undecided along with others whether this or that harm was inflicted, l) "either by the frequency of rain or by its excessive scarcity," or, as some m) prefer, joining both together: "after lasting rains, a raging drought or the heat of the sun." But Kimchi, as has been said, does not attribute it to abundance, but to a lack or scarcity of rain, which...

units.la: g) Jun. Trem. b) Psal. p. 472. i) In 4to Genev. 1607, k) Genev. 1641. in Fol. l) Pelican. m) Danæus. bres ,sœvientem siccitatem seu eslum solis. At Kimchi abundantiæ,ut dictum est, eam non tribuit,sed defectui vel inopiæ pluviarum, quæ etiam opinio est Abu Walid, cujus verba eo tendunt ut nihil aliud velint verba Abaschu Perudoth grana arefacta sunt, quam אלתשניע ואלתעטים לאמר אלקים אלהים התי יבשרת אלחביב החרת אלארץ אר לא ינזר עליהא מטר פלם תנבת exaggerare turpitudinem & magnitudinem famis, quæ illos obruebat, ita ut grana sub terra arefierent, quia pluvia non cadebat super ea, atque ita non poterant protuberare. R. Tanchum dicit etiam id contigisse per ingentem siccitatem, atque exinde putat monstrari posse cum locustis simul fuisse ibi pluviarum inopiam, id quod etiam ex sequentibus appareat (v. 20.) כי יבשו אפיקי מים alvei aquarum exaruerunt. Hanc expressionem (cui adjungi potest quæ habentur v. 19. Ignis consumsit pascua deserti, flamma inflammavit omnes arbores agri, & quæ sequuntur Vers. 20. ignis absumsit pascua deserti) argumenti loco habet prædictus Doctissimus Bochartus, magnam fuisse siccitatem,non vero humiditatis excessum,qua hæc facta sunt. Idem ex eo probat, quod hæc calamitas conjuncta sit cum destructione illa,quam inferebant terræ fructibus locustæ,& cætera ante dicta noxia animalcula,quia plerumque hæ bestiolæ abundant tempestate sicca,non humida & pluviosa,quæ ipsis interitum ciet, ut ex illis probat auctoribus, qui de natura illarum scripserunt;& hac ratione, ut observat,non dicenda sunt fata putrefacta, quod a superflua humiditate venit, quin potius evanuisse, in nihilum redacta, quod fit, cum marcida redduntur atque contrahuntur humiditatis defectu, qua notatione etiam accepisse עבש prædictum Abu Walid, jam ante nobis observatum est. Huic verborum explicationi operose nimis ac diu insistere coacti sumus ob nimiam diversitatem interpretationis, quam diversi interpretes tam diverse tradunt. De reliquis, quæ descriptionem ulteriorem calamitatis immissæ complectuntur, quamvis diversitas tanta inter illos non sit, nec omnibus tamen convenire satis apertum est. Nostrates habent,
units.tr: g) Junius and Tremellius. b) Psalm, p. 472. i) In the 4to Geneva edition of 1607. k) Geneva 1641, in folio. l) Pelicanus. m) Danaeus. showers, a raging drought or the heat of the sun. But Kimchi does not attribute it to excess of rain, as has been said, but to a lack or scarcity of rain. This is also the opinion of Abu Walid, whose words aim only at this: that the phrase Abaschu Perudoth grana arefacta sunt [Abaschu Perudoth: the seeds were dried up] is meant to magnify the foulness and greatness of the famine which overwhelmed them, so that the grains withered under the ground because rain did not fall upon them, and so they could not sprout. The verse al-tashnīʿ wa-l-taʿṭīm ... al-arḍ ... lā yanzil ʿalayhā maṭar fa-lam tanbut [the Arabic, in Hebrew letters] is, in his view, to be taken in this sense. R. Tanchum says that this too happened through an immense drought, and from this he thinks it can be shown that along with the locusts there was also a lack of rain there. This is also clear from what follows (v. 20): כי יבשו אפיקי מים [ki yibshu afiqei mayim], the channels of the waters have dried up. The aforementioned most learned Bochart uses this expression (to which can be added what is found in v. 19, Fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, a flame has burned all the trees of the field, and what follows in v. 20, fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness) as an argument that the drought was great, and not an excess of moisture, which brought about these things. He proves the same from the fact that this calamity is joined with the destruction which the locusts and the other harmful little creatures mentioned above brought upon the fruits of the earth, because these little beasts mostly abound in dry weather, not in damp and rainy weather, which brings about their death, as he proves from those authors who wrote about their nature. For this reason, as he observes, the things are not to be described as rotted, which comes from excessive moisture, but rather as vanished, reduced to nothing, which happens when things are made withered and shrivelled by lack of moisture. By this sense, as we have already noted, the aforementioned Abu Walid also took the word עבש [ʿbsh, mouldy]. We have been compelled to dwell on this explanation of the words too laboriously and too long, because of the great diversity of interpretation which different interpreters give so differently. As to the rest, which contain the further description of the calamity sent, although there is not such great diversity among them, it is nevertheless quite clear that they do not all agree. Our people have:

units.la: n) Ex Plin. Arist. ut & ex Tertulliano. habent, horrea sunt desolata, granaria destructa. Horrea אצרות Otzeroth, quæ vox significat & res in futurum usum conditas, & repositoria vel loca, in quibus conduntur, Latine Thesauri, & Græce Θησαυροί, ut e) non nemo interpretatus est. R. Salomon addit שיר ... ין ושין שבן vini & olei, verum non exprimit, num harum rerum copiam, an promtuaria intelligat; posteriora vero intelligere non levis conjectura est. Clarius mentem suam prodit Kimchi in eandem sententiam exponens: thesauri seu repositoria התבואה fructuum terræ sunt desolati (deserta, derelicta) quia nihil est, quod iis imponatur atque ita sunt vel jacent desolata. Unde manifeste liquet, plerosque vocibus licet diversis eodem tendere, cum habeant horrea, thesauri, cellæ, thecæ, reconditoria, granaria, omnesque hanc vocem sumant pro repositoriis, quibus aliquid imponitur vel quæ aliqua re implentur; licet alii generalius accipiant pro quoque rerum genere, alii strictius pro frumentorum granis, ut nostrates, quando reddunt, horrea, quod hic locus videtur præcipue flagitare, cum de iis, & quæ præcedunt, & quæ sequuntur, inprimis agant verba. Differt ab his versio Tigurina, quippe de rebus iis impositis sumit, reddendo: Vasta ta sunt quæ reposita fuerunt; & quæ antecedunt: computruerunt semina dispersa subter glebas suas, ita ut sibi apte hunc in modum cohæreant: Computruerunt semina diversa subter glebas suas, vasta ta sunt, quæ reposita fuerunt. Utrumque eodem redit, nimirum, defectus ordinariæ frumenti copiæ innuitur, qua gaudere solebant, cuiusque recondendæ repositoriis opus erat. Si frumentum deficit, horreis opus non est; si horrea sunt desolata, constat frumentum non posse ibi recondi, atque ejus curam haberi. At magis puto quadrare non tantum huic loco, sed & sequentibus verbis, de horreis vel repositoriis, in quibus dicta solebant recondere, ea exponere, quam de rebus ipsis; atque ea ratione videntur id etiam accepisse ex prisicis Chaldæus & Syrus, qui talem adhibent vocem, quæ & radice & significatione accedit hebraico אוצרות Otsraya, cellaria, vel ut Mercerus, Apotheca & Ιλαοι Autsre, horrea, & Græca Θησαυροί thesau.
units.tr: n) From Pliny, Aristotle, and also from Tertullian. They have: the barns are desolate, the granaries destroyed. The word for barns, אצרות [otzeroth], denotes both things stored up for future use and the places or repositories in which they are kept; in Latin treasuries, and in Greek θησαυροί [thēsauroi], as one person has rendered it. R. Solomon adds שיר ... ין ושין שבן [wine and oil], but he does not say whether he means the abundance of these things or the storerooms; to understand the latter is not a slight conjecture. Kimchi reveals his meaning more clearly, explaining to the same effect: the treasuries or storehouses of the produce of the earth (the deserted, abandoned ones) are desolate, because there is nothing that is placed in them, and so they lie desolate. From this it is clear that most writers, though they use different words, aim at the same thing, since they have horrea, thesauri, cellae, thecae, reconditoria, granaria, and all these words they take for repositories into which something is put or which are filled with something. Some understand the word more generally, for any kind of thing, others more narrowly, for grains of corn, as our people do when they render horrea, which this passage seems chiefly to demand, since the words both before and after it deal with these things. The Tigurine version differs from these, since it takes the reference to be to the things put in the repositories, rendering: The things that were stored up are laid waste; and what goes before: the scattered seeds have rotted under their clods, so that they hang together fittingly in this way: The diverse seeds have rotted under their clods; the things that were stored up are laid waste. Both come to the same thing, namely, that the lack of the usual abundance of grain is indicated, the abundance which they used to enjoy and for which storehouses were needed. If the grain fails, there is no need of barns; if the barns are desolate, it is plain that the grain cannot be stored there or looked after. But I think it fits better, not only with this passage but also with the following words, to explain these as the barns or repositories in which the things were usually stored, rather than the things themselves. For this reason the Chaldee and Syriac seem also to have taken it in this sense; they use a word which, both in root and in meaning, is close to the Hebrew אוצרות [otsraya], storehouses, or, as Mercerus has it, apothecae, and horrea, and the Greek θησαυροί [thēsauroi], treasuries.

units.la: e) Targ. thesauri, ut antea retulimus, eamque ob rationem hic repetimus, ut palam fiat, hic loci in quibusdam p) exemplaribus perperam legi ταυρόι, tauri, quia fortean δαμάλεις, juvencæ, in hac translatione præcesserant.
units.tr: e) Targum: treasuries, as we mentioned before, and we repeat it here for this reason, so that it becomes plain that in some copies here it has been wrongly read as ταυρόι [tauroi], bulls, perhaps because δαμάλεις [damaleis], heifers, had come before it in this translation.

units.la: In eandem sententiam dicta etiam sunt, quæ hæc proxime sequuntur, adeo ut Kimchi dicat, quod in eis העניין כפל geminet sensum, (i. e. repetat idem, licet diversis verbis) quatenus ממגורות Memguroth, ejusdem significationis est cum אצרות Otseroth, utraque repositoria denotante. R. Salomon tamen eas ita distinguere conatur, ut per Otseroth intelligat, in quibus reconditur vinum & oleum, per Memguroth, quibus recipitur triticum vel frumentum. q) Alii aliter accipiunt, scilicet, ut priori innuatur receptaculum frumenti & aliorum id generis vitæ necessariorum, posteriori receptaculum, quo vinum secluditur. Ita videntur accepisse LXX, cum alteram reddant θησαυροί, thesauri, alteram ληνοί torcularia, quemadmodum & Syrus primam exprimit per לוכל horrea, alteram per torcularia (ut & Arabica impressa per Maafer.) Eo nempe redit omnis inter eos diversitas, quod, observante Kimchi, vox utraque indefinite denotet aliquod repositorium vel locum, in quem colliguntur vel deponuntur res vitæ necessariæ, sive frumentum & vinum, sive aliquid hujus generis aliud. De posteriori voce ממגורות Memguroth, (quæ descendit a radice גור Gur, quatenus denotat colligere) dicit Aben-Ezra esse מלרות דרות dictionem peregrinam vel inusitatæ formæ, eo quod initio gemina ponatur littera ם m, cum una juxta regulam sufficiens fuisset, adeo ut debuisset legi מגורות Megurot, numerusque sit pluralis ex r) מגורה Megurah, qui occurrit Hagg. 2,19. quo in loco significat granarium. Hinc R. Tanchum [illegible, ~20 letters] Ejus numerus pluralis debuisset esse Megnroth, sed addita alia m ei, quæ nomen format,
units.tr: In the same sense is also said what immediately follows, so that Kimchi says that in these words the matter is doubled (that is, the same thing is repeated, though in different words), since ממגורות [memguroth] has the same meaning as אצרות [otseroth], both denoting repositories. R. Solomon, however, tries to distinguish them so that by otseroth he means those in which wine and oil are stored, and by memguroth those in which wheat or grain is received. Others take them differently, namely, that the first points to a receptacle for grain and other things of that kind necessary for life, and the second to a receptacle in which wine is kept. The Seventy seem to have understood it this way, since they render the one as θησαυροί [thēsauroi], treasuries, and the other as ληνοί [lēnoi], winepresses; and the Syriac also renders the first by לוכל [lukhal], barns, and the second by winepresses (as also the printed Arabic renders it by Maafer). All the difference between them comes to this, as Kimchi observes, that each word indefinitely denotes some repository or place into which things necessary for life are gathered or deposited, whether grain and wine or something else of this kind. Concerning the latter word, ממגורות [memguroth], which comes from the root גור [gur], in the sense of to gather, Aben Ezra says it is a foreign word or of an unusual form, because a double letter ם [m] is put at the beginning, whereas one would have sufficed according to the rule, so that it ought to be read מגורות [megurot], and the plural comes from מגורה [megurah], which occurs at Haggai 2:19, where it means a granary. Hence R. Tanchum [illegible] Its plural ought to have been megnuroth, but another m has been added to it, which forms the noun.

units.la: p) Basil. in sol. 1597. Et vid. Kimchi Concord. & Druf. q) Vide Riberam & Pet. a Fig. r) Grotius comparat cum ea Maguria, quo nomine Pœni horrea sua vocabant & villas. m:t, factum est Mammegurosh. At, quod confitetur non illi solum, sed & Iudæi alii cum Christianis, nil ea additione nec significatione nec constructione vocis, quæ simplicior est & regulari formæ magis accedens, infertur. Unus Kimchi observat Patrem ejus secus sentire, videlicet priorem ם m, voci essentialem non esse, sed particulam servilem, vel præpositionem ei præfixam, significantem de vel ex; ita ut sensus esse deberet ex granario (quodam) destructa sint; quanquam litera m ea vocali destituta sit, qua plerumque conjuncta ea significatione venit; loco enim ı habet ם. Huic accedit etiam Abarbinel, primam literam esse particulam præfixam, statuens, quæ idem significat ac מ Men, ob vel propter, atque tum alia significatione accipit nomen, scilicet, timoris, mutatoque constructionis ordine legi debere percupit: granaria sunt destructa & diruta propter timorem, scilicet hostium, quatenus timore horum correpti nec ferebant, nec metebant. At prior ratio ut simplicissima est constructione, ita & videtur planissima, quare cum plerisque tum nostratibus quoque merito probatur. Quod ad verbum הרמס Neherfu destructa sunt attinet, nullum dubium est, quin ruinas ac destructionem inferre denotet. Kimchi tamen hanc significationem conatur infringere, sic posse intelligi innuens בארו הרמס sunt ac si essent desolata vel diruta, quia nihil hucusque illis illatum est: Addit vero, si proprie hoc sumendum, ut re ipsa destructa dici possint, id ideo factum, quia nemo amplius eorum curam habebat, vel quotannis, ut solenne iis erat, reparabat deficiente protinus eorum usu & emolumento, atque sic prorsus esse periisse. Ratio vero istius negligentiæ, qua in ruinam ea vergere necesse erat, & quare minus ruinæ illorum obstent, exprimitur in sequentibus: Nam frumentum exaruit. Quæ cum addantur præcedentibus, factum mucidum factum est sub glebis suis, vel ejusdem rei repetitionem constituunt, vel si quid diversi habent, id significare videntur, q) quod superierat ex illa semente, nondum prorsus corruptum (vel quod inde expullulabat) ita in agro nacidum erat redditum, ut integritatem ac perfectionem suam minus assequi posset, quare nil relinquebatur granarius inferendum, unde
units.tr: p) Basel, in Sol. 1597. And see Kimchi's Concordance and Drusius. q) See Ribera and Peter of Figueroa. r) Grotius compares with it maguria, a name the Carthaginians used for their granaries and farmhouses. m:t, it has become Mammegurosh. But, as not only he but also other Jews together with the Christians admit, nothing is inferred from that addition either in the meaning or in the construction of the word, which is simpler and comes closer to the regular form. Kimchi alone observes that his father thought otherwise, namely, that the first letter ם [m] is not essential to the word but a servile particle, or a preposition prefixed to it, meaning from or out of; so that the sense ought to be out of the granary (some) were destroyed, although the letter m lacks that vowel which usually goes with that meaning; for instead of ı it has ם. Abarbanel also agrees, holding that the first letter is a prefixed particle which means the same as מ [men], because of or on account of, and then takes the noun in another sense, namely, of fear, and he wishes the order of construction to be changed to read: the granaries are destroyed and overthrown because of fear, namely of enemies, since, seized with fear of them, they neither carried in nor reaped. But the former explanation, as it is the simplest in construction, so it also seems the plainest; therefore it is rightly approved both by most and by our people as well. As for the word הרמס [neherfu], have been destroyed, there is no doubt that it denotes the bringing about of ruin and destruction. Kimchi, however, tries to weaken this meaning, suggesting that it may be understood as they are as if they were desolate or overthrown, because nothing has so far been done to them. He adds, however, that if it is to be taken literally, so that they may truly be said to be destroyed, this has happened because no one any longer took care of them, or repaired them each year as was customary for them, their use and profit having ceased at once, and so they have utterly perished. But the reason for this neglect, by which they were bound to fall into ruin, and why their ruin is less to be prevented, is expressed in what follows: For the grain has withered. Since these words are added to the preceding ones, the mouldy thing has become mouldy under its clods, they either form a repetition of the same thing, or, if they have something different, they seem to signify this: what remained from that seed, not yet wholly corrupted (or what had sprouted from it), had been so turned into a withered crop in the field that it could hardly reach its wholeness and perfection; so nothing was left which needed to be brought into the granary, for which there was neither any necessity nor any use for keeping it safe; and this explanation favours those who take the preceding word to mean granary, which properly suits grain, against those who take it for a wine-cellar.

units.la: q) Jon. 1 remel. eorum confervandorum nec ulla necessitas nec usus; atque hæc expositio pro illis facit, qui præcedentem vocem interpretantur, granarium, quod frumentis proprie convenit, contra illos, qui eam sumunt pro cella vinaria.
units.tr: q) Jon. 1. There is neither any necessity nor any use in keeping them; and this explanation supports those who take the preceding word to mean granary, which properly suits grain, against those who take it to mean a wine cellar.

units.la: Vocis הביש Hobish, nostratibus exaruit, plus semel ante mentio injecta est, ut v. 10. 11. 12. duplicique ratione sumi posse notatum, quatenus ad duplicem radicem referri patitur, videlicet ad יבש yabash, exarescere vel ad בוש Bosh pudefieri vel confundi, prout loci circumstantiæ, ubi occurrit, requirere videntur. Utraque significatio voci hic tribuitur, altera ab aliis, ab aliis altera. Primam amplectuntur nostrates, & non pauci cum antiquorum tum recentiorum. Sic LXX. ὅτι ἐξηράνθη σῖτος, quia triticum exaruit. Sic Syrus Vibesh oburo, & frumentum exaruit. Et Arabica impressa quia &c. Et interpretum recentiorum nonnulli: r) aruit aut s) exaruit, & e secuto, inquit Diodati, exaruit, & in t) alia editione, perīro per la siccita, periit per siccitatem. Sed sunt alii inter eos, qui altera significatione accipiunt, qua denotat pudefieri vel confundi. Ita Vulgatus quia confusum est triticum, quem sequuntur ex u) hodiernis non pauci, cum vel w) eodem verbo vocem exprimant, vel alio æquipollent: quod pudefactum sit; quid? quod nec Judæorum quorundam mens ab hac interpretatione prorsus aliena fit. Ita MS. Arabicum x) frumentum confusum est vel pudefactum. Ita R. Tanchum qui contra significationem exarescendi excipit, quod non fit conveniens dicere, frumentum exaruisse, eo quod innuitur, locustas illud comedisse. At non opus est mea ipsius opinione hac exceptione, si verba eo modo accipiantur, quo supra innuimus, scilicet pro repetitione verborum præcedentium, qua docetur, quid acciderit frumento in solo sub glebis; vel si accipiatur cum quibusdam pro eo, quod devoratum non erat a locustis, sed relictum; reliquisse autem r) Pagn. s) Munster. t) 4to 1607. Gen. u) Munst. w) Tig. Castalio, quippe sæda frumenta. x) Videtur vocem hebraicam retinere, quæ tamen ea significatione apud Arabes in usu non est. autem nonnihil improbabile prorsus non est, quanquam horrenda⌄ fuerit illarum destructio. Quod vero ad sensum hujus vocis pertinet, si hac ratione sumatur, certum est, illum proprie eam non accipere, ut significet pudorem vel confusionem, quippe quæ in frumentum non cadunt, sed figurate vel improprie pro defectu, vel frustratione, præcisione vel amissione, quo sensu etiam Chaldæus Paraphrastes reddit ײ, defecit; vel ut y) nonnemo ad rationem clariorem reddendam, cur ita accipiatur, exponit, defecit, & deficiendo homines confudit, pudefecit & ipse fructratum est; qui sensus æque congruit vocis significationi, qua denotat exarescere. Quæ porro collocantur opera ad ea insuper exquisite distinguendum, instituti nostri non est inquirere. Calamitatem hic describi nostra opinio est, quæ inferebatur a locutis &c. & siccitate proprie sumta⌄; eamque exponendi viam planissimam tritissimamque arbitramur. Quidam hostes hisce expressionibus præfiguratos esse statuunt, quorum⌄ non paucos esse ante tradidimus, omnem etiam jacturam & damnum hic descriptum iisdem tribuunt, eosdem putant omnes devorasse⌄ terræ fructus, eosdem z) conculcasse fata, eosdem destruxisse horrea, eosdem diruisse granaria, eoque frumenta, quæ humi jacebant, & in a) acervis suis congesta, exaruisse & effluendo periisse, quia non erat horreum, quo tegebantur & defendebantur a cœli intemperie; hinc Grotius ultima verba vertit: ideo b) fecit tritici, non quod tritici penuria causa exiterit, cur horrea rui lixiviisent, sed id potius adscribendum est defectui tectorum, quibus cum destituta essent horrea atque ideo omni intemperiei cœli expositia, factum est, ut exaruerint mucidaque reddita sint frumenta. Atque ita exponit Abarbenel particulam כי Ci, quam nostrates reddunt Nam per ולכן velacen, atque ideo; sicut aliquando etiam aliis in locis significare, ideo, propterea, quare, quamobrem, c) notatum est.
units.tr: The word הביש Hobish [Hobish], which our people render dried up, has been mentioned more than once before, at vv. 10, 11, 12, and it has been noted that it can be taken in two ways, since it may be referred to two roots: to יבש yabash [yabash], to dry up, or to בוש bosh [bosh], to be put to shame or confounded, as the circumstances of the passage where it occurs seem to require. Each meaning has been given to the word here, some following one and some the other. Our people, and not a few both of the ancients and of the more recent writers, embrace the first. So the Seventy: ὅτι ἐξηράνθη σῖτος [hoti exēranthē sitos], because the wheat dried up. So the Syriac: Vibesh oburo, and the grain dried up. And the printed Arabic: because, and so on. Some of the more recent translators: r) withered or s) dried up, and in what follows, dried up, says Diodati; and in the t) other edition, perīro per la siccita, that is, perished through drought. But there are others among them who take it in the second sense, which denotes to be put to shame or to be confounded. So the Vulgate: because the wheat is confounded, whom not a few of the modern writers follow in u), since they either express the word by the same verb w) or by one of equal force: which has been put to shame. Why? Because the mind of some Jews is not at all alien to this interpretation. So the Arabic manuscript: the grain is confounded or put to shame. So R. Tanchum, who, against the sense of drying up, objects that it is not fitting to say that the grain dried up, since it is implied that locusts ate it. But my own opinion does not need this objection, if the words are taken in the way we have indicated above, namely as a repetition of the preceding words, by which it is taught what happened to the grain in the soil under its clods; or if it is taken, with some, to mean what was not eaten by the locusts but left behind; and that leaving behind is x) not a little improbable, although their destruction was dreadful. As for the sense of this word, if it is taken in this way, it is certain that it is not used properly to mean shame or confusion, since these do not fall upon grain, but figuratively or improperly for failure, or disappointment, cutting off or loss. In this sense the Chaldee paraphrast also renders ײ [...], failed; or, as someone, to make the reason for so taking it clearer, explains it: it failed, and by failing it confounded men; it put them to shame, and was itself disappointed. This sense agrees equally well with the meaning of the word by which it denotes to dry up. What further labours are spent on distinguishing these things carefully is not our business to inquire. Our opinion is that the calamity is described here, which was brought about by the locusts, etc., and by drought taken in its proper sense; and we judge this to be the plainest and most commonly accepted way of explaining it. Some hold that enemies are foreshadowed by these expressions, of whom we have said before there are not a few; they also attribute to them all the loss and damage described here. They think the same enemies devoured the fruits of the land, trampled the crops underfoot, destroyed the barns and pulled down the granaries, and so the grain lying on the ground and heaped in its piles dried up and perished by running away, because there was no barn to cover and protect it from the inclemency of the sky. Hence Grotius renders the last words: therefore he made the wheat, not that the shortage of wheat was the cause why the barns were ruined and dissolved, but this is rather to be ascribed to the lack of roofs; since the barns were left without them and so were exposed to every inclemency of the sky, it came about that the grain dried up and was made mouldy. And so Abarbenel explains the particle כי Ci [ki], which our people render for, by ולכן velacen [velakhen], and therefore; as it has been noted that elsewhere it also sometimes means therefore, on account of this, why, wherefore.

units.la: Quamcunque autem viam ingressus fueris, ut rite intelligas hanc emphaticam & geminatam exprimendi rationem, qua ingentem⌄ illam
units.tr: Whichever way you go about rightly understanding this emphatic and doubled manner of expression, by which the Prophet describes that huge

units.la: y) Pet. a Fig. z) Vid. Ar. Mont. a) Grotius. b) Putat ביש vicinam habere significationem cum ובאש fœcuit. c) Vid. Concord. Noldii.
units.tr: y) Peter of Figueroa. z) See Arias Montanus. a) Grotius. b) He thinks ביש [bish] has a meaning close to ובאש [vebaash], became foul. c) See the Concordance of Noldius.

units.la: illam Propheta describit calamitatem, qua populus erat affictus & in posterum affligendus ea in regione, in qua antea omni genere deliciarum ad satietatem usque superfluus fructus erat magna copia omnibus illis bonis, quae ad vitae non tantum necessariam, verum & ad delicatam pertinent rationem, nec non ipsum fontem, unde haec universa in ipsum derivabantur; hanc, inquam, exprimendi rationem, nemini obscurum arbitror, in id potissimum esse adhibitam, ut, si omnino ad mentem voluissent revocare suam conditionem Judaei ac undecunque rite inspicere, de gravissima, qua in eos saeviebat Deus, admoneret ira atque ad seriam repentinamque commoveret resipiscentiam & conversionem ad DEum, ut ejulando, jejunando ac precando moestissima ante juberet cessare supplicia, quam penitus essent ab iis consumti & deleti. E contrario si minus ad ea attenderent eaque non aliter considerarent, quam quae fortuito erant illata, & quae tam cito possent evanescere, quam venerant, vel quibus aliunde remedium peti posset, quid aliud ea innui arbitreris, quam summa illorum stupiditas brutumque ingenium, quo minus iis afficiebantur, quam ipsa inter eos bruta? quorsum etiam ad ulteriorem eorum instructionem eos videtur in sequentibus ablegare, quo affectu mala ingruentia exceperint, ostendens:
units.tr: calamity with which the people were afflicted and were to be afflicted in the future in that region, in which before, in great abundance, superfluous fruit had been available to the point of satiety, with all those good things that pertain not only to the necessary but also to the delicate way of life, and also the very source from which all these things were derived to them: this manner of expression, I think, is obvious to no one, except that it was used chiefly for this purpose: that if the Jews had wished to call their condition to mind and to examine it properly from every side, it would have warned them of the very grave anger with which God was raging against them, and would have moved them to a serious and sudden repentance and conversion to God, so that by wailing, fasting and praying they might at once end the most sorrowful punishments before they were utterly consumed and destroyed by them. On the other hand, if they paid less attention to these things and did not consider them otherwise than as things that had come by chance, and that could vanish as quickly as they came, or for which a remedy could be sought elsewhere, what else do you think these things imply than the great stupidity of those people and a brutish disposition, by which they were moved less than the very beasts among them? To which end, for their further instruction, it seems that he sends them, in what follows, to learn with what feeling they received the evils that were coming upon them, showing:

units.la: 18. Quam ingemiscit animal? armenta boum sunt perplexa, eo quod nullum sit pascuum eorum: et- iam greges ovium desolantur.
units.tr: 18. How the beast groans! The herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are laid waste.

units.la: Quam d) quidam reddunt, quare &c. quod perperam aliis videtur, quocirca retinere malunt, quam &c. Prolata priora verba interrogandi forma arguunt amplitudinem rerum praedictarum, atque impetum & vehementiam qua perstringebant; quamobrem Chaldaeus ea forma interrogandi insuper habita affirmative reddit ingemiscit animal valde. Vox animal hebraice singularis numeri est, verum sumitur e) collective significatione plurali seu plura complectens; f) generale praeterea est nomen,
units.tr: How d) some render, why etc., which seems wrong to others, so they prefer to keep how etc. The earlier words, put as a question, show the greatness of the things foretold and the force and vehemence with which they struck. For this reason the Chaldee paraphrast, disregarding that interrogative form, renders it as an affirmation: the beast groans greatly. The word animal is singular in Hebrew, but it is taken e) in a collective sense, embracing several things in the plural; f) moreover, it is a general name,

units.la: d) Vulg. Pagn. Arab. MS. e) Pisc. f) Kimchi. Per. a Fig. nomen, cujus specialia postea exprimuntur sub nominibus bohm & vhim. Etenim בהמה Behemah, cum veniat generali significatione יקרא עין אלחיון אלמאשי dicitur de talibus creaturis vivis, quae incedunt quadrupedes, ut explicite habet Abu Walid: apposite ad بهيمة Bahimah, dialecto Arabica, quae g) denotat كل ذات لربع ولوقي الى quadrupedem quandam vivam creaturam quales etiam in aqua degunt; imo adhuc generalius يمسي لا حي كل quamcunque creaturam vivam sine distinctione. Abu Walid praedictus inquit אן לפט בהמה יקע עלי נוע ואחר ועלי אניאא כתירה Behemah, dici jam de uno genere (bestiarum) jam de pluribus, jam de quadam beftia particulari. Inter eam vero & חיה Chaiyah, (quae reperire est una cum illa Gen. 1, 25. ubi altera vertitur bestias terrae, altera boves) distinguere Judaeorum b) Magistros observatum est, ita ut posteriorem (chayah) feras bestias proprie denotare statuant, priorem vero (Behemah i)) domestica, cicuria, quorum servitio plerumque utuntur homines. Hoc igitur generali nomine non dubium est, quin fequentes species, quae armenta boum & greges ovium appellantur, comprehendantur, adeo ut in specie deinde Propheta velit innuere, quaenam potissimum spectet animalia juxta expositionem Kimchi, quae nobis valde probabilis est. Solet equidem ea vox, ut jam notavimus, pro aliis etiam animalium speciebus fumi ac praecipue, ut censet Grotius, pro equis, mulis, asinis, quando nihil aliud additur, ab Hebraeis, Chaldaeis, & Arabibus; atque hinc est, quod voce magis propria ab eis exprimitur, qui habent, k) jumentum, quae inprimis ejusmodi animal denotat, cujus opera in rebus bajulandis & trahendis, ut & in re agraria praesto est; ac fi non solum in genere spectaret has duas species boum & ovium, sed & quascunque alias; qua significatione probata necessario addendam esse duco interrogandi vel exclamandi notam etiam sequentibus verborum commatibus, quod ut
units.tr: d) Vulg. Pagn. Arab. MS. e) Pisc. f) Kimchi. Per. a Fig. name, whose particular kinds are expressed afterwards under the names bohm and vhim. For Behemah, in its general sense, is said of such living creatures as walk on four feet, as Abu Walid states explicitly, and it corresponds to the Arabic Bahimah, which denotes a certain living four-footed creature, of the kind that also live in water (kull dhāt arba'); and more generally still, any living creature without distinction (kull ḥayy). The aforesaid Abu Walid says that Behemah is used now of one kind (of beasts), now of several, now of a certain particular beast. Between this word and Chaiyah, (which occurs together with it in Gen. 1, 25. where the one is rendered beasts of the earth and the other cattle), the Jewish b) masters have been observed to distinguish, so that they hold that the latter (chayah) properly denotes wild beasts, and the former (Behemah i)) tame, domestic animals, whose service men mostly use. There is therefore no doubt that under this general name the following species, which are called herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, are included; so that the Prophet then wishes to point out, in particular, which animals he chiefly has in view, according to the exposition of Kimchi, which seems to us very probable. Indeed that word, as we have already noted, is also commonly used for other species of animals, and especially, as Grotius thinks, for horses, mules and asses, when nothing else is added, by the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Arabs. Hence those who have k) jumentum express it by a more proper word, which especially denotes that kind of animal whose work is at hand in carrying and dragging loads, and also in farming; as if it referred not only generally to these two species, cattle and sheep, but to any others. With this meaning established, I think a mark of question or exclamation must necessarily be added also to the following clauses, which

units.la: s) Armenta Bucera, Grot. – r) Tig. Jun. Trem. u) Kamus. 96) Ita & Syriac. & Arab. impressa. x) Merc. Drus. Capp. *) Buxt. Vind.
units.tr: s) Armenta Bucera, Grotius. r) Tigurine, Junius, Tremellius. u) Kamus. 96) So also the printed Syriac and Arabic. x) Mercer, Drusius, Cappel. *) Buxtorf, Vindiciae.

units.la: alibi in S. literis non inveniatur aut vox ipsa aut ejus forma; si vero inveniretur, non active significaret lugere vel flere, sed passive, lugeri vel deploreri. Verum non est, ut ex illorum interpretatione diversa diversam etiam colligamus lectionem. Quamvis enim ἰχλαυσαν non praecise significet perplexi esse, patet tamen luctum, fletum & lamentationem plerumque assiduos esse comites perplexae ac perturbatae mentis, atque ex eo mihi non leviter videntur peculiari hac expressione comprehendere, quicquid animi perplexitas secum fert, pisiid ipsum illi recte innuisse dicendi sint. Atque haec ratio conciliandi & facilior & mitior mihi videtur, quam conjecturarum talium conglobatio, quibus & in regulas & in proprietatem linguae impingitur, & activum cum passivo pro lubitu confunditur. Pari facilitate possunt & caeterorum translationes conciliari cum textu hebraico, quae non stricte adhaerent perplexitatis significationi. Hos inter prominet Vulgatus, qui habet, mugierunt, Munsterus, obmurmurant, & Castalio, plorant. Ratio hujus perplexitatis in illis traditur haec, quia illis nullum pabulum superest, omnibus alimentis ac pabulis destructis & absumptis a caulis, quas non multum ante inspeximus, ac in sequentibus adhuc inspecturi sumus. Hinc ut exaggeret Propheta calamitatem, quam describit, addit, non solum defore pabulum majoribus animalium generibus, quae majorem alimenti copiam requirunt; verum etiam minoribus, quae paucis contenta, quin & ipsis ovibus, quae parciori fruuntur pabulo, gramineque curtiori. Unde sic pergit; etiam greges ovium desolantur, hoc est, etiam hae tam tristi, tam desolatae subjectae sunt conditioni, ut non amplius habeant, quo sustententur. Emphasin, qua Propheta calamitatis immissae gravitatem describit, Kimchi arbitratur ineße particulae ☐ G.um, quam nostrates vertunt, etiam, eaque innui putant, adeo increbuisse calamitatem, ut nec minores quidem animalium greges, qui caeteroquin adhuc alimentum ibi inveniunt, ubi majora bene sunt pascua, tantum invenerint, quo fami suae consulerent. Vox יִשְׁ Hatson, nostratibus & aliis non paucis versa, ovium, ac si potissimum hoc genus animalium minorum spectaret, redditur a Vulgato & aliis voce largiori, pecorum (vel pecoris) traduntque ab erudito Judaeo Abu Walid, nomen esse ... quod comprehendat æque oves ac capras, ita ut juxta illum Arabice debuisset reddi غنم G.anam, quod etiam utramque speciem denotat, nulla vero ratione ضأن Ddan, quamvis in literis nulla diversitas; quia illud peculiare nomen est Arabibus, quo oves distinguuntur a capris. Pari ratione notat, quod interdum peculiariter dicatur de ovibus, quatenus distinctæ sunt a capris. (ut 1. Sam. 25, 2. ubi Nabot dicitur habuisse tria millia צאן Tson, ovium, & mille עזים caprarum.) Idem observavit etiam Kimchi, quod scilicet nomen sit commune הברהמות minoribus gregibus, videlicet הכבשים והעזים ovibus & capris, & quod nunc כולם כיורי ) omnes complectatur, jam uni alicui illorum z) speciei attribuatur, scilicet ovibus, ut in prædicto loco, 1. Samuel. 25, 2. Rursus quod interdum utrumque comprehendat, non tantum minora animalium, verum etiam majora, ita ut nomine בקר Bakar, intelligantur vaccæ &c. Atque eo significatu hanc vocem extare putat a) 1. Sam. 8, 17. Verum quod secus hic accipienda sit, ex eo liquet, quod expresse a voce בקר Bakar distinguatur, quæ majora pecora b) denotat, ut notatum est antea. Necesse igitur est, ut cum nostratibus aliisque nonnullis sumatur vel pro ovibus peculiariter, vel quibus etiam admistæ erant capræ, ut illis placet, qui reddunt pecus, Chaldæoque Syro ac Arabi, quorum priores habent ענו Ono, posterior غنم Ganam, quæ nomina utrique harum minorum pecudum generi communia esse videntur. De his dicitur hic נאשה Neeshamu, quod recentiores nostri interpretes reddiderunt, desolati sunt; alii antiquiores in eandem mentem, destruuntur, quod Græco ἠφανισμένοι respondet; Chaldæus habet שמם; Syrus ܐܬܬܐܝܢ; Arabicum MS. استوحشوا (desolati redditi sunt) Impressa Arabica انقرضوا; Vulgatus disperierunt; Munsterus, damno affecti sunt; Castalio, multi sabantur. Grotius desolati sunt,
units.tr: Nowhere else in Holy Scripture does the word itself, or any form of it, occur; and if it did, it would not mean actively "to mourn" or "to weep" but passively, "to be mourned" or "to be lamented." It is not the case, however, that from their differing translations we should infer a differing reading. For although ἰχλαυσαν [ichlausan] does not strictly mean "to be perplexed," it is plain that grief, weeping and lamentation are generally the constant companions of a perplexed and troubled mind. So it seems to me no slight thing that this particular expression comprehends whatever perplexity of mind brings with it, and that those who use it are rightly said to have hinted at this very thing. This method of reconciling the texts seems to me both easier and gentler than the piling up of such conjectures, which offend against the rules and the idiom of the language and confuse the active with the passive as they please. With equal ease the renderings of the others can also be reconciled with the Hebrew text, although they do not keep closely to the sense of perplexity. Among these the Vulgate stands out, which has mugierunt ("they bellowed"); Münster, obmurmurant ("they murmur against"); and Castalio, plorant ("they weep"). The reason for this perplexity is given in these words: because no pasture is left to them, all food and pasture having been destroyed and consumed by the sheepfolds, which we have not long since looked into, and which we shall examine further in what follows. Hence, to heighten the calamity he describes, the Prophet adds that pasture will fail not only for the larger kinds of animals, which need a greater supply of food, but also for the smaller, which are content with little, and even for the sheep themselves, which make do with sparser pasture and shorter grass. Whence he goes on: even the flocks of sheep are laid waste, that is, even these, so sad and so forlorn, are reduced to such a condition that they no longer have anything by which they might be sustained. Kimchi thinks that the emphasis by which the Prophet describes the gravity of the calamity sent upon them lies in the particle gam, which our people render "even," and they suppose it signifies that the calamity has grown so great that not even the smaller flocks, which otherwise still find food where the larger ones have good pastures, have found enough to provide for their hunger. The word hatson (יִשְׁ), rendered "of sheep" by our people and by not a few others, as though it chiefly regarded this kind of smaller animal, is given by the Vulgate and others by the wider word pecorum (or pecoris), "of cattle." And they report from the learned Jew Abu Walid that it is a name which comprehends both sheep and goats alike; so that, according to him, in Arabic it ought to be rendered ghanam, which also denotes both kinds, and by no means dhaʼn, although in the letters there is no difference; because the latter is a special name among the Arabs by which sheep are distinguished from goats. In the same way the word is sometimes used specially of sheep, insofar as they are distinguished from goats (as in 1 Sam. 25:2, where Nabal is said to have had three thousand of tson, sheep, and a thousand of izzim, goats). Kimchi also observed the same thing: that the name is common to the smaller flocks, namely to sheep and goats; and that while it comprehends them all, it may now be attributed to one of those two kinds, namely sheep, as in the aforementioned place, 1 Sam. 25:2. Again, it sometimes comprehends both, not only the smaller animals but also the larger, so that by the name bakar are understood cows, and so on. And he thinks this word bears that sense in 1 Sam. 8:17. But that it is to be taken otherwise here is clear from the fact that it is expressly distinguished from the word bakar, which denotes larger cattle, as was noted above. It is necessary, therefore, to take it, with our people and some others, either specially for sheep, or for those flocks among which goats were also mixed, as those prefer who render it pecus ("cattle"). The Chaldean and the Syrian and the Arab render it in the same way: the first two have ono (עָנוֹ), the last ghanam; and these names seem to be common to both kinds of these smaller cattle. Of these it is said here neeshamu (נאשה), which our recent interpreters have rendered they are desolate; others, older, to the same effect, they are destroyed, which corresponds to the Greek ἠφανισμένοι [ēphanismenoi]. The Chaldean has shamam; the Syrian has a word of the same root; the Arabic manuscript has istawhashū (they were made desolate); the printed Arabic has inqaraḍū (they have perished). The Vulgate has disperierunt ("they have perished"); Münster, they have been stricken with loss; Castalio, many have been killed. Grotius, they are desolate.

units.la: y) Ut Levit. 3,6. ubi nostr. græc. z) Ex denominatione unius speciei etiam collagi pos s quid de cæteris s tuum, licet vox eas non denotet. a) Ubi nostr. sfer. b) Quod quidam non tantum proprie referunt ad minora, sed generaliter ad omnia majora animalia, ut sunt, Equi, Boves, Asini & Cameli. Druf. sunt, quod ad literam hebraicam vocem sonare idemque significari asserit, ac ad paucitatem redacti sunt. Eodem hi omnes arripiunt sensu radicem אשם Asham cum שמם Shamam desolavit, destruxit, vastavit, qua significatione hic sumi R. Abraham Ezra & D. Kimchi volunt, ut & Hos. 13,16. & Esa. 24,6. At aliam etiam significationem habet ea radix, nimirum deliquit, reus fuit, reus factus aut peractus fuit, quo sensu accipit eam Tigurina reddens: & greges ovium culpa obnoxii facti sunt; quo suppono necessario intelligere obnoxios ipsi supplicio, vel talibus malis atque suppliciis, qualia possessores peccatis suis a Deo in se provocaverant, eos enim concernebant, qui peccatis se iis obnoxios reddiderant. Quod ad oves innoxias attinet, quid mali admittere poterant, quo talia in se derivare potuissent? Quod si eo pacto sumitur, optime congruit explicationi, quam tradit R. Salom. Jarchi, qua utramque radicis Asham significationem approbare videtur, quando dicit נתקלקלו באשמתם quod Mercerus interpretatur vastati sunt delicto suo, cui enucleando scite & ad rem appositum esse duco a quodam erudito c) viro, scilicet Israelitarum. Eadem interim fruuntur forte, ac si ipsi culpae fuissent obnoxii, fortisque suae sensum sat superque testantur gravi luctu ac gemitu, qui illorum possessores haud dubie debuisset movere, propter quos tanta tolerabant, ut veram ejus inquirerent causam, quae nulla erat alia quam peccata admissa, manusque supplices attollerent ad Deum, ut has plagas calamitatesque, quae etiam innoxias pecudes illorum culpa invaserant, benigne recedere jubeat. Hinc ea verba sic accipi posse constat, ut simul complectantur reprehensionem vel exprobrationem stupiditatis, qua correpti adeo non afficiebantur poenis immissis, quam miseILAE pecudes. Ipsi illarum boatus ac gemitus debuissent eos excitare. Quod cum minus fieri ab iis videret Propheta, omnisque advertendi mentem spes esset sublata, suo, quod non poterant non imitari, exemplo praeit, ut eos hocce modo instrueret viamque praemonstraret, in sequentibus:
units.tr: y) As in Lev. 3:6, where our [version has ...]; the Greek [...]. z) From the naming of one species something may also be gathered about the others, even though the word does not denote them. a) Where our [version has] ... b) Some refer this not only properly to the smaller animals, but generally to all the larger animals, such as horses, oxen, asses and camels. Drusius [holds that the verb] "are desolate" corresponds to the Hebrew word's sound and means the same as "are reduced to a small number". By the same reading all these take the root אשם (Asham) together with שמם (Shamam), "he desolated, destroyed, laid waste", in which sense R. Abraham Ezra and D. Kimchi wish it to be taken here, as also in Hos. 13:16 and Isa. 24:6. But this root has also another meaning, namely "he offended, was guilty, was made or declared guilty", and in this sense the Tigurine version takes it, rendering: "and the flocks of sheep have been made liable to guilt". By which we must necessarily understand "liable to punishment", or to such evils and punishments as the possessors had provoked upon themselves from God by their sins; for they were the ones concerned, who had made themselves liable to these by their sins. As for the innocent sheep, what evil could they commit by which such things might have come down upon them? But if it is taken in that way, it agrees very well with the explanation handed down by R. Solomon Jarchi, in which he seems to approve both meanings of the root Asham, when he says נתקלקלו באשמתם (they were ruined through their guilt), which Mercer translates "they were laid waste through their guilt". In unfolding this I judge that a certain learned man has said something apt and to the point: "namely of the Israelites". The animals meanwhile suffer, perhaps, as if they themselves had been guilty of the fault, and by their deep lowing and groaning they amply testify to their sense of their own misfortune, which ought undoubtedly to have moved their owners, on whose account they bore such great things, to inquire into the true cause of it, which was none other than the sins committed, and to lift up suppliant hands to God, that He might graciously command these plagues and calamities, which had invaded even the innocent beasts through their owners' fault, to withdraw. Hence it is plain that these words may be so understood as to include at the same time a rebuke or reproach of the stupidity by which those thus chastised were so little moved by the punishments sent upon them, that the wretched beasts ... Their own bellowing and groaning ought to have stirred them up. Since the Prophet saw that this was less than done by them, and all hope of drawing their attention was taken away, he goes before them by his own example, which they could not but imitate, so that he might instruct them in this way and show them the path, in what follows:

units.la: c) Jo. Leusden.
units.tr: c) Jo. Leusden.

units.la: 19. Ad te, o Domine, clamo: quia ignis consumfit d) pascua deserti, & flamma inflammavit omnes ar- bores campi.
units.tr: 19. To you, O Lord, I cry: for fire has consumed the d) pastures of the wilderness, and flame has burned up all the trees of the field.

units.la: e) Sunt qui hisce censent continuari verba Sacerdotum, quibus Propheta vult, ut lamententur propter ingressas plagas, quorum initium fecerat v. 15. f) Alii vero putant, prioribus verbis a Propheta innui gravitatem suppliciorum immissorum, quibus eo illos adducere volebat, ut animo sedulo volverent miseram suam conditionem, quam provocaverant & sibi ipsis & suis rebus, nec terra nec pecudibus exceptis; his autem declarari quid ipse faciat & facturus sit, unde exemplum capere fas erat, ad averruncandum ea, quibus premebantur, gravia mala. Nimirum preces & supplicationes fundendæ erant ad Deum, ut misericordia motus procul abs illis removeat ea mala, quæ denuo per partes exponere haud grave ducit, ut se ipsum exhibeat, quomodo populus, quocum sibi negotium erat, sese exhibere debebat, scilicet rebus his admodum permotum ac agnoscentem, quæ illata erant propter enormia peccata, pro yeris supplicis. Ad te, o Domine, clamo. Hoc unicum proponit medium ad removenda hæc ingentia mala, quæ describit, videlicet, preces ardentissimæ ad Deum, a quo immittebantur, & qui solus hæc amovere potis erat; easque tantummodo ad verum Deum, quem idcirco gloriosò eo nomine describit, quod ipsi soli convenit יהוה, unde a quibusdam recentioribus interpretibus retinetur tanquam nomen proprium, iisdemque literis consignatur g) Jehovah: Nostrates vero atque alii, & in genere omnes antiquiores accipiunt significatione Domini, idque non tantum hoc loco, sed alibi ubicunque occurrit. Pauca enim sunt loca, in quibus nostrates, quorum hic tantum a nobis habetur ratio, Jehovæ nomen retinent. Extat illud Ex. 6, 3. ubi habent, nomine meo Jehova non eram cognitus illis, ut & Psal. 83,18. cui soli nomen est Jehova; & Esa. 12,2. Dominus Jehova est fortitudo mea, & 26,4. In Domino Jehova est æterna fortitudo; nec aliorum memini, præterquam ubi aliquid
units.tr: e) Some think that these words continue the speech of the priests, in which the Prophet wants them to lament the plagues that have come upon them, which he had begun at v. 15. f) Others think that the Prophet's earlier words point to the severity of the punishments sent, by which he meant to bring the people to consider carefully their wretched condition, which they had brought upon themselves and their possessions, the land and the beasts not excepted. These words, on the other hand, show what the Prophet himself does and will do, and from this they could take an example for averting the grave evils that oppressed them. Prayers and supplications were certainly to be poured out to God, so that, moved by mercy, he would remove far from them those evils, which it is no trouble to describe again piece by piece. In this way he shows himself as the people with whom he had to deal ought to show themselves, namely deeply moved by these things and acknowledging, as true suppliants, that what was inflicted came because of their enormous sins. To you, O Lord, I cry. This alone sets out the means for removing these huge evils that he describes, namely most ardent prayers to God, from whom they were sent and who alone could remove them. And these prayers are addressed only to the true God, whom he describes with the glorious name that belongs to him alone, יהוה. For this reason some more recent interpreters keep it as a proper name and mark it with the same letters, g) Jehovah. Our writers and others, and in general all the older ones, understand it in the sense of Lord, and this is so not only in this place but wherever it occurs. For there are few places where our writers, whose view alone we take into account here, retain the name Jehovah. It occurs at Ex. 6:3, where they have "by my name Jehovah I was not known to them"; likewise at Ps. 83:18, "whose name alone is Jehovah"; at Is. 12:2, "the Lord Jehovah is my strength"; and at 26:4, "in the Lord Jehovah is everlasting strength." I do not recall others, except where something is added to that name
