units.la: Cum vero vox hebraica, nemine contradicente, nomen Dei proprium sit, quod nulli alii creaturæ communicari potest, quodque ipse memoriale suum vocat k) Hos. 12,5. eoque Propheta eum invocet, quid aliud significare voluit, quam solum verum Deum esse, qui calamitates ingressas & averruncare possit, & propter nomen suum dubio procul velit, si ea, qua decet, humilitate atque mentis contritione quæratur? Ad te, o Domine, כי אין מושיע זולתך quia nulla salus extra te. Expositerat jam antea has l) calamitates suis auditoribus, repetit tamen hic easdem, tanquam causam, ob quam solam Deum ardentissime ac patheticis terminis invocat. Nec difficile conjectu est, id propterea maxime factum, ut ab ipso hæc judicia profluxisse profiteretur, populum ad eandem confessionem moveret, Deumque simul instigaret, ut misericordia tangeretur ob eum, quo afficiebantur, vehementem eorum sensum. Ignis enim, inquit, devoravit pascua deserti &c. Quum exserat æstuans ignis elementum vim, devorando & consumendo, quicquid rei combustibilis est, quam allambit, adeo nota res est, ut, si hujus effectum alii rei tribueris, exitii summi tradi descriptionem, recte putes, terribilemque innui rerum destructionem ab eo, quod cum igne comparatur, aut ejus nomine venit ortam, ita ut non immerito consideran possit ceu m) nomen generale adversitatum, vel illarum rerum, quæ noxiam inferunt, aut ut descriptio ingentis alicujus mali, ab iis illati. Quæ annotare haud inconsultum duximus, quod plerique ferme interpretes ignis vocem hic non accipiant significatione propria; sed alia ejus loco substituant, quæ similitudinis quid cum eo habent, qua vim & perniciem inferunt. Longe tamen a se invicem dissentiunt, quid potissimum hoc loco innuatur. n) Sunt quibus locustæ cæterique noxii vermiculi, de quibus ante, videntur intelligendi, qui noxii quid habere dicuntur non absimile igni, quo destruunt quæcunque contactu suo contrectant. Hucadjerunt verba o) Plinii
units.tr: But since the Hebrew word, with no one contradicting, is God's proper name, which cannot be communicated to any other creature, and which he himself calls his memorial, Hos. 12, 5, and since the prophet calls on him by it, what else did he mean to signify than that the true God alone is the one who can avert the calamities that have come upon them, and who undoubtedly will do so for his name's sake, if he is sought with the humility and contrition of mind that befits? "To you, O Lord, כי אין מושיע זולתך [for there is no saviour besides you]." He had already set forth these calamities to his hearers, yet he repeats them here as the reason why he calls on God alone so ardently and in such moving terms. It is not hard to guess that this was done chiefly so that he might show that these judgments had flowed from himself, move the people to the same confession, and at the same time stir up God, so that he would be touched with mercy by their intense feeling of the suffering they undergo. "For fire," he says, "has devoured the pastures of the wilderness," etc. Since the glowing element of fire exerts its power by devouring and consuming whatever combustible thing it touches, the matter is so well known that, if you attribute the effect of it to another thing, you may rightly think that a description of utter ruin is meant, and that the terrible destruction of things is indicated as arising from that which is compared with fire, or named after it. So it may not unfairly be regarded as a general name for adversities, or for those things which bring harm, or as a description of some great evil inflicted by them. These points I thought it not unwise to note, because most interpreters here do not take the word fire in its proper sense, but put in its place something else that has a likeness to it in bringing force and destruction. Yet they differ widely from one another as to what is chiefly meant here. n) Some think that locusts and other harmful little worms, of which we spoke before, are to be understood, since they are said to have something harmful, not unlike fire, by which they destroy whatever they touch. To this the words of Pliny belong.

units.la: k) Vide notas in h. l. l) Kimchi. m) Flacius Illyr. Interdum ponitur pro re quasi salde ladente. n) Drufius. o) Objici contra hanc interpretationem posset, quod AbenEzra objecerat R. Japhet ex v. 10. aireos aquarum exaruisse (quod in locultas non quadrare.) nii de locustis: multa contactu adurunt. Eaque ratione comparative ea verba exponit Kimchi: כאלו אש ולהבה עכרה בהם כאשר velut ignis & flamma transfiit per illas, quum transfiit per eas locusta. p) Alii intelligunt nimium ardorem vel æ-ftum, quo omnia in terra combusta esse quibusdam observatum est, ut paulo ante annotavimus. Hinc annotant q) ardorem immoderatum solis vocari ignem, Pf. 83,14. Ut ignis exurit silvam, & ut flamma accendit montes; locaque solis ardore torrida חררים Chararim, exarefacta loca, Jer. 17,6. Si locustæ & æstus solis simul extitisse dicendi sunt, quod quidam probatum eunt, ut supra vidimus, nec omni prorsus ratione caret, ambo tunc ignis nomine comprehendi possunt: non est igitur ut has expositiones tanquam diversas notes, vel Chaldæum longe ab ultima abire, cum reddat קדרים תקיף כאשר violentus eurus tanquam ignis.
units.tr: k) See the notes on this passage. l) Kimchi. m) Flacius Illyricus. Sometimes it is used for a thing that burns, as it were, intensely. n) Drusius. o) It might be objected against this interpretation what Aben Ezra objected to R. Japhet, from verse 10, that the waters had dried up in the ditches, which does not fit locusts: they burn many things by contact. On that account Kimchi explains these words comparatively: as if fire and flame passed through them [כאלו אש ולהבה עכרה בהם כאשר], as when a locust passes through them. p) Others understand the excessive heat or drought, by which, as we noted a little earlier, everything on the earth has been observed to be burnt. Hence they note that the immoderate heat of the sun is called fire, Ps. 83:14: As fire burns the forest, and as a flame sets the mountains alight; and places scorched by the heat of the sun are called חררים Chararim, places made dry, Jer. 17:6. If the locusts and the heat of the sun are to be said to have occurred together, as some approve, as we saw above, and as it is not entirely without reason, then both can be comprehended under the name of fire. It is therefore not necessary to regard these explanations as different, nor to say that the Chaldee has moved far from the last, since it renders it as a violent east wind [קדרים תקיף] like fire [כאשר].

units.la: Alii accipiunt de inimicis ac detrimentis, quæ illorum invasione terræ erant illata. Ita Abarbinel dicit, eum loqui על צרים האיב de calamitate ab inimicis, non autem a locustis illata: & in eandem sententiam r) quidam Christianorum hoc tropo pictam belli imaginem volunt, quo etiam inclinat Munsterus, qui & in hanc sententiam habet: hostes per ignem & gladium omnia devastaverunt (s) igne proprie sumto); & in priorem: pascua sunt vermibus corrosa, ac sit ignis exuffiet ea. Quicquid vero per ea intelligatur, quibus hæc tristis regionis facies tribuitur, tanquam instrumentis, id extra dubitationis aleam positum est, a DEO esse accersita atque operi adhibita, suasque præterea vires non aliter in fruges terræ exeruisse quam ignem in combustibilia quæque. Instrumenta autem solummodo fuisse constat, quæ non nisi DEO jubente ac imperante operata sunt, id quod etiam eruditum quendam t) Commentatorem impulit, ut satius putaret, generaliori significatu ignem vindictæ ejus ardentis intelligere, quæ vocatur ignis zeli Ezech. 36, 5. & ardens indignatio, O quam
units.tr: Others take it to refer to the enemies and the losses that were inflicted on the land by their invasion. So Abarbanel says that he is speaking of the calamity inflicted by enemies, not by locusts, על צרים האיב. To the same effect, some Christians want the image of war painted by this trope, to which Munster also inclines, who also holds this view: enemies have laid everything waste with fire and sword (taking fire in its proper sense); and in the former sense: the pastures are gnawed by worms, and fire has consumed them. But whatever is understood by those things to which this sad appearance of the region is attributed, as instruments, it is placed beyond the reach of doubt that they were summoned and employed in the work by God, and that they put forth their power on the fruits of the earth no differently than fire on anything combustible. It is clear, however, that they were only instruments, which acted only at the command and order of God. This also led a certain learned commentator to think it better to understand, in a more general sense, the fire of his vengeance, which burns, and which is called the fire of zeal, Ezek. 36:5, and burning indignation, rather than to name something special by which God exercised his wrath against them.

units.la: p) Jun. Trem. Livel. Pifcat. Bochart. q) Livel. Bochart. r) Vide Merc. s) Hoffl. igniv, Ar. Mont. Incendio Chaldaeorum, Ribera. Bellum cum incendio conferetur quod omnia gaftat, Tarnov. ex Vinkel. t) Tarnov. Ita Gvalt. ifu fero bofilem rubrum vel potius borribilem Dei findictam denotat. quam speciale quid denominare, quo furorem suum DEus in eos exercuerit. Quid autem effecerit, quod hic ignis nomine venit, & in quam miserrimam conditionem omnia conjecerit, ex sequentibus videre est. Consumpsit, inquit, נאות Neoth pascua (vel ut in margine, habitacula) deserti, quae interpretationis diversitas vocis ambiguitatem notat. Quod etiam ex aliis diversis tum veterum tum recentiorum interpretationibus constat. LXX. habent τὰ ὠγῆα τῆς ἐρήμου, ut & Arab. impressa. Vulg. Lat. speciosa deserti, cui accedunt Tigur. amoenissima loca deserti, & non absimili ratione ꝯ alii, pascua & x)loca herbifera. Quos inter quidem nemo est, qui ab ea translatione plane discedit, quam in Textu habemus. At Chaldaeus pro eo habet דירות מרבצא Diroth Madbera, habitacula (vel mansiones, ut reddit Mercerus,) deserti. Simili modo Syrus & MS. Arabicum in eandem sententiam, habitationes deserti. Ex recentioribus Castal. Stationes (vel Mansiones in versu sequenti) saltuum. Junius & Tremellius habitacula deserti. Drus. habitacula vel habitationes deserti. Alii caulas, quo sensu nonnulli Judaei exponunt, ut R. Sal. Jarchi, Aben-Ezra & Kimchi, qui aliis verbis eas vocat אהלי הרעים pastorum mapalia. Et Rabbi Tanchum qui Arabice habet habitacula. LXX, quorum interpretationis rationem supra retulimus, reddunt hanc vocem Psal. 23. (vel juxta illos Psal. 22,2.) τόπον locum. Non dubito, quin interpretum quidam hujus vocis rationem habuerint, quatenus a Grammaticis ad hujusmodi refertur x) radices, quae jam hanc, jam illam significationem habent, cujus generis sunt נאה pulchrum, decorum esse, vel אוה y) expetivit, desideravit, vel נוה inhabitavit, ad quas singulas nomen hac forma potest referri; verum non minus constat, cum pluribus locis ea vox occurrat, quem vis eorum eo significatu accepisse, quem eo loco potissimum congruere arbitratus est.
units.tr: Jun., Tremellius, Livelius, Piscator, Bochart. q) Livelius, Bochart. r) See Mercer. s) Hoffmeister reads "igni", Arias Montanus: by the burning of the Chaldeans; Ribera: war is compared with fire because it devours everything; Tarnovius, from Vinkel. t) Tarnovius. So Gualtherus: it denotes a fierce and rather horrible vengeance of God, rather than something particular by which God exercised his fury against them. What he has done, which is here called fire, and into what most miserable condition he has cast everything, can be seen from what follows. He has consumed, he says, נאות Neoth pascua (or, as in the margin, habitacula) deserti. This diversity of interpretation marks the ambiguity of the word, which is also clear from the various other interpretations, both old and recent. The LXX have τὰ ὡραῖα τῆς ἐρήμου [the beautiful things of the desert], as does the Arabic in print. The Vulgate Latin has speciosa deserti, to which the Tigurine adds most pleasant places of the desert, and others, in a not dissimilar way, pastures and herb-bearing places. Among these there is certainly no one who departs entirely from that translation which we have in the text. But the Chaldee has for it דירות מרבצא Diroth Madbera, habitations (or dwellings, as Mercer renders it) of the desert. Similarly the Syriac and an Arabic manuscript, to the same effect, dwellings of the desert. Among the more recent, Castalio has stations (or dwellings, in the following verse) of the thickets. Junius and Tremellius habitations of the desert. Drusius habitations or dwellings of the desert. Others sheepfolds, in which sense some Jews explain it, such as R. Solomon Jarchi, Aben Ezra and Kimchi, who in other words call them אהלי הרעים tents of the shepherds. And Rabbi Tanchum, who in Arabic has habitations. The LXX, whose method of interpretation we have reported above, render this word at Ps. 23 (or, according to them, Ps. 22:2) as τόπον [place]. I do not doubt that some of the translators have taken account of the sense of this word, insofar as the grammarians refer it to roots of this kind, which now have this meaning, now that, of which kind are נאה to be beautiful, fitting, or אוה he desired, longed for, or נוה he dwelt, to each of which this form of the noun can be referred. But it is no less certain that, since that word occurs in several places, they have understood it in that sense which they judged most suited to the place.

units.la: Quantumvis igitur hæ significationes ad literam diversæ sint, sensu tamen æque omnes conveniunt, quippe plerumque loca deserti & camporum amœnissima, eaque herbis ac gramine abundantia ab iis eliguntur, qui gregum suorum curam agunt, quibus mapalia ac casas a civitatibus nimium remoti habitandi gratia struunt, ita ut altero nominato alterum necessario subintelligatur pascuaque vix ab habitaculis pastorum secerni possint. Sic etiam Kimchi ad sequentem versum, ubi eadem verba repetuntur, notat voce Neoth designare loca graminea (מקומות הרשא שהיו במדבר) quæ in deserto erant, eaque appellavit Neoth, caulas, quia pastores, qui in deserto habitant, mapalia sua ibi figunt, licet a cæteris habitaculis procul esse remota. Abludit parumper R. Tanchum, cui quidem vox reddenda videtur habitacula; quia vero habitaculis locum in deserto non dari animadvertebat, arbores innui putat الثنى ثلاوى الـيـهـا الوحوش ويستظل بها عـبـام الـطـرق ad quas feræ se recipiunt ut lateant, & viatores, ut umbra fruantur & refugium habeant. Quod cum sequentibus verbis annectatur, & flamma inflammavit omnes arbores campi, magis etiam declarat, quod in his dictum est. Ex his clare patet, quam facile conciliari possit quæ inter interpretes notata est differentia, quodque, sive pabula, sive loca amœnissima, sive pulchra, sive habitacula reddideris, quæ cuncta hoc nomen complectitur, eo sensus redeat, quo ab omnibus concipitur. Nimirum innuere velle Prophetam, quicquid rerum vel ad necessitatem, vel ad decorum, vel ad voluptatem spectat, tum hominibus, tum feris, idque non tantum in civitatibus, verum etiam in campis & desertis, destructum esse ab eo, quod hoc commate vocatur ignis, sequenti vero flamma, adeo ut nec hominibus ullus refugiendi locus, nec bestiis relictæ sint caulæ aut habitacula. Quæ omnia nomine pabulorum, habitaculorum deserti & omnium arborum campi, quarum hic etiam expressa est mentio, manifesto arguuntur. Quibus tamen calamitatum series nondum absolvitur, ut ex sequenti versu apparet;
units.tr: However much these meanings differ according to the letter, they all agree equally in sense, since for the most part the most pleasant places of the desert and plains, abounding in herbs and grass, are chosen by those who care for their flocks, and for the sake of dwelling there they build huts and cottages far too remote from the cities, so that when one is named the other is necessarily understood, and pastures can scarcely be separated from the dwellings of the shepherds. Thus also Kimchi, on the following verse, where the same words are repeated, notes that by the word Neoth he designates grassy places (מקומות הרשא שהיו במדבר) which were in the desert, and he called them Neoth, sheepfolds, because the shepherds who live in the desert pitch their tents there, although they are remote from other dwellings. R. Tanchum differs slightly, for whom the word seems indeed to be rendered habitations; but because he observed that there was no place for habitations in the desert, he thinks that trees are meant, to which the wild beasts retire in order to hide, and travellers to enjoy the shade and have a refuge. Since this is joined to the following words, and flame has set alight all the trees of the field, it declares even more clearly what has been said here. From these things it is plain how easily the difference noted among the interpreters can be reconciled, and that whether you render it pastures, or most pleasant places, or beautiful, or habitations, which all this name embraces, the sense comes back to the one that is conceived by all. Namely, that the Prophet wishes to indicate that whatever pertains to necessity, or to beauty, or to pleasure, for men and for beasts alike, has been destroyed by that which in this verse is called fire, and in the following flame, and not only in the cities but also in the fields and the deserts, so that there is no place of refuge left for men, nor sheepfolds or dwellings left for beasts. All these things are plainly indicated by the names pastures, dwellings of the desert, and all the trees of the field, of which mention is also expressly made here. Yet the series of calamities is not yet complete, as appears from the following verse.

units.la: 20. Etiam bestiæ agri clamant ad te, eo quod exarue- rint alvei aquarum, & ignis abfumferit pabula deserti.
units.tr: 20. Even the beasts of the field cry out to you, because the channels of the waters are dried up, and fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness.

units.la: Adeo conditione illorum miserrima Propheta afficitur, ut non ipse tantum ad Dominum clamet, verum & in consortium hujus assectus vocet agri bestias, easque maxime feras, quæ ) juga hominum fugientes in defertis ac montanis pabula sibi quærunt, quo locustæ penetrare non solent. Verbum, quo illarum clamor exprimitur, est תערוג taarog, quod etiam dicitur de cervo Pfal. 42, 1. כאיל תערג sicut cervus aspirat (vel glocitat, ut in nostra translatione ad marginem notatum,) ad alveos aquarum. Atque hoc verbo proprie exprimitur illorum clamor ac sonus. Attamen nec aliorum animalium eo excluditur vociferatio. Quod cum quidam interpretes animadverterent, generaliori etiam reddidere voce, ut vociferari, clamare, vel a) simili. Alia voce, at non alia mente exponunt LXX per ἀναβλέψαν, & Arabica impressa per ut & Latinus Vulg. suspexerunt; quibus etiam accedit Chaldæus מסבריא קרמך Mefabro Kadamac, spectant coram te, vel ut Mercerus, in te spirant. Qui cunctii in eo conveniunt, clamorem includere auxilii exspectationem & spem. Adjicit vero hic quædam verba Vulgatus, quæ nec in Hebræo, nec in ulla alia translatione inveniuntur, nempe, quasi area sitiens imbrem, quod Duacensis reddit; as a Garden bed, thirsting for a shower. Doctissimus Grotius conjicit, initio loco area fortean suisse scriptum cerva, quasi cerva sitiens imbrem: quod fi ita fit, nil amplius dicendum, quam ea periphrasi conatum esse exprimere emphafin vocis תערוג, quatenus proprie significat b) clamorem vel glocitationem cervi clamantis vel glocitantis præfiti ad alveos aquarum, ut doceret, sitientium bestiarum clamorem non minus esse c) vehementem, quam cervi. Alioquin respici, quis posset cogitare, ad תערוג quatenus notat sulcum, quo terra proscinditur ad recipiendum femen.
units.tr: So miserable is their condition that the Prophet is moved to call not only himself upon the Lord, but also to summon the beasts of the field into fellowship with this feeling, and especially those wild beasts which, fleeing the haunts of men, seek their pasture in deserts and mountains, where locusts are not accustomed to penetrate. The word by which their cry is expressed is תערוג taarog, which is also said of the hart, Ps. 42:1 כאיל תערג sicut cervus aspirat (or "bellows," as noted in the margin of our translation) ad alveos aquarum. By this word their cry and sound are properly expressed. Yet the outcry of other animals is not thereby excluded. Some interpreters, noticing this, rendered it with a more general word, such as to shout, to cry out, or a) something similar. The Septuagint, with another word but not another meaning, render it ἀναβλέψαν [anablepsan, looked up], and the printed Arabic does likewise, and the Latin Vulgate has suspexerunt [they looked up]. To these is added the Chaldee מסבריא קרמך Mefabro Kadamac [they look toward you], or, as Mercerus has it, "they breathe in you." All of these agree that the cry includes the expectation and hope of help. The Vulgate, however, adds certain words here which are found neither in the Hebrew nor in any other translation, namely quasi area sitiens imbrem [as a garden bed thirsting for rain], which the Douai version renders as a Garden bed, thirsting for a shower. The most learned Grotius conjectures that originally the word area was perhaps written cerva, so that the text read quasi cerva sitiens imbrem [as a thirsting hind for rain]. If that is so, nothing more need be said than that by this periphrasis they tried to express the emphasis of the word תערוג, insofar as it properly signifies the b) cry or bellowing of a hart calling out or bellowing, thirsting at the streams, so as to teach that the cry of thirsty beasts is no less c) vehement than that of the hart. Otherwise, who could think that it refers to תערוג insofar as it denotes the furrow by which the earth is cut open to receive the seed?

units.la: z) Kimchi fera, Grot. ut Syr. Arab. MS. a) Caftal. Munft.
units.tr: z) Kimchi: beast; Grotius: as the Syriac and the Arabic manuscript. a) Castalio, Münster.

units.la: b) Etsi Hieronymus eam in Pfal. 41. exponat area. c) Vide fis Pet. a Fig. men. Quod horum verborum constructionem attinet, nomen est pluralis numeri בהמות Behemoth bestiæ, & verbum singularis תערג Taarog, clamat, juxta literam, bestiæ clamat. Quod cum nec latinæ nec Anglicæ multisque aliis linguis minus congruat, visum fuit non nullis ita sensum supplere, bestiarum agri quæque glocitat, quod par esse putant, quoties talis constructio sese offert. Atque in eo sequuntur Aben-Ezram, qui reddit ארם כבאחר unaquæque earum. At hebraicam constructionem retinet Arabica tum MS. tum impressa, MS. omnes bestiæ agri clamat (impressa sursum spectat) ad te; quod proprie debebat esse, clamant & sursum spectant. Nec insolens est huic linguæ constructio verbi singularis fœminini generis cum nomine plurali, quæ ut suppleri non opus habet, ita sensum nequaquam mutat. Unde non levis conjectura est, eandem ejus habuisse olim rationem etiam Hebræos, adeo ut alia constructione verborum nexus non indigeat. Hunc autem clamorem bestias direxisse ad eundem dicit Propheta, quo ipse suum direxerat, nempe ad solum verum Deum: Omnes, inquit, clamant ad te, ac si ex ipsæ, quæ rationis, omnisque cognitionis DEI expertes, quamque nec recipere nec doceri possunt, naturali tamen instinctu providentiæ divinæ vestigia in his rebus cognoscerent, eamque, ut calamitatibus amotis inopiam, qua erant pressæ, suppleret, vehementibus clamoribus implorarent, qui ut iis proprii sunt, ita precationum loco apud DEum habentur. Idque phrasis clamare ad Dhum videtur innuere, similesque hujus farinæ alibi, ut Psalm. 104, 21. ubi habetur: Juvenes leones rugiunt ad prædam quærendo a Deo escam suam. Et Psalm. 14-, 9. Dat jumentis cibum suum, pullis corvorum qui clamant (i. e. ad cum) quod quidem in textu Originali non exprimitur, facile tamen subintelligitur, quare & in quibusdam versionibus expresse additur, ut in Græa τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις αὐτον, invocantibus eum, & in Arabica impressa الذين يصرخون qui clamant ad eum; ita & in nostra veteri Anglicana, qua plerumque Ecclesia utitur: qui clamant ad eum, & Job. 38, 41. expresse habetur: quis comparat corvis escam ipsorum, cum pulli eorum vociferantur ⟨Hebrew⟩, ⟨Hebrew⟩, El, El, ad Deum? Exinde certo certius apparet, illarum clamorem non aliter a Deo respici, ac si directe ad eum esset intentus. Caeterum ex adductis locis parallelis & hoc manifesto liquet, proprie tales hic innui creaturas, quales videmus descriptas, ita ut propria notatione haec verba de bestiis agri intelligenda esse non dubitemus, de quibus eadem ratione, qua bos dicitur agnoscere possessorem suum, & asinus praesepe domini sui Jesf. 1, 3. dici potest, cognoscere suo modo Deum tanquam illum, a quo habent existentiam, vitam & incolumitatem, idque luctibus ac clamore, inopia ac fortuna adversa ingruente, testari. Abarbanel vero indicari arbitratur per bestias agri alias gentes praeter Judaeos, quorum regionem sub potestatem suam redigebat, ac rivis illorum exsiccatis destruebat Nebuchadnezar, easque ipsas, quibus poculum excandescentiae bibendum dederat Deus Jer. 25, 15. &c. Huic adstipulatur Arias Montanus hic verbis: ut familiares & fidei domestici gregum & pecorum appellatione definiuntur; sic gentes etiam harum animantium agri generibus componi assimilarique solent. Ad haec vero quidam doctus d) Commentator excipit, gentes suis in calamitatibus non clamare ad verum Deum, quod bestiae agri hic fecisse perhibentur, sed ad Deos falsos. Et profecto non est, cur alia significatione hic accipiantur bestiarum nomina, quam propria. Quando autem harum clamorem ad ⟨Hebrew⟩ Dominum cum suo conjungit Propheta, non tantum magnitudinem ac calamitatis designatae indicare videtur universalitatem, qua homines aeque ac bestias spectabat, verum & populum, cui loquebatur, admonere, ut non solum ab ipso, sed & a bestiis agri exemplum caperent, quomodo se eo in statu deberent gerere, nimirum, ut vehementibus clamoribus ac ardentissimis precibus ad Dominum se verterent, quo mala vel prementia vel pressura, nisi seria poenitentia ea praverterent, averruncaret. Quod si minus, declarat e) stuporem eorum majorem esse, quam brutorum, cum magis ea videantur sentire ac clamoribus suis testari, quam homines, qui inde exemplum capere poterant, imo debebant, atque ad animum revocare & pudore affici, si tantam DEO non exhiberent reverentiam, quam illa exhibebant. Quae porro eum
units.tr: b) Although Jerome explains it in Psalm 41 as "area." c) See Pet. a Fig. men. As for the construction of these words, Behemoth, beasts, is a plural noun, and the verb Taarog, cries out, is singular; literally, the beast cries out. Since this does not agree well with Latin, English, or many other languages, some have thought it right to supply the sense as each of the beasts of the field cries out, which they consider appropriate whenever such a construction occurs. In this they follow Aben-Ezra, who renders it each one of them. But the Arabic text, both manuscript and printed, keeps the Hebrew construction: the manuscript has all the beasts of the field cries out (the printed text has looks upward) to you, where the sense should properly be they cry out and look upward. Nor is a singular feminine verb with a plural noun unusual in this language; it needs no supplying and does not change the sense at all. So it is not a weak conjecture that the Hebrews also once had the same usage, so that the sentence needs no other arrangement of the words. The Prophet says that these beasts directed their cry to the same one to whom he himself had directed his, namely to the one true God: All of them, he says, cry out to you, as if creatures lacking reason and all knowledge of God, who can neither receive nor be taught it, nevertheless by natural instinct recognised the traces of divine providence in these matters, and implored with loud cries that the want which pressed upon them should be relieved by the removal of calamities. Such cries are proper to them, and before God they are counted as prayers. The phrase to cry out to God seems to suggest this, and so do similar passages elsewhere, such as Psalm 104:21, where it is said: The young lions roar after their prey, seeking their food from God. And Psalm 147:9: He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens who cry (that is, to him), which is not expressed in the Original text but is easily understood; hence some versions add it explicitly, as the Greek has τοῖς ἐπικαλουμένοις αὐτον [to those who call upon him], and the printed Arabic has alladhina yasrakhuna [who cry out to him]; so also our old English version, which the Church mostly uses: who cry to him. And Job 38:41 expressly says: Who prepares for the raven its food, when its young cry out to God [El, El]. From this it appears more and more certainly that their cry is not regarded by God otherwise than as if it were directed to him in person. Moreover, from the parallel passages cited, this also is plain: the creatures here meant are properly such as we see described, so that we do not doubt these words are to be understood in their proper sense of the beasts of the field, of whom, in the same way that the ox is said to know its owner, and the ass the crib of its master (Isa. 1:3), it can be said that in their own manner they know God as the one from whom they have their existence, life, and safety, and that they bear witness to this by their groaning and crying when want and adverse fortune press upon them. But Abarbanel thinks that by the beasts of the field are indicated other nations besides the Jews, whose country Nebuchadnezzar brought under his power, and whose rivers he dried up and destroyed, and the very nations to whom God gave the cup of wrath to drink (Jer. 25:15, etc.). Arias Montanus agrees with him here in these words: As the familiar and faithful servants of the household are designated by the name of flocks and herds, so the nations are also commonly compared to and likened to the kinds of these living creatures of the field. But a certain learned d) commentator objects to this, that the nations in their calamities do not cry out to the true God, as the beasts of the field are here said to have done, but to false gods. And indeed there is no reason why the names of the beasts should be taken here in any sense other than the proper one. But when the Prophet joins their cry to the Lord [Adonai], he seems to indicate not only the greatness and universality of the calamity he describes, which bore upon men as well as beasts, but also to admonish the people he was addressing, that they should take an example not only from him but also from the beasts of the field, of how they ought to conduct themselves in that state, namely by turning to the Lord with loud cries and most fervent prayers, so that he might avert the evils that threatened or pressed upon them, unless they forestalled them by genuine repentance. And if not, it declares e) that their stupidity is greater than that of the brutes, since these seem to feel more and to bear witness by their cries than men do, who could and indeed ought to have taken an example from them, and to recall this to mind and be moved with shame if they did not show God the same reverence that the beasts showed. Dan. eum ac bestias movebat causa, quæque omnes denique terræ incolas debebat movere, ut ad Dominum clamarent, exhibetur sequentibus verbis: Eo quod exaruerint alvei aquarum. Ex quo illis sententiis, quarum mentionem fecimus, non leve accedit pondus, quibus calamitates hic designatas non tantum accidisse statuitur per volucres, locustas & hujusmodi alios vermiculos noxios, sed etiam peringentem siccitatem, vehementem ardorem, & pluviæ inopiam, qua f) exarescunt rivi ac torrentes, unde potum sibi quærunt pecudes ac feræ bestiæ, quorumque exficcatione necesse est, ut sitim tolerent, atque ea pereant. Qui istud malum inimicis adscribunt obstruentibus fontes, g) vel alio modo officientibus, ut flumina deficerent, allegare possunt, quod Sennacheribis nomine dicitur 2. Reg. 19,24. Ego exficco plantas pedum meorum omnes rivos locorum obsessorum. Abarbinel intelligit per ea invasionem Nebuchadnezaris in terram eorum; at planior videtur sententia prior. Quemadmodum autem eo declaratur fitis, quam ferebant potus defectu; ita ex sequentibus verbis apparet non habuisse unde ederent: ignis, inquit, abfumfit pabula deserti. Verum eadem hic habemus verba, quæ versu præcedenti, quocirca hic sufficiat, quod ibi dictum est. Id unum addere perplacet, quod h) Kimchi explanans vocem Midbar, quæ redditur desertum, fignificare autumet locum, ubi pecudes (vel bestiæ) pascuntur sive is sit a civitate remotus, sive propinquus, quemlibet talem locum; & non solum fylveftria, remota, desolata, & sterilia loca eo nomine venire. Quando igitur dicitur, ignem abfumfiffe pabula, quæ talibus plerumque locis inveniuntur, vel habitationes, ut alii volunt, aut hujusmodi loca, ubi pastores pabulum solent reperire, vel suas pecudes, pascere; significari constat nil rerum reliftum fuisse, aut amplius ibi reperiri, unde pafcerentur, atque ita inopia impulsas bestias, ut precum loco ad DEum clamarent. Atque exinde liquet, descriptionem in hoc capite lugubris dari famis, quæ homines æque ac befti s premebat, feriasque fimul adhiberi admonitiones, quomodo fe homines debeant gerere, & quo pacto tantam calamitatem a fe possint removere; quamvis non
units.tr: d) Christopher a Castro. e) Calvin, on Daniel. What moved the Prophet, and the beasts with him, and what ought to move all the inhabitants of the land to call upon the Lord, is shown in the following words: because the channels of the waters are dried up. From this, the opinions we have mentioned gain no small weight, by which it is held that the calamities described here came not only through locusts and other such noxious small worms, but also through a scorching drought, a fierce heat, and a lack of rain, by which f) the brooks and torrents dry up, from which cattle and wild beasts seek their drink, and with whose drying up they must endure thirst and perish. Those who ascribe this evil to enemies who block the springs, or who otherwise hinder the rivers from flowing, can cite what is said in the name of Sennacherib, 2 Kings 19:24: I have dried up with the soles of my feet all the streams of the besieged places. Abarbanel understands by these words the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar into their land; but the former opinion seems plainer. Just as the thirst which they suffered from lack of drink is thereby declared, so it appears from the following words that they had nothing to eat: fire, he says, has consumed the pastures of the wilderness. But here we have the same words as in the preceding verse, so what was said there suffices here. It is only pleasant to add one thing, that h) Kimchi, explaining the word Midbar, which is rendered wilderness, thinks it signifies a place where cattle (or beasts) graze, whether it be remote from a city or near it, any such place; and that not only wild, remote, desolate, and barren places come under that name. When it is said, therefore, that fire has consumed the pastures, which are commonly found in such places, or the dwellings, as others prefer, or places of this sort where shepherds are accustomed to find pasture for their flocks, it is clear that nothing was left, nor was anything more to be found there on which they could feed; and so the beasts, driven by want, cried out to God in place of prayers. And from this it is clear that in this chapter a description is given of a grievous famine, which pressed upon men as much as upon beasts, and at the same time that admonitions are given as to how men ought to conduct themselves and by what means they might remove so great a calamity from themselves; although not

units.tr: f) 1. Reg. 17,7. g) Ar. Mont. Grot. h) In rad. Ioel: the interpreters do not agree well about where that calamity was inflicted on them, nor about what calamity is meant. Some take it to be present, others future, but because of its certainty it is spoken of as if it had already happened or were present. The prophet pursues the same subject by the same method in the following chapter too, as will be clear to anyone who looks at it.
