units.la: Verf. 1. Clangite buccina (in margine vel lituo) in Sione, & date signum in monte meo sancto, tremant omnes incolae terrae; nam dies Domini advenit, nam propinquus est.
units.tr: Verse 1. Blow the trumpet (in the margin, or the cornet) in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble; for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand.

units.la: Buccinae quondam inter Judaeos & diversis occasionibus & inpeculiarem finem DEO ita ordinante adhiberi solebant. Quod tum ex aliis Scripturae locis, tum praecipue ex Num. 10,2. appareret, ubi & mandatum divinum extat, ut conficerentur, & usus, in quem essent adhibendae, nimirum (1.) ad convocandum coetum ut sacra exerceret, v.2.3. (2.) Ad imperandam profectionem castrorum. (3.) Ad signum dandum tempore belli, cum oppugnator eos oppugnaret, v.9. (4.) In die laetitiae & in solennitatibus eorum, nec non in principiis mensium. Quid autem rerum esset, cujus populum volebant admonere, diversis tubae sonis videntur expressisse. Hinc ad tertium ordinem hic tubae inflatus referri videtur, quare a) Rabbini verbis inimicus qui opprimit vos (vel (b) oppugnator qui oppugnat vos) intelligi censent quamlibet rem, quae illos oppugnabat, ut annonae caritatem, pestem, vel locustas (vel similia), ita ut aeque recte conveniat, quodcunque hanc calamitatem intulisse dixeris. Hinc descri-
units.tr: In former times trumpets were commonly sounded among the Jews, on various occasions and for particular ends that God had appointed. This appears from other passages of Scripture, but especially from Num. 10,2., where both the divine command that they be made and the uses for which they were to be employed are set out: namely (1) to summon the assembly to perform sacred duties, vv. 2, 3; (2) to order the setting out of the camp; (3) to give the signal in time of war, when an enemy attacked them, v. 9; (4) on days of joy and at their solemn feasts, and also at the beginnings of the months. Now the particular matter about which they wished to warn the people seems to have been expressed by different blasts of the trumpet. Hence the blast here seems to belong to the third kind. For this reason the rabbis, a) reading the words the enemy who oppresses you (or (b) the attacker who assails you), take them to mean whatever thing was attacking them, such as dearth of grain, plague, or locusts (or the like), so that it fits equally well whatever you say brought this calamity. Hence the descrip-

units.la: a) Maimon. Tad in Taaniotb. c. 1,1. b) Ainsworth. descriptionem hæc verba continent ingentis afflictionis, quæ ejus generis erat, ut tubæ sonitu illius merito deberet admoneri populus, quo miserrimæ fortis affectu tacti media prospicerent, quibus ab eaimmunes redderentur. Atque hæc admonitio magis eos debuisset afficere, quam excubitoris sonitus, cum revera tuba det signum. Repetit autem hæc admonens eandem rem diversis exprimendi formulis, nimirum הריעו & הקעו Clangite & date signum, ut magis magisque illorum mentem & affectus excitet לעורר הלבבות והתשובה ad excitandum animos eorum ad pœnitentiam, inquit Kimchi. Pari ratione & Sion, & mons sanctus eundem locum denotant, (ut Psal. 2, 6. præfeci Sioni monti sancto meo) qui cum effet congregationis folennis eorum locus, declarat quanti momenti res fit, ut ad unum omnes hujus sint conscii ac admoneantur. Hinc pergit: tremant omnes incolæ regionis, non tantum Hierosolymæ, sed & omnium aliarum civitatum. Idque tubæ sonitu plerumque iis notabatur, unde Amos. 3, 6. An buccina clanget, quin populus trepide accurrerit? quo audito communiter de quodam ingenti malo imminenti, quod timorem merito injiciebat, admonebantur. Atqui hujus generis & hanc rem esse, de qua Propheta loquitur, ut talem buccinæ sonum requireret, apparet ex descriptione ejus, quæ habetur in sequentibus verbis: nam dies Domini advenit, nam propinquus est. Dies Domini, id est, quo immissurus est regioni atrocissima judicia vindictamque sumturus de incolis, ob gravissima eorum peccata. Tali modo etiam exprimitur cap. 1, 15. ubi vide fis plura de hac expressione. Verum enim vero, ne fortean securi eandem vitæ rationem tenerent, quamvis territi, delaturum eum adventum suum & in eo retardaturum, sibi persuadentes, atque ita fe ipsos fallentes longe repellendo diem malí Amos. 6, 3. addit: advenit, propinquus est, ita ut, fi eum velint prævenire & fe immunes reddere ab omni periculo, necefle effet, ut fe fine mora conferrent ad inquirenda remedia, quibus id efficerent. c) Etenim quis sustinebit diem adventus ejus, aut quis consistet, fi apparuerit? Malach. 3, 2. Ut autem rite perciperent, res eorum esse in statu pessimo
units.tr: a) Maimonides, in Taanith, c. 1,1. b) Ainsworth. The description contains the words of a great affliction, of such a kind that the people should rightly be warned by the sound of the trumpet, so that, touched by the emotion of the most wretched fear, they might look about for means by which they could be made immune to it. This warning ought to have moved them more than the sound of a watchman's cry, since the trumpet really gives a signal. The speaker, moreover, repeats the same thing in different forms of expression, namely הריעו and הקעו (clangite and date signum), so that he may more and more stir up their minds and feelings, לעורר הלבבות והתשובה [to arouse their hearts and to repentance], as Kimchi says. In the same way, both Zion and the holy mountain denote the same place (as in Ps. 2,6: I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion), which, since it was the place of their solemn assembly, shows how important the matter is, so that all of them may be aware of it and be warned. He goes on: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, not only those of Jerusalem but of all the other cities as well. This was usually signalled to them by the sound of the trumpet, whence Amos 3,6: Shall the trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? When it was heard, they were generally warned of some great evil impending, which rightly struck fear. That this is the kind of thing the Prophet is speaking of, and that it requires such a sound of the trumpet, appears from the description given in the following words: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand. The day of the LORD is the day on which he is about to bring the most terrible judgments on the land and to take vengeance on its inhabitants for their very grave sins. This same expression occurs in ch. 1,15, where see more about this phrase. But truly, lest perhaps, though frightened, they keep to the same manner of life, persuading themselves that his coming will be put off and delayed, and so deceiving themselves by thrusting far away the day of evil, Amos 6,3 adds: cometh, is nigh at hand. So if they wish to forestall it and to make themselves immune from all danger, they must betake themselves without delay to seeking the remedies by which they could bring this about. c) For who shall abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? Malachi 3,2. But so that they may rightly perceive that their affairs are in the worst state

units.la: c) Vid. v. 11. hujus cap. pessimo periculique pleno, & a securitate expergiscerentur, terrorem istius diei porro describit.
units.tr: c) See v. 11 of this chapter. Full of the worst danger, and that they may wake up from their complacency, he goes on to describe the terror of that day.

units.la: 2. Dies tenebrarum & caliginis, dies nubis & obscuritatis, ut aurora panditur super montes: populus magnus & robustus, cui par non fuit a seculo, & post quem non amplius erit usque ad annos multarum generationum.
units.tr: 2. A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations.

units.la: Dies tenebrarum & caliginis &c ) Dies sane ater & calamitosus, multa secum ferens mala & afflictiones. Frequens est S. literis, per d) tenebras figurate denotare rerum miserrimum & calamitosum statum, sicut e contrario per e) lucem secundum & prosperum. Aliter tamen hoc loco a quibusdam accipiuntur tenebræ, nimirum pro tenebris aeris proprie, quibus regio tegenda esset ab iis, quæ erant eam invasura. Ita Kimchi הצרה נמשלה לחשך כמו שהשמחה Afflictio est similis tenebris, sicut latitia luci; vel alias, inquit, expositio est, כי מריב הארבה השכיח הארץ per multitudinem f) locustarum terram esse obscuratam, quomodo habetur Exod.10,15. Operiebant enim superficiem totius terræ illorum, ita ut obscuraretur terra. Hanc explicandi rationem omnium censet Piscator, convenientissimam verbis Prophetæ, ut id, inquit, ex frequentibus verbis apparet, de quibus lector accuratius judicari poterit, cum eorum justam rationem habuerit. Interim satius mihi videtur priorem recipere, utpote quæ magis cæteris omnibus expositionibus congrua est, sive per ea, quibus calamitas dicta ipsis illata est, intelligant locustas & similes noxias bestias, sive Chaldæos vel alios inimicos, qua in re plurimum eos differre in capite primo vidimus, nec in sequentibus adeo nulla erit occasio, quin cognitionem ejus rei haurire possimus. Hic autem porro hujus diei conditionem depingit, ut verba distinguunt Biblia nostra recens translata, quæ hæc verba cum præcedentibus aliis quibusdam conjungunt; vel ut alii g) non-
units.tr: A day of darkness and of gloominess, etc. Surely a dark and calamitous day, bringing with it many evils and afflictions. In Scripture it is frequent to denote by d) darkness, figuratively, the most wretched and calamitous state of affairs, just as, on the contrary, by e) light is denoted a happy and prosperous one. Here, however, some take darkness in another sense, namely properly as darkness of the air, by which the land was to be covered from those who were about to invade it. So Kimchi: Affliction is compared to darkness, as gladness to light (הצרה נמשלה לחשך כמו שהשמחה); or, he says, another explanation is (כי מריב הארבה השכיח הארץ) that by the great multitude of f) locusts the land is darkened, as is found in Exod. 10,15: For they covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened. Piscator thinks this way of explaining it the most suitable of all to the words of the Prophet, as, he says, appears from the frequent words, about which the reader can judge more carefully once he has grasped their proper sense. Meanwhile it seems better to me to keep the former, since it agrees more than all the other explanations, whether they understand by the calamity locusts and similar harmful creatures, or the Chaldeans or other enemies, a point on which we saw in the first chapter that they differ greatly. Nor in what follows will there be so little occasion that we cannot draw out knowledge of that matter. Here, however, he goes on to portray the condition of this day, as our recently translated Bibles divide the words, joining these words to the preceding ones; or as others g) refer them to what follows,

units.la: d) Amos. 5,18. &c. e) Es. 3,16. f) Vid. Rab. Sal. & Ab. Ezra. g) LXX. Arab. impress. Castalio. nonnulli, qui ea ad sequentia referunt,in quibus populum illum,qui hanc calamitatem illis illaturus erat, amplum & robustum populum nuncupat. b) Utram vero harum sententiarum sequamur,eodem sensus redit, five i) diem,five populum intelligamus esse, ut שחר Shachar, sicut auroram quæ panditur super montes. Eadem de his verbis interpretandis opinionum est differentia, quæ inter lucem & tenebras, quum scilicet per שחר lucem,alii tenebras intelligant. Si שחר Shachar generaliter vertatur,quod mea sententia commode fit, aurora, & lux intelligatur, subitum adventum innui apparet,amplamque rerum dictarum expansionem, ita ut impediri nequaquam poffit,non secus ac aurora, quæ fe momento pandit super cacumina montium, (ubi primo fe exhibet) quamvis longissime a fe invicem distent. Ita subitaneum eventum expressurus Efaias dicit cap.58,8. k) Tunc erumpet velut aurora lux tua & sanitas tua protinus effloref-cet. Licet vero apposita fatis & perspicua fit sententia,significatio-que vocis שחר Sahar; sunt tamen qui præferunt contrariam significationem,quam voci impingunt,tenebrarum. Sic Arias Montanus, de quo Chriftophorus a Castro: Solus Montanus intelligit de tenebris. Quo sensu fortean & a latinis Commentatoribus antiquitus acceptum. At liquet, omnia, quibus Montanus suam fulcit sententiam,apud Abarbinel extare,a quo etiam eam,ut reor,accepit. Hunc in finem notat,eandem radicem etiam denotare nigredinem & tenebras; atque inde & auroram nomine Shachar venire, quia est antelucanum tempus, tenebraque tunc temporis in unum quasi collectæ densiores, quam antea,ut habet Montanus; vel ut Abarbinel: quia tenebrarum nigredo nondum abiit,nec luce exoriente protinus supra terram est dispersa. At antiquior est multo ea interpretatio,quam ut illi foli vindicemus. Vetus ille Grammaticus Abu Walid profert eam tanquam a fe inventam, eamque illi præfert, qua alii vocem reddunt lucis nomine, cujus verba,cum liber non fit impressus, hic apponere lubet: Hæc est expo{b} Vid. Mercer. {i} Quidam eam ad utrumque referunt,dies ille & exercitus locustarum vel Babyloniorum. Pet. a Fig. {k} Druf. sitio aliorum in verbis כשחר פרוש ער הרויכם Cashachar parusb al baharim שבר אנתשאר אלגראר פי אלבלאר באנתשאר אלצו פי אלנו הרא קור גירנא ותשביהרר באנתשאר אלטלאם אולא, i. e. comparari expansionem locustarum in regione expansioni lucis in aere. Hoc est quod alii dicunt. Sed magis convenit comparatio cum extensione tenebrarum, sicuti dicitur Exod. 10, 15. Operiebant faciem totius terrae, ita ut obscuraretur terra. Verum R. Tanchum, qui dubio procul eum viderit ejusque sententiam expenderit, aliter censet, quippe postquam dixerat, se comparare אנתשאר אלגראר באנתשאר אלצו אנר אלצבאר extensionem locustarum cum extenfione lucis aurorae, addit משתק אלטלאם ... & dicitur (a quibusdam) Shachar hic esse tenebras, derivatum a Shachor nigrum esse, quia impediunt (vel velant) lucem sua multitudine, ita ut tenebrae inde pandantur super montes, juxta illud quod ante dicit, dies tenebrarum & caliginis, quod convenit cum eo, quod extat Exod. 10,15. Operiebant superficiem totius terrae. Verum inquit אלאור ואנסב אטהר prior sententia est magis perspicua atque convenientior. Attamen ex recentioribus Junius & Tremellius, etsi ab iis non abeant, qui vocem Shachar per auroram interpretantur, sensum tamen eundem fere statuunt, quem illi volunt, qui contrario significatu accipiunt vocem. Hinc est ut in versione addant vocem, quam putant subintelligendam, ut nubes aurora panditur super montes, ita ut ex illorum mente sic versus fluat: dies tenebrarum & caliginis, dies nubium & crassarum tenebrarum, ut nubes aurorae panditur super montes, & exponant, tempus tam injucundum & difficile, quam solet ille dies esse, quo exoriente nubes densissimae in montes assurgunt, quae solem coelumque obtegunt prima luce, aerem obscurant & minantur imbres certissimos. At sunt l) alii, qui mirantur eos in diversum abeuntes ab usitatiori translatione, quae tam apte verbis convenit. Et Piscator mavult omittere vocem nubis
units.tr: d) Amos 5,18, etc. e) Isa. 3,16. f) See Rabbi Salomon and Abraham Ezra. g) The Septuagint, the printed Arabic, Castalio, and some others, in which the Prophet calls that people which was about to bring this calamity upon them a great and strong people. b) Whichever of these opinions we follow, the sense comes to the same, whether we understand day or people (some refer it to both: the day and the army of locusts or of the Babylonians; Pet. a Fig.) as the dawn (שחר, shachar) which spreads over the mountains. Opinions differ on the interpretation of these words just as they differ between light and darkness, in that some understand shachar as darkness. If shachar is rendered generally as dawn, which in my view is fitting, and is understood as light, it appears that a sudden coming is signified, and a wide spreading of the things said, so that it cannot in any way be hindered, just as the dawn, which spreads in a moment over the tops of the mountains (where it first shows itself), though they are very far apart. So Isaiah, wishing to express a sudden event, says in ch. 58,8: Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily. Although the sense is sufficiently suitable and clear, and the meaning of the word shachar is clear, there are still those who prefer the opposite meaning which they attach to the word, namely darkness. So Arias Montanus, of whom Christophorus a Castro says: Montanus alone understands it of darkness. In this sense it was perhaps also taken by the Latin commentators of old. But it is clear that all the things on which Montanus bases his opinion are found in Abarbanel, from whom, as I think, he took it. To this end he notes that the same root also denotes blackness and darkness; and that from this the word shachar for dawn arises, because it is the time before daylight, when the darkness is then, as it were, gathered together more densely than before, as Montanus has it; or as Abarbanel: because the blackness of the darkness has not yet passed away, nor, when the light rises, is it at once scattered over the earth. But that interpretation is much older than that these men alone should claim it for themselves. The old grammarian Abu Walid puts it forward as if he had discovered it himself, and prefers it to the one by which others render the word with the name of light. Since the book is not printed, it pleases me to set his words here: This is the explanation of others in the words (כשחר פרוש על הרים, cashachar parush al haharim) [as the dawn spread over the mountains], the spreading of the locusts over the land is compared with the spreading of the light of dawn in the air (Arabic: intishār al-jarād fī l-bilād ka-intishār al-ḍaww fī l-hawā'). This is what others say. But the comparison fits better with the extension of darkness, as is said in Exod. 10,15: They covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened. But R. Tanchum, who without doubt saw him and weighed his opinion, thinks otherwise. For after saying that he compares the spreading of the locusts with the spreading of the light of the dawn (Arabic: intishār al-jarād bi-intishār ḍaww al-fajr), he adds (Arabic: wa-yuqāl, and it is said) by some that shachar here means darkness, derived from shachor, black, because by their multitude they block or veil the light, so that darkness is spread over the mountains, according to what he said before: a day of darkness and of gloominess, which agrees with what is found in Exod. 10,15: they covered the face of the whole earth. But he says, Arabic: al-awwal wa-anṣab azhar [the former is clearer and more suitable]. Still, among the more recent writers, Junius and Tremellius, though they do not depart from those who render shachar as dawn, nevertheless set down almost the same sense as those who take the word in the opposite meaning. Hence they add in their version a word which they think is to be understood, as clouds: as the dawn spreads over the mountains, so that, in their mind, the verse runs thus: a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness, as clouds of dawn spread over the mountains; and they explain it as a time as unpleasant and hard as that day usually is, when at its rising the thickest clouds rise over the mountains, covering the sun and sky with the first light, darkening the air and threatening the most certain rains. But there are l) others who wonder that these men depart in a different direction from the more usual translation, which fits the words so well. And Piscator prefers to omit the word clouds

units.la: l) Livel. bis & reddere: ut aurora, i. e. splendor solis orientis. Exinde liquet, hic ex mente & interpretatione quorundam describi subitum adventum ac latam expansionem dictæ calamitatis; ex aliorum vero, ejusdem magnitudinem & gravitatem, verbaque (prout alios hanc, alios illam rationem elegisse vidimus) tum cum præcedentibus, quibus ipsa describitur calamitas, tum cum sequentibus, quibus eorum traditur qualitas,qui calamitatem erant illaturi,conjungi posse. Hi vero dicuntur magnus & robustus populus. m) Iidem qui cap. 1, 6. natio vocantur, populi nomine hic vocari videntur. Eadem enim duplici nomine,quod idem significat,appellari posse,non est dubium. Verum majoris difficultatis res est, nec facile Commentatoribus extricabilis,ut supra vidimus,quinam potissimum eo nomine sint intelligendi. Sunt qui per eos intelligunt locustas, similesque noxias creaturas, quarum nomina cap. 1. inspeximus; alii inimicos, ut Affyrios & Babylonios; alii locustas nomine, sensu vero Assyrios. n) Plerique Judæorum intelligunt locustas; unus Abarbinel inimicos, quibus terram irruentibus, populantibus ac Judæos in captivitatem abducentibus tribuit,quicquid & antecedentibus & quibusdam fequentibus versibus continetur. In verbis clangite buccina &c. alludi asserit ad buccinæ clangorem anno Jubilæi Levit. 25. alio tamen fine; nempe ut quisque possessionis suæ,quam debebat capere,tum admonebatur, ita hic discessionis,qua in captivitatem migrandum erat, o) ut quisque ex possessione sua exiret, & a familia sua discederet in captivitatem. Per tenebrarum diem p) reliquaque verba,quibus ille describitur, innuit titulum vel denomi-nationem destructionis prioris templi atque afflictionum, quibus tunc temporis afficiebantur; per magnum populum &c. quos secum adduxerat Nebuchadnezzar adversus Hierosolymam. Inter Christianos hoc quoque olim diverse agitatum est,nec adhuc dum extricatum. Hieronymus dubius hæret, utram harum sententiarum sequi velit, cum
units.tr: l) Livelius, twice, renders it: as the dawn, that is, the brightness of the rising sun. From this it is clear that, in the view and interpretation of some, the sudden arrival and wide spreading of the said calamity is described here; while in the view of others, its size and severity are described, and the words may be connected both with what precedes, where the calamity itself is described, and with what follows, where the character of those who were to inflict it is set out (for we have seen that some have chosen this explanation and others that one). These people are called a great and mighty people. m) The same people who are called a nation in chap. 1:6 seem here to be called a people. There is no doubt that the same thing can be named by two words that mean the same. But the question of who in particular is to be understood by that name is more difficult, and the commentators cannot easily resolve it, as we saw above. Some understand by them locusts and similar harmful creatures, whose names we looked at in chap. 1; others understand enemies, such as the Assyrians and Babylonians; others understand locusts by the name but Assyrians in meaning. n) Most of the Jews understand locusts. Only Abarbanel understands enemies, to whom he assigns everything contained both in the preceding verses and in some of the following ones, namely those who would invade the land, lay it waste, and lead the Jews into captivity. He asserts that the words blow the trumpet etc. allude to the sounding of the trumpet in the year of Jubilee, Lev. 25, but for another purpose: just as each man was then reminded to take possession of his property, so here he is reminded of the departure into which he must go into captivity, o) that each man should go out of his possession and depart from his family into captivity. By the day of darkness p) and the other words by which the day is described, he hints at the title or designation of the destruction of the former temple and of the afflictions with which they were then being afflicted; and by the great people etc., which Nebuchadnezzar had brought with him against Jerusalem. Among the Christians this too has long been disputed in different ways, and it has not yet been settled. Jerome hesitates, uncertain which of these opinions he should follow, since

units.la: m) At secus videtur Danæo. n) Abu V Valid R. Sal. Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, R. Tanchum. o) Aliter Ar. Mont. p) Quo præcipue notari putat novus dies mensis Ab.
units.tr: m) Danaeus, however, seems to think otherwise. n) Abu Walid, R. Salomo, Aben Ezra, Kimchi, R. Tanchum. o) Others, Arias Montanus. p) He thinks this is chiefly pointed at by the new day of the month Ab.

units.la: juxta eum verba proprie accepta denotent locustas, figurate Chaldaeos, ita ut, dum locustas legimus, Babylonios cogitemus. Per metaphoram locustarum, inquit, describitur impetus Chaldaeorum. Nec habet, quo se vertat Cyrillus, cum id accipit vel de locustis, vel ἐξ ὁμοιότητος αὐτῶν, ex similitudine illarum de Assyrus atque ἐπ' ἀμφοῖν ἀληθὲς, de utrisque verum pronuntiat. Ita utrosque respici ait Theodoretus, tum locustas, tum inimicorum nubem. At Ruffinus ad locustas solas id refert. Ex q) recentioribus nonnulli, iisque magnae auctoritatis viri praecise exponunt de inimicis, Assyriis, vel Babyloniis; r) alii vero positive de locustis. Nec difficultate caret, hanc controversiam dirimere, cum ex utraque parte auctoritas tantorum virorum intercedat. Quare ita ea verba juxta literalem sensum explicare annitar, ut, quamvis ad locustas potissimum ea referam, quam sententiam prae caeteris his verbis puto congruam & maxime amplectendam, si cui tamen secus visum fuerit, genuinam tamen illorum habeat significationem. Adduntur autem huic populo duo epitheta רב Rab magnus & עצום Atsum, robustus; magnus, i. e. numero; tantus scilicet, ut juxta cap.1,6. מספר אין sit innumerus vel sine numero; & robustus, non quidem per se ac singulas, sed s) per eum, qui eas immittebat, cujusque virtute tam validae erant, ut totam regionem destruerent. Robustus enim qui efficit verbum suum, (per eas) ut infra dictum est v. 11. Adjicit: cui par non fuit a seculo & post quem non amplius erit usque ad annos multarum generationum. Quae populi descriptio eadem est atque ea, quam vidimus cap.1.v.2,3. ubi ex iis quaerit, num earum rerum, de quibus erat dicturus, tale quid fuerit temporibus suis, vel temporibus majorum suorum, ac monet, ut de hoc filiis suis narrent, & filii eorum filiis suis, & filii illorum generationi posterae, quibus plane idem declarat atque hoc loco; scilicet, par huic, quod nunc videbant, (vel mox visuri erant) non fuisse visum antecedentibus seculis, nec unquam visum iri sequentibus; sed quibuscunque demum id audire contingeret, nonnisi rei stuporis plenae, imo prodigii loco habitum iri, quale ne fando unquam auditum.
units.tr: according to him the words, taken in their proper sense, denote locusts, and figuratively the Chaldeans, so that while we read of locusts, we are to think of the Babylonians. By a metaphor of locusts, he says, the onslaught of the Chaldeans is described. Nor does Cyril know which way to turn when he takes it either of locusts, or of the Assyrians by likeness to them (ex homoiotētos autōn), and pronounces it true of both (ep' amphoin alēthes). So Theodoret says that both are regarded, both the locusts and the cloud of enemies. But Rufinus refers it to the locusts alone. Among the more recent writers, some, and men of great authority, explain it strictly of the enemies, the Assyrians or Babylonians; r) others, however, positively of the locusts. It is not easy to settle this dispute, since on each side stands the authority of such great men. Therefore I shall try to explain these words according to the literal sense in such a way that, although I refer them chiefly to the locusts, which view I think more suitable than the rest and most worthy of embrace, yet if anyone sees it otherwise, the words still keep their genuine meaning. Two epithets are added to this people: rab [רב], great, and atsum [עצום], mighty. Great, that is, in number, so great that, according to chap. 1:6, they are without number (mispar ein [מספר אין]); and mighty, not indeed in themselves and individually, but s) through him who sent them, by whose power they were so strong that they destroyed the whole region. For the mighty one who performs his word (through them), as it is said below, v. 11. He adds: there was none like it from of old, nor shall there be any more after it, to the years of many generations. This description of the people is the same as the one we saw in chap. 1:2, 3, where he asks them whether anything of the sort, of the things about which he was going to speak, happened in their own times or in the times of their fathers, and he urges them to tell it to their sons, and their sons to their sons, and their sons to the following generation. There he declares plainly the same thing as here, namely that nothing like what they now saw (or were soon to see) had been seen in the preceding ages, nor would ever be seen in the following ones; but whoever should happen to hear of it would regard it only as a thing full of astonishment, indeed as a prodigy, such as was never heard of

units.la: q) Calv. Munst. Grot. Duae. Genev. r) Jun. Trem. Pisc. Bochart. s) Vide not. in cap.1,6. ditum, vel alicubi oculis visum. Non videtur absona,quæ ex utroque loco, si per nationes vel populum locustas intelligamus, enascitur quæstio, quomodo, quod hic & ibi dictum est,cum eo conveniat, quod extat Exod. 10,14. ubi tam numerosæ locustæ super universam terram Ægyptiorum a DEO dicuntur missæ,ut ante eas non fuissent sic locustæ pares istis, & post eas non essent sic futuræ. Quo pacto hanc difficultatem solvant Commentatores, ad ea verba prolixe satis notavimus,nec est,quod hic pluribus ei enodandæ incumbamus, cum de novo sese hic offert. Verum non possum facere,quin in medium proferam, quod R. Tanchum, quamvis nihil novi completens facile lectori tædium possit adferre,hunc in locum annotavit. Verba ejus translata sic habent: Quod si hoc accipiatur de veris locustis, cum eo pugnabit quod Deus de locustis dicit, quæ inter plagas Ægyptiacas erant, ante quas non fuerant pares istis, & post quas non futuræ erant sic. Ad hanc contradictionem dirimendam rationem oportere habere loci t) quidam viri eruditi notant, cum,quod in Exodo extat, tantum concernat Ægyptum illasque locustas, quæ ibi tunc erant, & postea nunquam venturæ; ut e contrario hoc loco solam terram Israelitarum sermo propheticus respiciat, nec ultra extendi possit. u) Alii eo tendi his verbis censent, quod nunquam pares his fuissent, qua erant quatuor genera,quæ nominantur c. 14. cum tantum locustarum in priori loco mentio fiat. Sunt & qui statuunt has & similes loquendi formulas in prophetiis & libris Prophetarum non nisi hyperbolicas esse locutiones nec innui, veritatem rerum exacte verborum significationi debere respondere, sed verbis tam excessivis tantum denotari, quod magnum est, ac ordinariam naturæ rationem ac usitatum rerum, quas videmus, cursum longe excedit. Quod sequitur, translatum est in nostris Bibliis, a multis generationibus; at in margine notatum juxta literam legi, a generatione & generatione. Sic & recentiorum & veterum non pauci. Chaldæus quoque eadem ferme verba retinet quæ in textu hebraico sunt. Vulgatus Lat. usque in annos generationis & generationis.
units.tr: q) Calvin, Münster, Grotius, Duae, Geneva. r) Junius, Tremellius, Piscator, Bochart. s) See the note on chap. 1:6. ...spoken of, or seen with the eyes anywhere. The question that arises from both passages does not seem absurd, if by the nations or people we understand locusts: how what is said here and there agrees with what stands in Exod. 10:14, where locusts so numerous are said to have been sent by God over the whole land of the Egyptians that before them there had not been locusts like them, nor would there be such after them. How the commentators resolve this difficulty we have noted at some length on those words, and there is no need to labour at it again here, since it presents itself afresh. Yet I cannot refrain from bringing forward what R. Tanchum has noted on this passage, although it adds nothing new and may easily weary the reader. His words, translated, run thus: If this is taken of real locusts, it will clash with what God says of the locusts that were among the Egyptian plagues, before which there had not been such as these, and after which there would not be such. Certain learned men note that, to remove this contradiction, one must take account of the place: what stands in Exodus concerns only Egypt and those locusts that were there at that time and were never to come again; whereas, conversely, the prophetic discourse in this place regards only the land of the Israelites and cannot be extended further. u) Others think that these words aim at this, that there had never been such as these, which were of four kinds, named in chap. 1:4, since in the earlier passage only locusts are mentioned. There are also those who hold that these and similar forms of speech in the prophecies and books of the prophets are merely hyperbolical expressions, and that it is not implied that the truth of the matter must correspond exactly to the meaning of the words, but that by such excessive words only what is great is denoted, and what far exceeds the ordinary course of nature and the usual order of the things we see. What follows is rendered in our Bibles to many generations, but noted in the margin as read literally: from generation and generation. So too not a few of both recent and ancient writers. The Chaldee also keeps nearly the same words as the Hebrew text. The Latin Vulgate has unto the years of generation and generation.

units.la: t) Bochartus. u) R. Sal. Aben-Ezra,Kimchi. tionis. Ita & MS. Arabicum الي سنين ... [illegible, ~12 letters] & multæ versiones latinæ. Nec multum abludunt LXX. ἑως ἑτῶν εἰς γενεὰς γενεῶν: nec Arabica impressa الي سنين الي جيل الاجيال ad annos generationis generationum : Syrus [illegible, ~8 letters] usque ad annos generationis post generationem. Junius & Tremellius reddunt, ut nostrates in textu,ad annos multarum generationum, quod propria & genuina videtur explicatio verborum, quæ ad literam sonant, ad annos generationis & generationis. Repetitio vocis generationis, importat multitudinem vel pluralitatem, ɯ) non duas tantum sequentes generationes, sed longum temporis tractum post præsentem generationem, quamvis certis limitibus ac terminis non coarctatum, eatenus tamen limitibus circumscriptum, quatenus aliquando finem consequitur; idem est, ac si diceretur, non tam subito tale quid iterum accidet, nec x) cujusvis generationis erit; non, nisi post plures annos præter præsentem, vel proxime sequentem & fortean alios. Breviter: indicatur h. l. indefinite longum tempus, quamdiu DEO visum fuerit. Cum vero y) annorum hic mentio fit, verisimile est, eum temporis decursu denuo vel posse redire, vel certo rediturum esse, adeoque non præcise z) determinari, parem nunquam futurum, quod cum quidam annotarunt, ita exponunt: a) nunquam ultra, vel b) neque ullis seculorum annis futurus est. Qui hic locustas intelligi volunt, pro tempore longo indefinite sumunt, ut vidimus; qui vero inimicos, restringunt id ad tempus Romanorum, qui longo temporis spatio post Chaldæos erant venturi, ut ex Judæis habet Abarbinel & ex Christianis non pauci.
units.tr: t) Bochart. u) R. Salomo, Aben Ezra, Kimchi. ...of generation. So too the Arabic manuscript (ila sinin, "to years," ... [illegible, about twelve letters]) and many Latin versions. The Seventy do not differ much: heōs etōn eis geneas geneōn [ἑως ἑτῶν εἰς γενεὰς γενεῶν]; nor does the printed Arabic (ila sinin ila jil al-ajyal), to years, to generation of generations. The Syriac (... [illegible, about eight letters]) unto the years of generation after generation. Junius and Tremellius render, like our translators in the text, to the years of many generations, which seems to be the proper and genuine explanation of words that sound literally to the years of generation and generation. The repetition of the word generation implies multitude or plurality: not merely the two following generations, but a long stretch of time after the present generation, not confined within fixed limits and bounds, yet circumscribed by limits so far as it at some point reaches an end. It is the same as if it were said: such a thing will not happen again so suddenly, nor will it be of any generation; not until many years have passed beyond the present one, or the one immediately following, and perhaps others too. In short: here an indefinitely long time is indicated, as long as it shall seem good to God. But since mention is made here of years, it is likely that in the course of time it may return again, or will certainly return, and so is not precisely determined to be a thing that will never be matched again; which some who have noted this explain thus: a) never again, or b) it will not be in any years of the ages. Those who wish the locusts to be understood here take the long time as indefinite, as we have seen; but those who understand the enemies restrict it to the time of the Romans, who were to come after the Chaldeans after a long interval, as Abarbanel holds from the Jews, and not a few Christians from among the Christians.

units.la: 3. Ante
units.tr: 3. Before

units.la: §§) Ne duas tantum generationes accipe, sed pro scripturæ usu multas. Merc. x) Livel. y) Ar. Mont. z) Theodoret. Rib. Cast. a) Vat. b) Castr.
units.tr: Take the "two generations" not only as two, but as many, according to the usage of Scripture. Mercer x) Livelius y) Arias Montanus z) Theodoret. Ribera. Castro. a) Vatablus. b) Castro.

units.la: 3. Ante eos consumit ignis & post eos flamma inflam- mat; terra est ante eos sicut hortus Edenis, & post eos desertum desolatissimum, tamen nihil evadet eos.
units.tr: Before them the fire devours, and behind them the flame burns; the land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them a most desolate wilderness; yea, and nothing shall escape them.

units.la: Pergit hoc & sequentibus quibusdam versibus aliquibus sublimibus ac figuratis exprimere expressionibus circumstantias lugubres ac effectus, quibus praedicti magni & robusti, numerosi ac scelesti populi adventum conjunctum fore indicat. Primo dicit, ignis consumit ante eos, vel utin veteri Genevensi Anglicana, & plerique interpretes latini juxta textum hebraicum singulari numero, לפניו Lephanav, ante eum. Verum cum id referatur ad praecedentem vocem populum, quae collectiva adeoque multitudinem etiam singulari numero complectitur, parum refert quo numero ponatur, quod sequitur לפניו ante eum, vel ante eos. Haec vox prima est in textu originali & sic denotat ante. Non caret autem ambiguitate, cum non satis constet, sitne hic referenda ad praecedentem locum, an tempus, quia alibi indifferenter pro utroque sumitur. Hinc priori significatione accipitur a quibusdam, ab aliis posteriori, nec tamen fluit sensus ratio, quocunque modo sumant, quidve demum per populum intelligant. Idem dicendum de voce sequenti ואחריו Teacherau, & post eum vel eos. Potest enim pari ratione referri tum ad locum, qui erat relictus, tum ad tempus, quod superierat. Eorum qui ad locum videntur referre non sunt postremi LXX. reddentes c) τα ἐμπροσθεν αὐτὰ ἀπὸ ἀλλίστων καὶ τὰ ὀπίσω αὐτῶν ἀναπομένη Φλοξ. Quae sunt ante eum, consumit ignis, & quae post eum, accensa flamma, quod Cyrillus, qui de locutis id sumit, idcirco dictum putat, quia τὰς τῶν ἀκοῶν ἐμξηλάς, locutiarum irruptione, quicquid occurrit, profligatur, & si quid ab iis reliquitur, ἔργον καὶ αὐτὸ ἐσαι τῶν ἐπομένων τὰς πρώτας, hoc opus veritatem, quae priores sequuntur ad abfumendum ea. Eandem noxam illatam ab inimicis intelligi posse ait. Quorsum etiam exacte Vulgatus: Ante faciem ejus ignis vorans, & post eam exurens flamma. Quod ita exponit Hieronymus: Quicquid quid c In Arab. Imprell. quid attigerit, quasi vorax flamma consumet, nihilque post se derelinquet. Nec absimile illud R. Salom. Omnia absumit tanquam devorans ignis ante eas, & ardens flamma post eas; & Rab. Kimchi: Ubicunque sedem fixerit, est ante eas & post eas, ac fi ignis devorans & arsisset viridia quaeque ante eas, ut dicit, & post eas, quasi locus erant, ut (in praesentiarum) eratteftus. Hinc particulis ante & post hac ratione sumtis, comparatio est juxta illos locustarum & rerum ab iis gestarum cum igne & ejus detrimento, quod adfert plerumque rebus, quas adurit. Eaque comparatio satis concinnanis videtur ac conveniens locustarum naturae, quae ob noxiam, qua praedita sunt, qualitatem, eas dicuntur res c) adurere, quibus insident, ut si praviservatum est ad v. 7. cap. 1. Secus tamen sentit Doctissimus Bochartus, qui, quamvis de locustis sermonem esse ac eas innui per popuar. arbitretur, igni tamen nec ipsas comparari censet, nec earum res gestas ignis effectibus; verum aliud per ignem indicari, nimirum magnam siccitatem & ingentem ardorem, qui earum adventum praecedebat, sicut in praecedenti capite etiam ad v. 17. & 19. annotatum, ubi non tantum ejus, verum & aliorum opinionem attulimus. Quod vero attinet ad vocem ante eum, eam non denotare ait locum, sed tempus, adjiciens, utrobique agi de f) summa siccitate quae locustarum adventum praecessit & secuta est, quarum noxa illa omnia terrae virentia non secus atque ab igne & flamma erant adusta & absumta. Quocunque vero modo accipiatur, g) utrique optime congruit, quod sequitur: Terra est sicut hortus Edenis ante eos, & post eos desertum desolatisfimum. Ubi vocula haec ante & post rursum possunt referri vel ad locum vel ad tempus; ita ut sermo respiciat vel eam regionis partem, quo non penetraverant, & quam ulterius progredientes post se relinquebant. Ita Hieronymus: Quasi hortus Eden Adus & paradisus voluptatis omnis terra est, quam non tetigerunt: quasi solitudo & desertum quoque quid fuerit praedatus; sicut hortus & paradifus voluptatis (qualis olim erat hortus Edenis Genef.2, 8. &c. qui etiam hortus Dei vocatur phrasi usitata, qua denotantur loca jucundissima & amoenissima, ut Gen.13,10. Ezech.36,35.) est omnis terra quam non tetigerit (scil. hic populus) & quasi solitudo & desertum quicquid fuerit praedatus. Vel alias b) ante eorum adventum, & post eorum discessum esse regionem, quae tam amoena erat ante eorum adventum, ut descripta est, postquam discesserint, relictam esse prorsus desolatam. Haec sententia i) nonnullis etiam placet, qui priora verba sumunt de ordine loci; nec plurimum refert, utram selegeris, quippe nihil exinde oritur detrimenti rei, quae intenditur ac descriptione ingentis mali absolvitur; cujus extensio atque universalitas his exprimitur verbis: tamen nihil evadet eos, ut nostrates optime sensum exprimunt verborum regam pelitah lo haytah lo, ad literam: & ita ibi non erit evasio ei (vel k) abeo). Vox pelitah proprie quidem denotat l) evasionem, at non tantum pro m) actu evadendi usurpatur, sed & pro rebus vel personis, quae evadunt & superstunt. Ita ut nihil aliud his verbis, non erit evasio ei, indicetur, quam n) evaforem non futurum, vel nihil evasurum, nec o) reliquias remansuras superstites. Sic exponit ea Aben-Ezra Nihil est quod evasit (vel possit evadere) ei vel eis. Et Kimchi qua nihil earum rerum reliquerunt, quae nascuntur, quas non decit devoratas. Non autem hic interpretum unanimis sententia, cum, quod nostrates & supra dicti cum aliis attribuunt rebus, alii tribuant personis. Ex his LXX: καὶ ἀναστωξόμενοι ἐκ ἐστὶ αὐτοῖς, & qui salvetur non erit ei; & p) Arabica impressa Non est qui possit evadere, & Vulgatus Lat. nec est qui effugiat cum, quod h) Bochart. i) Mercer. k) Mercer. ei, i. e. ab eo. l) Drus. m) Aliis & res, Schindl. Stein alus, ut captivitas pro captivis & c. Drus. Eadem vox est v. 32. n) Non erit evasio. o) Reliquiae, superstites remanserit. p) Mss. Arabic. insigniter convenit cum Hebraeo. quod Hieronymus sic explicat: neque ullus poterit inveniri, qui illius effugiat manus. Syrus ܣܪܝܢ ... Nihil est, vel nullus (potest enim tum personis tum rebus accommodari indifferenter) quod queat ab eo liberari. Chaldaeus dilucide ad personas refert ואף שובא ... atque ita non est evasio illi (vel ab illo vel propter illum) pro impio. Recentiorum etiam quidam non reddidere nihil, sed q) nemo. Qui homines vel personas non evasuras volunt, non videntur per eos, quibus erant evasuri, intelligere locustas vel hujusmodi creaturas, sed inimicos; hi enim non illae homines infestant. Quamvis tamen bono etiam sensu ab illis, quibus interpretari placet nemo, locustae respici possent. Cum enim hi vermiculi omnes terrae fructus ad subsistendum aptos absumant, omnino ipsi homines generali hac devastatione dici possunt affecti, nemoque eorum iis evasisse, qui non illarum succubuerit noxae, & a generali fame fuerit immunis. Quia vero vocula פליט foeminini generis est, eamque significationem habet, quam supra tradidimus, rectius videtur referri posse ad res in genere, quam in specie ad personas, interpretatioque planior est, quae habet nihil, quam nemo. Inter eos, qui inimicos intelligunt per populum, non locustas, Abarbinel peculiari modo explicat verba, quae praecedunt: ante eos consumet ignis, & post eos flamma inflammat. Nimirum per ignem consumentem ante eos intelligit primam aciem vel exercitus frontem; per flammam inflammantem post eos, postremam aciei partem, quae quidem in aliis exercitibus plerumque claudiatur agmine foeminarum, liberorum, veterumque ac morbo confectorum militum ad pugnas inidoneorum; secus tamen fiebat apud Babylonios, quorum consuetudine talibus agmen claudebatur, qui cum flamma omnia adurente merito poterant comparari; & quando dicitur, nihil evadet eos, innui putat, quod accidebat Gedaliah filio Ahikam, & illis, qui relicti erant cum eo in terra Juda, quo non ita multo post r) Ismael filius Nethaniah, veniens eos occidebat, ita ut nullus eorum, quibus Nebuchadnezar pepercerat, superstes relictus fuerit.
units.tr: In this verse and the ones that follow, the prophet uses some lofty and figurative expressions to describe the dreadful circumstances and effects that he says will accompany the coming of this great, strong, numerous and wicked people. First he says, the fire consumes before them, as the old Geneva and English versions have it, and most Latin interpreters, following the Hebrew, have it in the singular: לפניו [lephanav], before him. But since this refers to the preceding word "people", which is a collective noun and so includes a multitude even in the singular, it matters little whether the word is before him or before them. This word is the first in the original text and so means before. It is not free of ambiguity, however, since it is not clear whether it refers to the preceding place or to time, because elsewhere it is used indifferently for either. Some therefore take it in the first sense, others in the second, and yet the sense does not follow, whichever way they take it, or whatever they finally understand by "people". The same must be said of the following word, ואחריו [acharav], and after him or after them. For by the same reasoning it may refer either to place, that which was left behind, or to time, that which remained. Those who seem to refer it to place include not the least of the Seventy, who render: τὰ ἐμπροσθεν αὐτὰ ἀπὸ ἀλλίστων καὶ τὰ ὀπίσω αὐτῶν ἀναπομένη Φλοξ [ta emprosthen auta...], what is before him the fire consumes, and what is after him the burning flame. Cyril, who takes the locusts to be meant, thinks this was said because by the irruption of the locusts whatever meets them is laid waste, and if anything is left by them, the first ones pursue it to consume it, a work of truth itself. He says the same harm inflicted by enemies may be understood. Hence also the Vulgate translates exactly: Before his face a devouring fire, and after him a burning flame. Jerome explains this: whatever it touches, the devouring flame will consume as if it were a fire, and it will leave nothing behind it. Not unlike this is what Rabbi Solomon says: it consumes everything like a devouring fire before them, and a burning flame behind them; and Rabbi Kimchi: wherever it fixes its seat, it is before them and behind them, as if a devouring fire had burned up every green thing before them, as he says, and behind them they were as a desert. Taking the particles before and after in this way, the comparison is, according to them, between the locusts and what they do and the fire with its destructive effect, which usually befalls the things it burns. This comparison seems quite apt and suits the nature of the locusts, which, because of the harmful quality they possess, are said to burn up the things they settle upon, as was noted above at chapter 1, verse 7. The most learned Bochart, however, thinks otherwise. Although he holds that the discourse concerns locusts and that they are hinted at by "people", he does not think they are compared to fire, nor that their deeds are compared to the effects of fire. Rather, he thinks fire indicates something else, namely the great drought and intense heat that preceded their coming, as noted in the previous chapter at verses 17 and 19, where we gave not only his opinion but others as well. As for the word before him, he says it denotes not place but time, adding: in both places the drought is meant, which preceded and followed the coming of the locusts, and by whose harm all the green things of the earth were burned and consumed no less than by fire and flame. However it is taken, what follows fits both readings very well: the land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness. Here again the little words before and behind may refer either to place or to time, so that the sense concerns either the part of the region which they had not entered, or that which they left behind as they advanced. Thus Jerome: the whole land which they have not touched is like the garden of Eden and the paradise of delight, and whatever they have plundered is like a solitude and a desert. Like a garden and a paradise of delight (such as the garden of Eden once was, Gen. 2:8 etc., which is also called the garden of God, a common phrase denoting most pleasant and delightful places, as in Gen. 13:10 and Ezek. 36:35) is every land which this people have not touched, and whatever they have plundered is like a solitude and a desert. Or otherwise: before their coming, and after their departure, the region was as lovely as it is described, and after they had departed it was left utterly desolate. This interpretation also pleases some, who take the first words as referring to order of place. It matters little which of these one chooses, since nothing of the thing intended is lost from it, and the description of the great evil is completed by this: the extent and universality of which are expressed in these words: yet nothing shall escape them. Our countrymen render the sense of the words regam pelitah lo haytah lo [רק פליטה לו היתה לו] very well, literally: and so there shall be no escape for him (or from him). The word pelitah properly denotes escape, but it is used not only for the act of escaping, but also for things or persons that escape and survive. So by these words, there shall be no escape for him, nothing else is indicated than that there will be no fugitive, nor anything escaping, nor remnants surviving. So Aben Ezra explains them: there is nothing that escaped (or could escape) him or them. And Kimchi: nothing of those things which grow has been left, which has not been devoured. But the interpreters are not unanimous here, since our countrymen and the aforementioned writers with others attribute it to things, while others attribute it to persons. Among these, the Seventy: καὶ ἀναστωξόμενοι ἐκ ἐστὶ αὐτοῖς [kai anaswzomenoi ek estin autois], and he who is saved will not be for them; the printed Arabic: There is no one who can escape; and the Latin Vulgate: nor is there anyone who may escape, which Jerome explains thus: no one will be found who escapes his hand. The Syriac: nothing, or no one (for it may be applied indifferently to persons or to things) which can be freed from him. The Chaldee clearly refers it to persons: and so there is no escape for him (or from him or on account of him) for the wicked. Some of the more recent writers rendered it not nothing but no one. Those who want the words to mean persons or people who will not escape do not seem to understand by those from whom they would escape the locusts or creatures of that kind, but enemies; for these are not the men who attack. Yet even in a good sense, those who prefer to translate no one could also refer to the locusts. For since these little worms consume all the fruits of the earth fit for sustenance, the men themselves may certainly be said to be affected by this general devastation, and none of them will have escaped who did not succumb to its harm and was immune from the general famine. But since the word פליט [pelit] is feminine, and has the meaning we gave above, it seems more correctly referred to things in general rather than to persons in particular, and the translation which has nothing is plainer than no one. Among those who understand the people to be enemies and not locusts, Abarbanel explains the preceding words in a peculiar way: before them the devouring fire consumes, and after them the flame burns. Namely, by the fire devouring before them he understands the first line of the army or the front of the host; by the flame burning after them, the rearmost part of the line, which in other armies is usually closed by a column of women, children, and old or sick soldiers unfit for battle. Among the Babylonians, however, it was otherwise, for by their custom such people closed the column, and they could rightly be compared to a flame that burns up everything. And when it is said, nothing shall escape them, he thinks it hints at what happened to Gedaliah son of Ahikam, and to those who were left with him in the land of Judah, whom not long afterward Ishmael son of Nethaniah came and killed, so that none of those whom Nebuchadnezzar had spared was left alive.

units.la: Quidam s) eruditus Commentator Latinus per ignem ante eos intelligi vult, atque alludi ad eum ignem, quem Chaldæi (quorum moribus Dei instar colebatur) exercitui suo præferebant, ut viam præmonstraret atque terrorem injiceret hostibus; neque minus ad cum, quo agmen claudebatur, quoque flammis subjiciebant, quicquid obviam veniebat. Quæ opinio quamvis ipsi quam maxime arrideat, neque inconcinna videatur observatio, tamen ad rem minus eam facere t) nonnulli judicarunt. Quodsi de inimicis accipiendum, planissima sententia est, omnia circumquaque u) flammis fore subjicienda destruendaque, quæcunque visum eorum subitura essent. Sed rectius mihi facere videntur, qui de locustis ea sumunt cæterisque vermibus antea nominatis, quæ & in sequentibus una cum rebus suis gestis aut gerendis porro describuntur.
units.tr: A certain learned Latin commentator wishes "fire before them" to be understood as the fire which the Chaldeans (among whose customs fire was worshipped as a god) carried before their army, to show the way and strike terror into the enemy, and likewise the fire with which they set alight whatever lay in their path at the rear of the column. Although this opinion greatly pleases him, and the observation does not seem unfitting, some have judged that it contributes little to the matter. If it is taken of the enemies, the plainest sense is that everything round about that was about to come under their sight would be set on fire and destroyed. But those seem to me to take it more rightly who understand it of the locusts and the other worms mentioned earlier, which are also described further on, together with their deeds done or yet to be done.

units.la: 4. Species eorum est tanquam species equorum, & ut equites, ita current.
units.tr: 4. Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and as horsemen, so they will run.

units.la: מראה Marehu, Visio, vultus, species, w) forma, facies est sicut species x) equorum. Non inusitatam fuisse comparationem locustarum cum equis, ex eo apparet, quod de locustis extat Apocal. 9,7. earum (quicunque etiam per eas denotentur) figuras (vel similitudines) similes esse equis ad prælium paratis. Quacunque autem alia in re earum cum equis similitudo consistat, vultum tamen, caput ac faciem earum præcipue respici nostra non minus quam aliorum est opinio. Ita in h. l. Theodoretus: Si quis accurate, inquit, satis locusta caput inspiciat, inveniet σφόδρα τῇ τῶν ἵππων εἰκονι ἀπομοιον simile capiti equi, quod & aliis recentioribus observatum, Bocharto referente, habemus. Idem de illis observant Arabes, quibus hoc creaturarum genus optime notum, ut ex verbis, quæ ex Historia creaturarum viventium Damari citat, videre est, quibus locustæ dicuntur imbecilles creaturæ, at quæ corpore ac aliis quibusdam corporis partibus referunt decem genera creaturarum fortiorum robustio-
units.tr: Marehu, Visio, vultus, species, w) forma, facies [מראה] is "like the appearance x) of horses." That this comparison of locusts with horses was not unusual appears from Revelation 9:7, where the figures (or likenesses) of locusts (whoever is meant by them) are said to be like horses prepared for battle. In whatever other respect their resemblance to horses lies, our view, like that of others, is that their face, head and countenance are especially in view. So Theodoret on this passage: "If anyone," he says, "examines the locust's head closely enough, he will find it very much like the image of a horse [σφόδρα τῇ τῶν ἵππων εἰκονι ἀπομοιον], that is, like the head of a horse," which, as Bochart reports, has also been noted by other more recent writers. The Arabs observe the same thing about them, and know this kind of creature very well, as can be seen from the words which Damari cites from his History of Living Creatures, where locusts are called weak creatures, yet in body and certain other bodily parts they resemble ten kinds of stronger and more robust creatures.

units.la: s) Sanctus. t) in Not. Angl. u) Grot. Quaqua illic omnia lucebunt incendiis. 66) cap. Cons. x) Schindl. ftiorumque. Atque primo loco tunc constituitur פוס ןישכ וצ cues equi, quod inter eos peculiari ratione exprimit Poeta quidam: celeres equi contulerunt in eas caput & os, ita ut commode hic commate primo locustæ dicendæ sint conferri cum equorum vultu, specie ac genuina forma. Cui addi potest, quod z) alii censent, consistere vim similitudinis in illarum ferocia, audacia, & procacitate, ut Job. 39, 19. &c. Dein iisdem rursus sequenti commate comparantur refpectu illarum impavidæ velocitatis in progrediendo his verbis: Et ut equites ita current. Equus enim ipse est qui currit, quamvis ab equite incitatus. Atque tanta celeritate omnia ante fe subvertent nemine contra eunte vel inhibente. Ex eo multi argumentum irrefragabile petere posse sibi videntur, quod proprie ea verba spectent locustas, non Chaldæos vel inimicos, quia dicuntur similes equis & equitibus. Erant enim revera inimici equites & equis inequitantes, non autem similes illis vel ipsi, vel eorum equi. Quidam illorum, qui inimicos intelligunt, ut hanc objectionem explodant, dicunt, literam ] ,c, Græcis redditam ως latinis sicut, ut plurimum quidem esse particulam similitudinis, at hoc loco non poni ωαρα-βολικως ad comparationem vel fimilitudinem denotandam; sed, quod & alibi frequenter, επιτατικως, ut Theodoretus ad intensionem significandam, & dicendi ea eminenter ac revera ita habere, quomodo dicta sunt, ita ut his verbis Species eorum est tanquam spectes equorum, innuere vult, equos revera præ fe ferre equorum aspectum; & sequentibus: & ut equites, ita current, illos ipsos fe exhibituros expeditos equites. Alii quidem comparativam significationem retinent, at volunt intelligi peditatum exercitus, ita ut ipsi tanti feroces apparerent, quam equi, & tam audaces ac celeres forent, quam equites.Pedites ipsi erant velociores, inquit Grotius. Et Abarbinel, postquam historiam retulit, quae ad rem plane non facit, ac si centauris compararentur, qui dicuntur semi-homines ac semi-equi, ad & dos putat hic illudi, addit non a vero protinus abhorrere, facies illorum fuisse magnas, ac membra robusta instar equorum, eorumque pedites tanta celeritate cucurrisse, quanta equites currunt equis. Verum atro carbone ea notat Bochartus dicens: Pedites cum equitibus conferri nolvim est, & inaudituri; &: quis Assyrius dixerit ut equites fuissent, cum revera equites fuerint, ingens magno numero, ut alibi describuntur Ezec. b. 27, 6. & 12. & 23. & cap. 26. v. 7. 10. 11. Habac. 1, 8. &c? Attamen b) alius est, qui in haec verba scribit: Non mirum est viros bellicosos comparari equis generosis, pedites equitibus, ad indicandum fortitudinem & celeritatem eorum. Ad me quod attinet, perspicue satis censeo comparationem hic fieri locustarum, & similium infectorum cum equis, quibus Deus utebatur ad judicia sua perficienda, quamvis imbelles videantur creaturae ac contemtui sint expositae, equi vero fortitudine ingenti ac facultate inclyti. Nec minus his congruet comparatio in verbis sequentibus, quibus adventus illarum ac facta aliis circumstantiis tradunt, nimirum tumultus ac strepitus magnus, quem erant facturae, comparatur cum strepitu currum super cacumine montium crepitantium & cum strepitu flammae consumentis stipulam, vel materiam combustibilem, & cum strepitu populi robusti ad praelium instructi.
units.tr: Footnotes: s) Sanctius. t) in the English Notes. u) Grotius: "Wherever there everything will blaze with fires." 66) chapter ... x) Schindler. ...and so the stronger and more robust creatures. And so the first place is then assigned to the horse, which a certain poet expresses in a special way among them: "swift horses have set their head and mouth against them," so that here, in the first clause, locusts are rightly to be compared with the face, appearance and genuine form of horses. To this may be added what others think, that the force of the likeness lies in their fierceness, boldness and insolence, as in Job 39:19 and so on. Next, in the following clause, they are compared again with respect to their fearless speed in advancing, in these words: "and as horsemen, so they will run." For it is the horse itself that runs, though urged on by the rider; and they will overturn everything before them with such speed that no one will oppose or check them. From this many think they can draw an irrefutable argument, namely that these words properly refer to locusts, not to the Chaldeans or the enemy, since they are said to be like horses and horsemen. For the enemy were in fact horsemen riding horses, and were not like them, either themselves or their horses. Some of those who understand the enemy, to explode this objection, say that the letter rendered in Greek as ὡς [ὡς] and in Latin as sicut is, for the most part, a particle of likeness, but here it is not placed parabolically [παραβολικῶς] to denote comparison or similarity, but, as often elsewhere, emphatically [ἐπιτατικῶς], as Theodoret does, to signify intensity; and that things are really as they are said to be. So by the words "their appearance is as the appearance of horses" he wishes to indicate that they really present the look of horses; and by the following words, "and as horsemen, so they will run," that they will show themselves as light-armed horsemen. Others indeed keep the comparative sense, but want it understood of the infantry of an army, so that they would appear as fierce as horses, and be as bold and swift as horsemen. "The infantry themselves were swifter," says Grotius. And Abarbanel, after relating a story that has nothing to do with the matter, thinks that since they are compared to centaurs, who are said to be half men and half horses, this is a jest about the shoulders here, and adds that it is not far from the truth that their faces were large and their limbs strong like horses, and that their infantry ran as fast as horsemen ride their horses. But Bochart rejects this with black charcoal, saying: "It is unwelcome and unheard of to compare infantry with cavalry"; and "who would say that the Assyrians were like horsemen, when they really were horsemen, in great numbers," as they are described elsewhere in Ezekiel 27:6, 12, 23, and chapter 26 verses 7, 10, 11, and Habakkuk 1:8 and so on? Yet another writer says in these words: "It is not surprising that warlike men are compared to noble horses, and infantry to horsemen, to indicate their strength and speed." As for me, I think it sufficiently clear that the comparison here is of locusts and similar insects with horses, which God used to carry out his judgments, although these creatures seem weak and are exposed to contempt, while horses are famous for great strength and ability. The comparison agrees no less with the following words, in which the other circumstances of their coming and their deeds are described: namely, the great tumult and noise they were going to make is compared with the noise of chariots crackling over the tops of mountains, with the noise of a flame consuming stubble or combustible material, and with the noise of a strong people drawn up for battle.

units.la: 5. Sicut strepitus Curruum super cacumina montium sa- liunt, sicut strepitus flamma ignis devorantis sti- pulam, sicut populus robustus instructus ad pra- elium.
units.tr: 5. As the noise of chariots leaping over the tops of mountains, as the noise of a flame of devouring fire consuming stubble, as a strong people drawn up for battle.

units.la: Verba כקול מרכבות על ראשי ההרים ירקרן Cekol Mirkavoth al-rosbe haharim yerakkedun, videntur duplici ratione posse construi, vel ita ut sonant, quod locustae salient (quae vox pro-pro
units.tr: The words Cekol Mirkavoth al-rosbe haharim yerakkedun seem able to be construed in two ways: either as they sound, that the locusts will leap over the tops of the mountains with such a noise as the leaping of chariots makes, a phrase that expresses the manner of their motion, or in the following way, which the words also allow:

units.la: b) Brentius.
units.tr: b) Brentius.

units.la: prie earum movendi rationem exprimit) super cacumina montium tali strepitu, qualem curruum saltatio edit, quare etiam a Junio & Tremellio sic reddita: Quasi strepitu curruum siper cacumina (vel cacuminibus) montium salient. Vt & Tigur. ante eos: Irruent strepitu quodam per cacumina montium, ut currus. Vel in hunc modum: sicut strepitus curruum, qui saltunt (vel quando saliunt) super cacu-mina montium, cum ellipsi, qua subintelligitur, vel qui, vel quando saliunt super cacumina montium, ita ut verba, saliunt super cacumina montium, quæ in priori sententia referuntur ad locustas, vel ad eos, qui hic cum curribus comparantur, in posteriori referantur ad currus, quibuscum comparantur. Posteriori ratione accipit ea Drufius & Syrus, quando reddit ... sicut vox currium, qui faciunt tumultum super cacumina montium. At prior ratio aliis interpretibus usitatior. Ita LXX. ὡς Φωνὴ ἀρμάτων ἐπὶ τὰς κορυφὰς τῶν ὀρέων ἐξαλλόντας, ut & impressa & MS. Arabica & Vulg. Lat. sicut sonitus quadrigarum super capita montium saliunt, & sic recentiores ferme omnes; in eo tamen differunt, utrum verba, super cacumina montium saliunt, ad locustas referenda sint, vel tantum saliunt ad eas; & cacumina montis ad currus. Mercerus quorundam d) Judæorum affirmat esse opinionem, omnia referenda esse ad locustas, quæ cacumina montis ascendunt, quo currus pertingere non possunt, ita ut quoad strepitum & saltum cum curribus conferantur, quia utrisque hoc proprium est; verum quod hoc facient in cacuminibus montium, id unum ad locustas pertinere. Ipse vero mediam harum ivit viam, qua ita distinguit verba, ut super cacumina montium jungat cum præcedentibus, sicut strepitus currum atque saliunt, referat ad locustas, quas tertia persona plurali vult, qua ratione verba ita fluunt: qualem strepitum currus super cacumina montium seciunt, talem faciunt locustæ saliendo (vel subtilibus). Quamvis enim in usu non fit, currus per talia loca trahi, attamen si traherentur, non est dubium, quin magnum strepitum sint edant.
units.tr: (…) with such a noise as the leaping of chariots makes. For this reason Junius and Tremellius render it thus: As with the noise of chariots they will leap over the (or the) tops of the mountains. So also the Tigurine version before them: They will rush with a certain noise over the tops of the mountains, like chariots. Or in this way: as the noise of chariots which leap (or when they leap) over the tops of the mountains, with an ellipsis, which is understood, either which or when they leap over the tops of the mountains, so that the words they leap over the tops of the mountains, which in the former sense refer to the locusts, or to those who are here compared with chariots, in the latter refer to the chariots with which they are compared. Drusius and the Syriac take it in the latter way, when they render it as the voice of chariots which make a tumult over the tops of the mountains. But the former interpretation is more common among other interpreters. So the LXX: like the voice of chariots leaping onto the summits of the mountains, as also the printed text, the Arabic manuscript and the Vulgate Latin: as the sound of chariots leap over the heads of the mountains, and almost all more recent writers likewise. They differ, however, over whether the words leap over the tops of the mountains are to be referred to the locusts, or only leap is referred to them, and the tops of the mountain to the chariots. Mercer affirms that it is the opinion of certain d) Jews that everything is to be referred to the locusts, who climb the tops of the mountains, where chariots cannot reach, so that they are compared with chariots as to noise and leaping, since both have this in common; but that they will do this on the tops of the mountains alone pertains to the locusts. He himself took a middle way, distinguishing the words so that over the tops of the mountains is joined with what precedes, as the noise of chariots, and they leap is referred to the locusts, whom he takes in the third person plural; in this way the words flow thus: the noise which chariots make over the tops of the mountains, such noise the locusts make by leaping (or by their slender bodies). For although it is not customary to drag chariots over such places, nevertheless, if they were dragged, there is no doubt they would make a great noise.

units.la: {d} Ita Abu-Ezra, Kimchi & Christianorum quidam: Qualem strepitum in brevi tempore edunt currus saltantis, talem saltant ceteri super cacumina montium salientes. Lysed. editurí,atque in eo vertitur similitudinis cardo. Verum enim vero, quæcunque fit disceptatio interpretum de horum verborum conftructione,id sane non scopo nec sententiæ nostræ quicquam præjudicat, contineri his verbis similitudinem ad exprimendum horridum strepitum, quem prædicti, qualescunq; etiam sint, adventu suo sunt editurí, & ad notandum terrorem, quo corriperetur populus earum tam terribilem ingressum videns. Quem autem strepitum locuftæ soleant facere ubi sunt,ex eo cognosci potest, quod Remigius ex illis, quorum territoria per eas infestari solent,refert,earum tantum esse strepitum, ut a sexto milliari audiri possit sonitus earum. At sufficiet ad horum verborum illuftrationem,cum de locustis fumuntur, unum addidisse ejusdem fere tenoris locum Apoc. 9,9. ubi de locuftis ibi nominatis dicitur, sonitus alarum ipsarum fuisse sicut sonitus curruum,equis multis currentibus ad prælium. Ex quo utroque loco conjuncto luculenter apparet, proprie hic respici ad locustas veras,& non inusitatam atque insolitam fuisse comparationem inter strepitum locustarum, quem motu suo concitant,& equorum conculcationem curruumque saltum, qui ingens esse solet. Hanc excipit alia comparatio in verbis sequentibus, qua formidabilis illarum strepitus, quem concitabunt, exprimitur, sicut strepitus flammæ ignis devorantis stipulam, talis e) strepitus, qualem ciet stipula igne adusta, quæ, quam crepitantem edat strepitum, nemini ignotum esse potest. Quando enim f) combustibilia,ut sunt stipula & lignorum detrimenta,injiciuntur igni,magnus exinde oritur strepitus. Cum hac expreffionis formula concidit, quod dicitur Eccles. 7,6. Ut crepitus spinarum sub olla &c. Priore in comparatione strepitus videtur existere ex illarum motu, saltu vel alarum reniigio; hic vero procul dubio ex illarum manducatione ac esu. Ita videtur hoc intellexisse Cyrillus, cum dicat: Ferunt, eas campos nunquam irruere fine strepitu,g) qualem quoque haud mediocrem edere solent dentibus suis arrodentes frumentum ante fe abactum & dejectum,non secus ac ventus abigit ignis flam-
units.tr: {d} So Abu-Ezra, Kimchi and certain Christians: The noise which chariots leaping make in a short time, such the others leap, leaping over the tops of the mountains. The hinge of the comparison turns on this. But whatever dispute there is among the interpreters over the construction of these words, it certainly does not prejudice our purpose or our meaning in any way: these words contain a comparison to express the dreadful noise which the aforesaid creatures, whatever they are, will make at their coming, and to note the terror which would seize the people who saw their so terrible entry. What noise locusts usually make where they are can be known from what Remigius reports from those whose territories are commonly harassed by them, that the noise of locusts is so great that their sound can be heard from six miles away. But it will suffice for the illustration of these words, since locusts are in view, to add one passage of almost the same tenor, Rev. 9:9, where of the locusts named there it is said that the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots, of many horses running to battle. From these two passages taken together it clearly appears that locusts themselves are properly meant here, and that the comparison between the noise of the locusts, which they stir up by their motion, and the trampling of horses and the leaping of chariots, which is usually great, was not an unusual or strange one. Another comparison follows in the words after this, by which the dreadful noise they will raise is expressed: as the noise of a flame of fire devouring stubble, such e) a noise as stubble makes when it is burnt by fire, whose crackling noise is known to everyone. For when f) combustible materials, such as stubble and the refuse of wood, are thrown into the fire, a great noise arises from it. With this figure of speech agrees what is said at Eccles. 7:6, Like the crackling of thorns under a pot, etc. In the former comparison the noise seems to arise from their motion, leaping or the rowing of their wings; here, without doubt, from their eating and consuming. So Cyril seems to have understood it, when he says: They say that they never rush over fields without a noise, such as they usually make no small amount of when they gnaw with their teeth the grain driven and cast down before them, just as the wind drives the flame of fire.

units.la: e) Drufius. f) Kimchi. g) ἀλλ' βλπχέαι, quia voce simul denotatur imbecillis & fortis; at magis conveniens videtur huic loco posterior significatio,Bochartus tamen reddit eam tenuem, at alii,non tenuem. flammam. Et Mercerus: qualis est strepitus flammæ ignis confumentis quæq; combustibilia, talis est & ejus plantas (vel res alimenta præbentes) erodentis strepitus. Et Pet. a Fig. Devorantium Locustarum strepitum declarat, b) magno strepitu volant, & in agros decidunt, & segetes dentibus commolunt. Atque sic idem hæc verba cum iis, quæ v. 4. exposuimus, ex mente illorum denotare dicenda sunt, qui & ibi locustas cum igne conferri statuunt. Hinc ex utroque hoc loco non difficile inferre possis, comprehendi ibi omnino locustas ac cum illis cætera hæc infecta sub nomine magni & ferocis populi (v. 2.) secum ferentis ignem, mœstissimosque eius effectus ubicumque edentis. Tertia comparatio continetur his verbis: sicut populus robustus ad prœlium. Ad ea connectenda cum præcedentibus i) quidam subintelligi volunt, repetique, vel ירקדון jerakkedun, saliunt ut; vel קול kol, strepitus, ut strepitus robusti populi. Atque ita erit populi hujus strepitus. Ubi posteriorem similitudinis partem inferri putant ex priori, quæ duntaxat exprimitur, idque consuetudinem communem esse eorum, qui ita sunt ordinati ad invadendum regnum. Sustollunt incomditum & trucem clamorem, quo injiciant populo terrorem, ut exponit hoc Kimchi verba hac ratione accipiens. Attamen k) aliis videtur satis, subintelligere, sunt sicut &c. est ut populus validus ad pugnandum instructus; ac si a descriptione strepitus quem edunt, transeunt ad ordinem, quo procederent opera sua exequentes. Digna hic est observatione diversitas hujus formulæ a præcedenti v. 2. ubi vocantur magnus & robustus populus; hic vero sicut robustus populus. Quod argumento est, eas priori loco vocari populum l) non proprie, sed figurate, quia simili modo, vel sicut populus sese exhibet, ita & hæ hoc vel illo modo sese sunt exhibituræ, ut idcirco illius nomine inferito vocentur; id quod non leve indicium videtur, nec m) Babylonios hic indigitari, nec alios ullos, inimico odio terram invasuros, sed revera locustas & hujusmodi vermiculos, qui a Deo immittebantur exsecuturi sua super eos judicia. Etenim hoc usu venire sunt, ut ad amplificandum minora atque extollendum ea cum majoribus conferanb) Bochart. i) Drufius. l) Bochart. l) Bochart. m) Pet. a Fig. {ter}tur, non contra majora cum minoribus, vel diminuendi ac vilipendendi causa ac in hujusmodi rebus, quibus ea antecedunt, quamvis in aliis multo sint iis inferiora. Quod in iis imitari. Quamus verba sunt &c. ratio, cur hic dicantur sicut populus robustus ad praelium, videtur esse rillarum numerus & vis inferendi damnum: numero sint sicut populus, ut ac potentia robustus, quales cognitas habemus telle experientia; o) quid locustae memorabilis & fortis quibus hoc unam incoraret reffere non possit? Ita Cyrillus de illis dicit, esse rem edacem & ... sed propter imminentem cupiam non facile expugnabilem, vel potius oppugnari difficilem, & illarum irruptionem esse ... rem in expugnabilem & hostibus ...
units.tr: e) Drusius. f) Kimchi. g) ἀλλ' βλπχέαι [the Greek as printed], because the word denotes at once what is weak and what is strong; but the latter meaning seems more fitting to this place. Bochart, however, renders it thin, while others render it not thin. And Mercer: as the noise of a flame of fire consuming whatever is combustible, so is the noise of the locusts devouring its plants (or the things that provide food). And Pet. a Fig. declares the noise of devouring locusts: they fly with a great noise, fall upon the fields, and grind the crops with their teeth. And so these words, together with those we explained at v. 4, are to be said to denote the same thing, in the mind of those who hold that locusts are compared with fire in that place as well. Hence from both passages one may easily infer that here are comprehended altogether the locusts, and with them these other pests, under the name of the great and fierce people (v. 2) bearing fire with them, and wherever they go producing the most sorrowful effects. A third comparison is contained in the words: as a strong people drawn up for battle. Some wish to supply, in connecting these with what precedes, either yerakkedun, they leap as, or kol, noise, as the noise of a strong people. And so it will be the noise of this people. They think the second part of the comparison is to be inferred from the first, which alone is expressed, and that this is the common custom of those who are thus arranged to invade a kingdom: they raise a disorderly and fierce shout, by which they strike terror into the people, as Kimchi explains these words in this sense.
