Yet k) to others it seems enough to supply: they are as etc.; it is as a strong people equipped for fighting; as if from the description of the noise they make they pass to the order in which they would advance in carrying out their work. A difference of this phrase from the preceding one in v. 2 is worth noting here, where they are called a great and strong people; here, however, as a strong people. This is an argument that in the former place they are called a people l) not properly but figuratively, because in a similar way, or as a people presents itself, so these will present themselves in this or that way, and therefore are called by its name; which seems no slight indication that neither the Babylonians are here indicated, nor any others who would invade the land with hostile hatred, but really locusts and such small worms, which were sent by God to execute his judgments upon them. For it is customary to compare smaller things with greater ones to magnify and exalt the former, not the reverse, nor to diminish or belittle; and in such matters the smaller ones precede, although in other respects they are far inferior to them. The reason why they are said to be like a strong people drawn up for battle seems to be their number and their power of inflicting harm: in number they are like a people, and strong in power, as we know from experience; what memorable and strong creature could they not overcome, which would hinder them with a single wall? So Cyril says of them that they are a devouring thing and ... but on account of the imminent danger not easily conquered, or rather difficult to overcome, and their irruption is ... an unconquerable thing and for enemies ...

units.la: i Illarum ordo ac pertinacia in progrediendo & rebus gerendis, cum addat sicut robustus populus, quo cum ea conserit, ad praelium instructus. Milites disciplina cultu quacunque esse offerat occasio, loca sua constanter tenere ordinesque servare solent. Quibus cum quando eas creaturas conserit de quibus hic loquitur, quid aliud in iis tenuiter, quod ordinem in suum aeque constanter in motibus suis servare sciant? Quem quam accurate servare soleant, ex eo patet, quod de iis legimus p) Prov. 30, 26. (ex translat. nostrat.) omnes procedunt turmatim; & evidentius Graec. praedunt tanquam ad praelium instructi ευτακτως, bono ordine, & Arab. impressa, ... ordine. q) Alii observant eas fixe locum suum tenere volantes ordine quadrato, lapidum instar in pavimento tessellato, nulla stationem suam unquam linquente vel mutante. Ita S. Hieronymus qui id oculis se vidisse affirmat. Pari ratione apud ... & Cyril invenies, earum ordinem tam stabilem esse, ut nulla unquam ratione eum intertubari sinant. Nec in contrariu quid afferunt r) Arabes, quibus ex maxime sunt notae, quia uno ore confitentur, eas sese in unum corpus compingere ... R 2 ut
units.tr: i Their order and persistence in advancing and carrying out their tasks is such that, when the text adds "like a strong people," it compares them to a people drawn up for battle with the enemy with whom they engage. Soldiers who are well trained and disciplined, whenever the occasion offers, usually keep their places steadily and maintain their ranks. When this text compares them to those creatures of which it speaks, what else is it saying about them, except that they know how to keep their order just as steadily in their movements? How carefully they usually keep it is clear from what we read of them in p) Prov. 30:26 (from our translation): "they all go forth by bands"; and more clearly the Greek has "they march as if drawn up for battle," in good order [εὐτάκτως], and the printed Arabic has "in order." q) Others observe that they hold their places fixed while flying, in square order, like stones in a tessellated pavement, never leaving or changing their station. So St. Jerome, who affirms that he saw this with his own eyes. In the same way you will find in ... and Cyril that their order is so stable that they never allow it to be broken in any way. Nor do the r) Arabs, who are very well acquainted with them, bring anything to the contrary, since they all agree that they fit themselves together into one body ... R 2 ut

units.la: z) Ut ... m ... exercitus con ruuntur cum loc suis ratione numeri, Bochart. part. post. p. 467. o) Hieron. c. 1. v. 6. p) Procul ari modo hunc locum interpretatur Bochart. quem vide part. post. p. 459. q) Vide Bochartum. r) Alii ... ut exercitum,in quo, priore ac duce se movente, caeterae se movent, & e contrario omnes resident, eadem residente; quare illarum gregem appellant s) מנדהם Mandhum, quae rem significat in ordine collocata; quippe tam exacte se in ordine posse redigere ac eum servare tradunt, ut militaris disciplinae videantur gnarae ac non secus eum, quam optimi strenuissimiq; milites, observare. Hoc respectu apta satis videtur comparatio, quae petitur a militibus ad praelium instructis. Quod si talem etiam cum aliis statuimus eas inferre strepitum, qualem milites inferunt, ad amplificandum adventus illarum terrorem id fieri constat. Horrenda certe res visu atque auditu esse debebat, quam tot circumstantiae, atque hic praedicuntur, erant comitaturae. Qua quam graviter populus necessario afficeretur, sequentibus tradit in verbis.
units.tr: z) As ... m ... an army is drawn up with its ranks in order of number, Bochart, part. post. p. 467. o) Jerome on chapter 1, verse 6. p) Bochart interprets this place very differently; see his part. post. p. 459. q) See Bochart. r) Others ... as an army, in which, when the leader moves first, the rest move, and conversely all halt when it halts; for this reason they call their flock Mandhum [מנדהם], which signifies things placed in order. They report that they can bring themselves into order and keep it so exactly that they seem skilled in military discipline and observe it no less than the best and most vigorous soldiers. In this respect the comparison drawn from soldiers drawn up for battle seems apt enough. But if we also hold that they make a noise such as soldiers make, it is agreed that this is done to heighten the terror of their coming. Surely the sight and sound of the thing must have been dreadful, which so many circumstances, and those predicted here, were to accompany. How heavily the people would necessarily be affected by it, the following words tell us.

units.la: 6. A conspectu eorum populus multum dolebit: omnes facies contrahent nigrorem.
units.tr: 6. At the sight of them the people will greatly grieve; all faces will gather blackness.

units.la: מִפָּנָיו Mippanau, a conspectu ejus, i. e. vere in oculis illius, vel ut Vatablus, prae metu ejus, scilicet adventus, populus יַחִילוּ yachilu, multum dolebit tanto nimirum t) dolore, quanto puerpera partus tempore. Vox enim, quamvis latiore significatione sumatur, ut plurimum tamen ei designando adhibetur dolori; quare, sicubi alio in loco usurpatur, non communes denotat dolores, sed horrendos, quibus ferendis vix pares sunt, qui eis premuntur. Quo factum, ut nostrates, ad pondus addendum significationi, vocula adjiciant multum, ac si eam necessario in se complecteretur verbi denotatio. Alii tamen eam tam plene atque expresse non exprimunt uno verbo generalioris significationis contenti, ut u) dolebunt, w) cruciabuntur, x) horrent, (vel y) contremiscunt.)
units.tr: מִפָּנָיו Mippanau, [from before him] i.e. truly before his eyes, or as Vatablus has it, from fear of him, namely of the coming, the people יַחִילוּ yachilu [will writhe] will grieve greatly, with a grief surely as great as a woman in labour feels at the time of birth. For the word, though taken in a wider sense, is for the most part used to denote that pain; so wherever it is used in another place it signifies not ordinary pains but dreadful ones, which those who are oppressed by them can scarcely bear. Hence our people add the little word greatly to add weight to the sense, as if the meaning of the verb necessarily included it. Others, however, do not express it so fully and clearly, content with a verb of more general meaning, such as u) will grieve, w) will be tormented, x) will shudder (or y) will tremble).

units.la: Quantum vero dolerent & quam graviter animo turbarentur, ex vultibus eorum pateret. Hinc addit: omnes facies contrahent nigrorem, vel ut in margine, ollam, quam propriam quidam statuunt signi-
units.tr: How greatly they would grieve, and how sorely they would be troubled in mind, would be plain from their faces. Hence he adds: all faces will gather blackness, or, as in the margin, a pot, which some take as the proper

units.la: {s} Kamus, ut & in Asap. t) Druf. Tarnov. u) Jun. Trem. ✠ LXX. x) Chald. y) Merc. Verbo Chald. ordinar. Syr. Bochart. significationem vocis פארור Parur, ac si eadem esset cum פרור Parur, sine litera ע, 4, quæ occurrit Num. 11, 8. ubi a nostratibus redditur, patina, ab aliis χύτρα, & ς.) olla vel lacabus, omnibus vas tale esse unanimi sententia consentibus, quo igni coquenda admoventur, pro quo cum accipitur, ad literam vertitur olla. Ita Vulgatus: redigentur in ollam; qua quid innuatur, per se manifestum est, & ab aliis in genere dictum, futuros esse colore a) ut ollas. Sic & Duac. qui ad literam fere exprimunt versionem Latinam, addunt similitudinis particulam in hoc loco: omnes facies fient sicut olla. LXX. πᾶν πρόσωπον ὡς πρόσκαυμα χύτρας, & Arab. impressa vestigiis eorum insistens quslibet facies est (vel erit) sicut adustio vel nigredo ollæ. Pari modo MS. Arab. omnes facies contraxerunt nigredinem ollæ. Chaldæus, omnes facies coopertæ sunt אכרומים כקדירא, fuligine atra ut olla. Syrus & omnis facies erit nigra sicut nigredo ollæ. In aprico est hos omnes pariter sentire, defumtam esse hanc comparationem hic a colore ollæ, non a materia vel metallo ejus, licet ejus cum facie comparatio alibi extet, ut Esa. 48,4. Supercilium eorum erat æneum; sed hic alio modo comparatum est. Unde factum est, ut, quotquot translationes inspeximus, æque omnes, nec recentioribus exclusis oculos non adeo intenderint ad ollam, quam ad ejus colorem, nostratesque reddiderint, nigrorem, præterquam quod ullam ollæ mentionem faciant, quam vox proprie denotat. Sic b) quidam tantum habent, nigredinem vel nigrorem. c) Alii luridum ollæ colorem. Alii d) pallorem, quam interpretationem omnibus aliis præfert Doctissimus Leusdenus, ut maxime huic loco convenientem, quamvis negari non possit vocem proprie denotare nigredinem; atque in eo Mercero accedere videtur, qui id explicat nigricantem pallorem. Omnium vero huc redit mens ac sententia, hac exprimendi formula innui hujusmodi faciei ac vultus alterationem, qua afficimur metu magno corre-
units.tr: {s} Kamus, as also in Asaph. t) Drusius, Tarnovius. u) Junius, Tremellius. ✠ LXX. x) Chaldee. y) Mercerus. In the Chaldee lexicon ordinarily, Syriac, Bochart: the meaning of the word פארור Parur, as if it were the same as פרור Parur, without the letter ע, which occurs in Num. 11:8, where our people render it pan, others χύτρα, and the sense is a pot or cauldron, all agreeing unanimously that it is a vessel in which things are put to be cooked over fire; and taken in that sense it is rendered literally "a pot." So the Vulgate: "they shall be brought to a pot"; what is meant by this is plain in itself, and others have said in general that they will become of colour like pots. So also the Douay, who render the Latin version almost word for word, add the particle of comparison here: "all faces shall become like a pot." The LXX: "every face as the burning of a pot," and the printed Arabic, following their footsteps: every face is (or will be) like the scorching or blackness of a pot. In the same way the manuscript Arabic: all faces have contracted the blackness of a pot. The Chaldee: all faces are covered with black soot like a pot. The Syriac: every face will be black like the blackness of a pot. It is clear that all these are of one mind, that this comparison is drawn here from the colour of a pot, not from its material or metal, although a comparison of the face with that is found elsewhere, as Isa. 48:4, "Their forehead was brass"; but here it is put in another way. Hence it happens that all the translations we have examined, even the more recent ones not excluded, have not fixed their eyes so much on the pot as on its colour, and our people have rendered it blackness, except that they make some mention of the pot, which the word properly denotes. So b) some have only blackness or darkness. c) Others the livid colour of a pot. Others d) pallor, an interpretation which the most learned Leusden prefers to all others as most suited to this place, although it cannot be denied that the word properly denotes blackness; and in this Mercerus seems to agree, who explains it as a blackish pallor. But the mind and meaning of all comes to this: that by this form of expression is signified an alteration of face and countenance such as we suffer when seized with great fear

units.la: z) Et Jud. 6,19. 1. Sam. 1,14. a) Kimchi. b) Jun. Trem. c) Tig. d) Calv. correpti atque perturbatione, cujus signum ca[?]le [?]. Nec longe abit ab hac mente interpretatio alia, quae huic prorsus contraria est eorum, qui nomen Parur dicunt non significare nigredinem, sed pulchritudinem, (tam hoc loco, quam Nahum 2, ubi eadem expressionis formula occurrit) a פאר, elegantia, nitor (per geminationem tertiae radicalis) ita ut oratio sit: Omnes fuerunt recolligerunt, retraxerunt, vel contraxerunt suam pulchritudinem. Nec abhorrent ab hac interpretandi ratione quidam non vulgaris notae Judaeorum, ut Abu-Walid & R. Tanchum reddentes Arabice e) recolligerunt vel contraxerunt suam pulchritudinem. Atque ita affixum respiciunt tanquam limitellectum nomine. Eandem etiam significationem putat habere hoc nomen Aben-Ezra, quam Peer, pulchritudo vel decus, & verbum de notare aliquid שיתקבץ quod contrahit vel colligit se ipsum, contrarium est יתפשט yitpashet, quod de re dicitur, quae se ipsum aperit atque denudat. Cui illustrandae adferunt, quod dicitur Lujus cap. & cap. 3, 15. & stellae retrahent suum splendorem; attendentes praecipue verbo אסף Asaph, & קבץ Kibats, qua utrumque significat non tantum colligere, congregare, sed & recipere, vel retraxit. Excipit vero contra hanc interpretationem Kimchi Parens, eamque minus propriam esse dicit, ut refert ejus filius, eo quod sua sententia verbum קבץ Kibats non sit ultimatum significatione congregandi in unum, vel recolligendi, quod jamjam praesens est, ut אסף Asaph; sed colligendi, quod disperium est vel non praesens. Quicquid vero subtilitatis horum verborum distincta significationi inesse putet, Rab. Tanchum tamen, cum utramque verborum significationem inter se confert, poteriorem, scil. quod reddunt recolligent vel recuperent suam pulchritudinem, & priorem quae reddunt, colligunt nigrorem vel pallorem, hanc dicit 1. e. conficere meliorem & planiorem sensum. quidem quod ad sensum attinet, quamvis ad literam diverse ...
units.tr: z) And Judg. 6:19; 1 Sam. 1:14. a) Kimchi. b) Junius, Tremellius. c) Tigurinus. d) Calvin. struck and disturbed, of which the sign is ... Nor is another interpretation far removed from this view, one quite contrary to it, of those who say that the name Parur does not signify blackness but beauty (both in this place and in Nahum 2, where the same form of expression occurs), from פאר, elegance, lustre (by doubling of the third radical), so that the sentence is: All of them have gathered in, drawn back, or contracted their beauty. Nor do some Jews of no ordinary note shrink from this way of interpreting, such as Abu-Walid and R. Tanchum, who render in Arabic they gathered in or contracted their beauty. And so they regard the suffix as a limitation of the noun. Ibn Ezra also thinks this word has the same meaning, namely Peer, beauty or glory, and the verb signifying something that contracts or gathers itself in, is the opposite of יתפשט yitpashet, which is said of a thing that opens and bares itself. To illustrate this they cite what is said in Joel 2:10 and 3:15, "the stars withdraw their brightness," paying particular attention to the verbs אסף Asaph and קבץ Kibats, each of which means not only to gather, to assemble but also to receive back or withdraw. Kimchi the Father, however, objects to this interpretation and says it is less proper, as his son reports, because in his view the verb קבץ Kibats does not carry the ultimate sense of gathering into one or gathering again, which is already present, as אסף Asaph does, but of gathering which is lost or not present. But whatever subtlety of distinct meaning he thinks inheres in these words, Rabbi Tanchum, when he compares the two senses of the verbs with each other, says that the latter, namely the rendering they will gather again or recover their beauty, and the former, which renders they gather blackness or pallor, i.e. make a better and plainer sense. Indeed, as far as the sense is concerned, although in the letter they are different ...

units.la: e) i. e. legitimus ... opponitur ... Bafats ... contrariε sibi invicem vilentur interpretationes, hoc tamen affirmare habeo. æque omnes harmonia elegantissima sibi invicem congruere, cum innuat ingentem vultus mutationem ac alterationem, quæ forma, qua erant prædita, est contraria, diversiqne nihil habet, sive facie dicas perdidisse pulchritudinem suam, sive collegisse pallorem vel rubrorem, cum uno remoto alterum in ejus locum succedat necesse sit. Ad nostrates quod attinet, eorum expositionem opinione atque autoritate plerorumque interpretum confirmatam videmus.
units.tr: e) That is, legitimate ... is opposed ... Bafats ... The interpretations seem to contradict one another, but I must affirm this: all of them agree very well with one another, since they all point to a huge change and alteration of countenance, contrary to the beauty they had. It makes no difference whether you say they lost their beauty or took on paleness or redness, since when one is removed the other must necessarily take its place. As for our own countrymen, we see their explanation confirmed by the opinion and authority of most interpreters.

units.la: Hinc ex præteritis satis superque patet ubi terribilis eorum adventus, qui a DEO erant missi ad exequendum sua judicia, describitur, quam justa esset incolis pavendi causa, & quam merito pavoris illius deberent edere signa & effectus. Idem ulterius amplificatur in quibusdam sequentibus versibus, ubi res eorum horrendæ, quibus gerendis irruentes operam darent, dilucide traduntur, ut v. 7.
units.tr: From what has gone before, it is clear enough, and more than enough, where the terrible coming of those who were sent by God to carry out his judgments is described, and how just a cause for fear this would be to the inhabitants, and how rightly they ought to show the signs and effects of that dread. The same point is developed further in some of the following verses, where their dreadful deeds, which they would rush in to perform, are clearly set out, as in verse 7.

units.la: 7. Current sicut potentes, scandent vallum ut bellato- res, & quisque procedet per vias suas & non per- vertet semitas suas.
units.tr: 7. They shall run like mighty men, they shall climb the wall like men of war, and each shall march in his own ways and not break their paths.

units.la: Current sicut potentes] i. e. procedent audacter, expedite ac constanter, nil reformidantes, nec transversum unguem a via decedentes. Qua expressione cursus innuit constantem ac indefessigatam processionem ex Psal. 19, 5. manifestum est, ubi sol dicitur, lætatur ut gigas ad currendam viam. Eadem vox est in utroque loco, nimirum גבור Gibbor, numeri singularis ibi, hic vero pluralis gibborim, quæ virum potentem ac robustum denotat, & a quibusdam ubique reddita per gigantes, quo nomine hujus generis ac conditionis hominnes plerumque venire solent. Idem in utroque loco est etiam verbum רוץ, ruts, sese mutuo currere, quod si fortitudinem juvenum ac velocitatem infert. Nec ullum dubium est, quin hac descriptione describetur, eos nunc suam h) strenue obituros, quod ulterius etiam appareat ex versu additis scandent vallum ut bellatores, non
units.tr: They shall run like mighty men: that is, they will advance boldly, nimbly and steadily, fearing nothing and not turning aside a finger's breadth from their way. By this expression of running is signified a steady and unwearied advance, as in Psalm 19:5, where the sun is said to rejoice like a giant to run its course. It is the same word in both places, namely גבור gibbor, singular there, but plural gibborim here, which denotes a powerful and robust man; and it is sometimes rendered everywhere as "giants," a name by which men of this kind and condition are usually called. In both places the verb is also the same, רוץ ruts, to run to one another, which implies the strength and swiftness of young men. And there is no doubt that by this description it is meant that they will now strenuously rush to their death, which further appears from the added words, they shall climb the wall like men of war, not

units.la: g) Cadmea ea enim cum fortitudine velocitas. Rib. Tarnov. h) Merc.
units.tr: g) For speed goes with strength. Rib. Tarnov. h) Merc.

units.la: non a cursu suo ac proposito ab aliqua re prohiberi fe sinent, nec valla munitissima quid ab iis immune reddent. Quæ ipsis occurrent, ὅιωε ἀμεὶνως κὰι δειμάτων ὑπαρχόσαι (ut ait Cyrillus) terroribus & pigritia superiores super ea fe tollent, quasi audacem irruptionem meditantes,ita ut 1) horti fepimento circumdati,æque illorum destructioni fuerint subjecti,quam campi patentes. Quo progressu, inquit, quisque procedet per vias suas & non pervertet semitas suas; non erit,quod illorum cursum vel impediat vel immutet, sed eo incedent ordine,quo ad aciem instructi, ut infra ex �r. videre est, ubi,quod dictum est,optime conspirat cum his verbis, ex nostrat. interpretatione, quisque procedet per vias suas. Secundum Vulgat. Viri in vijs suis gradientur; cui accedunt Duacens. the men shall march in their ways; quod perperam putat factum Ribera culpa librariorum,qui numero plurali expressum advertentes verbum, gradientur,nomen quoque plurali numero censuere exprimendum,ponendumq; esse viri loco,vir,quod ad literam respondet hebraic. איש ish, quod revera quidem denotat virum; at tali modo constructum idem valet ac singvli, ita ut k) verbum plurali numero proferatur necesse fit,quamvis nominis singulare retineatur, quo illorum,qui singulī multi erant, quisque sic fecisse intelligendus sit. Quisque eorum tam firmo ordine erat processurus per suam viam, ut peracto itinere nullus eam aliquo modo pervertisse dici posset,quocirca addit: Et non pervertent semitas suas. Quæ verba licet ex interpretatione nostrat. satis clara sint,nec dubius hæream,quin optime exprimant textus hebraici genuinam mentem; attamen cum multum inter se distent aliorum interpretationes, quod attinet ad literalem sensum vocis,quam nostrat. reddidere,pervertent, operæ pretium duxi mus eas paululum expendere, ut, qua ratione altera cum altera, omnesque denique cum Originali textu, quem exprimere omni nitu conantur, possint conciliari, cuivis sit perspicuum ac clarum. Verbum hebraic. est יעבטן yeabbetun, de quo l) R. Sal. Jarchi & m
units.tr: not allowing themselves to be held back from their course and purpose by anything, nor will the strongest walls make them immune from anything. Whatever stands in their way, (as Cyril puts it) being superior to terrors and sloth [ὅιωε ἀμεὶνως κὰι δειμάτων ὑπαρχόσαι], will raise themselves above it, as if planning a bold assault, so that, surrounded by a garden fence, they will be as subject to their destruction as open fields. By this advance, he says, each shall march in his own ways and not break their paths: there will be nothing to hinder or alter their course, but they will proceed in the order in which they are drawn up for battle, as may be seen below from the text, where what has been said agrees well with these words in our own translation, each shall march in his own ways. According to the Vulgate, men shall walk in their ways, to which is added the Douay version, the men shall march in their ways; Ribera wrongly thinks this arose through the fault of copyists, who, noticing that the verb shall walk was expressed in the plural, judged that the noun too should be expressed in the plural and that men should stand in place of man, which corresponds literally to the Hebrew איש [ish]. This word does indeed denote a man, but when constructed in this way it has the same force as each, so that the verb must be put in the plural, although the noun keeps its singular form; by this it is to be understood that each of them, who were many individually, did so. Each of them was to advance in such a firm order along his own way that, when the march was complete, no one could be said to have deviated from it in any way. Hence he adds: and they shall not break their paths. Although these words are clear enough in our translation, and I have no doubt that they express the true meaning of the Hebrew text well, nevertheless, since the interpretations of others differ greatly as regards the literal sense of the word our translators rendered break, I have thought it worth while to weigh them a little, so that it may be plain to anyone how they can be reconciled with one another, and finally with the original text, which they all strive with every effort to express. The Hebrew word is יעבטן [yeabbetun], on which 1) R. Sal. Jarchi and m

units.la: i) Pet. a Fig. k) Quod in latina lingua etiam usu venit. l) ... on est ei simile. m) ... nec soolum habet in Scriptura. Kimchi notat, in sacris literis alibi hoc sensu non inveniri, unde accuratius enucleare necesse est, quo sensu hoc loco usurpetur, quaque interpretes maxime nitantur ratione. Quem in finem hanc potissimum approbant viam id rite expediendi Grammatici Hebræorum. Primo ut ad cognitam usitatamque reducatur significationem radicis עבט Abat, aliquid dare vel accipere pignori vel depositi loco, quæ res vocatur עבוט Abot, & quia res hoc pacto tradita tamdiu retinetur ac in possessione manet, donec redimatur ab eo, qui eam oppigneravit, eo ipso accipere verbum עבט Ibbet signicationem, impedivit, inhibuit, vel tardavit & moratus est.
units.tr: i) Pet. a Fig. k) This also happens in the Latin language. l) ... is not like it. m) ... nor is it found only in Scripture. Kimchi notes that in the sacred writings it is not found elsewhere in this sense, so it is necessary to explain more exactly in what sense it is used here, and on what grounds the interpreters chiefly rely. To this end the Hebrew grammarians especially commend this way of rightly working it out. First, it should be traced back to the known and common meaning of the root עבט [Abat], to give something, or to take as a pledge, or in place of a deposit; such a thing is called עבוט [Abot]. Because a thing handed over in this way is kept for so long, and remains in possession until it is redeemed by the one who pledged it, the verb עבט [Ibbet] by that very fact takes the meaning to hinder, to restrain, or to delay and detain.

units.la: Quo respexit Paraphrastes Chaldaicus, quando reddit ולא־ נלאחת מעכבין ארחתהן nec morantur vias suas, vel moram faciunt in viis suis. Ad cujus se auctoritatem etiam quidam alii contulerunt, in quibus Abu Walid לא יעכבון non retardant se ipsos, vel moram faciunt in vias suas, quem interpretandi modum notat tum R. Tanchum, tum R. Kimchi, (etsi alios etiam notare non desinunt) quamque interpretationis rationem hujus verbi adduximus, R. Tanchum tradit his verbis משרק מן לעבוט עבוטי והו ארהן לאן ארהין מחביס מעאק עלי קימורי פכאכורי Deducitur ab abot (in leabot aboto Deut. 24, 10.) quod significat depositum (vel pignus) quatenus quod pignori datum est (vel in depositum traditum) reprimitur & inhibetur pro eo valore, quo redimendum est (vel donec pretium, quo oppigneratum est, solutum fit). Hinc evidentissimum censent, radicem continere significationem impediendi, impedimendi vel detinendi, qua non tantum a Chaldæo, sed & aliquibus recentioribus accipitur, ut a Pagnin. neque retardabunt itinera sua, & Munster nec tardi erunt in semitis suis, & in nostra translatione Anglicana antiquiore, qua communiter olim utebantur, and they shall not linger in their paths; & in ea, quæ ex Genevensi confecta est, and they shall not stay in their paths. 2. Sunt qui hac significatione quidem verbum admittunt, at non eodem, quo jam adduximus, usurpari contendunt respectu, sed longe alio, nimirum quatenus depositio dato res mutuo sumitur & per mutuum fœnus ab alio ad alium transfertur, ac si sonarent, Kimchio auctore in libro radicum, ויאמר ישאיל ... & non commodabunt viam suam alius alii, ut recte haec verba interpretatur Mercerus; perperam vero quidam n) alii, ut Vatablus notat: non interrogabunt ipse ab illo de semitis suis, quasi vel tantillum temporis non essent subsituri ut mutarentur viam ab alio. Gemina ratione, qua denotat mutuare vel commodare, videtur etiam recepisse MS. Arabicum, reddens & quisque procedet in sua via, & non dabunt (vel accipient) mutuo suas ipsorum vias, i. e. non recedent a suis viis, vel communicabunt eam alii aliis, sed quilibet suam ipsius constanter observabit. Quo pacto si verba recipiantur, elegantem expressionem ea complecti censet Doctus quidam o) Commentator, qua innuitur, quod non permutent inter se, vel non mutuent vias suas unus alteri, sed quod quilibet suam servet, ac cum tueatur locum, quem primo occupabat. 3. Non desunt qui secus plane hoc verbum accipiunt, non quatenus significat oppugnavit, sed quatenus idem valet quod עיר Iwet (quocum sono convenit literis mutatis) nimirum pervertit, curvum reddidit, vel obliquavit, quo sensu & in lingua Ilmaelitica usitatum esse Aben-Ezra & Kimchi auctores sunt. At recte p) Doctissimo L. de Dieu observatum, lexicographos Arabes hanc significationem verbi non dare, quomodocunque suo tempore ita usitatum invenerit Aben-Ezra, quamvis etiam negari non posset, quasdam ejus significationes extare, quibus ad eam queat reduci, ut fidit &c. Interea quam maxime probabile est, apud Hebraeos hac significatione venire, quam idcirco non vetusti modo, verum & recentiores secuti sunt interpretes. In eandem mentem LXX, καὶ ἃ μὴ ἐκκλίνωσι τὰς τρίβους αὐτῶν. Quos sequitur Arabica impressa ... & Syrus & Vulgat. Lat. non declinabunt a semitis suis. His ex recentioribus etiam accedunt non pauci, quorum interpretationes sunt: q) Neque de semitis suis deflectent. r) Nullus a semita sua deflectit &c. s) Non pervertet.
units.tr: This is what the Chaldee paraphrast had in view when he renders ולא נלאחת מעכבין ארחתהן [nor do they delay their ways], or make a delay in their ways. Certain others also appealed to his authority, among them Abu Walid, who has they do not delay themselves, or make delay in their ways. Both Tanchum and Kimchi note this way of interpreting the word (although they do not cease to note others also), and the reasoning for this interpretation of the word which I have cited is given by R. Tanchum in these words: it is derived from abot (in leabot aboto, Deut. 24. 10.), which signifies a deposit (or pledge), inasmuch as what has been given in pledge (or handed over as a deposit) is held back and detained until the price for which it was pledged is paid. From this they judge it most evident that the root contains the meaning of hindering, impeding or detaining. This sense is taken not only by the Chaldean, but also by some more recent writers, such as Pagninus, they will not delay their journeys; Münster, nor will they be slow in their paths; and in our older English translation, which was commonly used in former times, and they shall not linger in their paths; and in the one made by the Geneva translators, and they shall not stay in their paths. 2. There are some who admit the word in this meaning, but contend that it is used not in the sense we have just cited, but in a quite different one, namely, inasmuch as a thing is taken on loan and by lending is passed from one to another, as if the words meant, according to Kimchi as author in his book of roots, [and he will not lend], nor will they lend their way, one to another; as Mercerus rightly interprets these words. But some n) others wrongly render it, as Vatablus notes: they shall not ask him about their paths, as if they would not be going to stop even for the briefest time so that the way might be changed by another. In the same twofold sense, which signifies to borrow or lend, the Arabic manuscript also seems to have taken it, rendering: and each shall proceed in his own way, and they shall not give (or receive) their ways on loan, that is, they shall not depart from their ways, or share them with one another, but each shall constantly keep his own. If the words are taken in this way, a certain learned o) commentator thinks they embrace an elegant expression, signifying that they shall not exchange among themselves, or lend their ways to one another, but that each shall keep his own and hold the place he first occupied. 3. There are not lacking those who take this word quite differently, not as meaning to attack, but as having the same force as עור [iwet] (with which it agrees in sound when the letters are changed), namely, to pervert, to make crooked, or to bend aside; that this meaning was also in use in the Ishmaelite tongue Aben-Ezra and Kimchi testify. But the most learned de Dieu rightly observed p) that the Arabic lexicographers do not give this meaning of the verb, however Aben-Ezra may have found it in use in his own time; though it could not be denied that some of its meanings exist to which it could be reduced, as he trusts, etc. Meanwhile it is most probable that among the Hebrews it has this meaning, which is why not only older but also more recent interpreters have followed it. To the same effect the Septuagint have: καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐκκλίνωσι τὰς τρίβους αὐτῶν [and they shall not turn aside from their paths]. The Arabic printed text follows them, and so do the Syriac and the Latin Vulgate: they shall not turn aside from their paths. To these recent interpreters many others also add their renderings: q) Nor will they turn aside from their paths. r) No one turns aside from his path, etc. s) They shall not pervert.

units.la: n) Papn. Lex. o) Tarnov. p) Qui ex Aethiopica lingua eam explicari posse putat. q) Cal. r) Tig. s) Jun. Trem. pervertent vel t) obliquabunt semitas suas, u) non obturbabunt itinera illorum. Atque hi & qui sunt hujus generis alii ea videntur accepisse omnes significatione, qua conspirat cum Hiret, pervertit, nec est quod sententiam illorum nostrae posterioris translationi, quae ad subjecta referuntur praedicata, contrariam putes; quippe quae non tantum eam expresse tradit, sed & utrivis aliarum interpretationum applicari potest, quia omnes complectitur praedictas rationes, sive inliberi non potuisse dicas, sive alios alios non expulisse ex locis suis, sive se non coarctasse in viis suis, vel cum aliis commutasse, nec sibi invicem contrarios ordinem suum turbasse, utpote quibus cunctis illorum procedendi describitur ordo, qui quam concinnus futurus esset nec in sequentibus tradere desistit.
units.tr: n) Papn. Lex. o) Tarnov. p) Those who think it can be explained from the Ethiopic language. q) Cal. r) Tig. s) Jun. Trem. will pervert, or t) will bend their paths, u) will not disturb their ways. These and others of this kind all seem to have taken the word in the sense that agrees with Hiret, to pervert, and you should not think their view contrary to our later translation, which refers the predicates to the subjects. For that translation not only states this view outright but can also be applied to any of the other interpretations, since it includes all the aforesaid senses: whether you say that they could not be pushed in, or that some did not drive others from their places, or that they did not confine themselves in their ways, or exchanged places with one another, or disturbed each other's order. All of these describe the order of their advance, and the passage goes on to show how orderly that advance would be.

units.la: §. Nec unus alterum expellet, quisque per semitam su- am procedent, & quando cadent super ensem, non vulnerabuntur.
units.tr: §. Neither shall one thrust another aside; each shall march along his own path, and when they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded.

units.la: Ordinem locumque suum, quem primo occupabant, tam stricte servabunt, ut, quamvis sint numero pene infinito, tamen non sint se invicem praesuturi, vel submoturi, vel locum mutaturi, sed quisque illorum accurate semitam suam retenturi. Talem ordinem utplurimum in magnis exercitibus observari expedit, ne sibi ipsis verius inferat copiarum multitudo confusionem, quam inimicis suis damnum, atque in eo omnis militaris disciplinae vis sita est, utpote quo sine rerum successus non sperandus. Nam , cum alter alterum impedit confusione, quomodo pugnabunt? Exercitus vero pulchre dispositus, & ordine collocatus & amicis pulcherrimus videtur, & hostibus propemodum invictus & expugnabilis; atque egregia omni tempore ac loco a talibus tam pulchre dispositis exercitibus gesta esse nemini constare non poterit. Quod si haec verba ad inimicos referantur, ut quibusdam hoc placet, summam & fortitudinem eorum & belli peritiam, qua utraque praestantes ingentem pote-
units.tr: They will keep their order and place, which they first occupied, so strictly that, although they are almost infinite in number, they will not go before one another, or push one another aside, or change places, but each will keep his own path with care. It is useful that such order is generally observed in great armies, lest the multitude of troops bring confusion upon themselves rather than harm upon their enemies; in this lies the whole force of military discipline, since without it no success in affairs can be hoped for. For when one hinders another through confusion, how will they fight? An army well arranged, set in order, seems most beautiful to its friends and almost unconquerable and invincible to its enemies; and no one can fail to know that outstanding deeds have at all times and places been done by armies so finely arranged. If these words are referred to the enemies, as some like, it is plainly implied here that they had great strength and skill in war, by which, excelling in both, they could strike enormous terror.

units.la: {t} Merc. {u} Oecol. vid. Diodati Edit. in 4to. {ss} Livel. ex Xenoph. poterant injicere terrorem, hic innui manifestum est. Verum si ad locustas vermiculosque hujus generis alios spectare mavis, quae nostra cum aliis sententia est, quae cum nec rege gaudeant nec praefecto, qui agmen exacte disponat, & nihilominus tam catervatim ac ordinate procedant, idem de illis dici, quod de inimicis, quis ambigere potest? Manus DEI magna, ex cujus jubentis dispositione volitant, uti Hieronymus ait, debebat in illis agnosci, & plane constare, ejus hunc esse exercitum ab ipso instructum, & in incolas immissum (uti v. 25.) ad obeundum quoddam opus magnum, earumque adventus talem debebat illis terrorem incutere, qualis describitur v. 6. & inprimis, cum animo revolverent impavidam earum pertinaciam prosperumque omni ex parte successum, quo suo ordine & effrenato cursu progressurae essent, quod dilucidius etiam docet in sequentibus: & quando cadent super ensem, non vulnerabuntur. Qua audacia atque pervicacia forent, ex eo patet, quod non sint gladium formidaturae, ei insidere etiam audentes; quo vero successu ea peracturae essent, ex eo patet, quod sic faciendo non forent vulnerandae. Ita haec verba explicat x) Kimchi &c. Non est hic exercitus ut reliqui hostes, quos prohibebis, ne adversum te veniant gladio; sed castra metantur vel sedent super eos, nec vulnerantur, idque inquit ob levitatem earum. Ex his quidem satis superque constare poset hujus commatis sensus juxta translationem nostram, quam omnium maxime cum Textu Hebraico conspirare cognitum habemus; verum cum discrepantes quarundam vocum extent apud antiquiores interpretationes, par esse duco, iis recensendis ac enucleandis parumper inhaerere. Primo quod attinet verba nostratibus reddita: Nec unus alterum expellet, hebraice ... veish achiu lo yidchakun, & a quamplurimis in eandem mentem translata retinentibus cum nostrat. verbum significatione y) coarctandi vel expellendi; LXX utuntur voce, quae sensu videtur discrepare, reddentes ... ἀφέξεται.
units.tr: {t} Merc. {u} Oecol. see Diodati's edition in 4to. {ss} Livel. from Xenophon. They could indeed strike terror. But if you prefer to refer these words to locusts and other such small worms, which is our own view, since they have neither a king nor a commander to arrange their host exactly, yet advance in such close and orderly troops, who can doubt that the same may be said of them as of the enemies? The great hand of God, by whose ordering command they fly about, as Jerome says, ought to be recognised in them, and it should be plain that this host is his, equipped by him and sent against the inhabitants (as in v. 25) to perform some great work. Their coming ought to strike them with such terror as is described in v. 6, and especially when they consider in their minds their fearless stubbornness and the successful outcome on every side, with which they would advance in their order and unbridled course. This is taught even more clearly in what follows: and when they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded. That this would show their boldness and obstinacy is plain, since they would dare even to settle upon the sword without fear; and that they would accomplish their task successfully is plain, since by doing so they would not be wounded. So Kimchi explains these words, etc.: This is not an army like other enemies, whom you will keep from coming against you with the sword; but they encamp or settle upon them, and are not wounded, because of their lightness, as he says. From these things it can be clearly enough established what the sense of this verse is according to our translation, which we know agrees most of all with the Hebrew text. But since there are differing readings of certain words in the older interpretations, I think it right to pause a little on reviewing and explaining them. First, as for the words rendered by our countrymen, Nor shall one thrust another aside, in Hebrew ... veish achiu lo yidchakun [וְאִישׁ אָחִיו לֹא יִדְחָקוּן], and as very many have translated them to the same sense, keeping the English word in the sense of confining or driving out, the Seventy use a word that seems to differ in meaning, rendering ... [ἀφέξεται].

units.la: x) Ut & Abu VValid. y) Vulg. Lat. coarctabit. Eandem cum Hebr. vocem habent Chald. & Syr. Versiones, Lat. reliquae premunt, urgebunt, impellent, in eandem sententiam omnes. ἀφίξεται, quilibet non discedet a fratre suo, quos sequitur Arabica impressa وَيَشْكُرُ وَحِدٌ مِنْ أَخِيهِ لَا يَتَعَرَّضُ quisque eorum non fugiet a fratre suo, i. e. non separabunt se unus ab altero. Quo factum est, ut z) quidam conjecerint, eos loco yidchakun, legisse ירחקון irchakun cum ר loco ר a רחק rachak procul esse, distare, recedere. At fortean non opus esset statuere, aliter eos olim legisse quam hodie adhuc dum legimus, si latiori significatione acciperemus verbum רחק Dachak, quam plerumque obtinuit, premendi vel trudendi, nimirum, qua usus est Chaldaeus & Syrus repellendi, propellendi, vel expellendi; unde non inepte eam expressisse dixeris per abstinere, sugere, ab aliis se secernere, quod idem est ac propellere a se ipso. Porro quae proxime sequuntur, quisque per semitam suam procedent, & hebraic. נבר במסלתו ילכון Geber bimsillato yelecun, tanta eorum apud veteres aeque ac recentiores interpretes est discrepantia, ut vix inter se conciliari possint. Prima vox est גבר Geber, quae utplurimum significat virum, qui potentia, robore ac auctoritate pollet, שיש לו גבורה עד האישור qui potestatem habet in fœminam, uti eam exponit a) Kimchi, & proprie dicitur בני ארם de filiis hominum, quamvis eodem auctore hic tribuatur locustis vel eusmodi animalculis, quae ante contulerat cum גבוריים Gibborim robustis hominibus (v. 7.), eodemque modo adhibeatur atque praecedens איש ish, vir, quo horum quisque in specie denotatur. Altera vox est מסילה Mesillah, quae proprie significat aggestam, stratam vel tritam viam, & deducitur a סלל Salal, aggregavit vel contumulavit; attamen nec minus usitata est pro via vel semita. Quae cum cognita tritissimaque hujus vocis sit significatio, mirum omnino videtur, quod in Graeca translatione hujus nec vestigium nec volta exstat. Etenim habet καταβαρυνόμενοι ἐν τοῖς ὅπλοις αὐτῶν προςεύσονται, onerati procedent in suis armis (vel cum suis armis), quae hic convenientia cum hebraeo? Equidem, ut eas conciliaret, Capellus legisse eos, ait, loco גבר Geber vir (vel quisque) literis mutatis כבד Cabed gravis; At quomodo מסלתו Mesillato denotabit in suis armis, vel
units.tr: x) So also Abu Walid. y) The Vulgate Latin will confine. The Chaldee and Syriac versions have the same Hebrew word, and the other Latin versions press, will urge, will drive, all to the same sense. [ἀφίξεται], each one will not depart from his brother, which the printed Arabic follows: each one of them will not flee from his brother, that is, they will not separate themselves from one another. Hence some have conjectured that they read, instead of yidchakun, the word irchakun [ירחקון], with ר in place of ד, from רחק rachak, to be far off, to be distant, to withdraw. But perhaps there would be no need to suppose that they read differently from what we read today, if we took the verb רחק dachak in the wider sense it has mostly held, of pressing or thrusting, which is the sense used by the Chaldee and Syriac, of repelling, driving off, or expelling. Whence you might not unfittingly express it by to refrain, to shun, to separate oneself from others, which is the same as driving away from oneself. Moreover, the words that immediately follow, each shall march along his own path, Hebrew [גבר במסלתו ילכון] Geber bimsillato yelecun, have such disagreement among the older and newer interpreters that they can hardly be reconciled. The first word is גבר Geber [גבר], which generally means a man who is strong in power, vigour and authority, who has power over a woman [שיש לו גבורה עד האישור], as Kimchi explains it, and it is properly said of the sons of men, although on the same authority it is here ascribed to locusts or such small animals, which he had earlier compared with the גבורים Gibborim, the strong men (v. 7), and it is used in the same way as the preceding איש ish, man, by which each of them is denoted individually. The other word is מסילה Mesillah [מסילה], which properly means a raised, paved or beaten road, and is derived from סלל Salal [סלל], to heap up or to pile up; yet it is no less commonly used for way or path. Since the meaning of this word is well known and very familiar, it seems altogether strange that there is neither trace nor variant of it in the Greek translation. For it has [καταβαρυνόμενοι ἐν τοῖς ὅπλοις αὐτῶν προςεύσονται], weighed down, they will advance in their arms (or with their arms). How does this agree with the Hebrew? Indeed, to reconcile them, Capellus says they read, instead of גבר Geber, man (or each one), with the letters changed, כבד Cabed [כבד], heavy. But how would מסלתו Mesillato [מסלתו] denote in their arms, or what word would they have found in its place that might show a trace of this meaning?

units.la: z) Schindl. Capel. a) In rad. b) Druf. vel quam vocem illius loco eos invenisse conjiciet, quæ vel speciem hujus significationis præbeat? Si conjecturis quid promoveri posset, forte primam vocem Geber eos legisse eo modo, quo nunc se habet, statuendum est; at qua denotat fortem, magnum & robustum virum (quo pacto & alibi eandem vocem reddere solent per ἀνδρεῖος vir strenuus) quam deinde idem valere putasse, ac virum armorum vel in armis; quod autem ad verba ἐν τοῖς ὁπλοις in armis, quæ inclusa erant præcedenti voci, eorum loco scripsisse ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς in viis suis, quæ a librariis postea mutata in hac versione, at non in textu hebraico; nisi magis arrideat pro מכלתו legisse משלחתו vel mishlacatho in sua armatura. Quod equidem non adduco, ut hac ratione omnem difficultatem me expedire mihi videar; verum quia æque multum probabilitatis habet hæc, quam altera conjectura. De cætero cum Mercero dicendum: Græcorum lectio ad Hebræum textum applicari non potest, nisi sensum eos potius secutos dicamus, quasi etiam graviore armatura induti, non propterea impediantur, quo minus in armis suis via sua ᴠadant. Quid vero hac sua interpretatione respexerint, non est quod divinando adsequi fatiganus, cum plana sint, quæ in textu hebraico habentur, quibuscum non tantum nostra, verum & aliæ interpretationes insigniter conspirant, nec præcedentibus aut consequentibus ullo modo adversantur. A parte nostrarum inter cæteros, qui hoc commate literæ adhæ rent, Vulgatus latin. stat, cum reddat, singulí in calle suo ᴠadent; sequenti vero commate longius a nostratibus abest, quam Græca vel ulla alia veterum aut hodiernarum translationum, quod ex specimine, quod sumus daturi cum ex illa, tum ex aliis, luculenter apparebit. Verba Hebraica sunt ובער השלח יפלו לא יבצע Ubead hasshelach yippolu le yibtsau, apte nostratibus reddita, & quando cadunt super ensem (vel telum uti in margine) non ᴠulnerabuntur. Latina habet: & per fenestras cadent, & non demolientur, quod Duacens. vertunt, and through the windows they shall fall, and shall not shall take no harm, non contrahent damnum, uti ad marginem habet. Omnis difficultas ac discrepantia sita est in voce Shelaḥ, quamo-
units.tr: z) Schindler; Capellus. a) In the root. b) Drusius. Or what word would they have found in its place that might show a trace of this meaning? If anything can be advanced by conjecture, it must perhaps be assumed that they read the first word Geber as it now stands, but which denotes a strong, great and mighty man (in which way they often render the same word elsewhere by [ἀνδρεῖος], a valiant man), and then supposed that it also meant a man of arms or in arms. As for the words [ἐν τοῖς ὁπλοις], in arms, which were enclosed in the preceding word, that they wrote [ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς], in their ways, in their place, which later copyists changed in this version but not in the Hebrew text, unless it pleases more to have read מכלתו as משלחתו [משלחתו], mishlacatho, in his equipment. I do not bring this forward because I think that in this way I can clear up every difficulty for myself, but because this conjecture has as much probability as the other. Otherwise, it must be said with Mercerus: the Greek reading cannot be applied to the Hebrew text, unless we say they followed the sense rather than the words, as if being equipped with heavier armour they were not thereby hindered from going their way in their own arms. What they had in mind in their own translation it is not worth wearing ourselves out to reach by guessing, since the meaning of what is found in the Hebrew text is plain, and not only our translation but other interpretations agree with it remarkably, nor do they in any way conflict with what goes before or after. On our side, among others who keep close to the letter in this verse, the Latin Vulgate stands, since it renders each one will walk in his own path; but in the following verse it is further from ours than the Greek or any other version, ancient or modern, which will become clear from the specimen we are about to give from it and from others. The Hebrew words are ובער השלח יפלו לא יבצע [ובער השלח יפלו לא יבצעו], Ubead hasshelach yippolu le yibtsau, aptly rendered by our countrymen, and when they fall upon the sword (or weapon, as in the margin), they shall not be wounded. The Latin has: and they shall fall through the windows, and shall not be demolished, which the Douai translators render: and through the windows they shall fall, and shall take no harm, as the margin has it. The whole difficulty and disagreement lies in the word Shelaḥ, which

units.la: c) Satius alii ducunt passive verti, shall not be demolished, aor hunt. strates verterunt gladium, ille fenestras: quam significationem cur voci assignet, me prorsus latet, cum omnibus æque cognita ac probata sit significatione gladii, teli aut aliorum hujus generis armorum, eaque non semel alias in eadem Vulgat. usitata. Ejusdem notionis est Arabicum Salabo, & Chaldaicum שלחא; at nullibi, quod quidem cognoverim, fenestrarum significatione extat. Nec Hieronymus ullam adducit rationem pro hac interpretatione, nec alicujus allegat auctoritatem; attamen differentiam notat, qua verterunt LXX. ἐν βελεσιν super tela, quorum versionem hoc versu plane non putat expositionis ordini convenire. Verum hanc censuram magis spectare autumo verba præcedentia, quæ jamjam exposuimus, quam hanc vocem, quam haud impropria, sed usitata notione accipiunt, nec adeo erroris argui possunt, quantumvis ob id unum fere atro carbone ab eo sint notati. Quod perperam factum atque difficultati locum fecit, verba sunt quæ huic adjungunt. Præter antecedentia enim annectunt hic vocabulo βελεσιν vocem αυτῶν, illorum, quam Hebraicus Textus nescit, & quæ sensum plane invertit; quippe cum sine hac voce innuatur, casuros eos vel infesturos armis, quæ adversus se caperentur, cum ea vero significari videas, vel eos casuros cum d) suis ipsius armis, quæ tum etiam erigerent, cum alicubi residerent aut quiescerent, quæ Theodoreti opinio videtur: vel, alios esse casuros illorum armis, quæ est Cyrilli, quali populus cecidisset, i. e. fame periisset eo, quod terræ fructus alimentaque cetera consumerent dentibus, quos innui putat per illorum tela vel arma. Nec difficultate carent, quæ sequuntur לא יבשו lo yibtsau, ab eis reddita, non consummentur. Quibus Theodoretus indicari statuit, non iri expletum eos ea, quam exercerent, crudelitate; & Cyrillus, eos (scil. populum) nondum futuros immunes noxa æquo animo lata, qua terræ fructus erant affecti, verum & insuper laturos damnum, quod illorum civitatibus ac domibus essent daturi, uti sequitur. Ex illis totam hanc versus clausulam Arabica impressa sic translatam habet ... jacu-
units.tr: c) Others think it better to render the verb passively, "shall not be demolished," and they translate the word as "sword" (gladium), while the Latin renders it "windows" (fenestras). I am quite at a loss to see why this sense should be assigned to the word, since the meaning "sword, javelin," or some other weapon of this kind, is known and approved by everyone, and the Vulgate itself uses it elsewhere more than once. The Arabic Salabo has the same meaning, and so does the Chaldee שלחא [shelacha]; but nowhere, so far as I know, does it carry the sense of "windows." Jerome offers no reason for this rendering and cites no authority for it. He does note the difference from the Septuagint, who wrote ἐν βελεσιν [en belesin], "upon the javelins," and he judges that their rendering does not fit the order of the exposition in this verse. But I think this criticism applies more to the preceding words, which we have just explained, than to this word, which they take in its proper and ordinary sense. It cannot fairly be charged with error, however much it has been marked almost with black charcoal for this alone. The mistake that created the difficulty lies in the words they add here. For besides what goes before, they attach to the word βελεσιν the pronoun αυτῶν, "of them," which the Hebrew text does not have and which entirely reverses the sense. Without this word, the meaning is that they will fall or attack with the weapons that are directed against them. With it, you see that either they will fall "with their own weapons," which they would also raise whenever they sat or rested anywhere, as seems to be the opinion of Theodoret; or that others will fall "by their weapons," which is the view of Cyril, as if the people had fallen, that is, perished by famine, because the locusts would consume the fruits of the earth and the rest of its food with their teeth, which he thinks are signified by "their javelins or weapons." Nor are the following words free of difficulty: לא יבשו [lo yibtsau], rendered "shall not be consumed." Theodoret holds that these words indicate that they will not be sated with the cruelty they practise; and Cyril, that they (namely, the people) will not yet be exempt from the harm that was borne with equanimity by the fruits of the earth, but will also suffer damage that they will inflict on the cities and houses of those people, as the passage goes on. Of these, the printed Arabic has translated the whole closing clause of the verse thus: ... jacu-

units.la: d) Secus Mercerus, in suæ ipsorum ruunt jaculas. jaculisque suis corruent, & rem ad exitum non perducent. Qua ex versione patet eum legisse, quod & in quibusdam exemplaribus extare observatum est, συντελέσωσι, active, perficient, quam lectionem confirmat Interpres Syrus, qui ejus loco habet pre armorum suorum ponere cadent, & rem ad exitum non perducent. Quocunque vero modo hæ interpretationes inter fe conciliari possint, id saltem appareret, quod probandum nobis erat, quam maxime eas distare ab ea, quam noftrates existimant omnium maxime genuinam veritatique congruam, a qua non parum etiam differt Paraphraftes Chaldeus, qui posteriorem hujus commatis partem ita reddit singuli per callem suum procedunt ad locum quo missi sunt, e) trucidant (vel confligunt) nec recipiunt pecuniam. Unde non obscure liquet, accepisse eum hanc vocem Hashelach, quam plerique vertunt arma vel tela (solus latinus, fenefiras) usitata radicis significatione mittendi, acsi locum eonfumerent, quo erant missi, vel f) propter quem. Addit illi trucidant vel confligunt, quod in Hebraeo non est, quo additamento in opinionem adductus e Pet. a Fig. intellexisse eum hæc verba de inimicis potius quam de locustis. Ultimam denique vocem yebifau alia prorsus notione accipit, quam cæteri a nobis adducti interpretes, nimirum, qua significat pecuniam accipere, eoque innui putat, eos non esse sicut inimicos alios, qui pecunia contenti ære possent prohiberi, cum ei nequaquam inhiarent. Et quamvis recentiores in aliis ut plurimum noftratibus accedant, in eo tamen eorum nonnulli cum Chaldaeo sentiunt: quare abs re prorsus non erit, fi in hujus vocis significationem parumper inquiramus. In proclivi est diversis significationibus radicem Batsa gaudere, 1. Denotat quastum facere, vel inhiare lucro vel quassui, ut Prov. 27. qui deditus est quastui, & Habac. 2, 9. pidus quastus malı, atque alibi sæpenumero, eaque ratione hic Chaldaeus uti vidimus. Tigur. nec lucro inhiant. Alius (apud Vatablum)
units.tr: d) Mercer differs, rendering "they rush down upon their own javelins, and by their javelins they shall fall, and will not bring the matter to an end." From this version it is clear that he read what has been observed in some copies, συντελέσωσι, in the active voice, "they will accomplish." The Syriac interpreter confirms this reading, for in its place he has "they shall fall by the weapons they have set down, and will not bring the matter to an end." But however these interpretations may be reconciled with one another, at least this appears, which was what we needed to prove: they differ very widely from that rendering which our countrymen consider the most genuine of all and in agreement with the truth. The Chaldee paraphrast also differs from it considerably, for he renders the latter part of this clause thus: "each one proceeds by his own path to the place to which he was sent, and they slaughter (or fight) and do not receive money." From this it is not obscure that he took the word Hashelach, which most render "weapons or javelins" (only the Latin has "windows"), in the ordinary sense of the root, "to send," as if they would consume the place to which they were sent, or f) on account of which. He adds "slaughter" or "fight," which is not in the Hebrew, and by this addition he was led, following Pet. a Fig., to understand these words of enemies rather than of locusts. Finally, he takes the last word, yebifau, in an entirely different sense from the other interpreters we have cited, namely, that it means "to receive money," and he thinks it signifies that they are not like other enemies, who could be restrained by money or bribes, since they do not at all lust after it. And although more recent writers for the most part agree with our countrymen, some of them nevertheless side with the Chaldee on this point. Therefore it will not be out of place to inquire a little into the meaning of this word. The root Batsa is easily seen to have various meanings. 1. It signifies to make gain, or to lust after gain or profit, as in Prov. 27, "he who is given to gain," and Hab. 2:9, "greedy gain of evil," and often elsewhere; and in this way the Chaldee uses it here, as we have seen. The Tigurine version: "nor do they lust after gain." Another (in Vatablus):

units.la: e) Trucidant, utut alii trucidantur (Leusd.) vel trucidabuntur. Pet. a Fig. f) R. Sal. non fluxebunt s̈aritia: & apud Calv. non concupiscent: MS. Arab. ita ex hebraeo transtulit ... cadent post gladium, (vel arma) nec facient quaestum. (2.) Perficere vel ad finem deducere, ut Esa. 10, 12. ... cum perfecerit Dominus totum opus suum, & Lament. 2,17. ... perfecit sermonem suum. Quo sensu eam accepit Graeca, Arabica impressa & Syriaca. (3.) Concidere, praecidere, vulnerare &c. sicut Job. 6. v. 9. ... Vayiltseni & concideret me, & Esa. 38, 12. ... refectiurus est me, & Amos. 9,1. ... & percute eos (vel vulnera eos, uti ad marginem) & ita cum Passa convenit, (b & p. inter se commutatis) quae denotat vulnerare, quam significationem etiam confirmat R. Tanchum ex lingua Arabica, qua Badaa significat concidere, dissindere, vel in frustra comminuere, ut & in Chaldaica. Quocirca & apud eum & apud Abu Walid hic legimus ... non vulnerabuntur. Quo sensu nostrates quoque cum multis aliis accepisse videmus, quos inter & Vulgatus fortean habendus, quatenus g) demoliri quidam interpretantur per concidere, ac si diceret, concident se, vulnerabunt se; Quod ad verbum, etsi actívae formae hic sit atque aliis in locis etiam hic usurpatum inveniamus, Kimchi tamen notat esse Omed, intransitivum, & significationem habere passivam. Hisce jam diversis significationibus rite traditis, quarum quamque vel eligunt vel alteri praeferunt etiam viri magnae auctoritatis, quis est qui non videt, aequam nobis esse libertatem, parumque referre, quamcunque harum selegerimus, quippe auctoritate nobiscum sententium non erimus destituti. At si meum quoque judicium interponere liceat, eam prae caeteris maxime perspicuam duco sententiam ac interpretationem, qua acceperunt vocem nostrates & aliorum non pauci, quippe non solum tunc optime accedit indubiae significationi hebraicae vocis, sed & apte cohaeret cum praecedentibus & consequentibus. Quodque idcirco in medium adduxi, non nisi digressionis loco factum fuisse ingenue faterer, nisi secus me sentire jubaret tantorum virorum auctoritas, quibus alia ratione accipere eam vilum
units.tr: e) Trucidant, though others read "are slaughtered" (Leusden), or "shall be slaughtered." Pet. a Fig. f) R. Sal. "they shall not flow with greed," and in Calvin "they shall not covet"; the Arabic manuscript translates it from the Hebrew thus: "they shall fall after the sword" (or weapons), "nor shall they make gain." (2.) To "complete" or bring to an end, as in Isa. 10:12, "when the Lord has completed all his work," and Lam. 2:17, "he has completed his word." It is in this sense that the Greek, the printed Arabic and the Syriac take it. (3.) To "cut off," "cut down," "wound," and so on, as in Job 6:9, "that he would cut me off" (Vayiltseni), and Isa. 38:12, "he will cut me off," and Amos 9:1, "and strike them" (or "wound them," as in the margin). In this way it agrees with the Arabic Passa (with b and p interchanged), which means "to wound." Rabbi Tanchum confirms this meaning from the Arabic language, in which Badaa means "to cut down, to split," or "to crush into fragments," as also in Chaldee. Accordingly, both he and Abu Walid read here "shall not be wounded." Our countrymen, like many others, are seen to have taken it in this sense, and among them perhaps the Vulgate should be counted, insofar as some interpret g) demoliri as "to cut down," as if it said "they shall cut themselves down, they shall wound themselves." As to the word, although we find here and elsewhere that the active form is used, Kimchi nevertheless notes that it is Omed, intransitive, and has a passive sense. Now that these various meanings have been duly set out, and that each of them is chosen, or preferred to the others, even by men of great authority, who does not see that we have an equal freedom, and that it matters little which of these we choose, since we shall not lack authority for our opinion? But if I may add my own judgment, I count that sense and interpretation as the clearest of all, by which our countrymen and not a few others have taken the word. For not only does it agree very well with the undoubted Hebrew meaning of the word, but it also coheres fittingly with what precedes and what follows. I would frankly confess that I have brought this forward only as a digression, were it not that the authority of such great men, who seemed to them to take it in another way, bids me think otherwise.

units.la: {g} Ribera. visum fuit. Verum enim vero quod ad nos,non possumus,quin nostratium in sententiam eamus, qua ad sequentia tam directus etiam patet aditus, utpote quibus describitur, quid denique hic exercitus Dei sit facturus,cujus pertinacia æque ac agilitas in his & præcedentibus verbis tam luculenter erat depicta.
units.tr: {g} Ribera. But as for us, we cannot help going along with the opinion of our countrymen, for by it the way to what follows lies open and direct, since there is described what the army of God will finally do here, whose stubbornness and agility are so vividly depicted in these and the preceding words.

units.la: 9. Ultro citroque current in civitate: current in mu- ro, conscendent domos: intrabunt per fenestras, sicut fur.
units.tr: 9. They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up into the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.

units.la: Ultro citroque current &c.) Verbum hoc loco est ישקו jashokku,nec dubito quin proprie hic sit redditum,quippe descendit a radice שקק Shakak, ejusque derivata, uti notat b) Kimchi, proprie denotant התליכות בהתמרה continuum progressum (vel continuitatem gradus, ut in notis h. l. habet התמרה ההליכות). Ejusdem præterea statuit ille cum Aben-Ezra significationis esse, atque שוק Shok crus, locustasque præcipue indigitari,propterea quod crura earum sint longa & insuper, quia הילך תמיר ולאי ינוח אליו מעט gradiuntur assidue, & non quiescunt nisi paululum. At cujuscunque etiam ponderis sit hoc acumen,quod in hac interpretatione lateat, manifestum est satis superque,hoc verbum ea ratione, qua dictum est ante,accipi atque alibi etiam de locustis usurpari,ut Esa. 33,4. כמשק גביים שקק בן quod ex nostratium interpretatione habet: ut locustæ ultro citroque currunt, sic curret in eos. Nec obscure liquet eo significatu a quamplurimis interpretibus hoc loco accipi, quorum Vulgat. ingredientur; alii, per urbem i) gradientur, vel k) per civitatem ambulabunt, vel l) in civitate discurrent,vel m) civitatem percurrent,vel per n) civitatem current, vel o) urbem pervadent. Qui certe omnes alia significatione hoc verbum non sumunt,quibus jure merito etiam accenseas Interpr.Græc. habentes τὰς πόλεις ἐπιλήψονται; & Arabic. impressam horum æmulam ... occupabunt vel contingent civitatem; vel Syrum ... ascen-
units.tr: They will run to and fro, etc.) The word here is jashokku [ישקו], and I do not doubt that it is rightly rendered here in its proper sense, since it comes from the root Shakak [שקק] and its derivatives, which, as b) Kimchi notes, properly denote a continuous progress (or continuity of step, as the note on this passage has it [התמרה ההליכות]). Moreover, he agrees with Aben-Ezra that it is of the same meaning as Shok [שוק], a leg, and that locusts are chiefly meant, because their legs are long and also because they walk constantly and rest only a little [הילך תמיר ולאי ינוח אליו מעט]. But however much subtlety may lie hidden in this interpretation, it is plain enough and more than plain that the word is taken in the sense stated above and is used elsewhere also of locusts, as in Isa. 33:4, [כמשק גביים שקק בן], which in our translation reads: as locusts run to and fro, so shall they run upon them. And it is clear enough that many interpreters take it in this sense here: the Vulgate has ingredientur (they will enter); others have per urbem i) gradientur (they will walk through the city), or k) per civitatem ambulabunt (they will walk through the city), or l) in civitate discurrent (they will run about in the city), or m) civitatem percurrent (they will run through the city), or per n) civitatem current (they will run through the city), or o) urbem pervadent (they will overrun the city). All of these certainly do not take the word in any other sense, and among them one may fairly count the Greek interpreters, who have [τὰς πόλεις ἐπιλήψονται] (they will seize the cities); and the Arabic, a printed rendering similar to these, will occupy or will touch the city; and the Syriac ... will ascend.

units.la: b) In Not. i) Pag. Drufius. k Munst. l) Tig. m) Jun. Tremel. n) Pifc. o) Cast. asfecdent in civitatem & MS. Arab. effundent se ipsos (vel irruent simul) magna copia in civitatem. R. Tanchum (vel potius) concul-cabunt. Omnium vero longissime a recepta significatione abire videtur Chaldæus Paraphrastes vertendo in urbe armatur, vel in civitate armati, vel ut aliî distinguunt, & in civitate armati super murum excurrunt &c. ac si juxta illum yashakku valeret armatum esse, originemque traheret a armatura. In diversum etiam abit ab aliis interpretibus R. S. Jarchi, quando ait verbum significare cedere somnum, nec levis conjectura est, cum hanc vocem ea accepisse hic significatione, qua Isa. 33 accipi antea vidimus, quam planiorem reddit per Nobem, p) clamosum sonum, quæ interpretatio nulla omnino alia quam ejus unius auctoritate nititur, ut & ea, quam Chaldæus secutus est. Eas tamen nihilo secius videtur approbare Abarbinel, illique, cujus mentionem fecimus primo loco, quamque cum aliî tum nostrates sequi gavisi sunt, præferre, utramque harum ducens rectam. Nec prorsus latet hujus instituti ratio, quippe hac ratione melius hoc putat congruere iis, de quibus hic sermonem esse putat; non quidem locustis vel hujusmodi aliis creaturis, sed Babylonius, qui muris conscensis civitateque occupata triumphalia quidem sua clamore celebrarent, at non gulæ & deliciis sese in præsentiarum dederent, (quod aliis quidem hostibus usu venire solet) sed se ipsos accingerent ulterioribus pugnis. Cujus vestigiis insistit Arias Montanus in interlin. urbe crepabunt armis, cum P. Agninus vertera t, per urbem incedent. Grotius vero peculiari ratione: adversus urbem concrepabunt arma. Verum non est præter eam, cui nostrates inhærent, quæ magis videatur congruere & his verbis eorumque receptæ significationi, & sequentibus, quibus aperte satis declaratur, quid urbe quadam potiti in quavis ejus parte essent admissuri, nimirum nihil immune ab eorum assultibus futurum, etiam quod vel expugnari vel accedi antea prorsus ἀδύνατον. Current in muro. Habetur supra v. 7. scandent vallum, hic vero Bachomab jerutsun, current in vallo,
units.tr: b) In the Notes: i) Pagninus, Drusius; k) Münster; l) Tigurinus; m) Junius and Tremellius; n) Piscator; o) Castalio: will climb into the city; and the Arabic manuscript: will pour themselves out (or will rush in together) in great numbers into the city. Rabbi Tanchum (or rather): will trample. But the Chaldee paraphrast departs furthest of all from the accepted meaning when he renders it is armed in the city, or armed in the city, or, as others distinguish, armed in the city they run out upon the wall, etc., as if according to him yashakku meant to be armed and derived from armour. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi also departs from the other interpreters when he says the word means to cease from sleep. This is not a slight conjecture, since he has taken the word here in the sense in which we saw it previously taken at Isaiah 33, which he makes plainer by Nobem, a clamorous sound. That interpretation rests on no authority other than his alone, as does the one the Chaldean followed. Nevertheless Abarbanel seems to approve these, and he prefers the one with which he began, which both others and our own countrymen have been glad to follow, judging both to be right. The reason for this course is not hidden: he thinks this fits better with those of whom he takes the discourse to be, not indeed locusts or other creatures of this kind, but Babylonians, who, having climbed the walls and taken the city, celebrated their triumphs with a shout, yet did not at the moment give themselves over to gluttony and pleasures (as is usually the case with other enemies), but girded themselves for further fighting. Arias Montanus follows this track in the interlinear version, they will clamour in the city with arms, while Agninus translates, they will advance through the city. Grotius, for a peculiar reason, renders: the arms will clash against the city. Yet there is no other interpretation, apart from the one our countrymen adhere to, that seems to agree better both with these words and their accepted meaning, and with what follows, where it is plainly enough declared what those who had taken hold of some part of the city would do in any part of it: namely, that nothing would be immune from their assaults, even what before could in no way be stormed or approached [ἀδύνατον], impossible. They will run on the wall. In verse 7 above we have they will scale the rampart; here, however, Bachomab jerutsun, they will run on the rampart, vallo, namely because those who had occupied it, with nothing standing in their way, could proceed from one place to another, and so would halt their course.

units.la: p) Ad primam tamen significationem referri potest, si talis intelligatur sonus, qualem cruribus suis edunt, quod Mercero arridet. vallo, qui scilicet eum occupaverant, nulla re existente,quæ prohiberet ,quo minus ab uno loco ad alium procederent, atque ita cursum illorum sisteret. Quin imo nec domus civitatis ab iis reddentur immunes, Conscendent domos, non erit ulla earum tam alte exstructa, cujus fastigium non effent conscensuri,nec repagula forium tam arcte clausa,ut ingressu eos excluderent; quippe omni aditu exclusi, intrabunt per fenestras sicut fur. Furum est,hoc modo intrare domos, quas inveniunt opeffulatas,quod tum quotidiana testatur experientia,tum quod a Salvatore nostro prolatum est Job. 10,1. Qui non ingreditur per ostium, sed ascendit ex loco alio, ille fur est. q) Cæterum hoc loco non videtur respici timor, quo furum instar corriperentur, qui his verbis describuntur; sed declaratur tantum, quod ab ingressu nullo modo prohibere eos posset,five ostium clausum, five aliquid aliud invadentibus objectum, sed quod aliam statim intrandi viam reperturi effent, non formidantes altitudinem inurianem,nec aditu difficilia quæque. Atque sic ea verba, quibus impavida rerum gerendarum ratio traditur eorum, qui lis & præcedentibus verbis intelliguntur, optime quidem ac concinne accommodari possunt exercitui imperterrito ac glorioso, qualis erat Babyloniorum, quemque hic innui & alii & in his Abarbinel asserit. Verum quod non minus recte hic locus explicari possit de locustis vel hujusmodi aliis creaturis, quæ Deo sunt armorum loco,ex eo liquet,quod fcriptum extat Exod. 10,5. 6. quod operient faciem terræ ita,ut non posfit quisquam videre terram &c. & quod implebunt domos Pharaonis, domos omnium fervorum suorum, domos omnium Ægyptiorum &c. Hinc Hieronymus in h.l. nihil locustis inbnum est, utpote quæ non tantum occupabant campos, fruges & arbores, verum etiam civitates, domos,interioraque penetrant conclavia. Nec abludit ab eo Cyrillus. Et Theodoretus in eandem mentem dicit,altitudinem munium earum cursum non posse remorari, utpote quæ facile transcenderent muros atque furum instar intrarent domos per fenestras, quod,inquit ipse ceu oculatus testis,ὡ μοῦ οὐτὰ πολέμιων, ἀλλα ὑπὸ ἀκρίδων r) γιγνόμενον πολλάκις εἰσεσαμένα, non solum ab holli- bus, q) Mecc. Tarn. r) Qua ratione legendum esse ceulet Bochartus. bus, sed & a locustis fieri sæpe vidimus. Eodem spectant etiam sequentia, quibus simul exponitur, quam terribilis futurus sit earum adventus, quidque sit exspectandum ab iis non tantum violentia, sed & multitudine immane quantum excedentibus.
units.tr: p) Yet this may be referred to the first meaning, if the sound is understood as the kind they make with their legs, which Mercer favours. in the rampart, that is, those who had occupied it, with nothing standing in the way of their advancing from one place to another, and so halting their course. Indeed the houses of the city will not be immune from them either. They will climb into the houses: there will be no house so high-built that they would not climb to its roof, nor doors barred so tightly that they would shut them out from entering. Since they are shut out from every approach, they will enter through the windows like a thief. It is the way of thieves to enter houses by whatever way they find unguarded, as both daily experience testifies and what our Saviour said confirms: John 10:1. He who does not enter by the door, but climbs up some other way, is a thief. q) Otherwise, in this place, there seems to be no reference to fear, by which thieves are seized, as these words describe them; rather it is only declared that nothing could in any way prevent their entering, whether the door were shut or some other obstacle were set against those who attack, since they would at once find another way to enter, fearing neither any height nor any difficult approach. And so these words, which give the fearless manner of conducting affairs of those who are understood in the verses before, can very well and fittingly be applied to an army fearless and glorious, such as that of the Babylonians, which both others and Abarbinel in particular assert is meant here. But that this passage may be explained no less correctly of locusts or creatures of that kind, which are God's weapons, is clear from what is written in Exod. 10:5, 6, that they will cover the face of the earth so that no one can see the earth, etc., and that they will fill the houses of Pharaoh, the houses of all his servants, the houses of all the Egyptians, etc. Hence Jerome on this passage: nothing is more harmful than locusts, since they not only occupy fields, crops and trees, but also penetrate cities, houses and inner rooms. Cyril does not differ from him. And Theodoret, to the same effect, says that the height of walls cannot check their course, since they would easily pass over the walls and, like thieves, enter houses through the windows, which, he says, as an eyewitness, ὡ μοῦ οὐτὰ πολέμιων, ἀλλα ὑπὸ ἀκρίδων γιγνόμενον [not only by enemies, but by locusts is often seen to happen]. We have seen this done not only by enemies but also by locusts. The following also bear on this, by which it is set forth at the same time how terrible their coming will be, and what is to be expected from them: not only violence but also a multitude immeasurably exceeding all bounds.

units.la: 10. Contremiscet terra ante eos, cœli trement, sol & luna obtenebrabuntur, & stellæ retrahent suum splendorem.
