units.tr: 10. The earth shall quake before them, the heavens shall tremble, the sun and moon shall be darkened, and the stars shall withdraw their brightness.

units.la: רגזה ארץ Rageza arets, ad literam, terra contremuit, quippe præteriti temporis est hoc verbum & quiquuntur, coque modo a quibusdam versa: Sic Vulgatus Latin. Contremuit terra, moti sunt cœli, sol & luna obtenebrati sunt, & stellæ retraxerunt splendorem suum, qui tempore præterito omnia protulit, quod & factum invenis in Paraphrasi Chaldaica, in Versione Syriaca & MS. Arab. nec non in quibusdam versionibus recentioribus, quarum non postrema Interlinear. Movit se terra &c. Munst. contremuit terra, & commoti sunt cœli &c. Druf. commota est terra. Non desunt autem, s) qui ea præsenti tempore reddunt, contremiscit terra, &c. in quibus etiam Mercerus est, quamvis in Chaldaica versione, quam transfert, non aliud tempus extet, quam in textu hebraico. E contrario futuro quoque tempore non t) pauci sunt qui ea efferunt, quos etiam sequi nostrates juvat. Atque sic eos recte facere nullum est dubium; quippe hoc Prophetis non infrequens est atque inusitatum, præterito efferre, quod adhuc futurum est, idque ideo, quod a Deo determinata atque dicta æque certa sint, ac si essent jam jam facta. Quocirca parum refert, quo tempore verba interpreteris in rebus ad prophetias spectantibus, quales hoc loco sunt, etiam forma eorum potissimum videatur præteritum requirere. Magis hic habenda ratio est rei, quam formæ, atque ad illam præcipue, non ad hanc tempus est accommodandum. Atque ita quam facillime hæc expediri possunt. Verum majoris momenti quæstio est, quo sensu hæc verba sint sumenda, utrum significatione propria, qua revera foret, ut terra contremi-
units.tr: Rageza arets [רגזה ארץ], literally, the earth trembled, for this verb is in the past tense, and it has been rendered that way by some. So the Vulgate translator: The earth trembled, the heavens were moved, the sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness, which puts everything in the past tense. The Chaldee paraphrase also has this, as do the Syriac version and an Arabic manuscript, and among more recent versions, not the least is the interlinear one: The earth moved itself, etc. Münster: the earth trembled, and the heavens were moved, etc. Drusius: the earth was moved. Nor are there lacking those who render it in the present tense, the earth trembles, etc., and Mercerus is among them, although the Chaldee version he translates has no other tense than the Hebrew text. On the other hand, not a few render it in the future tense, the earth will tremble, etc., and our own writers are glad to follow them. There is no doubt that they do right, since it is not uncommon or unusual for the Prophets to express in the past what is still future, because what has been determined and declared by God is as certain as if it had already happened. Hence it matters little in which tense one translates the verbs in prophecies of this kind, such as these here, even if their form seems to call for the past. Attention must be paid to the thing rather than the form, and the tense must be adapted above all to the thing, not to the form. In this way these matters can be settled very easily. But a question of greater weight is in what sense these words are to be taken: whether in their proper meaning, so that the earth would in fact tremble,

units.la: s) Tig. Cattal. t) Pag. moveb. Jun. Trem. movebitur &c. tremiscerent, cœli tremerent, & sol & luna obtenebrarentur &c. anfigurata, qua aliud quid significaretur, quam verba primo aspectu ac proprie videntur suggerere. Etenim non levis, quæ hac de re agitatur penes interpretes, est controversia. Quidam proprie ea acciperevolunt prout sonant, atque in hanc sententiam inclinare videtur Theodoretus, cui admodum probabilis est propria verborum denotatio, licet ingenue fateatur, alio quoque haud incommodo posse accipi sensu. At cæteris quibuscunque significationibus explosis, in eo totus est Arias Montanus, ut omnem hinc procul removeat hyperbolen, qua indicari dicunt, homines tantummodo ob exercitum prædictum, (per quem Chaldæos, sive Assyrios, quod postremum tamen probabilius videtur, intelligat, nequaquam plane refert) tanto assectum iri metu, ut terra illis videretur tremere, cœlum concuti, atque sol & luna obtenebrari, quod loquendi genus Poetis familiare est ad magnum cum hominum terrorem, tum aliarum rerum perturbationem exprimendam. Id enim ait a Propheta jam esse traditum v. 6. A conspectu eorum populus multum dolebit: omnes facies contrahent nigrorem. Sed quæcunque hic proferuntur, simpliciter expectanda putat non secus atque ea, quibus prædicitur u) Luc. 21,25. Signa fore in sole & luna & stellis. Eandem quoque sententiam videtur amplecti Drusius, quando cum locustis simul tonitru contremuissestatuit cœlum, terræque motu concussam terram, quibus manifestum fieret atque indubitatum, exercitum hunc tot atque tantis prodigiis insignem nonnisi a Deo immitti; vel ut tanto majorem injiceret timorem populo profano, quo a peccatis eum deterreret, atque ad seriam perduceret pœnitentiam. Verum non obstant rationes, quotquot etiam pro literali sensu adferuntur, quin aliis ea sententia arrideat, quam rejicit Montanus; nimirum hyperbolica ratione esse prolata, quæ hic inveniuntur, non qua ad literam ea erant futura, sed qua ita afficiebantur homines, ut, quæ rara erant ac communem rerum rationem & ordinem excedebant, sibi imaginarentur, ac si revera ita se haberent. Atque hæc erat olim mens Hieronymi, non quod locustarum aut hostium tanta vis sit, ut possit movere cœlos, & terram tum-
units.tr: s) Tig. Cattal. t) Pag. moveb. Jun. Trem. movebitur etc. (the variant readings of Tigurinus, Catalan, Pagninus, Junius and Tremellius, "shall be moved"), "they would tremble, the heavens would tremble, and the sun and moon would be darkened," and so on, are figurative expressions, which signify something other than the words seem at first sight and in their proper sense to suggest. Indeed the question debated among the interpreters on this point is no slight one. Some want these words taken as they sound, and Theodoret seems to incline to this view, since the proper meaning of the words is quite probable to him, although he candidly admits they can also be taken in another, not unsuitable, sense. But with all other meanings rejected, Arias Montanus is wholly intent on removing every hyperbole from this passage. He says these things indicate only that men, because of the predicted army (by which he understands the Chaldeans, or Assyrians, though the latter seems more probable, and it makes no real difference), would be so seized with fear that the earth would seem to tremble to them, the heavens to be shaken, and the sun and moon to be darkened. This manner of speaking is familiar to the poets, to express both great terror among men and the disturbance of other things. For he says the Prophet has already stated this in v. 6, Before their face the people will be in great pain; all faces will gather blackness. But he thinks that whatever is set forth here must be simply expected, no differently from those things in which it is foretold, u) Luke 21:25, There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars. Drusius also seems to embrace this same view, when he holds that the heavens thundered together with the locusts and the earth was shaken by an earthquake, by which it would be made clear and beyond doubt that this army, marked by so many and such great portents, was sent by God alone, or in order to strike still greater fear into the profane people, so as to deter them from sins and bring them to serious repentance. But the arguments, however many are adduced for the literal sense, do not prevent others from favouring the view which Montanus rejects: namely, that what is found here is put in hyperbolic fashion, not because these things were going to happen literally, but because men were so affected that they imagined, as if they were really so, things which were rare and exceeded the common course and order of nature. This was also the mind of Jerome of old, not that the power of the locusts or of the enemy is so great that it can move the heavens and shake the earth, but that to those suffering adversity, because of the greatness of their terror, the heavens seem to fall and the earth to heave.

units.la: u) Vide sis Matth. 24,29. concutere, sed quod adversa patientibus pro terroris magnitudine & cælum ruere & terra fluctuare videantur. Denique (quod ad verba ultima) pro multitudine locustarum obtegentium cælum, sol & luna convertentur in tenebras & stellæ retrahent lumen suum: nimirum, dum lumen nubes locustarum in medio posita ad terram non sinut pervenire. Sic ea ille explicat, ad eundem fere modum ut Theodoretus, iis tantum exceptis, quæ ante notavimus. Nec Cyrillus multum videtur abludere, cum omnia ita perturbata fore a locustis putet, ὡς ἤδη δοκεῖν καὶ αὐτὸν δεδιν ηθαι τὸν ἐρχόμενον &c. ut jam & ipsum cælum concuti videatur, & sol ac luna atque etiam stellæ suum lumen quasi inhibere, cui etiam hic est ὑπερβολικὸς ὁ λόγος- hyperbolica locutio intolerabilem dolorumque refertam calamitatem indicans. Quam etiam veram pronunciat, etiamsi de hominum exercitu eam accipias.
units.tr: u) See Matt. 24:29. Shake, but that to those suffering adversity, because of the greatness of their terror, the heavens seem to fall and the earth seems to heave. Finally (as to the last words), because of the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the sun and moon will be turned into darkness and the stars will withhold their light, namely, while the cloud of locusts placed in between does not allow the light to reach the earth. He explains these things in almost the same manner as Theodoret, except for those points which we noted before. Nor does Cyril seem to differ much, since he thinks everything will be so disturbed by the locusts [ὡς ἤδη δοκεῖν καὶ αὐτὸν δεδιν ηθαι τὸν ἐρχόμενον], as if the very heavens seem to be shaken, and the sun and moon and even the stars seem as it were to restrain their light, and for him too this is a [ὑπερβολικὸς ὁ λόγος], hyperbolic expression, indicating a calamity intolerable and full of sorrows. He pronounces this true even if you take it of a human army.

units.la: Eodem videntur etiam respicere Commentatores Judaici, quorum Kimchi dicit omnia parabolice (vel figurate) significare gravitatem afflictionis. Hunc esse morem Scripturæ loquendi, ut Esa. 13,10. Stellæ cœlorum & sidera eorum non facient, ut luceat lux sua, tenebrosus erit sol ab exortu suo, & luna splendidam non edet lucem suam, & x) alibi. In eandem etiam mentem Abarbinel, cum verbis contremiscet terra innui velit, fore, ut incolæ regionis Judææ ea de causa contremiscant, atque ratione afflictionis ingentis dici, cæli tremunt, sol & luna obtenebrantur & stellæ retrahunt suum splendorem quod omne parabolica expressio sit calamitatum Judæorum, non secus ac ea, quibus Salomon utitur ad accidentalia illa designanda, quibus obruitur homo multis annis gravis (vel senectus y) dum non obtenebrescit sol. Ita ut præcipue z) spectet populum atque inhabitatores terræ, quicquid malorum vel adventus istiusmodi nubis locustarum, ut Kimchi, vel exercitus Babyloniorum, ut vult Abarbinel, erat illaturus. Illi enim cursu cœlorum imperturbato ac lumine solis, lunæ & stellarum grato hactenus infigniter gavisi adeo confusione obruti sunt, ut nihil non ipsis
units.tr: The Jewish commentators also seem to look to the same thing. Kimchi says that everything signifies the gravity of the affliction parabolically (or figuratively). That this is the manner of speaking in Scripture is shown by Isa. 13:10, The stars of the heavens and their constellations will not make their light shine; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not give forth its shining light, and elsewhere. Abarbanel also, in the same sense, wishes that by the words the earth will tremble it be signified that the inhabitants of the land of Judah will tremble for this reason, and that it is called by reason of the great affliction: the heavens tremble, the sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their brightness, because the whole expression is parabolic for the calamities of the Jews, just as those expressions which Solomon uses to designate those accidents by which a man burdened with many years is overwhelmed (or old age), while the sun is not darkened. So that it chiefly regards the people and the inhabitants of the land, whatever evils the coming of such a cloud of locusts (according to Kimchi), or of the army of the Babylonians (as Abarbanel holds), was going to bring. For they, who had hitherto rejoiced remarkably in the undisturbed course of the heavens and the light of the sun, moon and stars, are so overwhelmed with confusion that nothing is not to them

units.la: x) Ezech. 24, 29. y) Eccles. 12,2 quem etiam allegat Aben-Ezra. z) Aben-Ezra.
units.tr: x) Ezek. 24:29. y) Eccles. 12:2, which Aben-Ezra also cites. z) Aben-Ezra.

units.la: Tremunt hominos terræ.
units.tr: The men of the earth tremble.

units.la: ipsis conturbatum, nihil non prioris sueti ordinis expers vi sum sit, nec illis ipsis exceptis, quæ ordine suo omnibus aliis prælucent. Addit tamen idem Abarbinel sequentia verba cœli tremunt &c. ad literam posse intelligi, atque indicare putat, cœlos vires suas malignas in Ierusalem exserturos, cum ita Deum provocassent, ut merito faciem suam ab eo averteret. Placet quoque hæc parabolica sive hyperbolica verborum expositio quibusdam, ne dicam plurimis, recentioribus inter Christianos interpretibus, sive de locustis, sive de hostibus ea caeteroquin intelligant. Omnes enim eo redeunt, magnum hominum indicari motum, agitationesque animorum incitatas sive locustarum nube aerem contegentium, cœlosque obscurantium, sive multitudine atque ingenti tumultu hostium obvia quæque miscentium & in confusionem redigentium, ita ut omnia ipsis adeo viderentur consusa ac perturbata, ac si ea ipsa revera facta essent, quæ hic ad literam consignantur. Hinc Drusius, quamvis in diversum eum abire toto hoc versu antea viderimus, tamen ad ultima verba notat: ita videtur metu conflernatis. Citat quoque illum locum, quo illis, qui senio caligant, dicitur sol, lux & luna caligare obscurarique, Eccles. 12,2.
units.tr: Abarbanel nevertheless adds that the following words, the heavens tremble, etc., can be understood literally, and he thinks they indicate that the heavens will unleash their malign powers upon Jerusalem, since they had so provoked God that he justly turned his face away from them. This parabolic or hyperbolic explanation of the words also pleases some, not to say most, of the more recent Christian interpreters, whether they understand the locusts or the enemy by it. For they all come back to this: that a great stirring of men is indicated, and the agitation of minds aroused, whether by a cloud of locusts covering the air and darkening the heavens, or by the multitude and great tumult of the enemy mixing up and reducing to confusion whatever lies in their way, so that everything seemed to them so confused and disturbed, as if those very things that are written here literally had really happened. Hence Drusius, although we saw earlier that he goes off in a different direction on this whole verse, nevertheless notes on the last words: so it seems, with people dismayed by fear. He also cites that passage in which it is said of those who are dim with age that the sun, light and moon grow dark and are obscured, Eccles. 12:2.

units.la: Verum restat adhuc alia horum verborum interpretatio, quam nonnulli ea quidem per allegoriam dicta esse putant, sed volunt per terram intelligi homines, vel res inferioris conditionis, vel communis ordinis; per solem, lunam & stellas, qui insignioris sunt conditionis; per prædicata vero, quæ horum cuique assignantur, nimirum contremiscet, tremunt, & retrahent suum splendorem, illum ingentem pavorem atque calamitates, quibus quisque pro sua conditione atque statu erat corripiendus, cum ab hujus ignis ferocitate nihil quicquam immune foret. Nec desunt a) qui hanc interpretandi rationem approbant, quos inter & D. Stokius est in sua Paraphrasi, cujus verba „hic apponere haud supervacaneum reor: Potest per terræ motus „horrendos effectus intelligi pavor plebejorum & qui sunt ex „populi; per cœlorum superiorumque virium tremorem ruinamobiliū;
units.tr: There remains yet another interpretation of these words. Some think they are said allegorically, but want "earth" to mean men, or things of lower or common rank, and "sun, moon and stars" to mean those of higher rank. By the predicates assigned to each, namely "will tremble, they tremble, and withdraw their brightness," they understand that immense dread and those calamities with which each person, according to his condition and station, was to be seized, since nothing would be immune from the ferocity of this fire. Some <a> also approve this method of interpretation, among them Mr. Stokius in his Paraphrase, whose words I think it not superfluous to set down here: "The terror of commoners and of those of the people may be understood by the dreadful effects of earthquakes; the trembling of the heavens and of the higher powers by the ruin of mobile things;

units.la: a) Occolamp. Danæus omnibus rebus tum pavorem denuntiat futurum Joel cum mo-mu, quæ terra nomine designantur, tum etiam maximu ac eminentissimu, qua sol, luna ac stellarum vocabula hic comprehenduntur. bilium; tristis confusio omnium ordinū ac legum (quæ fe invicem" sequuntur) per solis atque lunæ obtenebrationem, nec non per" stellas, quæ splendorem suum consuetum retrahunt; interrostem" tam omnium spectatorum, quam harum inprimis illustrium perso-" narum, quas potissimum hæc calamitas spectat. Quomodocunque" vero hæc allegoria etiam possit probabilis reddi, imo, etiamsi de rei veritate nemini queat subire dubitatio; tamen hanc sententiam" huic loco tam apte non congruere, quam priorem, omnino perstum habeo, qua scilicet hyperbolice sumuntur verba, eaque, quæ minus ordinaria sunt in suo genere, talibus terminis concipiuntur, quæ rebus sublimioris naturæ proprie conveniunt. Mira certe res est, fateor, idque libenter, talia malorum instrumenta, sive locustas, sive hostes fortissimos intet homines juxta quosdam intelligas, tam terribilia, ut verba habent, esse effectura; verum omnis mirandi occasio protinus evanescet, si probe intellexerimus, quomodo & a quo hoc oneris ipsis sit impositum, cujusque viribus ac jussu, quicquid effecerunt, perpetraverint, quod ex sequentibus verbis pluribus videre est.
units.tr: a) Occolampadius and Danaeus: Joel announces that terror will come in all things, both those designated by the word earth and also the greatest and most eminent, which are comprehended here under the words sun, moon and stars. mobile things; a sad confusion of all orders and laws (which follow one another) through the darkening of the sun and moon, and likewise through the stars, which withdraw their customary brightness; in short, the destruction of all spectators, and especially of those illustrious persons whom this calamity chiefly concerns." However this allegory may be made probable, and even if no one can doubt the truth of the matter, I am entirely certain that this opinion fits this place no better than the former one does. The former is that words are used hyperbolically, and that things less ordinary in their kind are described in terms properly suited to things of a more sublime nature. It is indeed a remarkable thing, I admit and gladly so, that such instruments of evil, whether locusts or the most fierce enemies, which some understand as men, should be going to bring about things as terrible as the words say. But every occasion for wonder will immediately vanish if we have properly understood how and by whom this burden was laid upon them, and by whose power and command they carried out whatever they accomplished. This may be seen more fully from the following words.

units.la: 11. Et Dominus edet vocem suam ante exercitum suum: Nam campus ejus est valde amplus: Nam fortis est qui exsequitur suum verbum, nam dies Domini est magnus & valde terribilis, & quis potest eum sustinere?
units.tr: 11. And the Lord shall utter his voice before his army, for his camp is very great; for he is strong who executes his word; for the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, and who can endure it?

units.la: Variæ hic iterum horum verborum sunt interpretationes, at in eundem scopum, quotquot sunt, unanimi consensu collineant. Et Dominus,inquit, נתן קולו Natan kolo edet suam vocem, ad literam, dedit vel edidit suam vocem, quippe verbum temporis præteriti est, eaque forma a quamplurimis redditum. In quibus Vulgat. Et Dominus dedit vocem suam. Sic multi alii tum antiquiores, tum recentiores, ut Syrus ܢܬܬ yahab koleh, dedit suam vocem (utut latinus interpres reddat dabit) Chaldæus אריו
units.tr: There are various interpretations of these words here too, but however many there are, they all aim unanimously at the same goal. "And the Lord," he says, נתן קולו [Natan kolo] will give or utter his voice. Literally it is "gave or uttered his voice", since the verb is in the past tense, and very many render it this way. Among them is the Vulgate: And the Lord gave his voice. So do many others, both older and more recent, such as the Syriac, yahab koleh, gave his voice (although the Latin translator renders it "will give"), and the Chaldee [אריו].

units.la: u
units.tr: u

units.la: מיטרו ארים levavit verbum suum, quo cum convenit MS. Arabicum ﻭﻧﻮﺳ ﺳ ﺭﻓ levavit vocem suam. Ita quoque ex recentioribus Interlinear. & Munst. &c. At tempore futuro LXX. καὶ κύριος δώσει φωνὴν αὐτῆς, quorum vestigia premit Arab. impressa الرب يعطي ... Dominus dabit suam vocem, nec non alii b) recentiorum, quibus cum faciunt noitrates reddendo edet, locoque futuri hic positum esse tempus praeteritum c) quibusdam observatum est. d) Sunt etiam quibus praesenti tempore exponere complacitum fuit, edit vocem suam, vel sonitum edit. Atqui non est horum quisquam, qui linguae usu interpretationem suam non tueatur, quo, ut nosmet ipsi jam e) ante annotavimus, indiscriminatim hoc tempore utuntur Prophetae de rebus vel praesentibus, vel futuris, vel etiam praeteritis, ad denotandum illarum certitudinem ac necessitatem, ita ut loquendi formae nihil praejudicet, sive hoc judicium locustas aliasque supra memoratas bestiolas immissas jamjam orsum fuisse, vel adhucdum denunciatum tantum dixeris. Junius & Tremellius nihil hic definiunt, cum temporibus omnibus posthabitis per participium efferunt, quod ei congruit tempori, cui adjungitur. Jehova autem edente vocem suam ante copias suas &c. eqxus sufflinebit ... ? Verum nullius ferme momenti est haec differentia prae illa, quam invenimus apud interpretes circa verba: vocem suam, quando dicitur: Dominus edet vocem suam ante exercitum suum. Quid hic per vocem suam intelligendum sit, *) Judaeorum quorundam opiniones, quas primo loco adducimus, inprimis audiendae sunt, quibus per vocem Domini intelligunt verbum Domini ori Prophetarum suorum inditum, ut judicii gravitatem praedicerent, ac si significaretur, haec omnia ipsis ex improviso & fortuito non accidere, sed quibus satis superque a Prophetis essent pramoniti, ut ea ratione non cunctarentur ad frugem redire. At hanc interpretationem horum alius (Aben-Ezra) dicit אינבי על דרך השלש non ... rationem linguae. Hinc per vocem intelligit a) suam magnum, quem, Deo
units.tr: [מיטרו ארים] lifted up his word, with which agrees the Arabic manuscript, which reads (transliterated) rafaʿa ṣawtahu, lifted up his voice. So too among more recent writers the Interlinear and Münster, and others. But the Septuagint has the future tense: καὶ κύριος δώσει φωνὴν αὐτῆς [kai kyrios dōsei phōnēn autēs], "and the Lord will give his voice," and the printed Arabic follows their footsteps: (transliterated) al-Rabb yuʿti..., the Lord will give his voice. Likewise other recent writers, with whom our own translators agree in rendering will utter. Some have observed that the past tense is used here in place of the future. Others have preferred to explain it in the present tense, utters his voice, or utters a sound. Yet none of these fails to defend his rendering by the usage of the language, in which, as we ourselves have already noted, the prophets use this tense indiscriminately of present, future or even past things, to denote their certainty and necessity. So the form of the verb decides nothing, whether one takes this judgment to have already begun with the locusts and the other creatures mentioned above, or regards it as still merely announced. Junius and Tremellius settle nothing here: they set aside all the tenses and render it by a participle that agrees with the tense to which it is attached: But Jehovah, uttering his voice before his forces, etc. ...? Yet this difference is of almost no importance compared with the one we find among the interpreters about the words his voice, when it is said: The Lord will utter his voice before his army. As to what is to be understood here by his voice, the opinions of certain Jews, which we cite first, must above all be heard. By the voice of the Lord they understand the word of the Lord placed in the mouth of his prophets, to foretell the severity of judgment, as if it were meant that these things would not come upon them suddenly and by chance, but that they had been warned more than enough by the prophets, so that they should not hesitate in this way to return to soberness. But another (Aben Ezra) says of this interpretation: [אינבי על דרך השלש] "not according to the rule of the language." Hence he understands by his voice a great [voice], which, Deo

units.la: b) Pagnin. c) Vatabl. Pisc. d) Tig. Mere. Calvin. e) Viteb. in c. 1. v. 4. & praeced. verf. *) R. Salom. R. D. Kimchi, Abarbinel. a) Verf. 1. Deo sic dirigente, executores judiciorum excitabant, ut non inhabitatores terræ tantum, verum & ipsa terra, eo tremescerent, & quo b) alius alii animum addebat in c) rite exsequendis & obeundis muniis, quæ a Deo erant impositæ. Verum harum sententiarum priorem nimis frigidam censet Mercerus, posteriorem, quæ est Aben-Ezræ, longe alieniorem. Sequuntur itaque d) Christiani iique potissimum, qui per vocem suam intelligi volunt tonitru, quo adventus illorum præsentiæ suæ indicandæ causa, metusque faciendi in hominibus erat conjunctus. Quod enim vox Domini alias tonitru denotet, perquam notum est ex Psal. 18,13. & 29,3. &c. Quod tamen aliis non probatur, utpote qui haud necessarium ducunt, tam gravem aresque tam acriter ferientem vocem subintelligi, sed ordinem Dei, quo agmen suum vel campum, ut ipse ait, admirandum in modum armabat alacritate atque animo ei addito, ut voluntatem atque jussum ipsius rite obiret & exsequeretur, quod interdum e) plus animi addit, quam vox imperatoris milites hortantis. Atque sic faciendo probaret, ad neminem alium, quam ad se, spectaturas has copias, talique ordinis ratione ob campi magnitudinem & numerum opus fore, ut singuli ordinem suum servarent munusque suum præstarent, quod pro irresistibili vi ac pertinacia erant præstituri. Nam fortis est qui exsequitur suum verbum, i. e. qui verbi sui exsequendi eos dedit ministros atque hoc onus illis imposuit, is etiam instruet eos virtute atque potentia, ut nihil tam forte, nihil tam firmum futurum sit, quod eos vel cohibeat vel remoretur in mandatis ejus obeundis. Quocirca non difficile intellectu est, quanta essent obruendi calamitate, quorum in perniciem tantus exercitus erat instructus. Nam dies Domini est magnus & valde terribilis, & quis poterit eum sustinere? Dies Domini] f) Quo se ipsum manifestum reddet exercendo hujusmodi judicium in suos hostes, extraordinarius erit dies, isque valde terribilis propter calamitatem, quam per vindictæ suæ instrumenta Deus erat immissurus, ita ut nihil eum posset sustinere. Proferendi ratio fit.
units.tr: b) Pagnin. c) Vatabl. Pisc. d) Tig. Mere. Calvin. e) Viteb. on c. 1, v. 4, and the preceding verse. *) R. Salom., R. D. Kimchi, Abarbinel. a) Verse 1. With God thus directing, he roused the executors of the judgments, so that not only the inhabitants of the land but the land itself trembled at them, and one encouraged another b) to carry out and discharge rightly the duties c) that had been imposed by God. But Mercerus judges the former of these opinions too cold, and the latter, that of Aben Ezra, far too remote. Accordingly the Christians follow, and especially those who wish his voice to be understood as thunder, which was joined with the coming of those forces to indicate his presence and to produce fear in men. For that the voice of the Lord elsewhere denotes thunder is very well known from Psalm 18:13 and 29:3, etc. This, however, is not approved by others, who think it unnecessary to supply so heavy a voice striking so sharply, but take it to mean the order of God, by which he marshalled his host, or the field, as he says, in a wonderful manner, and added eagerness and courage to them, so that they might rightly carry out and perform his will and command. Sometimes he adds more courage than the voice of a commander encouraging his soldiers. And in doing so he would show that these forces would be directed at no one but himself, and that by such an arrangement of order, because of the size of the field and the number, it would be necessary for each to keep his own place and perform his duty, which they were going to carry out with irresistible force and perseverance. For he is strong who carries out his word, that is, he who has given ministers for executing his word and has laid this burden upon them, will also equip them with virtue and power, so that nothing shall be so strong or so firm that could restrain or delay them in carrying out his commands. Hence it is not difficult to understand how great a calamity was to overwhelm those for whose destruction so great an army had been arrayed. For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, and who can endure it? The day of the Lord f) When he shows himself by carrying out such judgment upon his enemies, the day will be extraordinary, and very terrible because of the calamity that God was going to send through the instruments of his vengeance, so that nothing could withstand him. The reason for the expression is given.

units.la: b) Verf. 10. c) Druf. d) Livel. Druf. e) Merc. f) Ira etiam appellatur supra cap. 1,15. Hinc talem diem ita vocari notat Maimonides, quo Dominus manifestat liberationem insignem aut executionem, eamque in finem hunc locum citat M. S. part. 2, c. 29. fit per quæstionem, quis sustinebit? qua protinus negatur in rerum natura esse, quod id facere queat. Omni doctrina ac eruditione conspicuus Bochartus reddit: Dominus dedit vocem suam ante exercitum suum, ut magna sint castra ejus & multus sit &c. Nam dies Domini est magnus & valde terribilis, & quis poterit eum sustinere? Quæ ita explicat: Dominus verbo suo f) multas conscripsit copias, ut graviter in peccatores judicium exerceat, quodque nemo sustinere possit. Atque ea ipsi videtur sententia Prophetæ, quamvis interpretes aliter sentiant. Quemadmodum vero in prioribus variantium discrepantium interpretationum ratio habita est, ita earundem habebimus etiam in sequentibus. Ubi enim nostrates habent: Nam fortis est qui exsequitur suum verbum. Vulgat. reddit, quia (scil. castra ejus) fortia & faciens verbum ejus. Græce: ὅτι ἰσχυρὰ ἔργα λόγων αὐτοῦ, quia opera verborum suorum sunt fortia, ut & Syriac. & Arabic. ... et forte est opus verbi sui, nec non Arab. impress. ... MS. Arab. ... Magnus vel fortis est qui facit suum verbum, pariter ut nostrates. At hujusmodi non sunt ità differentiæ, ut sensui vel minimam possint inducere variationem, quippe omnes eo tendunt, Prophetam illos hisce excitare velle, ut mente percipérent instans conditionis suæ periculum, credérentque certo futura esse, quæ tamdiu in prophetia sua minatus erat, judicia gravia, nisi ab ipsis prævenirentur, nec illorum propriis viribus posse prævenire, instrumentis licet exilibus ac cæteroquin facile repellendis a DEO adhibitis, quippe quæ non sua sponte agerent, sed jussu divino, qui hanc provinciam ipsis imposuerit, atque ejus virtute, cui resisti non posset: hinc nullam aliam evadendi adventus illorum terrorem restare viam, quam propositum redeundi cum DEO in gratiam pœnitentia feria, quo uno fortean moveri posset, ut datum revocaret, pœnæque ac calamitatis eum pœniteret, quam ipse infligere constituerat. Atque ex præcedentibus verbis ut loculenter
units.tr: b) Verse 10. c) Drusius. d) Livelius, Drusius. e) Mercerus. f) He is called wrath also above, chap. 1:15. Hence Maimonides notes that such a day is so named when the Lord displays a remarkable deliverance or execution, and to this end he cites this passage, M. S. part 2, c. 29. It is done by the question, who shall endure it? which is at once denied to exist in the nature of things, that anyone could do so. The very learned Bochart renders: The Lord gave his voice before his army, so that his camp is great and very numerous, etc. For the day of the Lord is great and very terrible, and who can endure it? He explains this thus: By his word the Lord has enrolled many forces, so that he may execute severe judgment upon sinners, and that no one can endure. This seems to me the sense of the prophet, although the interpreters think otherwise. Just as in the earlier passages I have taken account of the variant and differing interpretations, so I shall do also in what follows. Where our people have: For strong is he who carries out his word. The Vulgate renders: because (namely his camp) is strong and does his word. In Greek: ὅτι ἰσχυρὰ ἔργα λόγων αὐτοῦ [because the works of his words are strong], as also the Syriac and Arabic... and perhaps is the work of his word, and also the printed Arabic... the manuscript Arabic... Great or strong is he who does his word, likewise as our people. But these differences are not such as could introduce the slightest variation into the sense, since all tend to this: that the prophet wishes to rouse them to grasp in mind the danger of their present condition, and to believe with certainty that the grave judgments he had so long threatened in his prophecy are to come, unless they forestall them; and that they cannot forestall them by their own strength, even with instruments that are feeble and otherwise easily repelled, which God employs. For these would not act of their own accord but by divine command, which has imposed this task on them, and by his power, which cannot be resisted. Hence no way of escaping the terror of their coming remains except the purpose of returning to God into grace by timely repentance, which alone might perhaps move him to revoke what he had given, and to repent of the punishment and calamity he had determined to inflict. And from the preceding words, as it is plainly said...

units.la: f) Et nuncer & robore vertes dici posse, vel multos fuisse qui verbum ejus exegerunt, Deulusoblervat. ter apparet, quam necessarium sit hanc inire viam; ita in sequentibus ad eam eos adhortatur haud sine magna spe boni successus.
units.tr: f) And it may be rendered "and with strength" or "in strength", or that there were many who carried out his word. God observes how plainly it appears how necessary it is to enter upon this way; so in what follows he exhorts them to it, not without great hope of a good outcome.

units.la: 12. Quocirca ita nunc, inquit Dominus, convertimi- ni omnino ad me toto corde vestro, & jejunio, & fletu, & planctu.
units.tr: 12. Therefore now, says the Lord, turn to me with your whole heart, and with fasting, and weeping, and mourning.

units.la: ונם עתה נאם יהוה שבו ad literam: Nunc ergo dictum Jehovæ, convertimini. De constructione horum verborum notat Drusius particulas, nunc ergo, non esse conjungendas cum verbo convertimini, ac si dictum esset: Dominus dicit, nunc ergo, (vel jam tamen) convertimini; sed cum Dominus inquit, ita ut sonent: Dominus nunc ergo dicit, convertimini ad me: Sicut antea quam saepissime per Prophetas eos vocaverat, ita etiam nunc, jam adhuc, eos vocat, ut convertantur. g) Aliis tamen altera constructio arridet magis quia dictum putant a Domino: jam demum convertimini ad me; nec admodum magni refert, utri harum assentiaris; quippe utraque indicat, hujus generis quamvis essent judicia hactenus descripta ac denunciata, ut iis resistendis vel perferendis incolae terrae nequaquam forent pares, atque ideo res iplorum ad incitas plane viderentur redactae; attamen spei locum adhuc superesse, quam ferventissimas etiam inter minas ipse DEus fecerat, invitando eos atque vocando, ut ea, quae sibi horrenda pariter ac divina vindicta digna provocaverant, vel futura praevenirent, vel praesentia longe a se averruncarent. Cui vero aetati haec vocatio maxime congruat, Abarbinel ausus est determinare, cum ad illud tempus praecipue spectare dicat, quod delapsum est primo templo devastato atque Judaeis in Babylonia captivis, b) rationemque hic haberi liberationis ex captivitate posteriorisque templi aedificationis, ac si diceret: etsi ad frugem prius redire noluistis, quam ea omnia vos nisi ge corrumpuerunt; attamen & nunc post hanc destructionem ac captivitatem dicit vobis DEus, convertimini. Quo cum
units.tr: Literally: "Now therefore, the saying of Jehovah: turn" [ונם עתה נאם יהוה שבו]. On the construction of these words, Drusius notes that the particles "now therefore" are not to be joined with the verb "turn", as if it were said: the Lord says, "now therefore" (or "yet now") turn; but rather with "the Lord says", so that they sound: "the Lord now therefore says, turn to me." Just as before, he had very often called them through the prophets, so now too, "even now, yet again", he calls them to turn. Others, however, prefer the other construction, because they think it is said by the Lord: "at last, turn to me"; nor does it matter greatly which of these you accept. For each indicates that, although the judgments described and announced so far were of such a kind that the inhabitants of the land were in no way equal to resisting or enduring them, and therefore their affairs seemed utterly reduced to despair, yet there remained room for hope, which God himself had given even amid the most fervent threats, inviting and calling them, that they might anticipate what was coming, or, if it was present, far away avert what had provoked this horrible divine vengeance. To what period this call most fits, Abarbanel dared to determine: he says that it chiefly looks to that time which followed the destruction of the first temple and the Jews' captivity in Babylon, and that there is regard here to deliverance from captivity and the building of the later temple, as if he said: although you were unwilling to return to soundness before all these things corrupted you, yet even now, after this destruction and captivity, God says to you, "turn." With which

units.la: g) Tamen si vel nunc saltem resipuerint &c. Liv. D. Stok. Etiam in hoc ipso tempore articulo Ibem Venia reflare clamavit. Tarnov. b) הם רם לקדרת כירם שבי cum facere videtur Arias Montanus, quando dicit: In hoc loco divina illa Judaicarum rerum restitutio praedicitur, quae post certos annos, hoc est septuaginta, contigit; quod DEus ita effecit, ut fartam tectam servaret hanc nationem, ex qua magnus ille totius mundi redemtor erat progressurus; cum vero jus fasque non esset, in homines fideatque poenitentia caeteros maxima a DEO conferri beneficia, etiam hoc tempore & in hac conditione constitutos Judaeos hortatur, ut huncin finem sese converterent. At sibi ipsis eam interpretandi rationem peculiarem, per me licet, referverent. Sunt alii, qui, praeterquam quod judiciorum divinorum, nobis approbantibus, constituant executores dictas locustas atque caeteras belluolas, ut supra vidimus, his verbis tantum praescribi putant rationem illarum ingressum vel praevenendi, vel jamjam ingressas removendi. Nec in contrarium euntihic quicquam, qui ab hostibus id omne factitatum censent. Ea vero ratio atque praeveniendi via nulla alia erat, quam talis respiscentia, cujus his verbis depingitur natura ac conditiones, quae ex ulteriori verborum inspectione & ordine clarius patebunt. Convertimini, inquit, ad me. Quod secuti erant, quodque adhuc sequebantur vitae institutum, hujusmodi fuisse videtur, quod a Deo eos abalienabat, atque efficiebat, ut praesentia sua gratiosa eos non amplius dignaretur, sed praedicta illis mala minaretur, vel immitteret, ut sentirent, quam necessario esset vitae ratio mutanda, atque ab his viis recedendi, ut ad eum sese converterent, &ad ea quae ei placerent; ad me, inquit, id est, secundum Chald. lepulchrani, ad meum: cultum, ac si cultum ejus abnegassent, aliis sese mancipantes, vel idolis, vel peccatis, vel utrisque simul, a quibus etiam necessario erat recedendum, si ea, quae pr erat, ratione ad DEum sese convertere vellent, qui clamat ad eos: Convertimini ad me, Adai, eben me, omnino ad me, quae particula eben sive omnino nostratibus peculiaris e, atque in interpretatione addita, ut magnam illam emphasin exprimerent, quae in voce latet, pro designando respiscentiae modo, quae requirebatur; quippe tales esse debebat, ut non solum ad eum retrorsum respicerent, sed ut venirent protinus vel omnino ad me, ea scilicet qua erat animi integritate ac sinceritate, ut ex sequentibus apparet בכל לבבם corde vestro. Corde id faciendum erat, non externo tantum indicio, sed interno affectu eoque totius cordis שלא תורה התשובה (inquit Kimchi) ita ut non fit poenitentia cum (vel ex) corde & corde, non i) duplici ac fraudulento corde, non corde diviso inter DEum & illorum idola, vel alia peccata, quod, licet conversionis ad DEum aliquam prae se ferat speciem, aliis tamen rebus adhuc delectatur, quae ita illud occupant, ut DEus pariter cum iis nequaquam diligi atque coli possit. Atque hoc idem est, quod ad amorem ac cultum DEI quam maxime requiritur, ut fiat ex toto nostro corde, ex toto nostro animo, & ex totis nostris viribus Deut. 6,5. k) Additur ex tota nostra cogitatione, Marc. 12,30. ubi istud a Salvatore nostro repetitur primum atque maximum mandatum, quo sine caeteris rite observari non possunt. Opus autem ad id perficiendum inprimis est corde, quod, cum omnia unum movere ac dirigere debeat, manifestum est, eo deficiente, omnia exterioris hominis esse insufficientia & vana, imo maxime DEO odiosa. Hinc omnium illud primum exigit in respicientia, ut animo interno fiat. Quod demum omni ex parte perfectum sequi etiam debent externa, utpote quae nequaquam sunt negligenda, sed ita juxta normam, quam habent, reformanda, ut vel hinc appareat quomodo interna habeant; quippe his denique junctis omnis respicientiae ratio expletur. Hinc, posteaquam tradiderat, qua ratione cordis totius intima constituta esse deberent, ad exteriora progreditur, quae, quibus signis rite constituta sese deberent prodere, his verbis indicat: & jejunio, & fletu, & planctu. (1.) Jejunio, quo humilis redditur animus, cum e contrario nimium curando cuticulam inflatur atque inhibetur, quo minus suae conditionis cultusque divini fit memor. Exemplo sit Jesurun, qui saginatus ac pinguis recalcitravit, & Deum deseruit, qui cum fecerat, & vilipendit rupem salutis suae, Deut. 32,15. Atque ideo ut plurimum illud conjungitur in S. literis cum cultus divini studio ac precibus, quibus illud necessario accedere debet & a DEO mandatum, & a sanctis nullo non tempore observatum. (2.) Et fletu & planctu, 1) Psal. 12,3. 1. Chron. 12,38. 4) Matth. 4, 3. planctu, quæ etiam communiter signa sunt, quibus animus gravi dolore ac tristitia obrutus sese prodit ac affectus eos exprimit, quos vis accensi ulterius procedendo cæteras etiam passiones excitant doloremque magis magisque augent, atque l) ita in ipsam personam operantur, cujus non tantum relipiscentiam, verum & indicia ejus non levia promovent. Ut jam silentio præteream, quam habeant vim in aliis similes affectus excitandi atque ad pœnitentiam provocandi, quod inprimis maximo usui est in cœtibus publicis, ac diebus relipiscentiæ causa publice indictis, quales hic fuisse videntur, quo tempore admirandum certe in modum devotionem promovet, cum m) exemplo suo alter alterum provocet. Quare optime de his Abr. Montanus: Hac enim si pure sanctèque fiant, non quidem converso ipsa, sed laudatissima sunt conversionis argumenta. Quæ quibus postro requisitis gaudere debeat, ut ratam eam habeat DEus, ex sequentibus apparet.
units.tr: g) Yet if even now at least they repent, etc. Livy, D. Stock. Even at this very time, Venia reflare cried out. Tarnovius. b) [הם רם לקדרת כירם שבי] Arias Montanus seems to do this when he says: In this place that divine restoration of Jewish affairs is foretold, which came about after a certain number of years, that is seventy; which God so arranged that he preserved this nation safe and sound, from which that great redeemer of the whole world was to come forth. But since it was neither right nor lawful, he exhorts the Jews, even at this time and in this condition, to turn themselves to this end, since by God great benefits are conferred on men and on others who trust and repent. Yet let them, for all I care, have their own peculiar way of interpreting it. There are others who, besides holding (with our approval) that the said locusts and other beasts are executors of the divine judgments, as we saw above, think that these words only prescribe the manner of forestalling their entry, or of removing them as soon as they have entered. Nor do those who think that all this was done by enemies oppose anything here. But that way of forestalling and that method were no other than such repentance as is depicted in these words, its nature and conditions, which will appear more clearly from the further examination of the words and their order. Turn, he says, to me. What they had followed, and what their way of life still followed, seems to have been of such a kind that it estranged them from God and caused him no longer to deign to show them his gracious presence, but rather to threaten or send the evils foretold, so that they might feel how necessarily the manner of their life must be changed, and that they must withdraw from those paths, to turn themselves to him and to the things that please him. To me, he says, that is, according to the Chaldee paraphrast, to my worship, as if they had renounced his worship and surrendered themselves to others, either to idols, or to sins, or to both at once, from which also they necessarily had to withdraw if they wished to turn to God in the manner set forth, he who cries out to them: Turn to me [Adai, eben] me, altogether to me. This particle eben, or "altogether", is peculiar to our people, and was added in translation so as to express that great emphasis which lies in the word, to designate the mode of repentance that was required; for it had to be of such a kind that they would not merely look back to him, but would come at once, "altogether to me", namely with that integrity and sincerity of mind which appears from what follows: with all their heart [בכל לבבם], with your heart. It had to be done with the heart, not only with an outward sign but with an inward affection, and with the whole of the heart; repentance that is not from the heart and heart (Kimchi says) [שלא תורה התשובה], not with a double and deceitful heart, not with a heart divided between God and their idols or other sins, which, though it has some appearance of conversion to God, is still delighted by other things, which occupy it so that God cannot be loved and worshipped along with them. And this is the same as what is most required for the love and worship of God: that it be done with the whole of our heart, the whole of our soul, and the whole of our strength (Deut. 6:5). It is added: with the whole of our thought (Mark 12:30), where our Saviour repeats this first and greatest commandment, which cannot be rightly observed without the others. But the work of accomplishing this is above all of the heart, which, since it ought to move and direct all things, is plainly such that, when it is lacking, all outward man is insufficient and vain, and indeed most odious to God. Hence in repentance it requires first of all that it be done in the inner mind. Then, when this is perfected in every respect, the outward things must also follow, since they are by no means to be neglected, but are to be reformed according to the rule they have, so that it may appear from this how the inward things stand; for when these are finally joined together, the whole account of repentance is fulfilled. Hence, after he had set forth in what manner the inmost parts of the whole heart ought to be constituted, he proceeds to the outward things, which he indicates in these words, by what signs they ought to show themselves rightly constituted: with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning. (1.) With fasting, by which the mind is made humble, whereas on the contrary excessive care for the body puffs it up and hinders it, so that it is not mindful of its condition or of divine worship. Let Jeshurun be an example, who, fat and gross, kicked, and forsook God who made him, and despised the rock of his salvation (Deut. 32:15). And so for the most part this is joined in Holy Scripture with zeal for divine worship and with prayers, to which it must necessarily be added, both commanded by God and observed by the saints at all times. (2.) And with weeping and with mourning [Psalm 12:3; 1 Chron. 12:38; Matt. 4:3], which are also commonly signs by which the mind, overwhelmed with grave sorrow and sadness, reveals itself and expresses the affections which, when they are kindled, proceeding further excite other passions and increase the grief more and more, and so work upon the very person, promoting not only his repentance but also its not slight signs. Not to mention in silence the power they have to stir up similar affections in others and to provoke them to repentance, which is especially of the greatest use in public assemblies and on days of public appointment for the sake of repentance, such as these seem to have been, at which time they certainly promote devotion in a wonderful manner, since one provokes another by his example. Wherefore Abraham Montanus has said well of these things: For if they are done purely and holily, they are not indeed conversion itself, but most praiseworthy evidences of conversion. How God ought to be pleased with these, given the requirements just mentioned, that he may hold them acceptable, appears from what follows.

units.la: 13. Et scindite cor vestrum & non vestimenta vestra, & convertimini ad Dominum DEum vestrum; quia benignus est & misericors, tardus ad iram & multæ misericordiæ, & pœnitens super malo.
units.tr: 13. "And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil."

units.la: Judæis olim, ut de aliis gentibus jam nihil attingam, folenne fuisse in testimonium magnæ indignationis, mæroris ac doloris animi scindere vestes, tot loquendi formulis ac Sacrarum literarum exemplis manifestum est, ut omni prorsus opera vel unum exemplum adducendi supersedere possimus. Quod cum adeo in consuetudinem abiisset, non est dubium, quin ratione fucosa & in speciem adhibita æque id factum sit ac sincera, multisque indicia mæroris quidem ediderint, at a veritate rei quam maxime nonnunquam abhorrentia. Quapropter ad veram sinceramque relipiscentiam eos hic adhortatur Propheta, ut non intime tantum compungerentur animo propter nefas admissum fumnio dolore afficerentur, verum ut rei etiam ederent signa atque indicia omni fuco carentia, addito simul cautione contra hypocriseos malum, ipsos scilicet sibi maxime imposituros esse, cum DEum fallere conarentur. Quibus equidem horum externorum rituum usu illis adeo non interdicit religionem tuæ tueri, sed satis aptorum, ut potius eos quam maxime videatur requirere eo, quod ad illos ipse eos invitare haud gravetur. Unde luculenter patet, his in verbis non latere eorum interdictum, sed mandatum, ut recte ritéque fierent, nimirum, non ad ostentationem vanam speciemque externam, sed ut essent conjuncti cum interno affectu, ingenuaque cordis intentione, quod hic significat cor scindere, non vestimenta (scilicet) solum.
units.tr: That it was once customary among the Jews (not to mention other nations) to rend their garments as a sign of great indignation, grief and sorrow of mind is clear from so many turns of phrase and examples in Sacred Literature that I may spare myself the trouble of citing even one. Since this custom had become so common, there is no doubt that it was often done with a feigned and show-making pretence just as much as with sincerity, and that many people displayed signs of grief which, at times, were most remote from the truth of the matter. For this reason the Prophet here urges them to a true and sincere repentance: not merely to be pricked inwardly in their minds on account of the wickedness they had committed, nor only to be affected with the greatest sorrow, but also to show outward signs and tokens of this that are free from all pretence. He adds a warning against the evil of hypocrisy, since they would be deceiving themselves most of all if they tried to deceive God. Indeed, the use of these outward rites does not forbid them to uphold their religion; rather, it seems to be something very suitable, so much so that he seems chiefly to require it, since he does not hesitate to invite them to it. Hence it is plainly evident that these words do not hide a prohibition of such things but a command that they be done rightly and properly, namely not for empty show and outward appearance, but joined with an inward feeling and sincere intention of heart. This is what the phrase rend the heart, not the garments (that is, not only the garments) signifies.

units.la: Obvium est cuique primo etiam intuitu, quid sit vestimenta scindere, cum verba sint clara atque perspicua: at difficilius explicatu est, quid sibi velint verba corda scindere, cum figurata sint atque aliquid indicent, quod verba proprie non complectuntur. Etenim hic innuí tale quid, quod ad emendandum corrigendumque conducit animum, non autem ad destruendum, ut verba habent, quivis videre poterit. Quare cum opponantur sibi invicem cordis ac vestimentorum scissio, per cordis scissionem requiri mihi videtur talis cordis status atque conditio, qualem vestimenta scissa indicare solebant, nimirum contriti sumus ob communem peccatì suæ dolor, cum ardentissimo veniæ & absolutionis desiderio conjunctus, quo cum cor revera est affectum, vocatur cor contritum, aut, quod ad textum nostrum alludit, cor scissum & laceratum; quæ loquendi ratio etiam aliis linguis familiaris est, quibus ea quæ graviter affligunt, alicujus animum pungere, vel quempiam usque ad intima cordis ferire dicuntur. In eandem sententiam reddunt hæc verba a Paraphraste Chaldaico יאערי רשע לבכיך & auferte (vel abjicite) impietatem cordis vestri; ea sub cordis nomine complectente, quæ in corde residet vel ex eo potissimum procedunt, & (id) non cum dilaceratione vestimentorum vestrorum (scil. solummodo). Sunt qui lucem allundere conantur huic phrasi scindite cor vestrum, quatenus cum alia cam p) comparant, quæ est Deut. 14, 16. Circumcidetis
units.tr: Anyone can see at first glance what rending the garments means, since the words are clear and plain. But it is more difficult to explain what the words rend the heart mean, since they are figurative and point to something that the words do not properly express. For it is plainly implied here that something is required which serves to amend and correct the mind, not to destroy it, as the words might suggest, as anyone can see. Therefore, since the rending of the heart and the rending of the garments are set against each other, I think that by rending of the heart is meant such a state and condition of the heart as torn garments were wont to indicate, namely: we are crushed by grief over our common sin, joined with a most ardent desire for pardon and absolution. When the heart is truly affected in this way, it is called a contrite heart, or, to allude to our text, a rent and lacerated heart. This manner of speaking is also familiar in other languages, in which things that grievously afflict someone are said to pierce a person's mind, or to strike someone to the very depths of the heart. The Chaldee paraphrast renders these words to the same effect: [ יאערי רשע לבכיך ] and remove (or cast away) the impiety of your heart, comprising under the name of heart those things which dwell in the heart or proceed chiefly from it, and (this) not with the tearing of your garments (namely, only). Some try to shed light on this phrase, rend your heart, by comparing it with another phrase, Deut. 14:16. Circumcise

units.la: n) Pial. 51, 17. o) Kimchi ita sensum concipit: Si laceraveritis cor vestrum, & ab co malam emendationem abstulerit, non necesse habebitis scindere vestes vestras, ut homo scindit vestes tempore afflictionis & angustiæ. p) Aben-Ezra. itis praeputium cordis vestri, quod de substantia vel materiali quadam cordis parte accipi non potest, sed de removendis ejus corruptis qualitatibus, nec non de ejus stoliditate atque crassitie, ut habet eo loco Chaldaeus. Id enim seriae tandem resipiscentiae indicium est atque opus, quo sine, quacunque demum vel carnis, vel vestimentorum, vel exterioris hominis extiterint signa, vana esse atque nullius usus merito dixeris; cum e contrario incredibile, quantum conjuncta cum ea conducant tum ad alios ad eandem excitandum, tum ad genuinum ejus exinde petendum testimonium. Et quemadmodum illa circumcisio sine manibus vocatur Col. 2,11. ita & hic cordis circumcisio sine manibus efficitur, quarum utraque est in spiritu, non litera; de altera loquitur Rom. 2,29. atque consistit in exuendo corpore praeputorum carnis, Col. 2,11. Atque adeo vere poenitentis cordis nullum ossicium est majus, quam omnia ea peccata protinus excutere, quibus hactenus adeo assuetum erat, ut in naturam abierint & sic veluti pars reddita sint. Hinc quoque est, ut Judaeos haud desperare jubeat Propheta, quasi melioris fortunae spei non esset locus, sed ad Dominum converti, misericordiamque ejus humiliter implorare, in hunc modum atque finem omnes occultissimos cordis sui recessus, quasi dilacerando ac refricando, diligenti ac sedula inquisitione scrutati fuissent, omnia ejus abominanda detexissent, lacrymis & resipiscentia infucata abluissent, iisque in posterum planissime decrevissent, quamvis adeo prioribus Deum provocassent peccatis, ut vix revocari posse viderentur saevissima supplicia, quae immittere plus semel antea iis minatus fuerat. Et convertimini (inquit) ad Dominum Deum vestrum. Eadem occurrit adhortatio in praecedenti versu, ea tantum differentia, quod ibi ex ipsius DEI ore procedat ac sub ejus ipsius persona dicatur, convertimini ad me; cum hoc loco ex ore Prophetae procedant verba, quibus ita de DEO loquitur, ut simul addat, quae poterant in illis excitare q) audaciam & confidentiam eum convenientis, cui appropinquare alias veniti fuissent, ejusque de gratia desperassent, haud nescii quantopere eum irritassent, quibusque terribilibus minis ac judiciis sese illis per Prophetam suum revelasset. Nomina, quibus {q} Ephes. 3, 12. bus hic appellatur יהוה & Elohim, docent eum esse DEum & misericors, iudicu & gratiæ, neque misericordiæ neque condonationis limites habentem. In priore iis sese exhibuerat. Quare ut posteriorì scilicet gratiæ suæ eius in illos voluntas, sat superque etiam constaret, a loco affixum בית־אל hem Dei...
units.tr: n) Ps. 51:17. o) Kimchi understands the sense thus: If you rend your heart, and it has taken away the evil amendment from it, you will not need to rend your garments, as a man rends his garments in a time of affliction and distress. p) Aben Ezra. the foreskin of your heart, which cannot be taken of some substance or material part of the heart, but of removing its corrupt qualities, and also of its stupidity and thickness, as the Chaldee paraphrast has there. For this is at last the sign and work of a serious repentance, and though outward signs of flesh, garments or the outward man may appear, you may rightly call them empty and of no use without it. On the contrary, it is incredible how much such outward things, when joined with this inward repentance, help both to stir up others to the same and to obtain from it a genuine testimony. And just as that circumcision made without hands is called Col. 2:11, so here too the circumcision of the heart is effected without hands; each of these is in the spirit, not in the letter. The former is spoken of in Rom. 2:29, and consists in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, Col. 2:11. Indeed, the truly repentant heart has no greater duty than to shake off at once all those sins to which it had so long been accustomed that they have passed into its nature and so have become, as it were, a part of it. Hence the Prophet also bids the Jews not to despair, as if there were no room for hope of better fortune, but to turn to the Lord and humbly implore his mercy. To this end and in this manner, having searched out all the most hidden recesses of their hearts with diligent and careful inquiry, as if by tearing and scraping them open, and having uncovered all their abominable things, they should wash them away with tears and unfeigned repentance, and should resolve most plainly for the future, although they had so provoked God by their earlier sins that the most cruel punishments, which he had more than once threatened to bring upon them, seemed scarcely capable of being recalled. And turn (he says) to the Lord your God. The same exhortation occurs in the preceding verse, with this one difference: there the words proceed from God's own mouth and are spoken in his own person, turn to me; here the words proceed from the mouth of the Prophet, speaking of God in such a way that he adds what could stir up in them boldness and confidence in approaching one with whom they would otherwise have shrunk from coming and had despaired of his grace, though they well knew how greatly they had provoked him and with what terrible threats and judgments he had revealed himself to them through his Prophet. The names by which he is called here, יהוה and Elohim, show that he is God, and merciful, just and gracious, having no limits of mercy or pardon. In the former, he had shown himself to them thus. Therefore, that his will towards them in the latter, namely of grace, might also be sufficiently and more than sufficiently established, [the Prophet adds] from the place fixed as the house of God [בית־אל]...

units.la: Quo sibi eos adhuc tanquam proprium suum populum vindicat, sequi ipsum illorum Deum vocat. Etenim omni prorsus vacat dubio, DEum nequaquam eum desertum esse, quem sibi adhuc tanquam proprium asserit. At pluribus hoc declaratur, amplificatur ac confirmatur per alia epitheta ac proprietates, quæ rationis loco subjunguntur, ne ad eum converti vel ullum dubium vel moram nectant, nimirum, quia benignus est ac misericors. Conveniunt hæc attributa DEI cum illis, quibus nomen suum voluerat esse cognitum Exod. 34.6. Eadem quippe ibi inveniuntur verba priora, nec differunt nisi ordine, quæ initio sunt posita duo, quamvis a nostratibus diversimode reddantur. Ibi enim habent: misericors & benignus, longanimis & abundans probitate & fide; hic vero: benignus & misericors, tardus ad iram & multæ misericordiæ. Quod, cum ita visum fuerit nostratibus, quamvis ovum ovo non adeo simile sit, quam veritas utriusque hujus loci in textu hebraico huncin finem id factum esse fixeris, ut alterum conferamus ac explicemus ex interpretatione alterius, quoad sensum diversi nihil importantis. Ultimum vero attributum רבך־ו & pœnitet ipsum (vel pœnitens ut sit adjectivum notante Aben-Ezra) mali, cæteris in Exodo expresse non subjungitur, etiam ex sequentibus colligi facile potest, ubi dicitur, condonatio iniquitatem, defectionem & peccatum eorum enim condonatio s) involvit id, quod innuitur verbis pœnitens mali, quod immittere numatus fuerat. Magis patet horum attributorum priorum sensus cuiusque probe ea in piscicu, quam ut aliis verbis ea enodari operis sit. Difficiliora autem sunt intellectu quæ sequuntur, pœnitens fper malo, cum nonnulli antiqui habeat vox pœnitens. Nam passim dicitur, DEum alicujus rei pœnitere, ut Gen. 6, 6. Pœnituit DEum, quod secisset hominem, & 1. Sam. 15, 11. pœnituit eum quod constituisset Saulem Regem,
units.tr: By this he still claims them as his own people, calling him the God of them. For there is absolutely no doubt that God has not forsaken the one whom he still declares to be his own. But this is declared, enlarged and confirmed by many other epithets and properties, which are added as reasons, so that they should not hold back from turning to him through any doubt or delay, namely because he is gracious and merciful. These attributes of God agree with those by which he wished his name to be known, Exod. 34:6. Indeed, the same first words are found there, and they differ only in order, the two that are placed at the beginning, although our people render them differently. For there they have: merciful and gracious, long-suffering and abundant in goodness and truth; but here: gracious and merciful, slow to anger and of great kindness. Since this seemed good to our people, although one egg is not so like another, you will find that the truth of each of these passages in the Hebrew text was done for this end: that we may compare the one and explain it from the interpretation of the other, the sense being in no way different. But the last attribute, רבך־ו [and abundant in kindness], and repents (or, as Aben Ezra takes it as an adjective, repenting) of the evil, is not expressly added to the others in Exodus, though it can easily be gathered from what follows there, where it is said that he pardons iniquity, transgression and sin; for their pardon involves what is implied by the words repenting of the evil, which he had threatened to bring upon them. The sense of the earlier of these attributes is clearer to anyone who has properly considered them in their context, and it would be a work to explain them in other words. But what follows is more difficult to understand, repenting of the evil, since the word repenting has in some ancient authors a different sense. For it is said in many places that God repents of something, as in Gen. 6:6. God repented that he had made man, and 1 Sam. 15:11. he repented that he had made Saul king,

units.la: r) Ubi vant Elohim est nomen plurale. יהוה nomen gentis. Ar. Mont. Buxtorf. s) Mercer.
units.tr: r) Where the word Elohim is a plural noun. [יהוה] Yhwh is the name of the nation. Ar. Mont. Buxtorf. s) Mercer.

units.la: Regem, & Jon. 4, 2. non secus atque hoc loco, poenituit me mali, Sic Moses a Domino petit, ut se converteret, ne accenderetur ira sua & poeniteret eum iflius mali, quod proposuerit contra populum suum, Ex. 32,12. Verf. 14. habetur. Tuna poenituit Deum iflius mali, quod fecerat populo suo ... E contrario alibi in locis citatis, Deus non poenitere nec posse poenitere. Ita Num. 23, 19. Deus non est homo, ut mentiatur, aut filius hominis, quem poeniteat; & 1. Sam. 15. cum ea, quem ante adduximus, dictum erat, eum poenitentiam, v. 29. subjungitur: fortitudo Israelis non commutabit poenitentiam, neque poenitebit eum, non enim homo est, ut poeniteat eum.
units.tr: Regem, and Jon. 4, 2. just as in this place: it repented me of the evil. So Moses asks the Lord to turn, so that his anger may not be kindled and that he would repent of the evil which he had proposed against his people (Ex. 32:12). Verse 14 has it: so the Lord repented of the evil which he had spoken of doing to his people. On the contrary, elsewhere in the passages cited, God does not repent, nor can he repent. So Num. 23:19: God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent. And in 1 Sam. 15, after the words quoted above, with that repentance (v. 29) is added: the Strength of Israel will not change his purpose, nor will he repent, for he is not a man that he should repent.

units.la: Quae loca cum sibi invicem videantur contraria, manifestum est diversi sensu poenitentia & poenitere vocem, nempe, quatenus usurpatur proprie & potissimum de hominibus, quo tenus DEO non attribuitur, sed alio, quatenus etiam DEO convenit, attribui potest. Proprie igitur & striction significat accepta mentis eorum, de quibus sermo est, notat mutationem, qua mutati moerore afficiuntur propter aliquam rem, quae evenerat secus quam putabant, opinati erant, vel nunc probare vel ratam habere potuerunt, quamquam tamen ... infectam quidem vellent, ut tamen & pro vili eam emendarent, licet emendandi ... potestas, quod in hominibus ... lerum quae cadit & in eorum res ... De DEO vero ejusque facis certum est ... Immutabilis et atque ita ... quae ... Unde, quicquid hominibus potest videri in una vel altera mutatum, respectu ejus decreti non potest dici mutatum, sed ... opinionis, quam de ea re hominies concipiunt, ... plane alio modo ... tumque protinus ... illorum ... ita et ordinatus ... fiet ... super malo poenitentia, quando recipit cetera ... poenas ac mala, quae perfer ... in ... terre detinuiaverat, eo nempe loquendi more, quo ... & sic. & de suis actionibus utuntur. Unde revera nihil aliud est in DEO, super malo poenitere, quam resipiscentiam hominum acceptam ferre, ejusque causa hujusmodi plagas ac judicia removere ac temperare, quo non adeo mentem suam mutat, novumque decretum fuscit, quin potius conditioni faciat satis, quam prima illorum denunciatio completebatur, quemadmodum in omnibus minis eam contineri ipse declarat Jer. 7, 8. & 26, 3. Quid? quod nec cum promissionibus bonorum cuiquam factis aliter se res habet, quippe cunctæ conditione ea nituntur, ut in obedientia perseverent, quibus ex sunt factæ. Quod vero huius conditionis interdum nulla fiat mentio, ex eo forsitan fit, ne insuper habeant abjiciantque resipiscendi curam nimium sibi de ejus misericordia promittentes, & supra, quam promissio illius continet. Hac igitur mente ea verba reddit Chaldaeus [Hebrew] & revocat verbum suum ab inducendo (vel infligendo) malo, quo cum facit Syrus [Syriac] & avertens malum, nec non MS. Arab. [Arabic] & t) avertens se ab afflictione (vel ab infligendo malo). Quæ versiones planum nobis reddunt verborum sensum, cum non tantum ostendant, quid sit super malo poenitere, sed etiam una, cuius generis hoc mali sit, de quo hic sermo est, scilicet non peccati, sed poena hic habetur ratio; quorum cum utrumque intelligi possit, ambigue hoc verterunt interpretes antiqui iique haud mediocris auctoritatis, ut Graeci, [Greek] et Latin Vulg. & praesultabus super malitia, quod Ducaeus interpretantur, [Greek] malice. Quantumvis enim eo sensu interpretes haec verba sumant, quem antea expoluimus, ut ex Hieronymo, Cyrillo, & pluribus aliis apparet; attamen alia etiam ratione capi posse, ex impressa Arabica liquet, quæ Græcos sequitur reddendo [Arabic] quod latine idem est ac si dicas, & quem pœnituit fecerunt [Arabic]. Aliter tamen Cyrillus, qui, licet judicio suo alium sensum ferre possint verba in Graeca translatione, eam tamen opinionem
units.tr: Since these passages seem to contradict each other, it is clear that the words repentance and to repent have different senses: properly and chiefly when used of men, they are not ascribed to God, but in another sense, insofar as they fit God, they can be ascribed to him. Properly and strictly, then, the word signifies a change in the mind of those of whom we speak. It denotes a change by which men are struck with grief over something that has happened otherwise than they thought or supposed, something they could now approve or ratify, although they would have wished it undone, and would even have corrected it for the worse, if they had the power to correct it; this is so in men... Concerning God and his decrees it is certain... immutable... Hence, whatever may seem to men to have been changed in one way or another, cannot be said to be changed with respect to his decree, but only with respect to the opinion which men form about the matter... in a completely different way... to repent concerning evil then follows, when he receives the penalties and evils which they had deserved... in the land... by that mode of speaking in which they also use of their own actions. Hence in truth there is nothing else in God to repent concerning evil than to accept the repentance of men, and for its sake to remove and temper such blows and judgments, not that he changes his mind or makes a new decree, but rather that he satisfies the condition on which the first announcement was fulfilled, as he himself declares that this is contained in all threats (Jer. 7:8; 26:3). And what of it? The case is no different with the promises of good things made to anyone, since all of them rest on this condition, that they persevere in obedience, on which they were made. That this condition is sometimes not mentioned at all may perhaps be so that men do not disregard and cast off the care of repentance, promising themselves too much of his mercy, and more than his promise contains. With this mind, then, the Chaldee paraphrast renders the words: and he revokes his word from bringing (or inflicting) the evil; so also the Syriac: and turning away the evil, and likewise the Arabic manuscript: and turned away from the affliction (or from inflicting the evil). These versions make the sense of the words plain to us, since they show not only what to repent concerning evil is, but also of what kind this evil is, of which the discussion here treats: that is, the penalty, not sin, is here in view. Since either sense could be understood, the older interpreters, who were of no small authority, translated the phrase ambiguously: the Greek and the Latin Vulgate render it and repenting of the malice, which Ducaeus interprets as malice. For although these interpreters take the words in the sense we have explained earlier, as appears from Jerome, Cyril and many others, yet that they can be taken in another way is clear from the printed Arabic, which follows the Greek and renders it with words meaning, in Latin, the same as if you said and he whom it repented made them.

units.la: ¹) Quo cum convenient ex interpretibus lat. Castalio, qui se ab inferendo malo contineat. nem optimam esse dicit, qua, etsi peccatores affligere coeperit, tamen non diu post mitigatum iri statuitur, μεταχωσὲι γὰρ εὐκόλως επὶ τὸ βασιλευσθαι τὰ χρηστά, nam facile revertitur ad benignitatem, vel ad ostendendum benignitatem. Vocem praeterea Graecam (κακία) tum denotare impietatem vel malum ab hominibus perpetratum, tum malum hominibus illatum, res manifesta est, quippe in N. T. ita usurpatur, Matth. 6, 34. Quo vero sensu malitia accipiatur Vulgato, & hoc loco, & praedicto apud Matthaeum, Hieronymus in haec verba notat: Malitiam in hoc loco non contrarium virtutis debemus accipere, sed afflictionem. Atque ita naturam DEI, ejusque morem agendi hic describit Propheta, eum praecipue in finem, ut eo usque eos perducere, ut quam citissime, totoque pectore, ceu admonitio habet, ad Dominum sese converterent. Quod quidem ut facerent, non desistit ulterius in sequentibus verbis adjicere, quid emolumenti in eos haud dubie redundaturum sit, si ad mentem suam & admonitionem agere vellent.
units.tr: With them agrees, among the Latin interpreters, Castalio, who renders it as refraining from inflicting evil. Cyril, however, though his judgment allows the words in the Greek translation to bear another sense, holds this opinion to be the best: that God, even if he has begun to afflict sinners, is nevertheless determined not to continue long, for he easily turns to kindness [μεταχωρεῖ γὰρ εὐκόλως ἐπὶ τὸ χρηστεύεσθαι], that is, he readily reverts to benignity, or to showing benignity. Moreover, that the Greek word (kakia) denotes both impiety or evil perpetrated by men, and evil inflicted on men, is plain, since in the New Testament it is used so (Matt. 6:34). In what sense the Vulgate takes malice here, and in the passage mentioned in Matthew, Jerome notes on these words: We ought to take malice in this place not as the opposite of virtue, but as affliction. And so the Prophet here describes the nature of God and his manner of acting, chiefly to this end: to bring them to turn to the Lord as quickly as possible and with the whole heart, as the admonition requires. Indeed, to get them to do this, he goes on in the following words to add what advantage will undoubtedly accrue to them if they were willing to act on his mind and admonition.

units.la: 14. Quis scit, si convertetur & poenitebit, & relin- quet post se benedictionem, etiam sacrificium & libamen Domino Deo vestro.
units.tr: 14. Who knows whether he will turn and repent, and leave a blessing behind him, even a meal offering and a drink offering for the LORD your God?

units.la: DEum converti posse atque poenitere, praecedentibus in verbis omni asseveratione affirmaverat, nihilque propterea esse, cur gratiam ejus tam graviter afflicti desperarent, licet peccata illorum aeque ac plagae vel supplicia communem fortem longe excedant, atque ex eo animos eorum facile subire posset desperandi consilium reputantes, talem forsitan non esse eum, quo cum ipsis erat negotium, quali hic est descriptus. Verum enim vero postquam omnino persuasi erant de illius benigna voluntate, spem illis facit gratiam consequendi, quamvis non adeo simplicibus verbis, ne jam recuperatam crederent. Atque hinc est, quod per interrogationem ea proferatur, cum dubii nonnihil adhuc inesse videtur. u) Spem metu miscet, vel ad securitatem fovet aut desperationem venit illos in luto relinquit. Simile
units.tr: In the preceding words the prophet had affirmed with every assurance that God can turn and repent, and that there was therefore no reason for those so grievously afflicted to despair of his grace, even though their sins far exceed the common lot, as do their plagues or punishments. Yet they might easily be led to despair, reasoning that he was perhaps not the kind of God with whom they had to deal, as he is described here. But now that they were fully persuaded of his kindly will, the prophet holds out to them the hope of obtaining grace, though not in simple terms, so that they would not believe they had already recovered it. Hence the matter is put as a question, since some doubt still seems to attach to it. u) He mingles hope with fear, or fosters security, or brings them to despair, leaving them in the mire. Similar

units.la: u) Grotius. lem locutionem habemus apud Jon. 3,9. qua Rex Ninive ad resipiscentiam excitat populum, cujus interitus a Jona erat prædictus: Quis scit, an revertetur et pœnitebit Deum, ut revertatur ab æstu iræ suæ non pereamus. Ubi manifesto liquet ejus mentem ac intentionem non fuisse, ut eos adduceret in dubium, sed ut spem faceret gratiæ. Id tamen de hac expressione, quam dubiam æque diximus includere atque spem & confidentiam, annotare habemus, dubium non in eo consistere, an gratiam velit DEus exhibere iis, qui ad frugem vere redeunt, sed an velit ea supplicia averruncare eo, quo ipsi vellent atque optarent, modo.
units.tr: u) Grotius. We have a similar expression in Jonah 3:9, where the king of Nineveh stirs the people to repentance, whose destruction Jonah had foretold: Who knows whether God will turn and repent, and turn from the heat of his anger, so that we do not perish? There it is plain that his purpose and intention was not to cast them into doubt, but to hold out hope of grace.
