Yet we must note that this doubtful expression, which we have said contains both hope and confidence, does not concern whether God is willing to show grace to those who truly return to amendment, but whether he will avert those punishments in the way they themselves would wish and desire.

units.la: Nam ubi nefas admissum est, quod DEus atrocibus puniendi insecutus est minis, qui admissam culpam rite agnoscunt atque dolore propterea angunutur, nempe remissio culpæ & castigationis. Quod ad priorem, non est dubium, quin revera condonaturus sit vere pœnitentibus, quippe ei hoc proprium est & ab eo ipso non una ratione declaratum, imo ne secus quidem facere ipsi δυνατον. Quod vero culpa remissa etiam omnem castigationem remittere & amovere velit, utique promissum omni loco non est, unde qui unius certi sunt, alterum sibi, cur quoque persuadeant, non habent, quippe id ubique conferre non assolet, ut id satis patet in David, cui quantumvis culpam remittere promiserat, infanti tamen nequaquam pepercit, quem in adulterio ex Bathsheba progeneraverat, etsi vitæ ejus impetrandæ nec jejunio nec lachrymis parceret, dicens (non minus interrogando, quam Propheta hoc loco) Quis scit, si gratiam est mihi facturus Dominus ut vivat infans? 2. Sam. 12. v. 13. 14. & 22. Ita hic quæ videtur dubitatio inesse huic loquendi formulæ, non adeo concernit remissionem peccatorum eorum, qui resipiscentia vera ad DEum se convertebant, quam quidem remissionem pœnæ ac suppliciorum. In eo enim rei cardo vertitur, num ea velit mitigare, destructionemque, quam minatus fuerat, adeo limitare, ne sit totalis, sed prout habent verba, quæ sequuntur, ut relinquat post se benedictionem; quæ si cum prioribus conjunguntur, non videntur esse tam dubitantis, quam bene sperantis & opem Dei desiderantis; quippe non dubitabat, quin Deus,
units.tr: For where a wrong has been committed, and God has threatened grievous punishment, those who rightly acknowledge the sin committed and are therefore grieved by it, the forgiveness of guilt and of chastisement, is what is at stake. As for the former, there is no doubt that he will indeed pardon those who truly repent, since this is proper to him and has been declared by him in more than one way; indeed, it is not even possible for him to act otherwise. But that once guilt is forgiven he will also remove and take away all chastisement is not promised everywhere, so those who are certain of the one do not have grounds to be persuaded of the other as well, since this does not usually follow everywhere. This is clear enough in David, to whom God had promised the remission of his sin, yet who by no means was spared the infant born to him of Bathsheba in adultery, although he refused neither fasting nor tears to obtain its life, saying (no less by question than the prophet here): Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live? 2 Sam. 12:13, 14, and 22. Thus the apparent doubt inherent in this form of speech does not concern so much the forgiveness of sins of those who truly turned to God in repentance, but rather the remission of penalty and punishments. For the crux of the matter lies in whether he is willing to soften the destruction he had threatened, and to limit it so that it is not total, but as the following words have it, that he leave a blessing behind him. If these are joined with what precedes, they seem to express not so much doubt as good hope and a longing for God's help. For the prophet did not doubt that God,

units.la: x) Livel. y) Glass. Grammat. Sacra p. 497. Deus, quatenus gloria atque iustitia ejus permitteret, supplicia temporalia vel esset remoturus, vel ita mitigaturus, ut nonnisi in illorum bonum cederet, quibus paterne in eos esset animadversurus, non totalem destructionem illaturus. Atque is est genuinus sensus verborum, quatenus vertuntur per interrogationem dubitandique particulam & a nostratibus & multis aliis interpretibus, quae interpretandi ratio mihi videtur satis conveniens. Verum cum observatione deprehensum sit, hanc particulam a textu Originali non agnoscit, atque eam ab illis supplendi sensus causa esse adjectam, factum est, ut alii aliter haec verba expresserint, nimirum sine interrogatione vel huiusmodi dubitandi ratione. Hos inter Chaldaeus est, qui, sensu perrotum comma diverso, non habet, Quis scit, si &c. sed Qui scit penes se esse peccata, abscedat ab eu, & misericordia applicabitur ei &c. Quem sequitur R. Salomon, ut & Kimchi, qui posteaquam priori loco haec verba interrogative expositerat, aliam tamen postea addit interpretationem, qua idem putat dici ac is qui sciit viam poenitentiae, respiciat & Deum huius mali poenituit. Ex quibus omnibus satis liquet, quia in re a priori interpretandi ratione maxime abiint. Ad homines referunt verbum שוב jashub revertetur, quasi ad resipiscentiam illi vocarentur, quod ad Deum referunt priores. Quod etiam faciunt Chald. & R. Sal. in verbo ינחם poenitebit; quamvis id ad Deum referat Kimchi. At planior est magisque perspicua verborum sententia, si interrogandi forma legantur, ut nostrates multi; alii legere, quippe ea non tantum incitantur, sed & animus iis additur, ut ad benignum suum Deum, uti eos admonuerat, sese convertant, non amplius animo haerentes, sed confidentes fore, ut peccata, quibus in se tam gravia derivaverant supplicia, non impediant, quo minus ad illos vere ac sincere poenitentes convertatur atque eo ipsum poeniteat sensu, quo id ei diximus convenire, nimirum, ut immutet, quam tulerat sententiam ulterius eos affligendi, & e contrario benignum se iis exhibeat misericordiaeque non mediocria praebeat indicia. Hinc in Hebraeo est שוב ינחם revertetur & poenitebit, ut ad literam, aliis praecunt-bus.
units.tr: x) Livel. y) Glass. Grammat. Sacra p. 497. God, so far as his glory and justice would permit, would either remove the temporal punishments or soften them so that they would turn only to the good of those upon whom he would inflict them fatherly, and would not bring total destruction. And this is the genuine sense of the words, insofar as they are rendered by a question and the particle of doubt by our countrymen and many other interpreters, which method of interpretation seems to me quite appropriate. But since it has been observed with care that this particle is not recognised in the original text, and that it was added by them to supply the sense, it has come about that others have expressed these words differently, namely without a question or any such form of doubt. Among these is the Chaldee, which, with a sense quite different from the whole clause, does not have "Who knows whether," etc., but "He who knows that sins are with him, let him depart from them, and mercy shall be applied to him," etc. R. Solomon follows him, as does Kimchi, who, having first expounded these words interrogatively in the earlier place, nevertheless afterwards adds another interpretation, by which he thinks the same thing is said as "he who knows the way of repentance, let him look back, and God will repent of this evil." From all these it is clear enough in what matter they differ most from the first method of interpretation. They refer the word שוב [jashub, "will return"] to men, as if they were called to repentance, whereas the earlier interpreters refer it to God. The Chaldee and R. Solomon also do this with the word ינחם [yinnachem, "will repent"], although Kimchi refers it to God. But the sense of the words is plainer and more perspicuous if they are read in the interrogative form, as many of our countrymen read them; others also read them so, since by this they are not only stirred up but also given courage, so that they turn to their gracious God, as he had admonished them, not remaining in doubt but confident that the sins which had brought upon them such grave punishments will not prevent God from turning to them when they truly and sincerely repent, and from repenting, in the sense we have said suits him: namely, that he changes the sentence he had passed of further afflicting them, and on the contrary shows himself kind to them and gives no small signs of mercy. Hence in the Hebrew it is שוב ינחם [shub yinnachem], "will return and repent," literally, as others precede.

units.la: z) Cui accedere videtur MS. Arabicum. bus, reddidere nostrates. Ita olim etiam LXX: ἐπισρέψ͏ͅʹ καὶ μετα- τοῦ, quibuscunq;ut in omnibus fere,ita & hic facit Arab. impressa: At Vulgatus ad sensum magis, quam ad literam, convertatur & ignoscet. Syrus [Syriac text illegible, ~12 letters] [Syriac text illegible, ~10 letters] quis scit, si velit reverti & nostri misereri? Qua vero in re præcipue desiderabant ac sperabant DEum se illis benignum exhibiturum, atque reversionis & pœnitentiæ signum editurum, sequentibus exprimitur verbis: & relinquet benedictionem post eum, etiam sacrificium & libamen Domino Deo vestro. Tantam benedictionem, i. e. tantam fructuum terræ ubertatem, quibus dubio procul ad unum omnes erant hactenus orbati, ut haberent, quibus coram DEO suam lætitiam rursus testarentur offerendo tales oblationes, quales ex lege erant præscriptæ, quibusq; solis animum gratum pro beneficiis in se collatis exhibere poterant, quod certe placati erga se Dei jam magnũ foret a) indicium, cum ex eo constare posset, eum & expectare adhuc illorum servitium & eo insigniter delectari. Cum tristis rerum eorum supra describeretur facies atque conditio cap. 1, 9. & 13. ob quam maxima mœroris edere debebant signa, in cæteris quoque dictum erat, sacrificium & libamen est b) abscissum, vel c) detentum a domo Domini, v. 9. vestri Domini, v. 13. Ex quo intelligi potest, quam adhuc res illorum essent, cum non haberent, quo DEO officium debitum præstare possent, quod non tantum argumento est, ingenti eos laborale omnium rerum penuria, sed & simul a DEO esse rejectos, qui, cum illarum rerum usu atque ubertate eos privaret, sine quibus cultum ex lege præscriptum nequaquam præstare poterant, quid aliud significare voluit, quam, se nullum amplius commercium, nullum negotium cum illis velle, nec illorum servitio diutius deleniri. Quapropter si nunc illorum iterum defectum supplere dignaretur, non leve indicium esset, conditionem in melius mutatum si, DEum eos sibi tanquam suos adhuc asserere, benigna atque benevolá in eos adhuc esse voluntate, gratam atque acceptam habituram eorum resipiscentiam plagisque, quas acerrimas illis immiserat, non in-
units.tr: z) To this seems to agree the Arabic manuscript. Our countrymen rendered it as they did. So also formerly the Seventy: ἐπιστρέψει καὶ μετανοήσει [epistrepsei kai metanoesei], which the printed Arabic does almost everywhere, and here too. But the Vulgate translator, more to the sense than to the letter, has convertatur & ignoscet, "will turn and forgive." The Syriac [Syriac text illegible, ~12 letters] [Syriac text illegible, ~10 letters] who knows, if he will wish to return and have mercy on us? But in the matter in which they especially longed for and hoped that God would show himself kind to them, and give a sign of return and repentance, it is expressed in the following words: and he will leave a blessing behind him, even a meal offering and a drink offering for the LORD your God. Such a blessing, that is, such abundance of the fruits of the earth, of which without doubt they had hitherto all been deprived, so that they might have the means by which in God's presence they could again bear witness to their joy by offering such offerings as were prescribed by the law, and by which alone they could show a grateful mind for the benefits conferred upon them. Surely this would already be a great a) sign that God was appeased toward them, since from it it could be established that he still expected their service and took special delight in it. When the sad state and condition of their affairs was described above, 1:9 and 13, for which they ought to have shown the greatest signs of mourning, it was also said in the same place: the meal offering and drink offering are b) cut off, or c) withheld from the house of the LORD, v. 9; your LORD, v. 13. From this it can be understood how dire their situation still was, since they did not have the means by which they could render to God the service owed him. This is evidence not only of their great distress from the lack of all things, but also that at the same time they had been rejected by God, who, by depriving them of the use and abundance of those things without which they could by no means perform the worship prescribed by the law, meant nothing other than that he no longer wished any commerce or dealings with them, and was no longer to be appeased by their service. Therefore, if he now deigned to supply their lack again, it would be no slight indication that their condition had changed for the better, and that God still claimed them as his own, that he still had a kindly and benevolent will toward them, and that he would hold their repentance pleasing and acceptable, and would not impose the most severe plagues he had laid upon them.

units.la: intendisse ultimum eorum excidium,sed,qua tacito eos adhuc fovebat amore, emendationem atque revertendi consilium, ut ipsemet ad cos converteretur. Et cum ea inprimis largiretur,quibus ad cultum divinum quam maxime erat opus, quid aliud inde colligendum, quam acceptum eum haberi, eoque valde DEum adhuc delectari? Distinguunt equidem Magistri Judæorum judicia atque calamitates a DEO illatas ea ratione, ut shel Ahabah, castigationes amoris nominent, quibus relinquitur, quod ad perficienda sacra potissimum conducit atque exigitur, quippe hoc charitatis indicium putant,nihilque aliud a DEO tum intendi, quam ut d) benefacere idoneosque reddat eos beneficiis rite accipiendis,longe ea avertendo,quæ id impedire potuissent. Hinc si benedictione hujusmodi, qua servitium debitum præstare poterant, DEus commutaret tot tantaque in præcedentibus descripta mala, argumento esse recte conjicies, DEum eos amore adhucdum complecti,quid? quod nec hoc direction divina vacare arbitreris,quod ea cumprimis jubeantur expetere,quæ ad cultum divinum spectant, non autem quæ ad ipsorum præcipue privatam salutem, usum atque voluptatem conducunt. Quippe etiam ex eo cuique constare posset & non alium in finem a DEO eos fuisse castigatos, quam ut, amoris erga eos divini tot tantisque characteribus exstantibus,ipsorum quoque amor erga illum e) majora indies sumeret augmenta; & præcipuum eorum finem tum in rerum mundanarum desiderio, tum in largo atque effuso earum usu non alium esse debere quam cultum divinum, quem ut unum præstare summo amore ac promtitudine animi oportebat, ita summum certe nefas,rerum ubertatem non nisi voluptatum expletioni, mundanisque desideriis implendis impendere voluisse, quippe benedictionis nomine ut nihil hoc ipso magis est indignum; ita nihil dignius eo,quam si priori modo bona terrestria collocentur. Nec dubito, quin homines, quacunque calamitate pressi, hac mente preces ad DEum fundant, auxilio cito ut præsto sit illis, quin & hoc ipsum ad roborandum immane quantum conducat fidem atque liberationis spem, DEum eos, quamvis taliaminus
units.tr: had intended their final destruction, but, by the secret love with which he still cherished them, he intended amendment and a purpose of returning, so that he himself might turn to them. And since he bestowed these blessings above all on those who most needed them for the worship of God, what else can be gathered from this than that he still holds them acceptable and is still greatly delighted in them? The Jewish teachers, to be sure, distinguish the judgments and calamities inflicted by God on this ground, calling them shel Ahabah, castigationes amoris (chastisements of love). They hold that what is left is chiefly that which serves and is needed to perform the sacred duties. They regard this as a token of charity, and they hold that God then intends nothing else than d) to do good and to make them fit to receive his benefits duly, by turning away everything that could hinder this. Hence, if God were to exchange for such a blessing, by which they could render the service they owed, so many and such great evils as are described in the preceding verses, you will rightly conclude that God still embraces them with love. Indeed, do you not think that this too is no accident of divine direction, that they are commanded to seek above all those things which pertain to the worship of God, and not chiefly those which serve their own private salvation, use and pleasure? For it might also be clear to anyone that God chastised them for no other end than that, with such great and conspicuous marks of divine love towards them, their love for him might grow greater day by day. And their chief end, both in the desire for worldly things and in their generous and lavish use of them, ought to be nothing other than the worship of God. This they ought to render as their one duty with the highest love and readiness of mind. So it would be the greatest wickedness to wish to spend the abundance of things on nothing but the satisfying of pleasures and the fulfilling of worldly desires. Indeed, though it is the name of blessing that is most unworthy of this, nothing could be more worthy of it than if earthly goods were bestowed in the former manner. Nor do I doubt that people oppressed by any calamity pour out prayers to God with this mind, that he may quickly come to their aid; and this very thing greatly strengthens faith and the hope of deliverance, that God will hear them, though they deserve such things less, f) out of regard for his own glory and for the preservation and enlargement of his own worship.

units.la: d) Psal. 119,71. e) Hebr. 15, 6. &c. minus mereantur, esse auditurum f) respectu sui ipsius gloriae atque cultus sui sarti tecti servandi & amplificandi. Quando vero hic mentio fit sacrificii & libaminis Domino, quae cultus divini sub lege erant necessariae partes atque requisita, in propatulo est, omnes his inclusas esse partes ac res necessarias ad cultum divinum praestandum riteque perficiendum. Unus est vero Abarbinel, qui, nescio quo modo, haec sola, quae hic nominantur, respici, caeterasque benedictiones, quas juxta eum nec sperare poterant, nec ullas alias relictas habebant, excludi putet. Is enim calamitatem non tribuit fami vel annonae caritati locustarum atque infectorum aliorum vitio illatae, quo destructi sunt terrae fructus, unde sacrificia atque libamina conficiebantur; sed explicat verba priora, ut vidimus supra, de futura terrae templique prioris destructione, quam illis Chaldaei essent facturi, ita tamen ut simul vaticinium complectantur, quod non solum essent redituri servitutis jugo exoluti, sed & templum restauraturi, Hierosolymamque incolentes sacra secuti tractaturi, quantumvis non eodem splendore neque iisdem privilegiis stipata, quibus priora; quippe qui quidem sub templo secundo benedictionibus eo usque perfunderentur, ut sacrificia cibaria atque libamina Domino possent offerre, caetera vero signa inter eos perilluctria, prophetiam, Urim & Thummim, Arcam & Shechinah vel majestatis praesentiam cum aliis, quae ibi erant, non expectarent vel invenirent in templo secundo, sed opportunitas sacrificia offerendi sola redire vel restaurare eis. Ad cujus auctoritatem se etiam confert Arias Montanus, quamvis omnino non liqueat, qua ratione huic opinioni ex his verbis vel levissimum praebeat fulcimentum. Quocirca singularis atque ipsis solis propriae sententiae nomine hic apponere mihi libuit, cum nullum aliunde hujus unquam norim defensorem. Satius itaque fore autumo, eam sequi sententiam, quam supra expositmus, quae & probabilior est & multorum auctoritate nititur, qua tanta vel locustarum aliorumque infectorum vel hostium culpa statuitur praedicta rerum destructio, ut, unde
units.tr: d) Ps. 119:71. e) Hebr. 15, 6. &c. (God will hear them, though they deserve it less), f) out of regard for his own glory and for keeping in good repair and enlarging his own worship. When mention is made here of sacrifice and drink offering to the Lord, which were the necessary parts and requirements of divine worship under the law, it is plain that all the parts and things necessary for rendering and duly performing divine worship are included in these. There is, however, one writer, Abarbinel, who for some reason thinks that only these things named here are meant, and that the other blessings, which according to him they could neither hope for nor had left to them, are excluded. For he does not attribute the calamity to famine or to dearness of grain, or to the damage done by locusts and other pests, by which the fruits of the land were destroyed, from which the sacrifices and drink offerings were made. Instead he explains the preceding words, as we have seen above, as referring to the future destruction of the land and of the former temple, which the Chaldeans were going to bring about. Yet he holds that the prophecy also includes this: that they would not only return freed from the yoke of servitude, but would also restore the temple, and dwelling in Jerusalem would observe and carry on the sacred rites, though not with the same splendour or the same privileges as before. For under the second temple they would be blessed only so far that they could offer to the Lord the grain offerings and drink offerings, while the other signs, very much lacking among them, the prophecy, the Urim and Thummim, the Ark, the Shechinah or presence of majesty, along with the other things that were there, they would not expect or find in the second temple; only the opportunity of offering sacrifices would return or be restored to them. Arias Montanus also appeals to his authority, although it is not at all clear on what ground he gives this opinion even the slightest support from these words. Therefore I have thought fit to set down here this opinion, singular and peculiar to these men alone, since I have never known any defender of it from elsewhere. I think it better, then, to follow the view set out above, which is both more probable and rests on the authority of many. According to it the predicted destruction of things is laid to the fault of locusts and other pests or of enemies, so great that nothing would be left from which the lack of those needed to handle the sacred rites could be made up, and this while the former temple and the other privileges they had used were still intact.

units.la: f) Calvinus. unde inopia illorum suppleretur, quibus ad sacra tractanda opus erat, non esset reliquum, idque priori g) templo ceterisque, quibus usi erant, privilegiis adhuc integris.
units.tr: f) Calvin. So that nothing would remain from which the lack of those who were needed to handle the sacred things could be made good, and this while the former temple and the other privileges they had used were still intact.

units.la: Caeterum notanda est, antequam hinc discedamus, differentia, quae sese in constructione magis quorundam verborum, quam in sensu apud interpretes offert. Verba sunt: & relinquet benedictionem post eum. Quaeritur autem, quisnam sit, qui relinquet hanc benedictionem & quisnam intelligendus per eum, cum dicitur post eum, num ipse (eadem scil. persona) relicturus sit hanc benedictionem, vel alius quispiam, post quem eam relinquet? Sunt qui utrumque applicant ad *) magnum populum vel DEI **) exercitum, quo intelligunt locustas. Ita R. Salomo הנזיר והחסיל & Aben-Ezra, forsan Dominus convertetur והשאיר זרע החיל ברכה & relinquet ille exercitus benedictionem, ex qua conficiant sacrificium cibarium & libamen. Pari modo Drusius priori loco: post se locusta. R. David Kimchi priori loco intelligit DEum, posteriori locustas; ותאכל יתברך ישאיר &c. Et Deus relinquet post locustas benedictionem; si enim repugnaverit, procul hinc eas amovebit, & relinquet in germinantibus benedictionem, ut non omnia pereant, &, quod reliquum est, sit in benedictionem, & faciatis ex eo sacrificium & libamen, quod antea dixerat succesum de domo Dei. Ita Drusius cum aliis non paucis, posteriori loco k) post illum. Sunt qui utrumque referunt ad DEum, nimirum quod relicturus sit post se, i. e. post ea quae perpetraverat, i) ira deposita loco maledictionis, benedictionem. Atque haec sententia quidem translationi noftr. quam maxime accedit, nec non aliorum k) quamplurimorum, qui vocem interpretantur, post se. At non admodum multum refert, quamcunque illarum sequaris, quippe illud a DEO fit, quod ab ejus instrumento efficitur, unde ipse cessare etiam dicitur, quando illa, quibus usus erat instrumentis, agere cessant, quibus dixerat, eo usque progredimini, non ulterius. Sic & quod reliquum est, postquam mandatum ejus expleverunt, dici potest, reliquum esse post se. se. Quod Paraphrasten Chaldæum attinet, quem insuper habuisse jam ante notavimus initio versus interrogandi notam, in reliqua parte vertenda non est verecundior, cum, ut planiorem reddat suo modo sententiam, æque personam mutet, de qua sermo est, ac verborum significationem & constructionem, quando loco illorum, quæ hebraice sonant, si converteretur, & pœnitebit & relinquet benedictionem post eum, etiam sacrificium&c. supponit: Et quicunque respuerit, dimittentur ei peccata sua, & recipiet benedictiones & consolationes, eritque ejus oratio, sicut viri, qui offert oblationes & libamina in ade sanctuarii Domini Dei vestri. Verum cum non nisi literali verborum translationi studeamus, parum hunc auxilii ad nostrum institutum redundare posse quivis facile intelligit.
units.tr: Meanwhile, before we leave this point, a difference should be noted, which appears more in the construction of certain words than in the sense among the interpreters. The words are: and he will leave a blessing after him. The question is who it is that will leave this blessing, and who is to be understood by him, when it says after him: is it he himself (the same person) who is going to leave this blessing, or some other, after whom he will leave it? Some refer both to the *) great people or **) army of God, by which they understand the locusts. So R. Solomon, הנזיר והחסיל [the cutter and the locust], and Aben Ezra: perhaps the Lord will turn and leave a blessing [והשאיר זרע החיל ברכה], that army will leave a blessing, from which they may make the grain offering and drink offering. In the same way Drusius, taking the first sense: after itself the locust. R. David Kimchi understands God in the first clause and the locusts in the second: ותאכל יתברך ישאיר [and God will leave after the locusts a blessing]. And God will leave after the locusts a blessing; for if they resist, he will drive them far from here, and will leave a blessing in the growing things, so that not everything perishes, and what is left becomes a blessing, and you make from it a sacrifice and a drink offering, which he had said before would be cut off from the house of God. So Drusius, with not a few others, takes the second sense: after him. Some refer both to God, namely that he is going to leave, after himself, that is, after the things he had done, a blessing, his anger laid aside in place of a curse. This view agrees very closely with our translation, and with that of many others who render the word as after himself. But it matters little which of these you follow, for that is done by God which is done by his instrument, and so he is also said to cease when the instruments he used cease to act, to whom he had said thus far you shall go, and no further. So too what is left, after they have carried out his command, can be said to be left after itself. As for the Chaldee paraphrast, whom we have already noted above had the question mark at the beginning of the verse, he is no more faithful in the rest of the rendering: in order to make the sense plainer in his own way, he changes the person spoken of just as much as the meaning and construction of the words, since for the Hebrew words, if he shall turn, and repent, and leave a blessing after him, even a meal offering, etc., he substitutes: And whoever shall repent, his sins shall be forgiven him, and he shall receive blessings and consolations, and his prayer shall be like that of a man who offers oblations and drink offerings in the house of the sanctuary of the Lord your God. But since we aim only at a literal translation of the words, anyone can easily see that this can bring little help to our purpose.

units.la: 15. Clangite tuba in Zion, sanctificate jejunium, convocate cœtum solennem.
units.tr: Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly.

units.la: 16. Congregate populum, sanctificate congregationem, congregate senes, congregate parvulos & sugentes ubera: egrediatur sponsus e cubili suo & sponsa e conclavi suo.
units.tr: 16. Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, gather the elders, gather the little ones and those who suck the breast. Let the bridegroom go out of his chamber and the bride out of her closet.

units.la: 17. Fleant sacerdotes ministri Domini inter vestibulum & altare, & dicant: Parce Domine populo tuo, & ne des hereditatem tuam in opprobrium: ut dominentur eis nationes, quare dicent in populis, ubi est Deus eorum?
units.tr: 17. Let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep between the porch and the altar, and say: Spare thy people, O Lord, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the nations should rule over them. Wherefore should they say among the peoples, Where is their God?

units.la: Eadem hic sunt verba, quæ initio hujus capitis, Clangite tuba in Zion quæ ut eadem occasione, ita eundem in finem adhibita hic esse merito sibi quisque persuadeat. Abarbinel tamen auctor est, utriusque loci diversam esse rationem atque occasionem, priorique loco hæc verba esse prolata, ut invasionis terræ, quæ a Chaldæis erat futura, captivitatis suæ, destructionis templi prioris, atque postea restaurationis eos admoneret; cum posteriori loco tantum habeatur ratio destructionis templi posterioris, exilii, quo nunc multantur, & restaurationis, quam anxie expectant בגאולה רעתיר in redemtione adhuc futura, cujus verba ita habentur in cap. 2. vers. 1. שנבא בהן ער שני הגיורי וחרבנית חרבן ביתי ראשון ופקירתו בפרשה הראשנה והרבן בית שני וגאולה בפרשה השנית. Nec ab eo hic iterum multum discedit Arias Montanus, quando his & sequentibus verbis describi putat omnes eas calamitates, quibus a Romanis, Hierosolyma late direpta, Judæi fuere pressi, prioribus vero eas, quas illis intulerant Assyrii & alii hostes. At non est, ut in sententiam suam nos adducere possit, cum nihil aliud agitet Abarbinel hoc suo conatu, quod luculenter patet, quam ut eas prædictiones in hac prophetia eludat, quarum complementum necessario adversus eum atque Judaicæ religionis asseclas probat Messiam venisse; quas si concesseris nondum expletas esse, eum necdum venisse e vestigio colligit atque homines eum adhuc venturum expectare jubebit, ut ex postea dicendis luculentius apparebit, in specie ex v. 28. Quam ob causam multo videtur planior rectiorque horum verborum interpretandi ratio, qua hæc præcedentium statuuntur complecti repetitionem, nec alia occasione, nec alium in finem esse repetita, quam ut magis magisque eos ad resipiscentiam feriam incitaret & adhortaretur, postquam & ejus necessitatem iis ostenderat & nullum extra eam extare medium, quo imminentia gravissima judicia a se possent amovere, probaverat. Quandoquidem peccandi lues totam invaserat nationem, atque exinde DEus etiam a tota natione sumebat pœnas; necesse equidem erat, ut conjunctis manibus conjunctisque viribus ea remedia adhiberent, quibus peccatorum veniam perinde ac pœnæ remotionem possent impetrare. Quod ne impigre facerent, secunda vice atque serio iterum eos hujus rei admonet, publicum jejunium in resipiscentiæ infucatæ testimonium omnibus sine exceptione indicens. Id enim est, ad quod hic eos vocat, methodumque ejus vel formam præscribit, ut ex verbis, quæ ordine suo sumus explicaturi, apparet.
units.tr: These are the same words as at the beginning of this chapter, Sound the trumpet in Zion, and each may rightly be persuaded that they are used here for the same occasion and to the same end. Abarbanel, however, holds that the circumstances and occasion of the two passages differ: in the earlier place these words were uttered to warn them of the invasion of the land that was to come from the Chaldeans, of their captivity, of the destruction of the former temple, and afterwards of its restoration; whereas in the latter place account is taken only of the destruction of the second temple, of the exile under which they are now punished, and of the restoration they anxiously await, in the redemption still to come [בגאולה רעתיר]. His words on chap. 2, verse 1 run thus: [שנבא בהן ער שני הגיורי וחרבנית חרבן ביתי ראשון ופקירתו בפרשה הראשנה והרבן בית שני וגאולה בפרשה השנית]: that is, that we prophesy about them until the second exile; in the first section, the destruction of the first temple and its deposit; and the destruction of the second temple and the redemption in the second section. Arias Montanus does not depart much from him here, since he thinks that by these and the following words are described all those calamities by which the Jews were oppressed when Jerusalem was widely plundered by the Romans, whereas the earlier words describe those which the Assyrians and other enemies had brought upon them. But he cannot draw us to his opinion, since Abarbanel by this effort aims at nothing else, as is clearly evident, than to evade those predictions in this prophecy whose fulfilment necessarily proves, against him and the adherents of the Jewish religion, that the Messiah has come. If you concede that they are not yet fulfilled, he at once infers that he has not yet come, and will bid men still to expect his coming, as will appear more fully from what we shall say later, especially from verse 28. For this reason the method of interpreting these words seems much plainer and more correct, by which they are held to contain a repetition of what goes before, repeated for no other occasion and to no other end than to urge and exhort them more and more to repentance, after he had shown them its necessity and proved that there was no other means outside it by which they could turn away the most grievous judgments now at hand. For the plague of sin had invaded the whole nation, and God was therefore exacting punishment from the whole nation. It was necessary, indeed, that they should apply, with joined hands and united strength, those remedies by which they could obtain the pardon of their sins as well as the removal of the punishment. Lest they should be slack in doing this, he admonishes them a second time, and seriously, of this matter, appointing a public fast to bear witness to their repentance, which is not feigned, and summoning all without exception. For this is what he calls them to here, and he prescribes the manner or form of it, as appears from the words which we shall explain in their order.

units.la: Clangiue
units.tr: Sound ye the trumpet

units.la: {1} Jun. Trem. Danæus. Clangite tuba in Zion } Qua occasione tuba inter eos clangendum erat, supra notavimus ad v. 1. Nec obscure ex sequentibus verbis liquet, quare hic tuba clangere jubeantur. Nimirum vocandi erant, ut solenniter congregarentur ad publicum jejunium, ad humilitatem & fundendas preces ad DEum, ut benigne averteret, quas illis denuntiaverat, calamitates, quas aut jamjam ferebant, aut proxime subituri erant, sive locustis &c. sive hostibus inferentibus juxta diversas, quas non una vice inspeximus, opiniones. Unde patet, clangorem hunc tubæ tum ad primum, tum ad tertium referri posse eorum, quos ad v. 1. notavimus, usum. Clangendum vero erat tuba in Zione, quæ v. 1. vocatur mons ejus sanctus, veluti alibi, mons sanctitatis Zion, Psal. 2,6. quo, sicut de Hierosolyma dicitur, ut m) totum quidem partis nomine interdum venire solet tribus Domini ad testimonium Israelitarum, i. e. ad arcam, quæ in templo erat, ut celebrarent nomen Domini, Psal. 122,4. ubi plerumque solenniter conveniebant religionis exercendæ gratia. Cum locum conveniendi iis assignet, declarat quanti sit ponderis & quam late pateat, quod debebant facere: Erat enim a DEO jussum, ut publice indiceretur, quare secus fieri non poterat. Nec quemquam id latere poterat, quippe promulgatio eo in loco fiebat, ubi maximus populi ex omni parte regionis erat concursus, unde omnibus æque facile innotescebat, quod ut eos ad id eodem in loco perficiendum attrahebat, ita eo quoque faciebat, ut idem in n) omnibus totius regionis aliis locis & synagogis eodem tempore observaretur. Quid autem hic promulgandum sit, docent sequentia verba, ubi quædam ejusdem rei etiam observandæ proponuntur circumstantiæ sanctificate jejunium קִרְאוּ עֲצָרָה convocate cœtum solennem (vel diem interdicti, ut in margine ad cap. 1,14.) Eadem enim verba hebraica supra habuimus, quorum mentem atque interpretationem, quia sufficienter ibi tradidimus, imprasentiarum plura addere supervacaneum foret.
units.tr: {1} Junius, Tremellius, Danaeus. Sound the trumpet in Zion: We noted above, at verse 1, on what occasion the trumpet was to be sounded among them. And it is plain enough from the following words why they are here bidden to sound the trumpet. Namely, they were to be summoned to gather solemnly for a public fast, for humility and for pouring out prayers to God, that he might graciously turn away the calamities he had threatened, which they were either already suffering or were about to suffer shortly, whether from locusts etc. or from invading enemies, according to the different opinions which we have not looked at just once. Whence it is clear that this sounding of the trumpet can be referred to both the first and the third of those uses which we noted at verse 1. The trumpet was to be sounded in Zion, which at verse 1 is called his holy mountain, and elsewhere the mountain of holiness, Zion (Psalm 2:6). By this name, as it is said of Jerusalem, the whole is sometimes denoted by the part, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, that is, to the ark which was in the temple, to give thanks to the name of the Lord (Psalm 122:4), where they usually gathered solemnly for the sake of performing religion. In assigning them the place of assembly, he declares how weighty the matter is and how widely it extends, what they had to do. For it had been commanded by God that it should be publicly proclaimed, so it could not be done otherwise. Nor could anyone be ignorant of it, since the proclamation was made in that place where the greatest crowd of people came from every part of the region; whence it was equally easy for all to learn of it. And this, which drew them to the same place to carry it out, also had the effect that the same observance was kept at the same time in all the other places and synagogues of the whole region. What is to be proclaimed here, however, the following words teach, where certain circumstances of the same observance are also set forth: sanctify a fast, [קִרְאוּ עֲצָרָה] call a solemn assembly (or a day of restraint, as in the margin at chap. 1:14). For we had these same Hebrew words above, and since we have there given their sense and interpretation sufficiently, it would be superfluous to add more here.

units.la: Verf. 16. Congregate populum] i. e. operam date ut congregentur o) ad publicas supplicationes. Sanctificate congregationem] De verbo קַדְּשׁוּ Kaddeshu sanctificate, quod etiam extat in versu præcedenti,
units.tr: Verse 16. Gather the people: that is, take care that they gather for public supplications. Sanctify the congregation: Concerning the word [קַדְּשׁוּ, kaddeshu, sanctify], which also occurs in the preceding verse,

units.la: m) Vct. a Fig. in v. 1. Danæus. n) Danæus. o) Pisc. Tarnov. denti, & ut diximus cap.1,14, priori loco quod dictum est, huic non incommode applicari poterit. Eandem huic congruere significationem, quam illi,notat R. Tanchum,quam putat esse praeparandi vel ordinandi, qua ratione etiam h. l. est in MS. Arab. praeparate congregationem, qua voce quamvis praeparatio communis alibi plerumque denotatur, locus tamen videtur postulare talem, qualis in usu erat ad quoddam p) officium sacrum obeuntibus, nimirum jejunium solenne omnibus regulis ac circumstantiis observatis, quae ad id rite perficiendum in lege erant traditae. Levitis inprimis congregandi onus hic esse impositum Autor est H. Grotius. At latius extendi vox patitur, quam ut iis solis applicetur, quodque omnis generis & conditionis includat homines, ex sequentibus elucescit, ubi nominatim recensentur, Senes, parvuli, sugentes ubera, sponsus, sponsa & sacerdotes. Congregate senes. Per Senes, idem omnigena eruditione praeditus vir intelligi putat tum illum summum senatum, tum illos qui urbibus singulis praesident. Eandem etiam hic habemus vocem, quam supra c.1,14. ubi quae de ea sunt dicta, etiam hic locum habere possunt, scilicet quod applicari possit ac soleat non tantum senatoribus, qui gravitate atque dignitate eminent, sed etiam illis, quorum graves sunt anni. q) Magis tamen hic respici exactae jam aetatis viros, praeterquam quod magis propria atque strictior tum sit vocis significatio, inprimis videntur exigere sequentia, ubi illis e diametro quasi opponuntur parvuli & sugentes ubera. Cur vero in specie hi congregari jubeantur die solenni totius nationis, ad resipiscentiam jejunio & supplicationibus testandam, probabiliter r) nonnullis videtur idcirco factum, tum quia propter peccatorum multitudinem magis erant coram DEO rei, tum ut caeteris suo exemplo praelucerent, eidem poenitentiae viae ut insisterent. Quando praeterea illis subjunguntur parvuli & sugentes ubera, indicio est, neminem ab hac congregatione populi & mandato sanctificandi fuisse exclusum & exemptum ulla excusationis specie; quippe non tantum insignes flore juventutis & quibus suo stabant robore vires, quinque exinde
units.tr: m) Vatablus, on verse 1; Danaeus. n) Danaeus. o) Piscator, Tarnovius. [fragment of the note] and, as we said at chap. 1:14, what was said there of the former place may fittingly be applied here as well. R. Tanchum notes that it has the same meaning here as there, namely to prepare or to ordain; and in the Arabic manuscript the sense is likewise prepare the congregation. Although this word usually denotes common preparation elsewhere, the place seems to demand such a preparation as was used by those who performed a sacred office for a certain p) service, namely a solemn fast, with all the rules and circumstances observed which were handed down in the law for carrying it out duly. The author H. Grotius holds that the burden of gathering is here laid chiefly upon the Levites. But the word admits of a wider extension, so that it is not to be applied to them alone, and it includes men of every kind and condition, as appears from what follows, where they are named one by one: elders, little ones, those who suck the breast, the bridegroom, the bride and the priests. Gather the elders. By elders the same man, endowed with learning of every kind, thinks is meant both that highest senate and those who preside over individual cities. We have the same word here as above at chap. 1:14, and what was said of it there may also hold here: namely, that it can be applied, and commonly is, not only to senators who are eminent for gravity and dignity, but also to those whose years are advanced. Yet that men of already ripe age are more particularly meant here is indicated, besides the fact that the sense of the word is then more proper and stricter, chiefly by what follows, where little ones and those who suck the breast are set, as it were, directly opposite to them. Why these in particular are bidden to be gathered on the solemn day of the whole nation, to attest by fasting and supplications their repentance, is probably explained by some r) writers as follows: partly because on account of the multitude of sins they were more guilty before God, and partly so that by their example they might shine a light for others to walk in the same way of repentance. Moreover, when little ones and those who suck the breast are added to them, it is a sign that no one was excluded from this gathering of the people and the command to sanctify, nor exempted under any pretext of excuse. For not only those who were distinguished by the bloom of youth and whose strength stood firm in their vigour, and who were therefore more fit to undertake the very hard duties of humility, were to be gathered for this purpose, but also those utterly worn out with age, whose aged limbs now tottered, down even to the little ones who filled the air with their plaintive wails.

units.la: p) Calv. Merc. q) Brenn. r) Calvin. Danaeus. exinde magis erant pares obeundis perquam duris humilitatis ossiciis, hunc in finem erant congregandi, sed & senio quam maxime confecti, quorum jam titubabant seniles artus, ad parvulos usque, qui querulis implebant vagitibus auras, quibusque languebant in corpore vires. Adeo enim in omnes penetraverat judiciorum vis atque vehementia, ut nequaquam poslent ab invicem sejungi, veniam his mediis quaerentes, quae ad eam impetrandam adhibenda erant. Quapropter excusandi caeteri non erant, quamcunque etiam causam praetexuerint officium suum declinandi aut sese congregationi subducendi.
units.tr: p) Calvin, Mercerus. q) Brenner. r) Calvin, Danaeus. They were all the more fit for the very hard duties of humility, and for this purpose they were to be gathered. Even the aged, whose failing limbs already trembled, were to come, and the infants too, who filled the air with plaintive cries and whose bodies were weak. The force and severity of the judgments had reached all of them, so that they could not be separated from one another, seeking pardon by those means which were to be used to obtain it. Therefore the rest were not to be excused, whatever pretext they might offer for avoiding their duty or withdrawing from the congregation.

units.la: Congregate parvulos & sugentes ubera ]
units.tr: Gather the infants and those at the breast ]

units.la: Non est, quod propter horum nullius criminis reorum peccata istis, quas ferebat, plagis putes nationem correptam fuisse, vel potuisse eos capere resipiscentiae rationem ejusque genuinum finem. Cur autem, inquies, & illi congregari jubentur, ut officii, quod hic injungitur, habeant rationem? Plana ejus est ratio, si probe expenderis, fas esse DEO patrum delicta multare in filiis, quo patres gemitibus atque doloribus filiorum suorum cognitis eo magis atque citius, intentiorique studio moveantur ea a DEO efflagitare remedia, quibus eorum malorum immunes reddantur, quorum gravitati sua causa sunt una secum involuti infantes innocentes, quique alia ratione ab iis liberari non possunt. Nec est exigua spes eo citius obtinendi a DEO opem, quod parvulorum ac infantium gemitu facile se moveri patiatur. Etenim qui pabulum praebet corvorum pullis vociferantibus, voces parvulorum insuper non habebit. Quam sollicitam eorum etiam curam habeat, quam teneram, in exercendis in nationes judiciis, ex eo apparet, quod ad Jonam dicit, qui missus erat, nuntiatum Ninivitis interitum, quando causam interponit, cur illis serio resipiscentibus suam velit mutare sententiam: Nonne parcerem Ninive civitati maximae, in qua sunt plures duodecim myriadibus hominum, qui non norunt discernere inter dextram suam & sinistram, jumentaque multa? Jon. 4, 11. Edixerat illorum rex in solenni, quod celebrabant, jejunio, ne homines & jumenta gustarent quicquam, nec pascerentur, nec aquas biberent, unde probabile est infantes non fuisse exemtos,
units.tr: You must not think that the nation was chastised with these blows on account of the sins of these infants, who were guilty of no crime, or that they could grasp the reason for repentance and its true end. You may ask, however, why they too are ordered to be gathered, so that they may have a share in the duty enjoined here. The answer is plain, if you weigh it carefully: it is lawful for God to punish the sins of fathers in their sons, so that the fathers, having learned of the groans and sufferings of their children, may be moved all the more quickly and with more earnest zeal to ask God for those remedies by which these evils may be averted. The innocent infants are involved with them in the weight of these evils, through no fault of their own, and cannot be freed from them in any other way. Nor is there little hope of obtaining help from God more quickly, since he allows himself to be readily moved by the cry of little children and infants. For he who gives food to the young ravens when they cry out will not disregard the voices of little children. How careful and how tender he is in carrying out judgments upon the nations appears from what he says to Jonah, who was sent to announce the destruction of the Ninevites. When he gives the reason why he is willing to change his sentence, now that they have repented in earnest, he says: Should I not spare Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons who cannot distinguish between their right hand and their left, and also much cattle? Jon. 4, 11. Their king had decreed, in the solemn fast which they kept, that men and beasts should taste nothing, neither feed nor drink water. From this it is probable that the infants were not exempted,

units.la: ad quos uti humiliandi ratio atque edictum haud dubie spectabat, ita eorum peculiarem rationem habuisse DEum gratiam exhibiturum ex adductis liquet verbis. Quodque persuasum eflet antiquis, citius se posse impetrare veniam, si supplicantibus sibi una adjungerent infantes, ex eo palam fieri videtur, quod scriptum extat in libro Jud. c. 4. 9. 10. 11. 12., ubi infantes una adducti dicuntur, ut humilimo ac supplici animo exclamarent apud DEum Israelis unanimiter contentione magna. Quo etiam faciunt verba Kimchi, quando dicit, congregari illos cum caeteris juberi [Hebrew] ut sint omnes in uno coetu & fleant parvuli ac fugentes vmmma [?] famem suam, & adulteres humiliantur fletu illorum & respiciat; DEus autem benignus, endas misericordia sua miseretur clamoris parvulorum. Quemadmodum vero nulla hinc poterat eximi aetas, quam partes suas ageret in hoc humiliationis publicae actu; ita nullae erant circumstantiae, quarum praetextu quis potuisset excusari. Quod si cuiquam hac in re indulgendum fuisset, utique recens nupti eximendi, qui in lege eo tempore a publicis excusabantur officiis, ut a disciplina militari tempore belli aliisque hujusmodi casibus. Sic enim habet, quod extat Deut. 24, 5. Quum duxerit quis uxorem nuper, non exibit in militiam, neque imponetur ei onus ullus rei, sed immunis erit domi suae unum annum & exhilarat suam uxorem, quam duxit. At hujusmodi quid illis hoc humiliationis publicae actu non concedebatur. Ergo dicitur, inquit, Ipsi ergo quid sponsi nubunt... & sponsa e thalamo suo. Equidem iis non licebat quidem aliter, in lectum eiusdem, aliis muneribus jussa persolventibus, sed una cum caeteris in id incumbendum iis erat, ut publicam decus caeterunt calamitatem etiam ipsi, ut impleret id vel quin caeterum solemnia carum solemnitatem celebrata. Pofhac vero denique esset, DEO ad alia eos avocante, quaecunque lectus gluna thalami fecerit, dus exigebat commendatarque. Quod enim periculo tunc consortio conjuncta forent, ex Jrel. 22. 13. & Psalm. 3; Ec Mes. Domini Dei exercituum ad illorum, & ad Iohannis & benedictio ad & gaudium &c. ne vivam, si expressis aliqui impetravit, ni eum est tr ... Dominus Deus exercituum. Nec erat circa id temporis, portis: quo DEus ad humilitatis officia publica eos vocabat, ulli excusationi locus. Quare qui id operam daturi hic vocantur, li se subdolcre ei volui Tent, quid aliud feriiTent, quam quod vi nd, tam divinam ulterius provocaTent, cum re probe facta reconciliationis summa foret spes, quam non nisi his medius obtineri posse praedictum erat. Egrediatur igitur publicae calamitatis tempore etiam sponsus & sponsa, libertate, qua alio tempore fas erat frui, laetandi cuticulam quoque ucandi praecisa, alter quidem e cubuli suo, altera ex concl.avi suo, ut cum caeteris omnium conditionum eorum, quibus humillimum suum publice testabantur animum, fiant participes. Vox Chuppah, nostratibus conclave, eodem modo ab interpretibus generali vocabulo exprimitur diversis linguis, quod denotat thalamum, qua notatione sumitur Pfalm. 19,5. Ita Chaldaeus בירא cum quo convenit Syrus & Graec. & Arab. imprefl. quod idem notat atque hebraic. חדר quo nomine hic venit sponsi conclave & redditum est cubile & ab eo in MS. ac si Synonymae essent hae voces. Eandem quoque sententiam fovet R. D. Kimchi, qui idem statuit esse ac חדר; adjicit tamen etiam aliam, quam ferre possit, nimirum החליים והעריים שיחיפים עליים ביסו ornamentis, quibus se obtegebat diebus d.spons.sationis (vel nuptiarum.) Neque adeo refragatur vocis denotatio, cum utramque signifacionem admittat, quippe cujus origo accellenda a חפה Chaphah obtegere, unde ad quodvis tegumentum denotandum apta. Idem autem verborum sensus, utram denique approbaveris, nempe, omnis nuptiarum pompa insuper debebat haberi, festiva quaeque atque laetitiae signa evanescere, sponsus e contrario una cum sponsa societatem congregatorum petere, atque simul cum caeteris solennes humilitatis ritus celebrare, moerorisque & relipiscentiae indicia edere, ut tum corda illorum recte riteque assicerentur, tum DEus moveretur, ut vices illorum vere doleret ac eorum miseretur. Posteaquam vero coetus ex diversis populi gradibus ac ordinibus collectus erat, proxime vocantur Sacerdotes ad officia sua obeunda. Fleant Sacerdotes, ministri Domini inter vestibulum & altare. Vocantur hoc loco, ut & supra cap. 1,9. ministri Domini, & vers. 13. ministri altaris, & ministri Dei nostri. Hi jubentur flere, quo quidem non excluduntur alii ne idem faciant; sed ut aliis exemplo suo præeant, quorum cumprimis erat divina strenue curare, altoque ad ea recte facienda impellere atque dirigere. Quod sit ab iis pro populo intercedentibus, non secus putandum est, ac si ab omnibus factum esset, quippe eadem mente cuncti actiones ac ritus illorum sequi debebant. Jubentur flere ob peccata & calamitates suas juxta ac totius populi, cujus & supra admonebantur cap. 1,13. quia sacrificium & libamen erat abscissum a domo Domini sui. Locus, ubi munus suum debebant præstare, nominatim hic quoque describitur, nimirum inter האולם Haulam & מזבח Mizbeach, vestibulum & altare. Quid sit אולם Ulam vel vestibulum, apparet ex 1. Reg. 6,3. Quid per altare intelligat, ex 2. Paral. 8,12. patet, videlicet illud, quod a Salomone exstructum dicitur ante portam in atrio interiore domus Domini (Ezech. 1,16.) non illud alterum, quod erat intra in loco sacro vel templo, quamvis Druss aram suffimenti intelligi velit. Verum enim vero plus nos esse profecturos reor in eruendo hoc loco ex delineatione quarundam partium templi vel atriorum ejus, quam in quodam veteri MS. Maimonidis invenio, cujus titulus fert Commentarium in Mishnajoth tractatus Middoth textus Talm. ubi hoc ordine ea tradit, ut ad orientem collocet (1.) עזרת הנשים Ezrat hannashim, atrium mulierum. (2.) עזרת ישראל Ezrat Israel, atrium Israelis (vel populi vel hominum). (3.) עזרת הכהנים Ezrat haccohanim, atrium Sacerdotum, in quo erat מזבח Mizbeach, altare. (4.) אולם vestibulum, ulma quod erat היכל Heical, templum (vel locus sacer) atque in eo מזבח הזהב Mizbeach hazzahab, aureum altare (scilicet suffimenti) & mensa & candelabrum, & (5.) קדש הקדשים Kodesh hakkodashim, sanctum sanctorum. Atqui locus hic descriptus non alius videtur esse juxta hanc delineationem, quam spatium vel ea pars atrii Sacerdotum, quod erat inter altare & vestibulum, in quo atrio illi solebant stare atque holocausta sua præparare.
units.tr: for the humbling and the decree undoubtedly looked to them as well, and from the words quoted it is clear that God would show grace to them in a particular way. That the ancients were persuaded that they could obtain pardon more quickly if they joined their infants with them in supplication is plainly shown by what is written in the book of Judges, ch. 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, where infants are said to have been brought along so that, with the most humble and suppliant spirit, they might cry out together before the God of Israel with great earnestness. The words of Kimchi agree with this, when he says that they were commanded to be gathered with the rest [Hebrew], so that all might be in one assembly, and the little ones and those at the breast might weep over their hunger, and the adults might be humbled by their weeping; and the good God, in his mercy, may have regard and pity for the cry of the little ones. Just as no age could be exempted from playing its part in this public act of humiliation, so there were no circumstances on whose pretext anyone could be excused. Yet if anyone were to be indulged in this matter, it would certainly be the newly married, who in the law of that time were excused from public duties, such as military service in time of war and other such burdens. For this is what is written in Deut. 24, 5: When a man has recently taken a wife, he shall not go out to war, nor shall any business be laid upon him, but he shall be free at home for one year and shall make glad his wife whom he has taken. But nothing of this kind was granted to them in this public act of humiliation. Therefore it is said, Let the bridegroom go out of his chamber and the bride out of her closet. Indeed, they were not allowed otherwise to lie down in their bed, performing other duties commanded to them; but together with the rest they were bound to devote themselves to this, that they might share in the public calamity, and in this way the solemn festivity was to be turned into mourning. Afterwards, when God called them to other tasks, whatever the bed and the chamber had done, it was required and commended. For what had been joined in fellowship at that time would be in danger... The Lord God of hosts. Nor was there, at that time when God called them to public duties of humility, any room for excuse. Therefore those who are summoned here to this work, if they tried to withdraw from it, would do nothing else than provoke the divine anger further, since the hope of a complete reconciliation was in question, which had been foretold could be obtained only by these means. Let the bridegroom and the bride therefore also go out in the time of public calamity, the liberty which at other times they were permitted to enjoy, of rejoicing and of feasting, being cut off; the one indeed from his chamber, the other from her closet, so that together with the rest of all conditions they may share in the humility they publicly professed. The word Chuppah, which our people call chamber, is rendered by the translators in various languages by a general term meaning bridal chamber, and this meaning is taken in Psalm 19, 5. So the Chaldee has [bira], with which the Syriac, Greek and Arabic agree, and which means the same as the Hebrew [chadar], the word used here for the bridegroom's chamber, rendered bed; and in the manuscript these words are treated as if they were synonyms. Rabbi Kimchi also favours the same view, holding that it is the same as [chadar]; yet he adds another meaning which it can bear, namely the ornaments with which they covered themselves on the days of the betrothal (or of the nuptials) [Hebrew]. Nor does the meaning of the word oppose this, since it admits both senses, its origin being derived from [Chaphah], to cover, whence it is suitable for denoting any covering. The sense of the words, whichever of these you approve, is the same: that all the pomp of the wedding must be laid aside, all festive signs and tokens of joy must vanish; the bridegroom, on the contrary, together with the bride, must seek fellowship with the gathered people and, along with the rest, perform the solemn rites of humility, and display the signs of mourning and repentance, so that their hearts may be rightly and properly affected, and God may be moved to truly grieve over their condition and have mercy on them. After the assembly had been gathered from the various ranks and orders of the people, the priests are next called to perform their duties. Let the priests, the ministers of the Lord, weep between the porch and the altar. They are called here, as above in chap. 1, 9, the ministers of the Lord, and in verse 13, the ministers of the altar, and the ministers of our God. They are commanded to weep; not that others are excluded from doing the same, but so that they may go before the others by their example, since it was especially their task to take diligent care of divine matters and to urge and direct the people to do them rightly. What they do when they intercede for the people is to be regarded no differently than if it had been done by all, for all were bound to follow their actions and rites with the same mind. They are commanded to weep over their sins and calamities, just as over those of the whole people, of which they were also reminded above in chap. 1, 13, because the sacrifice and the drink offering were cut off from the house of their God. The place where they were to perform their office is also named here, namely between [Haulam] and [Mizbeach], the porch and the altar. What Ulam, or porch, means appears from 1 Kings 6, 3. What he means by the altar is clear from 2 Chronicles 8, 12, namely that altar which is said to have been built by Solomon before the gate in the inner court of the house of the Lord (Ezek. 1, 16), and not that other one which stood within, in the holy place or temple, although Drusius wishes the altar of incense to be understood. But indeed I think we shall make more progress in explaining this place from a diagram of certain parts of the temple or its courts, which I find in an old manuscript of Maimonides, whose title is Commentary on the Mishnah, tractate Middoth, text of the Talmud. There he sets them out in this order, placing towards the east: (1.) [Ezrat hannashim], the court of the women. (2.) [Ezrat Israel], the court of Israel (or of the people or of men). (3.) [Ezrat haccohanim], the court of the priests, in which was the [Mizbeach], the altar. (4.) [Ulam], the porch, which was the [Heical], the temple (or holy place), and in it the [Mizbeach hazzahab], the golden altar (namely of incense), and the table and the candlestick; and (5.) [Kodesh hakkodashim], the holy of holies. Yet according to this diagram the place described here seems to be nothing other than the space, or that part of the court of the priests, which lay between the altar and the porch, in which court those priests used to stand and prepare their burnt offerings.

units.la: {*} Livel. Ezech. 8, 16. illud spatium, quod est inter altare & vestibulum, dicitur atrium interius. Quo de loco hoc videtur accipere Kimchi, cuius verba haec sunt: Ibi enim stabant Sacerdotes ad fungendum ministerio sui & sublato ministerio, ut dixit cap. 1, 9. succisum est sacrificium & libamen a domo Domini, ibi in loco ministerii sui stabant, & precentur ad DEum benedictum in domo sanctuarii ejus (qua ultima voce omne, quod ad templum tum internum tum externum concernit, cum complecti mihi persuadeo). Eundem locum intelligit etiam Aben-Ezra, cum explicationis loco dicat Non est rectum, flere in templo coram me, quod recte ab eo notatum dicit Abarbinel, adjiciens non fas esse flere in sanctuario DEI. Extra igitur atque ante illud jubentur flere, hoc autem loco, ut quidam notant, prohibitum erat signa moeroris edere. Nec alium fuisse locum opinio est, quo inter templum & altare occisus est Zacharias Matth. 23, 35. ubi totum nominatur templum, cujus vestibulum respicitur, tanquam pars ejus. Cur autem hoc loco cum primis jubeantur flere, praeter jam adductas rationes aliae haud improbabiles adferuntur: 1. ob loci opportunitatem, qua sic erat situs, ut populus ex atrio exteriori (separato ab illo interjecto pariete exiguo trium tantum cubitorum) advertere posset gestus lamentabiles motusq; sacerdotum summopere demissos, atque per illos ad similes producendos vehementius commoveri, ut alii aliis conjungerentur generali humilitatis actu. 2. Ut eo in loco stantes, qui erat inter templum Dei & atrium populi, perinde ac intercessores pro peccatis eorum intercedentes comparerent, vel 3. in signum summae demissionis, quia sententiam se indignos esse plane, qui propius ad DEum accederent procul stantes &c. Luc. 18, 13. x) Sunt qui putant, cum ad planctum & preces convertentur post altare, id factum esse, postquam DEum sacrificii placarunt jamjam reddiderant. At satis clare constat tum ex cap. 1, 17. tum ex hoc v. 14. illis nec fuisse nec foreac offerendum ulla sacrificia, eamque ob causam, quemadmodum ante a fronte exporrecta,
units.tr: {*} See Ezek. 8, 16. The space that lies between the altar and the porch is called the inner court. Kimchi seems to take it in this sense, and his words are these: For there the priests stood to perform their ministry, and when the ministry was taken away, as he said in chap. 1, 9: the sacrifice and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the Lord; there they stood in the place of their ministry, and they prayed to the blessed God in the house of his sanctuary (by which last word I am persuaded he means everything that concerns the temple, both inner and outer). Aben-Ezra also understands the same place, since in explaining the text he says: It is not right to weep in the temple before me. Abarbinel rightly notes this, adding that it is not lawful to weep in the sanctuary of God. They are therefore commanded to weep outside and in front of that place, but in this place, as some observe, it was forbidden to show signs of mourning. Nor is it thought to have been another place where Zechariah was slain between the temple and the altar, Matt. 23, 35, where the whole temple is named, of which the porch is regarded as a part. Besides the reasons already adduced, other not improbable reasons are given why they are commanded to weep especially in this place: (1) because of the suitability of the spot, which was so situated that the people in the outer court, separated from the inner by a low wall only three cubits high, could see the mournful gestures and very humble movements of the priests, and be moved more strongly by them to produce similar ones, so that they would join one another in a general act of humility; (2) so that those standing in that place, which lay between the temple of God and the court of the people, might appear as intercessors interceding for their sins; or (3) as a sign of the utmost submission, since they are fully convinced that they are unworthy to come nearer to God, standing afar off, etc., Luke 18, 13. x) Some think that when they turned to lamentation and prayers behind the altar, this was done after they had already appeased God by the sacrifice. But it is quite clear, both from chap. 1, 17 and from this v. 14, that no sacrifices were offered to them then, neither in front nor behind, and for that reason, just as before they were set forth in front, and they were accustomed to perform such duties with a cheerful mind, such as prayers and thanksgivings;

units.la: z) Merc. Ar. Mont. inquit eo ipso etiam in loco liberi flere, ubi alias las non erat. u) Episcop. Hallii Paraphras. vv) Merc. Calvin.. x) Ch. a Cast. cta, mentequc alacri solebant hujusmodi perfungi officiis, ut sunt preces gratiarumque actiones; ita ejus loco jam vocari ad ibi plorandum, cujus rei ut probabiles possunt adferri rationes, jamque a nobis etiam allatæ sunt; ita nulla pro superiori sententia hic extat, quocirca nec operæ pretium duco ullam aliunde petere vel anxie inquirere ut eo in loco fieret, a DEO erat ordinatum, hinc opus fuisse, nemo non videt, iis, ut id eo etiam perficerent modo, quo ab eo erat iussum, atque ibi potissimum mœroris ederent indicia tam pro suis ipsius, quam totius populi peccatis & calamitatibus, precesque supplices funderent tum pro se, tum pro populo. Preces enim hic etiam adjunguntur, quibus indicarent non oculos tantum eorum, sed & animum revera occupasse mœrorem, quodque facerent, non facere solum calamitatis gravitate pressos, sed ex merito atque ingenti propter admissa peccata dolore. Quocirca addit, & dicant, formam precandi, quidve dicere debeant præscribens, nimirum: Parce populo tuo Domine; qua innuitur, tum quam graviter eos deberet movere atque afficere & illorum propria & populi conditio, tum qua ratione possent sperare operamque navare, ut in gratiam cum illis rediret Deus. Dicendum erat: parce tuo populo. Quibus ipsi agnoscunt, se obnoxios esse pœnis eisque maxime commeritis, & divinam gratiam se magnopere desiderare, neque aliunde auxilium posse sperare, quam ab eo; eum merito ad vindictam adversus se esse provocatum, meritoque in se animadvertere, judiciaque sua exercere. Varia præterea hic sunt argumenta, quibus eum movere poterant, ut peccata condonaret atque longe averruncaret plagas, inprimis vero quod sibi ipse eos adscivisset, quod eum agnoscerent pro solo vero DEO, quod miserorum maxime doleret vices, ejusque gloria & honor inprimis in eo verteretur. Primum in eo consistit, quod ipse eos appellet suum populum suamque hæreditatem. Secundum inde liquet, quod eum debeant appellare voce יהוה Jehovah ex interpretatione nostratium Domine, quod nomen ipsi proprium erat, neque cuiquam alii tribuebatur quam vero DEO. Tertium a sympathia defluntum ex eo patet, quod in contumeliam darentur gentesque illis dominarentur, si in judiciis suis exequendis pergeret parcendique nullum iniret Viver tenuerunt. Huic accedit quartum, quod nullo calumniatis fine iumpol to in populis dicerent, ubi est Deus eorum? quippe qui exlade argumentum in nectere possent, non esse ipsum praestando ea, quae fecerat maioribus eorum, promissa, vel multo deteriorem, quam verba sua prae se ferrent, unde non nisi occasio daretur idololatriae inomen ipsius atque gloriam conviritus lacessendi. Quod argumentum aliis non jj semel in S. literis adhibetur ad DEum movendum, ut se talem praberet, qualem populus ejus afferebat atque profitebatur, ne in vanum viderentur omnem suam in eo collocare fiduciam, nec inimicis integrum foret objicere, quasi fidentibus sibi nihilo plus posset conferre solatii auxiliisque quam conferebant gentium DEI suis cultoribus. Nec leve illud esse ad DEum exorandum, non tantum manifestum est ex Mose & David aliisque sanctissimis viris, qui hunc in finem co usi sunt, ut Exod. 32, 12. Num. 14, 13. 15. 16. &c. Deut. 9, 28. Psal. 79, 9. 10. & 115, 20. Dan. 9, 19. verum &: ex eo potissimum, quod ex sanctissimo ejus ore prodiit, quo nominatim declaravit, se populo suo parcere, quem caeteroquin profligaret memoriamque ejus ex mortalibus deleviset, nisi ab inimico indignationem metuisset, ne hostes idolorum haberent occasionem se insolentiter gerendi atque dicendi: Excelsa manus nostra est, nec Dominus haec operatus est, Deut. 32, 26. 27. & in eandem sententiam Ezech. 20. 9. 14. 44. & v. 21. 22. Verba Limshal bam Goim notarat. in textu reddiuntur, ut dominentur eis gentes, similique modo etiam alii interpretibus in genere. Ad marginem tamen adjecerunt, velut diversam interpretationem, ut natura dilerio adverse est. Ita enim ea explanat R. Salomon Jarchi, qui verbum Imshal loco exponens, dicit ... esse eiusdem ... gubernationis cum Mashal veshemshal, quod etiam extat alibi, ut Isai. 49. 7. ubi Israelitae a DEO defectantes dicuntur tore Leshammah lemashal ... bicol hashamaim, in sinopterm in parabolam & in dicterium apud {y} ... Danaus: juxta morem reprehensionis blasphemum Rabshakeh 2. Reg. 18, 34. pud omnes populos. Ita & 1. Reg. 9, 7. & Jerem. 24, 9. quibus in loc̄is, cum nomen משל proverbium malo vsurpetur sensu, pro convicio, opprobrio & disterio, eodem accipi posse verbum arbitratum esse in propatulo est, qua ratione verborum sensum satis {z}convenienter fluere putavit. At generalior est, qua id accipiunt alii, significatio dominandi, quam uti approbat etiam Hieronymus, ita eximè manifestum atque evidens id esse putat, quod hactenus erat dubium, scilicet, quinam hic intelligendi sint calamitatis illatæ vel inferendæ auctores, locustæne cum cæteris noxiis vermiculis, an inimici? Indicio quippe eam censet expressionem non esse hic sermonem de illis vermibus vel infectis, sed de {a}hostibus illorum inter nationes. Pariter id accipit Cyrillus, quamvis satis apte de locustis etiam intelligi posse adserere non gravetur. In recentioribus est Calvinus, qui quoque exinde huic sententiæ fulcrum quærit, quando ait: Ideo rectius est, quod multi putant contexi sermonem de locustis, atque absonum plane a mente Prophetæ. At id ferventi ejus animo dandum est. Fuere alii, ut ante eum, ita & post eum, quibus argumenta ejus ad incudem vocare integrum fuit. Attamen non pauci sunt, qui iis rejectis proniores sunt in eam sententiam, quod recte equidem, imo quod necessario de damno illo sit sumendum, quod ab locustis divino jussu immissis fructusque terræ destruentibus iis sit illatum, atque illæ in præcedentibus sine dubio proprie etiam respiciantur. Ita id ex Judæis accepisse videtur Aben-Ezra, cum per opprobrium intelligit רעב famem, & verba, ut dominentur eis nationes, huncce in modum explicat: Nam famelici fugient ad eas, quo si venerint, non erit in eis robur ad pugnandum. Simili ratione Kimchi: Ne des in opprobrium hæreditatem tuam, ut dominentur eis nationes כי כשרים רעב בארץ ישראל &c. Quum enim esset famés in terra Israel, exinde multi ex ea, ad peregrinandum in terra Ægypti & in terra Palæstinorum propter famem, ac dominabantur eis nationes, quum peregrinarentur in terra eorum. Ita ut juxta hos & alios, qui eundem interpretandi modum sequuntur, hoc modo verba fluant, ut paraphrasi ea ex Christianis {b}quidam bene expressit: Parce populo tuo ut hæreditatem {z} Mercer. {a} Sic & Lyr. {b} Petr. a Figur. ferendo ab eo locustarum illam plagam, quæ si amplius desæviérit & consumserit fuerit, extremam inducet famem, atque ita populus tuus cogetur ad levandam famis necessitatem in regiones gentium transfugere, & apud eas pro pane servire & imperium earum, nec non opprobria sustinere, non secus ac olim in Ægyptum confugerunt & servi facti sunt. Hanc quoque approbant ex Christianis Calvino multo {c}recentiores, multo etiam saniorem censent, nimirum, hostes quidem volunt hic dici dominaturos illis, eos tamen non esse, sed vermiculos ante descriptos, quorum damnis illatis eo usque forent redigendi, ut fame coacti contenderent ad eas gentes, iisque sese submitterent, vel in potestatem earum redigi non difficiles forent. Cæterum cum hoc versu dicitur: fleant Sacerdotes inter vestibulum & altare, manifesto constat, ea, quæ hic dicta sunt, accidisse, templo cum vestibulo cæterisque ad illud spectantibus adhuc integro ac salvo, ad quod Sacerdotibus adhuc dabatur accessus, atque in eo officiis muneri suo propriis defungendi libertas, quod equidem sententiæ contrarium est, qua ad tempus putat respicere Abarbinel, quod destructo templo elapsum est, imo ad secundum templum, conditionisque hodiernam fortem, comparans cum hac expressionis forma, quæ habentur cap. 1, 9. 13. 14. & 16. & 14. hujus cap. Verba, quibus summam mentem prodit, eo redeunt, se non posse intelligere hæc verba, ne des hæreditatem in opprobrium ut dominentur iis gentes כי אם [?] [?] עד הגלות הארוך הזה אשר אנחנו בו לחרפה בידי ארם [?] nisi de diuturna captivitate, in qua nunc versamur, in opprobrium in manibus Edomitarum, & planctum hic descriptum non esse alium, quam captivitatis שבכי העם והתאבלו בגדותם כי מהשבים qua populus fleuit atque mœruit captivus tot annos. At quomodo id factum dici potest inter vestibulum & altare? Necessario igitur id ad ea referri debet, quæ facta sunt templo adhuc sarto tecto.
units.tr: z) Mercerus, Arias Montanus, says that the free men wept in that very place where the others were not allowed to be. u) Bishop Hall, Paraphrase. vv) Mercerus, Calvin. x) Cf. Castellio. Although they were accustomed to perform such duties with a cheerful mind, as prayers and thanksgivings, the place was now called to weeping there instead. As for the reasons that can be offered for this, we have already brought them forward. Since no other view is found here, I think it not worth the trouble to seek elsewhere or anxiously inquire why it happened in that place. Everyone sees that it was ordained by God, and that it was needful that the priests should do this in the manner that God had commanded, and that there, above all, they should show the signs of sorrow, both for their own sins and for the sins and calamities of the whole people, and pour out suppliant prayers both for themselves and for the people. For prayers are also added here, by which they would show that grief had truly taken hold not only of their eyes but of their minds, and that they were doing this not merely because they were pressed down by the gravity of the calamity, but out of genuine and great sorrow for the sins they had committed. Therefore he adds and let them say, prescribing the form of prayer and what they ought to say, namely: Spare your people, O Lord. By this is indicated how gravely both their own condition and that of the people ought to move and affect them, and by what means they could hope and labour that God might be reconciled to them. They ought to say: spare your people. By these words they acknowledge that they are liable to punishments, and that they deserve the greatest of them, and that they greatly need divine grace and can hope for help from no other source than from him; that he has rightly been provoked to vengeance against them, and rightly takes action against them and exercises his judgments. Besides, there are various arguments here by which they could move him to pardon sins and to avert the plagues far away. Above all, there is that he had adopted them for himself, that they acknowledged him as the only true God, that he would especially grieve for the sufferings of the wretched, and that his glory and honour would chiefly be concerned in it. The first lies in the fact that he calls them his own people and his inheritance. The second is clear from the fact that they must call him Jehovah, which in our translation is rendered Lord; this was his proper name, and was given to no one but the true God. The third, drawn from sympathy, appears from the fact that the nations would be given over to scorn and would rule over them, if he went on executing his judgments and undertook no sparing. To this is added a fourth: that the nations should not say, without any reproach, where is their God? For they could make this an argument, that he was not keeping the promises he had made to their forefathers, or was doing much worse than their words declared, so that nothing but an occasion would be given for idolatry and for provoking the name and glory of God to reproach. This argument is used more than once in Holy Scripture to move God, so that he might show himself such as his people described and professed him to be, lest they should seem to have placed all their trust in him in vain, and lest the enemies should have the chance to object, as if God could give no more comfort and help to those who trusted in him than the gods of the nations gave to their worshippers.
