That this is no small thing for appeasing God is clear not only from Moses and David and other most holy men, who used it to this end, as in Exod. 32:12; Num. 14:13, 15, 16, etc.; Deut. 9:28; Ps. 79:9, 10, and 115:2; Dan. 9:19, but chiefly from the fact that it came forth from his most holy mouth, in which he declared by name that he would spare his people, whom otherwise he would destroy and blot out their memory from among mortals, had he not feared the indignation of the enemy, lest the enemies of the idols should have occasion to act and speak insolently: Our hand is high, and the Lord has not done these things, Deut. 32:26, 27; and to the same effect Ezek. 20:9, 14, 44, and vv. 21, 22. The words limshol bam goyim, noted in the text, are rendered that the nations may rule over them, and similarly other translators in general. In the margin, however, they have added, as a different interpretation, that the nature of the thing is adverse. For thus Rabbi Solomon Jarchi explains them, who, expounding the word mashal, says that it is of the same governance as mashal veshemshal, which also occurs elsewhere, as in Isa. 49:7, where the Israelites who revolt from God are said to be a byword and a proverb among the nations, that is, a parable and a taunt, according to the custom of reproach, as the blasphemer Rabshakeh in 2 Kings 18:34 [mashal]. So also in 1 Kings 9:7 and Jer. 24:9, in which places, since the noun mashal, proverb, is used in a bad sense for reproach, disgrace and taunt, it is plain that the same verb may be taken in the same sense, by which reasoning he thought the sense of the words flowed quite suitably. But the more general meaning, by which others take it, is to rule. Jerome approves this, and thinks it most manifest and evident, which until now was doubtful, namely, who are here to be understood as the authors of the calamity inflicted or to be inflicted: the locusts together with the other harmful worms, or the enemies? For by his judgment this expression does not speak of those worms or the infected ones, but of their enemies among the nations. Cyril likewise takes it this way, although he does not hesitate to assert that it can also be understood quite aptly of the locusts. Among more recent writers is Calvin, who also seeks a support for this opinion from it, when he says: Therefore it is more correct, which many think, that the discourse is about the locusts, and this is plainly absurd to the mind of the prophet. But that must be granted to his fervent spirit. There were others, both before him and after him, whose arguments it was fair to bring to the anvil. Nevertheless, there are not a few who, rejecting these, are more inclined to that view, and rightly so, indeed necessarily so, that the loss must be taken as that which was inflicted by the locusts sent by divine command, destroying the fruits of the earth, and that those locusts are without doubt properly regarded in what goes before. Thus Aben Ezra seems to have received it from the Jews, when by reproach he understands hunger (ra'av), and explains the words that the nations may rule over them in this way: For the famished will flee to them, and if they come there will be no strength in them for fighting. In a similar manner Kimchi: Do not give your inheritance to reproach, that the nations may rule over them, because there was a famine in the land of Israel, and from it many went out to sojourn in the land of Egypt and in the land of the Philistines because of the famine, and the nations ruled over them while they sojourned in their land. So that according to these and others who follow the same manner of interpreting, the words flow in this way, as a certain Christian has well expressed it in a paraphrase: Spare your people, so that they do not hand over your inheritance to reproach, by bearing that plague of locusts, which, if it rages further and has consumed, will bring on extreme famine; and so your people will be forced to flee to the regions of the nations to relieve the necessity of famine, and to serve for bread among them and to endure their rule and also their reproaches, just as once they fled into Egypt and became slaves. Much more recent Christians also approve this, along with Calvin, and think it far saner, namely that the enemies are indeed meant here as going to rule over them, yet they are not the enemies, but the little worms described before, by whose inflicted damage they would be reduced so far that, compelled by famine, they would hasten to those nations and submit themselves to them, or would not be difficult to bring under their power. Moreover, when in this verse it is said: let the priests weep between the porch and the altar, it is plainly evident that the things said here happened while the temple, with its porch and the other things pertaining to it, was still whole and safe, to which access was still given to the priests, and the liberty to perform the offices proper to their duty there. This, to be sure, is contrary to the opinion of Abarbanel, who thinks that it looks to a time after the temple was destroyed, indeed to the second temple and the present condition of affairs, comparing it with this form of expression found in chap. 1:9, 13, 14, 16, and chap. 14 of this book. His words, in which he states his main view, come to this: that he cannot understand these words, do not give your inheritance to reproach, that the nations may rule over them, except of the long captivity in which we now are, in reproach, in the hands of the Edomites, and that the lament described here is none other than the captivity's, in which the people wept and mourned for their sins, since they were captives for so many years. But how can it be said to have happened between the porch and the altar? Therefore it must necessarily be referred to those things which were done while the temple was still standing whole and covered.

units.la: Hinc postquam ad generalem eos hortatus erat humilitatem, solennemque pœnitentiam, propter calamitatem, qua erant presli, vel quam reformidabant, formamque ejus præscripserat, ne nullum putarent habitura esse ea apud DEum locum, & ut rite etiam peragerent,
units.tr: Having thus exhorted them to general humility and a solemn repentance, because of the calamity that pressed them or that they dreaded, and having prescribed its form, lest they think such efforts will have no place with God, and so that they may also carry out properly what he had commanded, he declares in the following words that their actions will not be without a favourable result, and that God will follow them as surely as if he had already passed by.

units.la: {c} Piscat. Mercer. Drus. Tarnovius. rent, quæ jusserat, proximis declarat verbis, haud sine prospero fore effectu illorum actiones, eumque tam certo illas secuturum, ac si jamjam prateriisset.
units.tr: {c} Piscator, Mercerus, Drusius, Tarnovius. He declares in the next words that their actions, which he had commanded, will not be without a prosperous effect, and that God will follow them as surely as if he had already passed by.

units.la: 18. Tunc zelabitur Dominus terram suam & misere- bitur populi sui.
units.tr: 18. Then the LORD will be zealous for his land and will have pity on his people.

units.la: Ita quidem nostrates & alii nonnulli hæc verba tempore futuro interpretantur, zelabitur &c. miserebitur, cum eodem etiam extent hebraica יקנא yekaneh & ירחם yachmol. Verum cum illis præfixa sit conjunctio ו ve &, quæ plerumque in præteritum commutat tempus futurum, quibusdam etiam placuit ea præterito tempore exprimere, zelatus est, misertus est. Ita Chaldeus ורחם & קנא peperit & misertus est. Græc. καὶ ἐζήλωσε & καὶ ἐφείσατο, zelatus est & pepercit; & Syrus ܩܢܐ Utam, ܪܚܡ Uchos; & Arabica utraque غار wagara وشفق washphaka, cuncti versioni Latinæ accedentes & zelatus est & pepercit; Duacenf. and our Lord hath been zealous, and hath spared. Et ex recentioribus etiam quidam, ut Munster. commotus est zelo &c. nec non Junius & Tremellius. zelotypus affectus Jehovah terræ suæ, clementia usus est erga populum suum. Nemo est, qui hæc verba secundum regulam & prædicta ex ratione recte præterito tempore verti ambigat. Quod tamen nihilominus tempore futuro possint accipi, ex alia haud incoguta evidens est observatione, quam ut alibi sat superque tradidimus, ita haud paucis exemplis etiam suffulcitur, scilicet hunc esse Prophetis morem, ut de futuris non aliter loquantur, ac si jam essent præterita, vel hanc ob rationem, quod tam certo sint futura, quæ a DEO determinantur, ut non secus ac jam revera facta jure merito possint haberi. Atque hujus generis hanc formam esse, opinio est non ut unius. Approbant eam Iua interpretatione Nolbates non minus, quam ei alii. Notat ad ea verba Aben-Ezra, quod ad alia jam notalle dicitur, כי רבר נגזר יהוה ויאמרו הנביאים ער לעין עבר Prophetæ (f) solent.
units.tr: This is how our people and some others translate these words in the future tense, "will be zealous" and so on, "will have pity", although the Hebrew yekaneh [יקנא] and yachmol [ירחם] stand in the same form. But since they are preceded by the conjunction ve [ו], "and", which usually changes the future tense into the past, some have also chosen to render them in the past tense, "was zealous, had pity". So the Chaldee has veqana [וקנא] and verachem [ורחם], "was zealous and had pity"; the Greek has kai ezēlōse [καὶ ἐζήλωσε] and kai epheisato [καὶ ἐφείσατο], "was zealous and spared"; the Syriac has Utam and Uchos; and the Arabic has both wagara and washphaka. All of these agree with the Latin version, "was zealous and spared"; the Douai version has "and our Lord hath been zealous, and hath spared." Among more recent writers, some, such as Münster, render "he was moved with zeal," and Junius and Tremellius render "the zealous Jehovah was affected toward his land and showed mercy to his people." No one doubts that these words can rightly be rendered in the past tense according to the rule and the context. Yet they can equally be taken in the future tense, as is clear from another observation not unknown to scholars, which I have already set out fully elsewhere and which is supported by quite a few examples: it is the custom of the Prophets to speak of future things as if they were already past, either because what is determined by God is so certain that it may rightly be counted as already done. That this is the form of such expressions is not the opinion of one man alone. Aben-Ezra, commenting on these words, supports this interpretation no less than others do, as it is said he has already noted elsewhere: ki davar nigzar YHWH vayomru hannebi'im 'ad le'in 'ever [כי דבר נגזר יהוה ויאמרו הנביאים ער לעין עבר], "the Prophets are accustomed to speak..."

units.la: e) In cap. 1,7. f) Ita & Aharb. silent loqui de re, quae decreta est, ut fit, pars temporis praeteritum. Hinc meliora vult Pharaon verba Jani: & Tremellii, jam zelotypia offendit est ita: tunc zelotypia adversus & clementia ut ita, quia ipsa fontis hoc signaculum futuri postulat, etsi regularis sit alterius constructio & ex usu coniunctionis ꝩ, quae voci praefixa est. Attamen in contrarium hoc docti simus Lyra. Censet enim, Prophetam [illegible, ~6 letters] non ostendere, quod factur as dicturus sit Deus, sed quod jam dicere non fecerit, nimirum, quod respicientia facta illiusque ritibus, aliquos hortatus erat eos recte perachi se ipsum offendere et violum pro terra illorum atque benignum, auferendo ea quae inerat judicia, ita ut duo his verbis significare voluerit Prophetam, & a DEO admonitos ꝩ 11. 13. 15. 16. jam relinquisse eaque omnia fecisse, ad quae eos hortatus fuerat Propheta; & DEum ipsum ab illis removisse mala, quae peccatis sibi acciderant, atque liberationis multorumque bonorum promissionibus eos solatum esse. Quod ipsi moveri poterit dubium ab objicientibus, nullam hujus eorum respiciendi publicae, congregationis in hunc finem solennis & jejunii celebrati in sacris literis esse mentionem, nullius plane arbitratur momenti, cum multa sint loca, in quibus talium reticentia occurrit, quae facta esse nemo in dubium vocare poterit. Exemplo loco adducit Jesaiam, quam jussit Deus Isa. 7, 3. &c. ut cum filio suo Shear-jashub ad Ichaz le conferret, quod ut factum fuit, nemo ambigit ita nulla plane huius facta mentio. Sic cum Mose praeceptum erat, ut ad Pharaonem iret, eique & servis sui colluvionem animalium immissum in dementiret, nisi populum Israelitarum dimitteret, ilatio nulla facta mentione ejus, quid fecerit Moses vel responderit Pharaon (cf. v. 24, loquitur, DEum illam colluvionem immisisse. Itaque sub intelligendum est: haec DEI mandata cum Moses ad Pharaonem perrexisset, illi obtemperare renuisset, tunc advenit a Jehova musca ꝩ &c. Quae omnia ut ad literam ita tamen modo sunt facta: Hac mea sententia moderate progressio sententia est, quae a dolloribus exemplo clarius. Idem fortean sentire videtur Hieronymus, qui aliquantum multo eil eum cum omnia quoque tempore praesentia interpretatio sit. Nec certum habeo, num ab aliquo alio haec sententia ad metidem unquam
units.tr: e) On chapter 1:7. f) Likewise Aharb. [Aharon?] is accustomed to speak of a thing that has been decreed as if part of the time were past. Hence Pharaoh prefers the words of Jani, and that of Tremellius, "now zeal has been offended," is thus: "then zeal against and mercy, as it were," because the very seal of the future demands this, although the other construction is regular and follows the usage of the conjunction vav attached to the word. Nevertheless the learned Lyra holds the contrary. For he thinks that the Prophet [illegible, about six letters] does not show what God is going to do or say, but what he has not yet said; namely, that, looking back at the deeds and rites of the people, he had exhorted them to carry them out properly, and that God, being gentle and kind toward their land, had removed the judgments that were in it, so that by these words the Prophet wished to signify that, having been admonished by God, they had now left their sins and done all that the Prophet had urged them to do; and that God himself had removed from them the evils that had befallen them because of their sins, and had comforted them with promises of deliverance and many good things. This doubt may be raised by objectors: that there is no mention in Scripture of any solemn public gathering of the congregation for this turning back, nor of any fast celebrated for this purpose. Lyra thinks this is of no weight at all, since there are many places where the silence about such things occurs, and no one could doubt that these things were done. He cites as an example Isaiah, whom God commanded (Isa. 7:3, etc.) to go with his son Shear-jashub to Ahaz; and, although it was done, no one doubts that no mention of it is made. So too when Moses was commanded to go to Pharaoh and to threaten him and his servants with a swarm of animals sent into their land unless he let the Israelites go, there is no mention of what Moses did or what Pharaoh answered (cf. v. 24), but it speaks of God having sent that swarm. Therefore it must be understood thus: when Moses had gone to Pharaoh with these commands of God and Pharaoh had refused to obey, then there came from Jehovah a fly, etc. All of these things were done just as they are written, but only in this way. This is my view, a moderate progression of meaning, which is made clearer by the examples given. Perhaps Jerome seems to think the same, since he interprets the whole thing as present in time. Nor am I certain whether this opinion has ever been put forward by anyone else.

units.la: A a 2 quam fit vocata. Noftrates, ut & sequentium temporum alii, qui dubio procul ejus sententiam sciverunt, futuro tempore, quæ hic dicta sunt, accipiunt, prophetiamque ejus, quod futurum erat, potius habent, quam narrationem præteritorum, etsi propter g) certitudinem ita exprimatur, quod notatum est antea, ut revera actum esse putares: Etenim non est temporum apud DEum ulla distinctio; quod facturus est, non est secus quam jamjam factum, omnia ei sunt præsentia, & quod futurum est non est, aliter, ac si fuisset. Time zelabitur Dominus terram suam ויקנא יהוה לארץ zelfus erit, i. e. magno affectu afficietur, ita, ut quod noxium, quod damnosum ei, procul remoturus, quodque in bonum ejus cedat, procuraturus, h) destructioni æque ac inimicorum opprobriis tandem imponendo finem. Perspectum est i) observatione linguæ hebraicæ peritis, in bonam partem accipi hoc verbum, quando construitur cum præfixo ל le, ut hoc loco, atque denotare, sollicitum esse de ejus salute, de quo sursum patur; in malam vero partem sumi, quando construitur cum præfixo ב be, suspicionemque mali notare in eo, qui zelotypia afficitur, vel, alicui male velle. Quantumvis vero alibi ita usurpetur, ut etiam significet vindicare, vindicari; manifestum tamen est, hic non nisi benignam in eum denotare voluntatem, de quo dicitur. Apprime itaque ejus sententiam exprimit Chaldæus per ירחם & Dominus parcet. Hujusmodi autem verba, quæ passionem vel animi affectum notant, cum k) DEO tribuuntur, non significant, ut alibi, ni fallor, notatum est, eum talibus esse obnoxium affectibus, quibus homines sunt obnoxii; sed quos effectus in hominibus plerumque habent tales afsectus, iidem nobis humano more exhibentur hujusmodi loquendi formulis in Deo. Quocirca zelotypus esse hic nihil aliud est, quam benevolentia ac favore eam terram prosequi. Quod ut expredictus de verbi constructione aliquatenus patet; ita magis adhuc conflat ex altero ei adjuncto verbo, & miserebitur populi sui ועמו רחם. Quo quidem innuit, se pro justa sua severitate, quam communiter erant, eos non esse tractaturum, sed seria pœnitentia facta communi. {blurred}ordinis: benigne condonaturum, malaq; commerita longe remoturum: id quod futurum ex eo magis confidere poterant, quod talibus utaentibus, qui relationem propiorem notant, quibusque illi cos ... alterit, ut maiorem adhuc eorum videatur habere curam, quam ... aliis populi, dicens, suam terram & sui populi. Unde non potuit non animus iis accedere, fore ut peculiari modo iis etiam succurrat, benignitatemque largam exhibeat non solum auferendo ab hostibus, quo quidem maxime videtur hic versus respicere, sed etiam largiendo bona, ut pluribus id declarat versu sequenti.
units.tr: Our people, as well as others of later times who doubtless knew his opinion, take the things said here in the future tense, and regard his prophecy as concerning what was to come rather than a narrative of past events, although on account of the g) certainty it is expressed as noted above, so that you would think it had really happened. For there is no distinction of times with God; what he is going to do is no different from what is already done, all things are present to him, and what is future is no different from what has been. Then the LORD will be zealous for his land, vayqanna YHWH le-artso [ויקנא יהוה לארצו], "will be zealous", that is, he will be affected with great feeling, so that he will remove far away what is harmful and damaging to it, and will procure what turns to its good, h) putting an end both to destruction and to the reproaches of its enemies. Those skilled in the Hebrew language have observed i) that this verb is taken in a good sense when it is construed with the prefix le [ל], as here, and denotes concern for the welfare of the one about whom it is spoken above; but it is taken in a bad sense when it is construed with the prefix be [ב], and it indicates suspicion of evil in the one who is moved by jealousy, or ill will toward someone. However, although elsewhere it is used so as to mean also to avenge, to be avenged, it is clear that here it denotes only a kindly disposition toward the one of whom it is said. The Chaldee especially expresses this sense by verachem [ורחם], the Lord will spare. Now expressions of this kind, which denote passion or emotion, when they are ascribed to God, do not, as I think has been noted elsewhere, mean that he is subject to such feelings as men are subject to; rather, these effects that such feelings usually produce in men are shown to us in human manner by such forms of speech about God. Hence to be zealous here means nothing other than to pursue that land with goodwill and favour. This is shown to some extent by the construction of the verb; it is confirmed even more by the other verb joined to it, and he will have pity on his people [ועמו רחם]. By this he indicates that, for all his just severity, which they had deserved in common, he would not deal with them according to it, but, when a serious common repentance had been made, would pardon them graciously and remove far away the evils they had deserved; and they could be more confident of this because he uses such terms as denote a closer relation, by which he seems to have even greater care for them than for the other people, saying his land and his people. Hence their minds could not but take heart that he would help them in a particular way, and show a generous kindness not only by taking them away from their enemies, which this verse seems chiefly to concern, but also by bestowing good things, as he declares more fully in the following verse.

units.la: 19. Et respondebit Dominus & dicet populo suo: Ecce, ego mittam vobis frumentum, & vinum, & oleum, & satiabimini eo, & non amplius vos dabo in opprobrium in gentibus.
units.tr: 19. And the Lord will answer and say to his people: Behold, I will send you corn, and wine, and oil, and you shall be satisfied with them, and I will no longer give you up to reproach among the nations.

units.la: Vertit hunc rursus Vulgatus cum caeteris, respondit &c. Et Hieronymus uti usquequeque versum exponens in haec verba scribit: Zelatus est Dominus terram suam, quam primus quasi alienam contemserat, & passus est locum a ... populari, & in tantum pepercit poenitentibus, ut ... digna ... reliquisse ... fuerat divertetque &c. Verum uti plerique consueverunt, quod non ... ante, zelatus est & miserebitur ponitur, pro zelatur & miserebitur, ut habent nostrat.; iterum respondit &c. fine dubio, fine mora vel dilatione responderit &c. praecedentibus scilicet, eo quo par erat modo, in quae antecedentibus verbis ... illis ... in primis ... infucatae testimonium, quibus faciendi le populum ... poterant. Quid respondunt & dicturus vel compensaturus est ... ex sequentibus liquet: Ecce ego mittam vobis frumentum, vinum, & oleum, & satiabimini eo. Ecce, cognoscite quod confidimus certo fore compensaturus, est ... nobis contraxerunt ... frumentum &c. Quam tempestiva & praeclara ... atque ... conveniens adeoque grata fuerit responsio ... quam ... quae ... dicens ... fe reversurum revertentibus illis, locumque accedentibus datum, ... rum.
units.tr: The Vulgate, with the others, renders this again as he answered, etc. And Jerome, explaining the verse throughout in these words, writes: The Lord was jealous for his land, which at first he had despised as if it were foreign, and he allowed the place to be ... by the people, and he spared the penitent so far that ... he had left worthy ... and he turned aside, etc. But, as most have been accustomed to do, the phrase he was jealous and will have mercy is put for he is jealous and has mercy, as our people have it; he answered again, etc., undoubtedly answered without delay or postponement, namely to the preceding things, in the manner that was fitting, in which the preceding words ... those ... above all the testimony of the unfeigned ... by which they could make the people ... . What he answers, and what he is about to say or to make good, is clear from what follows: Behold, I will send you corn, wine, and oil, and you shall be satisfied with them. Behold, know that we confidently trust he will make good ... they have contracted from us ... corn, etc. How timely, how splendid, ... and how fitting, and so welcome, the answer will have been ... which ... saying that he would return when they returned, and a place was given to those approaching ... .

units.la: {y} II Cap. turum, ex iis non obscure patet, quæ in hoc libro habetur ius sun[?] de[?]pta. Præcedenti enim capite v.4. dicitur. Quod reliquerit ruca, s[?]s[?]... disse locustam, & quod reliquerat locusta, comedsse melolontha, & quod reliquerat melolontha, comedsse bruchum. Et v.4. Mostum ... s[?]... ... slorum ore, dentes fuisse dispositas in vastitatem &c. v. 7. & v. 10. Destatum frumentum, mistam exaruisse, oleum languisse, mistæ vites pernisse, omnes arbores agri aruisse, tantamque rerum inopiam ea omnia esse factam, ut non tantum gaudium ex plena fructuum vitam (spectantium perceptione in eos redundatum) exaruerit a domo hominum; sed & sacrificia & libamina cohibita fuerint, a domo DEI, lætitiaq; & gaudium exscissa v.16. quid? quod jumentum ingemiscit & perplexa essent armenta boum, quia nullum erat pascuum &c. v.18. &c. Quibus expressionibus quid aliud innuit censendum, quam usque adeo ad incitas hujusmodi annonæ caritate & extrema fame illos fuisse redactos, ut ad levandam famis necessitatem ad alias gentem confugere coacti sint in summum sui opprobrium, quasi DEum non haberent, qui ipsis auxilio esse possit, c.2.v.17? Quid igitur gratius, quid magis convenien & tempestivum accidere potuit hominibus tam deplorata conditione immersis atque animo pœnitenti a DEO solatium petentibus, quam quod summa affirmatione affirmat Propheta, fore, ut a DEO consequantur certam ac celerem conditionis suæ immutationem, quæ superant, qui nunc laborabant, inopiam in plenam omnium bonorum conversionem percepcionem, non tantum ratione ac mensura competenti, sed ad satietatem usque, ita ut ad alios confugere auxilii causa non foret opus, modo ut in DEum omnem collocarent spem, & fiduciam, qui omni defectu explendo sufficiens esset? Dicit DEum illis misericordiam esse frumentum, & vinum, & oleum, quæ omnia necessaria sunt ad vitam & tam jucundam, eaque tanta copia, ut ad satietatem lætorum suppeteretibus s[?]: quibusvis necessariis tum ad privatum ipsorum usum, tum ad sacrificia, oblationes juxta ac libamina in domo DEI, lætitia ac gaudio perfruentur. Nec ampliu̇s gentium oppositiones s[?] expositi, nec apud eas pro pane inseruiunt, ne cum-
units.tr: {y} Chapter II. It is clear enough from what is found in this book, ... the right ... . For in the preceding chapter, verse 4, it is said: What the cankerworm left, the locust has eaten; and what the locust left, the bruchus has eaten. And verse 4: ... the mouth of lions, their teeth were set for destruction, etc. Verse 7 and verse 10: The corn is spoiled, the new wine is dried up, the oil languishes, the vines have perished, all the trees of the field are withered, and such was the scarcity of all things that not only was joy in the full fruits of life (which redounds to those beholding them) dried up from the house of men, but also sacrifices and drink offerings were withheld from the house of God; and joy and gladness were cut off, verse 16. Moreover, the cattle groan and the herds of oxen are perplexed, because there was no pasture, etc., verse 18, etc. What else can be supposed to be hinted at by these expressions, than that they had been reduced, by the dearth of such a harvest and by extreme famine, to such a point that, to relieve the necessity of hunger, they were compelled to flee to other nations, to their great shame, as if they had no God who could help them, chapter 2, verse 17? What therefore could have happened that was more welcome, more fitting and timely to men plunged in so desperate a condition and seeking comfort from God with a penitent mind, than what the Prophet affirms with the highest assurance: that they will obtain from God a certain and swift change of their condition, that the want they were then suffering will be turned into a full conversion and receipt of all good things, not merely in a fitting measure, but even to satiety, so that there would be no need to flee to others for help, provided only that they placed all their hope and trust in God, who is sufficient to supply every lack? He says that God's mercy to them will be corn, and wine, and oil, all of which are necessary for life and so pleasant, and in such abundance that, being satisfied, they will enjoy them, both for their private use and for sacrifices and offerings, as well as drink offerings in the house of God, with joy and gladness. Nor will they any longer be exposed to the oppositions of the nations, nor serve them for bread, lest ...

units.la: *) Vide v.16. **) Ut dispergantur ad quærendum panem. Ab. Ferr. in Lamen. p.6. tenuu illis essent tanquam populus indigens, cujus DEus non parcetaccurrendo, vel quo plane deferuisset. Ita enim haec reddit Chaldaeus, neque dabo eos amplius היסודי כסיא opprobria famis inter populos, id est, ut R. Salomon hoc exponit שיקראו איתכם ut appellent vos pane tarentes (vix óibus haerentes). Quod vero hic est, mittam vobis frumentum & vinum, Chaldaeus interpretatur, esse benedicam (vel benedicam) vobis frumento & vino, quod ita explicat Kimchi: faciam vobis germinare arbores agri et fructum terrae. Quod ut fieret, necessarium erat, ut quae damnum tolerant vel efferunt illatura fructus destruendo, colliberentur vel renovarentur, ne quid amplius obstaculi esset, quo minus pristinis commodis uti liberent. Atque eo inprimis spectat versus sequens, quo nominatim promittit, omnia se esse remoturum, quae hactenus tolerarant aut tolerranda saltem imminebant.
units.tr: *) See verse 16. **) That they be scattered to seek bread. Ab. Ferr. in Lamentations, p. 6. ... to them, as a people in want, whom God would not spare by running to their aid, or by which he would plainly have ceased. For the Chaldee paraphrase renders it thus: neither will I give them any more [היסודי כסיא] a reproach of famine among the nations, that is, as R. Solomon explains it, [שיקראו איתכם] that they may call you, those who are dying of hunger (scarcely cleaving to bones). But what is here, I will send you corn and wine, the Chaldee renders as: I will bless you with corn and wine, which Kimchi explains thus: I will make the trees of the field and the fruit of the earth to sprout. In order that this might happen, it was necessary that those things which caused loss or which would bring forth fruit should be destroyed, that they be removed or renewed, so that there would be no further obstacle to their using their former advantages. And the following verse especially bears on this, in which he promises by name that he will remove all the things which they had hitherto endured, or which at least were threatening to be endured.

units.la: 20. Et procul removebo a vobis exercitum ab aquilo- ne, & compellam eum in terram aridam & desola- tam, faciem ejus ad mare orientale, & extremum e- jus usq; ad mare extremum, & foetor ejus ascendet, & malus odor ejus ascendet, quia patravit magna.
units.tr: 20. And I will remove far from you the army from the north, and will drive him into a dry and desolate land, with his face toward the eastern sea and his hinder part toward the western sea. His stench shall come up, and his foul odour shall ascend, because he has done great things.

units.la: Exercitum ab aquilone: Et hatsephoni, ab aquilone, hoc enim verba continent, quod us adiecit exercitum noltrates, quem illi ligi hic putarunt, ut diverso imprimendi characterere lignificarent. Quod tamen in quibusdam aliis translationibus non occurrit. Graecis ea interpretantibus τὸ ἀπὸ βορρᾶ. Vulgat. Lat. eum qui ab aquilone est, Syr. Arab. impreff. quod sic vertit Lat. cum qui est ex aquilone, (quamvis verba ita proprie forsitan non habeant) MS. Arab. eum qui est a Chaldaeis. Unde huic instrumenta, quae praecedentibus describuntur, vocaverat DEus exercituum suum. Hoc loco additur ei epitheton ab aquilone, quod valet, vel qui removeat ab aquilone, vel qui versus aquilonem erat collocatus.
units.tr: "The army from the north": the Hebrew is hatsephoni, "from the north," and these are the words that the translators of our own version rendered by adding "the army," which they thought had to be supplied here, marking the addition with a different type to show it. This addition is not found in some other translations. The Greeks render it τὸ ἀπὸ βορρᾶ [to apo borra, "the one from the north"]. The Vulgate has "him who is from the north"; the printed Syriac and Arabic, which the Latin renders "the one who is from the north" (though perhaps the words do not properly have that sense); and a manuscript Arabic has "him who is from the Chaldeans." Hence God calls the instruments described in the preceding verses "his army." Here the epithet "from the north" is added, which means either "one who removes from the north" or "one who was stationed toward the north."

units.la: Exinde igitur magna inter interpretes orta est o) dissensio, quinam potissimum sint intelligendi, locustæne & hujusmodi vermiculi tanta multitudine eos infestantes, fructusque terræ devorantes, et hostes terram invadentes spoliantesque. Ita R. Tanchum אלי צפון appellat eum ab aquilone; vel vocatur aquilonaris, ceu est (ut a quibusdam dictum) propter adventum suum, nempe, adventus locustarum erat a parte Erak (vel Chaldæx) ita erat adventus hostium, si cum illis conferuntur. Pari modo R. Salomon dicit, exponi posse de exercitu locustæ, vel alia ratione, dicipulo veniente ex Aquilone Regum Assyriæ. Nec Cyrillus longe ab hic abit, cum de Assyriis exponat, qui versus aquilonem habitant. Attamen subjungit, fi quis de locustis accipere velit, quatenus ex aquilonaribus Judæx partibus veniunt, nil esse quod hanc expositionem infringere possit. Verum alii sic unam approbant, ut alteram plane reiiciant. Inter Judæos est Abarbinel, qui ut totus in eo est annotavimus ante, ut de hostibus omnia exponat, ita epithe-ton huc congruere putat Assyrios, Babylonios, & Romanos, quorum duo priores magis ad euro-aquilonem, posteriores ad caurum respectu Judæx habitabant, eosque omnes hac voce comprehendi, ac, quicquid Judæis illatum, ab eis esse illatum, nequaquam a locustis alisque ad literam descriptis infectis, quodque hic dicitur futurum, factum esse jam prioribus, & futurum posterioribus (populi.) Sunt autem p alii, qui Assyrios hic tantum denotari arbitrantur, qui Sennacherib Duce terram invadebant tempore Hezekiæ. q) Alii Chaldæi, qui Judæos in captivitatem abduxerant; r) alii Assyrios duxerunt, quorum exemplo omnium hic denotatio est respectu ad terram Israelis habito. Verum quascunque cum quasque pro sua tempore...
units.tr: From this there has arisen a great disagreement among the interpreters as to who are chiefly to be understood: locusts and such small worms that, in such great numbers, attack them and devour the fruits of the land, or enemies who invade and plunder the land. R. Tanchum calls him el tsafon [אלי צפון], that is, appellat eum ab aquilone; or he is called northern, as some have said, propter adventum suum, that is, because the locusts came from the direction of Erak (or the Chaldeans), and the enemies came from the same direction as compared with them. In the same way R. Salomon dicit, that it may be explained of the army of locusts, or in another way, of a leader coming from the north, the king of Assyria. Nor does Cyrillus depart far from this, since he explains it of the Assyrians, who dwell toward the north. Yet he adds that if anyone wishes to take it of the locusts, inasmuch as they come from the northern parts of Judea, there is nothing that can overturn this explanation. Others, however, so approve one interpretation that they plainly reject the other. Among the Jews there is Abarbinel, who, as I noted earlier, explains everything of enemies, and thinks the epithet fits the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Romans, the first two of whom lived more toward the north-east, and the last toward the north-west, with respect to Judea; and he thinks all of them are comprehended under this term, and whatever was inflicted on the Jews was inflicted by them, and by no means by locusts and other things described literally; and what is said here as future has already happened in the former times and will happen in the later (peoples). Others, moreover, think that only the Assyrians are denoted here, who invaded the land under their leader Sennacherib in the time of Hezekiah. Others say the Chaldeans, who had led the Jews into captivity; others name the Assyrians, whose example shows that the whole denotation here is with respect to the land of Israel. But whatever ...

units.la: o) Chaldæi superbæ populum. Alii inimicum. Psic. alii exercitum. Pañ. aliis Judæis Chaldæi. Thes. Arabiana ex Psener. adjicit, i.e. Assyrios. q) Cap. a Cast. r) Vide sis eundem & Riberam. sententia adducat rationes, adeo apte tamen dictis præcedentibus æque, ac sequentibus. Prophetæ non convenire videntur, quamquæ aliorum est non minus eruditione insignium virorum,qui non nulli locustas, caeterosque prædictos vermiculos hic denotari volunt. Hos enim & Aben-Ezra & Kimchi (quos s) alii sequuntur) dici autumant הצפיני ab aquilone, quod venirent צפון ממארץ ex angulo aquilonis: (quamvis ex eo argumentum petat Hieronymus, de Assyriis hoc dici, non de locustis, quod ab austro ex verius veniant quam ab aquilone) t) alii tamen satius putant intelligi earum eam partem, quæ occupaverat latus aquilonare Hierosolymæ; vel aquilonarem partem illarum, quas dicit, procul se remoturum ab eis, & compulsurum in terram aridam & desolatam, id est, commentantibus Ab. Ezra & Kimchi, in terram, ubi morientur, quia ibi non invenient, quo vescantur, nimirum in Arabia deserta, Bocharto autore, Junius & Tremellius intelligunt per eum ab aquilone, partem quam in Aquilonem a regione vestra depulsurus sum, locoque ejus, quod in textu est, compellam eum, reddunt depellam ex eo, i. e. ex eo exercitu, ad partem scilicet meridianam, ubi est desertum illud horrendum, de quo Deut. 8,15. At meridianæ earum partis hic nullam extare mentionem Bochartus regerit, quia, cum Hierosolyma sita esset in extrema meridiana parte terræ Canaan, pauca erant respectu urbis & sub aliis comprehensæ, ita ut hæc verba compellam eum, ad aquilonarem spectent partem, cujus injecta est mentio, & sequentia cum facie ejus ad mare, ad eam illarum partem, quæ ad mundi faciem, i. e. ortum. Quod hic hebraice est, ejus faciem, Junius & Tremellius reddunt, primum agmen; eam autem partem dicit se compulsurum ad vel in mare orientale, i. e. in mare mortuum, quod Hierosolymæ ad orientem erat, vel ut alii, in lacum Genezareth vel Tiberias. Quod autem ad postremum ejus, cum aliis innui putat occidentalem ejus partem, eamque depulsurus est in extremum mare; i. e. occidentale seu meridianum, quo quæ venturæ erant, essent perituræ, omnesque interituræ; & ejus fœtor, inquit, ascendet, & צחנתו Tsachanato malus odor ascendet, quæ postrema vox alibi in Sacris literis non invenitur. s) Druf. Caftal. t) Jun. Trem. Livel. Bochart.
units.tr: (Notes:) The Chaldeans, proud people. Others, the enemy. Psic., others, the army. Pañ. Others, the Jews, the Chaldeans. The Thes. Arabiana, from Psener, adds: that is, the Assyrians. q) Cap. a Cast. r) See the same and Ribera. Some adduce reasons, so apt for the preceding words as well as the following ones, yet they do not seem to fit the prophet. There are others of no less learned men who want locusts and the other aforementioned worms to be denoted here. For Aben-Ezra & Kimchi (whom others follow) say that the northern one means from the north, because they came from the corner of the north, (although Jerome takes an argument from this, that it is said of the Assyrians and not of locusts, because they came from the south rather than from the north). Others, however, think it better to understand the part of them that occupied the northern side of Jerusalem, or the northern part of those whom he says he would remove far from them and drive into a dry and desolate land; that is, as Ab. Ezra & Kimchi comment, into a land where they will die, because there they will find nothing to eat, namely in the desert of Arabia, according to Bochartus. Junius & Tremellius understand by "from the north" the part which I will drive from your region toward the north, and in place of the text's compellam eum they render depellam ex eo, that is, from that army, to the southern part, where is that dreadful desert of which Deut. 8:15. But Bochartus objects that no mention of a southern part of them appears here, since Jerusalem lay in the extreme southern part of the land of Canaan, and the parts that lay south of it were few compared with the city and were included under other names. So these words I will drive him refer to the northern part, whose mention has been introduced, and the following words, with his face toward the sea, refer to that part of them which lies toward the face of the world, that is, the east. What is here in Hebrew, his face, Junius & Tremellius render "the first army." But he says he will drive that part toward or into the eastern sea, that is, the Dead Sea, which lay east of Jerusalem, or, as others say, into the lake of Gennesaret or Tiberias. As for "his hinder part," others think it denotes his western part, and he will drive it into the furthest sea, that is, the western or southern sea, so that what was to come would perish and all would be destroyed. And his stench, he says, shall ascend, and tsachanato [צחנתו], his foul odour shall ascend; this last word is not found elsewhere in Holy Scripture.

units.la: Quia vero cum priori באשׁ ,cujus significatio usitatior est, conjunćta est, apparet (quod n) Rabbinis observatum est) ejusdem fere cum illa lignificationis efle, ita ut hoc loco הכביר כביר fnfus fit duplicatus, vel eadem res diversis expressa verbis, ut ... dicit, & ab omnibus fere interpretibus pro malo & fœtido intelle sumitur, exceptis Græcis eorumque w) interpretibus, qui in quibusdam exemplaribus habent ὁ ἐρευγόμενος αὐτῆ svetus ejus, quod tamen librariorum culpa factum elle Bochartus censet, cum debuissent scribere ꜧ) βρωμός; quam antiqua quædam exemplaria habuisse non obscure liquet ex Arabic. impressa, quæ ex iis est versa, quippe quæ ... ejus ascendet, & odor ejus attolletur. Quibus equidem nihil aliud innuitur, quam magnum illarum numerum iis in locis perisse aut fame necatum, aut in mare præcipitatum, quarum deinde cadavera ejecta fuissent in littus, id quod evenire locustis ex mukus fi immuntis fide dignis Auctoribus usitatis & ex illis a Bochart° citatis constat. Sufficiet in præsentiarum, opinor, (i, quod narrat Hieronymus, in medicum adducam. Dicit enim, le suo tempore vidisse agmina locustarum & obtexisse Judæam, quæ postea versus surgentes mare primum & novissimum præcipitatæ sunt. Paucisque interjectis ita pergit: Cumque littora utriusque maris acervis mortuarum locustarum quas aquæ evomuerant, implerentur, putredo earum & fœtor in tantum noxius fuit, ut aërem quoque corrumperet, & pestilentia ramen jumentorum quam hominum gigneretur. Ex quibus facile intelligi potest, quid minantia hæc DEI verba contineant & qua ratione velit ucrec cum vindictæ suæ instrumentis antea descriptis, si ad literam eam intelligamus de locustis atque similibus vermiculis, quorum non ina in prioribus sunt tradita. Qui de hostibus ea exponunt, veri gratia de Assyriis, Chaldæis, Romanis, vel id genus aliis, ut videmus hæc eorum descriptionem ad literam difficulter admodum expresse possunt. Quicunque autem hoc exercitu ab aquilone, ut non str. vertere collibuit) intelligantur, quæ etiam harum expressionum interpretationes
units.tr: But because it is joined with the former word, ba-ash, whose meaning is more common, it appears (as the Rabbis have observed) to have nearly the same meaning as that word, so that here the expression is doubled, or the same thing is expressed in different words, as ... says; and almost all the interpreters take it to mean "bad" and "fetid," except the Greeks and their translators, who in some copies have ὁ ἐρευγόμενος αὐτῆς [ho ereugomenos autēs], "its belching," which, however, Bochartus thinks was an error of the copyists, since they should have written βρωμός [bromos, "stench"]. That some ancient copies had this is clear from the printed Arabic, translated from them, which has "its stench shall ascend, and its odour shall be lifted up." By these words nothing else is indicated than that a great number of them perished in those places, either killed by famine or hurled into the sea, and their carcasses were then cast up on the shore. That this happens to locusts is established by trustworthy authors commonly cited and by those cited by Bochartus. For the present, I think it will suffice to bring forward what Jerome relates. For he says that in his own time he saw swarms of locusts that covered Judea, and afterward, driven toward the seas, they were cast into the first and the last. And after a few intervening words he goes on: "When the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts which the waters had cast up, their rottenness and stench became so harmful that it corrupted the air too, and a pestilence was produced, more among the beasts of burden than among men." From these things it can easily be understood what these threatening words of God contain, and for what reason he wished to connect them with the instruments of his vengeance described earlier, if we understand them literally of locusts and similar small worms, which were not so described in the previous passages. Those who explain these things of enemies, namely of the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Romans, or that kind of others, as we see, can hardly express their description literally. But whatever is understood by this army from the north, as some have preferred not to say, and whatever explanations of these expressions are finally given, it is plain and clear that God, through his threatening words, promises to the people who are truly and sincerely repentant that he will deliver them from those things and make them immune from every...

units.la: w) R. Sal. Ab. Ezra. ꟼ) Vide Cyrillum. x) Vide Drufii Conjectanca. tiones demum dentur, planum est atque perspicuum, DEum minacibus suis verbis promittere populo vere atque sincere poenitenti, se eos esse ab illis liberaturum atque immunes redditurum ab omni, quae imminere iis amplius videretur, clade, quanta & quam gravia hactenus illis etiam intulerant supplicia, quod in posterum, ut crederent etiam, eum esse facturum, DEus ipse suam interponit magnam potentiam. Eo enim cum primis spectant verba sequentia כי הגדיל לעשות quae notrat in textu interpretati sunt, quia patravit magna, & in margine, ad literam verius, quia magnificavit facere. Anglica, quae ex Geneven. confecta est, quia exaltavit se ipsum ea faciendo, ut & altera antiqua Anglicana versio cum quibusdam aliis linguis diversis, quae etsi in exprimendi ratione nonnihil differant, facile tamen inter se conciliari possent, modo in eo convenirent, de quo hic fit sermo, quidve innuat particula כי Ci, quae hujus clausulae prima vox est, & priorem versus partem cum posteriori connectit. Etenim non una hujus particulae est acceptio, quarum, quae ad institutum nostrum aliquid faciunt, haec inprimis sunt: y) Quia, cum postquam, etsi, quamvis. Nostrates & plerique alii eam hic accipiunt significatione prima, scilicet quia, atque; sic videtur rationem exponere, cur DEus eo velit agere modo, quo in praecedentibus dixerat. Tunc vero differentio inter interpretes oritur, cuinam sequentia debeant applicari, hostibus busne, an lodis vel Deo, & quisnam horum dicendus sit patrasse magna, aliis alteram, alteram aliis defendentibus. Qui hostem in praecedentibus ubique spectari putant, sive Assyrium & Chaldaeum, f. alium, de eodem & hoc loco sermonem esse, autumant, rationemque in illis reddi, cur DEus in eum ita animadvertere velit, ut in praecedentibus dictum est, scilicet quia patravit magna, vel magnificabit facere, velut Vulgatus habet, quia superbe egit, & a DEO cum esset missus ad populum castigandum, z) crudelitatem suam ipsius citra modum exercebat & petulantia quavis, effrenataque insolentia utebatur omnia ex sua, non alterius vi & potentia ratus se inferre & facere. Quae interpretatio ut satis videtur conveniens verbis; ita y) dubium haud mediocre nec tit illis,
units.tr: w) R. Sal. Ab. Ezra. ꟼ) See Cyril. x) See Drusius, Conjectanea. It is plain and clear that God, in these threatening words, promises the people who are truly and sincerely repentant that he will deliver them from those enemies and free them from every disaster that seemed about to fall on them, however great and grievous the punishments they had already suffered. That they should also believe he will do this, God himself adds a great assurance of his power. For the following words, כי הגדיל לעשות, which the text renders in the translation as quia patravit magna, and which the margin gives more literally as quia magnificavit facere, are chiefly aimed at this. The English version made from the Geneva Bible has quia exaltavit se ipsum ea faciendo, and so does another old English version, as well as several other versions in various languages. These differ somewhat in wording, but they could easily be reconciled with one another, provided they agree on the point under discussion, namely what the particle כי (ci), the first word of this clause, means and how it connects the first part of the verse with the second. For this particle does not have just one meaning. Among those meanings that bear on our purpose, the most important are these: y) because, when, after, although, even though. Our countrymen and most others take it here in its first sense, namely because, and so it seems to explain why God wishes to act in the way he had said before. But then the interpreters disagree about which party the following words should be applied to, the enemies or the locusts or God, and which of these is to be called the one who has done great things; some defend one view, some another. Those who think the enemy is always in view in the preceding verses hold that the Assyrian and the Chaldean, or some other enemy, is the subject here too, and that the reason given for God's wishing to punish him in the way already described is because he did great things, or will go on to do them. So the Vulgate has quia superbe egit (because he acted proudly), and when he had been sent by God to punish the people, z) he exercised his cruelty without measure, used every kind of wantonness and unbridled insolence, and thought that he was inflicting and accomplishing everything by his own power and not another's. This interpretation seems to fit the words well enough; yet y) not a small doubt arises for those who take the locusts as the subject,

units.la: y) Vid. Schindl. Nold. Conc. z) Esa. 47, 6. a) Lyra & Pet. a Figur.
units.tr: y) See Schindler, Noldius, Concordance. z) Isa. 47:6. a) Lyra and Petrus a Figueroa.

units.la: illis, qui a locustis stant, non posse deiis proprie dici superbiæ atque insolentiæ esse reas, superbe agere, vel magnificare fe, vel suo arbitratu hæc fecisse, cum nonnisi duētu naturæ agant, quocunque veniunt, vel a DEO mittuntur, ut judicia sua aliquandiu exequantur. Unde colligere absonum plane non est, quosdam inde esse inductos, cum præcedentia non nisi de locustis exponant, ut ad eas hæc non referant, sed ad DEum, cujus nomen hic fubintelligendum volunt, uti versu fequenti exprimitur cum iisdem adjunctis verbis, verbumque patrabit magna, exponant tempore præfenti, patrat, vel futuro, patrabit: Atque hujus opinionis sunt viri haud mediocri eruditione conspicui. Sic equidem Junius & Tremellius, quia magnifice Jehovah agit; cujus loco Piscator substituit, aget, & Caftalio, tam magna ille faciet, ad marginem notans, scilicet Jehovah, de quo, cum sermo incideret, Lively inquit, quod valde probo. At immanis est, qua laborant verba, hac ratione sumta, anomalia, quippe tunc prima persona mutatur in tertiam, nimirum cum initio versus sit, ego removebo, &c. clausula habet, ille faciet: Quod cum Drufius vidisset & ad incudem revocasset, eos, dicit, b) ideo non esse secutos, quia c) Hebraï omnes in locusta consentiunt, & Chaldæus Paraphr. Jonathan interpretatur, quoniam multa mala patrabit (ארי אטגי למעבר בישי) Quapropter de locustis ea cum non paucis aliis intelligit, de quibus Vulgat. quia superbe egit; quæ interpretatio fi sequenda, verba metaphoricè intelligenda esse notat d) Pet. a Figue, quia superbia in locustas non cadit; atque tunc nihil aliud significant, quam quod alii ad literam magis expresserunt, fecerunt magna: quo etiam spectat, quod olim observavit Ruffinus, superbe eum egisse pronuntians, haud vitio mentis, verum magnitudinem calamitatis expressit. At quare, qui a DEO missus erat ad hoc faciendum, quique hoc faciebat non ex ulla sua ipsius mala intentione, erat puniendus, quia hoc faciebat? Ad hanc litem dirimendam statui posset particulam כ Ci, quæ hic vertitur, quia, non adeo præcise respicere ad verba immediate præcedentia, removebo &c. & compellam &c. sed & ad ea simul quæ præcedunt, quibus
units.tr: who take the locusts as the subject: can they properly be said to be guilty of pride and insolence, of acting proudly or magnifying themselves, or of having done these things by their own choice, since they act only by the impulse of their nature, wherever they go, or because they are sent by God to carry out his judgments for a time? So it is not absurd to infer that some have been led to refer these words not to the locusts but to God, whose name they wish to be understood here, as it is expressed in the following verse with the same added words. They render the verb patrabit magna in the present tense, patrat, or in the future, patrabit. Men of no small learning hold this opinion. Thus Junius and Tremellius render quia magnifice Jehovah agit (because Jehovah acts magnificently); Piscator puts aget (will act) in its place; and Castalio gives tam magna ille faciet (he will do such great things), noting in the margin scilicet Jehovah (that is, Jehovah). When this matter came up, Lively said of it, quod valde probo (which I greatly approve). But the difficulty with this rendering is a monstrous anomaly, since the person changes from first to third: the verse begins with I will remove, and so on, while the clause has he will do (ille faciet). Drusius saw this and examined it again, and says that they did not follow it, b) because all the Hebrews agree on the locusts, and the Chaldee paraphrast Jonathan translates it, because he will do many evils (ארי אטגי למעבר בישי). For this reason he understands these words of the locusts, along with a number of others, to whom the Vulgate's quia superbe egit refers. If this interpretation is to be followed, the words must be understood metaphorically, as d) Petrus a Figueroa notes, since pride does not apply to locusts. Then they mean nothing other than what others have expressed more literally, fecerunt magna (they did great things). Here too belongs what Rufinus once observed, pronouncing that he acted proudly, not from any fault of mind, but expressing the greatness of the calamity. But why should the one who was sent by God to do this, and who did it not from any evil intention of his own, be punished because he did it? To settle this dispute, one could hold that the particle כ (ci), translated here as because, does not refer so precisely to the words immediately before, I will remove and I will drive, but also to the things that precede them, by which

units.la: b) Druf. c) R. Sal. Ab. Ezra. Kimchi. d) Id quod de locustis metaphorice intelligitur, quibus proprie non consenit superbia. quibus dicitur: Dominus zelabitur suam regionem & miserebitur populo suo. Atque sic tanquam effectus gratiæ & misericordiæ suæ sutura erat remotio horum instrumentorum a sua, quam intulerant, clade, quia patraverant magna, imo tanta, quantis volebat terram suam atque populum affligi. Hæc etiam videtur sententia Kimchi, qui in hæc verba commentatur: כי הארבה הגדיל לעשות רע באר והאר יח' ריחם עד הארץ וריחין quia locustæ magnificavit facere malum in terra, at Deus benedicendus misertus est (vel miserebitur) terra & occidit (vel occidet) eam. Quod quasi uno ictu omnem præcidit objectionem, quam faciunt illis, qui a parte locustarum stant, etiamsi כי Ci vertatur, quia. Verum enim vero sunt alii qui multo planiorem autumant evadere sententiam, si aliarum significationum quædam subfituatur, postquam vel etiamsi, quarum primam approbat vir admodum Reverendus Diodati, qui Italice reddit: dopo che haura fatte cosa grande, postquam fecit magna. Alteram vero Reverendus e) M. Gatakerus, qui ita mentem suam prodit: quamvis magna gesserit, locustarum scilicet agmen illud, exterminabitur tamen, & internecioni dabitur, fætore solo pene relicto. Nec video quid adversus harum quamvis excipi possit, quin insigniter æque omnes conspirare atque eo inprimis redire statuendum; etsi hæ noxiæ creaturæ a DEO ex justa ira immissæ, ad vindictam sumendam de terra propter peccata populi, magna ei jussu ipsius intulerant damna, eas tamen non plus potuisse inferre quam DEus permittebat, quocirca postquam magna patraverant, quæ merito injiciebant populo timorem, atque diutius ea in re perstare volebant & exitio vastatique nihil non dare, DEum tamen resipiscentia illorum permotum, ut offenderet ad se eas spectare, suum exercitum esse & non nisi jussu suo ea peragere, non permissurum esse ut noxæ quid amplius inferrent, sed eas ita esse remoturum, repensurumque, quod dederant, damnum, ut populus ei reconciliatus non haberet quod amplius eas timeret. Quoniam vero tam terribiles eas hactenus senserant, denuo tali opus erat ad fidem faciendam iis asseveratione, qualem habemus in verbis sequentibus. Antequam autem eam propius
units.tr: b) Drusius. c) R. Sal. Ab. Ezra; Kimchi. d) This is said metaphorically of the locusts, to whom pride does not properly belong. which it is said: The Lord will be jealous for his land and will have pity on his people. And so, as an effect of his grace and mercy, the removal of these instruments from his land would follow, from the ruin they had caused, because they had done great things, indeed as great as he wished his land and people to suffer. This also seems to be the view of Kimchi, who comments on these words: [כי הארבה הגדיל לעשות רע באר והאר יח' ריחם עד הארץ וריחין] because the locust magnified to do evil in the land, but God, blessed be he, had mercy (or will have mercy) on the land and destroyed (or will destroy) it. This cuts off, as it were at one blow, every objection that those who take the side of the locusts raise, even if כי is rendered because. Indeed, there are others who think the sense becomes much plainer if one of the other meanings is substituted, after or even though. The most Reverend Diodati approves the first, rendering it in Italian as "after he has done great things" (postquam fecit magna). The Reverend M. Gataker, for his part, states his view thus: although they did great things, that is, that host of locusts, they will nevertheless be destroyed and put to ruin, leaving scarcely anything but a stench. I do not see what can be objected to these views, except that they all agree remarkably well and must in the end come back to this: although these harmful creatures were sent by God in just anger to take vengeance on the land for the people's sins, and by his command had inflicted great losses, they could inflict no more than God permitted. Therefore, after they had done great things, which rightly struck fear into the people, and wished to persist in this and to give up nothing to destruction and devastation, God, moved by their repentance, would, as it were, take offence at their regarding themselves as his army and acting only by his command, and would not allow them to do any further harm, but would remove them and make good the loss they had caused, so that the people, reconciled to him, would have no reason to fear them any more. But since they had hitherto felt these creatures to be so terrible, a solemn assurance of this kind was needed to win their trust, such as we have in the following words. Before we look at them more closely,

units.la: c) In Adversariis. inspiciamus, non abs re fore arbitrantur directionis loco a sicere quasdam allegoricas expositiones, quas inde arcessunt quidam atque inter eos Cyrillus, qui ea interpretatur de Christo, qui tenus ex nobis expellit τὴν ἀκρίδα τὴν νοητὴν, locustas mentem nostram occupantes, i. e. eas Daemonum legiones, quas in orco ita conclusit, ac in mare praecipites dedisset, foetoremque eorum reddidisset odiosum, qui antea adeo non erat cognitus; inprimis vero, quam nobis tradit Kimchi, f) aliique notant ab antiquis Judaeis esse relictam, nimirum, ea verba spectare ad adventum Messiae ac per הצפוני Hatzephoni, (quod utplurimum redditur, cum qui a septentrione est) denotari (juxta aliam, quam vox fert, significationem) abscondLtum quendam, id est, secundum illos יצר הרע שצפון יעמר בלבי שיר אורם figmentum malum, quo plerumque intelligunt, malam concupiscentiam, naturalem corruptionem, vel peccatum originale (malum gentile) qui absconditus est & stat in corde hominis, & per ea, Expellum eum in terram aridam & desolatam, locum ubi non inveniuntur homines ad contendendum cum illis; & per faciem ejus ad mare Orientale, conjecisse eum oculos suos in primum sanctuarium & vastasse illud; & per extremum ejus usque ad mare novissimum, conjecisse eum oculos suos במקרש שני והחריבו ... arum & illud vastasse & occidisse discipulos suos ... & quando dicitur: Et ascendet foetor ejus, & ascendet putredo ejus, idem esse ac שנאי ... finit quinque gentes seculi & contendut cum sacribus Israelis, i. e. cum Israele, quod ex eo cum primis apparet, quod vocem שנאי omiserit yalkut, ejusque loco habeat cum illis, i. e. cum Israele. Denique patravit magna, juxta R. Abba, denotare cum magis esse occupatum in vespillis spiritum: quam in reliquis omnibus. Hactenus allegorica expositio veterum Rabbinorum a Kimchi citata, quae ut mihi persuadere minus potuit ad literam eos tali modo expositisse, quam ejus vox aeque significat abscondidum ac absconditum ac al quem a spectantem, ita & ipsa esse minus censeo, quam apte, ut ostendam, haec periphrasis verbis bis
units.tr: c) In the Adversaria. Let us look at some allegorical expositions which they think will not be out of place as a guide here, and which some draw from this passage. Among them is Cyril, who interprets it of Christ, who drives out from us the spiritual locust [τὴν ἀκρίδα τὴν νοητὴν], the locusts that occupy our mind, that is, those legions of demons which he shut up in hell, hurled headlong into the sea, and made their stench odious, though it had not been so well known before. Above all there is the exposition that Kimchi hands down to us, and that others note was left by the ancient Jews. According to it, these words look to the coming of the Messiah, and by the word Hatzephoni [הצפוני], which is mostly rendered "the one from the north", is denoted (according to another meaning the word bears) a certain hidden one, that is, as they say, the evil inclination, which lies hidden in the north and stands in the heart of man. By this they commonly understand evil concupiscence, natural corruption, or original sin (the evil of the nations), which is hidden and stands in the heart of man. By the words "I will drive him into a dry and desolate land", a place where there are no men to contend with them; by "his face toward the eastern sea", that he has cast his eyes on the first sanctuary and laid it waste; and by "his hinder part toward the utmost sea", that he has cast his eyes on the second sanctuary [במקדש שני] and laid it waste, and killed his disciples. And when it says "his stink shall come up, and his ill savour shall come up", this is the same as the haters, who end the five nations of the age and contend with the sacrifices of Israel, that is, with Israel. This appears first from the fact that the Yalkut omits the word "haters" and has in its place "with them", that is, with Israel. Finally, "he has done great things", according to R. Abba, denotes that the spirit is more occupied in burying the dead than in all the rest. So far the allegorical exposition of the ancient rabbis, cited by Kimchi. It could persuade me less that they expounded the words literally in this way than that the words equally signify "hidden", "a hidden one" and "one who is in the north". So I think this exposition too is less apt than it should be, as I will show: this periphrasis does not agree well with the words, nor does it draw a very good sense from them.

units.la: f) Talkut R. Salom. bis conveniat, neque quam belle sese habeat, quem ex iis elíciunt sensum. Id tantum unum adjicere expedit, si ingenue largiantur haec verba non nisi ea complecti, quae tempore Messiae futura erant ad subigendum inimicum absconditum, qui se abdit, excedit, & bellum excitat in corde hominis, omnino ea tempore Christi Domini nostri per eum factitata esse dicendum, ita ut eum solum verum esse Messiam vel ex his colligere possimus, nec ullum alium unquam expectare venturum opus habeamus. Ejus enim unius doctrina docti sumus, ac per gratiam ejus capaces reddití, ut exuamus veterem hominem, qui per fallaces corruptus est concupiscentias, atque merito vocatur יצר הרע yetser hara, innata corruptio, quam per יצר הרע abscondítum (ut reddunt) intelligi volunt; & renovemur spiritu mentis nostrae, & induamus novum illum hominem, qui secundum Deum conditus est in justitia & sanctimonia vera, Ephes. 4, 22. 23, 24. Nam cum eo vetus ille homo crucifixus est ut abolcatur corpus peccati, ne nos amplius serviamus peccato, nec peccatum regnet in nostro mortali corpore, ut auscultemus ei in cupiditatibus corporis, neque sistamus membra nostra arma injustitiae peccato, sed sistamus nos Deo, ut ex mortuis vivos & membra nostra arma justitiae Dei, peccato non amplius nobis dominante, Rom. 6, 6. 12. &c. Propter hoc manifestatus est Filius Dei, ut dissolveret opera diaboli, 1. Joh. 3, 8. Ita ut certissime atque omni ratione praestitum sit a Domino nostro Jesu Christo, quodcunque statuant Judaei his verbis innuí ac tempore Messiae requiri, tanquam verum adventus ejus indicium, adeo ut, si ex ea re adventus Messiae certissimum colligendum est argumentum (ut sua expositione videntur confiteri) merae sit in iis pertinaciae signum, si inficias ire adhuc volunt. Hanc eorum expositionem oppugnat Ribera congruamque minus eam censet, primo quia de hostibus exteris cum diu sermo fuerat, s. phoni non poterit reddi abscondítum aliquid, aliquid naturale sive formale ut ita, ut est ea naturalis concupiscentia; deinde quia videntur expectare, ut Messiae tempore hoc innatum originale malum protinus expellatur ex corde hominis, quod sanae doctrinae contrarium est. At in eo mihi videtur mentem eorum pervertere, cum inter eos hoc vulgatissimum sit atque decantatum, quamdiu pii sint victuri ח ה ש צ נ ו... nlhcm נלחמים עם יצרן certamen sibi fore cum sua ipsius concupiscentia; unde luculenter fatis elucescit, nil aliud sententiam illorum ferre, quam quod id temporis plus roboris atque virium sint accepturi ad id oppugnandum & subigendum. Arias Montanus vero & hanc sententiam optime congruere verbis, & eo modo intelligi posse putat, uti diximus. Si quis tamen secus censeat cum Ribera,non est quod hac in parte cum eo contendamus,illo potissimum verborum sensu contenti, qui preffius adhaeret literae,cum tam manifestum nobis statim hoc ipso in capite occurrat testimonium de Christo,ut & litera stricte retenta negari non possit. Hinc a literali expositione, quam antea horum verborum dedimus, transeamus ad ea quae fequuntur v. 21.
units.tr: Let me add only this one thing, if they frankly concede that these words embrace only what was to be done in the time of the Messiah, namely the subduing of the hidden enemy, who hides himself, withdraws, and stirs up war in the heart of man, then it must be said that all this was accomplished by our Lord Jesus Christ at the time of his coming. From this alone we may gather that he is the only true Messiah, and that we have no need to expect any other to come. For we have been taught by his doctrine alone, and through his grace we have been made able to put off the old man, who has been corrupted by deceitful lusts, and who is rightly called יצר הרע [yetser hara, innate corruption], which they wish to be understood through the hidden (as they render it) יצר הרע. And we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new man, who after God is created in true righteousness and holiness, Eph. 4:22, 23, 24. For our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer serve sin, nor sin reign in our mortal body, that we should not obey it in the lusts of the body, nor yield our members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but yield ourselves to God, as those that are alive from the dead, and our members as weapons of righteousness to God, sin no longer having dominion over us, Rom. 6:6, 12, etc. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil, 1 John 3:8. Thus it has been most certainly and in every way accomplished by our Lord Jesus Christ, whatever the Jews maintain is hinted at by these words and required in the time of the Messiah, as a true sign of his coming. So much so that if the certain argument for the coming of the Messiah is to be drawn from this matter (as they seem to confess in their own exposition), it is a sign of mere obstinacy in them if they still wish to deny it. Ribera attacks this their exposition and thinks it less suitable, first because, since the discussion had long been about foreign enemies, tsephoni cannot be rendered as something hidden, something natural or formal, as this natural concupiscence is; and secondly because they seem to expect that in the time of the Messiah this innate original evil will at once be expelled from the heart of man, which is contrary to sound doctrine. But in this I think he misreads their meaning, since among them it is most common and widely sung that as long as the pious live they will have a struggle with their own concupiscence: נלחמים עם יצרן [nilḥamim im yetsaram, they fight with their inclination]. From this it clearly appears that their opinion amounts to no more than this, that at that time they would receive more strength and power to attack and subdue it. Arias Montanus, however, thinks that this opinion also agrees very well with the words and can be understood in the way we have said. If anyone nevertheless thinks otherwise with Ribera, we need not contend with him on this point, being content with the sense of the words that adheres more closely to the letter, since at once in this very chapter there meets us such a clear testimony concerning Christ that it cannot be denied if the letter is strictly kept. Hence let us pass from the literal exposition, which we gave earlier of these words, to what follows, v. 21.

units.la: 21. Ne timeas terra, exulta & laetare: Nam Domi- nus faciet magna.
units.tr: 21. Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD will do great things.

units.la: Quid aliud poterant quam omnis generis mala timere, qui ante audiverant tot horrenda supplicia praedici,quaeque vel initia sua jam sumserant,vel necessario erant sumtura v. 1. jubebantur omnes etiam habitatores terra tremere propter diem Domini; & hic dies appellatur v. 11. vere terribilis. At contraria prorsus ratione hic agitur,qua jubentur non tantum non timere, sed & exultare & laetari. Quod tantam conditionis atque status ipsorum infert immutationem,resipiscentia erat, quae exigebatur abiis, v. 16.17. rite peracta ac praestita. Quamdiu juga detrectare pergebant Domino, eumque inimicum habebant, ratio erat atque occasio continuo timendi,flendi & ejulandi (cap. 1,5.) & lugendi, nec aliud quid tunc temporis monebantur; at postquam in gratiam erat reditum cum eo resipiscentia,jubentur non timere, sed exultare & laetari. Ne timeas terra, exulta & laetare. Terra, i.e. terra Israel, ut addit explicationis causa Chimchi, idem esse putat, ut porro explanat Kimchi, ac fi dictum est ישבי ne timeant incolae terrae Israel. Cui non absimile est,quod notat Aben-Ezra, vocem ארמי explanans, quando dicitur terra luget, pro ישבי incolae terrae cap. 1,10. & ita quoad vocem ארץ terra cap. 2,10. contrenuifcet terra pro ארץ אנשי homines terrae. Cum enim ipsa terra, ad quam sermo hic per prosopopœiam dirigitur, talium affectuum minus capax sit, manifestum est atque perspicuum, eam duntaxat dici ab omni liberari metu, atque exultare & lætari, quando occasio ita sese gerendi offert iis, quorum incolumitas, lætitia & exultatio ex ejus unius pinguetudine & prosperitate pendet. Ea enim erat quæ iis g) depromebat cibum, vinum ad cor eorum lætificandum, oleum ad faciem eorum nitidam efficiendam, & panem ad cor eorum fulciendum, fœnum ad jumentorum, & herbam ad hominis usum. Exinde cum his similibusque tam necessariis ad vivendum rebus producendis jußa esset supersedere, non poterat non tam tristis rerum facies existere. Contra vero cum jamjam omnem jubeatur deponere metum, ejusque loco gaudere & lætari, quid aliud innui censendum, quam eam rursus expletum iri omnibus hujus generis bonis, quæ fiduciam illorum possent firmare animumque addere, quorum ex ea omnis dependebat salus. Et ne ullo pacto in dubium vocarent, quam hic eis injungit timorem abjiciendi, exultandi & lætandi justam occasionem, exhortationi suæ addit Propheta rationem, qua ea nititur, ac non leve inde sumit pondus. Nam Dominus faciet magna. Dominum posse magna facere, ubicunque ipsi etiam collubitum sit, sive cœlis sive in terra, res erat, quæ in dubitationem eos adducere non poterat, quibus cognita erant tot ejus miranda coram majoribus suis patrata. Quapropter cum magna se esse facturum promittit, tam certo ea esse factura persuadere sibi poterant, ac si jam essent facta. Et si verum fateri velimus, verbum הגדיל Higdil proprie significat, fecit magna, neque tantum a plerisque antiquis, verum & a nonnullis recentioribus ita redditum est; ut a Chaldæo ארי אסני יי לחעבר a LXX. ὅτι ἐμεγάλυνε κύριος τὸ ποιῆσαι; & a Syro ܠܡܓܕܠ ܡܝܢܝ ܕܝ ܩQuia Dominus exaltavit se ipsum facere, licet interpres latinus futuro tempore id efferat, quoniam Dominus magnifice aget; in versione Arab. utraque, in MS. لأن الرب عظم & in impressa أن الله كان صنع Nam Dominus magnefecit sua opera vel suas actiones. Quos omnes sequun-
units.tr: What else could those who had earlier heard of so many dreadful punishments foretold, punishments that had either already begun or were bound to come (v. 1), do but fear every kind of evil? They were told to "tremble, all the inhabitants of the land, because the day of the LORD is coming," and this day is called "truly terrible" (v. 11). Here, however, the command is entirely different: they are told not only "not to fear" but to "exult and rejoice." This brings about so great a change in their condition and state because the repentance demanded of them (vv. 16, 17) had been duly carried out and performed. As long as they went on refusing to bear the yoke of the LORD and counted him their enemy, there was a reason and occasion for constant fear, "weeping and wailing" (ch. 1:5) and mourning, and at that time they were given no other instruction. But after repentance had restored them to favour with him, they are bidden "not to fear" but "to exult and rejoice": "Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice." "Land," that is, the land of Israel, as Kimchi adds by way of explanation, is taken to mean the same as if it had been said, "let the inhabitants of the land of Israel not fear." Not unlike this is what Aben-Ezra observes, explaining the word "mourns" in the sense of "the land mourns" (ch. 1:10) for "the inhabitants of the land," and so with the word "land" in ch. 2:10, where "the land trembles" stands for "the men of the land." For since the land itself, to which the speech is addressed by prosopopoeia, is less capable of such feelings, it is clear and evident that it is said to be freed from all fear and to exult and rejoice only when the occasion of so acting presents itself to those whose safety, gladness and exultation depend on the fruitfulness and prosperity of that land alone. For it was the land that yielded to them g) food, wine to gladden their heart, oil to make their face shine, and bread to strengthen their heart, hay for the cattle and herbs for the use of man. Since they had been ordered to abstain from producing such things, so necessary for living, the face of affairs could not but be very sad. On the contrary, now that they are commanded to lay aside all fear and in its place to rejoice and be glad, what else is to be understood than that the land will be filled again with all such blessings, which could strengthen their confidence and give courage to those on whom all their safety depended. And lest they should in any way doubt the justice of the occasion for casting off fear, and for exulting and rejoicing that he here enjoins on them, the Prophet adds to his exhortation the reason on which it rests, and from it draws no slight weight: For the LORD will do great things. That the LORD is able to do great things wherever it pleases him, whether in heaven or on earth, was something that could not make doubtful those who knew of so many marvels he had wrought before their fathers. Therefore, when he promises that he will do great things, they could be as sure that these would be done as if they had already been done. And if we wish to speak the truth, the word higdil [הגדיל] properly means "he has done great things," and it has been rendered thus not only by most of the ancients but also by some more recent writers: as by the Chaldee [paraphrast] "Ari asni Adonai le-ha'avar" ...; by the Seventy, "because the LORD has magnified to do" [ὅτι ἐμεγάλυνε κύριος τὸ ποιῆσαι]; and by the Syrian, "Lemgadal mayni di..." [Quia Dominus exaltavit se ipsum facere], "because the LORD exalted himself to do." Although the Latin translator renders it in the future tense, "because the LORD will act magnificently"; in the Arabic version, both forms appear: in the manuscript, "li-anna al-rabb 'azzama," and in the printed text, "anna Allah kana sana'a," "for the LORD magnified his works or his actions."

units.la: {g} Psal. 104, 14. 15. sequuntur etiam recentiores, & inter eos Munsterus : agendo magniſicè egit ; & interlin. magniſicavit Dominus ad h. l. faciendum ; nolitrat. vero, quibuscum faciunt non 1) pauci alii, malunt id futuro reddere : aget vel faciet, cum, refragante quamvis textu hebraico, non arbitrentur innui, quod jam fecerat, sed quod erat certo factu rus, ratione Sacris litteris usitata qua, quod a DEO determinatum est, non secus pronuntiatur, quam jam, am effectum. Iisdem verbis, excepto nomine ירושלם quod hi deest, videlicet Hygdil leafolb concluditur versus praecedens, quicunque ic; quod in opinionem quosdam adduxit, eandem utramque loci esse sententiam, subjectumque nullam aliud, quam DEum, qui praecedenti versu cum non habeatur, subintelligendus. Quod tamen minus probatur aliis, cum, quod etiam magis audet nobis, de iis potius instrumentis putent sermonem esse, quibus DEus usus erat ad exequendum judicia sua, in populum sibi refractarium, atque ita bi invicem esse oppositi quamvis eadem sint verba cum ibi per ישׁ Hish in, ut Chaldaeus exponit, intelligendā sint 2) hoc loco autem per כוב Tobin bona. Facile tamen differentia verborum hujus & illius loci reconciliari potest, quippe ab eodem fonte profluxerunt & bona & mala. Nimirum a DEO erant, quamvis, quod ibi factum est, malum ab hujusmodi instrumentis illatum fit, quae in hunc finem ab eo erant adhibita, hoc loco autem, quod bene factum erat ab eo immediate oriretur.
