Nihil etiam refert, quod ibi de locustis dicatur Jiwm tua magna, quippe id propterea factum, quia potestatem hic faciendi is largiebatur idem DEus, qui hic dicitur fecit, magna, quatenus non tantum ea potestate illa rursum exuebat, sed & ea ipsa quae tantum potestate videbantur armata, ab oculis omnium removebat resarciendo populo, quod se permutente dederant, damnum ita ut eidem poteltas, quae inimicis videpti erat causa nietu, Jonas facere recouciliata, causa fuit securitatis. Pari ratione termonem suum ad bellas agri dicit cauffingue dulcis us alloquii folatonque licet ratione carent dilcernendi atque caum um, magnam tamen sentire poterant ut mutationem & pacis conciliationis,
units.tr: Psalm 104:14, 15. Recent writers also follow these, and among them Münster: acting magnificently he acted magnificently; and the interlinear version: the Lord magnified to do. But a good many others, including those with whom I agree, prefer to render it in the future, he will act or he will do. Although the Hebrew text resists this, they do not think what he had already done is meant, but what was certain to be done. Holy Scripture commonly speaks in this way: what has been determined by God is declared no differently than if it had already been accomplished. The preceding verse ends with the same words, except that the name Jerusalem is absent here, namely Hygdil leafolb. This has led some to think that both passages have the same sense and that the subject is none other than God, who must be understood here since he is not named in the preceding verse. Others regard this as less probable, and think, with greater boldness, that the reference is to those instruments by which God carried out his judgments against the refractory people, so that the two passages are opposed to each other. The words are the same, since there Hish [ישׁ] is to be understood as evil, as the Chaldee paraphrast explains, while here Tobin [טוב] means good. Yet the difference between the words of this place and that can easily be reconciled, since both good and evil flow from the same source. Certainly both come from God, although what was evil there is inflicted by such instruments as were employed by him for this purpose, whereas here what was done well arises immediately from him. Nor does it matter that there the locusts are said to have their great army (Jiwm); this is because the same God who is here said to have done great things gave them that power, and he later stripped them of it, and also removed from sight those very things which seemed armed only with power, making good to the people the loss they had incurred. The power which had been a cause of fear to enemies became, through reconciliation, a cause of safety. By a similar reasoning he speaks to the beasts of the field, and to the creatures which lack the ability to discern and understand, yet could nonetheless perceive a great change and the restoration of peace, the sweet comfort of a reconciled address, which they had lost while they were subject to divine wrath, and now enjoy in the present grace restored by him. For this reason he addresses them in this manner:

units.la: b) Vel ut fa erit, in margine. 1) Sagn. Tig. Cast. Jun. Tremel. 2) Vide Aben-Ezra, Kimchi. mis, qua divinæ iræ cum populo erant subjectæ,& præsentis, qua gratia ejus restituta fruebantur; quocirca eas hunc in modum alloquitur:
units.tr: b) Or "as it would be", in the margin. 1) Sanct., Tigur., Cast., Jun., Tremell. 2) See Aben Ezra and Kimchi. ...which were subject to divine wrath, and which now enjoy the present grace of God restored to them; wherefore he addresses them in this manner:

units.la: 22. Ne timeatis, bestiæ agri: nam pascua deserti ger- minant, nam arbor adfert fructum suum, ficus & vitis dant virtutem suam.
units.tr: 22. Fear not, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring up; for the tree beareth its fruit, the fig tree and the vine give their strength.

units.la: Dictum est supra de his bestiis agri cap. 1,18. ingemuisse eas & perplexas fuisse, & v. 20. Bestiæ campi ad te clamant,cujus rei hæc additur ratio,quia nullum pascuum erat earum,& quia alvei aquarum exaruerant, & ignis absumserat pabula deserti. Hic vero, ne sic pergant vocare vel glocitare, vel ut ostendatur, nullam amplius fore causam sic faciendi,jubentur deponere metum,eo quod contrario modo omnia sese essent habitura, unde sibi de necessariis possent providere, quorum indigentia ad tantam antea glocitationem erant impulsæ. Et quamvis alveorum aquarum hic nulla fiat mentio, patet tamen, ut Kimchi observat, eorum impletionem iis comprehendi formis, quibus cæteris defectibus mederi velle dicitur,in primis quando pascua deserti,quæ ignis antea absumserat,dicuntur nunc germinare. Hinc merito hoc inter magna habendum est DEI factum, quo tantam desolationem, qua frugifera terra in meram solitudinem, pastum & hominibus & bestiis abnuentem, erat versa,momento commutaturus erat potentia sua in hortum Edenis, necessariaque omnia suppeditaturus ad utrorumque & usum & voluptatem. Id enim certo futurum sat superque declarant verba. Sicuti autem arida pascua erant germinatura; ita & arbor,quæ supra dicitur exaruisse cap. 1,12. & ficus & vitis, quæ ibi quoque dicuntur elanguisse & aruisse,daturæ erant suam virtutem, i. e. edituræ uberrimos fructus, id quod omnium erat maximum, quod ab iis expeti posset. Quid igitur immutationis illis ipsis esset illaturus status rerum beneficio DEI illis reconciliati immutatus,proximesequenti versu exhibere contendit.
units.tr: This was said above of these beasts of the field, at 1:18, that they groaned and were perplexed, and at v. 20, "The beasts of the field cry also unto thee." The reason given for this is that they had no pasture, "and the rivers of waters are dried up, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness." Here, however, they are told to lay aside their fear, so that they will not go on crying out or lowing, and so that it may be shown that there will be no longer any cause for doing so. For all things were going to turn out the opposite way, so that they could provide for themselves what they needed, the want of which had driven them to such great lowing before. And although no mention is made here of the rivers of water, it is plain, as Kimchi observes, that their filling is included in the forms by which he is said to wish to remedy the other defects, especially where the pastures of the wilderness, which the fire had previously consumed, are now said to spring up. Hence this must rightly be counted among the great works of God: that by his power he would in a moment change such a desolation, in which the fruitful land had been turned into mere wilderness, denying food both to men and to beasts, into the garden of Eden, and would supply everything necessary for the use and pleasure of both. For the words declare sufficiently that this will certainly come to pass. But just as the dry pastures were going to sprout, so also the tree, which above is said to have "dried up" (1:12), and the fig and the vine, which there too are said to have "languished" and "withered," were going to give their strength, that is, to yield most abundant fruit, which was the greatest thing of all that could be desired from them. What change of circumstances, brought about by God's favour toward the people reconciled to him, was going to bring about this change in them, he sets forth in the next verse.

units.la: 23. Et exultate filii Sionis & lætamini in Domino DEO vestro: nam dedit vobis temperiuam pluviam moderate, & faciet descendere vobis pluviam, temperiuam pluviam, & serotinam pluviam in primo mense.
units.tr: 23. Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month.

units.la: Filii Sionis, i. e. vos incolæ Hierosolymæ, cujus pars erat ædificata in monte Sion. Qui antea erant vocati, ut ad Dominum reverterentur flendo ac lugendo in pœnitudinis signum, iidem jam ad frugem posteaquam redierant, Deumque idcirco sibi reconciliaverant, jubentur exultare in Domino DEO suo. In Domino, non adeo in affluenti rerum bonarum ubertate, quam quod relipiscentia ea adepti essent vel adepturi, quibus hactenus, non secus ac l) bestiæ illæ ægri in præcedentibus verbis, fuerunt privati, favoremque ejus illi conciliassent, qui illis donandis benignitatem suam erga eos renovabat sibique illos vindicabat, ut illorum DEus. Addit enim, ne ulla ratione de ejus magna dubitarent benignitate, Nam dedit vobis pluviam temperiuam moderate &c. dedit, vel ut m) alii, dabit, i. e. tam certo, ac si jam dedisset, tempore perfecto pro futuro posito ad innuendam certitudinem, ut antea vidimus.
units.tr: "The children of Zion" means you, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, a part of which was built on Mount Zion. Those who had before been called to return to the Lord, weeping and mourning as a sign of repentance, now, after they had returned to him and thereby reconciled God to themselves, are bidden to rejoice in the LORD their God. "In the Lord," not so much in the abundant plenty of good things, as in the fact that they had obtained or were about to obtain repentance, by which they had hitherto been deprived of these things, just as those beasts had been deprived of pasture in the preceding verses, and had won his favour, which renewed his kindness towards them in bestowing these things and claimed them for himself, as their God. For he adds, lest they doubt in any way his great kindness, "For he hath given you the rain moderately," etc. "He hath given," or, as others have it, "he will give," that is, as surely as if he had already given it, the perfect tense being used for the future to indicate certainty, as we saw earlier.

units.la: Eth hammoreh lisdakah. Quæ a nostrat. in textu redduntur, temperiuam pluviam moderate, at in margine addidere, tanquam aliam interpretationem, quam verba quoque ferunt: Doctorem justitiæ; quia ratione ea interpretatus est Vulgatus & recentiorum plerique. At variæ sunt & magnæ de iis interpretum altercationes, quæ potissimum ortæ sunt ex ambigua significatione verbi Morech, quod sine distinctione significat vel doctorem, vel pluviam. Radix hujus verbi quæ in primis triplici gaudet significatione. Primo, quæ propria est jactum, ejaculatum vel jaculis petit. Secundo, pluit, dejecit. Tertio, docuit, instituit. Nec differt quia nomen derivativum morech, quippe primo denotat jaculatorem vel sagittarium, ut 1 Sam. 31 3. & 2 Sam. 11, 24. Secundo pluviam, ut
units.tr: "Eth hammoreh lisdakah." Our translators render this in the text as "moderately," but in the margin they added another interpretation, which the words also bear: "the teacher of righteousness." The Vulgate and most of the more recent writers followed this sense. But there are many and great disputes among the interpreters about this, which arise chiefly from the ambiguous meaning of the word morech, which without distinction means either "teacher" or "rain." The root of this word, which especially enjoys a threefold meaning, is: first, what is proper to it, "to cast, to hurl" or "to shoot at with missiles." Second, "to rain, to pour down." Third, "to teach, to instruct." Nor does the derivative noun morech differ, for it primarily denotes a "thrower" or "archer," as in 1 Sam. 31:3 and 2 Sam. 11:24. Second, "rain," as in

units.la: l) Calv. m) Jun. Tremel. Dedit,pro dabit. Druf. ut Pf. 84, 7. & hoc versu paulo inferius interpretibus quibusvis confitentibus. Tertio Doctorem, ut Job. 36, 22. Esa. 9, 15. Habac. 2, 18. &c. Quod primam concernit, non videtur ullo modo huic loco convenire; de posterioribus autem magna intercedit inter interpretes contentio, ut diximus, utra harum sit eligenda. Si numero Auctorum standum sit, ultimam illarum cæteris esse præstituram, certum habeo. Præferunt etenim illam non tantum Vetus Latin. & qui illius versionem sequuntur, veluti authenticam, sed & alii multi recentiores, qui interpretantur vel sequuntur aliorum versiones, sive lingua latina, sive aliis vulgaribus. Ita Pagnin. Doctorem illum justitiæ, Tigur. & Castalio, Doctorem ad justitiam, Munst. qui doceat justitiam; nec non duæ versiones Hispanicæ, quarum una a Christiano quodam concinnata privilegio gaudet Ducis Ferrarensis, quæ habet, fernador de justitia, doctorem justitiæ; altera a Judæo, meo judicio, parata, at Inquisitoribus probata, in eandem sententiam habet, & amostrador de justedad. Atque eorum vestigiis qui insistunt, multi sunt, iique non vulgaris notæ ac eruditionis, ut jam nominibus illorum parcam. Quin & Judæorum non pauci eandem vocis significationem probant, veluti Paraphrasta Chaldæus, qui reddit אתיב לכן יתמלכון כוזבן restaurabit vobis doctorem vestrum (vel ut alii doctores) in justitiam, & R. Salomon, qui ita hæc exponit, Prophetæ vestri לשוב אלי כדי לצדק אתכם המוריים qui vos docent אתככם redeunt ad me ad justificandum vos, vel ut MS. habet אליו כדו לצדק אתככם ad cum ut vos justificet. Ita R. Japhet, quem citat AbenEzra, per המורה Hammoreh intelligi vult הנביא שהוא מירה צדק אותם בדרך Prophetam, qui docebit eos viam justitiæ, ita ut bonum illis obveniat. Pariter eam accipit Abarbinel verba huncce in modum exponens: Sed vos filii Sionis, in primis præ cæteris omnibus nationibus exultate & lætamini in Domino Deo vestro; nam in eo habebitis gaudium perfectum tempore captivitatis vestræ, nam dabit vobis doctorem justitiæ (vel informatorem ad justitiam) והוא מלך המשיח שיורו ארץ הדרך ילכו בו ואת המעשה אשר יעשון Et is est Rex Messias, qui eos docebit viam, in qua debent ambulare, & talia quæ debent agere. Verum non æque conveniunt in eo, quinam hoc doctore
units.tr: l) Calvin. m) Junius and Tremellius: "he gave," for "he will give." Drusius, as in Ps. 84:7, and in this verse a little lower, all interpreters agreeing. Third, "teacher," as in Job 36:22, Isa. 9:15, Hab. 2:18, etc. As to the first, it does not seem to fit this place in any way. On the other two, there is, as we said, great contention among the interpreters as to which of these should be chosen. If we must go by the number of authors, I am certain that the last of these will be preferred to the others. For not only the Old Latin and those who follow its version, as if it were authentic, prefer it, but also many other more recent writers, who either interpret or follow the versions of others, whether in Latin or in other vernacular tongues. So Pagninus: "the teacher of righteousness"; the Zurich Bible and Castalio: "a teacher to righteousness"; Münster: "who will teach righteousness"; and also the two Spanish versions, one of which, put together by a certain Christian, enjoys the privilege of the Duke of Ferrara, and reads fernador de justitia, "a teacher of justice"; the other, prepared by a Jew, in my judgment, but approved by the Inquisitors, has to the same effect & amostrador de justedad, "and a showing of righteousness." And there are many who follow in their footsteps, men of no common reputation and learning, whose names I will now spare. Indeed, not a few of the Jews too approve the same meaning of the word, as the Chaldee paraphrast, who renders restaurabit vobis doctorem vestrum [he shall restore to you your teacher] (or as others, "teachers") "to righteousness"; and Rabbi Solomon, who explains these words thus: "Your prophets," who teach you, "return to me in order to justify you"; or as a manuscript has it, "to him, that he may justify you." So also Rabbi Japhet, whom Aben Ezra cites, wishes that by hammoreh is understood the prophet who will teach them the way of righteousness, so that good may come to them. Likewise Abarbanel takes the words, explaining them thus: "But you, children of Zion, above all other nations, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, for in him you will have perfect joy in the time of your captivity; for he will give you a teacher of righteousness (or an instructor to righteousness)," and this is "the King Messiah, who will teach them the way in which they must walk, and the deeds which they must do." But they do not agree so well about who is to be understood as this teacher

units.la: fit intelligendus, qui tam insigniter conveniunt in significatione vocis. Sunt qui innui volunt n) quosdam Prophetas, veluti Haggaeum, Zachariam, Malachiam &c. p) alii Esaiam, alii Regem Hamam,ut q) Ruffinus; at plerique Messiam vel Christum,eandem omnes dum amplectuntur vocem. Ex altera parte alii sunt,tum Judaei, tum Christiani, qui potiorem habent denotationem pluviae,veluti ad planiorem sensum multum facientem, atque huic loco magis convenientem. Horum non infimus est Aben-Ezra,qui opinione recensita cujusdam R. Japhet, ut vidimus, inquit, sententia sua מורה Moreh hic idem esse, quod ירה yoreh (quam vocem Deut. 11, 14. reddidere primam pluviam). Ita idem hic denotare quod ירה yoreh putat Kimchi, quam cum dicit se daturum לצדקה litsdekah in justitia (vel ad justitiam) eam justitiam intelligit, quam faciebat illis, quum transfibat super scelus eorum & visitabat eos pluvia. Eidem significationi subscribit etiam R. Tanchum, & cum dicitur לצדקה ad justiam, idem valere censet,vel quod בצדקה, i.e. in aequitate, postquam ad me respiciens reverti sunt, vel quod in gratia sine merito Vestro, vel in, vel a vobis, vel a veltra parte. Sic & MS. ex Hebraico concinnatum, qui dedit vobis Albakir, temperatiam pluviam ad aequalitatem (vel justa mensura). Diverli recentiores interpretes tam in latina, quam aliis linguis hanc significationem praeferunt; ita Calvinus,dum utriusque mentionem facit,de altera dicit: non videtur ferre hunc sensum circumstantia loci, cum Propheta jam loquatur ad illos de temporalibus beneficiis (non autem de spiritualibus,de quibus non disserit usque ad v. 23. inhisce praecedentibus verf.) ut illos veluti per gradus instrueret ad illa rite accipienda, & quod propterea hic debuerit verti per pluviam; cui succinunt Junius & Tremellius: ipsum imbrem temperatum justo tempore. Pa- riParirer Diodati in versione sua Italica: e' ka dista pregna gmissamente, dedit pluviam juste. Sic & Gallica translatio Genevæ typis impressa Anno 1637. la pluye selon justice (nec alias deesse autumo, quas mihi neque videre neque percepisse contigit); & cum hac concordant novissimi nostri translatores, quos sequimur, ponentes in textu, temperatiuam pluviam, quod & alii aliciunt, veluti Genevenses pluviam. LXX. hic suggerunt differentem ab omnibus hisce aliis interpretationem, qua reddunt τα βρώματα εις δικαιοσύνη, cibos in justitiam, (vel æquitatem) vel ut alia s) apographa habent, δικαιοσύνης justitiæ, quibus consentit Syrus. cibos ad æquitatem. Verum enim vero ita horum interpretatio cum t) quodam accipi potest, ut non alio quidem modo hæc vertisse, nec alio sensu vocem morch accepisse, quam quatenus significat pluviam, dicendi sint, sed ejus loco tantummodo expressisse effectum & intellesisse causam, quatenus nimirum pluvia tempestiva interveniente ex terra proveniebant res alimentariæ, eoque pacto idem cum cæteris sensisse, qui verterunt pluviam.
units.tr: whom they so remarkably agree in the meaning of the word. Some want it to be hinted at as certain prophets, such as Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, etc.; others Isaiah; others King Hama, as Rufinus; but most, while all embrace the same word, mean the Messiah or Christ. On the other side are others, both Jews and Christians, who prefer the meaning "rain," as making for a plainer sense and fitting this place better. Not the least among these is Aben Ezra, who, having recorded the opinion of a certain Rabbi Japhet, as we have seen, says in his own view that moreh here is the same as yoreh (which word in Deut. 11:14 they rendered "the former rain"). So Kimchi too thinks that here it denotes the same as yoreh; and when he says that he will give litsdekah ("in righteousness," or "to righteousness"), he understands by that righteousness which he showed them when he passed over their wickedness and visited them with rain. Rabbi Tanchum also subscribes to the same meaning, and when it is said litsdekah ("to righteousness") he judges it to mean either bitsdekah, that is, "in equity, after they returned, looking to me," or "in grace, without your merit," or "in or from you, or on your part." So also the manuscript put together from the Hebrew reads: "who gave you albakir, temperate rain in equal measure" (or in just measure). Various more recent interpreters, both in Latin and in other tongues, prefer this meaning. Thus Calvin, while mentioning both, says of the second: "the context of the place does not seem to bear this sense, since the prophet is already speaking to them about temporal benefits (not yet about spiritual ones, which he does not discuss until v. 23 in these preceding verses), so as to instruct them, as it were by steps, to receive those rightly; and therefore it ought here to be rendered by 'rain.'" Junius and Tremellius agree: "the rain itself, tempered at the just time." Diodati in his Italian version likewise: e' ka dista pregna gmissamente, "he gave rain justly." So also the French translation printed at Geneva in the year 1637: la pluye selon justice, "the rain according to justice" (nor do I think there are lacking others which I have neither seen nor happened to learn of); and with this our most recent translators agree, whom we follow, putting in the text "temperate rain," which others also adopt, as the Genevan Bible has "rain." The LXX here suggest an interpretation different from all these others, rendering τα βρώματα εις δικαιοσύνη [the food for righteousness], "food to righteousness" (or equity), or, as other copies have, "of righteousness," with which the Syriac agrees: "food to equity." But their rendering can be taken in such a way that they did not translate it in another way, nor understood the word morech in another sense than as meaning "rain"; rather, they expressed only its effect in its place and understood the cause: namely, that by the timely rain, the food came up from the earth; and thus they agreed in sense with the others who rendered it "rain."

units.la: Caterum quam nostrates in Textu reddunt vocem moderate, & in margine notant proprie haberi, secundum justitiam, Anglicana ex Genev. concinnata vertit, pluviam justitiæ; Verum e vadhuc alia vetus translatio, quæ recentioribus accedit: qui dedit vobis moderatam pluviam. Perquam cognita præterea atque usu multiplici probata significatio vocis Tsedekah est justitia, cujus tamen latitudo non tantum, quod justum & æquum est, comprehendit, sed etiam quod beneignitatis atque beneficentiæ nomine venit, imo ne u) veracitatis quidem notatione excepta (qua ratione Arabibus admodum frequens est & familiaris) atque harum quædam locum habere potest pro subjecta materia & convenientia loci. Quod ad hunc locum attinet, omnes æque bene ei convenire accentuo. acceptiones haud temere dixeris, quippe DEus pluviam iis poenitentibus largiri volebat,ut ipse se justum exhiberet in gratia ea præstanda, quam promiserat peccatoribus resipiscentibus. Talis vero pluvia quid aliud esse debebat, quam indicium magnæ ejus benignitatis & liberalis erga eos voluntatis, quæ decidere debebat n) justo tempore & x) justa mensura (quod nostrates voce moderate innuere puto) ad succurrendum illorum inopiæ; non in defectu, ne impedimento esset, quo minus produceret terra uberes fructus, qui non arescerent; nec in excessu, ne y) corrumperentur & putrescerent. Quamvis non desint Interpretes, quorum alii hanc, alii aliam significationem radicis in specie videantur magis magisque respicere, atque verbis exprimere; attamen omnes inter se reconciliari possunt, si reddatur secundum justitiam, quandoquidem sine hac interpretatione cæteræ una consistere nequeunt.
units.tr: But as for the word which our countrymen render in the text as moderate, and note in the margin as properly meaning according to justice, the English version adapted from the Geneva Bible renders it the rain of righteousness. There is also another old translation, which agrees with the more recent ones: who gave you the moderate rain. The meaning of the word Tsedekah is well known and has been proved by many uses: it is justice. Its range, however, covers not only what is just and fair, but also what goes by the name of kindness and beneficence, and even (as is very common and familiar among the Arabs) truthfulness. Some of these senses may have a place, according to the subject matter and the fitness of the passage. As far as this passage is concerned, one could hardly say that all these senses suit it equally well. God was willing to give rain to these penitent people so that he himself would show himself just in bestowing the grace he had promised to sinners who repented. Now what else ought such rain to be than a sign of his great kindness and generous will towards them? It was to fall n) at the right time and x) in the right measure (which I think our countrymen meant by the word moderate) to relieve their want. It was not to fall in deficiency, which would hinder the earth from producing rich fruits that would not wither, nor in excess, lest the fruits y) be spoiled and rot. Although there is no shortage of interpreters, and some seem to attend more and more to one meaning of the root and others to another, and to express it in words, yet all can be reconciled with one another if it is rendered according to justice, since without this rendering the others cannot stand together.

units.la: Porro ut benevoli ejus erga illos animi & benignitatis abundantiam iis declararet, proximis in verbis addit: & faciet descendere vobis pluviam, tempestivam pluviam & serotinam pluviam: גשם Geshem, pluviam, quæ vox in z) genere magis significat pluviam, cum posteriores duæ moreh tempestiva pluvia & malkush, serotina pluvia, eas in specie denotent, quæ certo decidunt tempore: a) prior quidem in vel post sementem, quæ efficit ut frumentum crescat; posterior tempore messis, quæ efficit ut ad justam maturitatem perveniat. Hinc est ut alibi etiam ita conjungantur, veluti Deut. 11,14. ubi distinguuntur ut diversæ pluviæ species, generali pluviæ nomine retento, præter quam quod generale nomen ibi est מטר Matar (quod eandem significationem obtinet apud Syros & Arabes) cum hoc loco fit גשם Geshem, quod indicio est ejusdem esse significationis hoc, ut diximus, cum eo, atque exinde non solum impetuosam denotare pluviam five nimbum, ut b) quidam videntur suggerere; sed pluviam c) in genere, locoque מורה moreh ibi fit ירה yoreh, eadem cum priore significatione, quamvis litera prima diversa. Pari modo posteriores duas con-
units.tr: Further, to show them the abundance of his benevolent mind and kindness, he adds in the next words: and he will cause to come down for you rain, the early rain and the latter rain (z) geshem [גשם], rain, which word in its general sense means rain). The other two, moreh [מורה], the early rain, and malkush [מלקוש], the latter rain, denote in particular those that fall at a fixed time: a) the first, indeed, after the sowing, which makes the grain grow; the second at harvest time, which makes it come to full ripeness. Hence it is that they are joined together elsewhere too, as in Deut. 11,14., where they are distinguished as different kinds of rain, the general name of rain being kept, except that there the general name is matar [מטר] (which has the same meaning among the Syrians and Arabs), whereas in this passage it is geshem [גשם]. This is evidence that this word, as we have said, has the same meaning as the other. Thus it does not only denote a violent rain or downpour, as b) some seem to suggest, but rain c) in general. And in place of moreh [מורה] there stands yoreh [ירה] there, with the same meaning as the former, although the first letter differs. In the same way the other two are joined together.

units.la: §§) Pifcat. x) Livel. y) Vide cap. 1,17. z) Calvin. a) Druf. b) Kimchi Rad. c) Reuchl. Concord. conjungit D. Jacobus epist. 5, 7. iisdem nominibus græce eas vocans ὄψιμον & πρόιμον, quibus LXX. hoc loco uti sunt, & a nostratibus ibi redditæ, matura & serotina pluvia, uti hic tempestiva & serotina pluvia.
units.tr: §§) Piscator. x) Livelius. y) See chapter 1:17. z) Calvin. a) Drusius. b) Kimchi, Radices. c) Reuchlin, Concordance. St. James joins them in Epistle 5:7, calling them by the same Greek names, ὄψιμον [opsimon] and πρόιμον [proimon], which the Seventy use in this passage, and which our countrymen there render the early and latter rain, as here the early and latter rain.

units.la: Quandoquidem autem vox מוֹרֶה moreh & forma & literis congruit cum ea, quæ paulo ante præcessit, atque omnium interpretum unanimi sententia hic pluviæ notionem obtinet, argumentum ex eo d) nonnulli videntur petere, quod alia sua significatione debeat accipi priori loco, nimirum doctoris. At non est, quod adeo urgeat, diversa significationis ratione ut accipiantur, quippe utrumque locum (primum etiam, ut ad unum omnes exponunt alterum, per pluviam) eodem modo exponentes ταυτολογίας rei reddi haud possumus, quin potius cum cæteris verbis conjuncta magni sint ponderis mirabilemque emphasin habeant ad exprimendum, uti notavimus, plenam mensuram & perfectionem benedictionum divinarum in illos collatarum: Cum enim priori loco promiserat, se daturum illis tempestivam pluviam moderate, vel secundum justitiam, quæ pro tempore videbatur sufficiens, hoc loco videtur subjicere; imo ne hanc quidem, sed & omnem convenientem pluviam justo suo tempore, sicuti tempestivam, ita & serotinam, ita ut ejus benedictio nulla in re foret imperfecta aut manca, sed omni egestati succurrens, quovis etiam tempore, occasione sic postulante, quod ulterius innuere videtur sequenti בראשית nostratibus: in the first month, imo primo mense; qua ratione etiam præcedentes Anglicanæ translationes legunt. Cæterum ingens hic iterum est differentia inter interpretes, cum nec qua versionem, nec qua sensum horum verborum concordent. Sunt qui cum nostratibus subintelligunt e) mensem, cui quidem nominatim subjicit Chaldæus Paraphrastes, in mense Nisan, cujus interpretandi ratio si approbanda, necesse est, auctore Piscatore, ut hujus temporis designatio referatur ad posteriorem vocem מלקוש malkosh, serotinam pluviam; inter eam enim & moreh, tempestivam pluviam, intererant tempestates live
units.tr: Since the word מוֹרֶה [moreh] agrees in form and letters with the one that came just before it, and by the unanimous opinion of all interpreters here has the sense of rain, some seem to argue from this that it must be taken in its other meaning in the first place, namely of a teacher. But there is no reason to press this, for the two places cannot be taken in different senses. If both are explained in the same way (even the first, as all expositors explain the second, by rain), no tautology is involved. Rather, joined with the other words, they carry great weight and have a remarkable emphasis for expressing, as we have noted, the full measure and perfection of the divine blessings bestowed on them. For when he had promised earlier that he would give them the early rain moderately, or according to justice, which seemed sufficient for the season, here he seems to add: not only this, but every fitting rain at its proper time, both the early and the latter, so that his blessing would be imperfect or deficient in nothing, but would relieve every want at any time, as the occasion demands. This he seems to hint at further in the following word בראשית [bereshith] which our countrymen render in the first month, or rather in the first month; the earlier English translations also read it this way. Still, there is again a great difference among the interpreters, since they agree neither in the translation nor in the sense of these words. Some, with our countrymen, supply the word e) month, which the Chaldee paraphrast indeed adds by name: in the month of Nisan. If this method of interpretation is to be approved, it is necessary, on the authority of Piscator, that the mention of this time refer to the latter word מלקוש [malkosh], the latter rain. For between it and moreh, the early rain, there were seasons or months.

units.la: sive menses, quibus una & altera, plerumque f) spatio diversorum mensium, cadebant; ita ut non facile fit intellectu, quomodo uno mense utraque cecidisse dicenda fit. Judæi, qui eandem viam fequuntur, miraculo hanc difficultatem expedire conantur, quæ factum statuunt, ceu ex aliis id refert Kimchi, ut ambæ descenderint eo anno pluviæ eodem mense, adeo ut, cum antea nunquam ulla pluvia eo mense descendisset, primo die mensis Nisan five Martii, decideret tempestiva pluvia, quæ communiter folebat decidere mense Marchefvan vel Octobris; rursusque die quinto, intra quod dierum fpatium seminabant fruges, quæ ad diem decimum sextum ad maturitatem perveniebant, adeo, ut decursu undecim dierum, per has duas pluvias, quæ secus plane ceciderant, quam aliis annis, eandem perfectionem fruges adipiscerentur, quam alias nonnisi sex mensium spatio adeptæ erant. Eandem huc referunt historiam R. Salomo, & Aben-Ezra, qui credidisse videtur factum בםעשרי נם loco prodigii, fecundum illud quod dictum est v. 21. quoniam magnificavit Dominus facere. At ne nostram faciamus causam eorum, qua hæc historia creditu difficilis videretur, etsi versionem illorum (videlicet in mense primo) probamus, inprimis facit ea nota, qua de serotina pluvia tantummodo id accipiendum esse statuitur, quæ erat tunc danda, priore sua tempestate antea rite data. Sic accepisse ea videtur Kimchi, cujus expolitio est, DEum pluviam, quæ vocatur Moreb, demiliffe tempore suo, quod erat mensis Marchesvan, similique modo Malkosh five serotinam pluviam demiliffe tempore suo, mense primo, qui est Nisan, qua ratione & noftrates opinor intellexisse, quia fubjecere comma inter verba, tempestivam pluviam, & sequentia; quod omisere inter serotinam pluviam & in primo mense. Verum enim vero alii hujus loci difficultatem sic tollere conantur, ut nullam rationem habeant mensis, quem alii hic fubintelligi volunt. Absurdum prorsus autumnat R. Tanchum ad vocem ראשון primo adjici הורש לאן ךלך ליס ךלך אאן אלמטר הראשון primo mense, qui est Nisan quia, f) Aquorum una ad alteram sex minimum menses solent intercedere. Merc. ימים רבים multi dies Aben-Ezra. quia, inquit, hac g) non est justa tempestas pro pluvia. Quocirca cum aliis non paucis aliam vocis versionem praefert, qua probata non una iterum eorum explicandorum ratio est. Duplici enim modo explicari posse putat. (1.) Ut per בראשׁית in primo, intelligatur פיאור קתור primo ejus tempore, vel primo ejus tempestatis; quam primum erit tempestivum vel necessarium. Quo cum facit hac in parte versio Junii & Tremellii, primo quoque tempore, ut & Castalionis, in primis, i. e. ut R. Livelius explicat h), mature, cum primum ea opus est. Quam expositionem ut primo loco tradit hic Rabbi, ita & op tinia esse videtur. (2.) Ut juxta aliorum, quam refert, opinionem idem valeat atque כראשׁן (sicut primo vel antea) scil. כחאלכם אלאילי uti in (vel juxta) vestro primo vel priori flatu, scilicet antequam ultimo correpti essent poenis ob sua peccata. Ita quoque reddunt LXX, καθὼς ἐμπρῶτεν, sicut antea (vel ut prius) & Arabica, quae illos sequitur ﻟﺮ ﺠﻜﻲ ﻣﻪ nec non Syriaca ut antea, & Vulgat. lat. sicut in principio, quo sensu etiam non i) pauci recentiorum accipiunt. Id quod in opinionem k) nonnullos perduxit, diversa haec ab iis olim esse lecta, nimirum loco בראשין Barishon, in primo, כראשין Carishon, sicut primum. Haud dubie, inquit Drusius, de LXX differens, legerunt כ pro ב. Quod tamen non facile dixerim eos fecisse, sed potius subintellexisse particulam C. ca sicut, quamvis non sit expressa (sicuti alibi saepe ubi, Ribera, Autore, omittitur) vel tantundem putasse valere in primo, vel priori, quod sicut antea. Ita videmus intellexisse Judaeos, de quibus R. Tarnchum loquitur, qui omni dubio procul non aliter legerunt quam hodie legimus. Quod idem affirmat Abarbinel, qui בראשין hic tantum significare dicit, ac si dictum esset כבראשנות, sicut primo, vel in prioribus temporibus, ita ut in his verbis promissio contineatur שיתברכו תבואורת הארץ כאשר היו ביטי קדם fructus terrae fore benedictos sicut prioribus diebus. Unde sat superque liquet, non opus
units.tr: or months, in which one or another rain, usually in the space of different months, fell; so that it is not easy to understand how both could be said to have fallen in one month. The Jews, who follow the same way, try to resolve this difficulty by a miracle. They assert that it was a fact, as Kimchi reports from others, that both rains came down that year in the same month, so that, although no rain had ever fallen in that month before, on the first day of the month Nisan, or March, the early rain fell, which usually fell in the month Marcheshvan, or October. Then on the fifth day, within which span of days they sowed the grain, which came to ripeness by the sixteenth day, so that in the course of eleven days, through these two rains which fell quite differently from other years, the crops attained the same perfection which they usually reached only in a span of six months. R. Solomon and Aben Ezra refer the same story here, and Aben Ezra seems to have believed the thing happened bannes [בנס], by a miracle, according to what was said in v. 21.: for the Lord hath done great things. But lest we make our case rest on this story, which would seem hard to believe, even though we approve their rendering (namely in the first month), the chief point which favours it is that the note declares that of the latter rain only that is to be understood which was then to be given, the earlier rain having already been properly given in its own season. Kimchi seems to have understood it this way, and his explanation is that God sent down the rain called Moreh at its own time, which was the month Marcheshvan, and in a similar way sent down Malkosh, or the latter rain, at its own time, in the first month, which is Nisan. In this way, I think, our countrymen also understood it, since they placed a comma between the words the early rain and what follows, which they omitted between the latter rain and in the first month. But others try to remove the difficulty of this passage in such a way that they take no account of the month which others want to be understood here. R. Tanchum thinks it entirely absurd that the phrase הראשון [harishon], the first, should be added to the word for month in the sense of the first month, which is Nisan, because at least six months usually intervene between one rain and the next. Mercerus, citing Aben Ezra, says that it is many days (ימים רבים [yamim rabbim]), because, he says, this is not a proper season for rain. Wherefore, with not a few others, he prefers another rendering of the word, and once this is approved there is again another way of explaining them. For he thinks they can be explained in two ways. (1) So that by בראשית [bereshith], in the first, is understood at its first time, or at the first of its season, that is, as soon as it will be timely or necessary. With this the translation of Junius and Tremellius agrees, at the first opportunity, as does that of Castalio, chiefly, that is, as R. Livelius explains it, early, as soon as there is need of it. R. Livelius gives this explanation first, and it seems to be the best. (2) So that, according to the opinion of others which he reports, the phrase has the same force as כראשון [kerishon] (as at first or before), namely as in your first, or former, breath, that is, before they were seized by the last punishments for their sins. So also the Seventy render it, καθὼς ἐμπρῶτεν [kathōs emprōsthen], as before (or as formerly), and the Arabic version, which follows them, and the Syriac as before, and the Latin Vulgate as in the beginning, in which sense also not a few of the more recent writers take it. This has led some to the opinion that these were read differently in former times, namely in place of בראשין [bareshin], in the first, כראשין [kareshin], as at first. Doubtless, says Drusius, speaking of the Seventy, they read כ for ב. I would not readily say they did this, but rather that they understood the particle C, ca, as, though it is not expressed (as often elsewhere where where is omitted, according to Ribera), or thought it meant the same as in the first or before, which is as before. So we see the Jews, of whom R. Tanchum speaks, understood it, who without doubt read it no differently than we read it today. Abarbanel affirms the same, who says that בראשית here means only what would be said as כבראשנות [kevaresh-noth], as at first, or in former times, so that the promise contained in these words is: the fruits of the land shall be blessed as in former days. Whence it is quite clear enough that there is no need

units.la: g) Nescio unde. Ita & Tarnovius, quod hac pluvia in illo mense non fit data. h) Apposite Calvinus in tempore suo, i. e. unamquamque pluviam tempestive & opportune; & Grotius: Sementis & messis tempore commodus dabit tempestates. i) German. & Pet. a Fig. k) Drusius, Mercer. &c. Tarnov. Pet. a Fig. opus esse ulla diversa lectione, cum perspicuus sit satis verborum sensus, si illorum sequamur & versionem & interpretationem.
units.tr: g) I do not know where from. So also Tarnovius: that in that month this rain is not given. h) Aptly Calvin: in its time, that is, each rain seasonably and opportunely; and Grotius: at the time of sowing and harvest he will give suitable showers. i) German. and Pet. a Fig. k) Drusius, Mercer, etc. Tarnov. Pet. a Fig. There is no need of any different reading, since the sense of the words is plain enough if we follow their version and interpretation.

units.la: Quantumvis igitur, qui priore loco diversi sunt in reddenda voce מורה moreh, sive per doctorem sive pluviam, posteriori loco insigniter concordent interpretando eam unanimi consensu pluviam temporalem; attamen non eadem hic utrorumque est verborum mens & sententia. Qui primo loco habent doctorem, illorum non pauci per pluviam hic intelligunt spiritualia bona, quae ad regnum Christi pertinent, l) veluti prosperum Evangelii successum ejusque propagationem, quae frumenti instar futura erat, quod temporaliter pluvia benigne irrigatum crescit & augmenta indicis majora capit; vel m) copiam fructuum & bonorum spiritualium per Christum, n) gratiam praevenientem & cooperantem, & o) copiam doctrinae & auxiliorum Dei, quibus aliisque id genus expressionibus verba accipiunt, ut eorum non nemo dicit, p) allegorice & principaliter, ceu notavimus. Illi vero, qui primo loco habent pluviam, utrobique intelligunt juxta literam benedictionem temporestivae pluviae, qua tales boni effectus erant producendi, quales verbo praecedenti memorantur ac ulterius verbo sequenti describuntur, quam explicandi rationem uti sequimur tanquam caeteris longe planiorem, ita proximis verbis ea etiam quam maxime accedit, etsi non desint qui allegorice & sequentia intelligunt. Verba sunt haec:.
units.tr: Although those who in the former place differ in rendering the word מורה (moreh), whether as "teacher" or as "rain", agree remarkably in the latter place in interpreting it as temporal rain by unanimous consent, nevertheless the meaning and sense of the words is not the same for both. Those who in the first place have teacher understand by rain, not a few of them, spiritual goods that pertain to the kingdom of Christ, l) such as the prosperous success of the Gospel and its propagation, which was to be like grain that, watered benignly by temporal rain, grows and takes greater increase; or m) the abundance of fruits and spiritual goods through Christ, n) preventing and cooperating grace, and o) the abundance of teaching and the help of God. With such expressions and others of this kind they take the words, as one of them says, p) allegorically and principally, as we have noted. But those who in the first place have rain understand in both places, according to the letter, the blessing of seasonable rain, by which such good effects were to be produced as are mentioned in the preceding verb and described further in the following verb. We follow this method of explanation as far plainer than the rest, and with the following words it agrees most closely, although there are not lacking those who understand the following words allegorically too. The words are these:

units.la: 24. Et area implebitur tritico, & dolia redundabunt vino & oleo.
units.tr: 24. And the threshing floor shall be filled with wheat, and the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.

units.la: Hisce verbis nihil aliud describitur, quam magna conditionis illorum, qua antea erant pressi, immutatio. Frumentum ante dicitur c. 1, 10. vastatum, mustum arefactum, oleumque languisse, & v. 17. horrea desolata & granaria destructa, quia non erat, quod illis imponeretur, munera-que & libamina succisa, v. 9. & quae sunt hujusmodi alia summam denotantia penuriam omnium rerum necessariarum. Atque
units.tr: These words describe nothing other than the great change in the condition of those who were previously oppressed. Earlier the grain is said (c. 1, 10.) to have been laid waste, the new wine dried up, and the oil languished, and (v. 17) the barns desolate and the granaries destroyed, because there was nothing to be stored in them, and the offerings and drink offerings cut off (v. 9), and other things of this kind that denote a total lack of all necessary things. And

units.la: l) Mercerus & Ribera & Ch. a Castro. m) Tirin. n) Menoch. & vide Ar. Mont. o) Intellige gratiam auxiliam & doctrinam. p) Tirinus. Atque ita erat, quamdiu perduelles perseverabant DEI, ejusque manum & judicia sentiebant. At posteaquam ad DEum sese jam converterant, DEusque ad illos atque in gratiam eos rursum receperat, omnia sese contraria ratione habent, omniumque rerum bonarum copiam non sibi defore sunt persuasi, quæcunque verbis concipi possent. Area horreorum eorum implebuntur tritico & dolia illorum abundabunt vino & oleo. Videntur his tribus, tritico, (vel frumento) vino & oleo, omnia comprehendi ad hominis usum necessaria. Sicuti enim q) harum defectu ut plurimum annonæ caritas vel fames & omnium bonarum rerum ad vivendum necessariarum inopia describitur, ita e contrario harum abundantia fertilitas & talium rerum copia innuitur. Hujusmodi autem hic promittuntur ad satietatem, imo ad abundantiam usque. Verbum השיקו Hesbiku, redditum abundabunt, non invenitur, quod sciam, alibi in S. literis hac forma & significatione, quæ hic requiri videtur, præterquam hoc loco & rursus c.3,13. id quod mea sententia in diversum egit interpretes, ut minus inter se conveniant in eo vertendo. Interlinearia, ut ab Ariæ Montano sunt correcta, habent in textu, stridebunt torcularia, quæ sequitur Tigur. quamvis in margine ambo habeant, redundabunt. In quo sectari videntur R. Salomonem, qui nescio cujus auctoritate, nisi sua ipsius nitens, ait significare השמערת קו כשהקקילוח ירד edere sonum, cum fluxus descendit ex torcular in (vel per) vas; addit enim insuper יקב הביר proprie esse foveam vel fas, quod est ante torcular. Quare etiam Drusius veteris versionis torcularia, in lacus torcularis mutat, sicut Junius & Tremellius vertunt, torcularium lacus, quod recipit, quicquid est expressum. Aben-Ezra eodem hic sensu accipi vult, quo est משיקורת Mashikoth Ezech.3,13. quod nostratibus redditum est per tangeres, seu uti in margine, osculari, quæ vocis propria significatio est. Quid vero innui velit eo, non declaravit. Si divinando quid assequi possimus, forsan id voluisse non temere conjeceris, quod vino & oleo abundante opus foret diversis vasis ad illa recipienda, aliis propius appositis, ut spatium ea capere posset. At quæ ibi est vox, derivatur a verbo
units.tr: l) Mercerus, Ribera and Ch. a Castro. m) Tirinus. n) Menoch., and see Ar. Mont. o) Understand grace, help and teaching. p) Tirinus. And so it was as long as the rebels persisted and felt the hand and judgments of God. But after they had now turned to God, and God had received them again into favour, all things stand in the opposite relation, and they are persuaded that no abundance of good things, however it might be conceived in words, will be lacking to them. The threshing floor of their barns shall be filled with wheat, and their vats shall abound with wine and oil. It seems that by these three, wheat (or grain), wine and oil, everything necessary for human use is comprehended. For just as by the lack of these, as a rule, a dearth of food or famine and a want of all good things needed for living are described, so conversely their abundance points to fertility and a plenty of such things. Such things are here promised to the point of satiety, indeed to overflowing. The verb השיקו [Hesbiku], rendered shall abound, is not found, as far as I know, elsewhere in the Holy Letters in this form and meaning, which seems to be required here, except in this place and again c. 3, 13; in my opinion this has led the interpreters in different directions, so that they agree less among themselves in translating it. The interlinear versions, as corrected by Arias Montanus, have in the text the winepresses shall creak, which the Tigurine version follows, although in the margin both have shall overflow. In this they seem to follow R. Salomon, who, on the authority of I know not whom, unless resting on his own, says that it signifies השמערת קו [making a sound], to give forth a sound, when the flow comes down from the winepress into (or through) the vessel; for he adds further that יקב הביר [the pit of the winepress] is properly a pit or trench, which lies before the winepress. Therefore Drusius also changes the old version's winepresses into the vat of the winepress, as Junius and Tremellius translate, the vat of the winepress, which receives whatever is pressed out. Aben-Ezra wishes it to be understood here in the same sense as משיקורת [Mashikoth] in Ezek. 3, 13, which our people rendered touch, or, as in the margin, kiss, which is the proper meaning of the word. But what he wished to convey by it he did not explain. If we can guess something by conjecture, perhaps it is not rash to suppose that, with wine and oil abounding, different vessels were needed to receive them, others placed closer so that there would be room to hold them. But the word there is derived from the verb

units.la: q) Pet. a Fig. verbo נשך Nashak, quod osculari valet atque inde etiam sese contingere vel hujus simile; cum secus habeat quæ hoc loco est, quippe defcendit a שוך Shok, cujus nomen inde deductum שוק Shok crus juxta ac plateam denotat. Ea autem forma, qua hoc loco est verbum, plerisque five Judæis, prædictis tantummodo exceptis, five Christianis, accipitur significatione effluendi vel redundandi. Hinc reddit Chaldæus ישיפון, nec aliud pronunciat Kimchi, significare, quam הציפו heesifphu, א ציף, & R. Tanchum (ut & MS. Arabicum) arabice habet ﻳﺼﻔﻮ, quæ cuneta in eandem sententiam conspirant & notant supernatare, fluere, vel superfluere, ut & quam habent LXX, ὑπερχυθήσονται, Vulgat. Lat. redundabunt, Syrus MS. Arabicum Arab. impressa quæ recte satis eo, quo noftrates usi sunt, exprimuntur, redundabunt. Cui vero nominis prædicti significationi verbum cumprimis sit vindicandum, dubii non nihil habet. Pereruditus Nicol. Fullerus ad illam referendum putat, qua denotat crus instrumentum currendi, unde primaria ejus significatio, currere, discurrere, excurrere, quasi diceretur, crurare, atque exinde metaphorice in rebus cruribus destitutis, effluendi ac redundandi notio. E contrario ad alteram ejus significationem id referunt Junius & Tremellius, qua notat plateam (licet pari jure ad priorem etiam possit referri, quatenus platea locus est currendi, in quo populus discurrit) quando reddunt, plateasque perfundent torcularium lacus musto & oleo, ac si ita propter abundantiam effluerent, ut per plateas etiam liquores hujusmodi discurrerent. Quicquid autem de derivatione & deductione verbi acute disputetur, manifestum est ex sequentibus, ingentem hic eo omnium rerum innui abundantiam. Quodsi autem amplius quid addendum, optime ejus significatio illustrari & confirmari potest ex usu ejusdem thematis in lingua Arabica, quam cognitum habemus omnium maxime cum Hebraica convenire. In ea enim a themate ﺳﻮﻙ Saka denotat impellere vel concitare, sexta ﺗﺴﺎﻭﻙ tafavvaka, se invicem sequi & tam arcte ire, ut alius alium premat vel trudat, & septima ﺍﻧﺴﺎﻙ Enfaka (ut GroGrotius notat ex Dictionario Ebn. Maruph) fluxit & progressus est ad denotandum abundantiam, per quam res rebus succedunt. Qui allegorico horum verborum sensui adhærent, hic iterum intelligi volunt r) Evangelii diffusionem per totum orbem. s) Sunt qui in specie verbis: & area implebuntur tritico, innui rentur plenitudinem gratiarum & virtutum ecclesiis particularibus a Christo suppeditatarum, quæ significantur per arcas, oliveta & vineas, sicuti per torcularia (vel vasa) in quibus vinum & oleum exprimitur, Gymnasia, Monasteria, Collegia &c. atque ita persecutiones & tribulationes, quibus vinum sapientiæ & fortitudinis, ac oleum consolationis divinæ exprimitur & hauritur. Quomodocunque autem hæc verba comparando huic vel illi rei applicari possint, literalis tamen expositio mihi planissima videtur & hoc loco & in proxime sequentibus versibus, in quibus ulterius declarat, DEum cuncta ea bona velle collocare in vere pœnitentes, quibus eos antea ob commissum nefas privaverat justa pœna immissa, atque iterum t) exhilarare pro diebus, quibus eos afflixerat, & annis, quibus experti erant malum. Quocirca ipse ad eos inquit per os Prophetæ ושלמתי &c.
units.tr: q) Pet. a Fig. (Petrus a Figueroa) on the Hebrew verb Nashak, which means "to kiss" and from this also to touch oneself or something similar. The verb here is different, since it derives from Shok, whose noun Shok, meaning "leg" and also "street" [shoq], is derived from it. Most people, whether Jews (apart from those already mentioned) or Christians, take the form of the verb used here in the sense of overflowing or running over. Hence the Chaldee gives yeshiphon, and Kimchi says it means nothing other than heesifphu [hziphu], from tzaph. R. Tanchum (as also the Arabic manuscript) has yaṣfū in Arabic. All of these agree on this sense and mean to float on top, to flow, or to overflow. So too the Septuagint has [hyperchythēsontai] (will be poured over), the Vulgate Latin has redundabunt (will overflow), and the Syriac manuscript and the printed Arabic express it well enough with the same word our people used, redundabunt. But it is somewhat doubtful to which of these senses the verb should above all be assigned. The very learned Nicol. Fullerus thinks it should be referred to the sense in which crus denotes an instrument of running, so that its primary meaning is to run, to run about, to run out, as if it were said to leg it, and from this, metaphorically, the notion of flowing over and overflowing in things lacking legs. On the other hand, Junius and Tremellius refer it to the other sense, in which it means street (although it could equally well be referred to the first, since a street is a place for running, where people run about), when they render it: the streets of the winepress will be flooded with must and oil, as if from abundance they would overflow in such a way that such liquids would run about through the streets. Whatever is subtly argued about the derivation and root of the verb, it is clear from what follows that an immense abundance of all good things is implied here. If anything more is to be added, its meaning can be very well illustrated and confirmed from the use of the same root in the Arabic language, which we know agrees most of all with Hebrew. In it, from the root Saka, it means to drive on or to stir up; the sixth form, tafavvaka, means to follow one another and go so closely that one presses or thrusts another; and the seventh, Enfaka (as Grotius notes from the Dictionary of Ebn Maruph), means to flow and advance, to denote the abundance by which things succeed one another. Those who cling to an allegorical sense of these words wish it to be understood here again as r) the spreading of the Gospel throughout the whole world. s) Some, in particular, take the words and the threshing floors will be filled with wheat to imply the fullness of graces and virtues supplied by Christ to the particular churches, which are signified by chests, olive groves and vineyards, just as by winepresses (or vessels) in which wine and oil are pressed out: gymnasia, monasteries, colleges, and so on, and thus persecutions and tribulations, by which the wine of wisdom and strength, and the oil of divine consolation, is pressed out and drawn off. However these words may be applied to this or that thing by comparison, the literal exposition seems to me most plain both here and in the verses that immediately follow, in which he further declares that God wishes to bestow all those good things on those who truly repent, of whom he had previously deprived them on account of the wickedness they had committed, by the just punishment sent upon them, and again t) to gladden them in return for the days in which he had afflicted them, and the years in which they had experienced evil. Wherefore he says to them through the mouth of the Prophet: and I will repay, etc.

units.la: 25. Et restaurabo vobis annos, quos comedit locusta, bruchus & volvox, & eruca & meus ingens ex- ercitus, quem misttebam in vos.
units.tr: 25. I will restore to you the years that the locust, the bruchus, the volvox and the eruca have eaten, my great army which I sent against you.

units.la: Quod annis aliquot ante illis illatum erat damnum ab his creaturis voracibus, quæ omnes fructus terræ ita vastabant, ut, unde subsisterent, nil quicquam relictum esset, porro illis rependere disciupit redendo extraordinariam copiam eamque ad usum illorum præservando. Locusta, bruchus, volvox & eruca, omnes eædem sunt, quæ supra memorantur cap. 1. inverso licet ordine. Ibi enim חגגי haggezem, volvox, primum locum occupat, cum hic extet ultimo; unde non leve argumentum petit doctissimus Bochartus probaturus uno anno atque simul venisse, qui hic nominantur, vermiculi, non autem per vices singulas, alio genere veniente hoc anno, alio altero, ut ex Judæis non-
units.tr: Because the loss that these voracious creatures had inflicted on them some years earlier, when they laid waste all the fruits of the land so that nothing was left by which they could subsist, God now promises to repay them with an extraordinary abundance, and to preserve it for their use. Locust, bruchus, volvox and eruca are all the same creatures mentioned above in chap. 1, though in reverse order. There the word חגגי haggezem, volvox, stands first, whereas here it stands last. From this difference the very learned Bochart draws no slight argument to prove that the worms named here came in one year and at the same time, and did not come in successive swarms, one kind one year and another the next, as some of the Jews [would have it]

units.la: r) Mercer. s) R. Menoch. t) Psal. 90,15. nonnulli volunt; quippe tunc non conjecisset in annum quartum, quam dixerat alibi venisse primo, ut in illum locum notavimus. Verofimile hinc est omnes simul venisse atque vastando confumsisse aliquot annos, uti vox הַשְּׁנִים bashanim, annos, numero plurali expressa indicat. Vocat eas, meus ingens exercitus quem mittebam in vos, quas supra v. 11. vocaverat, valde magnum campum. Quinam intelligendi sint per hunc exercitum & campum, utique patet ex nominibus locustæ, bruchi, volvocis & eruca, vel hujusmodi creaturarum quæ hebraice hic extant & a nostratibus sic redduntur. An tales fuerint exacte, vel aliæ similis generis, non satis nobis liquet his in regionibus degentibus. Ratio vero, cur eas exercitum suum vocet, hæc est, quod eas in illos mittebat. Etenim non fortuito veniebant, neque ex ulla ordinaria atque naturali causa, sed erant ab eo immissæ, ut facerent ejus voluntatem muniaque ejus gnaviter obirent. Eadem autem hic iterum enascitur quæstio, quæ diu jam ante in hac propheti a agitata est, imo a quarto versu primi capitis, num per hæc nomina ad literam intelligendæ sint istæ prædictæ creaturæ, an quidam alii cum illis collati, quoad damnum ab iis illatum? sunt, iiq; non pauci qui propria significatione ea accipiunt, nec apud eos difficultatem habet, quod exercitus Dei vocentur, quibus hæc creaturæ penitius atque multo familiarius sunt cognitæ. Sic inter Arabes trita est & cognita expressio locustarum sub nomine exercitus Dei, imo ab ipso u) Mahumede usurpata, qui eas interficere prohibuit, eo quod essent exercitus Dei omnipotentis, decantatumque est inter eos, locustam cecidisse in ejus manus, vel ante eum, cujus alis inscriptum erat [Arabic] Hebraice [Arabic] Nos sumus exercitus maximi Dei. Nec quicquam refert, quam fabulosa sit hæc historia, cum nostro proposito satis sit conveniens, & sufficienter probet denominationem hanc exercitus Dei congrue satis ac proprie applicari posse locustis. Quantumvis enim id minus sit inscriptum illarum alis, apparet tamen, eas esse tales ex rebus, quas ab eo missæ & adhibitæ quam
units.tr: r) Mercer. s) R. Menoch. t) Psal. 90,15. some hold; for then he would not have reached the fourth year, when he had said elsewhere that they came in the first, as we noted at that place. It is therefore likely that they all came together and, by devastating, consumed the land for several years, as the Hebrew word הַשְּׁנִים bashanim, years, in the plural number, indicates. He calls them my great army which I sent against you, the same that he had called a very great field in verse 11 above. Who are to be understood by this army and field is clear enough from the names locust, bruchus, volvox and eruca, or from creatures of this kind, which are given here in Hebrew and rendered thus by our own people. Whether these were exactly such creatures, or others of a similar kind, is not clear to us, living in these regions. The reason why he calls them his army is that he sent them against them. They did not come by chance, nor from any ordinary and natural cause, but were sent by him so that they might do his will and diligently perform his commission. Here, however, the same question arises again which has long been debated in this prophet, indeed from the fourth verse of the first chapter: whether these names are to be understood literally of the creatures just named, or of certain others compared with them in the damage they did? There are not a few who take them in their proper sense, and for them there is no difficulty in their being called the army of God, since these creatures are known to them much more intimately and familiarly. Thus among the Arabs the expression the army of God for locusts is common and well known; indeed Mohammed himself used it, forbidding them to be killed because they were the army of Almighty God. And it is told among them that a locust fell into his hand, or before him, on whose wings was written We are the great army of God [in Hebrew]. Nor does it matter how fabulous this story is, since it is sufficiently suited to our purpose and sufficiently proves that this name army of God can fitly and properly be applied to locusts. For although it is less certain that such words were written on their wings, it nevertheless appears that they are such from the things which, sent and employed by him, they very often committed, not unlike those which the greatest and bravest armies of men could carry out for the destruction of some region. So there is no reason to object to those who hold that this is said properly of locusts; nor does the genius of the language forbid it being so understood. Indeed the verb to eat, which is used to express the damage done, fits them remarkably well. As for the Vulgate rendering my great strength, or others in the same sense my great power or might, when above it had been rendered army, this makes no difference, for the Hebrew word in both places is the same, namely חיל Chail, which admits both meanings and is equivalent in this case. They are rightly called the army of God on account of their multitude, but his great power and strength on account of the great things they carried out at his command. Apart from the fact that these words can conveniently be taken of locusts and other such noxious insects, they are also explained in another way by others, namely of men, enemies, and the authors of the damage inflicted. Thus the Chaldee paraphrast expounds this verse: And I will repay (or restore) to you good years for the years, in which דכוו יתכין עממיא איומיא ולישנא ושלטונא ומלכותא פורענות חילי רבא רשלחיא בכן peoples, nations, tongues and princes (or principalities) and kingdoms (or ordained for vengeance; or x) as others have it, the vengeance of my great army) my great army, which I sent against you, plundered you. Kimchi says that his meaning was that this is a prophecy of things to come in the time of the Messiah. Abarbanel thinks that by these are indicated the four kingdoms which were also indicated earlier (1:4), and he affirms that they are signified under the names of the four devouring creatures, and are called by God my great army which I sent against you, כי הכם היו חיל השכם ושלוחי השבחתו להעניש ארת ישראל עד ירחם because they were the powers of God and the messengers of his providence to punish Israel; and so he thinks that great abundance of good things is promised here, which they ought to enjoy once freed from captivity. To pass over in silence others who

units.la: u) Damiri. quam sæpissime perpetraverunt, non absimiles iis, quæ a maximis fortissimisque exercitibus hominum ad regionis alicujus destructionem peragi possent. Adeo ut non sit, quod contra illos excipias, qui hoc de locutis proprie dictum volunt; nec linguæ genius retragatur, quo minus de iis ita accipiatur, quinimo verbum comedendi, quod ad damnum illatum exprimendum usurpatur, insigniter illis congruit. Quod Vulgat. Lat. reddat, fortitudo mea magna, vel w) alii in eandem mentem, magna mea potentia, vel vis, cum antea redditum esset v. n. exercitus, nullam differentiam infert. Hebræa enim vox utroque loco eadem est, nimirum חיל Chail utramque significationem admittens, atque hoc in casu æquivalens. Vocantur merito Dei exercitus propter multitudinem, magna autem ejus potentia & sortitudo propter magna, quæ ejus jussu perpetraverant. Præterquam autem quod commode hæc verba sumi possunt de locutis atque hujusmodi aliis noxiis infectis, alia etiam ratione ab aliis explicantur, videlicet de hominibus, hostibus & auctoribus illati damni. Ita hunc versum exponit Chaldæus Paraphrastes: Et redpendam (vel restaurabo) vobis annos bonos pro annis, quibus דכוו יתכין עממיא איומיא ולישנא ושלטונא ומלכותא פורענות חילי רבא רשלחיא בכן populi, nationes & linguæ & principes (vel principatus) atque regna vindicta (vel in vindictam ordinata; vel x) ut alii, vindicta magni mei exercitus) exercitus meus magnus, quem immisi in vos, diripuerunt vos, cujus mentem fuisse ait Kimchi, quod sit prophetia futura temporibus Messiæ. Abarbinel putat, per ea innui quatuor regna, quæ & antea (c. 1, 4.) fuisse indicata, affirmat sub nominibus quatuor vastantium creaturarum eaque vocata a DEO meum magnum exercitum, quem immisi vobis כי הכם היו חיל השכם ושלוחי השבחתו להעניש ארת ישראל עד ירחם quia erant DEI potestates & legati providentia ejus ad puniendum Israelem, atque sic bona hic promitti arbitratur magna copia, quibus deberent frui captivitate exsoluti. Ut alios silentio nunc præteream, qui eandem
units.tr: u) Damiri. They have very often carried out deeds not unlike those that the greatest and bravest armies of men could accomplish in the destruction of some region. So there is no reason to object to those who want this to be said of locusts in the proper sense. Nor does the genius of the language forbid taking it that way; indeed the verb to eat, which is used to express the damage done, fits them remarkably well. That the Vulgate renders it my great strength, or w) others to the same effect my great power or force, whereas earlier it had been rendered my great army, makes no difference. For the Hebrew word is the same in both places, namely חיל Chail, which admits both meanings and is equivalent in this case. They are rightly called God's army because of their number, and his great power and strength because of the great things they carried out at his command. Besides, although these words can fittingly be taken of locusts and other such harmful pests, others explain them in another way, namely of men: the enemies and authors of the damage inflicted. So the Chaldee paraphrast expounds this verse: And I will repay (or restore) to you good years for the years in which the peoples, nations, tongues and princes (or princedoms) and kingdoms, dekhu yathkhin ammayya ayomaya ulishana ushilṭana umalkuta purʿanuta, took vengeance (or were ordained for vengeance; or x) as others have it, for the vengeance of my great army), my great army which I sent against you, plundered you. Kimchi says that his meaning was that this is a prophecy referring to the times of the Messiah. Abarbinel thinks that the four kingdoms, which were also indicated earlier (c. 1, 4.), are hinted at here; he maintains that they are meant under the names of the four devouring creatures, and that they are called by God my great army, which I sent against you, because they were the powers and legates of his providence to punish Israel, in Hebrew, ki hakkem hayu chayil hasheqem u-shelukhei hashbachato lehaanish et Yisraʾel ad yeraḥem, and so he holds that great abundance of good things is promised here, which they were to enjoy when freed from captivity. To pass over in silence others who follow the same method of explanation,

units.la: §§) LXX. & Arab. impressa. x) Merc. & Pet. a Fig. dem explicandi rationem sequuntur, Grotius his denotari autumat Phulem, z) Teglathphalasarum, a) Salmanasarem, & b) Sennacheribum quatuor Reges Assyriæ, qui regionem Israelis & Judæ invadentes magno illam afficiebant damno lateque diripiebant. De quovis horum dici posset esse DEI exercitum & ab eo missum, sicuti ipse dicit de Assyriis, esse virgam suæ iræ & baculum in manu eorum, suam indignationem, Esa. 10,5. Quæcunque autem ab illis erant perpetrata, ex ejus concessa potestate fiebant, non ex sua ipsorum, citra quam despectui erant vilissimorum vermiculorum instar, quos quam facillime destruere poterat, ut ex eo apparet, quod Sennacheribo ejusque exercitui contingebat, Esa. 36. &c. Hinc quæ sunt contemtissimæ omnium creaturæ, a DEO cum sint armatæ, non minus populum aliquem affligere possunt, quam si essent earum maximæ fortissimæque; ut videre est in plagis Ægyptiacis. Quare non opus est, ut hic a litera discedamus & ad figuram confugiamus in harum imbecillium creaturarum locum substituentes potentissimos reges & nationes. Sufficiebant hæc animalcula divino jussui satisfaciendo in puniendo populo malitioso, æque pariter ac illorum quisquam: Nec minus opus est cum aliis ad continuam allegoriam confugere, secundum quos promissa hæc felicitas nulla alia c) foret, quam qua sub Christo & Evangelio essent fruituri, quæ longe excederet eam, qua fruiti erant effœtis temporibus sub lege obnoxii morti & diabolo; vel benedictiones hic spirituales innuerentur, sive res ad d) animæ felicitatem pertinentes atque isti divini fructus, quos terra (vel solum) humanæ naturæ, femine ac virtute Christi locupletata producit; vel his dictis creaturis noxiis denotarentur e) diaboli sive f) exercitus inimicorum spiritualium cum suis tentationibus; vel fructibus diversorum annorum significaretur g) verus DEI cultus, qui nullus erat plane inter gentes, perditus maxime inter Judæos, quamdiu a gentibus opprimebantur. Quæ allegoriæ quibusdam videntur apertius spectare verba; at mea sententia id rectius dici posset
units.tr: §§) LXX. & Arab. impressa. x) Merc. & Pet. a Fig. follow the same method of explanation. Grotius maintains that these denote Phul, z) Tiglath-pileser, a) Shalmaneser, and b) Sennacherib, four kings of Assyria, who invaded the territory of Israel and Judah, inflicting great damage and plundering widely. Of any of these it could be said that he was God's army and was sent by him, just as he himself says of the Assyrians that they were the rod of his anger and the staff in their hand, his indignation, Isa. 10,5. But whatever was perpetrated by them was done by his granted power, not their own, and they were otherwise held in contempt, like the most worthless little worms, which he could destroy with the greatest ease, as appears from what happened to Sennacherib and his army, Isa. 36, &c. Hence creatures that are the most despised of all, when they are armed by God, can afflict a people no less than if they were the greatest and bravest. This may be seen in the plagues of Egypt. Therefore there is no need for us to depart here from the letter and take refuge in a figure, substituting the most powerful kings and nations in place of these feeble creatures. These little animals sufficed to satisfy the divine command in punishing a wicked people, just as well as any others. Nor is there any need, with others, to take refuge in a continuous allegory, according to which this promised happiness would be nothing other than that which they were to enjoy under Christ and the Gospel, which would far exceed that which they enjoyed under the law, subject to death and the devil, in the barren times; or spiritual blessings would be meant here, that is, things pertaining to the happiness of the soul, and those divine fruits which the land (or ground) of human nature produces, enriched by the seed and power of Christ; or by these said harmful creatures would be denoted the devil, or the army of spiritual enemies with their temptations; or by the fruits of different years would be signified the true worship of God, which was entirely absent among the nations, and most lost among the Jews while they were oppressed by the nations. These allegories seem to some to be favoured more openly by the words; but in my opinion it could be said more correctly

units.la: y) 2. Reg. 15,19. z) 1. Paral. 5,26. 2. Reg. 15,29. d) 2. Reg. 17,3. b) 2. Reg. 18,13. Esa. 36,1. 2. Paral. 32,1. &c. c) Mercer. d) Ar. Montanus. e) Monoch. f) Sa. g) Vet. a Fig. h) Ribera. set de literali sensu,quo,non secus atque in precedentibus hujus prophetiæ non una vice dictum est, declaratur, quæcunque ante sunt descripta aut iis prædicta, a DEO propter peccata illis esse immissa loco pœnæ, atque has dictas vilissimas creaturas fortem ejus esse exercitum,cui ut resistere non erant pares,ita nec se ipsos immunes reddere,quod decursu quorundam annorum comprobatum erat,unde, ne totalis ipsis immineret interitus atque exitium, haud immerito vereri poterant; verum posteaquam resipuerant atque in gratiam cum eo rursus redierant, eos esse animadversuros,etiam DEum,cujus directione hæc fiebant,atque cujus potestate & jussu hæc agebant atque magna perpetraverant, majoraque minari videbantur,æque facile eas posse removere (ut v. 20.) im[illegible, ~3 letters]od majus est,& posse & velle resarcire omnem noxam & damn[illegible, ~3 letters]quodvis, quo ab illis fuerant affecti. Ita ut, cum omnis generis inter eos hominibus tunc temporis esset justa occasio ejulandi & lachrymandi propter ingentem rerum penuriam & miseriam qua erant obruti,non amplius habituri essent occasionem sic se gerendi,sed alio eoque plane contrario modo faciendi,ut in sequentibus est descriptum & promissum.
units.tr: y) 2 Kings 15:19. z) 1 Chron. 5:26. 2 Kings 15:29. d) 2 Kings 17:3. b) 2 Kings 18:13. Isa. 36:1. 2 Chron. 32:1, etc. c) Mercer. d) Ar. Montanus. e) Monoch. f) Sa. g) Vet. a Fig. h) Ribera. But the literal sense, which is declared (as has been said more than once in the earlier parts of this prophecy), is this: whatever has been described before or foretold in these verses was sent by God upon them as a punishment for their sins. These so-called most worthless creatures are his strong army, which they were not able to resist, and which they likewise could not free themselves from, as had been proved over some years. Hence, lest total ruin and destruction should overtake them, they had good reason to fear. But after they had come to their senses and returned again into favour with him, they would find that God too, by whose direction these things were done, and by whose power and command they were carried out and great harm inflicted, and who seemed to threaten still greater things, could just as easily remove them (as in v. 20), and that it is a greater thing both to be able and to be willing to make good every harm and loss with which they had been afflicted by those creatures. So, although at that time people of every sort among them had just cause for wailing and weeping because of the great scarcity and misery by which they were overwhelmed, they would no longer have occasion to behave in that way, but would act in another and quite opposite manner, as is described and promised in what follows.

units.la: 26. Et comedetis in plenitudine, & saturabimini, & laudabitis nomen Domini Dei vestri, qui fecit vobiscum mirabiliter, & populus meus nunquam confundetur.
units.tr: 26. And you shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wonderfully with you; and my people shall never be put to shame.

units.la: Plana sunt ad literam, quam sequimur,hæc verba,in quibus illis promittitur,fore ut,cum aliquot retro annis magna rerum laboraverant penuria & egestate,abundantem jam habeant copiam omnium necessariorum non tantum ad vitam hilarem vivendam,sed & ad desideriis suis extremis plane satisfaciendum,ut non aplmius habituri sint ullam occasionem murmurandi vel seditiose se gerendi & plura postulandi, sed e contrario nomen Domini DEI sui laudandi, qui secum tam mirabiliter egerat omnia liberaliter præbens,quibus opus erat, quæque exoptare poterant; qua ratione etiam contumeliæ, qua antea gentes eas propter paupertatem afflecerant,finis imponebatur, batur, DEO eos tanquam populum suum vindicante curamque ipsorum gerente, qui nunquam, quos sibi asserit, confundi patietur, quasi non omnisufficiens iis esset, qui omnem fiduciam in eum collocant. At non omnis verborum vis in descriptione ingentis rerum copiæ sit a est, verum complectuntur insuper una cum his benignam divinæ benedictionis promissionem, qua futurum erat, ut iis frue-rentur, riteque sentirent animo divinam in se collatam gratiam, cum sine hac benedictione & gratia possent habere, quod ederent, & edere; nec tamen saturari (vel ad satietatem) & bibere, minime vero affatim (vel ad ebrietatem) i) Hagg. 1,6. Malum, quod Ecclesiastes dicit vidisse sub sole, obviumque valde inter homines, quando DEus divitias dat viro, ut ejus animæ nulla re destituatur, qua delectetur, cum huic non faciat copiam fruendi, Eccles. 6, 2. Hoc donum Dei est, si DEus dat divitias & facultates, & facit ei copiam comedendi ex illis & percipiendi partem suam, Eccles. 5, 19. Atque id ipsum est quod hic illis promittit, fore, ut comedant in plenitudine & saturentur (quod probe mea sententia innui putant verbis אכלו ואכלתם) & comedenda comedetis, i.e. habebitis quod edatis, quotiescunque opus erit, & nunquam inopia laborabitis, donec ad satietatem comederitis desideriosque omni ex parte satisfeceritis). Præterea aliud quoque malum est idque non adeo infrequens inter homines, ut k), quando comederint & saturati fuerint, oblivisceantur DEI & dicant in animo suo: Virtus mea & robur manus mea paravit mihi opulentiam hanc, Deut. 8, 12. 14. 17. (Hos. 13, 6.)
