Quæ agendi ratio cum in maledictionem hominibus vertat has benedictiones, & ne apud hos sic quoque vertantur, simul promittit se daturum illis animos, ut cognoscerent datorem gratumque erga eum exhiberent animum, ut nunquam desineret iis benefacere. Ita enim ait: Et laudabitis nomen Domini Dei vestri, qui egit vobiscum mirabiliter. Quibus innui manifestum est eos, uti eum laudandi jam habituri essent commodam occasionem, ita & in tantos effusum iri affectus, ut revera appareret, illos sentire, quam mirabiliter DEus cum illis egisset, magnaque, ut supra v. 21.
units.tr: These words, which we follow literally, are plain. In them it is promised that, although for some years past they had suffered great scarcity and want, they will now have an abundant supply of all necessities, not only to live a cheerful life but also to satisfy their every desire completely. So they will have no further occasion to grumble, to act seditiously, or to demand more; on the contrary, they will praise the name of the Lord their God, who has dealt so wonderfully with them, bestowing generously all that they needed and all that they could wish for. By this means too, the insults which the nations had heaped upon them because of their poverty were brought to an end, since God was vindicating them as his own people and taking care of them. He will never allow those whom he claims as his own to be put to shame, as if he were not all-sufficient for those who place all their trust in him. But the whole force of the words does not lie merely in the description of an immense abundance of goods; they also include, along with this, a gracious promise of divine blessing, by which they would enjoy these things and would rightly perceive in their hearts the grace of God bestowed upon them, since without this blessing and grace they could have something to eat and yet not be satisfied (or filled to the full), and drink but not be filled to drunkenness. Haggai 1:6. The evil which Ecclesiastes says he has seen under the sun, and which is very common among men, is that when God gives a man riches so that his soul lacks nothing it desires, yet does not give him the power to enjoy them. Eccles. 6, 2. It is a gift of God when God gives riches and wealth and grants him the ability to eat of them and to receive his portion. Eccles. 5, 19. This is exactly what he promises them here: that they shall eat in plenty and be satisfied (which, in my view, they rightly take to be signified by the Hebrew words akhlu ve-akhaltem [אכלו ואכלתם], to be eaten, you shall eat), that is, you will have something to eat whenever it is needed, and you will never labour in want, until you have eaten to the full and have satisfied your desires in every way. Moreover, there is another evil, and one not so uncommon among men: k), when they have eaten and been satisfied, they forget God and say in their hearts: My power and the might of my hand have gained me this wealth, Deut. 8, 12. 14. 17. (Hos. 13, 6.) Since this way of acting turns these blessings into a curse for men, and so that they may not be turned into a curse among them in this way, he at the same time promises that he will give them hearts to recognise the giver and to show a grateful attitude towards him, so that they will never cease to receive good things from him. For he says: And you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wonderfully with you. By these words it is plainly implied that they would not only have a convenient opportunity to praise him, but would also be moved by such strong feelings that it would truly be evident that they perceived how wonderfully God had dealt with them, and how great things he had done for them, as v. 21. said above.

units.la: i) Mich. 6, 14. k) Et vide Deut. 32, 15. & Prov. 30, 9. v. 21. dicit,fecisset. Mirandum equidem necessario videbatur,quod, cum totius regionis fruges aut nutrimenta a prædictis vorantibus creaturis antea effent abfumtæ, nunc improvisa immutatione non‐ tantum eas fit remoturus (ut est v. 20.) verum & compensaturus, quicquid devoraverant. l) Quidam arbitrantur his verbis comprehendi miraculum atque in eo consistere, quod jam uno anno illis velit restituere, quantum quatuor præterlapsis annis redundaffet, ni a locustis fuisset abfumtum. Atque ita Deus cum illis aget, ut populus ejus nunquam fit confundendus. Quamdiu ab eo defectionem faciebant, atque ille sibi eos non afferebat, ex dictis apparet, pudore ac consufione fuisse correptos. Hinc cap. 1, 11. jubentur agricolæ erubescere. Quod vero tota natio eum deferuisset & ab eo etiam abnegata aliis nationibus opprobrio cessisset, manifestum est tum ex eo, quod jubentur orare v. 17. parce populo tuo, & ne da hæreditatem tuam in opprobrium &c. tum ex promissione, v. 19. quod non amplius eos effet expositurus opprobrio in gentibus. Quo in statu eos fuisse vel esse jamjam, nemini dubium esse potest. Idque eo tempore quo DEus eos rejecerat, & quam male effet in eos affectus, exhibere volebat; at posteaquam pœnitudine illum sibi reconciliaverant, adeo, ut sibi eos rursum vindicaret, alio modo rem processuram certi sunt. Removebitur omne opprobrii genus & ejus causa, cum id firmum atque indubium populi ejus fit privilegium, quod nunquam fit confundendus. Quo fundamento autem id sibi promittere poterant, ex proxime sequentibus patet.
units.tr: i) Mic. 6:14. k) See also Deut. 32:15 and Prov. 30:9. v. 21. Indeed, it seemed necessarily to be a matter for wonder that, since the crops and provisions of the whole region had been consumed by the aforesaid devouring creatures, God would now, by an unforeseen change, not only remove them (as in v. 20) but also make good whatever they had devoured. l) Some think that the miracle is comprehended in these words and consists in this: that he is willing to restore to them within a single year as much as would have been produced in four years past, had it not been consumed by the locusts. And so God will deal with them so that his people shall never be put to shame. That, while they were turning away from him and he was not bringing them good things, they were seized with shame and confusion is clear from what has been said. Hence in chap. 1:11 the husbandmen are commanded to be ashamed. That the whole nation had deserted him and, having been denied by him, had become a reproach to the other nations, is plain both from the fact that they are bidden to pray, v. 17: spare your people, and do not give your inheritance to reproach, etc., and from the promise in v. 19 that he would no longer expose them to reproach among the nations. That they were in this state, or were just about to be, no one can doubt. And this was at the time when God had rejected them and wished to show how evil things had turned out for them. But after they had reconciled him to themselves by repentance, so that he claimed them again as his own, they are assured that the matter would proceed in another way. Every kind of reproach and its cause will be removed, since it is the firm and undoubted privilege of his people that they shall never be put to shame. On what foundation they could promise this to themselves is clear from what follows immediately.

units.la: 27. Et scietis me esse in medio Israelis, & me esse Do- minum Deum vestrum & nullum alium: & popu- lus meus nunquam confundetur.
units.tr: 27. And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God and none other: and my people shall never be ashamed.

units.la: Hujusmodi beneficia & boni effectus, ut sunt evidentia signa, quibus DEus sibi populum tanquam suum vindicat, præsentiamque suam gratiosam ac peculiarem providentiam in eum luculenter exhibent, ita ex iis debent cognoscere ac persuasi esse, DEum ad conversio-
units.tr: Such benefits and good effects, which are clear signs by which God claims his people as his own and plainly shows his gracious and special providence towards them, should lead them to know and be persuaded that God is also turned to their conversion,

units.la: l) Quod idem cum aliis sentit Kimchi, Tarnovius. versionem eorum quoque conversum,atque in medio illorum esse, peculiarique jure sese exhibere DEum illorum in peculium eos sibi afferentem,neque ullum alium esse,qui fecisset aut posset facere tanta,quanta fecerat & facturus erat pro illis, tum,quibus affligebantur, procul removendo,tum, quibus afficiebantur, benigne procurando, idque tam extraordinario modo,ut non nisi illius infinita potentia faftum fuisse dici possit,sicut ex peculiari hoc calu patet,quo eas, quas in poenam illorum immiserat locustas,non tantum arcebat, sed & extraordinaria ubertate, quod illis intulerant damnum,pensabat. Ad insolita mala,quibus obruendi erant Israelitæ rebelles ac fœdifragi, etiam hoc accedebat, quod effent dicturi : Nonne obvenerunt nobis mala hæc, quod Deus noster non est in medio nostrum? Deuter. 13,17. Hic vero contrario modo fe res habet. Nimirum ex eo, quod DEus mirabiliter effet acturus cum populo resipiscente, eosque annos restauraturus,quos locustæ &c. comederant atque ingenti omnium rerum affluentia beaturus &c. cognoscere debebant, DEum esse in medio eorum, atque Dominum DEum eorum & nullum alium. Quando dicitur DEum esse in medio illorum, nihil aliud indicatur,quam eum esse paratum ad clamores eorum , atque omni occasione iis auxilium præbendum; additis autem verbis, Dominum DEum illorum, quod, cum omnium fit Dominus, peculiari ratione sibi eos vindicet ac respiciat tanquam peculiarem suum populum, cujus majorem velit curam habere, quam ullius alius in ordinandis rebus, quæ in illorum bonum cederent; Cum vero adjicitur nullum alium, quod nullus alius DEus fit inter eos,quos aliæ gentes, vel illi ipsi, cum abnegarent eum, colebant, qui tanta posset facere, quanta ipse nunc faciebat,& poterat & volebat in gratiam illorum continuare. Hinc experientia hujus rei certi redditi non possunt ullatenus confundi propter hunc cultum,vel in colendo eo aliquid invenire, quod iis dedecori esse queat, quasi fiduciam suam collocarent in quendam,qui nec velit nec possit ipsis auxilio esse,cum illis benefaceret quavis data occasione, potentem pariter ac benignum
units.tr: l) Kimchi and Tarnovius hold the same view. God is turned to them and is in the midst of them, and he shows himself to them by a special right, claiming them for his own possession, and there is no other who has done or could do such great things as he has done and will do for them, both in removing far away what afflicted them and in lovingly providing for what benefited them. He did this in so extraordinary a way that it can only be said to have been done by his infinite power, as is clear from this particular event, in which he not only kept away the locusts he had sent as punishment for them, but also made up for the damage they had caused with an extraordinary abundance. To the unusual evils by which the rebellious and treacherous Israelites were to be overwhelmed, this was also added, that they would say: Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not in the midst of us? Deut. 13,17. Here, however, the situation is the reverse. Namely, from the fact that God was going to deal wonderfully with a repentant people and restore to them the years that the locusts etc. had eaten, and bless them with a great abundance of all things etc., they ought to know that God is in the midst of them, and that he is their Lord God and none other. When it is said that God is in the midst of them, nothing else is indicated than that he is ready to hear their cries and to give them help on every occasion. But by adding the words their Lord God, it is shown that, since he is Lord of all, he claims them for himself in a special way and regards them as his peculiar people, whose welfare he wishes to care for more than that of any other in ordering the things that would turn to their good. When it is added and none other, the meaning is that there is no other God among those whom the other nations, or they themselves when they denied him, worshipped, who could do such great things as he now did, and who both could and wished to continue them for their good. Hence, having been made certain by experience of this, they cannot in any way be put to shame for this worship, or find in worshipping him anything that could bring them disgrace, as if they had placed their trust in someone who neither would nor could help them, though he would do them good on any given occasion, being at once powerful and kind,

units.la: m) Kimchi. n) Grot. in Matth. 18,20. Pfal. 90,5. o) Pfal. 14. 148.20. p) Kimchi. q) Hof. 13,4. gnum sese iis tam infinita ratione exhibens,ut nullus alius ei par posfit censeri. Atque hinc est, quod confirmationis atque summae certitudinis causa hic repetat: & populus meus nunquam confundetur. Populus meus, qui perseverat in fide ac constans est in me colendo, nunquam confundetur, nunquam spe sua ac fiducia in DEum excidet; sed persuadeat sibi, fore, ut omnia promissa sua solvat,ad exoptatum deducat finem atque ex omnibus afflictionibus & malis,quae ei accidere possent, liberet, quibus opprobrio posset exponi,& pudefieri,& confundi, nisi cum eo esset & in medio ejus,atque promtus paratusque ad eum liberandum. Haec exponendi ratio verborum plana videtur ac literae satis conveniens,juxta quam a nostratibus apte sunt versa. Verum sunt alii, qui alio modo ea vertunt atque inde etiam alio intelligunt לעולם leolam,a nostratibus & aliis reddita unquam, & cum adjuncta particula negativa nonnunquam, ab aliis vertitur in sempiternum, vel r) perpetuo, quasi diceret: licet interdum affligerentur, calamitateque afficerentur, attamen semper futurum exitum bonum,ut non haberent adversarii quod irriderent illos & dicerent: vbi jam est illorum Deus? quod optime congruit cum praecedentibus & ad ea rite intelligenda multum conducit,quippe quo prohibemur, ne semper feramus judicium de conditione filiorum Dei ex praesenti illorum statu vel calamitatibus, sed ex fine & exitu, quem DEus illis dare constituit, qui certe talis erit,quo pudore non suffundentur,sed in gaudium & gloriam illorum cedet,li non hoc momentaneo tempore, attamen in s) vita futura, cum interea illos sustineat suo solatio & spe certa, quae non finit eos t) confundi, sed potius efficit, ut u) glorientur de afflictionibus, quam ut languescant insque succumbant, aut a DEO se relictos esse imaginentur; verum quod in iis paternum erga eos animum x) manifestet, euramque eorum gerat eos humiles reddendo & probando, ut benefaciat illis ad finem usque, Deut. 8, 2. & omnia dirigit in bonum diligentibus eum, Rom. 8, 28. Interea hic reperiunt, quid faciant, sive sint totae nationes, sive quisque in specie, si nolint pudefieri vel confundi ullo tempore, vel ulla occasione,nimirum ut propius sese conferant ad Deum,eumque
units.tr: m) Kimchi. n) Grot. on Matt. 18:20. Ps. 90:5. o) Ps. 14. 148:20. p) Kimchi. q) Hos. 13:4. showing himself to them in a way so infinite that no other can be considered his equal. And so it is that, for the sake of confirmation and the greatest certainty, he repeats here: and my people shall never be ashamed. My people, who persevere in faith and are constant in worshipping me, shall never be ashamed, shall never fall from their hope and trust in God; rather, let them be persuaded that he will fulfil all his promises, bring them to the desired end, and deliver them from all the afflictions and evils that might befall them, by which they could be exposed to disgrace, be put to shame, and be confounded, unless he were with them and in their midst, ready and prepared to deliver them. This way of explaining the words seems plain and quite suited to the letter, and according to it they have been translated aptly by our people. But there are others who translate it in another way, and hence also understand leolam [לעולם] differently. Our people and others have rendered it never, and with a negative particle not ever, while others translate it for ever or perpetually, as if he meant: although they might sometimes be afflicted and struck by calamity, nevertheless the outcome would always be good, so that their adversaries would have nothing to mock them with, saying: where is their God now? This agrees very well with what goes before and helps greatly to understand it rightly, for it forbids us to judge the condition of the sons of God always from their present state or calamities, but from the end and outcome which God has determined to give them. That outcome will certainly be such that they will not be covered with shame, but will turn to their joy and glory, if not in this momentary time, yet in the future life, while meanwhile he sustains them with his comfort and sure hope, which does not allow them to be confounded, but rather makes them glory in their afflictions, so that they do not grow faint or give in, or imagine that they have been abandoned by God. Rather, he shows his fatherly heart towards them and cares for them by humbling and proving them, that he may do them good in the end, Deut. 8:2, and works all things for good for those who love him, Rom. 8:28. Meanwhile they find here what they should do, whether whole nations or each person individually, if they do not wish to be put to shame or confounded at any time or on any occasion: namely, that they draw closer to God and

units.la: r) Tig. s) Per. a Fig. t) Rom. 5, 5. u) Rom. 5, 3. x) Heb. 12, 5. que solum & nullum alium pro Deo suo agnoscant, ut ab eo recipiantur tanquam ejus peculium. Etenim talibus tantum promissio hic facta est; atque hi sunt, qui eam ita probatam animadvertent,ut in salutem ipsorum quovis modo tendat, utque exinde agnoscant & sciant,DEum,ut hic descriptus est,in medio esse illorum, Dominum illorum Deum,& non esse ullum alium prater eum parem ordinandis rebus in illorum bonum.
units.tr: r) Tig. s) Per. a Fig. t) Rom. 5:5. u) Rom. 5:3. x) Heb. 12:5. acknowledge him alone and no other as their God, so that they may be received by him as his own possession. For this promise is made here only to such people, and these are the ones who will see it so proved that it tends in every way to their salvation, and who will therefore acknowledge and know that God, as he is described here, is in the midst of them, is their Lord God, and that there is no other besides him who is equal in ordering things for their good.

units.la: Praeter hasce significationes vocis לעולם leolam, quibus reddi potest vel unquam, vel perpetuo, & cum particula negativa conjuncta, nunquam, non in aeternum, non perpetuo, alia est notio vocis, qua nonnunquam usurpatur pro longo temporis spatio, cujus tamen finis non fumus ignari. Quo sensu hic eam accipit Lyra dicens, eam non x) importare perpetuitatem. Ut & y) Grotius,qui eam explicat, per longum tempus, quamdiu vivet Ezechias,cujus tempore status pacatus atque rerum felicitas erat promissus, 2. Reg. 20,9. Esa. 39, 8. At quantumvis alibi eo sensu non infrequens fit particulae significatio, justo tamen arctius hic videtur restringi promissio Dei ad hunc populum,quem eo nomine sibi vendicat,ac fi tantum foret pro tam exiguo temporis spatio, non vero privilegium eorum perpetuum,quo unquam fruiti erant & semper ac certo erant fruituri. Certum est atq; indubium plane,verba a Propheta prolata ad Judaeos in specie esse directa respectu status ac conditionis diversae,quam subierant vel subituri erant (f. invasione Assyriorum,ut cum aliis hoc ille accipit,five ut alii ad lteram magis, fame per locustas cita,quae omnes terrae fruges late devorabant) quamdiu in peccatis ac rebelli statu perseverarent, cui tamdiu justitia divina volebat eos subjici, donec feria resipiscentia reverterentur ad DEum: quod utrumque in praecedentibus verbis est descriptum, quorum prius exponebat illos ludibrio ac pudori coram caeteris nationibus, posterius illud opprobrium removebat omnemque ejus occasionem. Unde certitudo hujus immutationis, tanquam res per fe plana & certa,his verbis subjicitur :populus meus nunquam confundetur. Ita ut ad eos in specie videatur respicere idque
units.tr: Besides these meanings of the word לעולם leolam, by which it can be rendered either ever or perpetually, and, with a negative particle, never, not for ever, not perpetually, there is another sense of the word, in which it is sometimes used for a long span of time, whose end, however, is not unknown to us. In this sense Lyra takes it here, saying that it does not import perpetuity. So also Grotius, who explains it as a long time, for as long as Hezekiah lives, in whose time a peaceful state and prosperity of affairs had been promised, 2 Kings 20:9; Isa. 39:8. But however much in other places this meaning of the particle is not uncommon, the promise of God to this people, whom he claims as his own by that name, seems here to be restricted too narrowly, as if it were only for so short a span of time, and not a perpetual privilege which they had always enjoyed and always would certainly enjoy. It is certain and quite beyond doubt that the words spoken by the Prophet are directed in particular to the Jews, with respect to the different state and condition which they had undergone or were to undergo (either, as he takes it with others, the invasion of the Assyrians, or, as others take it more literally, the famine brought on by the locusts, which devoured all the fruits of the land far and wide), for as long as they persisted in sin and a rebellious state, to which divine justice wished them to be subject for so long as they did not return to God by sincere repentance. Both of these are described in the preceding words: the first exposed them to mockery and shame before the other nations, while the second removed that disgrace and every occasion for it. Hence the certainty of this change, as a matter plain and certain in itself, is added in these words: my people shall never be ashamed. So that it seems to refer to them in particular, and that

units.la: x) Alias Jubilaei tantum designat spatium. y) Et alii, vide fis Pet. a Fig. que pro exiguo temporis spatio; ad omnes vero in genere, qui fe_ dignos reddunt titulo populi DEI, & quamdiu illum sustinere fatagunt. Quamvis enim ad hunc casum in specie applicatur,res tamen videtur axioma continere generale, quod semper locum habet in_ populo DEI, nimirum omnia z) operari in eorum bonum, qui conftanter DEO adhærent, ut nunquam pudore sint confundendi, sed occasionem nanciscantur in statu suo gaudendi ac gloriandi, utique habentes a) promissionem tam hujus quam futuræ vitæ. Profpera eorum conditio etiam in hac vita non b) una vice in sacris literis depiͤta est, tum hujus vel illius in specie, tum quod totas concernit nationes. Quemadmodum vero illi, qui hanc promissionem nimis adstringunt ad tempora Ezechiæ, multum magnitudini & gratiæ ejus detrahunt, dum intra illud tempus eam tantummodo coarctant; ita ex altera parte non minus ei detrahit Abarbinel, quando nimis protrahit illud tempus, quo implenda est hæc promissio. Statuit enim, ei non prius futurum esse locum, quam fuerint restaurati atque exfoluti ex ultimo suo exilio, sub quo adhucdum gemunt, & Meffiæ dies, quem jam venisse negant, venerint; in quo certo certius falluntur, ac fe ipsos miserrime frustrantur beneficio hujus factæ promissionis, quod pertinaciter incredulitati suæ inhærent, qua fe ipsos eo privaverunt jure, ut jam non amplius ejus sint populus, cum tamen beneficia non nisi ad ejus populum pertineant. At ut rejicienda est plane hujus de ea re sententia, ita nec assentiri possumus illis ex Christianis interpretibus, qui cum præcedentia verba allegorico sensu acceperunt, ut vidimus, etiam hic arbitrantur tantum esse promissionem talium spiritualium bonorum, qualia conferenda erant in c) Christum, per quem corrupta nostra natura est restituta, atque pudor & consusio legis & peccati per salutarem Evangelii doctrinam sunt sublati.
units.tr: x) Elsewhere it denotes only the span of a Jubilee. y) And others (see Pet. a Fig.) take it for a brief span of time. But it applies to all in general who make themselves worthy of the name of the people of God, for as long as they strive to keep that name. For although it is applied here to this particular case, the words seem to contain a general axiom that always holds for the people of God, namely that all things z) work together for the good of those who cling steadfastly to God, so that they are never to be put to shame, but find occasion to rejoice and glory in their state, since they have the a) promise of both this life and the life to come. Their prosperous condition is described in Holy Writ b) more than once, both in this or that particular instance and in what concerns whole nations. But just as those who restrict this promise too narrowly to the time of Hezekiah diminish its greatness and grace, by confining it to that period alone, so on the other side Abarbanel no less detracts from it when he stretches out too far the time in which this promise is to be fulfilled. For he holds that the place will not come until they have been restored and freed from their last exile, under which they still groan, and until the days of the Messiah, whose coming they deny, have arrived. In this they are deceived more certainly than certain, and they utterly cheat themselves of the benefit of this promise, since they obstinately cling to their unbelief, by which they have deprived themselves of the right to be his people any longer, although the benefits belong only to his people. But just as his opinion about this matter is to be rejected outright, so we cannot agree with those Christian interpreters who, having taken the preceding words in an allegorical sense, as we have seen, likewise think that this is a promise only of such spiritual goods as were to be conferred through c) Christ, through whom our corrupt nature has been restored, and through the saving doctrine of the Gospel the shame and confusion of the law and of sin have been removed.

units.la: Verum enim vero quo denique modo hæc verba applicueris, vel ad quoscunque ea referre complacitum fuerit, si literæ habenda sit aliquatenus ratio, quam nos inprimis sequi constituimus, in specie videntur ad illius temporis Judæos respicere, quos hic allocutus est
units.tr: Indeed, however these words are applied, or to whomever it may be pleasing to refer them, if regard is to be had to the letter, which we in particular have resolved to follow, they seem especially to look to the Jews of that time, whom he here addresses.

units.la: z) Rom. 8, 28. a) 1. Tim. 4, 8. b) Deuteron. 11. v. 13. 14. & Cap. 28, 1. &c. Psalm. 91. c) Mercer. Propheta, conditionisque illorum, ut antea vidimus & diximus, fortem innuere, quam aut olim subierant, aut jam jam subibant, aut in posterum erant subituri. Non admodum autem refert, quo tempore ea sumas, quippe lingua prophetica, quæ sunt apud DEum præsentia, non secus sunt censenda, quam quæ præterierunt, ac jamjam sunt confecta. Dicitur de illis, quod gravibus peccatorum suorum irritamentis tam miseram in se derivaverant calamitatem & plagam d) annonæ caritatis atque famis, quam illis inferebant locustæ & aliæ noxiæ bestiolæ terræ fructus penitus destruentes, ut coram cæteris nationibus esset opprobrio, ignominiæ atque risui. Quocirca admonebantur, ut sicria pœnitudine ad DEum sese converterét ad hæc mala evitanda, promissione adjecta, fore, ut ita faciendo gratiam apud DEum invenirent, qua in pristinum favorem rursum eos reciperet, vindicans sibi eos pro suo populo ac perpetrans pro iis tanta, ut, quamdiu in eo statu essent permansuri, non diutius, imo non amplius pudore suffundendi forent. Quæ promissio hujusmodi concepta est verbis ut in genere ad omnes, quamvis in specie ad præsentem eorum conditionem hic respiciat, omnique tempore applicari possit; populus meus nunquam confundetur. Quando enim absolute accipiuntur, omnibus æque, qui ita DEO adhærent, ut populus ejus vocari mereantur, promittunt futurum, ut nulla re unquam egeant, quæ saluti illorum conducat, sive ad spiritualem, sive ad temporalem hanc vitam pertineat, deo ut spe ac fiducia in eum collocata nunquam excidant, neque in cultu, quem ei præstant, confundantur. Verum, ut diximus, magis videtur hic in specie ad eos spectare atque innui, se esse eorum regionem redacturum in alium florentem statum, quo omnibus temporalibus bonis magna abundantia & ubertate iterum affluerent, quibus propter peccata admissa ac rebellionem in DEum factam hactenus erant privati.
units.tr: z) Rom. 8.28. a) 1 Tim. 4.8. b) Deut. 11.13, 14; ch. 28.1, etc.; Ps. 91. c) Mercer. They point to the condition of the prophet and of those people, as we have seen and said above, and to the fortune that they had either undergone in the past, or were then undergoing, or were going to undergo in the future. It does not much matter at what time you take these things, since in prophetic language what is present before God is to be regarded no differently from what has passed and is now all but accomplished. It is said of them that, by the weighty provocations of their sins, they had brought upon themselves so wretched a calamity and blow: d) the dearth and famine that the locusts and other harmful little creatures of the earth inflicted, destroying the fruits of the land utterly, so that they became a reproach, a disgrace and a laughingstock among the other nations. For this reason they were admonished that they should turn themselves to God with true repentance in order to avoid these evils, with the promise added that by so doing they would find grace before God, by which he would receive them back into his former favour, claiming them for his own people and bestowing on them so much that, for as long as they remained in that state, they would no longer be covered with shame, indeed no longer at all. This promise is framed in words that, while in general addressed to all, look here particularly to their present condition, and can be applied at any time: my people shall never be put to shame. For when taken absolutely, they promise to all alike who cling so to God as to deserve to be called his people, that they will never lack anything that conduces to their salvation, whether it pertains to this spiritual life or to this temporal one, so that hope and trust placed in him will never fail, nor will they be confounded in the worship they render him. But, as we have said, here it seems rather that he is looking particularly to them and hinting that he will restore their region to another flourishing state, in which they would again abound with all temporal goods in great plenty and fertility, of which they had hitherto been deprived on account of the sins they had committed and the rebellion against God.

units.la: Quod autem ad spiritualia attinet, expresse ea satis continentur in verbis sequentibus.
units.tr: As for spiritual matters, these are expressly contained in the following words.

units.la: 28. Et
units.tr: 28. And

units.la: d) Id. Merc. ad literam, ad probrum famis hoc pertinet, quo inter gentes laborabant.
units.tr: d) Id. Merc. Literally, this pertains to the reproach of famine, under which they were suffering among the nations.

units.la: 28. Et erit post hæc, effundam spiritum meum super omnem carnem, & filii vestri & filiæ vestræ prophetabunt, senes vestri somnia somniabunt & juvenes vestri visiones videbunt.
units.tr: 28. And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.

units.la: 29. Atque etiam super servos & super ancillas diebus illis effundam spiritum meum.
units.tr: 29. And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit.

units.la: Pergit hic in promissis gratiam spirantibus faciendis. At alius plane generis ac naturæ sunt hæc, quam quæ fecerat in præcedentibus. Unde fortean occasionem nactus est Abarbinel, ut hunc librum Joelis in duas prophetias vel duos sermones propheticos divideret, quarum altera his verbis initium sumeret: Quo cum facere videntur, qui eandem ob rationem novum ab his verbis incipiunt caput. Magna erant certe promissa præcedentia; at multo sunt majora hæc, altiorisque ac sublimioris naturæ. Illa temporalia erant, si exprimendi formas respexeris, (quamvis ulterius ea extendant nonnulli) hæc plane spiritualia, quæ, quo tempore essent conferenda & in quos eroganda his declaratur verbis: (1.) Tempus exprimitur, והיה אחרי כן vehayah achare chen, & erit post hæc, post ea promissa antea præstita. Spiritualia, quæ hic promittuntur, ut dignitate longe excedunt & naturæ excellentioris sunt, quam temporalia ante promissa, ita & ante & præ illis spectanda juxta monitum Salvatoris nostri Matth. 6,33. ut regnum cœlorum quæramus primo, non dubii, quin cætera quoq; hujus vitæ, ut alimenta & vestitus, adjiciantur nobis. At complacitum fuit hic benignissimo DEO (pem facere prius minus necessariorum, ut e) imbecillitati eorum indulgeret, cui hæc magis erant obvia, & quia præsens necessitas ea inprimis exigere videbatur, ut hac ratione magis magisque perducerentur ad cognitionem ejus, omnium donorum bonorum largitoris, propiusque indies ad eum appropinquantes ac in ejus populum adoptati desiderio etiam tangerentur cæterorum meliorum bonorum, quæ hoc loco se esse largiturum pollicetur. At quodnam est illud tempus constitutum, quod expri-
units.tr: Here he goes on to promises that bestow grace. But these are of a quite different kind and nature from those he had made before. Hence perhaps Abarbanel seized the occasion to divide this book of Joel into two prophecies or two prophetic discourses, the second of which begins with these words; and those who begin a new chapter with these words for the same reason seem to do likewise. The promises that went before were certainly great, but these are much greater, and of a higher and more sublime nature. Those were temporal, if you regard the form of expression (although some extend them further), whereas these are plainly spiritual. The time at which they are to be conferred, and upon whom they are to be bestowed, is declared in these words: (1) The time is expressed by vehayah achare chen [והיה אחרי כן], and it shall be after these things, that is, after the promises made before and the benefits already granted. The spiritual goods promised here, just as they far exceed in dignity and are of a more excellent nature than the temporal promises before, so are they to be looked for before and above those, according to the warning of our Saviour, Matt. 6.33, that we should seek the kingdom of heaven first, with no doubt that the other things of this life, such as food and clothing, will be added to us. But it pleased the most gracious God here to make the lesser and less necessary things first, so that he might indulge their weakness, to which these things were more obvious, and because the present need seemed especially to demand them, so that by this means they might be led more and more to the knowledge of him, the giver of all good gifts, and, drawing nearer to him day by day and being adopted into his people, might also be moved by longing for the other and better goods that he promises here to bestow. But what is the time appointed that is expressed

units.la: e) Calvin. exprimitur his verbis ;] אחרי כן posthac, nimirum post ea prædicta facta & præstita, vel eo tempore, quod ea sequetur? Non est,quod hic anxie inquiramus rationes, quibus alii nituntur, qui id referunt vel ad temporaf) Jehosophatis (cujus vallis postea memoratur c.3, 12.) quo tempore multos fuisse Prophetas ex eo apparet,quod multi dicuntur venisse ad Elisæum g) 2. Reg. 2, 15. vel ad tempora,quibus floruit Esaias, ut b) Grotius videtur statuere, quando verba sequentia (super omnem carnem) ita exponit, i.e. super multos, non super Esaiam solum; vel nescio quæ alia hoc genus i) conjectant. S. Petrus omnium auctoritate sua nos reddit certissimos de complendo promissorum hoc tempore Act. 2, 17. ubi hunc locum citans non obscure docet, eo tempore præstita esse ac completa, quæ hic dicuntur, atque ita tempus expressum est per אחרי כן Achare chen, post hac. Hoc est, inquit, populo attonito, cum tam miranda, quæ antea nunquam viderat nec fundo usquam audiverat, Spiritus Sancti videret dona in Apostolos collata, nec,unde descenderent, cognoscere posset, hoc est, quod dictum est per Prophetam Joelem: Et erit in ultimis temporibus &c. Ait hanc prophetiam tunc temporis esse expletam, quo dilucide arguit,antea nullum fuisse tempus, quo id præstitum ac factum esse dici posset; atque pariter opus haud esse, ut posthac aliud ejus implendi tempus expectetur, ac si omni ex parte nondum esset etfactum,quod hic prædictum est,sed tum aliqua hujus prophetiæ pars,quæ isti tempori esset propria,tunc completa. Atqui hoc tempus non erat aliud,quam illorum dierum spatium post Christi adventum & ascensionem in cœlos elapsum, quo, captivis abductis in captivitatem, dedit hominibus dona Ephes. 4, 8. eadem etiam, quæ hic sunt, promissa,ita ut planam nobis sternat viam ad To אחרי כן Achare chen, post hac, intelligendum de tempore post Christum, quod communiter appellatur, Messiae dies. Quod hic cumprimis observandum est, eo redit, quod Propheta hic dicat Achare chen,post hac, cum S. Petrus habeat ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις, ultimis diebus. At hanc diversitatem tantummodo sitam esse in verbis,nequaquam autem ingredi eorum sensum, sed idem utramque expressionem complecti,quidam etiam
units.tr: e) Calvin. It is expressed by these words: achare chen [אחרי כן], after this. Does it mean, after the things foretold and done and bestowed, or at the time that will follow them? There is no need for us to inquire anxiously into the reasons by which others strive to refer it either to the times of f) Jehoshaphat (whose valley is mentioned afterwards, ch. 3.12), at which time there appears to have been many prophets, since many are said to have come to Elisha g) 2 Kings 2.15, or to the times in which Isaiah flourished, as b) Grotius seems to hold, when he explains the following words, upon all flesh, to mean upon many, not upon Isaiah alone; or to some other conjectures of this kind. S. Peter makes us entirely certain by his authority concerning the fulfilment of this promise at this time, Acts 2.17, where, citing this passage, he plainly teaches that what is said here was then bestowed and completed. And so the time is expressed by achare chen [אחרי כן], after this. This is, he says, to the astonished people, when they saw the gifts of the Holy Spirit conferred upon the Apostles, so wonderful as they had never seen before nor heard of anywhere, and could not understand whence they came: this is what was spoken by the Prophet Joel: And it shall come to pass in the last days, and so on. He says that this prophecy was fulfilled at that time, by which he clearly argues that there was no earlier time at which it could be said to have been performed and done; and likewise that there is no need to look for another time of fulfilment afterwards, as if what is foretold here had not yet been done in every respect, but some part of this prophecy belonging to that time had then been completed. Yet this time was nothing other than the space of those days that elapsed after the coming and ascension of Christ into heaven, when, having led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men, Eph. 4.8, and the same promises that are here were given, so that he lays a plain path for us to understand to [אחרי כן] achare chen, after this, as referring to the time after Christ, which is commonly called the days of the Messiah. What is especially to be noted here comes to this: that the Prophet here says achare chen, after this, whereas St Peter has in the last days [ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις]. But some of the most learned Jews do not hesitate to admit that this difference lies only in the words, and does not enter into their sense, but that both expressions embrace the same thing.

units.la: f) Vide Aben-Ezra a quodam R. Mose. g) Et cap. 4,38. b) Quem vide in h. l. & in Act. 2. i) vide Rufsin. ctiam doctissimorum Judæorum fateri non detrectant. Ita R. David Kimchi: אחרי כן Achare chen idem sensu est quod באחריתהימים Beacharith hayamim, in nouissimis diebus Isa. 23. ubi Christi adventus describitur, ad cujus tempora cum non paucis aliis suæ gentis confitetur hæc verba pertinere, licet promissorum præslitorum adeo non curam habeat, ut iisdem convictus fateatur eum jam venisse, quippe cujus adventum cum cæteris suæ nationis pertinaci mente perneg at. Dies itaque Messiæ omni dubio procul nobis hic intelligendi sunt hac Prophetæ expressione, post hæc, quam exponit S. Petrus ultimis diebus, quibus DEus, secundum illum, tam extraordinaria dona volebat in homines collocare, eaque tam extraordinaria ratione, mensura & gradu atque in tot ac tales personas, ut in sequentibus verbis est expressum. Evincit enim id præclare & auctoritas Apostoli divino spiritu afflati, & evidentia operum factorum & verborum proprietas ususque cognitus. Atqui hi dies non nisi Evangelii tempus erant, quo verbum confirmatum est subsequentibus signis, Marc. 16,20. Deo attestante primis ejus prædicatoribus signis & variis miraculis & Spiritus Sancti donationibus suo arbitratu, Hebr. 2,4. Nam extra omnem dubitationis aleam positum est, hanc prophetiam non posse dici ullo priori tempore rite completam. Quid? quod nec hoc inficias iri queat, hæc eo tempore fuisse eo modo visa, quo hic sunt prædicta, ut pluribus hoc evincemus, exposituri & bona dona his verbis descripta, quæ conferenda erant, & personas, in quas erant collocanda. 1. Dona] i. e. copiosa mensura Spiritus Dei, copiosa, inquam, mensura; id enim significat verbum hoc loco adhibitum אשפך atque redditum effundam, non simpliciter conferre, sed magna abundantia conferre, ampliore significatione. Quod dicit, k) effundam Spiritum meum, qui est fons & auctor, in prædictas personas, necessario denotat se impleturum esse eos omnibus donis & beneficiis, quæ sunt ejusdé Spiritus S. l) effectus, & ubi ejus dona & operationes apparent, ibi dicitur datus, vel receptus ab hominibus, quotquot illorum
units.tr: f) See Aben-Ezra, as cited by a certain R. Moses. g) And ch. 4, 38. b) See it on this passage and on Acts 2. i) See Rufinus. Nor do the most learned of the Jews refuse to admit this. Thus R. David Kimchi: Achare chen [אחרי כן] has the same sense as Beacharith hayamim [באחריתהימים], in the latter days, Isa. 23., where the coming of Christ is described. He refers these words to the time of Christ, together with not a few others of his nation. Yet he so little regards the promises already fulfilled that, though convinced by them, he confesses that the Messiah has already come, whose coming he stubbornly denies together with the rest of his nation. Without any doubt, then, we must understand the days of the Messiah here by the Prophet's expression after these things, which S. Petrus explains as in the last days, when God, according to him, wished to bestow such extraordinary gifts on men, and in such an extraordinary manner, measure and degree, and upon so many and such persons, as is expressed in the following words. For this is clearly shown both by the authority of the Apostle, inspired by the divine Spirit, and by the evidence of the deeds done, and the proper use of the words as it is known. Yet these days were nothing other than the time of the Gospel, in which the word was confirmed with the signs that followed, Mark 16:20, God bearing witness to its first preachers with signs and various miracles and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will, Heb. 2:4. For it is beyond all doubt that this prophecy cannot be said to have been properly fulfilled at any earlier time. What more? Nor can it be denied that these things at that time appeared in the very way in which they are foretold here. We shall prove this at length, expounding the good gifts described in these words, which were to be bestowed, and the persons upon whom they were to be placed. 1. The gifts: that is, an abundant measure of the Spirit of God, an abundant measure, I say, for this word used here, ashpokh [אשפך], rendered I will pour out, signifies not merely to bestow, but to bestow in great abundance, with a fuller meaning. When he says k) I will pour out my Spirit, which is the fountain and author, upon the said persons, he necessarily signifies that he will fill them with all the gifts and benefits which are the l) effects of the same Holy Spirit. Wherever his gifts and operations appear, they are said to be given or received by men, as many as there are of them,

units.la: k) Confer cum hac expressione Esa. 44,3. diversa licet hebræa voce ibi extante, Act. 2,17. Rom. 5, 5. Tit. 3,6. l) 1. Cor. 12,11. gratia spiritualis in nobis est, quæ sunt effectus Spiritus Sancti. Drus. Danæus. Sp. Piscat. inum sunt, ac quantum etiam differant, cum cuique adhic, & de eo, hoc loco, quisque certus reddatur, ut infra id dicturi sumus. Quæ porro hic sunt in textu Hebraico, nostrates & alii interpretes reddunt אֵת רוּחִי Eth Ruchi, meum spiritum, LXX. atque Apostolus Petrus eam citans, ἀπὸ τῆς πνεύματός μου, ex Spiritu meo. Quam τῶν LXX. vitiosam quidam advertunt, ac minus exactam; imo quod m) perpetuam verterint, diminuentes gratiosam DEI promissionem, ac si particulam aliquam Spiritus sui Deus promitteret. Quod tamen dicere nobis religio est, cum eo modo videamus S. Petrum agere hunc locum citantem, qui certe non secutus esset pravum τῶν LXX vel alicujus alius sensum, sed genuinam verborum mentem expressisset. Manifestum est ex diversa interpretatione verborum præcedentium, Apostolum sese non alligare auctoritati illorum, sed exprimere tantum genuinam sententiam verborum Prophetæ, quæ ipsi suggerebantur atque ab eodem Spiritu docebantur, quo agitatus erat Propheta. Nec est revera, quod aliqua ratione differat expressio Græca ab hebraica, vel majus quid hæc innuat, quam illa. In propatulo enim est, illam omnino notare 1. inexhaustam abundantiam hujus Spiritus, quæ omnibus implendis sufficiens est. 2. Donationes Spiritus esse multas ac diversas idoneos reddentes homines diversis illis muniis obeundis, quæ gloria Dei & ecclesiæ vel populi salus requirat, omniaque hæc prædicta bona dona, licet plurima ac varia, ab eodem descendere Spiritu. Et quid amplius literalis hebraici Textus interpretatio, effundam spiritum meum, suggerere potest? Equidem id non potest dici innui, totum Spiritum cuique personæ æquali ratione ac mensura conferendum esse, cum id vim inferat citato loco Hebr. 2, 4. & 1. Corinth. 12, 4. &c. nec leve indicium hujus rei hoc loco est, quando enumerantur diversæ donationes in sequentibus in diversas personas collocandas, ita ut interpretatio græca utroque in testamento nullo modo, quod in textu hebraico est, extenuet, sed insigniter enucleet, has diversas donationes (ut diximus) pandens, quæ generali nomine Spiritus sunt comprehensæ atque dilucide posteà traditæ; nec non eas personas, in quas erant conferendæ. Antequam vero
units.tr: k) Compare with this expression Isa. 44:3, though a different Hebrew word is found there; Acts 2:17; Rom. 5:5; Tit. 3:6. l) 1 Cor. 12:11. spiritual grace is in us, which are the effects of the Holy Spirit. Drusius, Danaeus, Piscator. And how far they differ, since each person is still to be made certain of this in this place, as we shall say below. What is in the Hebrew text here, our countrymen and other interpreters render Eth Ruchi [את רוחי], my spirit; the Septuagint, and the Apostle Peter citing it, render from my Spirit [ἀπὸ τῆς πνεύματός μου]. Some note that the Septuagint is faulty and less exact in this, indeed m) because they have rendered it perpetual, diminishing God's gracious promise, as if God promised some particle of his Spirit. Yet it is a scruple for us to say this, since we see St. Peter handling this passage in the same way when he cites it, and he certainly would not have followed a faulty sense of the Septuagint or of anyone else, but would have expressed the genuine meaning of the words. It is manifest from the different rendering of the preceding words that the Apostle did not bind himself to their authority, but only expressed the genuine sense of the Prophet's words, which were suggested to him and taught by the same Spirit by whom the Prophet was moved. Nor is it really the case that the Greek expression differs from the Hebrew in any way, or implies anything greater than it does. For it is plain that it signifies, first, the inexhaustible abundance of this Spirit, which is sufficient to fill all things; second, that the gifts of the Spirit are many and diverse, making men fit to discharge those various offices which the glory of God and the salvation of the Church or people require; and that all these promised good gifts, though very many and various, proceed from the same Spirit. And what more can the literal interpretation of the Hebrew text, I will pour out my spirit, suggest? Indeed it cannot be said to imply that the whole Spirit is to be given to each person in equal manner and measure, since that would do violence to the cited passages, Heb. 2:4 and 1 Cor. 12:4, etc. Nor is this a slight indication in the matter here, when the diverse gifts are enumerated in the following verses as to be placed in diverse persons. So the Greek rendering, in both Testaments, in no way waters down what is in the Hebrew text, but clearly brings it out, unfolding these diverse gifts (as we have said), which are comprehended under the general name Spirit and afterwards plainly set forth, and likewise the persons upon whom they were to be conferred. Before, however, we subject either of these two to examination,

units.la: m) Calvin. alterutrum horum examini subjiciamus, consideran-dum venit nobis verborum vestigiis insistentibus nomen quoddam generalius, quopersona comprehenduntur, quod est כל בשר Col Basar,omnis caro; כל Col, omnis, est nota, quod scimus, universalitatis, & בשר basar,caro, vox ampla, quæ & cæteras omnes creaturas & homines denotat. At cognitum habemus, vocem כל omnis tum hoc loco, tum alibi restrictiori accipi sensu, adeo ut non quemvis omnis generis notet, sed omnia genera vel quosdam omnium generum & cujusvis conditionis; atque vocem בשר caro denotare cumprimis homines, non alias creaturas. Hac ratione כל omnis, usurpatur 2. Reg. 8,9. ubi Hazael dicitur duxisse secum muneris loco טוב כל משק omne bonum Damasci, i. e. ut nostrates optime interpretati sunt, ex omni bona re Damasci, ex quovis genere bonorum aliquid. Quod autem attinet ad בשר basar caro, quod non denotet, ut diximus, omnes vivas creaturas, sed בני ארם (n) in specie homines, ita usurpatur Psal. 145,20. Omnis caro, (i. e. omnis generis homines) benedicat nomini sancto,& Esa. 66,23. omnis caro venient ad servicendum coram me, ait Dominus; atque hac tantum notione eadem vox בשר Bashar in usu est Arabibus, ut in specie tribuatur inter creaturas cæteras hominibus, unde Adam vocatur illis Abu Bashar, pater hominum, vel humani generis. Huc usque tam Christiani quam Judæi insigniter conveniunt, generalem vocis significationem limitibus certis esse coercendam; verum ulterius procedunt Judæi, in quo adstipulari illis nequaquam possumus, cum ad solos Israelitas hæc adstringant, omnesque alias hominum nationes juxta ac alias creaturas excludant; quid? quod ne ad illos quidem Israelitas pertinere putent, qui non in terra Israelis habitant. Ita Aben-Ezra, super omnem carnem מקום ראוי להנכחי בארץ ישראל i. e. in terra Israel, qui est locus accommodatus ad votici-nandum. Ut & Kimchi, super omnem carnem, i. e. de Israelitis (intelligendum) dignis in quibus sit Spiritus Sanctus, qui & voce כל omnis intelligi putat הגדולים והקטנים magnos & parvos inter eos. His arctius hanc prophetiam adhuc constringit Grotius, cum super omnem carnem idem vult valere quod super multos.
units.tr: m) Calvin. Let us consider, following the traces of the words, a more general name by which persons are comprehended, namely col basar [כל בשר], all flesh. Col [כל], all, is a known mark of universality, and basar [בשר], flesh, is a wide word, denoting both all other creatures and men. But we know that the word all is taken here, and elsewhere, in a more restricted sense, so that it denotes not any kind whatever of all things, but all kinds, or some of all kinds and of every condition; and that the word flesh denotes especially men, not other creatures. In this way all is used at 2 Kings 8:9, where Hazael is said to have taken with him, as a gift, all the good of Damascus [טוב כל משק], which our countrymen have rightly rendered of all good things of Damascus, some of every kind of good thing. As for flesh, which, as we have said, does not denote all living creatures, but (n) men specifically [בני ארם], it is so used at Psalm 145:20, all flesh (that is, men of every kind) shall bless his holy name, and at Isa. 66:23, all flesh shall come to worship before me, saith the Lord. And only in this sense is the same word bashar used by the Arabs, so that among other creatures it is assigned specifically to men; whence Adam is called by them Abu Bashar, father of men, or of the human race. Up to this point Christians and Jews agree remarkably, that the general sense of the word is to be restrained within certain limits. But the Jews proceed further, and in this we can by no means agree with them, since they confine these things to the Israelites alone, excluding all other nations of men as well as other creatures. Indeed they do not think it pertains even to those Israelites who do not dwell in the land of Israel. Thus Aben-Ezra on all flesh: a place suitable for prophesying, in the land of Israel. And Kimchi, on all flesh, that is, (it is to be understood) of the Israelites worthy to have the Holy Spirit in them; who also thinks that the word all is to be understood of great and small among them. Grotius constrains this prophecy still more narrowly, since he wants upon all flesh to mean the same as upon many.

units.la: n) Vide Kimchi & Ainsio. multos, non super Efaiam solum, ac si ne quidem ad Israelitas pertincaret extra illud Prophetæ tempus. Idem facit o) R. Joseph Albo, qui ad exiguam totius Israelis partem eam refert, non ad omnes, neque ad alias nationes, ita ut juxta illum sensus esset, super quendam ex omni carne (ex illis) quamvis non idoneus foret vel pararetur ad vaticinandum (vel muneri prophetico initiatus & in eo educatus.) Verum enim vero quod laxiori significatu hæc verba sumenda sint, eventus atque complementum eorum dilucide evincit, qui prophetiarum optimus est interpres, illarumque sensum maxime reddit obvium & clarum.
units.tr: n) See Kimchi and Ainsworth, over many, not only over Isaiah, as if the promise did not even extend to the Israelites beyond the prophet's own time. o) R. Joseph Albo does the same. He refers it to a small part of all Israel, not to everyone and not to the other nations, so that on his reading the sense would be: upon someone from all flesh (from among them) who, though not fit or prepared to prophesy (or trained and educated in the prophetic office), would be given it. But that these words must be taken in a looser sense, the outcome and fulfilment of them make clear. Outcome is the best interpreter of prophecies, and it renders their sense most plain and obvious.

units.la: Non admodum a vero abhorret, Judæos olim, cum Evangelii primo prædicaretur, (imo & ipsum Petrum) eandem fovisse sententiam cum illis, qui recentioris ævi sunt a nobis citati, promissa scilicet dona Spiritus S. non nisi ad suam nationem pertinere atque in eam tantum effusum iri. Verum secus sunt docti ex eo, quod Cornelio & ejus familiæ contigerat, quod argumenti loco erat, in gentiles quoque effusa esse Spiritus S. dona, Act. 10, 45. Eadem ibi vox est effundendi in descriptione eventus, quæ hoc loco in promissione, (quam, uti diximus, ille citat Act. 2, 17. eundem in finem) quod indicio est id hic fuisse præstitum, quod vi hujus prophetiæ erat expectandum, atque factum, ut id rite confieret, adeo ut per omnem carnem necessario intelligendi sint quidam ex omnibus, vel quædam hominum genera, nullo respectu habito, cujusnam sint regionis, sexus, ætatis vel conditionis. Quippe in Christo, quoad ordinaria beneficia & privilegia, quorum tempora, ut vidimus, hæc prophetia spectat, neque p) Judæus est neque Græcus, neque servus neque liber, neque mas neque fœmina, Gal. 3, 28. sed omnes sumus idem in Christo Jesu, ad omnes pari jure spectant promissa Spiritus DEI, omnesque iis tali modo atque mensura instruentur, prout ejus gloriæ atque ecclesiæ incremento propriæque saluti optime conducet. Id quod non obscure ex sequentibus liquet, ubi in specie magis docet, tum quænam sint imprimis illæ personæ, tum quæ spiritualia ad eas spectantia bona, quæ hisce terminis tam generalibus comprehenduntur. Verum priusquam
units.tr: It is not far from the truth that the Jews of old, when the Gospel was first preached (even Peter himself), held the same opinion as those more recent writers we have cited: that the promised gifts of the Holy Spirit pertained only to their own nation and would be poured out on it alone. But the learned have been taught otherwise by what happened to Cornelius and his household, which served as proof that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were poured out on Gentiles also (Acts 10:45). In that passage the word for "pour out" is the same as in the promise here, and in describing the event Luke uses it of the same thing that Peter cites from this prophecy (Acts 2:17) for that purpose. This shows that what was to be expected by the force of this prophecy was in fact done, and done properly. So "all flesh" must necessarily be understood as some from all, or certain kinds of people, without regard to what region, sex, age or condition they belong to. For in Christ, as far as ordinary benefits and privileges go, to which times this prophecy looks as we have seen, "there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female" (Gal. 3:28), but we are all one in Christ Jesus. The promises of God's Spirit apply to all on equal terms, and all are equipped in such a way and measure as will best serve his glory, the growth of the Church, and their own salvation. This is plain enough from what follows, where he teaches more specifically both which persons are chiefly meant and which spiritual goods belonging to them are comprehended under these very general terms. But before we spend our effort on these matters,

units.la: *) Ihkarim I. 2. c. 10. p) Rom. 10, 12. quam his considerandis operam nostram collocemus, opus erit diversam quorundam sententiam inspicere, quam fovent de voce caro, quæque nimium quantum abest ab ea, quam memoravimus. Eam autem nobis suggerit R. Salomon Jarchi, qui per בשר כר Col bafar intelligi voluit מי שנעשה לבו רך כבשר eum cujus factum est cor tenerum more carnis, allegatis argumenti loco pro hac vocis notione his verbis q) Ezech. 2,19. Ponam inter eos spiritum novum, & amovebo cor lapideum a carne eorum, & indam ei cor carneum. Quo videtur probare vocem caro accipi posse pro tenero carneo corde; verum non multum promovebit hac duorum locorum collatione, quandoquidem cor carneum ibi promittitur, tanquam donü atq; effectus Spiritus Dei; cum hoc loco habeatur pro corde, quod præparari debebat ad spiritum recipiendum. Interim sunt, r) quibus hæc sententia R. Salomonis non videtur displicere; de qua autem Mercerus ita suum judicium interponit: Non est, inquit, ex phrasi hebraei sermonis, quo col bafar denotare debet omnes mortales, i. e. omnes homines; Pariter omnino ut Abarbinel censet, qui eam non nisi ratione ורש vel ut expositionem allegoricam approbat, non autem pro interpretatione propria recipit. Ipse vero sentit, col bashar, omnem carnem כל בשר ... rebena comprehendere omnia hominum genera, cujuscunque nationis sint, quare neque Aben-Ezra assentitur, neque his aliis interpretibus, qui Spiritus promissionem hic factam ad solos Israelitas restringunt, cum indubiæ sit veritatis, vocem בשר b.ssar, quando cui tribuitur, laxioris esse significationis. Præterea & in rebus promissis ab illis differt, quando vocem רוח spiritus, non accipit cum illis pro peculiari Prophetiæ spiritu, sed pro eo, qui communior est, spiritu notitiæ, aut qui in cognitione DEI eos instruet. Dona enim prophetiæ, quorum in sequentibus fit mentio, etiam Israelitis vindicat, iisque inter eos, qui eorum recipiendorum forent capaces. Quod cum ita sit verbaque necessario ulterius extendi debeant, mente concipere non possum, cur adeo restricte s) quidam ea accipiant, ut ad Judæos magis spectasse hæc promis-sa
units.tr: *) Ikkarim I. 2. c. 10. p) Rom. 10:12. we must examine the different opinion some hold about the word flesh, which is far removed from the one we have mentioned. This opinion is suggested by R. Solomon Jarchi, who wished col bafar [כל בשר] to mean "he whose heart has been made tender like flesh [מי שנעשה לבו רך כבשר]", citing in support of this sense of the word Ezek. 2:19: "I will put a new spirit within them, and I will take away the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh." From this he seems to prove that the word flesh can be taken to mean a tender fleshy heart. But this comparison of two passages will not carry him far, since there a fleshy heart is promised as a gift and effect of the Spirit of God, whereas here it is taken to be the heart that had to be prepared to receive the Spirit. Yet there are some to whom this opinion of R. Solomon does not seem objectionable. Mercerus gives his judgement on it thus: "It is not," he says, "from the idiom of the Hebrew language, by which col bafar ought to denote all mortals, that is, all men." Abarbanel likewise thinks, who approves it only as an allegorical exposition, by way of ורש [rash], and does not accept it as the proper interpretation. He himself holds that col bashar, "all flesh" [כל בשר], rebbena, comprehends all kinds of men, of whatever nation they may be. Therefore neither does Aben Ezra agree, nor the other interpreters who restrict the promise of the Spirit made here to Israelites alone. For it is beyond doubt that the word bashar [בשר], wherever it is applied to someone, has a looser meaning. Moreover, he differs from them also about the things promised, since he does not take the word ruach [רוח], "spirit," with them as the special spirit of prophecy, but as the more general spirit of knowledge, or the one that will instruct them in the knowledge of God. For he claims for Israelites the gifts of prophecy, which are mentioned in what follows, and claims them among those who would be capable of receiving them. Since this is so, and the words must necessarily be extended further, I cannot understand why some interpret them so narrowly as to say that these promises looked chiefly to the Jews,

units.la: {q} Ut & cap. 36,26. {r} Lyra, (quamvis ad Judæos pariter & Gentiles etiam trahi posse arbitretur) & Tarnov. {s} Chr. a Castro. fa pronuntient,gentesque admissas ad harum rerum participationem non ex debito promissionis illis factæ,sed ex gratia,qua postea earundem participes factæ sunt. Erat certe,quod & initio notavimus,tam laxis terminis hæc prophetia concepta,ut & eas includeret,imo non_ effet,nec posset unquam dici completa, nisi præstita essent hæc promissa etiam gentibus, atque in eas non minus quam in Judæos effusa & collata essent hæc dona. Facto jam initio de promissis suis,generalibus his terminis inclusis,quod effusurus sit Spiritum suum (quo omnia ejus dona comprehendi possent) in omnem carnem(quo omnes filios hominum complectitur) in specie nunc it declaratum_, quænam Spiritus dona inprimis hic intelligat,& in quos homines & quomodo ea sint conferenda. Bona, quorum hic facit mentionem, non videntur solum illis hominibus conferri in ipsorum proprium_ ac privatum usum, sed ut aliis etiam iis prodessent & in illorum bonum operarentur, voluntatem DEI illis patefaciendo,viam ad eum_ perveniendi sternendo, doctrinam ejus propagando, atque eos pro virili ædificando. Primum quod promittitur,est prophetia, secundum somnia,tertium visiones. Personæ,in quas primum dicitur conferendum,sunt eorum filii & filia,secundum senes, tertium juvenes.
units.tr: {q} See also chapter 36:26. {r} Lyra (although he thinks it can also be drawn to Jews and Gentiles alike) and Tarnovius. {s} Christopher a Castro. and that the Gentiles were admitted to a share in these things not by any debt owed from the promise made to them, but by grace, through which they later came to share in the same things. Certainly, as we noted at the start, this prophecy was conceived in terms so wide that it includes them. Indeed, it would not be, nor could ever be called, fulfilled unless these promises had also been made to the Gentiles, and these gifts poured out and bestowed on them no less than on the Jews. Having now settled that he will pour out his Spirit, included under these general terms (by which all his gifts can be comprehended), upon all flesh (by which he embraces all the sons of men), it is now declared more specifically which gifts of the Spirit he means in particular, and on which men and in what manner they are to be conferred. The benefits he mentions here seem to be given to these people not only for their own private use, but so that they may also benefit others and work for their good: by revealing God's will to them, by preparing the way for them to come to him, by spreading his teaching, and by building them up as far as they are able. The first thing promised is prophecy, the second dreams, the third visions. The persons on whom it is said first to be conferred are their sons and daughters, second old men, third young men.

units.la: Quod ad primum donum Prophetiæ attinet,id proprie atque_ peculiari modo spectare arbitratur Abarbinel ad Israelem, vel in illis completum iri ea rerum restauratione,quam expectant (בני הנאילה) Licet enim prius Spiritus vocabulum ad alias nationes æque ac ad eos pertinere concedat,hoc loco tamen id Israelitus solis asserit & מכנים מהם hujusmodi inter eos qui se rite ad illud præparaverint; nec id unquam ad alias nationes pertinuisse, nec illis præstitum iri ullo tempore statuit,ut habent ejus verba מרה שלא היו ולא יהיו בשאר הגוים. At cum certo constet, hoc donum una cum_ cæteris hic tantum in specie recenseri (uti jam diximus) cum sub generali Spiritus nomine comprehenderetur, idque ejusdem naturæ esse cum cæteris, quæ in eo comprehenduntur,necessario sequitur, & illud ad omnes pertinere,qui nomine omnis carnis innuuntur, i.e. ad omnes hominum nationes,cujuscunque sint conditionis & sexus, ut denominatio filiorum & filiarum exhibet.
units.tr: As for the first gift, prophecy, Abarbanel thinks it looks properly and in a particular way to Israel, or that it will be fulfilled in them in that restoration of things which they expect (the sons of the redemption [בני הנאלה]). For although he allows that the word "Spirit" applies to other nations as well as to them, here he asserts it for Israelites alone, and only for such among them [מכנים מהם] as have duly prepared themselves for it. He holds that it has never belonged to other nations, nor will it be given to them at any time, as his words state: that it neither has been nor will be among the other nations [מרה שלא היו ולא יהיו בשאר הגוים]. But since it is certain that this gift is listed here only in particular (as we have said), while it was comprehended under the general name "Spirit", and since it is of the same nature as the others comprehended in it, it necessarily follows that it applies to all who are indicated by the name "all flesh", that is, to all nations of men, whatever their condition and sex, as the designation "sons and daughters" shows.

units.la: Quantûmvis etiam affixum ⊐⊃ chem, Vefiri, hoc promiss[?] illis solis videatur vindicare, ad quos Propheta locutus est, nimirum Judæis illius temporis; attamen absit procul, ut ad eorum filios tantum illud restringamus, quasi illorum tantum filii ac filiæ cæteris omnibus posthabitis respicerentur, cum potius cæterorum omnium filii ac filiæ non minus ac illi sub generali nomine omnis carnis comprehendantur. Etenim cum promissio tam late pateat, ut vox infert, non est cur arctioribus vinculis eam hic esse limitatam arbitremur; sed persuasi simus ad omnes æque indiscriminatim pertinere, etiam ad filios ethnicorum fidelium, quoscunque t) Deus advocaverit; quippe qui æque ac Israel secundum carnem essent capaces donorum Spiritus DEI recipiendorum. Filii Vestri & filiæ prophetabunt. Annorum hic rationem haberi sub nomine filiorum & filiarum autumat Kimchi, qui forent adhuc בניערות in pueritia sua, puelli & puellulæ, ut ita dicam כמו שמואל הנביא uti Samuel propheta, r. Sam. 3. qui Domini erat constitutus Propheta ab, imo in ipsis teneris annis. Quod si ita sit sumendum, omnes hic habentur ætates; senes quippe sequuntur & juvenes, quod argumento est, nullam esse u) ætatem, quæ non sit capax donorum spiritus DEI recipiendorum. Quid? quod nec sexus sit ulla exceptio, cum ex denominatione filiorum & filiarum patet, tum ex serie exemplorum, quam nobis exhibent S. literæ de feminis vatibus. Act. 21,9. dicitur Philippus habuisse quatuor filias, quæ vaticinabantur. Idem videre est ex eo, quod Paulus prohibeat, ne mulier vaticinetur detecto capite, 1. Cor. 11,5. Tandem & id illorum v) denominatione docemur, promissa divina non tantum pertinere ad patres, verum ad liberos quoque; Ad vos pertinet promissio, & ad Vestros filios, & ad omnes remotiores &c. Act. 2,39.
units.tr: Although the suffix ⊐⊃ chem, meaning "your", seems to claim this promise for those alone to whom the prophet spoke, namely the Jews of that time, yet far be it from us to restrict it to their sons only, as if only their sons and daughters were regarded and all others set aside. Rather, the sons and daughters of all others are no less than theirs comprehended under the general name "all flesh". For since the promise extends so widely, as the word itself implies, there is no reason to think it is limited here by narrower bounds. We should be persuaded that it applies to all equally and without distinction, even to the sons of believing Gentiles, whomsoever God has called (t). For they are just as capable as Israel, according to the flesh, of receiving the gifts of the Spirit of God. "Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." Kimchi holds that the age of the children is taken into account under the name of sons and daughters, since they would still be בניערות [benei 'ar'ot], in childhood, boys and little girls, as it were, like Samuel the prophet (1 Sam. 3), who was appointed a prophet of the Lord even in his tender years. If it is to be understood in this way, every age is included here: old men follow and young men, which is evidence that there is no age (u) which is not capable of receiving the gifts of the Spirit of God. And what of sex? No exception is made here either, as is clear both from the designation "sons and daughters" and from the series of examples which the Holy Scriptures give us of women prophets. In Acts 21:9 it is said that Philip had four daughters who prophesied. The same can be seen from the fact that Paul forbids a woman to prophesy with her head uncovered (1 Cor. 11:5). Finally, we are taught by their designation (v) that the divine promises pertain not only to the fathers but to the children too: "The promise is to you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off," etc. (Acts 2:39).

units.la: Proximo loco sub nomine omnis carnis jam notati sequuntur x) senes, in quos illud Spiritus S. donum conferendum est, ut somnia somniaturi sint, quos excipiunt eorum juvenes, in quibus se ita manifestabit Spiritus, ut Visiones Visuri sint. y) Maimonides distributioni huic personarum attendens eamque indefinite referri animadvertens ad quamvis hominum aetatem, quae ipsi non videbatur par ulli verae prophetiae gradui, accipienda haec verba non solum censet de illis, qui propheticis quibusdam donis veris erant instructi, verum etiam deiis, qui quaedam praedicere aut docere audebant augurando vel divinando, quatenus & hi prophetarum nomine gaudebant, ut prophetae Baal & lucus; atque scriptum extat Deut. 13,1. Si inter vos surrexerit Propheta vel somniator somniorum.
units.tr: Next, under the name "all flesh" already noted, come the old men (x), on whom that gift of the Holy Spirit is to be bestowed, "so that they will dream dreams." They are followed by "their young men," in whom the Spirit will manifest himself so that they "will see visions." (y) Maimonides, attending to this distribution of persons and noting that it is referred indefinitely to any age of men, judged that it did not match any true degree of prophecy. He thinks these words should be taken not only of those who were endowed with certain true prophetic gifts, but also of those who dared to predict or teach by augury or divination, since these too enjoyed the name of prophets, like the prophets of Baal and the grove. It stands written in Deut. 13,1: "If there arise among you a prophet or a dreamer of dreams."

units.la: Ad hanc expositionem, ut aures obturet lector, petit Abarbinel optans ardentissime, nunquam in chartam conjecta fuisse haec verba manifesto falsa, ut quivis ratione praeditus facile capere potest. Nam qua ratione in mentem alicui venire potest, cum extraordinariam benedictionem a DEO hic promittat Propheta, eum nominare atque intelligere hujusmodi affectatas prophetias, quae DEO omnino displicent, atque in lege ejus severe sunt prohibitae; & quomodo possit eas vocare suum spiritum, i. e. ut exponit hoc Chaldaeus meum sanctum Spiritum, quem in eos effusurus est? Unde necessario sequitur, non alia hic innui somnia ac visiones, quam quae DEum habent auctorem, quaeque ipse in lege pollicetur, & verae prophetiae revelationisque divinae non infimi gradus sunt. Si est propheta ex vobis, per visionem me ipsum notum faciam ei, & alloquar illum per somnium, ait Dominus Num. 12, 6.
units.tr: Abarbanel, to stop the reader's ears against this interpretation, begs, most ardently wishing that these words, manifestly false, had never been set down on paper, as anyone endowed with reason can easily grasp. For by what reasoning can it come into anyone's mind that, when the Prophet here promises an extraordinary blessing from God, he means and understands such affected prophecies, which altogether displease God and are severely forbidden in his law? And how could he call them "his spirit," that is, as the Chaldee paraphrast expounds it, "my holy Spirit," which he will pour out upon them? Hence it necessarily follows that no dreams or visions are meant here other than those which have God as their author, which he himself promises in the law, and which are not of the lowest degree of true prophecy and divine revelation. "If there is a prophet among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision, and speak to him in a dream," says the Lord, Num. 12,6.

units.la: Senes vestri somnia somniabunt &c.) Observat hic Kimchi & post eum Abarbinel, non addidisse hic Prophetam universalitatis notam, omnis, uti in praecedentibus fecerat, sed indefinite tantum dixisse, vestri senes & omnes vestri juvenes; non autem, omnes senes vestri & juvenes vestri, quod hanc ob causam factum dicunt, ut de iis tantum intelligatur, qui ex illis sunt מוכנים Mucanim, apti aut rite praeparati ad dona recipienda, imo ab ipsa eorum conceptione, ut Maimonides a Kimchi citatus habet. Idem etiam locum habet in verbis praecedentibus, filii vestri & filiae vestrae, quod tamen notare insuper habuerunt. Perquam facile autem intellectu est lectori, ut non est expressa
units.tr: "Your old men shall dream dreams," etc. Kimchi observes, and after him Abarbanel, that the Prophet has not added here the mark of universality, "all," as he had done in the preceding clauses, but has spoken only indefinitely: "your old men and your young men," not "all your old men and your young men." They say this was done so that it would be understood only of those who are מוכנים (Mucanim), that is, fit or duly prepared to receive the gifts, indeed from the very moment of their conception, as Maimonides, cited by Kimchi, has it. The same holds for the preceding words, "your sons and your daughters," which they nevertheless also noted. It is quite easy for the reader to understand that, since no express mark of universality, "all," is present, none is to be understood or can have a place.

units.la: y) Morch. Neb. L 1. c. 32. expressa universalitatis nota, omnis, ita nec subintelligendam esse, nec ullum habere posse locum. Etenim non erant instructi universi iisdem donis, ut illi omnes, in quos effusus erat Spiritus, potuissent prophetare, vel divinas haberent revelationes per somnia aut visiones; nunquam hoc tali modo erat factum, atque exinde etiam non promissum, quippe DEus revera in effectum deduxit quicquid promiserat. Stetit enim promissis suis, quae in hac prophetia fecerat DEus, Christo in coelum sublato, cum miranda Spiritus S. dona in fideles conferret, ita ut multi iis essent praediti in omnibus ecclesiis, tum Gentilium, tum Judaeorum. Exempli loco potest esse Ecclesia Corinthi, ubi tanta eorum frequentia erat, ut consultum duceret z) S. Paulus, vices eorum loquendi circumscribere limitibus, ne alius alium interturbaret. Attamen non omnes erant Prophetae, neque omnes eadem Spiritus dona recipiebant, neque eadem mensura omnes. Numquid omnes (inquit, Ecclesiae illius membra alloquens,) sunt Apostoli? a) numquid omnes Prophetae? numquid omnes doctores? numquid miraculorum editores? &c. minime gentium. Sed postquam mentionem injecerat diversorum modorum, quibus Deus effundit suum spiritum in eos, qui Evangelium Christi amplectebantur, eodem capite v. 11. ait, haec omnia efficere unum eundemque Spiritum, dispertientem cuique, ut vellet, sive sint Judaei sive gentes, servi aut liberi, v. 13. vel ut Prophetiae hujus verbis utamur, filii et filiae, senes vel juvenes, liberi vel servi et ancillae: tribuens differentiam horum diversorum donorum uni beneplacito DEI, uti & Heb. 2,4. Hinc beneplacitum ejus est potius, quod illos debet Mucanim, aptos reddere, (ut Judaei requirunt) quam ulla naturalis eorum constitutio, vel, ut volunt, propria industria. Donum est ejus, & quod illos aptos facit ad id recipiendum, quod recipiunt, & quod datur. b) Potest Deus quocunque tempore non solum munera sua conferre, sed etiam suscipientes ad id aptos efficere.
units.tr: (y) Morch. Neb. L 1. c. 32.) Indeed, not all were furnished with the same gifts, so that all on whom the Spirit was poured out could prophesy or have divine revelations through dreams or visions. This had never been done in that way, and so it was not promised in that way either, since God in fact brought to effect whatever he had promised. For the promises God made in this prophecy stood firm after Christ was taken up into heaven, when he bestowed the wonderful gifts of the Holy Spirit upon the faithful, so that many were endowed with them in all the churches, both of the Gentiles and of the Jews. The church at Corinth may serve as an example, where there was such a multitude of them that St. Paul thought it advisable to restrict their turns of speaking within limits, so that one would not disturb another (z). Yet not all were prophets, nor did all receive the same gifts of the Spirit, nor all in the same measure. "Are all apostles?" he says, addressing the members of that church. "Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all workers of miracles?" etc. By no means (a). But after mentioning the diverse modes by which God pours out his Spirit upon those who embraced the Gospel of Christ, he says in the same chapter, v. 11, that "all these things one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each one as he wills," whether they are "Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free" (v. 13).
