Or, to use the words of this prophecy, "sons and daughters, old men or young men, free or servants and handmaids." He attributes the difference of these diverse gifts to the one good pleasure of God, as also Heb. 2,4 does. Hence his good pleasure is what makes them fit (Mucanim), as the Jews require, rather than any natural constitution of theirs or, as they hold, their own industry. The gift is his, and it is what makes them fit to receive what is given. God can at any time not only confer his gifts, but also make those who receive them apt for them (b).

units.la: Eadem verba Apostoli responsum nobis suppeditant ad aliam quaestionem dirimendam, quam hic facit Abarbinel, cur hic somnia tribuantur senibus, visiones juvenibus? Posset equidem haec quaestio facillimo
units.tr: The same words of the Apostle supply us with a response for settling another question which Abarbanel raises here: why are dreams attributed to the old and visions to the young? This question could indeed be resolved with the greatest ease,

units.la: z) 1. Cor. 14, 29. a) 1. Cor. 12, 29. b) Pet. a Fig. Tho. Aq.
units.tr: (z) 1 Cor. 14,29. (a) 1 Cor. 12,29. (b) Pet. a Fig. Tho. Aq.

units.la: facillimo negotio expedire, fi ex DEI arbitrio hæc pendere dicerentur, nihilq; eum velle aut facere sine gravissima ratione, quamvis, cur ita velit ac faciat, ratiocinii nostri imbecillitatem longe superet; attamen in eo hic totus est Abarbinel, ut rationem assignet, cur voluntatem suam DEus revelet ac cognitum faciat, quid fieri velit, senibus per somnia & juvenibus per visiones. Eam autem non nisi in diversa temperamenti harum ætatum constitutione sitam esse censet, qua altera huic, altera alii generi longe est aptior. Cum igitur hæc Prophetiæ genera nimium quantum differant, senes, inquit, aptiores sunt Spiritus influxum recipiendi per somnia, idque לרוב לחות המקרי propter abundantem humorem, quo hæc ætas plerumque redundat, atque propter imaginariæ facultatis vel phantasiæ operationes augmentum indies capientes ex tot hominibus eorumque operibus vilis & cognitis; juniores vero, quibuscum aliter se res habet, qui tanto humore non scatent quorumque tot phantasiis facultas imaginatrix haud occupatur, aptiores sunt visionibus. c) Alii alias hujus rei rationes adducunt, quas inter nomen est postrema, quod sublimior nobiliorque prophetiæ gradus sit somnia somniare, quam visiones videre; eaque de causa primum sit promissum senibus, qui ætatis ratione majori sunt digni reverentia & honore, cum alterum gradus inferioris etiam inferioribus ætate sit dicatum; Atqui hæc est ratio quam Ribera tuetur. Non desunt tamen d) alii, qui contrarium probare contendunt, nimirum visiones sublimioris esse naturæ, quam somnia; quia majoris momenti res est homines vigilantes detrahere a contemplatione rerum sensibilium, quibus occupati sunt, atque ad rerum supernaturalium contemplationem elevare, quam tales effectus operari in anima, quæ jam somnio est sopita & a rebus sensibilibus abstracta. Etenim tunc demum excellere censet somnia, quando DEus immediate illis in somnio loquitur juxta illud quod ante citatum est, Num. 12,6. alloquar illum per somnium; quando autem dormientibus eædem visiones præsentantur, quæ vigilantibus, dormientis somnia inferioris arbitratur gradus, quam vigilantis visiones. Caete-
units.tr: if it were said to depend on the decision of God, and that he wills and does nothing without the most serious reason, although why he wills and does so far exceeds the weakness of our reasoning. Yet Abarbanel's whole aim here is to assign a reason why God reveals his will and makes known what he wishes to be done: to the old through dreams and to the young through visions. He thinks that reason lies only in the different temperament of these ages, by which the one is far better suited to one kind of revelation and the other to another. Therefore, since these kinds of prophecy differ greatly, the old, he says, are more apt to receive the influx of the Spirit through dreams, and this because of the abundant humour, לרוב לחות המקרי (lerov lechoth hamiqri, "by the abundance of moisture of chance"), with which this age commonly overflows, and because of the operations of the imaginative faculty or phantasy, which daily gain increase from so many men and their works seen and known. The younger, with whom matters stand otherwise, who do not teem with such humour, and whose imaginative faculty is not occupied with so many phantasies, are more apt for visions (c). Others adduce other reasons for this matter. Among these the last is that dreaming dreams is a higher and nobler degree of prophecy than seeing visions, and for this reason the promise is first made to the old, who by reason of age are worthy of greater reverence and honour, while the other, the lower degree, is dedicated also to the younger in age. This is the reason which Ribera defends. Nevertheless there are not lacking others (d) who contend for the contrary, namely that visions are of a higher nature than dreams. For it is a weightier matter to draw waking men away from the contemplation of the sensible things with which they are occupied and to raise them to the contemplation of supernatural things, than to produce such effects in a soul already lulled by sleep and abstracted from sensible things. Indeed, he thinks dreams are then truly excellent when God speaks to the dreamer immediately in sleep, according to what was cited above, Num. 12,6: "I will speak to him in a dream." But when the same visions are presented to sleepers as to the waking, he judges the dream of the sleeper to be of a lower degree than the vision of the waking.

units.la: c) Ribera. d) Thom. Aqu. ab eo citatus.
units.tr: (c) Ribera. (d) Thomas Aquinas, cited by him.

units.la: Cæterum hanc quæstionem,cur somnia tribuantur scenibus,visiones juvenibus,ex his verbis & necessario nasci,& hac ratione solvi posse autumat. Verum non video cur ei solvendæ tam anxie inhæreant, cum intellexisse sufficiat, mentem horum verborum non esse aliam, quàm Deum Spiritus sui ingentè promittere mensuram,quam constituto tempore, nullâ a donis ejus recipiendis ætate exclusa,conferre velit,ne ipso quidé excellentissimo prophetiæ dono excepto, in senes æque ac juvenes,prout ecclesiæ suæ censebit commodum,quibus voluntatem suam revelet per somnia & visiones, revelationum propheticarum tritas vias. Kimchi inter somnia & visiones talem nonstatuit differentiam, qualis cæteroquin grammatica quadam distinctione ex stricta verborum significatione posset erui, cum propius spectet dormientes alterum, alterum vigilantes,quamvis minus probabile sit,somnia huic, visiones alteri ætati peculiares esse. Verba enim sic explanat והנביאים תחזיון להם במראה החלום Et erit illis prophetia in visione somnii, quasi non essent distincta somnia & visiones,sed qui uno instrueretur, alterius etiam esset particeps,visionesque etiam locum haberent in somniis,ita ut quodvis nomen quibusvis revelationibus imponi posset,cuicunque etiam fieret ætati. Nec desunt visionum exempla,quas senes pariter atque juvenes videre. Eminet inter cæteros eo revelationis genere Cornelius Act.10,3. & Petrus eodem capite v.17. &c.11,5. De Ananiaquoque extat,Dominum eum allocutum esse per visionem, Act.9,10. Sic & Paulo legimus obvenisse visionem cap.16,9. Virquidam Macedo apparebat ei noctu orans,ut ad se veniret in Macedoniam. Atqui hi omnes in senibus sunt habendi; attamen non dicitur eos somnia somniasse,sed visiones vidisse. Quod de Paulo scriptum extat,quod aliquis noctu ei apparuerit, somnii speciem præ se ferre haud improbabile, est,nec alio venit nomine S. Hieronymo hæc in verba scribenti: senes quoque viderunt somnia, quando Paulus jam senex audivit virum Macedonem &c. id quod cum cæteris hujus generis exemplis liquidò confirmat,visiones juvenibus solis non esse peculiares, & idem revelationis genus nonnunquam denotari visionum & somniorum denominatione,ut hæc verba,senes somniabunt somnia & juvenes videbunt vi-siones, fiones, non argutam suppeditent distinctionem inter haec duo revelationis divinae genera, sed utriq; aetati certo affirment, Deum cum illis esse communicaturum haec Spiritus prophetici dona, jam hac, jam illa ratione pro arbitratu suo; quamvis non desit , cui pro Synonymis ea accipere placet, ut omnem ita praecidat occasionem disputandi, quae cui sit praeferenda donatio, etsi magis in visiones inclinet, si inter ea collatio instituenda sit. Verum non operae pretium est huic rei diutius hic insistere, quocirca altera divisionis nostrae pars jam est rimanda, qua Deus dicitur tam liberaliter esse effusurus Spiritum suum super omnem carnem, ut omnis aetatis non secus ac utriusque sexus personae sint receptura ex gratia & benignitate ejus. Quod ut pluribus in sequentibus verbis indicaret, magisque innotesceret, nullam conditionem hominum ab hoc privilegio esse exclusam, ita progreditur.
units.tr: Moreover, he claims that this question, why dreams are attributed to the old and visions to the young, must necessarily arise from these words and can be solved in this way. But I do not see why they cling so anxiously to solving it, since it is enough to understand that the intention of these words is nothing other than that God promises to pour out his Spirit in immense measure, which at an appointed time, with no age excluded from receiving his gifts, he will bestow, not even excepting the most excellent gift of prophecy, upon old men as well as young, as his church shall judge fit. To these he will reveal his will through dreams and visions, the well-worn paths of prophetic revelation. Kimchi did not establish between dreams and visions such a difference as might otherwise be drawn from the strict meaning of the words by some grammatical distinction, since it more properly regards sleepers in the one case and the waking in the other. Yet it is less probable that dreams are peculiar to one age and visions to the other. For he explains the words thus: והנביאים תחזיון להם במראה החלום ("And the prophets will have a vision in the appearance of a dream"), as if dreams and visions were not distinct, but he who was instructed by one would also share in the other, and visions would also take place in dreams, so that any name could be imposed on any revelations, whatever the age of the recipient. Nor are there lacking examples of visions which old men and young men alike saw. Among others, Cornelius stands out in this kind of revelation (Acts 10,3), and Peter in the same chapter, v. 17, etc., and 11,5. Of Ananias too it stands written that the Lord spoke to him through a vision (Acts 9,10). So too we read that a vision came to Paul (chap. 16,9), when a certain man of Macedonia appeared to him at night, praying that he come over into Macedonia. Yet all these must be counted among the old, and nevertheless it is not said that they "dreamed dreams," but that they "saw visions." That it is written of Paul that someone appeared to him at night is not improbable as a dream-like appearance, nor does St. Jerome come to it under another name when he writes these words: "The old also saw dreams, when Paul, already old, heard the man of Macedonia," etc. This, together with the other examples of this kind, clearly confirms that visions are not peculiar to the young alone, and that the same kind of revelation is sometimes denoted by the name of visions and sometimes by that of dreams. So these words, "your old men shall dream dreams and your young men shall see visions," do not supply a subtle distinction between these two kinds of divine revelation, but assure both ages that God will communicate with them these gifts of the prophetic Spirit, now in this way, now in that, as he pleases. Although there is no lack of one who likes to take them as synonyms, so as to cut off every occasion of disputing which gift is to be preferred, even if he inclines more to visions should a comparison between them be drawn. But it is not worth the effort to dwell longer on this matter here. Therefore the other part of our division must now be explored, in which God is said to be going to pour out his Spirit so liberally upon all flesh that persons of every age, no less than of either sex, will receive it from his grace and kindness. That he might indicate this more fully in the following words, and make it more clearly known that no class of men is excluded from this privilege, he proceeds thus.

units.la: 29. Atque etiam super servos & ancillas &c.] atque etiam; quorum cum praecedentibus verbis connexione docetur, alio respectu haec esse dicta, quam precedentia, non quidem de illorum sexu vel aetate, sed de conditione, cui erant adstricti; adeo ut, alienae licet subjecti essent potestati servileque munus obirent, non minus, ac qui sui juris essent, nec dominatum agnoscerent, capaces forent reddendi donorum Spiritus S. recipiendorum.
units.tr: 29. And also upon the servants and the handmaids, etc.] "And also": from the connection with the preceding words it is taught that these words are said with a different reference than the preceding ones. They are not about the sex or age of those people but about the condition to which they were bound. So, although they were subject to another's power and performed servile duties, they were no less capable of receiving the gifts of the Holy Spirit than those who were their own masters and acknowledged no lord.

units.la: In his diebus] Dies, de quibus hic sermo est, non sunt alii, quam regnum Christi, in quo nulla rerum differentia est, quae ad reditum eorum ad Deum atque ad potestatem privilegiis hujus regni fruendi pertinent, nulla hic est differentia inter servum & liberum, Gal. 3,28. Ille qui vocatus est in Domino, cum servus esset, is Domini libertus est. Idem qui liber vocatus est, is Christi servus est, 1. Cor. 7,22. Verba hebraica ita plane sonant, uti a nostratibus ad literam sunt expressa, eorumque sensus non alius certe videtur, quam a nobis est suppeditatus. At paulo aliter ea citantur a S. Petro Act. 2,18. Primo enim non indefinite dicit, super servos & ancillas, qua ratione hebraice habent עַל הָעֲבָדִים וְעַל הַשִּׁפְחוֹת al haabadim veal hashphacoth, sed cum
units.tr: In those days] The days of which this passage speaks are none other than the kingdom of Christ, in which there is no difference of conditions that bears on their return to God or on their right to enjoy the privileges of this kingdom. Here there is no difference between slave and free, Gal. 3,28. He who was called in the Lord, being a slave, is the Lord's freedman. He who was called being free is Christ's slave, 1 Cor. 7,22. The Hebrew words clearly sound as our countrymen have rendered them literally, and their sense certainly seems to be no other than what we have supplied. But St Peter cites them somewhat differently, Acts 2,18. For first, he does not say indefinitely upon the servants and the handmaids, which in Hebrew is [עַל הָעֲבָדִים וְעַל הַשִּׁפְחוֹת al haabadim veal hashphacoth], but with

units.la: {e} Petr. a Fig. Magis placet ut somnia & visiones pro eodem accipiantur. Possunt etiam intelligi omnia visa prophetica, quae fiunt sive in somno sive vigilia, &c. cum affixo subjuncto: ἐπὶ τὰς δούλας μου, καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς ἁμάς μου, super meos servos & meas ancillas, uti & Vulgata hic habet: sed & super servos meos & ancillas, quod aliquatenus videtur sensum immutare atque verborum significationem, quasi non proprie notarentur illi, qui nutus heriles observabant, aliisque hominibus subjecti erant, sed ad omnes omnium hominum ordines ac conditiones verba haec spectarent, ne summatibus quidem exceptis, cum & magnatibus laudi ducendum titulo filiorum DEI appellari; atqui ea ratione ad eosdem omnis generis homines respicerent, qui ante denotati sunt.
units.tr: {e} Peter of Figs. It is more pleasing that dreams and visions be taken as the same thing. All prophetic sights may also be understood, whether they occur in sleep or in waking, etc. With the added suffix: [ἐπὶ τὰς δούλας μου, καὶ ἐπὶ τὰς ἁμάς μου], upon my servants and my handmaids, as the Vulgate also has here: "but also upon my servants and handmaids". This seems somewhat to change the sense and the meaning of the words, as if those were not properly designated who watched for the nods of masters and were subject to other men, but as if these words referred to all ranks and conditions of men, without excepting even the great, since it is a matter for praise for the nobles too to be called by the title of sons of God. Yet in that way they would refer to the same kinds of men as were named before.

units.la: At quod eo sensu non sint accipienda, sed ad servilem ac communem hominum sortem referenda, haud incongrue f) quibusdam observatum est una nobiscum statuentibus, servos meos & ancillas meas hic non denotare omnis generis homines, qui vere in DEum credunt eumque colunt, sed eos cumprimis, qui servorum jugum subibant, adhuc inter homines. Quibus significari in proclivi est, & eos ipsos, non obstante illorum dejecta forte, a DEO dignos reddi tum iri omnibus his praeclaris & extraordinariis Spiritus S. donis accipiendis, non secus ac illorum dominos vel aliquem eorum, qui maxime sit sui juris conditionisque inter homines valde insignis & eximiae. Quapropter in tales hunc locum quadrare arbitror personas, quae sunt hujus conditionis, cujuscunque demum sint sexus, licet hujusmodi hic innui censeat Calvinus per servos & ancillas, qui antea prophetiae dono fuerant instructi; hisque verbis tam abundantem Spiritus Sancti effusionem denotari, ut & illi, in quos antea erat elapsus, multo majori mensura eum essent accepturi. Quemadmodum S. Petrus hunc locum citans loco ejus, quod hebraice habet, effundam spiritum meum, dixerat ex meo spiritu, ita & hoc loco agit. Nam quae Spiritus S. dona in eos essent conferenda, in textu hebraico, ut videmus, non est expressum. Ex eo autem, quod apud S. Petrum legimus, apparet, donum esse prophetandi; quippe addit, quod Textus hebraicus non agnoscit, καὶ προφητεύσουσι, licet neque hoc loco, neque apud LXX ulla hujus rei vola aut vestigium. At sufficiens argumentum est nobis ejus auctoritas, quod ita accipi debeat.
units.tr: But that these words are not to be taken in that sense, but are to be referred to the servile and common lot of men, has been noted, not inappropriately, by some who agree with us, namely that "my servants and my handmaids" here do not denote all kinds of men who truly believe in God and worship him, but especially those who bore the yoke of servitude among men. It is obvious that these are meant, and that even they, despite perhaps their abasement, would be made worthy by God of receiving all these remarkable and extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit, just as their masters, or any of them who are most their own masters and are very distinguished and eminent in rank among men. Therefore I think that this passage fits persons of this condition, of whatever sex they may be, although Calvin thinks that by "servants and handmaids" such people are hinted at who had previously been endowed with the gift of prophecy; and that by these words an abundant effusion of the Holy Spirit is signified, so that those upon whom he had previously fallen would receive him in a much greater measure. Just as St Peter, citing this passage, in place of what the Hebrew has, "I will pour out my spirit", said "from my Spirit", so he does here too. For which gifts of the Holy Spirit were to be conferred on them is not expressed in the Hebrew text, as we see. But from what we read in St Peter, it appears that the gift is of prophesying; for he adds what the Hebrew text does not acknowledge, [καὶ προφητεύσουσι], "and they shall prophesy", although neither in this place nor in the Septuagint is there any trace or sign of this matter. But his authority is a sufficient argument for us that it ought to be understood thus.

units.la: f) Druf. Veil.
units.tr: f) Drusius, Veil.

units.la: Accedit huic interpretandi rationi etiam Arabica MS. versio, quae habet ואירצאד עלי אלעביד ועלי אלאמאנה אצב נבותי atque etiam super servos & ancillas g) effundam prophetiam meam. Quod e diametro contrariatur Judaeorum axiomati pervulgato b) אין הנבואה שירה אלא ער חכם גבור ועשיר Propheta non reficiet super aliquo, nisi sit sapiens, fortis & dives, vel ut Grotius illud citat in Att. 2,18. Spiritus Sanctus non requiescit super animam pauperis. Iidem dicunt prophetiam non relidere t) מתיך עצביר ubi homines in maerore versantur. Quibus impulsus Abarbinel proprie haec accipit de servis & ancillis, uti verba sonant. Putat enim per Spiritum non posse hic intelligi donum prophetiae, sed tantum notitiam & cognitionem eorum mu̇eris ואמנכם העבריים והשפחורת שמפני עבדיהם יהיו הטיר בעצבן לא יוכלו להנבא אבר ישפוך השם ארץ רוחו עליהם רל רוח רעה יראת השם Iterum ait: at quod ad servos & ancillas, quia propter servilem eorum conditionem perpetuo versantur in maerore vel calamitate, non possunt apte esse ad prophetandum (vel obtinere prophetiae gradum) sed Deus effundet super eos suum Spiritum, nimirum, Spiritum cognitionis & timoris Domini.
units.tr: The Arabic manuscript version also agrees with this method of interpreting, which has [wa-irsad ʿala al-ʿabid wa-ʿala al-amanah asib nubuwwati], "and also upon the servants and the handmaids I will pour out my prophecy" (g). This directly contradicts the commonly known axiom of the Jews [אין הנבואה שורה אלא על חכם גבור ועשיר], Prophecy rests upon no one except the wise, the strong and the rich; or, as Grotius cites it on Acts 2,18: the Holy Spirit does not rest upon the soul of a poor man. The same people say that prophecy does not rest [מתיך עצביר] where men dwell in sorrow. Impelled by this, Abarbanel takes these words properly of menservants and maidservants, as the words sound. For he thinks that the Spirit cannot here be understood as the gift of prophecy, but only as the knowledge and recognition of their duty: [ואמנכם העבריים והשפחורת שמפני עבדיהם יהיו הטיר בעצבן לא יוכלו להנבא אבר ישפוך השם ארץ רוחו עליהם רל רוח רעה יראת השם]. Again he says: "but as for the servants and the handmaids, because on account of their servile condition they are perpetually in sorrow or calamity, they cannot be apt for prophesying (or obtain the degree of prophecy); but God will pour out his Spirit upon them, namely the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord."

units.la: Kimchi hic nullam quaestionem movet, nec quoad illos, qui vocantur servi & ancillae, cujusnam scilicet illorum foret conditio, nec quoad dona Spiritus, quae super eas dicuntur effundenda. At sic modo ille constringit verba, cum per hos dictos servos & ancillas, qui praedicto privilegio fruentur, non nisi eos putet innui, qui gentibus prognati in terra Israel adhuc essent victuri servientes Dominis Israelitis, quasi sic faciendo tantum horum Spiritus S. donorum participes reddendi essent, quorum servi alibi non forent capaces. Verum non latet talis limitatio in verbis, ultimus etiam ea allegata extendit S. Petrus; ad quosvis scilicet servos utriusque sexus, qui ad Deum in Christo essent conversi. Aben-Ezra inquit השיבו הטורות qui conversi sunt ad legem Dei, haud dubie, ad legem Mosis; at nos fr-miturι
units.tr: Kimchi raises no question here, either about those who are called servants and handmaids, what their condition precisely was, or about the gifts of the Spirit which are said to be poured out upon them. But he restricts the words in this way, since by the said servants and handmaids who enjoy the aforementioned privilege he thinks only those are meant who, born among the nations, were still to live in the land of Israel as servants to Israelite masters, as if only by doing so would they be made sharers in these gifts of the Holy Spirit, whereas servants elsewhere would not be capable of them. But such a limitation is not hidden in the words, and St Peter extends them, last of all, by the authority of the passage cited, to any servants of either sex who had been converted to God in Christ. Aben Ezra says [השיבו הטורות], "who turned to the law of God", undoubtedly to the law of Moses; but we, [...]

units.la: g) Omissum est in hu dictus. b) Morch. Neb. l. 2. c. 31. i) Morch. Neb. 2 c. 3. miori auctoritate S. Petri, dicimus ad legem Christi aut ad Evangelium, quod in eos dies erat promissum, qui per Christi adventum illustriores facti sunt diebus legis, utpote in quibus nulla amplius restat differentia inter sortem vel conditiones hominum, Col. 3. collat. cum Eph. 6. quibusque nullum est dubium, quin praestitum sit, quod Deus promiserat, quamvis omnium eorum tam particularia exempla non habeamus. Quod vero ad conditiones hominum, luculenter apparet, omnes indifferenter prophetiae pariter ac aliis Spiritus Sancti donis fuisse instructos. Quid per prophetiam plerumque denotetur, quispiam simul ac eam vocem audiat, intelligere potest; attamen rursus cognitum est atque pervulgatum, eam laxiori interdum sensu sumi, quam proprie significat.
units.tr: g) Omitted in the text cited. b) Morch. Neb. l. 2. c. 31. i) Morch. Neb. 2 c. 3. with the greater authority of St Peter, we say it is to the law of Christ or to the Gospel, which was promised for those days, the days which by the coming of Christ were made more illustrious than the days of the law, since in them no further difference remains between the lot or conditions of men (Col. 3, compared with Eph. 6), and for whom there is no doubt that what God had promised was granted, although we do not have particular examples of all of them. As to the conditions of men, it clearly appears that all alike were endowed with prophecy as with the other gifts of the Holy Spirit. Anyone who hears the word can understand what is usually meant by prophecy; yet it is again known and commonly accepted that it is sometimes taken in a looser sense than it properly signifies.

units.la: 30. Et ostendam miracula in cælis & in terra, sangui- nem & ignem & columnas fumi. 31. Sol convertetur in tenebras, & luna in sanguinem, antequam dies magnus & terribilis Domini ve- niat.
units.tr: 30. And I will show wonders in heaven and in earth, blood and fire and pillars of smoke. 31. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord come.

units.la: Expositis his extraordinariis Spiritus S. donis praecedentibus duobus versiculis, quae temporibus Christi benigne conferre volebat in fideles, fidosque suos servos cujuscunque aetatis, sexus, conditionis, & nationis, non tantum in eorum solatium, verum & in ecclesiae suae aedificationem, progreditur hic enumerando ea terribilia ac horrenda, quae etiam exhibere volebat, ut improbos terreret omnibusque sui timorem injiceret. Multa certe haec verba laborant difficultate, cum neque liquido appareat, quid iis rebus innuatur, neque quorsum pertineant & quo tempore sint dicenda completa.
units.tr: Having set out the two preceding verses, which describe the extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit that he was graciously willing to bestow on the faithful in the time of Christ, and on his faithful servants of every age, sex, condition and nation, not only for their comfort but also for the building up of his Church, the prophet now goes on to enumerate the terrible and dreadful things that he also meant to display, so that he might terrify the wicked and strike fear of himself into everyone. Certainly these words are very difficult, since it does not clearly appear what things are signified by them, or to what they pertain, or at what time they are to be fulfilled.

units.la: Miracula & signa prodigiosa, quae hic exhibiturus est, erunt בשמים ובארץ bashamaim ubaaretz, in cælis & in terra. S. Petrus ea citans explicandi forma ait, miracula in cælo supra, & signa in terra infra, τέρατα ἐν τῷ ἀέρᾳ ἄνω, καὶ σημεῖα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κάτω. Licet LXX simpliciter habeant, uti hebraice est: τέρατα ἐν ἀέρᾳ, καὶ
units.tr: The miracles and prodigious signs which he is about to display will be בשמים ובארץ (bashamaim ubaaretz), in heaven and in earth. St Peter, quoting this passage, explains it by saying: wonders in the heaven above, and signs on the earth beneath [τέρατα ἐν τῷ ἀέρᾳ ἄνω, καὶ σημεῖα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κάτω]. The Septuagint simply has, as the Hebrew does: wonders in the air, and

units.la: ΧΩΙ ΕΝΙ ΤΗΣ ΓΗΣ, miracula in cœlo & super terra; quod argumento est eum in citandis verbis ex veteri Testamento se non constrinxisse versioni LXXrali, sed expressisse tantum eorum sensum eo modo, quo optime sciebat planissime cum constare. Inter miracula, quæ dicit se esse exhibiturum, primo loco recensetur sanguis, quod ad ea pertinere videtur, quæ futura erant in terra. Quamvis enim post cœlos nominetur, relata tamen locantur ante ea, quo referuntur. Quæ collocandi ratio, notante Aben-Ezra, non infrequens est facis literis, nimirum, ubi duæ res memorantur, ut incipiant initio exponere, quæ ad secundam pertinent, postea vero tandem ad primam redeant. Sanguis Sanguinis prodigiosi & portentosi quaedam exempla ex Autoribus ethnicis citantur a doctissimo D. Livel. veluti sanguineæ pluviæ sanguineorum puteorum, ac scaturiginum, cruentique maris, quæ miseræ cladis triste præsagium habebantur. In Sacris literis legimus aquas & rivorum & scaturiginum in Ægypto in extraordinarium vindictæ divinæ signum conversas esse in sanguinem, ut in terrorem conjiceretur cor durum Pharaonis. Quod hic calamitatis ingentis futuræ sit præsagium, ex eo apparet quod sequitur: Antequam dies magnus & terribilis Domini veniat. k) Quidam interpretum hoc explicant de insolita effusione sanguinis in bellorum tumultibus hinc inde exortis; alii intelligunt 1) imbres & colores sanguineos; m) alii idem hic innui censent, quod postea his verbis innuitur: Luna in sanguinem convertetur. At certum est, hic constitui signum ab illo plane diversum, nimirum magis est vero, belli portendi sanguinea, quam sanguinem in eis effusum, etsi non sit expressum, qua ratione hic sanguis prodigii loco futurus sit. Atqui men ipse Salvator etiam bella sanguinea statuit signa instantium magnorum malorum, Matth. 24, 6. 7. Præ se ferunt certe hæc verba quandam extraordinariam sanguinis profusionem futuram in portentum ac ingentem populi consternationem; quo modo autem ea fit futura, non definiunt, & fortean alia etiam posset esse sanguinis profusio.
units.tr: and ΧΩΙ ΕΝΙ ΤΗΣ ΓΗΣ [and on the earth], that is, wonders in heaven and upon the earth. This is evidence that in quoting the Old Testament he did not bind himself to the Septuagint version, but only expressed its sense in the manner he knew would plainly agree with it. Among the miracles which he says he will display, blood is mentioned first, which seems to belong to those things that were to happen on the earth. For although it is named after the heavens, the things related are placed before those to which they refer. This arrangement, as Aben-Ezra observes, is not uncommon in the Scriptures: namely, where two things are mentioned, they begin by explaining what pertains to the second, and afterwards return at last to the first. Blood Certain prodigious and portentous examples of blood are cited from ethnic authors by the most learned D. Livel., such as rain of blood, wells and springs of blood, and a bloody sea, which were held to be sad forebodings of miserable disaster. In the Sacred Letters we read that the waters of the rivers and of the springs in Egypt were turned into blood as an extraordinary sign of divine vengeance, so as to strike terror into the hard heart of Pharaoh. That this is a presage of immense calamity to come appears from what follows: before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes. k) Some interpreters explain this of an unusual effusion of blood in the tumults of wars breaking out here and there; others understand 1) rains and blood-coloured clouds; m) others think that the same thing is meant here as is signified later by these words: the moon shall be turned into blood. But it is certain that a sign is here set down that is plainly different from that, namely that the blood-stained wars are foretold as a sign rather than the blood poured out in them, although it is not expressed in what way this blood will be a prodigy. Yet the Saviour himself also named bloody wars as signs of great evils about to come, Matt. 24:6, 7. These words certainly suggest a certain extraordinary outpouring of blood to come, as a portent and a great consternation of the people; but in what manner it will happen they do not define, and perhaps some other outpouring of blood could be meant.

units.la: k) Pet. a Lig. Ribera. Tar. Sa. Menoch. Grot. Act. 2. 1) Anon. Bibliotheca Jo. Menoch. Tirin. licet in alia etiam ita ac Ipiat, uti Ap. 8, 8. ubi mare sanguis fluens sanguis, quem majori copia putat fusum in sub Antichristo. profusio, quani in bellorum cladibus. Proximo loco sequitur ignis. Extant diversa exempla ignis,quo DEus mirando ac extraordinario modo usus est ad supplicia fumenda de peccatoribus atque terrorem incutiendum animis hominum,idque diversa plane ratione. Super Sodomam & Gomorrham prodigiosa ratione dimisit pluviam sulphuris & ignis a Domino e coelis, Gen. 19, 24. Inter plagas portentosas Ægyptiacas & hanc leginus, quod grando deciderit,cui erat ignis permistus, Exod. 9, 23. 24. Cum accensus esset ira Dominus propter populum quem ibundum, ignis Domini in eos exarsit eo loco, quem postea in ejus rei memoriam appellarunt thabheram, Num. 11, 3. & Num. 11, 35. egressus est ignis a Domino & abfumfit ducentos quinquaginta illos viros,qui offerebant suffitum. Ad preces Elia 2. Reg. 1, 10. ignis descendebat e coelo & consumebat praefectum & quinquaginta,qui veniebant comprehensum eum. In quibus omnibus historiis miraculi vicem subit,quia eorum nulla ordinaria ratio dari potest. Qua ratione & hoc loco esse debet, licet non sit definitum quo pacto id futurum sit,id quod variis conjecturis & opinionibus locum fecit. Abarbinel in iis hoc habet miraculis,quæ exhibituros erat in coelis,quo significari censet השמים עליהם בריר ואכני אלגבש אשר בתוכם האש DEum immuffurum esse super eos grandinem ingentesque grandines lapides, quibus immissus erit ignis, referens illud, ni fallor, vel ad id, quod acciderat in Ægypto, vel ad dictum Psalmistæ: grando & prunæ ignes Psal. 18, 12. 13. vel quod est Ezech. 38, 22. ubi DEus minatur se pluviam esse mifurum super Gog & Magog (quos hic cum caeteris Judæis putat respici) lapidum ingentis grandinis, ignis & fulguris. n) Alii hoc intelligunt de horrendis fulguribus vel infolitis igneis meteoris o) in coelis, sive p) aere (quæ & inter ethnicos putabantur magnam stragem portendere). Sunt & qui de q) ignibus linguis, quibus Spiritus S. descendebat super discipulos,hic prophetiam edi autumant Act. 2, 3. r) Alii autem exponunt de insolitis incendiis genti- n) Kimchi, Druf. Rib. &c. o) الذي تكسب الس ... quæ coelis tribuuntur ob altitudinem loci,quem occupant. R. Tanchum. p) Livel. q) Hieronym. Mercer. r) Grot. Kibera. gentibus incendiis, quibus delendæ forent civitates & urbes eo,quod tempore hic notato gerendum esset,bello. s) Alii generalem illam hic prodi arbitrantur conflagrationem,qua totus mundus igne periturus est ultimo die. Quænam harum opinionum maxime sit probabilis,rectius judicari poterit,quando scrutati fuerimus, cui tempori hæc inprimis sint vindicanda, quidve per proximum signum ut intelligendum,quod cæteris subjungitur nomine columnarum fumi. t) Quidam, juxta sensum præcedentibus verbis affictum,intelligunt sumum, qui ex illis rebus ascendet,quæ fulguribus sunt tactæ & accensæ,de quibus acceperant vocem ignis. u) Alii rationem suam explicandi sequentes, sunt de fumo,qui ascenderet ex civitatibus hostium opera accensis. w) Alii de fumo qui oriturus est ex concrematione totius mundi. x) Alii ad eum respici volunt,qui simul descendebat in igneis linguis, Act. 2. Columnæ fumi] Ita videntur appellari propter figuram, qua recta linea ascendunt columnæ instar. Vox lingua originali est תמרורת Timroth a תמר denotans palmam, unde transfertur ad proceram & rectam columnam, & hoc loco ad sumum, quatenus ascendendo se contorquet ea figura. y) Sensu non differt ab eo quod dicitur עמוד עשן Jud.2,40. utraque enim vox & columnam & palmam significat, atque convenit fumo ascendenti לשברור כרי sicuti illæ sunt figura. LXX magis attendentes materiæ quam formæ ejus, reddunt ἀτμίδα καπνὸς ut & Syrus ܥܡܘܕܐ ; & Vulgat. Lat. vaporem fumi. Arab. impress. quoque ; omnes de vapore fumi; At MS. Arab. ex Hebræo concinnatum ; quæ verba,si recto sunt scripta,necessario inferunt rectas & æquales fumi ascensiones. R. Tanchum vero verbis, quæ ultatiora
units.tr: k) Pet. a Lig., Ribera, Tar., Sa., Menoch., Grot., Act. 2. 1) Anon., Bibliotheca, Jo. Menoch., Tirin. Although they also take it in other ways, as in Rev. 8:8, where the sea turns to blood, they think a greater quantity of blood is poured out, a larger flood than in the disasters of wars, under Antichrist. Next follows fire. There are various examples of fire, which God used in wonderful and extraordinary ways to exact punishment from sinners and to strike terror into the minds of men, and in quite different ways. Over Sodom and Gomorrah God sent, in a prodigious manner, a rain of sulphur and fire from heaven (Gen. 19:24). Among the portentous plagues of Egypt we read also that hail fell mixed with fire (Exod. 9:23, 24). When the Lord was kindled to anger against the murmuring people, the fire of the Lord blazed among them in the place which they afterwards called Taberah, in memory of this event (Num. 11:3 and Num. 11:35): fire came out from the Lord and consumed those two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense. At the prayer of Elijah (2 Kings 1:10) fire came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty who had come to seize him. In all these histories a miracle takes the place of the ordinary course, since no ordinary explanation can be given for them. In the same way, a miracle must be meant in this passage, although it is not defined how this will happen, which has given room to various conjectures and opinions. Abarbanel holds that among those miracles which were to be shown in the heavens, this is meant, which he takes to signify [השמים עליהם בריר ואבני הברד אשר בתוכם האש], that God will rain down upon them hail and great hailstones, in which fire will be sent, referring this, if I am not mistaken, either to what happened in Egypt, or to the saying of the Psalmist, hail and coals of fire (Ps. 18:12, 13), or to what is in Ezek. 38:22, where God threatens that he will rain upon Gog and Magog (whom he thinks are meant here along with the other Jews) great hailstones, fire and sulphur. n) Others understand this of terrible lightnings or unusual fiery meteors o) in the heavens, or p) in the air (which even among the heathen were thought to portend great slaughter). There are also those who claim that the tongues of fire, in which the Holy Spirit came down upon the disciples, are here prophesied (Acts 2:3). r) Others, however, explain it of unusual fires among the nations, by which cities and towns were to be destroyed, because the war noted at this time was to be waged. s) Others think that this is a prophecy of that general conflagration by which the whole world is to perish by fire on the last day. Which of these opinions is most probable can be judged more correctly once we have examined to what time these things are chiefly to be assigned, and what is to be understood by the next sign, which is named with the words pillars of smoke that follow the others. t) Some, following the sense of the words just before, understand the smoke that will rise from those things which are struck and set on fire by the lightnings, from which they took the word fire. u) Others, following their own explanation, take it of smoke that would rise from cities of the enemy set on fire. w) Others take it of smoke that is to arise from the burning of the whole world. x) Others want it to refer to the one who also came down at the same time in tongues of fire, Acts 2. Pillars of smoke] They seem to be so called because of their shape, by which they rise straight up like columns. The word in the original language is תמרורת Timroth, from תמר, meaning palm tree, whence it is carried over to a tall and straight column, and here to smoke, insofar as, as it rises, it twists itself into that shape. y) In sense it does not differ from what is said as עמוד עשן (Judg. 20:40), for each word signifies both a column and a palm, and what agrees with rising smoke is that they are in the shape of [pillars]. The Seventy, paying more attention to the matter than to the form of it, render it ἀτμίδα καπνὸς, and so also the Syriac ‘ammuda; and the Vulgate Latin vapour of smoke. The printed Arabic also; all of the vapour of smoke; but the manuscript Arabic, drawn up from the Hebrew, [has words which, if they are written correctly, necessarily imply straight and even ascents of smoke]. R. Tanchum, however, in the words which...

units.la: z) Lyra. Sa. Men. Tirin. Pet. a Figuero,qui id etiam referri posse censet ad novum illud & infernale tormentorum inventum. t) Kimchi. Druf. u) Grot. w) Tirin. x) Merc. y) R. Tanch. Kimchi, propterea quod palma arbor est sublimis & rectus & æqualis,rem sublimem & rectam ei assimilant. z) ab eadem radice notat proceram veterem arborem, ut fersan debet esse a palma,qua ratione ad literam respondet hebraico תמרורת. tatiora sunt, inquit columna su- [Arabic text, illegible, ~12 letters] mi altum ascendentes [Arabic text, illegible, ~10 letters] qui refert columna formam propter spissitudinem suam [Arabic text, illegible, ~6 letters] & extensionem. Chaldaeus habet יטורין yiturin, columnas. Quidam intelligi volunt densas & obscuras nubes: Verum quicquid intelligatur hoc loco, necesse est, ut sit hujus generis, quod non est usitatum vel ordinarium, sed miri quid ac insoliti in se contineat veluti signa sequentia. v. g.
units.tr: z) Lyra. Sa. Men. Tirin. Pet. a Figuero, who thinks this may also be referred to that new and infernal invention of artillery. t) Kimchi. Druf. u) Grot. w) Tirin. x) Merc. y) R. Tanch. Kimchi says that because the palm is a tall, upright and straight tree, they liken a lofty and straight thing to it. z) From the same root it denotes an old tall tree, as it perhaps should be from the palm, and in this way it corresponds literally to the Hebrew תמרורת [tamrurot]. R. Tanchum, however, in the words that follow, says a column of smoke rising high [illegible Arabic] which represents the form of a column [illegible Arabic] because of its thickness [illegible Arabic] and extension. The Chaldee paraphrast has yiturin [יטורין], columns. Some want it understood as dense and dark clouds. But whatever is understood here, it must be of such a kind as is not usual or ordinary, but contains within itself something wonderful and unusual, like the following signs, for example.

units.la: v. 31. Sol convertetur in tenebras & luna in sanguinem. Haud absimilis exprimendi ratio fuit v. 10. Sol & luna obtenebrabuntur, ubi etiam expositum est, quid hoc significare velint. Quod ad hunc locum attinet, magnopere hic iterum discrepant interpretes, multis horum luminarium eclipsin intelligentibus, qua & lumen suum amissura sunt, & colorem commutatura. Eclipses enim eorum plerumque incutiunt hominibus metum, & solent praenuntiare esse calamitatum venientium etiam secundum naturam suam (ut ait Arias Montanus) i.e. quando ex cognitis & naturalibus oriuntur causis, nedum si praeter naturae ordinem hujusmodi accidant. Et si quid prodigiosi ac insoliti in illis accidere debeat, ut hic praedictum est, id in illorum eclipsibus esse haud temerarie dixeris, si de illis haec verba exponas. Et luna in sanguinem quibus Kimchi innui censet ejus sanguineum aspectum, si eclipsis sit non perfecta; quando autem persecta est, eam apparere nigram. Ejus verba sunt haec כשיהיה הקדרות [Hebrew text, illegible, ~20 letters] i.e. Quando eclipsis est perfecta, luna est nigra; quando autem non est eclipsis perfecta, est rubra instar sanguinis. Id quod fieri Aben-Ezra notat, cum fuerit procul a capite Draconis, & caudae ejus sex gradibus propinquior, quod semper putat portendere bella. Alii per solis conversionem in tenebras, ejus intelligunt obscurationem propter illum fumum undique surgentem, de quo dictum; & per luna conversionem in sanguinem,ejus sanguinolentum colorem, quo apparebit propter multum sanguinem infra fusum ex solo in aerem attractum.
units.tr: v. 31. The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood. The manner of expression is not very different from v. 10. The sun and moon shall be darkened, where it has also been explained what they wish this to mean. As for this place, the interpreters again disagree greatly, many understanding it of an eclipse of these luminaries, by which they will lose their light and change their colour. For their eclipses usually strike fear into men, and they are wont to foretell calamities coming, even according to their own nature (as Arias Montanus says), that is, when they arise from known and natural causes, much more if such things happen beyond the order of nature. And if anything prodigious and unusual ought to happen in their eclipses, as is foretold here, one could hardly rashly say that it does so, if you expound these words of them. And the moon into blood: Kimchi thinks this suggests its bloody appearance if the eclipse is not complete; but when it is complete, it appears black. His words are these: [כשיהיה הקדרות ...] that is, When the eclipse is complete, the moon is black; but when the eclipse is not complete, it is red like blood. Aben-Ezra notes that this happens when the moon is far from the head of the Dragon and nearer to its tail by six degrees, which he always thinks portends wars. Others understand by the turning of the sun into darkness its obscuring, on account of that smoke rising on every side, of which it was spoken; and by the turning of the moon into blood, its bloody colour, in which it will appear because of the much blood poured out on the ground and drawn up into the air.

units.la: Atque hi omnes literali sensu haec verba accipiunt, eaque omnia signa prodigiosa revera esse apparitura autumant, quae quoque sententia est quorundam interpretum inter Judaeos, ut observatum est Kimchi, qui etiam adjicit de Aben-Ezra, cum haec verba exponere כמשמע ad litteram, quasi tempore hic assignato futura sint haec prodigia; at alia mente esse Mosen Maimonid. qui haec & huic similia exponat על דרך משל sensu parabolico vel figurato de afflictionibus, quae populis evenient: Portenta ejus opinione significare ingentes afflictiones & bella allegorice & figurate, non ad literam intelligenda, uti & quod ante dictum est de locutarum denso agmine Joel 2:10. Sol & luna obtenebrabuntur &c. omniaque quae infra dicuntur cap. 3,15. ad eladem Gog & Magog referenda. At non unus est nec ejus sententiae primus auctor hic Rabbi; sunt & inter Christianos, qui eandem fovent sententiam iisque multo antiquiores eo. Ruffinus enim statuit non esse futuram tantam rerum perturbationem, vel insolita ac portentosa signa revera in coelo & in terra, sed tantummodo in animis populi attoniti, qui tanto terrore esset afficiendus, ut tota rerum facies ipsi videretur immutata, sol conversus in tenebras, luna in sanguinem, cunctaque igne & fumo correpta atque implera. Idem & e) recentiores nonnulli sentiunt, cum non ad literam, sed metaphorice haec verba fumant, phrasibusque, sol convertetur in tenebras, luna in sanguinem, ejusmodi innui calamitates velint, quae omnia eos solatio prorsus essent privatura.
units.tr: All of these take these words in a literal sense, and they maintain that all these signs will really appear as prodigies. This is also the opinion of some interpreters among the Jews, as Kimchi has observed, who also adds about Aben-Ezra that, when expounding these words, he says [כמשמע] literally, as if these prodigies were to occur at the time assigned here. But Moses Maimonides, who expounds these and similar words [על דרך משל], has a different mind, in a parabolic or figurative sense, concerning the afflictions that will come upon the peoples. In his opinion the portents signify great afflictions and wars allegorically and figuratively, and are not to be understood literally; and so too what was said before about the dense army of locusts, Joel 2:10, The sun and moon shall be darkened, &c., and everything that is said below, chapter 3:15, is to be referred to the ruin of Gog and Magog. But this Rabbi is not the only one, nor the first author of this opinion; there are also among the Christians those who foster the same view, and who are much older than he. For Rufinus held that there would not be such a great upheaval of things, or unusual and portentous signs really in heaven and on earth, but only in the minds of the astonished people, who would be so struck with terror that the whole face of things would seem changed to them: the sun turned into darkness, the moon into blood, and everything seized and consumed by fire and smoke. Some more recent writers also feel the same, when they say that these words are not to be taken literally but metaphorically, and that the phrases the sun shall be turned into darkness, the moon into blood wish to suggest calamities of that kind, all of which will utterly deprive them of comfort.

units.la: Obscervat h. l. R. Tanchum ישׁ per metaphoram vel figuram hic reges & regna conferri cum stellis, quod recentiores opinantur fieri cum sole & luna, atque his horrendis signis, quae illis dicuntur futura, eas denotari calamitates, quibus obruendi sunt. Pœnas quae affligentur hic summa auctoritatis fore procul dubio significatur, inquit Drusius. Nam eos solis & lunæ nomine designat Prophetæ.
units.tr: Here R. Tanchum observes that by metaphor or figure kings and kingdoms are compared with the stars, which more recent writers think is done with the sun and moon, and that by these dreadful signs which are said to be coming for them, calamities are denoted by which they are to be overwhelmed. That the punishments which will afflict them here will undoubtedly be of the highest authority is signified, says Drusius. For the prophet designates them by the names of sun and moon.

units.la: e) Calvin. Dan. Tarnov. Et in eandem mentem Tarnovius: f) Sunt qui allegorice in hoc versu per solem & lunam personas summæ auctoritatis notari existimant, in quos, cum aliorum in exemplum cultui divino incumbere strenue debuissent, propter defectionem suam acrius multo quam in cæteros animadvertetur talibus suppliciis, quæ omnem illorum gloriam & splendorem protinus obscurum reddent atque instar eclipsis obsuscabunt.
units.tr: Calvin. Daneau. Tarnovius. And to the same effect Tarnovius says: Some think that in this verse the persons of highest authority are allegorically denoted by the sun and moon, on whom, since they ought to have zealously devoted themselves to the worship of God as an example to others, punishment will be meted out much more severely than on the rest because of their defection, and such punishments will at once make all their glory and splendour dark, and will obscure them like an eclipse.

units.la: Abarbinel per solem & lunam g) hic intelligi vult ארום וישמעאל Edom & Ifmael (i. e. sua lingua Christianos & Mahumedanos) eorumque bella, quæ circa terram sanctam gerent, & solis nomine (quo præfiguratur Edom) in tenebras converti, atque lunæ (qua Ismael refertur) in sanguinem mutatæ inmui נקמתם vindictam, quæ de illis est fumenda. At non est ulla ratio, cur hoc loco sit deflectendum a literali sensu verborum, cum potius apertissimum sit, tum solem tum lunam accipiendos esse propria significatione, illorumque aspectus mutatione hic descripta revera describi hujusmodi portenta, quæ tempore a Deo constituto futura sunt, quod in sequentibus exprimitur his verbis: antequam magnus & terribilis (sive ut Act. 2,20. insignis) dies Domini venerit. Verum hic ingens enascitur difficultas, quæque non facile videtur expediri posse, quodnam scilicet his describatur tempus, & quando sint futura, quæ hic prædicuntur.
units.tr: Abarbanel wishes to understand here by the sun and moon [אדום וישמעאל] Edom and Ishmael (that is, in his language, Christians and Mahumedans) and their wars which they wage about the holy land; and that by the name of the sun (by which Edom is prefigured) they are turned into darkness, and the moon (to which Ishmael is referred) is changed into blood, which is intended to indicate [נקמתם] their vengeance, which is to be taken on them. But there is no reason why in this place one should turn aside from the literal sense of the words, since it is rather most clear that both the sun and the moon are to be taken in their proper meaning, and that the change in their appearance described here really describes such portents as are to come at the time appointed by God, which is expressed in what follows in these words: before the great and terrible (or, as in Acts 2:20, the notable) day of the Lord comes. But here a great difficulty arises, which does not seem easy to resolve: namely, what time is described here, and when the things foretold here are to happen.

units.la: Verissima est, quam h) Maimonides tradidit, regula ביום ... eum diem (vel quemvis diem) quo accidet aliquod ingens beneficium (vel prosperitas) aut aliquod magnum infortunium aliquid magnopere proficuum vel noxium, vocari terribilem diem Domini. Qua ratione & supra v. 11. illum diem, quo locustæ venturæ erant super eas, vocat diem DEI magnum & terribilem valde, quem nemo sustineret. Etsi igitur indubium sit certum, hic diem certumque tempus ejusmodi epithetis descriptum denota-
units.tr: The rule that Maimonides gave is most true: [ביום] the day (or any day) on which some great benefit (or prosperity) or some great misfortune happens, something greatly profitable or harmful, is called the terrible day of the Lord. By this reasoning, in verse 11 also, he calls the day on which the locusts were to come upon them the great and very terrible day of God, which no one could endure. Although therefore it is certain that the day and time described by epithets of this kind are denoted here,

units.la: {f} Vide fis Pelican. qui in eandem mentem interpretatur prius de Imperio Romano & sapientia Domini; posterius de Judæis sanguinem Christi in capita sua deriv n ibus. g) Cætera enim loca, uti v. 10. & c. 3,15. alia ratione intelligit, priorem de destructione Israelis, posteriorem de vindicta in alias gentes. h) Moreh. c. 29. i) Desunt hæc verba in hebraicis versionibus. ri; attamen cum plures reperiantur dies, ad quos possit commode satis referri, factum est ut in varias interpretes sententias iverint scrutantes, quisnam eorum cumprimis sit, qui in specie hic denotetur. Prædictus Maimonides hoc respicere existimat diem ingentis {ℓ} cladis, qua affectus est Sennacherib, prope Hierosolymam. Quæ eadem est opinio Ruffini, quem non longe ante citavimus, ex Christianis. Atque ne illis objiceretur talia, quæ hic describuntur, non esse facta eo die vel ante hunc diem, ad figuratum sermonem se recipiunt, quo intelligunt hæc de illis calamitatibus & ingenti consternatione, qua Judæi erant correpti propter ejus instantem invasionem, {s} donec DEus illucescere juberet illum magnum & terribilem diem, quo in caput ejus referebatur clades, qua Judæos volebat delere. Quodsi autem minus se probaret hæc expositio, inquit Maimonides יכין וצף חלאך גוג עלי ירושלם ביומי המלך המשיח erit destructio destructionis Gog prope Hierosolymam diebus Regis Messiæ, quam sententiam alii etiam Judæorum in exponenda hac prophetia sequuntur: כאנרי, ישיר בהרי אלנבורי ארי, inquit R. Tanchum, מלחמרי גוג ומגוג videtur hac prophetia indicare bellum Gog & Magog, quatenus magna est convenientia inter hoc & illud quod describitur Ezech. 38,22.&c. Ita & Kimchi ad illud refert tempus ruinæ Gog & Magog, & populi quem facient ascendere secum, quo tempore hujusmodi erunt luminarium eclipses, ut hic sunt descripta ejus reisigna & præsagia. Pari ratione procedit Abarbinel verba faciens de his prodigiosis ac mirandis signis אין כסק כי הוא מה שביאר יחזיאר במלחמרי גיג ומגוג שיהיר שם רכם הרג העצום בארץ &c. i.e. non est dubium quin idem hic describatur, quod Ezechiel describit, nimirum bellum Gog & Magog: præterquam enim quod sanguis ingentis cladis fuerit in terra & igne, & columnæ fumi, DEus pluet super eos ex cælis ignem & sulphur, & horrendam tempestatem &c. quapropter diem, qui hic vocatur magnus & terribilis dies Domini, exponit יום גאולרי עמו diem redemptionis (vel restaurationis) populi
units.tr: {f} See Pelican, who in the same vein interprets the first part of the Roman Empire and the wisdom of the Lord, and the latter of the Jews who would bring the blood of Christ upon their own heads. g) For he understands the other places, such as v. 10 and chapter 3:15, in another way: the former of the destruction of Israel, the latter of vengeance on the other nations. h) Moreh, c. 29. i) These words are lacking in the Hebrew versions. However, since several days can be found to which it may fitly be referred, it has come about that interpreters, searching, have gone into various opinions as to which of them is especially, and in particular, the one denoted here. The aforementioned Maimonides thinks this refers to the day of the great slaughter by which Sennacherib was struck near Jerusalem. This is also the opinion of Rufinus, whom we cited not long before, among the Christians. And lest it be objected to them that such things as are described here were not done on that day or before that day, they take refuge in figurative speech, by which they understand these things about those calamities and the great consternation with which the Jews were seized on account of his imminent invasion, {s} until God should command that great and terrible day to dawn, on which the disaster was to be turned upon his head, by which he wished to destroy the Jews. But if this explanation seemed less acceptable, says Maimonides, [יכין וצף חלאך גוג עלי ירושלם ביומי המלך המשיח] the destruction of the destruction of Gog near Jerusalem will be in the days of the Messianic King, an opinion which other Jews also follow in expounding this prophecy: [כאנרי ישיר בהרי אלנבורי ארי] says R. Tanchum, [מלחמרי גוג ומגוג] this prophecy seems to indicate the war of Gog and Magog, inasmuch as there is great agreement between this and what is described in Ezek. 38:22, &c. So also Kimchi refers to that the time of the ruin of Gog and Magog, and of the people whom they will bring up with them, at which time there will be such eclipses of the luminaries, as are described here, with their signs and omens. Abarbanel proceeds by the same reasoning, speaking of these prodigious and wonderful signs: [אין כסק כי הוא מה שביאר יחזיאר במלחמרי גיג ומגוג שיהיר שם רכם הרג העצום בארץ] etc., that is, there is no doubt that the same thing is described here which Ezekiel describes, namely the war of Gog and Magog: for besides the fact that there will be blood of a great slaughter in the land, and fire and columns of smoke, God will rain upon them from heaven fire and brimstone and a horrible tempest, etc. Therefore he explains the day which is here called the great and terrible day of the Lord as [יום גאולרי עמו] the day of the redemption (or restoration) of his people

units.la: {ℓ} 2. Reg. 19, 35. &c. {s} Ruff. populi sui, in cujus conspectu & prope quem hoc erit bellum. Dies autem Domini erit magnus propter populi sui redemtionem, & terribilis propter sumtam de hostibus ejus vindictam.
units.tr: 2 Reg. 19:35, etc. Ruff. of his people, in whose sight and near whom this war will take place. The day of the Lord will be great because of the redemption of his people, and terrible because of the vengeance taken on his enemies.

units.la: Ut autem rite hac de expositione verborum feramus sententiam, necesse est, ut paululum hinc digrediamur quam potest fieri, brevissime scrutatum, quosnam per Gog & Magog intelligant, & quo tempore existiment illud funestum bellum eorumq; exitium esse suturum, quod ipsum habent magnum & terribilem diem Domini. Atque in eo nemo nos, quod sciam, magis & melius erudire potest quam R. Tanchum in suis notis, quas fecit in Ezech. 38, 2. ubi frequentior est τῶ Gog & Magog mentio, quam ullibi alias in V. Testamento. Hic autem expresse habet הרא בלא שך קבאל אלתרך ואלתתר ובלארהם m) Hi sine ullo dubio sunt tribus Turcarum & Tartarorum eorumque regiones; atque eorum originem arcessit ex Gen. 10, 2. ubi recensentur inter filios Japhet Gomer & Magog &c. Hos, inquit, multi alii sequentur in bello, quod memoratur apud Ezech. quamvis praecipuus hic nominetur Gog omnium illorum rex. Hactenus de personis. Quod ad tempus attinet & quidnam eo tempore illis sit suturum, de eo iterum sic infit הרה אלקצ בלא שך מן אלמיאויר Hac descriptio dubio procul inter promissa est, quorum completio adhuc expectatur, eo scilicet modo, quo ibi est descripta tale quid nullo unquam tempore ante fuit, nec aliquid propius illi (accedit) praeterquam boc אנחא מכצור בבנתא תכן ככיב אנתמאע ישראל אלי בראהלם וקבר החצן אלבלאר ותעמירתא adventui est designatum posthac futurum, quam Israel in proprium suum regnum restitutus fit, & antequam muniverint atque incoluerint suas civitates, id quod ex v. 8. & 11. &c. liquere dicit. Idem etiam probabile putat hoc esse bellum cum eo, quod describitur Zachar. 14. quamvis in circumstantiis & expressionibus non nihil differat, cum idem
units.tr: But in order to pass a proper judgement on this explanation of the words, we must digress briefly from here and examine, as concisely as possible, who they understand by Gog and Magog, and at what time they think that deadly war and its destruction, which they hold to be the great and terrible day of the Lord, will take place. As far as I know, no one can instruct us in this more fully and better than R. Tanchum in his notes on Ezek. 38:2, where the mention of Gog and Magog is more frequent than anywhere else in the Old Testament. There he says expressly: These without any doubt are the tribes of the Turks and Tartars and their regions [hā'ulā' bilā shakk qabā'il al-Turk wa-al-Tatār wa-bilādahum]. He derives their origin from Gen. 10:2, where Gomer and Magog are listed among the sons of Japheth. These, he says, many others will follow in the war recorded in Ezekiel, although Gog is named as the chief king of them all. So much for the persons. As to the time, and what will then befall them, he again begins: This description is without doubt among the promises whose fulfilment is still awaited [hādhihi al-qiṣṣa bilā shakk min al-mawā'īd], namely in the way it is described there: such a thing never happened at any time before, nor anything nearer to it, except this, which is appointed to come hereafter, after Israel has been restored to its own land, and before they have fortified and inhabited their cities. He says this is clear from vv. 8 and 11, etc. The same man also thinks this war probably the same as the one described in Zech. 14, although it differs somewhat in circumstances and expressions, since

units.la: m) Confer cum his, quae ab Arabib. perhibentur de ججوج & ماجوج, de quibus consule Geogr. Arab. Clim. 5. part. 9. 10. & Maginum. idem tempus interim respiciat prophetia utraque,quod,inquit,futu-rum est ואנחנו הבן ילך בער אנתנאצ ישראל אלי כלארהם postquam Israel in proprium regnum suum restitutus erit, idque בער טהור ארצנו המלך המשיח post adventum nostri Domini Regis Messiæ, quem optat מהרה יגלה ut celerrime manifestetur. Atque hæc sunt ejus verba,quæ late hic recensere e re nostra duximus,quia codex ille non est impressus, ex quibus jam sat superque constat, quid per Gog & Magog existimet intelligi, ad quorum exitium magnum & terribilem diem Domini referunt, qui,cum juxta eum aliosque Judæos adhuc expectandus fit, eamque solam explicationem horum verborum selegit Maimonides, ad alteram cladem scilicet Sennacheribis referri non potest. At Christiani,qui firme credunt & consitentur Mes-siam diu venisse, huic assentiri non possunt, licet nec alteri opinioni assensum præbeant, quocirca alio modo ea exponere annisi sunt, quem multo putant probabiliorem, quam alterutram horum expositionem. Attamen in eo iterum non omnes eadem statuunt. Sunt qui hic ad destructionem Hierosolymæ & templi respici opinantur, quæ a Chaldæis sub Nebuchadnosore vastata sunt. Alii ad eorum seconda cum rursus essent ædificata,destructionem a Romanis, quam ar tecedebant horrenda ejus generis signa, ut hic memorata sunt,quemadmodum memoriæ prodidit Josephus libro septimo de Bello Judaico, quo tempore apparebat gladius igneus,& horrendus Cometa,quorsum n) nonnulli etiam referunt, quæ a Salvatore prædicuntur prodigia o) Matth. 24,29. &c. Ita & p) Grotius sentit, nimirum quatenus a Joele sunt prolata verba, spectare destructionem,quam judaicæ nationi intulere Chaldæi; quatenus a S. Petro, quæ postea illis illata est a Romanis,quorum temporum quodvis jure merito appellari potest magnus & terribilis dies Domini. Alii hunc diem tempo ris Christi circumscribunt,ad hoc alii,alii ad illud referentes. q) passionis & resurrectionis diem, quo tempore magna portenta dicuntur edita ab his dictis non abhorrentia,inter quæ etiam refertur Solem
units.tr: both prophecies look to the same time, which, he says, will come after Israel is restored to its own kingdom [ba'd an yurudda Isrā'īl ilā mamlakatihim], and after the coming of our Lord the King Messiah [ba'd bo'o adonenu melekh ha-mashiach], whom he prays may be revealed speedily [meherah yigalleh]. These are his words, which we have thought it useful to recount here at length, because that manuscript is unprinted. From them it is now sufficiently clear what he takes Gog and Magog to mean, and for whose destruction they refer the great and terrible day of the Lord. Since, according to him and other Jews, this is still to be expected, and Maimonides chose this sole explanation of these words, it cannot be referred to the other destruction, namely that of Sennacherib. But Christians, who firmly believe and confess that the Messiah has long since come, cannot assent to this, although they do not assent to the other opinion either. Therefore they have striven to explain the words in another way, which they think much more probable than either of these explanations. Yet even here they do not all hold the same view. Some think the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple by the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar is meant here. Others refer it to their second destruction, after they had been rebuilt, by the Romans, which was preceded by such horrible signs as are mentioned here, as Josephus recorded in book seven of The Jewish War, when a fiery sword appeared and a dreadful comet. To this some also refer the portents foretold by the Saviour, Matt. 24:29, etc. So also Grotius thinks: insofar as the words were uttered by Joel, they look to the destruction the Chaldeans brought upon the Jewish nation; insofar as they were uttered by St Peter, to the one later inflicted on them by the Romans. Either of those times may rightly be called the great and terrible day of the Lord. Others confine this day to the time of Christ, some referring it to this event, others to that: the day of Christ's passion and resurrection, at which time great portents are said to have been produced, not at odds with these statements, among which the sun is also said

units.la: n) Hammond. o) Marc. 13,24. & Luc. 21,11. p) In Act. 2. q) Vide Ch. a Castro & Mercer. de Hieronym.
units.tr: n) Hammond. o) Mark 13:24 and Luke 21:11. p) On Acts 2. q) See Ch. a Castro and Mercer on Hieronymus.

units.la: Solem r) obscuratum, cum hoc loco fertur in tenebras conversus, quod & s) lunæ accidisse quibusdam non inprobabile est, quantumvis in Evangelio nulla hujus rei mentio, Evangelistis quippe, S. Johanne testante, omnium rerum in specie accuratam curam non habentibus. Sub eo quoque t) concludunt Pentecostes diem, quo tam miranda ratione effusus est Spiritus Sanctus, ut S. Petrus dicat, id ipsum jam esse completum, quod a Propheta hic dictum est. At cum arduum nimis fit omnia hæc signa vindicare uni eidemque tempori jam jam elapso, ipseque dicat, fe hæc esse ostensurum ante hunc diem, non in eo, vel post eum, alii rectius putant hunc diem accipere de ultimo die judicii, fecundo Christi adventu & fine mundi, qui dies omnium suffragio meretur κατ' ἐξοχὴν vocari magnus & terribilis dies Domini, cujus ante adventum omnia portenta, tum quæ hoc loco sunt descripta, tum quæ etiam ab Evangelistis recensentur, certo sunt futura. Hinc certissima multis habetur expositio de eo die hoc exponere, licet hæc etiam u) reliquo tempore, quod intercurrit inter Christi adventum primum & fecundum, locum habere posse quibusdam ita persuasum fit, ut quicquid horum prodigiorum apparuit, vel ulla illustri hujus intervalli periodo apparebit, jure merito ad complementum hujus prophetiæ pertineat, adeo ut nequaquam neceffarium fit, ut omnia uno eodemque tempore fiant, vel ad illum ultimum omnium diem referventur. Caeperunt hæc in paffione Christi, (atque postea die pentecostes, ut S. Petrus in prædicto loco Act. 2. testatur) ereversit in excidio Hierufolymitano per Titum (quo a quibusdam hic locus refertur) sed perfecte complebuntur sub finem mundi ante extremum judicium & excidium universi, (quod tempus proprie hic respici non paucis persuasum est) ait doctus x) quidam interpres. Atque certum habeo, quicquid opponi possit, fi ad alia tempora referatur, quando de hoc similiter, infigniter ei epitheta hic data congruere. Etenim hoc summo jure meretur dies Domini vocari ac magnus dies propter magna quæ in eo sunt futura, & terribilis dies propter judicia, quæ exercebuntur in omnes, qui unquam
units.tr: to have been darkened, turned into darkness here. That the moon too was affected in this way, some think not improbable, although there is no mention of this in the Gospel; the Evangelists, as St John testifies, did not take exact care over every particular. Under this heading they also include the day of Pentecost, on which the Holy Spirit was poured out in so wonderful a way that St Peter says what the Prophet said here has already been fulfilled. But since it is too difficult to claim all these signs for one and the same time, now long past, and since he himself says that he will show these things before that day, not in it or after it, others more rightly take this day to be the last day of judgement, Christ's second coming and the end of the world. By general agreement this day deserves to be called κατ' ἐξοχήν the great and terrible day of the Lord, and before its coming all the portents, both those described here and those recorded by the Evangelists, will certainly occur. Hence to many this explanation of the day seems the most certain. Yet some are so persuaded that this also can take place in the remaining time that runs between Christ's first and second coming, that whatever of these portents has appeared, or will appear, in any notable period of this interval, rightly belongs to the fulfilment of this prophecy. Thus it is by no means necessary that all these things happen at one and the same time, or be referred to that last day alone. They began in Christ's passion (and afterwards on the day of Pentecost, as St Peter attests in the place cited, Acts 2), they were carried further in the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus (to which some refer this passage), but they will be perfectly fulfilled at the end of the world, before the last judgement and the destruction of the universe (a time which many are persuaded is properly meant here), says a learned interpreter. And I am certain that whatever objection may be raised, if it is referred to other times, these epithets given here fit remarkably well with this day. For the day of the Lord rightly deserves to be called great on account of the great things that will happen in it, and terrible on account of the judgements that will be executed upon all who have ever

units.la: r) Luc. 21. 45. s) Mercer. t) Consule Chrift. a Caltro. u) Gvaiter. & Juu. Tremel. x) Tirin.
units.tr: r) Luke 21:45. s) Mercer. t) See Chr. a Castro. u) Gvaiter and Juu. Tremel. x) Tirin.

units.la: quam in mundo vixerunt, quo cœli magno fragore interibunt, elementa ferventi ardore dissolventur, & terra, & quæ sunt in ea res, conflagrabunt, 2. Pet. 3, 10. ἐπιφανὴς, nisignis certe & illustris erit hic dies propter ejus magnitudinem, metum ac terrorem, quibus erit conjunctus; qua explicatione mea quidem ipsius opinione necessitas tollitur statuendi, quod quidam faciunt, aliter legisse olim hebræa apographa quam quæ hodie legimus. Cui opinioni occasionem fecit epithetorum ultimum dici Domini datum, quod apographa nostra legunt הנורא Hannora, quod denotat terribilis vel horrendus, eoque sensu ab omnibus interpretibus redditur ac derivatur a ירא timuit. Hinc opinantur, LXX & S. Petrum, qui cum illis concordat, olim in apographis suis, quibus usi sunt, secus legisse, nimirum י) הנראה bannirceh, apparens, a radice ראה raah vidit, percepit, eoque reddidisse ἐπιφανὴς, quam vocem nostrates Act. 2, 20. (ubi a S. Petro diximus ea esse citata) expresserunt per insignis. Interpres Latin. τῶν LXX illustris. Verum illorum hypothesis mihi videtur nec necessaria, nec probabilis: (1.) quia LXX diversis aliis locis, ubi eadem vox occurrit, atque hebraice non secus habet, atque hic נורא Nora, eodem modo eam exprimunt, sicuti hic per ἐπιφανὴς, itaut, si propter illorum versionem lectio hebraica est mutanda, necessario in omnibus illis locis mutanda sit, at probabile non est in probato quodam hebraico apographo tam sæpe esse aberratum totque differentias occurrere altero pro altero sumto. (2.) Quia vox נורא Nireah eam emphasin non videtur habere, quam materia subjecta, juxta ac græca vox ἐπιφανὴς exigit. Nimirum aliquid extraordinarium, insigne & illustre, nec non præ aliis eminens denotare debet; cum ea simpliciter dicat id quod visum est vel apparens, nec quod sciam ullili majori emphasi prædita in S. literis extet, id quod argumento esse arbitror, hic non adeo aptam esse ad circumstantias hujus dici exprimendas, præcipue cum antecedenti voci הגדול magnus subjungatur, ut ei ponderis quid addat atque illustret; sicuti fieri assolet, ubi epitheto
units.tr: lived in the world, when the heavens will pass away with a great noise, the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up, 2 Pet. 3:10. [ἐπιφανής] that is, notable, certainly this day will be remarkable and illustrious on account of its greatness and the fear and terror joined with it. By this explanation of mine, in my own opinion, the necessity disappears of positing, as some do, that the Hebrew copies once read differently from what we read today. The occasion for this opinion was the epithet given last to the day of the Lord. Our copies read it as הנורא [hannora'], which denotes terrible or dreadful, and in this sense all interpreters render it and derive it from יָרֵא, feared. Hence they think that the LXX, and St Peter who agrees with them, read differently in the copies they used, namely הנראה [hannir'eh], appearing, from the root ראה [ra'ah], saw, perceived, and so rendered it ἐπιφανής, which our people express in Acts 2:20 (where we said St Peter quotes it) as notable. The Latin translator of the LXX has illustris. But their hypothesis seems to me neither necessary nor probable. (1.) Because the LXX, in various other places where the same word occurs, and where the Hebrew has נורא [nora'] just as here, express it in the same way, as here by ἐπιφανής. So if the Hebrew reading must be changed on account of their version, it would have to be changed in all those places too. But it is not probable that in a certain approved Hebrew copy there was so often an error, producing so many variants by one being taken for another. (2.) Because the word נורא [nora'] does not seem to have the emphasis that the subject matter requires, as the Greek ἐπιφανής does. Namely, it ought to denote something extraordinary, notable and illustrious, and eminent above others; whereas the Hebrew word simply means what is seen or appearing. As far as I know, there is no word of greater emphasis in the Holy Scriptures. I take this as an argument that it is not very apt for expressing the circumstances of this day, especially since it is joined to the preceding word הגדול [hagadol], great, so that it should add weight to it and illustrate it, as is usually the case when an epithet

units.la: י) Capel. ut & Schindl. putant eosdem ea ratione legisse Deut. 1,19. verum cum nostri codicesibi quoque non habeant ἐπιφανὴς sed φαβρεάν parum auctoritatis habet.
units.tr: Capellus and Schindler think that they read Deut. 1:19 in this way. But since our manuscripts also do not have ἐπιφανὴς there, but φοβερὰν [terrible], it carries little authority.

units.la: epitheto epithetum subjungitur; cui ponderi addendo equidem vox Nareeh rem denotans, quæ est visa, non par esse videtur, quamvis silentio prætereundum non sit vocem græcam ἐπιφανὴς non tantum significationem ferre magni, sed etiam insignis propter aliquid, quod apparens hunc diem super alios dies magnos extollet. Unde colligi posset prædictos interpretes haudquaquam legisse aliter quam נורא Nora, nihilque aliud voluisse innuere, quam aliquid excessive magnum propter affectum, quem in spectatoribus ciebit, idemque indicare, quod faciunt, aliis locis eandem vocem reddentes per μέγας ingens, χαλεπὸς difficilis, θαυμαστὸς vel θαυμαστὸς mirabilis, vel ῥαταιὸς fortis, vel φοβερὸς terribilis, quibus locis eodem sensu vox nostratibus & aliis reddita est, atque hoc loco, scil. terribilis, horrendus, quo sensu nunquam, quod quidem patet, Græcos invenio ea reddidisse, quæ descendunt a radice ראה raah, vidit, præterquam מורא moreah, Zephan. 3, 1. ubi nostrates habent sordidus, vel (uti in margine) gulosus sive abdomini serviens, sicuti quibusdam in deteriorem partem tunc accipitur; Græci autem ἐπιφανὴς illustris, sive conspicua, fortean propter deperditum statum, ob quem civitas ibi corripitur. Cum igitur apertissimum sit, eandem vocem apud Græcos sæpe extare, ubi hebraice est נורא Nora, quæ hoc loco habetur, atque e contrario vocem נראה nireah nullibi ab illis ita esse versam, qua ratione audebimus textum mutare hebræum, propter illorum versionem, & non potius legemus, ut habet hodie Hebræus codex, nora, vocemque significatione, quæ infigniter huc quadrat, exprimemus per ἐπιφανὴς? Hæc certe conciliandi ratio multo tutior est, quam violentiam inferre textui diversa lectione, cujus antea nemo rationem habuisset. Ea enim, quam sequimur, confirmatur unanimi suffragio non tantum recentiorum, sed & antiquiorum interpretum, qui typographia nondum inventa vixerunt, locis diversis ac tempore diverso, ita ut nequaquam dici possit, omnes idem secutos esse apographum, qui eodem sensu eam reddidere vocem, quem hodie ex Hebræa lectione adhuc elicimus. Ita Chaldæus vertit דחילה Dechila, ut & Syrus: vetus Latinus terribilis. MS. Arab. almochawraph, omnes in eandem mentem terribilis sive horhorrendus; Hinc in eam adducimur sententiam, nec LXX alio modo eam exprimere voluisse sua interpretatione, quam ut significaret insignem & illustrem diem, ad injiciendum terrorem, quippe denotatur dies supra apparens, quæ apparet supra alios & conspicuus est, qui, uti ex præcedentibus apparet, necessario magnum debebat inferre terrorem, licet hoc non expresse addant, sed subintelligendum relinquant.
units.tr: epithet, an epithet is added to it. To add weight to this, the word nareeh, which denotes what is seen, does not seem a fitting choice, although it should not be passed over in silence that the Greek word ἐπιφανὴς [illustrious] bears not only the sense of great but also of conspicuous on account of something, since what appears will raise this day above other great days.
