From this it could be gathered that the aforementioned interpreters did not read anything other than nora [נורא], and wished to indicate nothing more than something excessively great because of the feeling it will stir in those who witness it. This is also what they indicate elsewhere, where they render the same word by μέγας [great], χαλεπὸς [difficult], θαυμαστὸς or θαυμαστὸς [wonderful], ῥαταιὸς [strong] or φοβερὸς [terrible]. In those places the word was rendered by our translators and others in the same sense as here, namely "terrible" or "horrible". In this sense I never find the Greeks rendering words derived from the root raah [ראה], "to see", except moreah [מורא] at Zeph. 3:1, where our translators have "filthy", or (as in the margin) "gluttonous" or "serving the belly", which some take in a worse sense; the Greeks, however, have ἐπιφανὴς [illustrious] or "conspicuous", perhaps because of the lost state on account of which the city is there rebuked. Since it is therefore most evident that the same Greek word often occurs where the Hebrew is nora [נורא], as it is here, and conversely that nireah [נראה] is nowhere rendered so by them, by what reasoning shall we dare to alter the Hebrew text on account of their version? Should we not rather read, as the Hebrew codex has today, nora, and express it by ἐπιφανὴς [illustrious] in a sense that fits this place remarkably well? This method of reconciliation is certainly much safer than doing violence to the text with a different reading, which no one had previously considered. For the reading we follow is confirmed by the unanimous agreement not only of recent but also of older interpreters, who lived before printing was invented, in different places and at different times, so that it cannot be said that they all followed the same copy. They rendered the word in the same sense that we still draw from the Hebrew reading today. Thus the Chaldee paraphrast renders it dechila [דחילה], as does the Syriac; the old Latin version has "terrible"; the Arabic manuscript has almochawraph, all in the same sense, "terrible" or "horrible". Hence we are led to the view that the Seventy in their translation intended to express nothing other than a notable and illustrious day, fitted to strike terror. For what is denoted is a day appearing above others, which is conspicuous among them, and which, as is clear from what precedes, must necessarily bring great terror, although they do not add this expressly but leave it to be understood.

units.la: Evicto vero ita vocem debere legi atque intelligi, quæstio enascitur, quomodo verba hujus & præcedentis versus, minas & terrorem præ se ferentia, cum præcedentibus congruant, qui sunt bonis promissis atque solatio plena? Cui solvendæ cum primis habenda est ratio personarum diversarum, ad quas ea referuntur, sive de quibus ibi sermo est. Erant inter eos, qui revera populi DEI nomen merebantur, quosque sibi DEus etiam vindicat hoc nomine meus populus, qui non forent confundendi, qui ad eum se converterebant, totoque animo ei adhærebant. Ad eos in primis spectabant promissa facta, qui etiam adhuc debent esse persuasi, fore, ut, quicquid periculorum sive rerum horrendarum immineat, ab omnibus redditantur immunes. At sunt præterea, qui se eo modo non gerunt, sed contra DEum se efferunt atque in rebellione, qua ab eo defecerunt, pertinaciter perseverant, & hi sunt super quos horrenda illa venient, quæ hic sunt prædicta, magno cum horrore atque sine ulla spe immunitatis sive evadendi, ita ut promissa bonorum, ac minæ malorum egregie hic fiant & conjungantur sine ulla rerum contradictione. Eadem ratione agit Salvator noster tantum prædicens mororem atque nationum confusionem, ut homines eorum metu & expectatione examinarentur &c. attamen eodem commate jubet eos suspicere, manusque attollere, quoniam illorum liberatio instaret, Luc. 21, 28. Quæ ratio, ut ex præcedentibus dilucide apparet, ita eam sequentia quam evidentissime confirmant, quibus ita progreditur:
units.tr: Once it is established that the word must be read and understood in this way, the question arises: how do the words of this verse and the preceding one, which carry threats and terror, agree with what comes before, which is full of good promises and consolation? To solve this, above all one must consider the different persons to whom these things refer, or of whom the discourse there speaks. Among them were those who truly deserved the name of the people of God, and whom God also claims by this name, "my people"; these must not be confused with those who turned to him and clung to him with their whole heart. The promises made looked above all to these, who must still be persuaded that whatever dangers or dreadful things threaten will leave them all unharmed. But there are also others who do not conduct themselves in this way, but rise up against God and persist stubbornly in the rebellion by which they have fallen away from him; and it is upon these that those dreadful things will come, which are foretold here, with great horror and without any hope of immunity or escape. Thus the promises of good things and the threats of evils are set side by side here, and joined together without any contradiction. Our Saviour acts in the same way, foretelling only sorrow and the confusion of nations, so that people would be tested by their fear and expectation, etc.; yet in the same verse he bids them to look up and lift their heads, since their deliverance was at hand (Luke 21:28). This reasoning, as is clear from what precedes, is also most evidently confirmed by what follows, where the passage proceeds thus:

units.la: 32. Et erit, quicunque invocaverit nomen Domini, li- berabitur: quia in monte Sion & in Jerusalem, erit liberatio, sicut Dominus dixit, & in residuis, quos Dominus vocabit.
units.tr: 32. And it shall come to pass that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be delivered: for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be deliverance, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call.

units.la: והיה Vehajah, imo, etsi tam magnus atque terribilis fuerit hic dies omnibus destructionem inferens, ut vix ac ne vix quidem ulli relictum via effugiendi esse mala; tamen hic a Domino declaratur, qua ratione ab iis immunes reddi possint, annexa asseveratione liberatum certo iri, quotquot huic viae inlliterint, mediunque commendatum in usum suum adhibuerint, nimirum, qui nomen DEI invocaverint, quicunque (inquit) cujuscunque demum sit nationis, sexus, vel conditionis: ejusdem enim videntur haec verba extensionis esse, atque ea, quae expositimus v. 28. ita ut horum promissorum nil solis Judaeis vindicari posset, quibus (non autem de quibus) tunc temporis in specie loquebatur, sed quicunque, sive Judaeus, sive gentilis, cujuscunque etiam conditionis, fidem DEO rite habuerit, & in fide ejus nomen in auxilium invocaverit, eo ipso tempore cum aliis nec spes nec locus auxilii fuerit, illud certo inveniet. Hinc Paulus eadem verba citans Rom. 10, 13. cum Graecorum sive gentilium, tum Judaeorum statui applicat. Invocare nomen Domini equidem in specie notat ardentissimas fundere preces, ut auxilio velit esse DEus; attamen necessario etiam in eo concluditur sincera obedientia & vera ejus cognitio, & quod omnium primum est, firma in eum fides cum hujusmodi aliis attributis fidelissimi servi DEI. Quam vanum enim fuerit catenus oquin vocare, Domine, Domine, ex eo apparet, quod scriptum extat Matth. 7, 21. Eadem precandi via cum aliis, quae preces gratas reddere possunt, conjuncta, a Salvatore nostro nobis ostenditur, ubi de eodem magno die, uti maxime probabile est, de quo Propheta loquitur, verba facit, eamque tanquam unicum medium horrenda ejus effugiendi commendat Luc. 21, 36. Vigilate igitur, omni tempore orantes, ut digni censeamini haec omnia eventura effugiendi & consistendi coram filio hominis. Chaldaeus Paraphrastes reddit haec כ-- רצי בשמא הוי בשם יהוה omnis qui invocaverit in z) nomine Domini, ut interpres Lat. habet, vel a) per nomen Domini; qua versione, quamvis nihil aliud innuat, quam quod alii etiam eo exprimunt, b) nomen Dei invocabit; attamen ut ad literam verba exprimit, ita docet quid in primis opus fit in invocatione nominis Domini, ut ea apud DEum fit accepta & grata, nimirum, ut invocatio hæc fiat in nomine Domini Jesu, in quo vera etiam in eum fide accedente adeo efficax semper erit, ut liberandi sint, quicunque ita preces suas fundere sategerint. Hoc, inquam, suggerit nobis versio Chaldaica; sed fi verum fateri volumus, ipse hebraicus Textus est, qui ad literam a c) quibusdam hocce modo vertitur: omnis qui invocaverit in nomine Domini. Mercerus existimat præpositionem ב in, quando cum voce שם sbem nomen, conjungitur, majorem inferre emphasin, quam fi simpliciter dictum effet invocaverit Dominum, Dominum scilicet in vel per illud verbum invocare, quo ipse fe nobis cognitum dedit, quod nomen ejus vocatur, cui rei illustrandæ lumen affundit ex verbis quæ citat ex S. Johanne: DEum nemo vidit unquam; unigenitus filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse exposuit, Joh. 1, 18. Ita ut invocare in nomine, seu nomen Domini fit, Deum invocare fiducia promissionis, quam Christus de cœlo ad nos attulit; unde & λόγος dicitur & imago DEI, quod in Christo DEus patefecit, quo in nos fit animo: Qua explicatione nihil nos aliud docet, quam quod a Chaldæo Paraphrafta (ut vidimus) suggestum est, eas scilicet, quæ hic requiruntur preces, efficaces tum fore ad eos liberandos ab illo magno & terribili die Domini, quando fiant in nomine Domini, i. e. Christi atque vera in eum fide sint conjunctæ. Non est quod hic erroris arguam noftratium aliorumque interpretationem, qui simpliciter habent, invocaverit nomen Domini; cum id tantum adjecerim, ut appareat, quid textus originalis & Chaldæus suggerant ad genuinam formam & constitutionem eorum, quibus invocantibus promissio hic facta est, ut illum obtineant finem quem hic dicuntur obtenturi, qui, qua in re constat, in sequentibus pluribus declarabitur. Quam habeant in genere vim preces rite constitutæ & omnia bona obti-
units.tr: And it shall be [והיה Vehajah]. Indeed, though this day shall be so great and terrible, bringing destruction on all, that hardly, or scarcely at all, will any way of escape remain for anyone, yet here the Lord declares by what means they may be made immune to these evils, with the assurance added that all who enter upon this way and apply the appointed remedy will certainly be delivered. These are, namely, those who call upon the name of God: whoever (he says), of whatever nation, sex or condition they may be. For these words seem to have the same extent as those we explained at verse 28, so that none of these promises could be claimed by the Jews alone, to whom (not concerning whom) he was then speaking in particular. Rather, whoever, whether Jew or Gentile, of whatever condition, has rightly held faith in God and in that faith has called upon his name for help, will certainly find it at that very time when others have neither hope nor place of help. Hence Paul, quoting these same words at Rom. 10, 13., applies them to both the Greeks or Gentiles and the Jews. To call upon the name of the Lord indeed signifies in particular to pour out most fervent prayers, that God would be pleased to help; yet it is necessarily also implied in this sincere obedience and true knowledge of him, and, first of all, firm faith in him, together with the other attributes of the most faithful servants of God. For how vain it would be merely to say, "Lord, Lord," appears from what is written at Matth. 7, 21. Our Saviour shows us this way of praying, joined with the others that can make prayers acceptable, where he speaks of the same great day, as is most probable, of which the Prophet speaks, and commends it as the only means of escaping its dreadful evils: Luc. 21, 36. Watch therefore, praying at all times, that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man. The Chaldee paraphrast renders these words כ-- רצי בשמא הוי בשם יהוה whoever calls in the name of the Lord, as the Latin translator has it, or by the name of the Lord, which (although it means nothing other than what others also express by it) shall call upon the name of God, but as it renders the words literally, so it teaches what is chiefly needed in calling upon the name of the Lord, so that this invocation may be accepted and pleasing to God: namely, that the invocation be made in the name of the Lord Jesus, in whom, with true faith in him joined to it, it will always be so effective that all who have striven to pour out their prayers in this way shall be delivered. This, I say, the Chaldean version suggests to us. But if we wish to speak the truth, it is the Hebrew text itself, which some render literally thus: whoever shall call in the name of the Lord. Mercerus thinks that the preposition ב in, when it is joined with the word שם shem, name, brings greater emphasis than if it had been simply said shall call upon the Lord, namely the Lord in or through that word by which he has made himself known to us, which is called his name. He throws light on this matter from the words he cites from St. John: No one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him, Joh. 1, 18. So that to call upon in the name, or the name of the Lord, means to call upon God in the confidence of the promise which Christ brought to us from heaven; whence he is also called the Word and the image of God, because in Christ God revealed himself to us in his own mind. This explanation teaches us nothing other than what the Chaldee paraphrast (as we have seen) has suggested: namely, that the prayers required here will be effective for delivering those who pray from that great and terrible day of the Lord, when they are offered in the name of the Lord, that is, joined with Christ and with true faith in him. There is no need here for me to accuse our own interpreters and others of error, who simply have whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord; I have only added this so that it may appear what the original text and the Chaldee suggest for the genuine form and character of those who, calling upon him, are given this promise, so that they may obtain the end which here they are said to obtain. What this consists in will be explained more fully in what follows. What power rightly constituted prayers have in general to obtain all good things and to avert all evils

units.la: ε) Bib. Polygl. a) Ita ex interpret. lat. Merceri. b) Merc. Pet. a Fig. c) Jun. Trem. obtinendi, & quæcunque sunt mala avertendi, non una vice in S. literis explicatur. Quicunque a Patre meo per meum nomen postulaverit, dabit vobis, inquit Salvator nostler Joh. 16, 23. Quod hic impetraturi sunt, in eo consistit, quod sint liberandi a terrore magni Domini diei. Quicunque invocaverit nomen Domini, liberabitur יִמָּלֵט immalet. Quo in verbo magnam d) quidam arbitratur latitare emphasin multo quidem majorem, quam si verbo quodam usus esset, quod simplicem haberet significationem servandi, quippe quo innuebat, quanquam omnium rerum conditio tam afflicta & desperata foret, ut nemini ulla reliqua esset spes ingentia evadendi mala omnibus indiscriminatim interitum ultimum minantia, ita ut ad incitas nihil non videretur redactum, fideles tamen servos DEI, qui semet ei offerendo & potentiæ ac gratiæ ejus maxime nitendo eum invocaverint, certo liberatum iri ab horrendis rebus eo magno & terribili die futuris, atque eum illis fore diem e) introeundi in lætitiam Domini sui, ac eum assequendi statum, quo immunes porro redderentur ab omni metu & malo. Quod ut persuasum habeant certo esse futurum, vel ratio constaret cur ita sit futurum, subnectit verba quæ sequuntur: Quia in monte Sion & in Jerusalem erit liberatio, sicut Dominus dixit. Dies hic descriptus dicitur magnus & terribilis, unde omnium rerum interitus videatur dependere; attamen Domini dies est, ab eo sunt ordinata, quæ tunc fient & peragentur, adeo ut non æque in omnes indiscriminatim mala sint sævitura, sed asylum eo die habituri fideles servi DEI, & qui ei firme & mordicus adhæserint, & f) invocarint eum in monte Sion & Jerusalem (vera ecclesia DEI) illis, inquam, atque omnibus ejus verbis membris erit ab iis omnibus liberatio. Hæc illis erit instar Arcæ Noah, quo uti ille sese conferebat, cum DEus g) diluvium toti mundo impiorum inveheret, ita & illis in ea erit liberatio, cum interea sint perituri, qui extra eam erunt.
units.tr: Bib. Polygl. a) So from the Latin translation of Mercerus. b) Merc. Pet. a Fig. c) Jun. Trem. is explained in Scripture not on one occasion: Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you, says our Saviour, Joh. 16, 23. What they are going to obtain here consists in this, that they shall be delivered from the terror of the great day of the Lord. Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be delivered [יִמָּלֵט immalet]. In this word some think there lies a great emphasis, much greater than if he had used a word that had the simple meaning to save, since he thereby signified that, although the condition of all things is so afflicted and desperate that no one has any remaining hope of escaping the great evils threatening all without distinction with final destruction, so that everything seems reduced to extremity, yet the faithful servants of God, who by offering themselves to him and relying most on his power and grace have called upon him, will certainly be delivered from the dreadful things that will happen on that great and terrible day, and that for them that day will be the entrance into the joy of their Lord, and the attainment of a state in which they will be made immune from all fear and evil from then on. That they may be persuaded this will certainly happen, he adds the words that follow, which give a reason why it will be so: For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be deliverance, as the Lord has said. This day is described as great and terrible, on which the destruction of all things seems to depend; yet it is the Lord's day, and the things done and accomplished on it are ordained by him, so that it will not rage equally and without distinction against all evils, but the faithful servants of God, and those who have clung firmly and tenaciously to him and have called upon him in Mount Zion and Jerusalem (the true Church of God), will have a refuge on that day. For them, I say, and for all the members of that Church, there will be deliverance from all these things. This will be to them as the Ark of Noah was to him, to which he withdrew when God brought the flood upon the whole world of the wicked. So also in the Church there will be deliverance for them, while those who are outside it will perish.

units.la: Quod si mons Sion & Jerusalem hic accipiatur ad literam de illis locis, qui hisce nominibus proprie significantur, ubi illo tempore erat templum DEI sive domus precationum, quo h) ascendebant tribus,
units.tr: But if Mount Zion and Jerusalem are here taken literally, of those places properly signified by these names, where at that time was the temple of God, or house of prayer, to which the tribes went up,

units.la: d) Calvin. e) Marc. 13,13. f) Psal. 145,18. g) 1. Pet. 3,5. h) Psal. 122,4. tribus, tribus Domini ad testimonium Domni ut celebrarent nomen Domini & invocarent eum; illorum hoc expositioni faveret, qui magnum diem Domini de calamitatis die exponunt, qua essent obruendi, Sione & Hierosolyma & templo præcipuo & unico loco veri divini cultus destructo, vel ut erat factum antea tempore Sennacherib, vel postea illis iterum ædificatis, ut ex antedictis diversis diversorum vidimus opinionibus, atque ita ad eos hoc spectaret, qui tunc temporis sunt liberati ac servati. At rectius videtur aliis hæc nomina accipi proprie, sed figurate pro ecclesia DEI. Cum enim ibi esset primo i) sata, atque inde in totum mundum transplantata, idem nomen etiam una cum ea gerebat. Ita ut, quam late etiam esset sparsa doctrinaque evangelii prædicata, mons Zion & Hierosolyma, dicitur etiam in extremis terræ partibus. Atqui hac notione probata ingeniter congruet ei expositioni, quam nos omnium pronunciationem planissimam tutissimamque, qua scilicet per diem magnum & terribilem Domini intelligi putant ultimum DEI judicium, atque his verbis liberationem promittit eo ipso die omnibus veris ecclesiæ membris & asseclis, quos Dominus vocabit & qui invocabunt nomen Domini, i. e (ut Mercerus ait) Christi, idque vere ac demisso animo, quippe non quilibet; qui dicit Domine, Domine, in regnum cœlorum intrabit, Matth. 7,21. Id quod omnino fore, ne quid dubii animis illorum inhæreret, verbum ac promissum Domini subjunctum habent, ita enim ait: sicut Dominus dixit; quod mea ipsius sententia nihil aliud respicit, quam k) quod vel ab eo ipso hoc loco, vel ab aliis Prophetis alibi dictum erat; cum minus probare possim ad quendam peculiarem hic spectari locum, ut quidam volunt, ut ex illis R. Salomon ad Deut. 28,30. l) alii ad Deut. 32,43. Kimchi ad Ezech. 4,3. qui eum ad tempus Senn.acherib refert, quo ut dictum ante hunc diem Domini fuisse completum quidam asserunt. Ex his diversis locis a multis aliis allatis, quibus dicitur DEus dixisse, quod Propheta hic dicit, dilucide apparet, sufficientem esse rationem hoc ita intelligi, quod per Prophetas DEus id dixerit, præterquam quod in specie ad
units.tr: Calvin. Marc. 13,13. 1. Pet. 3,5. Psal. 145,18. Psal. 122,4. the tribes, the tribes of the Lord, to bear witness to the Lord, to praise the name of the Lord and call upon him; this would favour the view of those who explain the great day of the Lord as a day of calamity, on which they would be overwhelmed, Zion and Jerusalem and the principal temple, the one place of true divine worship, being destroyed, either as had happened earlier in the time of Sennacherib, or afterwards when they had been rebuilt again, as we have seen from the various opinions of various men mentioned above. So it would refer to those who were then delivered and saved. But it seems more correct to others that these names are taken properly but figuratively for the Church of God. For since it was first sown there and then transplanted into the whole world, it bore the same name along with it. So that, however widely it had been scattered and the gospel doctrine preached, Mount Zion and Jerusalem are said to be in the furthest parts of the earth. Indeed, once this sense is proved, it agrees ingeniously with that explanation which we consider the plainest and safest of all, namely that by the great and terrible day of the Lord they understand the final judgment of God, and in these words he promises deliverance on that very day to all the true members and adherents of the Church, whom the Lord shall call and who shall call upon the name of the Lord, that is (as Mercerus says) of Christ, and that truly and with a humble spirit, since not everyone who says, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, Matth. 7,21. That this will certainly come to pass, and that no doubt may cling to their minds, they have the word and promise of the Lord added, for he says: as the Lord has said. In my own view this refers to nothing other than what was said either by him in this very place or by other Prophets elsewhere. I can less readily grant that a particular place is here in view, as some wish, such as R. Solomon on Deut. 28,30. among them, others on Deut. 32,43. Kimchi on Ezek. 4,3., who refers it to the time of Sennacherib, at which, some assert, what was said before about this day of the Lord was fulfilled. From these various passages, cited by many others, in which it is said that God spoke what the Prophet says here, it is clear that there is a sufficient reason for understanding it thus: that God said it through the Prophets, apart from the fact that in particular it may be referred to this or that passage where it seems to be stated.

units.la: i) Oportebat prædicari pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes incipiendo ab Hierosolyma, Luc. 24,47. k) Merc. l) Fil. Tarnov. ad hunc vel illum locum referatur, ubi id dictum extare videtur. Et sic efficiamus quod Propheta ipse m) dixerat a v. 22. ad hunc locum usque, satis superque liquet, DEum etiam per ipsum promissse filiis Israel liberaturum esse. Caeterum & hoc modo cum quibusdam haec verba explicari possent, ut, sicut Dominus dixit, idem valeat quod, sicut DEus decrevit & proposuit. Eo nempe redit summa verborum, ut certiores reddat hujus liberationis tam sancte promissae illos, qui se ad eam obtinendam reddiderint dignos. Mentio illorum erat inclusa hisce verbis praecedentibus: quicunque nomen Domini invocaverit, quos in sequentibus porro ita describit: & in reliquis quos Dominus vocabit. Verba hebraice habent ובשרידים אשר יהוה קרא, Ubsaridim asher Jehovah kore, quae ad literam transtulit nostra Anglicana & cum plerisque aliis consentit. Verum alio modo ea posse reddi Abarbinel auctor est, videlicet, & in reliquiis, qui invocabunt nomen Dei; at praeterquam quod praecedentium tum nonnihil repetitio esset, verbis ita translatis, verbum potius deberet esse plurali numero, ut nomen Iheridim, quod tunc nominativum referret, cum jam singularis numeri ad Dominum magis proprie referri videatur. Verum quocunque modo id caeteroquin solvi possit, non est praeter illum, qui hanc interpretandi viam sequitur. Omnes enim in universum vocem Jehovah, uti & nostrates nominativi loco habent, atque a verbo putant regi, eosque notari, quos Dominus vocaturus esset. Atque ea ratione porro declarare vult Propheta, ut diximus, quinam liberandi sint, prout commate primo habet, atque intente Sion & Jerusalem, veluti in secundo, ubi eadem quidem personarum est descriptio, at diversa exprimendi ratione, relpectu diversarum qualitatum, quibus alii invocabunt nomen Domini, alii vocabuntur a Domino, vel quos Dominus vocabit. Hinc a o) quibusdam observatum est, conjunctionem 1, 1, & hic non habere, quod & aliud venit, vim copulandi atque conjungendi sequentia cum praecedentibus, sed expositendi atque declarandi, quorum antea mentio erat habita, idemque hoc loco valere ac nempe. Scilicet in reliquiis, quos vocat Dominus. Non quod alii sint reliquiae ab illis, quae in Sion & m) Rom. n) Merc. Pet. a Fg. o) Tor. Grot. Jerusalem invocaverint nomen Domini & auxilium invenerint, quos Dominus vocabit, iique Judæi æque ac gentes, quanquam in specie id p) quidam accipere volunt de gentibus, quæ evangelio fidem habituræ essent, quod primo Judæis prædicatum erat; q) alii rursus de Judæis in Christo adunitis & cum gentibus in unum gregem & unum ovile coeuntibus. At optime reconciliari possunt, si de veris utriusque generis accipiatur fidelibus, quo sensu & illi accipiunt, licet ad hos propriè magis quam ad illos respicere existiment. Certum equidem est numerum eorum, si conjungantur, valde augeri, possunt tamen nihilominus non nisi r) residui vocari respectu ingentis eorum multitudinis, ad quos hæc verba non spectant, quique a Domino non sunt vocati.
units.tr: i) Repentance and remission of sins were to be preached among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem, Luke 24:47. k) Merc. l) Let Fil. Tarnov. refer this to whichever passage it seems to be found in. And so we may conclude that what the Prophet himself m) had said from verse 22 down to this place makes it abundantly plain that God would also, through him, deliver the children of Israel. Moreover, in this way some have been able to explain these words, that "as the Lord has said" may mean the same as "as God has decreed and purposed." The sum of the words is evidently this: to make certain of this liberation, so solemnly promised, those who have made themselves worthy of obtaining it. The mention of these was contained in the preceding words, "whoever calls on the name of the Lord," whom he goes on to describe in what follows as "and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call." The Hebrew reads [ובשרידים אשר יהוה קרא], Ubsaridim asher Jehovah kore, which our English version renders literally, and in agreement with most others. But Abarbanel assures us that it can be rendered otherwise, namely, "and among the remnant who call upon the name of God." Yet apart from the fact that this would be a somewhat tedious repetition of what precedes, the verb ought then to be in the plural, as the word Iheridim would be the nominative, whereas the singular seems to refer more properly to the Lord. However that may be otherwise resolved, there is no way out except for one who follows this line of interpretation. For all of them, in general, take the word Jehovah as the nominative, as our people also do, and think it governs the verb, and that it marks those whom the Lord was going to call. And by this reasoning the Prophet wishes to declare further, as we have said, who are to be delivered, as he has in the first verse, and especially Zion and Jerusalem; and, as in the second, where the same description of persons is given but with a different way of expressing it, with respect to the different qualities by which some "call upon the name of the Lord," and others "are called by the Lord," or "whom the Lord shall call." Hence some have observed that the conjunction and is not here merely copulative, joining what follows to what precedes, but explicative and declarative, of those whom he had mentioned before; and that here it has the force of namely: "among the remnant whom the Lord calls." Not that there are other remnants apart from those who in Zion and Jerusalem have called upon the name of the Lord and found help; m) Rom. n) Merc. Pet. a Fg. o) Tor. Grot. The "whom the Lord shall call" are Jews as well as Gentiles, although some specifically want this to be understood of the Gentiles who were going to believe the gospel, which was first preached to the Jews; q) others again of the Jews united in Christ and coming together with the Gentiles into one flock and one fold. But these can be very well reconciled if it is taken of the true believers of both kinds, in which sense they too take it, although they think it refers more properly to the one than to the other. It is certain that their number, when combined, is greatly increased; nevertheless they can only be called a remnant r) in comparison with the vast multitude of those to whom these words do not apply, and who have not been called by the Lord.

units.la: Vox, quæ hic redditur residui, hebraice est שְׁאִירִים Sheridim, quæ eos denotat, qui supersunt, cæteris direptis; vel qui periculà & destructionem, quæ aliis imminent, evadunt. Quod nomen unà cum radice sive verbo, unde originem trahit, occurrit Josu. 10. v. 20. והשאירים שרוד מהם vehasseridim saradu mehem, quod reddunt nostrates, reliqui qui supererant ex eis: Interlinearis, & superstites superfuerunt ex eis: LXX καὶ διασωζόμενοι διεσώθησαν, & superstites evaserunt. Idem alibi conjungitur cum verbo cognatæ significationis שריד ופלט sarid upalit, Jerem. 42, 17. ubi nostrat. habent, (qui) supererit sive evadet; Græci autem idem utroque denotant ratione, uno utrumque expresserunt σωζόμενοι salvandus. Unde liquido constat LXX non minus, quam aliis cognitam fuisse ac familiarem notionem vocis seridim, qua eos notat, qui supersunt vel qui salvantur ab hujusmodi malis, quibus alii corripiuntur; quare merito disquisitionem venit, cur hoc loco, cui hæc notio videtur aptissima, alia eam exprimant voce, quæ alienæ plane est significationis, ut siωζόμενοι εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, quæ tam parum affinitatem habet, altera cognita significatione videtur habere, ut in opinionem suam uerit non paucos legisse ipsos olim aliter in hebræo, quam hodie, side. videlicet הַמַּשְׂרִים, quod passive sumtum atque Mebuffarim lectum revera significat ac reddi potest ευαγγελιζόμενοι, i. e. ut versio latina in Bibl. Polyglot. habet, evangelizati, qui accepere bona nuntia (nova vel promissa bonorum, vel evangelium) a בשר Bisfer, nuntiatum, (& in specie quidem, s) rem bonam & laetam, & in passivo si in usu esset, quippe in sacris literis non extat, denotaret talia nuntia accipere, ut ευαγγελίζομαι in lingua graeca, quamvis & in ea magis in usu est activum) quo modo etiam hic interpretatur Hieronymus ex graeca versione, annuncians, prout in diversis graecis apographis legitur, nec non singulari numero ευαγγελιζωμενος. Ita Capellus post diversos alios legerunt מבשרים. At tanta est certe inter Mebuffarim & Seridim differentia in sono juxta ac in literis, ut vix ac ne vix quidem capi possit, quomodo librarius aliam pro alia substituerit. Quod vero a multo & antiquo tempore eodem modo lectum sit, sicuti hodie, Seridim, ex eo apparet, quod reperitur in fragmentis versionis t) Theodotionis, qui hebraicam vocem haud vertendo legebat ἐν σαρδίν in Sardin, nec non ex eo, quod Hieronymus refert, hebraice legi שרידים Seridim, quod Judaei loci nomen existimant, quasi dictum esset, in Morte Son & in Jerusalem & in Seridim (quos notet Judaeos non obviam ei; extat enim, quod sciam, in nullo illorum commentario, nec ejus alibi fit mentio praeterquam in fragmentis Theodotionis). At it ita non legissent LXX, ut illi supponunt, unde factum dixeris illos vocem hanc ea notione transtulisse, quae substitutae propria erat, non illi quae reperitur hodie in Hebraico Textu? Ipsam hujus rei rationem attingere, ut dicuat mihi quidem non arrogem, quid? quod ne dimittando quidem assequi idaudeam; tamen non odeisse lin ites me non esse transgressurum mihi persuadeo, si huic nodo solvendo hanc non improbabilem subjiciam viam ac rationem. Eadem significatione evadendi, effugiendi ac libertate fruendi accepisse vocem שרידים Seridim dicendi sunt (prout fecisse conflat Jer. 42, 17. ubi uno verbo expressisse propterea duo vidimus; verum ne eandem vocem repeterent, vel quandam dam
units.tr: The word rendered here as remnant is in Hebrew שְׁאִירִים, Sheridim, which denotes those who survive when the rest have been plundered, or who escape the peril and destruction that hang over others. This noun, together with the root or verb from which it derives, occurs in Joshua 10:20, where the Hebrew reads והשאירים שרוד מהם [vehasseridim saradu mehem], which our people render "the remnant of them who were left of them," the Interlinear "and the survivors survived of them," and the Septuagint καὶ διασωζόμενοι διεσώθησαν, "and the survivors escaped." The same word is elsewhere joined with the verb of cognate meaning, שריד ופלט [sarid upalit], Jeremiah 42:17, where our people have "(who) shall remain or escape," while the Greeks express both by one word, σωζόμενοι, "saved." Whence it is clear that the Septuagint knew the meaning of seridim as well as others did, the meaning by which it denotes those who survive or who are saved from such evils as overtake others. Why, then, in this place, where this sense seems most apt, do they express it by another word of a wholly different meaning, namely εὐαγγελίζεσθαι ["to evangelize"]? This has so little affinity with the Hebrew that, in the other known meaning, it seems to have led some to the opinion that the Hebrew text was once read differently from today, namely as הַמַּשְׂרִים, which, taken passively and read Mebuffarim, really means and may be rendered εὐαγγελιζόμενοι, that is, as the Latin version in the Polyglot Bible has it, evangelized, those who have received good tidings (new or promised good things, or the gospel) from בשר [bisser], "to announce." (And in particular, to announce a good and joyful thing; and in the passive, if it were in use, for it does not occur in Sacred Scripture, it would denote to receive such tidings, as εὐαγγελίζομαι does in Greek, although in Greek the active is more commonly used.) In this way Jerome also interprets it from the Greek version, announcing, as is read in various Greek copies, as well as the singular participle εὐαγγελιζόμενος. So Capellus, after various others, read מבשרים. But the difference between Mebuffarim and Seridim is certainly so great, both in sound and in letters, that it can scarcely, if at all, be understood how a copyist could have substituted one for the other. That it was read in the same way, as Seridim, from a very early and ancient time, as it is today, appears from the fragments of the version of Theodotion, who, translating the Hebrew word not at all, read ἐν σαρδίν as Sardin; and also from what Jerome reports, that the Hebrew reads שרידים, Seridim, which the Jews regard as the name of a place, as if it had been said "in the death of the Son, and in Jerusalem, and in Seridim" (which, I think, the Jews would note as not relevant to it; for, as far as I know, it is found in none of their commentaries, nor is it mentioned anywhere except in the fragments of Theodotion). But would the Septuagint not have read it as they suppose, so that one may say they translated this word in that sense which belonged to the substituted word, and not in the sense found today in the Hebrew text? I do not presume to touch on the very reason for this matter, so as to tell it to others; indeed I cannot even reach it by conjecture. Yet I persuade myself that I shall not be overstepping the bounds if, to loosen this knot, I offer the following not improbable way and reasoning. The word שרידים, Seridim, should be taken in the same sense of escaping, of getting away, and of enjoying freedom; (as it is clear they did in Jeremiah 42:17, where they expressed two things by one word, as we have seen; but so that they would not repeat the same word, or some form of the same root) (as the Syriac does: first, in the sense of liberation, ḥᵃ Meshauzbutho, "liberation"; second, ḥᵃ Meshauzbe, "those liberated"), it seemed better to them to supply another word, which indeed would not correspond literally to the Hebrew but would be suitable to this place, and, since what precedes and follows does not oppose it, would give the sense in this way: "and on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who are saved, as the Lord has said, καὶ εὐαγγελιζόμενοι ὃς κυρίῳ ἀπέσταλται ["and those evangelizing, as the one sent by the Lord"], and the rest who are to receive the Gospel" (that is, good tidings, namely deliverance), "whom the Lord has called." Since the Hebrew word looks more to the number of those to whom deliverance is promised, they put in its place a word which rather sets forth their qualities. Not that I suppose they thought this was the proper meaning of the word they were translating, but because these joyful tidings and the promise of deliverance pertained to all those, and to those alone, whom the Lord was going to call.

units.la: Hæc vel hujus similis planior mihi videtur atque tutior via conciliandi Textum Hebraicum & versionem Græcam hujus vocis, quam Hebraicam mutare, ut conveniat cum versione Græcorum. Quatione simul supponimus ita olim auctores hujus versionis etiam scripsisse, prout hodie apud eos legimus. De eo enim Drusius videtur dubitare, quando allegans hanc vocem εὐαγγελιζόμενοι dicit: vera hæc lectio; At hac quæstione extricanda nunc lubens supersedebo.
units.tr: This, or something like it, seems to me a plainer and safer way of reconciling the Hebrew text with the Greek version of this word, rather than changing the Hebrew to agree with the Greek translators. In this way we also assume that the authors of that version wrote what we read in them today. Drusius seems to doubt this, since, citing the word εὐαγγελιζόμενοι [euangelizomenoi], he says: this reading is genuine; but I will gladly set aside this question for now and not pursue it.

units.la: Ex sequentibus porro apparet, quomodo residui, quibus solis liberatio hic promissa est, digni habeantur selecti numeri nomine, scil. ex sola libera DEI gratia. Cujus ne ipsi essent ignari, adjicit, quos Dominus vocabit אשר יהוה קרא asher Jehovah kore. Vox kore est participium, quod simpliciter notat, vocans, qua ratione etiam vertitur in interlineari versione. Necesse igitur est, ut tali in constructione verbum substantivum subintelligatur ac cum eo conjungatur, ut ad aliquod restringatur tempus, sive sit præsens, præteritum vel futurum, quorum cuique participium rite factum inservit, quomodocunque subintellectum verbum collocetur, id quod vel praesenti, præterito aut futuro tempore fit; vel interdum tantum ufurpatur uno, u) nunc hoc, nunc illo, veluti sensus loci requirit. Quod ad participium hujus loci attinet, utuntur eo interpretes quovis tempore. Sunt iv) qui reddunt vocat, tempore praesenti: x) alii vocatvit, praeterito, ut LXX ἐκλήτα, Syrus ܩܪܐ kero, Arab. impressa ܟܬܒ ut & Chaldaeus in paraphrasi sua, licet diversa significatione in eandem mentem: alii tempore futuro, ut Vulgatus cum quibusdam aliis, vocaveri, Castalio vocabit, quo cum faciunt y) nostrates. Nec alieni quid infert materiae subjectae, quippe eadem erit Dei vocatio, quae hic innuitur, quo demum cunque accipias tempore, cum omni tempore haec sit certa. Quare inquirendum est potius, quid sibi velit haec eorum vocatio. Vox kore in genere notat, advocare vel vocare aliquem ad aliquam rem sive propositum, sed nonnunquam in specie magis adhibetur in peculiari quodam casu. Hinc est quod R. Salomon dicat, eam notare vocatos ad convivium vel ad ministerium Regis, idemque valere quod hazmanah, praeparatio, destinatio, constitutio ad aliquid, atque ideo invitatio; quare a Chaldaeo redditur, cujus verba z) quidam ita interpretantur: quos Dominus destinat; a) alii praedestinavit; b) alii invitat. David Kimchi hic intelligi vult tales, quos DEus vocabit meos servos & amicos, vel alias vocatione magnitudinis & gloriae, qua eliget ut magnificiat eos & glorificet, qui alibi nominantur Kerium, nostratibus renovati, ut Num. 1,16. & Ezech. 23,23. Interlinearis altero loco, convocati, altero invitati. Aben-Ezra exponit per decernit (sive decrevit sive decernet). Qua expositione innuunt DEum hic dici eos vocare, qui erunt reliqui, quibus promissa est liberatio, quippe ad unum omnes peculiarem hic respici existimant vocationem, quae vulgarem ac communem longe excedat.
units.tr: It further appears from what follows how the remnant, to whom alone liberation is promised here, are regarded as worthy of the name of the chosen, namely from the free grace of God alone. Lest they be ignorant of this, he adds whom the LORD calls [אשר יהוה קרא, asher Jehovah kore]. The word kore is a participle, which simply means calling, and it is rendered in this way in the interlinear version. It is necessary, then, that in such a construction a substantive verb be understood and joined to it, so that it is restricted to some tense, whether present, past or future, to any of which a properly formed participle may serve, however the understood verb is placed; and this happens either in the present, the past or the future tense, or sometimes it is used in only one of them, now this, now that, as the sense of the passage requires. As for the participle in this place, the translators use it in whatever tense they like. Some render it calls in the present tense; others called, in the past, as the Seventy have ἐκλήτα [eklēta], the Syriac has kero, the printed Arabic has katab (as also the Chaldee paraphrast does in his paraphrase, though with a different meaning leading to the same sense); others in the future tense, as the Vulgate with some others has will call, Castalio will call, and our own people do likewise. Nor does this difference bear on the subject matter, for it will be the same calling of God that is indicated here, whichever tense you take, since this calling is certain at every time. Therefore we should rather inquire what this calling of theirs means. The word kore in general means to summon or to call someone to some matter or purpose, but sometimes it is used in a more specific sense in a particular case. Hence R. Solomon says that it signifies those called to a feast or to the king's service, and that it has the same force as hazmanah, meaning preparation, appointment, establishment for something, and therefore an invitation; so it is rendered by the Chaldee, whose words some interpret thus: whom the LORD appoints; others predestined; others invites. David Kimchi wants this to be understood of those whom God will call his servants and friends, or else by a calling of greatness and glory, by which he will choose them to magnify and glorify them, who elsewhere are named Kerium, which our people call renewed, as in Num. 1,16. and Ezek. 23,23. The Interlinear renders it in the one place summoned, in the other invited. Aben Ezra explains it as decrees (whether he decreed or will decree). By this explanation they imply that God is here said to call those who will be the remnant to whom liberation is promised, since they all think that a special calling is meant here, one far beyond the common and general calling.

units.la: Verum enim vero ut planiorem reddamus huius loci sensum, sic procedendum nobis esse reor. Vocatio DEI accipi potest (1.) laxiori notione pro vocatione, qua omnes generaliter vocantur per
units.tr: But in truth, to make the sense of this passage plainer, I think we must proceed in this way. The calling of God may be taken (1) in a looser sense, for the calling by which all are generally called through
