units.la: Porro qui hisce titulis hic ornantur, nominatim vocantur Israel, & si verum fateri volumus, hæc natio, quatenus eo nomine ab aliis distinguitur, quæ erant ante tempora Evangelii, hoc solo quoquetitulo s) peculiariter cognitus erat; at postquam in vulgus editum est Evangelium, & nomen & hi tituli communes redditi sunt omnibus eis, qui fidem ei habent, cujuscunque sint nationis, sive tribus Israelis,sive alicujus alius, omnes hi sunt populus Dei, & t) hæreditas Dei, & Israel Dei, etiam tota ecclesia verorum fidelium; ita ut utriq; æquo jure hæc expressio applicari possit. Quicquid enim DEUS unquam Israeli olim impertiebat vel impertire voluit, vi istius relationis, qua populus ipsius erat,propter majores ejus,quibuscum primum sanxerat fœdus; idem facit & facere adhuc perget omnibus christianis ex ea relatione, qua in Christo ab eo sunt recepti. Sunt qui hæc verba & res dictas intelligunt alii de hoc spirituali Israelesolum, alii de altero secundum carnem, alii de utroque, & in utroque completa, quippe utriusque & veteris Israelis & novi Israelis eadem causa, eadem desponsatio divina,eadem quoque promissio
units.tr: Moreover, those who are adorned here with these titles are named expressly "Israel." And if we wish to tell the truth, this nation, insofar as it was distinguished from others by that name, that is, those who were before the times of the Gospel, was known particularly by this title alone; but after the Gospel was published abroad, both the name and these titles have been made common to all those who have faith in it, of whatever nation, whether of the tribe of Israel or of any other. All of these are "the people of God," and t) "the inheritance of God," and "the Israel of God," even the whole Church of true believers; so that this expression can be applied to both with equal right. For whatever God once bestowed, or wished to bestow, upon Israel, by virtue of that relation by which they were his people, on account of their forefathers, with whom he first made covenant, the same he does, and will continue to do, for all Christians, by that relation by which they have been received by him in Christ. There are those who understand these words and things said of the spiritual Israel alone, others of the other, according to the flesh, others of both, and fulfilled in both; for there is the same cause of both the old Israel and the new Israel, the same divine betrothal, and also the same promise.

units.la: missio agendæ causæ utrique, cum omnes, quicunque erant, vel sunt, ejus sint populus, ejus hereditas, ejus Israel, ejus ecclesia. Hinc a u) quodam ita explicantur hæc verba: Populum suum vocat electos omnes, quos etiam Israelis nomine comprehendit &c. Adeo ut non tantum loquatur de eo populo, neque de eorum hostibus solum; ut verba ad literam sonant, sed de electis hujus æque ac ecclesiæ gentium, & de omnibus qui electos persequuntur. Populus enim ille figura erat Ecclesiæ; & ejus hostes typus omnium qui sanctos persequuntur. Alludit (inquit w) alius ad captivitatem Babylonicam & Judæ destructionem a Chaldæis factam, quæ typus erant earum vastationum, oppressionum & miseriarum, quæ ab inimicis ecclesiæ fiunt fidelibus. Non equidem nomine populi Israelis ii tantummodo intelligendi sunt, qui sunt Israelitæ secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum, i.e. veri cultores DEI, qui ab infidelibus & improbis persecutionem patiuntur & affliguntur. x) Alius: Israel, de quo loquitur, non est ille externus vel carnalis, sed spiritualis, de quo supra cap. 2, 28, 29. & qui vocatur Israel Dei, Gal. 6,16. Unde etiam liquet, quomodo illa, quæ sequuntur, sint accipienda, videlicet per ea, quæ Israel quondam secundum carnem passus est, metaphorice signisicari, quæ verus Dei Israel semper patitur, vel passus est. Postea quam vero declaravit, quibuscum disceptaturus ac contenturus sit in judicio, jam pergit in specie designare in verbis sequentibus, de qua re disceptatio foret, vel quam causam imprimis sit acturus: quos dispersèrunt in nationibus & terram meam divisèrunt &c. אשר פזרו בגוים Asher pizzeru Baggoim y) quos (vel quem) dispersèrunt &c. Alii reddunt, quia dispersèrunt eos vel eum; quandoquidem vox Asher nonnunquam ponitur pro כי z) quia sive quod (atque tum supplendum est eos vel eum) in nationibus (scilicet cum captivos eos abducerent ex sua in aliam regionem. Syrus hæc verba passive reddit qui dispersi sunt in nationibus. Hinc Kimchi spectari putat ad Titum ejusque exercitum, ושמו ארץ ישראל ופזרו יושביה בין הגוים qui
units.tr: populus, his inheritance, his Israel, his church, since all who were or are his belong to him. Hence a u) certain writer explains these words thus: He calls all the elect his people, whom he also comprehends under the name of Israel, and so on. So he does not speak only of that people, nor only of their enemies, as the words sound literally, but of the elect of this people as well as of the church of the Gentiles, and of all who persecute the elect. For that people was a figure of the Church, and its enemies are a type of all who persecute the saints. Another writer (he says) alludes to the Babylonian captivity and the destruction of Judah by the Chaldeans, which were types of the devastations, oppressions and miseries that the enemies of the church inflict on the faithful. Indeed, by the name of Israel people are not to be understood only those who are Israelites according to the flesh, but according to the spirit, that is, the true worshippers of God, who suffer persecution and affliction from unbelievers and the wicked. x) Another: The Israel of whom he speaks is not the outward or carnal one, but the spiritual one, of whom above in chapter 2, verses 28 and 29, and who is called the Israel of God, Gal. 6:16. Hence it is also clear how the things that follow are to be taken: namely, that what Israel once suffered according to the flesh is metaphorically signified by what the true Israel of God always suffers, or has suffered. Having now declared with whom he is going to dispute and contend in judgment, he proceeds to name specifically, in the following words, what the dispute will be about, or what cause he will chiefly plead: whom they have scattered among the nations and divided my land, and so on. Hebrew: Asher pizzeru baggoim [אשר פזרו בגוים], y) whom (or who) they have scattered, and so on. Others render it because they have scattered them (or him), since the word asher is sometimes used for ki [כי], z) because or that (and then them or him must be supplied), among the nations (namely, when they led them away captive from their own land into another region). The Syriac renders these words in the passive: who were scattered among the nations. Hence Kimchi thinks they refer to Titus and his army, with the Hebrew: ushemu eretz Yisrael ufizzeru yoshveha bein hagoyim [ושמו ארץ ישראל ופזרו יושביה בין הגוים], who

units.la: {u} Ribera. {w} Menoch. {x} Tarnov. {y} Drus. {z} Quod dispersèrint eum per gentes. qui defolarunt terram Israel ejusque incolas inter gentes disperserunt. At excipiunt contra hanc ejus opinionem, primo a) quod non possint omnes nationes proprie dici, quos secum adducebat Titus, illorum instar, quibuscum DEus hic disceptaturus est. Secundo b) quod Judæi eo ipso tempore, quo regionem invadebat, titulum populi ejus ac hæreditatis Israelis sustinere haud possent, eo quod Christum abnegaverant crucique affigendo protinus rejecerant. Quæ rationes etiam faciunt ad destruendam sententiam Abarbinelis, qua de Chriftianis & Mahomedanis hoc exponit, diverso temporis intervallo in Judæorum terram irruentibus, eamque, incolis inde pulsis, inter fe dividentibus. Pari ratione & c) illis objici potest, qui de Assyriis & Chaldæis alisque gentibus Judæis vicinioribus, quarum auxilio nitebantur, intelligunt, quod omnium nationum titulum non mereantur. Atq; hæ objectiones inprimis adhibentur ab illis, d) qui ad captivitatem Babylonicam atque terræ Judææ destructionem alludi censent, easque typum gerere volunt earum vastationum, spoliationum & injuriarum, quibus hostes jugiter afficiunt ecclesiam & coetum fidelium, quos persecuti sunt atque in exilium egerunt, terra eorum (quam suam vocat DEus) bonisque & facultatibus inter fe divisis. e) Per ea, quæ Israel fecundum carnem passus est (quia in peculiarem populum eum DEus asciverat) metaphorice significat, quæ verus Israel DEI, Ecclesia Christi, passus est, vel adhuc f) patitur ab ejus hostibus, qui his descriptis malis vel aliis similibus eam urgent in diversis nationibus fideles dispergendo atque eorum terram dividendo.Suam Terram DEus hic vocat illorum regionem, atque hoc nomine olim veniebat peculiari ratione terra Israel, quia g) Israel erat populus ejus. Ita adhuc sibi venditat, quicquid ad eos pertinet, non secus ac illos ipsos; Hinc qui in jus illorum involare audeat eosque eo privare ac injuria afficere gestiat, vindicem eum sentiet haud aliter, ac fi in eum ipsum hæc omnia admisisset.
units.tr: {u} Ribera. {w} Menoch. {x} Tarnov. {y} Drus. {z} That they scattered him among the nations. who laid waste the land of Israel and scattered its inhabitants among the nations. But against this opinion of his they object, first a) that all the nations cannot properly be called those whom Titus brought with him, like those with whom God is here going to dispute. Second b) that the Jews, at the very time when he invaded the region, could not bear the title of his people and the inheritance of Israel, since they had denied Christ and, by fixing him to the cross, had at once rejected him. These arguments also tell against the view of Abarbanel, who explains this of the Christians and the Muslims, invading the land of the Jews at different intervals of time and dividing it among themselves after driving out its inhabitants. By the same reasoning, c) the objection can be made to those who understand it of the Assyrians and Chaldeans and other nations nearer to the Jews, on whose help they relied, since they do not deserve the title of all the nations. And these objections are chiefly brought forward by those d) who think that an allusion is made to the Babylonian captivity and the destruction of the land of Judah, and wish these to be a type of the devastations, plunderings and injuries with which the enemies constantly afflict the church and the assembly of the faithful, whom they have persecuted and driven into exile, dividing their land (which God calls his own) and their goods and property among themselves. e) By what Israel suffered according to the flesh (because God had taken them as his peculiar people) he metaphorically signifies what the true Israel of God, the Church of Christ, has suffered, or still f) suffers from its enemies, who press upon it with the evils described or others like them, scattering the faithful among the various nations and dividing their land. God here calls their region his own land, and by this name the land of Israel was once in a special sense called, because g) Israel was his people. So he still claims as his own whatever pertains to them, no differently than them; hence whoever dares to invade their rights and desires to deprive them of these and harm them will find him an avenger, no differently than if he had committed all these things against himself.

units.la: a) Pet. a Fig. b) Mercer. c) Grot. d) Menoch. Sa. e) Ribera. f) Vel patietur: prophetico enim more verba accipimus, quo sub præterito non tantum continentur, quæ facta sunt, sed & quæ futura, donec Deus universos ad judicium vocaverit. g) Menoch. Terram populi mei, atque adeo meam.
units.tr: a) Pet. a Fig. b) Mercer. c) Grot. d) Menoch. Sa. e) Ribera. f) Or, will suffer: for we take the words in the prophetic manner, under which the past tense includes not only what has been done but also what is to come, until God calls all to judgment. g) Menoch. The land of my people, and so also mine.

units.la: Peculiari ratione intelligit Hieronymus hæc verba, & terram meam diviserunt, ac si divisa esset terra diversis accersitis idolis ac idololatriæ generibus in eam regionem, ubi unum antea DEum erant cultu prosecuti; at multo planior videtur exponendi ratio, quam priori loco adduximus, qua, inter se eam illos divisisse atque in usum suum occupasse, statuunt.
units.tr: Jerome understands these words, and they have divided my land, in a special sense, as if the land had been divided by bringing in various idols and kinds of idolatry into that region, where previously they had worshipped the one God alone; but the explanation we cited first, which holds that they divided the land among themselves and occupied it for their own use, seems much plainer.

units.la: Quæ vero in specie sint rationes, ob quas cum hostibus disceptare velit, recensere pergit proxime in sequentibus verbis hocce modo:
units.tr: What the specific reasons are for which he wishes to dispute with his enemies he goes on to set out in the words that immediately follow, in this way:

units.la: 3. Et projecerunt sortem super meum populum, & derunt puerum pro meretrice, & puellam vendi- derunt pro vino ut biberent.
units.tr: 3. And they cast lots upon my people, and gave a boy for a harlot, and sold a girl for wine that they might drink.

units.la: Quibus verbis significat, populum ejus adeo contemtim habitum fuisse, tantaque contumelia affectum, qua neminem afficerent, quem vel alicujus facerent vel communi demum haberent loco. Sortem enim super eos, quos in h) captivitatem redegerant, projiciebant, nulla alterius præ altero ratione habita, quasi plane indigni essent ulla electione, ut eos inter se dividerent. Qui i) mos dividendi eos per sortem, quos captivos reddiderant bello, in multo usu antiquis fuisse videtur. Alludi quippe ad eum in aliis locis compertum habemus, veluti Nahum. 3,10. Et de honoratis ejus projecerunt sortem, & Obad. v. 11. & super Jerusalem jecerunt sortem. Verum equidem est, id accipi posse de divisione vel k) bonorum, agrorum & possessionum illorum, vel personarum. At quomodocunque acceperis, ingens hinc in eos redit contumacia, quæ tamen nihili censenda præ illa, quæ continetur in verbis sequentibus: & derunt puerum pro meretrice. Quod ad hæc verba, in diversum eunt hic nimium quantum interpretes tum in assignanda significatione vocis זנה zonah, quam reddidimus, meretrice, tum in concipiendo sensu, si hæc interpretatio probetur. Quod ad significationem vocis attinet, sunt qui alio modo eam interpretantur, quatenus scilicet vox quoque denotat alimentum, ac si eadem esset cum זן zan,
units.tr: By these words he signifies that his people were held in such contempt and subjected to such insult as no one would inflict on a man whom they esteemed or even regarded as an ordinary person. For they cast lots over those whom they had led into h) captivity, taking no account of one person above another, as though they were wholly unworthy of any choice, so that they might divide them among themselves. The i) custom of dividing by lot those whom they had made captives in war seems to have been in common use among the ancients. Indeed, we find that it is alluded to in other places, as in Nahum 3:10, And they cast lots for his honourable men, and Obad. v. 11, and they cast lots upon Jerusalem. It is true that this may be understood of the division of the k) goods, fields and possessions of those people, or of their persons. But however you take it, a great arrogance returns upon them from this, which yet is to be counted as nothing beside that which is contained in the following words: and gave a boy for a harlot. On these words the interpreters disagree greatly, both in assigning the meaning of the word זנה zonah [זנה], which we have rendered harlot, and in conceiving the sense, if this interpretation is approved. As to the meaning of the word, there are some who interpret it otherwise, namely because the word also denotes food, as if it were the same as זן zan,

units.la: h) Sors jacitur ubi est contemtus. Calvin. i) Druf. k) Mercer. צ.מ, sive מזון Mazon, a radice און aluit, quæ hanc {l} notionem fert, quo quidem pacto satis egregie sequentibus congruit, quibus dicuntur vendidisse puellam pro vino; nimirum, pro vino puellam, puerum pro alimento dedisse dici possunt; verum satius habent alii, iique fere plurimi hanc derivari vocem a radice זנח zanah [?] fortatus est, atque hoc loco, ut & alibi, quam sæpissime & communiter denotari meretricem, cum alibi alia notione non extet. Tum vero haud difficultate vacat, quo sensu hoc sit accipiendum, quando vertitur pro meretrice, num sit applicandum ad illud abominandum sodomiticum scelus, ac si meretricis gesserit vices; an vero pretii loco datus sit puer meretrici pro corporis ejus prostitutione. Priori modo accipit hoc Hieronymus, aliique nonnulli; plerisque autem aliis perplacet sententia posterior, m) quam & sequentia magnopere videntur confirmare, ubi adjicitur, & vendiderunt puellam בין Beyain, pro vino, id est, pro pretio vini. Vero itaque simillimum est, & quod præcedit בזונה Bazonah, pro meretrice, eodem præfixo ב be, exponi debere, pro mercede meretricis. Ita & Chaldæus באגר זנותא pro pretio sive mercede meretricis. Nec non Syrus Bagar zanoyotho, pro mercede meretricum. Quibus concinit MS. Arabicum [illegible, ~12 letters] & dederunt puerum pro pretio meretricis. Et LXX, ἐδωκαν τὰ παιδάρια πόρνας, quorum vestigia premens Arabica impressa habet [illegible, ~12 letters] & dabant pueros pro meretricibus. Quæcunque autem harum sententiarum probetur breviter, inquit R. Tanchum, sensus eo redit [illegible, ~30 letters] cos vendidisse liberos (populi DEI vel) Israelis, quos captivos reddebant, pretiumque eorum contulisse in suas voluptates & turpissimas libidines, id quod maximum certissime eorum arguit contemtum, tantamque ignominiam, qua nulla major ac abjectior excogitari potest, quippe tam
units.tr: h) The lot is cast where there is contempt. Calvin. i) Drusius. k) Mercerus. צ.מ, or מזון Mazon [מזון], from the root און aluit [אנן, to feed], which bears this {l} meaning; and this indeed fits quite well with the following words, in which they are said to have sold a girl for wine. That is, one may say that they gave a girl for wine and a boy for food. But many others, and indeed most of them, prefer to derive the word from the root זנח zanah [זנח, he has been forsaken], and to take it in this place, as often and commonly elsewhere, as denoting a harlot, since it occurs nowhere else in another sense. Then indeed it is not without difficulty in what sense this should be taken when it is rendered for a harlot: whether it is to be applied to that abominable sodomitical crime, as if they had acted in the place of a harlot; or whether the boy was given to a harlot as the price for her prostitution of her body. Jerome and some others take it in the former way; but to most others the latter opinion is much more pleasing, which the following words also seem greatly to confirm, where it is added, and they sold a girl בין Beyain [בעד?], for wine, that is, for the price of wine. It is therefore most likely, and the preceding בזונה Bazonah [בזונה], for a harlot, with the same prefixed ב be, should be explained as for the hire of a harlot. So also the Chaldee בגר זנותא for the price or hire of a harlot. Likewise the Syriac Bagar zanoyotho, for the hire of harlots. The Arabic manuscript [illegible] agrees with these, and they gave a boy for the price of a harlot. And the LXX, ἐδωκαν τὰ παιδάρια πόρνας [they gave the boys for harlots], which the printed Arabic follows closely, has [illegible] and they gave boys for harlots. Whichever of these opinions is approved, says R. Tanchum briefly, the sense comes back to this: [illegible] they sold the children (of the people of God or) of Israel, whom they made captives, and they put their price into their own pleasures and most shameful lusts. This most certainly proves their contempt to be very great, and such great disgrace, than which none greater or more abject can be imagined, since they were held in such a wonderfully despised way.

units.la: {l} Quod recte ita verti putat celebris ille Grammaticus Abu VValid. m) R. Tanchum. tam mirandum in modum vilipendebantur, ut nulli dubitarent eos, ut quidam volunt, projicere pro rebus abjectissimis sordidisve, ut sunt scortandi ac potandi libidines. Utut vero hujusmodi sortis vel populi Dei Israelis olim, vel Christianorum huc usq; nulla in historiis fiat mentio, eam tamen subiisse olim, vel subituros, sive ad praeterita, sive ad futura haec pertinere censeas, res est manifestissima horum verborum testimonio suffulta.
units.tr: {l} This is rightly rendered thus by that famous grammarian Abu Walid. m) R. Tanchum. So that they did not hesitate to cast them away, as some want, for the most abject and filthy things, such as the lusts of whoring and drinking. Yet although no mention is made in histories of such a lot, either of the people of God Israel of old or of Christians up to now, whether you think this applies to the past or to the future, it is a most plain matter, supported by the testimony of these words, that they once underwent it, or would undergo it.

units.la: 4. Imo quid tibi mecum, Tyre & Sydon, & omnes termini Palaestinae? Nunquid retributionem mihi reddetis? Et si retribuitis mihi, cito & velociter reddam retributionem vestram in caput vestrum.
units.tr: 4. Indeed, what have you to do with me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the borders of Palestine? Will you repay me? And if you repay me, I will swiftly and speedily return your repayment upon your own head.

units.la: Postquam praecedentibus in verbis v. 2. praedixerat in genere, quod esset disceptaturus cum omnibus gentibus de populo suo, atque in judicium vocaturus ob eas, quibus haereditatem suam affecerant, injurias, in specie jam & nominatim exprimit eorum quosdam, quibus litem sit moturus, nimirum Tyrum & Sydonem & omnes terminos Palaestinae. Hanc vero disceptationem orditur a quaestione, qua quicquid injuriarum illarum erat, injuste ac citra omne meritum & causam factum esse docet, quod se dignos reddiderant, ut ea severitate cum illis ageret, qua minatus erat. Populi, qui hic nominantur, sunt Tyrus & Sydon & omnes termini Palaestini, h. e. incolae horum locorum, quos vicinos sive conterminos fuisse terrae Israelis non uno loco apparet, quo eorum in S. litoris injicitur mentio. Ut autem horum verborum juxta ac sequentium v. 5. 6. 7. 8. genuinum eliciamus sensum, necesse est ut paulo limatius exactiusque ex historia eruamus, tum quo malorum genere ab iis affecti sint Judaei, quamdiu Israel DEI erant, tum quo poenarum genere correpti sint postea juxta illud, quo hic dicuntur, corripiendi. Cum autem nullus locus alibi occurrat, unde haec accurate peti possent, in literalem horum verborum sensum tanto majori studio inquirendum puto, cum utriusque rei descriptionem suggerat. Ampleditur quippe non tantum ea quae faciebant,
units.tr: Having said earlier in the preceding words, v. 2, in general terms that he would contend with all the nations concerning his people, and would summon them to judgement for the injuries by which they had afflicted his inheritance, he now expresses by name, in particular, some of those with whom he is about to bring suit, namely Tyre and Sidon and all the borders of Palestine. He begins this dispute with a question, by which he shows that whatever injuries those were, they were done unjustly and without any merit or cause on their part, since they had made themselves worthy that he should deal with them with that severity with which he had threatened. The peoples named here are Tyre and Sidon and all the borders of Palestine, that is, the inhabitants of these places, which are shown to have been neighbours or borderers of the land of Israel in more than one place, where mention is made of them on the Sea coast. But in order to draw out the genuine sense of these words, as well as of vv. 5, 6, 7, 8 that follow, it is necessary that we bring out from history, a little more finely and exactly, both the kind of evils by which the Jews were afflicted while they were the people of God, and the kind of punishments by which they were afterwards seized, according to what is said here, to be seized. Since no other place occurs from which these matters could be accurately sought, I think we must inquire into the literal sense of these words with all the greater zeal, since it suggests a description of each thing. For it sets forth not only what they did,

units.la: n) Tarnov. ciebant, verum & quo pacto in eos effet animadvertendum, quanquam immane quantum discrepant interpretes, num omni fuppliciorum genere jamjam sint correpti, vel adhucdum corripiendi, vel in totum, vel magna ex parte? Quocirca ordine hæc verba exponenda sunt nobis, ut & accuratius ea inspiciamus & de toto negotio limatius feramus judicium. Ita autem habent וגם מרי את לי צר וצירון Vegam mah attem li tzor Vetzidon. Vegam,imo, ad literam,atque ita; Vulgato licet,verum. Qua particula docet,cum aliarum etiam remotiffimarum gentium tanta maneat pœna, quæ toti populo DEI ruinam & interitum intentaverant, neque has exemtum iri, licet potentia cæteris multo effent inferiores; verum cum amicitiæ ac auxilii loco, cui ferendo ex jure viciniæ erant obligati, pro viribus maximo etiam affecerant damno, certo esse futurum ut & hæ suppliciis illis non eximantur, quibus afficiet cæteras DEus; sed in specie in judicium vocentur propter ea, quæ fecerant,atque pro meritis suis cum reliquis puniantur,utpote quæ immerito hæc secerant atque injuriæ in ipsum DEum erant reæ. Hinc aperte in hæc verba erumpit: quid tibi mecum? לי li, mecum,quasi sibi ipsi effent facta, quæ facta erant populo suo. Ita interpretando simul exprimit sensum MS. Arabicum ואיצא איש כאן לכם מע אמתי אנתכם צור וצירינא אתר atque ita quid erat vobis cum natione mea (five populo) o populo (vel incolæ) Tyri & Sydonis? Qua ratione etiam intellexisse videtur R. David Kimchi, cum ita exponat לי מרי ולכם &c. Quid mihi vobiscum? (vel quid negotii est, vel erat mihi vobiscum?) שבאתם לארצי &c. quia venistis in terram meam, qui, quum fitis vicini mei, debueratis populo meo benefacere. At non ita fecistis, sed cum vidistis venisse adversum eos Reges populorum, illis vos adjunxistis, ad referendum spolia & prædam. Unde apparet cum DEO illis negotium fuisse,cum dicantur negotium habuisse cum populo ejus, quippe sibi asserit, quæ populum suum respiciunt,ut ad v. 2. jamjam notavimus, atque id est quod plerisque consentientibus infert vocula לי mecum. Differt hoc loco quam maxime a communi interpretatione Chaldæus hunc in modum verba reddens ואף מנא אתין אתן חשבין קרמי Atque ita quanti estimati estis apud me? quocum etiam convenit Syrus ܐܬܘܢ ܫܒܝܢ ܩܪܡܝ cujus momenti estis apud me Tyre & Sydon? &c. Eodem videntur etiam respicere LXX. illis in o) exemplaribus quae habent καὶ τί ὑμῖς ἐμοί; quos Arabica impressa imitatur atque ita vertit فماذا انتم لي et quid vobis mecum? (quamvis alia exemplaria sint, quae propius ad communem interpretationem accedunt, cum habeant τί ἐμὲ καὶ ὑμῖν juxta Cyrillum, quid mihi & vobis?) Si ad mentem Chaldaei atque eorum, qui cum eo faciunt, verba interrogandi forma legantur, nihil aliud ea complecti in aperto est, quam exprobrationem stultitiae illorum, qui sibi videntur satis idonei ad resistendum DEO, quasi non esset par vindicta sumenda de ignominia, qua eum afficiunt, qui populum suum laedunt. Verum majorem veritatis speciem prae se fert altera exponendi ratio, qua cum illis videtur expostulare velle propter nefas in populum suum citra ullum meritum admissum atque per illum in se, cujus causam sibi ipse vindicat ac tuetur. Quare, sive, ob quam causam ita mecum egistis, o Tyre & Sydon & omnes termini Palestinae? Quid sit Tyrus & Sydon vel ejus incolae, verbis proprie acceptis, manifestum est, uti diximus, ex crebra earum mentione in sacris literis. Quod autem ad verba attinet, omnes termini Palestinae, quae hebraice sic habent וכל גבולות פלשת becol geliloth Pelesbet, variam a variis fortiuntur interpretationem. Sunt qui Geliloth pro nomine loci proprio habent & ad Galilaeam respici putant. In quorum numero sunt LXX vertendo: καὶ πᾶσα Γαλιλαία ἀλλοφύλων, & omnis Galilaea peregrinorum, & ad eorum mentem Arabica impressa جليل الغرببة & omnis Galilaea nationum peregrinarum. Quibus etiam accedit Syrus ܟܠ ܓܠܝܠܐ & omnis Galilaea Palestinae. At exemplis cum destituta sit vox גלילות Geliloth, quod numero plurali proprii nominis loco ponatur, alii recentiores aeque ac vetustiores, ni fallor, pro appellativo habent notionem terminorum, limitum, sive confinium. Ita olim Chaldaeus, qui hunc in modum vertit כל תחומי פלשתאי omnes limites (vel termini) Phili-
units.tr: n) Tarnov. they were doing, but also in what manner they were to be punished. Although the interpreters differ enormously, have they already been seized by every kind of punishment, are they still to be seized, or is the punishment total or largely so? Therefore these words must be expounded in order, so that we may examine them more accurately and form a more polished judgment on the whole matter. They read thus: [וגם מה אתם לי צר וצידון] Vegam mah attem li tzor Vetzidon. Vegam means, indeed, literally and so; the Vulgate renders it verum, but. This particle teaches that, although the punishment remains great even for other very distant nations which had threatened ruin and destruction to the whole people of God, these will not be exempt, even though they were far inferior to the others in power. But since they had inflicted the greatest damage, to the extent of their strength, instead of the friendship and help which they owed by the right of neighbourhood, it is certain that these too will not be exempted from those punishments with which God will afflict the rest. Rather, they will be called to judgment in particular for what they had done, and will be punished along with the others according to their deserts, since they had done these things undeservedly and were guilty of injury against God himself. Hence he breaks out plainly in these words: quid tibi mecum? [לי li] mecum, with me, as if the things done to his own people had been done to himself. By translating in this way, the Arabic manuscript at the same time expresses the sense: [Arabic: wa-ayḍan mā kān lakum ma'a umatī, anṭum Ṣūr wa-Ṣaydā'?] and so what was there between you and my nation (or people) O people (or inhabitants) of Tyre and Sidon? By this reasoning R. David Kimchi also seems to have understood it, since he explains it thus: [לי מרי ולכם] What is it to me and to you? (or what business is there, or was there, between me and you?) [שבאתם לארצי] etc. because you came into my land, you who, being my neighbours, ought to have done good to my people. But you did not do so; rather, when you saw the kings of the peoples come against them, you joined yourselves to them, to carry off the spoils and the plunder. From this it appears that the dispute was with God, since they are said to have had a dispute with his people; for he claims as his own whatever concerns his people, as we have already noted at v. 2., and this is what the little word [לי] mecum implies, as most agree. This passage differs very much from the common interpretation in the Chaldee paraphrast, who renders the words thus: [ואף מנא אתין אתן חשבין קרמי] And so how highly are you esteemed before me? The Syriac agrees with this: [Syriac: Atun shibin qmai] of what worth are you before me, Tyre and Sidon? etc. The Seventy also seem to have had the same in view in those copies o) which read [καὶ τί ὑμῖν ἐμοί;] which the printed Arabic imitates, and so translates: [Arabic: fa-mādhā antum lī?] and what are you to me? (although there are other copies which come nearer to the common interpretation, since they have [τί ἐμὲ καὶ ὑμῖν] according to Cyril, what to me and to you?). If the words are read in the interrogative form according to the mind of the Chaldee paraphrast and of those who agree with him, it is clear that they contain nothing but a rebuke of the folly of those who think themselves sufficiently able to resist God, as if the vengeance due for the disgrace they inflict on him who harms his people were not to be exacted. But the other mode of exposition shows a greater appearance of truth, by which God seems with them to wish to complain about the wrong committed against his people, without any merit on their part, and through them against himself, whose cause he himself claims and defends. Why, or for what cause, have you dealt thus with me, O Tyre and Sidon, and all the borders of Palestine? What Tyre and Sidon, or their inhabitants, are, taking the words in their proper sense, is clear, as we have said, from their frequent mention in the sacred letters. As to the words all the borders of Palestine, which in Hebrew read thus: [וכל גבולות פלשת] becol geliloth Pelesbet, they receive various interpretations from various scholars. Some take Geliloth as the proper name of a place, and think that Galilee is meant. Among these are the Seventy, who render it [καὶ πᾶσα Γαλιλαία ἀλλοφύλων] and all Galilee of foreigners; and in agreement with them the printed Arabic has [Arabic: wa-kull Jalīl al-gharbiyya] and all Galilee of the foreign nations. To these the Syriac also adds [Syriac: kul Gelila d-Pelesta] and all Galilee of Palestine. But since the word [גלילות] Geliloth has no examples of being used in the plural as a proper name, others, both more recent and more ancient, if I am not mistaken, take it as a common noun meaning borders, limits, or boundaries. So the Chaldee paraphrast formerly, who renders it thus: [כל תחומי פלשתאי] all the limits (or borders) of the Philistines, and the Arabic manuscript: all the parts (or borders) of Palestine. In the same way it has been observed that Abu Walid and R. Tanchum use this word to denote borders and limits.

units.la: e) Sic in Polyglot. p) Vide Grotium in h.l. & in Matth. 8,26. Philistinorum, & M. S. Arabicum omnes partes (vel termini) Palestinæ. Pari modo observatum est ab Abu Walid & R. Tanchum hanc vocem denotare terminos, limites. Geminum huic habet Latinus, numero singulari pro plurali posito, quem interpretandi modum in genere fere omnes recentiores sequuntur, ne nostratibus quidem exceptis. At alii iterum insistunt viæ in altero nomine reddendo LXX. quam præter impressam Arabicam cæteri omnes ignorant, cum haud pro nomine proprio habeant; verum non dubitant illud interpretari, per peregrinorum vel peregrinarum gentium. Atque familiare hoc revera illis est, quotiescunque Palæstinæ vel Philistinorum nomen occurrit; verum ut nemo dubitat hoc esse nomen regionis proprium perquam notæ, ita manifestum est etiam satis, hic potius accipi proprie, alterumque Geliloth eo sensu, quo vidimus, atque ita a nostratibus & aliis non inepte esse reditum, termini Palestinæ, adeo ut regiones ac populi sint, qui hic nominantur, Judæorum vicini, qui crudeliter ac inhumaniter cum illis egerant. Quibus verbis ita acceptis non obscure patet, minas in primis hic fieri incolis horum locorum. Sunt tamen qui sub nominibus horum locorum comprehendi autumant adhuc alios præter illos, qui simili modo agunt, atque ex eodem nomine vocari aut indicari merentur, veluti illi, qui ita agunt cum ecclesia DEI & ejus populo, sicuti olim agebant cum Judæis, cum nomen suum adhuc strenue tuerentur. Hinc est, q) qui sub his nominibus depingi vult omnem improbum populum, & sub Judæorum nomine omnes ingenuos fideles, omnesque electos DEI, cujuscunque sint etiam nationis. Alii exempli causa hæc nomina adducta statuunt, quæque hic dicuntur futura incolis horum locorum, qui fideles servos Dei in V. T. persequebantur, de iis intelligenda cupiunt, quæ contingent aliis nationibus, quæ ullo unquam tempore sese præbebunt inimicos DEI ac ipsius populi. In eandem igitur mentem hæc verba ita ωαςφοβ D. Stokius: Vos qui estis tam jurati hostes Christianis, quam olim Tyrii & Sydonii Judæis. Sic ab r) aliis respiciuntur tanquam exemplum sive typus hostium
units.tr: e) So in the Polyglot. p) See Grotius on this passage and on Matt. 8.26. The Arabic manuscript has of the Philistines, and all the parts (or borders) of Palestine. In the same way, Abu Walid and R. Tanchum have observed that this word denotes borders, limits. The Latin translator has a similar rendering, using the singular for the plural, and nearly all modern interpreters follow this manner of translating, our own countrymen included. Others, however, cling to the Septuagint's rendering of the other word, peregrinorum or peregrinarum gentium, though apart from the printed Arabic, all the rest are unaware of it, since they do not take it as a proper name, yet they do not hesitate to render it so. This is indeed their habit whenever the name of Palestine or of the Philistines occurs. But just as no one doubts that this is the proper name of a very well-known region, so it is also quite plain that here it is rather to be taken in its proper sense, and that the other word, Geliloth, is to be understood in the sense we have seen. Thus our own countrymen and others have not unreasonably rendered it the borders of Palestine, so that the regions and peoples named here are neighbours of the Jews who treated them cruelly and inhumanly. Taken in this way, the words clearly show that threats are directed here chiefly at the inhabitants of these places. Yet there are some who think that under the names of these places are comprehended, besides those who acted in this way, others who deserve to be called or designated by the same name, such as those who act thus towards the Church of God and his people, just as the Jews once acted towards them while they still vigorously defended their name. Hence some, q) want all wicked people to be depicted under these names, and under the name of Jews all honest believers and all the elect of God, of whatever nation they may be. Others, adducing these names as examples, hold that what is here said will befall the inhabitants of these places, who persecuted the faithful servants of God in the Old Testament, and they wish these words to be understood of what will happen to other nations which at any time show themselves enemies of God and of his people. In this same sense Dr Stokes renders these words: You who are as sworn enemies of Christians as once the Tyrians and Sidonians were of the Jews. Thus others, r) regard them as an example or type of enemies of the household of the Church, who, drawn by certain motives, feign zeal for piety for a time, but when occasion offers, break out with the poison hidden in their minds.

units.la: q) Vid. Christ. a Castro. r) Gualterus. um domesticorum Ecclesiæ, qui rationibus quibusdam adducti pietatis studium simulant ad tempus, data tamen occasione exserunt latens animi venenum. Quinam autem his nominibus innuantur, vel sub iis una comprehendantur, facilius erit judicare, postquam consideraverimus, quam ob rem cum illis expostulet & quomodo propterea cum illis lit acturus, id quod sequentibus declarat verbis inquiens: הגמיל אתכם משלמים עלי, Nunquid retributionem mihi reddetis? Et si retributitis mihi, cito & velociter reddam retributionem vestram in caput vestrum. Quorum verborum obscuritatem, qua videntur involuta, ut rite expediamus, notandum est vocem גמול Gemul, retributionem, & bono & malo accipi sensu, uti & verbum, cujus hic extat participium: ואם גמלים אתכם & si retributionem facitis sive in bonam, sive in malam partem; verum in malam hic accipi partem ipsa res loquitur. Porro & hoc observatione dignum est, haec verba significare tum, quod ab aliquo fit in compensationem alicujus praecedentis negotii, tum quod prius fit, quam ulla data sit occasio praecedens negotium compensandi, quam ad utramque notionem hic respici non obscure patet ex ipsis verbis; & ad primam quidem, cum dicitur הגמול haggemul attem meshallemim li, numquid retributionem mihi reddetis (vel redditis)? Etenim nomen verbo reddendi notione conjunctum requirere videtur, ut accipiatur pro השבת גמול recompensationis redditione pro aliqua re facta; ad alteram autem, quando incipit: ואם גמלים אתכם עלי nostratibus interpretantibus, & si mihi retribuitis, ubi significat התחלת הרעה initium inferendi malum (sive, quod id faciant loco priore); qua ratione haec accipit Kimchi utramque significationem "hujusmodi paraphrasi concinne exprimens: Quid rei est, quod vos "mihi male facitis? an putatis vos vindictam de me sumere, quod vo"bis male fecerim? quid mali vobis feci? quod si dixeritis, vos ex vo"bis ipsis (vestra sponte) nunc mihi malum facere, (qui enim Israeli "male facit, ejus intentio est mihi male facere, quia sunt filii mei) si "ita est, velociter reddam retributionem vestram in caput vestrum." Sic ejus expositio hoc loco habet; a qua non procul absunt, quæ s) alibi s) Lib. Radicum. alibi tradit de significatione radicis ⁿ⊐ɔ. Eundem fere in modum ea quoque explicat Abarbinel, præterquam quod gemina utatur interrogatione: Num male vobiscum egi (vel malum vobis feci) quod mihi retributionem meam redditis? Vel quanquam nihil in vos mali admiserim, an in me id admittere incipitis? Quæ explicandi ratio satis perspicua apparet, quapropter & t) quorundam suffragiis merito, mea sententia probatur. Succinde in eandem mentem earn transfert Castalio: Utrum mihi vos refertis, an potius confertis? vel ut alii: u) utrum cogitatis mihi referre, an inferre injuriam? Etsi non desunt qui eandem significationem retributionis utroque loco servant; an retributionem mihi reddetis? & si mihi retribuitis; ac si utrobique respiciatur aliquid, quod DEus (vel populus ejus) in eos admisisset antea, de quo jam cuperent ultionem sumere, ita ut priore loco fit quæstio propósita, num hoc in animo habeant, atque posteriore loco declaratio, quid sit iis facturus, si hoc constituissent, ubi secundo loco interrogatio evanescit (quam constituunt qui diversa significatione verbum accipiunt) ejusque loco particula DN im; si, habetur conditionalis, qua supposita, quæ sequuntur, infert, scilicet, si hoc facere constituissent, etiam esse facturum, quod sequitur; qua ratione etiam a perquam w) multis aliis redduntur. Sic ea exprimere videntur Chaldæus; & Vulgatus Latinus, qui ita habet: Et si ulciscimini vos contra me, cito & velociter reddam vindictam vobis supra caput vestrum. Verum sunt x) qui & altero loco quæstionem requirt censent, atque DNI, & si, idem esse ac an? imo illi ipsi ita putant, qui reddunt si, & Gomelius accipiunt significatione vel retribuendi, vel priore loco faciendi. Hinc Mercerus: DNI vein & si, interrogativæ intelligit; Gamul autem interpretatur inferre. Et Drusius: Hic si sumitur pro an, & retributionem reddere pro injuriam facere. Pariter statuit Grotius particulam si poni pro an, qua significatione Latino Vulgato dicit frequentem; ita ut pergat interrogando hunc in sensum: An hanc vicem mihi rependitis & hoc mihi redditis? nempe pro tot in vos collatis beneficiis. At in diversum
units.tr: q) See Christ. a Castro. r) Gualterus. of the Church's household enemies, who, drawn by certain motives, feign zeal for piety for a time, yet when occasion is given they bring out the hidden poison of the mind. Who exactly is indicated by these names, or comprehended under them together, will be easier to judge once we have considered why God complains against them and how he will therefore deal with them, as he declares in the following words: [הגמיל אתכם משלמים עלי] "Will you repay me? And if you repay me, I will swiftly and speedily return your recompense upon your own head." To clear up the obscurity of these words, which seem involved, it must be noted that the word gemul [גמול], "retribution," is taken in both a good and a bad sense, as is also the verb of which the participle occurs here: [ואם גמלים אתכם] "and if you make a return, whether for good or for ill." But that it is taken here in the bad sense the matter itself makes clear. Moreover, this too is worth noting: these words signify both that something is done in return for some preceding deed, and that it is done before any occasion has been given to repay a preceding deed. That both senses are intended here is plainly clear from the words themselves. In the first case, when it is said haggemul attem meshallemim li [הגמול אתם משלמים לי], "Will you repay me (or render)?", the noun seems to require the verb "to render" in the sense of making a return for something done: [השבת גמול] "the return of a recompense." In the second, where it begins "and if you repay me" [ואם גמלים אתכם עלי], our countrymen translating "and if you repay me," it means [התחלת הרעה] the beginning of inflicting harm (or, that they do it in place of the former). Kimchi takes both senses in this way, neatly expressing them in the following paraphrase: "What is the matter, that you do evil to me? Do you think you take vengeance on me, because I have done evil to you? What evil have I done to you? But if you say that you yourselves now do evil to me (for whoever does evil to Israel, his intention is to do evil to me, since they are my sons), then I will quickly repay your recompense upon your own head." Thus his explanation stands here, and not far from it are the things he elsewhere teaches about the meaning of the root [גמל], in his s) Book of Roots. Abarbanel explains it in almost the same way, except that he uses a double question: "Have I dealt badly with you (or done you evil), that you repay me my recompense? Or, though I have committed no wrong against you, do you begin to commit it against me?" This method of explanation appears clear enough, and therefore, in my view, it is rightly approved by the votes of t) several scholars. Castalio briefly renders it to the same effect: "Do you bring back to me, or rather heap upon me?" or, as others have it, u) "Do you intend to repay me, or to inflict an injury?" Although there are those who keep the same sense of "repayment" in both places, "Will you repay me? And if you repay me?" w) as if in both places something is being considered that God (or his people) had previously permitted against them, for which they would now wish to take vengeance: so that in the first place the question is put, whether they have this in mind, and in the second the declaration of what he will do to them if they had resolved it. In the second place the question disappears (as those who take the verb in a different sense maintain), and in its place the particle im; if, is taken as conditional, which, once supposed, infers what follows: namely, that if they had resolved to do this, he would also do what follows. In this way it is also rendered by very many others. So the Chaldee paraphrast seems to express it, and the Latin Vulgate, which has: "And if you take vengeance against me, I will quickly and speedily render vengeance to you upon your own head." But there are x) those who think that in the second place too a question is required, and that "im, if" is the same as "whether?" Indeed those who render it "if" think so themselves, and they take the verb in the sense either of repaying or of doing first. Hence Mercer understands "im" and "if" as interrogative, but interprets gamul as "to inflict." And Drusius: "Here if is taken for whether, and to repay is to do an injury." Likewise Grotius holds that the particle if is put for whether, a usage which he says is frequent in the Latin Vulgate, so that the question continues in this sense: "Do you repay me in this way, and render me this?" namely, for so many benefits conferred on you. But in the opposite direction

units.la: t) Mercer. Cast. Drus. Livel. quibus etiam accedit MS. Arab. u) Drusius & Livel. w) Tig. Pagn. Munst. x) Drusius. sum abit in altero verbo reddendo cum גמלים Gomelim accipit notione compensandi ac rependendi, quod iis factum erat, idque bono sensu, non malo, ut habent cæteri. Huc facit, quod habet R. Salomon, qui retributionem illis redditum iri putat pro viginti urbibus, quas Salomon dederat regi Tyri. Quibus LXX olim videntur struxisse viam, qui interrogative legunt particulam posteriore loco, verbumque, quod sequitur, notione retribuendi sumunt, atque ita distinguunt commata, ut vidimus, interpretando: ἡ μνησικακεῖτε ὑμεῖς ἐπ' ἐμοί; quæ Arabica impressa ita ad literam exprimit أو ذكرتم vel, an recordamini (vel retinetis in animo vestro) malum adversus me? At contraria ratione agit MS. Arabicum, quod uno commate verba cum sequentibus conjungit (id quod & alios facere antea vidimus) atque cum præcedentibus ita reddit An reddit is mihi retributionem, & si mihi prius faciatis malum, cito & velociter reddam retributionem vestram in caput vestrum. Syrus habet redditis mihi retributionem? quod in Bibliis Polyglottis ita interpretantur, quod si beneficiis me cumulatis; quod meo judicio potius reddendum: sed si reponitis (vel confertis in me) retributiones debitas mihi, quippe vox Chublo, æque bene, imo multo melius sic vertitur, quam beneficia, cum significat retributionem, vel debita.
units.tr: t) Mercer, Castalio, Drusius, Livelius, to whom the Arabic manuscript also adds its support. u) Drusius and Livelius. w) Tigurinus, Pagninus, Münster. x) Drusius. he goes on to the other verb, rendering gomelim [גמלים] in the sense of compensating and repaying what had been done to them, and in a good sense, not a bad one, as the others have it. To this agrees what R. Salomon has, who thinks the return will be made to them for the twenty cities which Salomon gave to the king of Tyre. For these the LXX seem to have paved the way, who read the particle in the second place as interrogative, and take the verb that follows in the sense of repaying, and so punctuate the clauses, as we have seen, in translating: [ἡ μνησικακεῖτε ὑμεῖς ἐπ' ἐμοί] "Or do you bear a grudge against me?" The printed Arabic renders this word for word as aw dhakartum ["or do you recall"] (or do you keep in mind) evil against me. But the Arabic manuscript proceeds by a different method: it joins the words with what follows in one clause (as we saw others do before), and renders with what precedes: "Does he render me a return? And if you first do me evil, I will quickly and speedily return your recompense upon your own head." The Syriac has "Do you render me a return?" which in the Polyglot Bibles they interpret as "since you heap benefits upon me"; in my judgment it should rather be rendered: "but if you repay (or heap upon me) the due returns to me," since the word Chublo, equally well, indeed much better, is rendered thus than as "benefits," since it means a return or what is due.

units.la: Hisce atque similibus huc usque allatis inprimis respici constat ad usitatam significationem radicis Gamul, rependendi, vel retributionem reddendi alicui ob aliquid, quod antea vel re ipsa in aliquem contulit, vel contulisse arbitratur, qua notione a quibusdam altero accipitur commate, ab aliis utroque. Verum secus hic sentit magnus ille Grammaticus Abu Walid, quippe altera significatione utroque loco venire sentit, scilicet conferendi priore loco sine provocatione vel ulla occasione antea data. Cum vero משלמים Meshallemim mim priore loco extet atque ad significationem rependendi videatur restringendum, eo quod plerumque id denotat, utramque significationem admittere hanc vocem notat & conferendi prius & rependendi. Quod ut magis appareat, ipsius verba apponenda esse censeo, cum in explicanda radice שלם Shalem ita scribat:
units.tr: These and similar examples, cited so far, show that the principal reference is to the usual meaning of the root Gamul, to repay, or to render a recompense to someone for something he has previously done for, or is thought to have done for, another. Some take the word in this sense in the second clause only, others in both. The great grammarian Abu Walid, however, thinks otherwise. He holds that it bears the other meaning in both places, namely to confer something first, without any provocation or occasion given beforehand. But since Meshallemim stands in the first clause and seems to be restricted to the sense of repaying, because it usually denotes that, I note that this word admits both meanings: to confer first and to repay. So that this may appear more clearly, I think his own words should be set down, since in explaining the root שלם Shalem he writes as follows:

units.la: וקר חכין הרר אללגרר לגיר אל- מכאפאר כר ללאילאי כמא כאנת לגר נמור פי הרין אלמענין איצא, i. e. Hæc vox non tantum usurpatur notione rependendi, sed & priore loco conferendi, prout etiam vox Gamul utraque hac significatione in usu est; cujus rei in exemplum, etiam hæc verba citat הגמיל אתם משלמים עלי ואם גמלים אתם עלי גמר Gamal utraque loco, quo habetur & haggemul & gomelim, ut & de משלמים Meshallemim dicit utrobique לא ידלון אד nihil aliud denotare quam initium, ac utraque innui אילא ואבתריא באלפער quod fit loco priore, & initium inferendi. Qua in re ei accedit R. Tanchum, cujus verba quoque, cum ejus liber impressus non sit, subjicienda reor האתין אללגתין אעני גמר ושלם קר יכינאן במעני אלאילא אבתריא ובמעני אלמכאפאריא עלי מא הקרם פקולרי הגמור אתם משלמים עלי ואם גומלים מן אלמעני אלאור וקולרי אשוב גמילכם מן אלמעני אלתאני והריא אלאסתפאם מנריא תע עלי סביר אלתהריד, i. e. Hæ duæ voces Gamul & Shillem veniunt jam significatione inferendi prius, jam rependendi, quod antea erat illatum. Cum itaq; dicatur Haggemul attem Meshallemim alai veim gomelim attem alai, priore significatu accipiendum est; quod autem subjicitur in verbis sequentibus: Ashib gemulcem, posteriore notione venit rependendi, & interrogatio à Deo fit rationes interminationis. Pari ratione notat Abu Walid de radice גמר Gamal eam significare conferre priore loco, vel initium facere sive באלאחסאן או באלאסאר bene sive male agendi. Ita ut juxta eum verba huncce in modum sumi possint: an vestra sponte, vel sine provocatione aut occasione data injuria me afficitis? nisi a R. Tanchum {†}) alibi proditum esset hac significatione לא non nisi in z) bonam partem fumi; quod tamen, si verba ejus recto stent talo, qua ratione dici possit, non video, quippe inter exempla, quibus probatur notatio haec priore loco faciendi, quaedam etiam recensentur, ex quibus non obscure patet in malam accipi partem. Exempli loco sit quod extat, Gen.50,15. והשב ישיב לנו ארר כרי הרער אשר גמלנו אתו Et omnino nobis rependet illud malum, quod intulit mus ipsi. Ubi גמל Gamal omnino & priore loco faciendi & male faciendi notione accipitur, quapropter tum Abu Walid, qui eum aetate praecessit, quemque in non paucis secutus est, tum R. Kimchi existere dicunt, hanc vocem significare & priore loco facere, & male benefacere. Postquam enim a) Abu Walid ejus rei quaedam exempla adduxerat, idque inprimis, quod citavimus, cum aliis nonnullis, in haec verba definit כלרי אולא ואבתרי באלאחסאן או באלאסאר omnia haec significant prius facere & ordiri sive bene sive male faciendo. Et b) R. Kimchi pleno ore pronunciat denotare התחלת הטובות או הרער prius facere sive bene sive male. Quare ex mente illorum verba sumi possunt de malo vel injuria, quam intulerant, praeterquam quod essent nulla re antea lacessiti. Ex quibus illorum observationibus ac diversis, quas dedimus, verborum interpretationibus (quibus forsitan plures possent addi) nec non ex eorum diversa distinctionis ratione, qua vel una vel duae interrogationes constituuntur notae, manifestum equidem est, ea diversimode juxta literam posse verti; verum non est quod eorum sensum aliquo modo infringant, utpote omnes eo redeunt, DEum cum illis expostulare propter injurias populo suo illatas, quas non secus respicit atque sibi ipsi factas, eaque propter in sequentibus minitari futurum, ut pro meritis suis cum illis agat. Verba ita habent קל מהר kal meheerab, cito & velociter reddam גמלכם Gemulcem, retributionem
units.tr: "i.e. This word is used not only in the sense of repaying, but also in the sense of conferring first, just as the word Gamul is in use in both senses. As an example of this he cites also the words הגמיל אתם משלמים עלי [haggemul attem meshallemim alai] and ואם גמלים אתם עלי [ve-im gomelim attem alai], where Gamal occurs in both places, namely haggemul and gomelim. As for Meshallemim, he says that in both places it denotes nothing other than a beginning, and that both senses are implied: one which is done in the first place, and the initiating of an infliction." R. Tanchum agrees with him. Since his book has not been printed, I think his words too should be given: "These two words, Gamul and Shillem, come sometimes in the sense of inflicting first, sometimes of repaying what was previously inflicted. Therefore when it is said, הגמול אתם משלמים עלי [haggemul attem meshallemim alai], and ואם גמולים אתם עלי [ve-im gomelim attem alai], it must be taken in the first sense. What is added in the following words, Ashib gemulcem, comes in the later sense of repaying, and the question put by God is the reason for the threat." In the same way Abu Walid notes that the root גמר Gamal means to confer first, or to make a beginning, whether bene or male agendi, that is, doing good or doing evil. So, according to him, the words may be taken in this way: "Do you of your own accord, or without provocation or occasion given, injure me?" Unless R. Tanchum {†}) had stated elsewhere that in this sense the word is taken only in a good sense, I do not see how that could be said with correct sense, since among the examples by which this meaning, to do first, is proved, some are listed which clearly show that it is taken in a bad sense. An example is Gen. 50.15: והשיב ישיב לנו את כל הרעה אשר גמלנו אתו [veheshiv yeshiv lanu et kol ha-ra'ah asher gamalnu oto], "And surely he will repay us all the evil which we did to him." Here גמל Gamal is taken in the sense both of doing first and of doing evil. For this reason both Abu Walid, who preceded him in time and was followed by him in many things, and R. Kimchi say that this word means both to do first and to do evil or good. For after a) Abu Walid had brought forward some examples of this, and especially the one we have cited, along with some others, he concludes in these words: כלהא אולא ואבתרא באלאחסאן או באלאסאר [kulluha ula wa-ibtada bi-l-ihsan aw bi-l-isar], "all these mean to do first and begin, either by doing good or by doing evil." And b) R. Kimchi plainly asserts that it denotes התחלת הטובות או הרעה [hatchalat ha-tovot o ha-ra'ah], "the beginning of good things or of evil," that is, to act first, whether well or ill. Hence, in their view, the words may be taken of an evil or injury that they had inflicted, although they had not been provoked by anything before. From these observations of theirs, and the various interpretations of the words that we have given (to which perhaps more could be added), and also from the different way they punctuate, so that either one or two questions are marked, it is clear indeed that the words can be rendered in different ways according to the letter. But there is no reason why these should in any way undermine their sense, since all come back to this: that God expostulates with them on account of the injuries inflicted on his people, which he regards no less than as done to himself, and therefore threatens in what follows that he will deal with them according to their deserts. The words read: קל מהרה [kal meheerab], "quickly and speedily I will repay" גמלכם [gemulcem], "your recompense"

units.la: {†}) In Lexico suo Morshed. in גמל. z) Quo posito hunc sensum videtur suppeditare verborum, quae mihi prius facitis פצלא מתקרמא tanquam beneficium praecedens, ea cito vobis compensabo. a) In radice גמל. b) In Rad. & Com. in h. l. nem vestram in caput vestrum. Vox גמול Gemul, quæ hic repetitur, omnibus consentientibus denotat rependere vel reddere illis id, sive retribuere, quod contulerant. Quod dicit, cito & velociter, intelligendum est, se id esse facturum vel magna velocitate, quandocunque, vel quam primum ipsi lubeat, ita ut obstaculo aut impedimento esse non possent, neque c) temporis ratio de ullo id præveniendi remedio permitteret iis cogitare; vel se d) talem esse, tantaque potentia præditum, qui ita agere posset, quamprimum ac quandocunque collibitum esset, præterquam quod ab aliquo posset impediri. Atque eo sensu videntur id recipere, qui nominis loco habent vocem קל kal. Ita Munster: Leve est, ut velociter reddam retributionem vestram &c. Tigur. Facile est ut & ego &c. velociter rependam &c. Vatablus epitheti loco habet ac Deo accommodat: festinus cum celeritate. Calv. velux &c. atque eodem modo Piscator: levis festinatione &c. Qui etli omnes pro adjectivo id habeant, eatenus tamen differre ipsos videmus, ut priores descriptionem hic tradi putent actionis, posteriores autem agentis; quibus MS. Arabicum videtur concinere קלל סרעי qui est levis celeriter. Quantumvis autem sensu non admodum inter se discrepant, literali tamen constructioni illi magis adhærere mihi videntur, qui primam vocem קל kal pariter ac sequentem מהרה meberab, pro adverbio habent, ut duæ ejusdem significationis voces conjunctæ majorem exprimerent emphasin ac certitudinem ejus rei, quæ hic dicitur futura. Hac ratione a nostratibus sumitur, qui, prout vidimus, reddunt cito, in quo conveniunt cum multis aliis & veteribus & recentioribus diversis linguis, quibus scripserunt. In eandem enim sententiam habet Chaldæus קליל Kalil (quod literis fere congruit voci hebraicæ) LXX. ὀξέως, cui insigniter mea opinione respondet Arab. impress. Beheddat, licet a latino interprete reddatur, cum ira (rectius forte cum impetu sive celeritate); Syrus ܒܥܓܠܐ quam latinus exprimit, brevi; Vetus latinus, cito; Quod etiam faciunt multi interpretum recentiorum diversis linguis, ita ut exigua vel nulla sit differentia inter hanc & sequentem vocem מהרה
units.tr: {†}) In his Lexicon Morshed, under גמל. z) Given this, the sense of the words seems to be: "What you first do to me, as a previous benefit, I will quickly repay to you." a) Under the root גמל. b) In the Root and Commentary on this passage. "...upon your own head." The word גמול Gemul, which is repeated here, denotes, by general agreement, to repay or render to them what they had conferred, or to requite. As to "quickly and speedily," it must be understood that he will do it with great speed, whenever or as soon as it pleases him, so that they could not be obstacles or hindrances, nor would the shortness of time allow them to think of any remedy to prevent it. Or else that he is such a one, endowed with such great power, that he could act thus as soon and whenever he pleases, without being hindered by anyone. And in this sense those seem to receive it who take the word קל kal as a noun. Thus Munster: "It is light, so that I quickly render your recompense," etc. The Tigurine version: "It is easy, so that I too..." etc., "I will quickly repay," etc. Vatablus takes it as an epithet and applies it to God: "swift with speed." Calvin: "swiftly," etc., and in the same way Piscator: "light with haste," etc. Although all of these take it as an adjective, we see that they differ so far that the former think a description of the action is given here, the latter of the agent. The Arabic manuscript seems to agree with the latter: קלל סרעי [qall sar'i], "who is light and swift." However, although they do not differ much in sense, those seem to me to adhere more closely to the literal construction who take both the first word קל kal and the following מהרה meherah as adverbs, so that two words of the same meaning, joined together, express more emphasis and certainty about the thing which is here said to be future. In this way our own people take it, and render it "quickly," in which they agree with many others, both ancient and recent, in the various languages in which they wrote. For the Chaldee has to the same effect קליל Kalil (which nearly corresponds in letters to the Hebrew word), the Seventy ὀξέως [oxeōs], to which in my opinion the printed Arabic Beheddat notably corresponds, although the Latin translator renders it "with anger" (perhaps more rightly "with impetus" or "speed"); the Syriac b'ʿagela, which the Latin expresses as "briefly"; the Old Latin, "quickly." Many recent translators in various languages also do the same, so that there is little or no difference between this word and the following מהרה.

units.la: {c} Ar. Mont. {d} Brenn. מהרה Meherah, utraque adverbialiter accepta, praeterquam quod altera alteri addat pondus sive emphasin, uti diximus: quare consultum est nonnullis una voce eas exprimere superlativo gradu, e) velociss ime, quae sola inferre videtur quod ambae ejusdem significationis repetitae requirunt; vel nullam conjunctionem eis interponere, ut sunt in lingua originali, Kal Meherah, & quibusdam interpretibus, uti vulgato, cito, velociter; vel cum conjunctione, ut planior aequabiliorque fluat sermo, ut habent nostrates & f) alii, cito & velociter. Hac expressione Abarbinel censet innui Tyri & Sydonis judicium (locis his proprie acceptis) non delatum iri בסוף הגלורת כשאר האימורי ad finem captivitatis Judaeorum, uti caeterarum gentium, sed multo maturius fore, quodque hoc loco praedicitur, completum revera esse tempore, quo Alexander Magnus templo secundo adhuc integro eas evertebat. Quid alii sentiant de ratione ac tempore, quo haec respiciant ac complementum suum habeant, ex sequentibus patebit. Hoc loco praedicit se constituto tempore in eas esse animadversurum tam largiter ac efficaciter, ut appareret se justam hanc reddidisse retributionem pro iis malis atque injuriis, quibus eum affecerant, afficientes populum suum atque ea, quae ad eum spectabant & super quibus nomen ejus erat invocatum, vel quae sua vocabantur aut ejus nomine. Quam iniquae autem eorum fuerint actiones, utpote quibus quam maxime provocabatur, sicut in prioribus hisce verbis describitur in genere; ita jam indicatur, quaenam illae in specie fuerint, his sequentibus:
units.tr: {c} Ar. Mont. {d} Brenn. Meherah [מהרה], both taken as adverbs, except that the second adds weight or emphasis to the first, as we have said. For this reason some have thought it best to render the two words with one superlative, e) most swiftly, which alone seems to convey what the two repeated words of the same meaning are meant to express. Others leave out any conjunction between them, as they stand in the original, Kal Meherah, and some interpreters render it as the Vulgate does, swiftly, quickly. Others add a conjunction so that the sentence flows more plainly and smoothly, as our people do, and f) others, quickly and swiftly. By this expression Abarbinel thinks it is indicated that the judgment on Tyre and Sidon (taking these places in their proper sense) will not come at the end of the Jews' captivity [בסוף הגלות כשאר האומות], as it will for the other nations, but will come much sooner, and that what is foretold here was in fact fulfilled at the time when Alexander the Great overthrew these cities while the second temple was still standing. What others think about the reason and time to which these words refer, and when they are fulfilled, will become clear from what follows. Here God foretells that at the appointed time he will take vengeance on them so fully and effectively that it will be plain that he has made a just repayment for the evils and injuries by which they had afflicted him, afflicting his people and the things that belonged to him, over which his name had been invoked, or which were called his own or were his by name. How wicked their actions were, since they provoked him most grievously, is described in general in the preceding words; now it is shown in particular what these actions were, in the following words:

units.la: 5. Nam argentum meum & aurum meum accepistis & intulistis mea optima desiderabilia in delubra vestra.
units.tr: 5. For you have taken my silver and my gold, and carried my goodly pleasant things into your temples.

units.la: Quid hic intelligendum sit per id, quod dicitur argentum meum, & aurum meum, & mea optime pretiosa, non eadem omnium interpretum est opinio. Ex Judaeis est Aben-Ezra, qui de eo haec exponit, quod Reges Judae illis dederant vel שויחר או לפרין השכויים muneri, vel in redemtionem captivorum. Quem etiam Drusius sequitur
units.tr: What is meant here by "my silver and my gold, and my goodly pleasant things" is not agreed among all the interpreters. Among the Jews, Aben-Ezra explains it as referring to what the kings of Judah had given to them either as a bribe [שוחד] or for the ransom of captives [לפדיון השבויים]. Drusius also follows him.

units.la: e) Jun. Tremel. f) Sic & LXX & Syrus. quitur inquiens : aurum populi mei, quod viri pro redemtionis pretio solverent aut muneris loco inferrent ad vos. Kimchi idcirco DEum sibi tribuere putat argentum & aurum Israelitarum, quod illis dederat. Geminum huic habet Abarbinel; ita ut auferendo ea ab illis ipsum iis privarent, vel auferrent quae ejus erant; ejus quippe erat argentum, ejusque aurum totius Israelis, quatenus id ab eo illis erat datum, adeo ut jure merito dicere posset meum est argentum, meum (est) aurum totius Israelis.
units.tr: e) Jun. Tremel. f) So also the LXX and the Syriac. He says: "the gold of my people, which men paid as the price of redemption, or brought to you as a gift. Kimchi therefore thinks that God claims for himself the silver and gold of the Israelites, which he had given to them. Abarbinel holds a twofold view of this: that by taking these things away from them they deprived them of what was his, or carried off what belonged to him; for the silver was his, and the gold of all Israel, insofar as it had been given to them by him, so that he could justly say, the silver is mine, the gold is mine, of all Israel."

units.la: Sunt interpretum Christianorum g) nonnulli, qui eorum premunt vestigia. Alii tamen veteres aeque ac recentiores intelligunt per ea illud b) argentum, aurum, & pretiosa vasa, quae in templo Deo erant dicata, eamque ob causam sua. Grotius vero ab altera stat parte intelligendo non quae templi erant & Babylonem avecta sunt, sed quae erant populi sui, & a Chaldaeis, capta urbe, vicinis vendita sunt. At non est quod impediat, quo minus de utroque sumatur alterumque altero comprehendi statuatur. i) Argentum populi mei vel argentum Templi mei, vel utrumque & populi mei & templi mei. Quo etiam videtur propendere Calvinus non dubium esse, inquiens, quin bonis suis populum spoliaverint, eaque de causa fuerint rei ac correpti, quamvis in specie, quia abstulerant sacra templi vasa. Argentum & aurum & desiderabilia pretiosa populi ejus revera erant ipsius, hinc justa de causa fit, quod in rationem vocat eos propter ea, quae abstulerant. Quippe ita agendo injuriam ei faciebant apertam, qui possessores eorum pariter ac quae eo ingenere possidebant, sibi vindicat. Verum major injuria ipsum, quod nemo negabit, afficiebant auferendo ea, quorum possessor nullus erat alius cognitus praeter ipsum, nempe thesauros & ornamenta aedis ejus peculiaris, ipsi uni separata & consecrata, quibus quantumvis non egeat, nec propterea dici posset iis delectari ob aliquod bonum, quod sibi inde redundet; attamen quia indicia erant ac signa grati animi, cultus atque obedientiae populi a se ipso ordinata, in deliciis ea habebat atque accipiebat tanquam ab illis data, quae ipse illis dederat. Magna erat in se ipsa injuria.
units.tr: Some of the Christian interpreters g) follow in their footsteps. Others, however, both ancient and modern, understand by the silver, gold and precious vessels those that had been dedicated to God in the temple, and for that reason call them his. Grotius, on the other hand, takes the opposite view, understanding them not as things of the temple that were carried off to Babylon, but as things belonging to his own people, which the Chaldeans sold to their neighbours after the city was taken. But there is no reason why we should not take both, and hold that one is included in the other: the silver of my people, or the silver of my temple, or both my people's and my temple's. Calvin also seems to lean this way, saying there is no doubt that they had plundered his people of their goods, and for that reason were guilty and rebuked, though in particular because they had carried off the sacred vessels of the temple. The silver, gold and precious treasures of his people really belonged to him, and so it is with good reason that he calls them to account for what they had taken. By acting in this way they did him a plain injury, since he claims for himself both the owners of such things and the things they owned of that kind. Yet a greater injury, as no one will deny, they inflicted on him by taking away things of which he had no other known owner but himself: the treasures and ornaments of his own house, set apart and consecrated to him alone. Though he has no need of them, and cannot be said to take pleasure in them for any good that comes back to himself, nevertheless, because they were tokens and signs of the grateful heart, worship and obedience of his people, which he himself had ordained, he held them dear and received them as if they had been given by those to whom he himself had given them. The injury in itself was great.

units.la: g) Merc. Pet. a Fig. Grotius, D. Stokins &c. b) Hieronym. Cyrill. Tarn. i) Piscat. injuria harum rerum ablatio; verum major fit ac atrocior ex eo, quod eas intulerant in sua delubra לחיכליהם lehheicelehem. Vox designat vel k) Palatia vel Templa; verum majoris videtur emphasis interpretatio Templorum, qua crimen eorum immane quantum aggravatur, quippe non ea tantum auferebant a Deo ac in privatum usum convertebant, sed & in majorem ignominiam ac contemtum Dei, quasi eo multo superiores, publice collocabant in delubris idolorum suorum, haud secus ac si Deo victoriam extorserint. Quod cum a Tyro & Sydone & terminis Palaestinae hic factum dicatur, haud alienum a vero videtur eos, quorum hic dantur nomina, socios fuisse l) Chaldaeorum in diripienda urbe Hierosolyma & templo, quo nomine prae caeteris hic corripiuntur; in sequentibus autem ob ea inprimis, quae in personas ipsas admiserant.
units.tr: g) Merc. Pet. a Fig. Grotius, D. Stokins &c. b) Hieronym. Cyrill. Tarn. i) Piscat. The injury lay in the removal of these things; but it becomes greater and more atrocious from the fact that they carried them into their own temples, lehheicelehem [לחיכליהם]. The word means either palaces k) or temples. But the rendering temples seems to give the greater emphasis, since it aggravates their monstrous crime: they not only took these things away from God and turned them to private use, but also set them up publicly in the temples of their idols, to greater shame and contempt of God, as if they were far superior to him, just as if they had wrested victory from God. Since this is said here of Tyre and Sidon and the borders of Palestine, it seems not far from the truth that the peoples named here were accomplices of the Chaldeans l) in the sacking of the city of Jerusalem and the temple, for which they are rebuked here above others; but in what follows they are rebuked chiefly for what they had done to the persons themselves.

units.la: 6. Filios etiam Judae & filios Hierosolymae vendidistis Graecis, ut eos procul amoveatis a termino suo.
units.tr: 6. You have also sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the Greeks, so that you might remove them far from their border.

units.la: Quod dicitur eos vendidisse filios Judae & Hierosolymae, id ita accipit Kimchi, ut intelligat vel parvulos quos suffurabantur Judaeis, interea dum essent in terra sua; vel in eos quos venientes ac facientes cum hostibus eorum, cum in captivitatem abducebant eos, captos in illorum manus tradebant, atque sive hos sive illos innui putes, Graecis vendebant, qui procul remoti erant a terra Israel, ne ultro in terram suam redirent. Quod idem ante eum succinctioribus expressit verbis Aben-Ezra שלקחתם במלחמה או בגניבה quos cepistis in praelio, aut furto. Sunt qui existimant, per filios Judae & filios Hierosolymae non necessario intelligendos esse tantum puerulos; sed & m) adultiores quosvis incolarum Judae vel civitatis Hierosolymae, qui vocantur earum filii, quare Castalio vertit, Judaeos & Hierosolymitanos, uti & loco proximo, quod dictum est filiis Graecorum ad literam, interpretantur & nostrates & alii non pauci simpliciter Graecis. Verba enim hebraica ita habent לבני היונים libne hayevanim, a n) veteribus interpre-
units.tr: Kimchi takes the words "the sons of Judah and Jerusalem" to mean either the little children whom they kidnapped from the Jews while they were still in their own land, or those whom they captured by coming to terms with their enemies and handing them over to those enemies when they led them into captivity. Whichever of these you take them to mean, they sold them to the Greeks, who lived far from the land of Israel, so that they could not easily return to their own land. Aben-Ezra expressed the same thing more briefly: "whom you took in war or by theft" [שלקחתם במלחמה או בגניבה]. Some think that by "the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem" we need not understand only small children, but also m) any adult inhabitants of Judah or the city of Jerusalem, who are called their sons. For this reason Castalio translates "Judaeans and men of Jerusalem". In the nearby verse, the words "to the sons of the Greeks" are rendered literally by our own translators and by many others simply as "to the Greeks". The Hebrew reads לבני היונים [libne hayevanim], which the older translators rendered literally. n) Some more recent writers have done the same, and our translators note the same in the margin, even though their text reads what is chiefly meant.

units.la: k) Quidam codices LXX legunt ελαιας alii παιδας. l) Drufius. m) Druf. Tarn. n) Chal. LXX, Syr. Arab. Vulg. Lat. terpretibus ad literam expressa,ut & a nonnullis recentioribus, filiis Græcorum, quo modo & ad marginem notant nostrates, quanquam in textu habeant,quid potissimum innuatur,non quidem pueri ætate, sed populus hujus nationis, quippe hac voce Javanim in specie designantur Græci a patre suo Javan,filio Japhet, Gen. 10, 2. ita appellati, unde propria sua dialecto vocantur Jones. Non desunt tamen,qui id nomen non ad eos præcipue referendum esse arbitrantur,sed sub eo etiam comprehendi omnes reliquas gentes,(quia cæteris hæ eminebant & earum lingua reliquæ utebantur) sensu quidem sat amplo, quo S. Paulus eam vocem accipit,quando in Judæos ac Græcos dispertiens omnes populos posteriore nomine omnes eas complecti videtur gentes, quæ Judæi dici nequeunt,uti Rom. 1,16. 2. 9. 10-3. 9. & 29-10. 12. Gal. 3,28. Coloss. 3, 11. Sive igitur per Græcos illi intelligantur qui proprie ita nominantur, (quibus magnum ab omni ævo fuit cum incolis Tyri & rerum aliarum & hominum commercium, ut o) apparet ex Ezech. 27,13.) sive alii,quibus id nominis tribuitur,id saltem constat procul fuisse remotos a Judæa,unde procul dubio non essent redituri, ex eo quod adjicit: ut eos procul amoveatis a termino suo, i. e. a regione sua vel limitibus ejus. Iniquis Tyri ac Sydonis conterminorumque Palæstinæ sive eorum, qui hoc nomine innuuntur actionibus in populum suum admissis,hocce modo descriptis,proximis duobus versibus Deus subjungit,quid ab iis provocatus agere velit tum respectu populi sui,tum respectu hostium & suorum & illorum.Quid acturus sit respectu populi, ita declarat: 7. Ecce, ego suscitabo eos de loco, quo vendidistis eos, (respectu hostium autem) convertam retributionem vestram in caput vestrum. 8. Et vendam filios vestros & filias vestras in manus filiorum Judæ, & vendent eos Sabais, genti longinquæ: quia Dominus locutus est.
units.tr: k) Some manuscripts of the LXX read "olives" [ελαιας], others "children" [παιδας]. l) Drusius. m) Drusius, Tarnovius. n) The Chaldee, LXX, Syriac, Arabic, Vulgate and Latin translators. The meaning is not children by age, but the people of this nation, since by the name Javanim the Greeks are particularly designated, called after their father Javan, son of Japheth (Gen. 10:2).
