From this they are called Jones in their own dialect. Yet there are some who do not think this name refers chiefly to them, but that under it all the other nations are also included, since these nations stood out above the rest and the rest used their language. This is a fairly broad sense, the one in which St Paul takes the word when he divides all peoples into Jews and Greeks, and by the latter name seems to embrace all the nations that cannot be called Jews (Rom. 1:16; 2:9-10; 3:9; 10:12; Gal. 3:28; Col. 3:11). Whether, then, by "Greeks" we understand those who are properly so named, with whom Tyre had great trade in goods and people in every age (as appears from Ezek. 27:13), or others to whom this name is given, this at least is certain: they were far removed from Judea, and so without doubt they would not return. This is clear from what follows, "so that you might remove them far from their border", that is, from their region or its boundaries. After the wicked deeds of Tyre, Sidon and the neighbours of Palestine, or of those indicated by this name, against God's people, which are described in this way, God adds in the two following verses what he will do in response, both towards his own people and towards their enemies and yours. He declares what he will do towards his people thus: 7. "Behold, I will raise them up from the place where you sold them, and I will turn your recompense upon your own head. 8. And I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation, for the Lord has spoken."

units.la: *) Grotius.
units.tr: *) Grotius.

units.la: Quæ verba ad literam insigniter ita explicat Abarbinel: Ego eos „restaurabo operam navando,ut revertantur ex eo loco,quo vendi„diftis eos, atque per illorum manus convertam retributionem ve„ftram in caput vestrum; siquidem filii vestri ac filiæ ab eis venden„tur Sabæis, genti quæ procul remota est a regione vestra. Quando vero dicit הנני מעירם &c. Ecce ego suscitabo eos ex loco, quanquam vox p) proprie significet suscitare ex somno vel huic simile; tamen hic idem videtur valere ac q) reduces facio; ita ut eos, qui protinus videantur amissi ac oblivioni traditi (prout homines somno sopiti vel mortui non sunt conspicui) resuscitare velit ac efficere,ut in regionibus illorum appareant, a quibus tam longe erant dissiti & remoti. Ita Chaldæus: הא אנאי מיתי לחון בנלאי Abducam eos publice &c. Quod porro attinet ad ea verba,vendam filios vestros &c. in proclivi est, verbum vendere non posse accipi significatione propria,qua in alius jus ac usum transit res pretio accepto; id quod de Deo dici nequit, sed ea qua significat rem alicui tradere, ut plenum in eam ac super ea habeat jus & potestatem disponendi tanquam cum re ære suo redemta. Quo sensu verbum vendere etiam r) alibi sumitur.HincDeus dicitur vendidisse Israelitas in manus inimicorum suorum, Jud.2.14-3. 8-4.2. & 10.7. ex quibus cum liberarentur,rursus Psalmista dicit, Deum vendidisse populum suum בלאי הון fine pretio (uti reddit Vulgatus) vel ut noftrates,nihilo,& in margine, fine divitiis. Certum, equidem est, vendere accipi pro vendere pretio dato in præcedentibus, filios Judæ &c. vendidistis Græcis, & in sequentibus, & vendent eos Sabæis; at secus fe res habet,cum de Deo sermo fit,ubi nihil aliud est,quam dare vel tradere in illorum manus & potestatem,confentiente etiam Kimchi,qui ita exponit illud אמסרם בירם tradam eos in manum eorum. Quod cum minus observaverint quidam,occasionem iis dedisse putat Drufius reddendi ביר בני יהורה Beyad Beni Jehudah, opera filiorum Judæ,quod tamen,eodem censente,male exponunt. Ita tamen revera habet Caftalio,& Vatablus & Mercerus;at antiquior est multo hæc verborum interpretatio. Eodem enim modo id accepisse videtur MS. Arabicum interpretando עלי יד בני יהורה alai
units.tr: Abarbanel explains these words literally and admirably as follows: "I will restore them by working so that they return from the place to which you sold them. Through their hands I will turn your recompense upon your own head, since your sons and daughters will be sold by them to the Sabeans, a nation far removed from your region. When he says הנני מעירם, 'Behold, I will raise them up from the place', although the word properly means to rouse from sleep or something similar, here it seems to have the same sense as 'I will bring back'. So he means to raise up and make appear in the regions of those from whom they were so far separated those who seem to have been lost and forgotten at once (just as men who are asleep or dead are not visible). The Chaldee has הא אנאי מיתי לחון בנלאי [ha anai meiti lechon bnalai], 'I will bring them out publicly', etc." As for the words "I will sell your sons" etc., it is obvious that the verb "to sell" cannot be taken in its proper sense, in which a thing passes into another's right and use for a price received. That cannot be said of God. It must be taken in the sense of handing a thing over to someone, so that the one who receives it has full right and power to dispose of it as if he had bought it with his own money. In this sense the verb "to sell" is used elsewhere too. Hence God is said to have sold the Israelites into the hands of their enemies (Judg. 2:14; 3:8; 4:2; 10:7). When they were set free from these, the psalmist again says that God sold his people bela hon [בלאי הון], that is, "without price" (as the Vulgate renders it), or, as our translators have it, "for nothing", and in the margin, "without riches". It is certain that in the preceding words, "the sons of Judah" etc. "you sold to the Greeks", and in what follows, "and they will sell them to the Sabeans", the verb means to sell for a price given. But it is otherwise when the subject is God, where it means nothing other than to give or hand over into their hands and power. Kimchi agrees, and he explains that phrase אמסרם בירם [amsarem beyadam] as "I will hand them over into their hand". Since some have paid less attention to this, Drusius thinks it gave them occasion to render ביד בני יהודה [beyad beni yehudah] as "by the work of the sons of Judah", though, in his judgement, they explain this wrongly. Yet this is in fact how Castalio, Vatablus and Mercerus have it, but this interpretation of the words is much older. The Arabic manuscript seems to have taken it the same way, rendering עלי יד בני יהודה [alai yad bani yehudah], "by the hand of the sons of Judah".

units.la: p) Tarnov. q) Drus. r) Drus. alai yad bani yehudah, manu filiorum Juda. Vulgatus autem habet, s) in manibus filiorum Juda, quamvis a Duacens. exprimatur: into the hands of the children of judah. Dubium equidem non est, בְּיַד beyad pariter significare in manu & in manum, nec video id sensui quodam modo officere, quamvis constructionis diversa sit ratio; quid enim aliud est vendere manu, quam eos tradere in illorum manus ad vendendum vel disponendum cum illis pro lubitu?
units.tr: p) Tarnovius. q) Drusius. r) Drusius. The Vulgate, however, has "s) into the hands of the sons of Judah", although the Douai version expresses it as "into the hands of the children of Judah". There is no doubt that בְּיַד [beyad] means both "in the hand" and "into the hand" alike, and I do not see that this works against the sense in any way, even though the construction differs. For what else does it mean to sell by the hand, than to hand them over into their hands, to be sold or disposed of by them as they please?

units.la: Quae proxime sequuntur, Et vendent eos Sabæis genti longinquæ, ubi hebraice est שְׁבָאִים Shebaim jam olim in diversum traxerunt interpretum curas. LXX reddunt: καὶ πωλήσουσιν αὐτὰς εἰς αἰχμαλωσίαν, &c. & vendent eos in captivitatem genti procul distantι &c. Ita & Arabica impressa illorum æmulatrix & tradent eos captivos genti quæ procul est; nec conjectu difficile est, qua ratione eo sint impulsi, quippe vox שְׁבָא Shabah, quam pro nomine derivativo habebant, Hebræis ut & Chaldæis, Syris & Arabibus significat in captivitatem abducere, atque hoc loco, captivitates vel captivos, qua ratione censet Hieronymus debuisse potius verti, & ab Arabe ita versam vidimus. Verum cum alibi hujusmodi appellativi nominis forma non occurrat, pro nomine proprio ab aliis hic habetur populi vel gentis ita appellatæ, scilicet Sabæorum, prout etiam regio eorum nuncupatur Seba vel Sabah, unde reliquæ *) versiones Græcæ τοῖς σεβαῖμ, vel †) τοῖς σεβαίοις; Syrus ܫܒܐ; Vulgatus Latinus, Sabæis, & omnes fere recentiores interpretationes in genere. MS. Arabicum ليحيل يمن Leahlil yaman, populo yaman; quo simul explicat, quem populum intelligat per eos, qui hic vocantur Sabei, nimirum, incolas yaman vel Arabiæ felicis; nullosque alios, qui vel ipsi vel eorum regio pari nomine possit insigniri, uti aliis quidem complacitum fuit, eosque inter Hieronymo, qui eos putat fuisse populum trans Indiam, cujus regionis juxta eundem & Regina fuit Sebæ, quæ veniebat auditum sapientiam Salomonis 1. Reg. 10. unde nobis etiam adhuc thus adferri statuit.
units.tr: The words that come next, "and they will sell them to the Sabeans, a distant nation", where the Hebrew is שְׁבָאִים [Shebaim], have long drawn the attention of translators in different directions. The LXX render: "and they will sell them into captivity to a nation far distant", etc. The printed Arabic, which imitates them, has "and they will hand them over as captives to a nation that is far off". It is not hard to guess what led them to this. The word שְׁבָא [Shabah], which they took as a derived noun, means to lead into captivity in Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic, and here it means captivities or captives. Jerome thinks it ought rather to be translated in this way, and we have seen an Arab translate it so. But since a form of this kind of common noun does not occur elsewhere, others take it here as a proper name of a people or nation so called, namely the Sabaeans, just as their region is also named Seba or Sabah. Hence the other Greek versions have τοῖς σεβαῖμ [tois sebaim] or τοῖς σεβαίοις [tois sebaiois]; the Syriac has "Shaba"; the Latin Vulgate has "Sabaeis", and almost all more recent translations in general. The Arabic manuscript has leahlil yaman, "to the people of Yaman", by which it also makes clear which people it means by those here called Sabei, namely the inhabitants of yaman, or Arabia Felix. It admits no others who could be designated by the same name, either themselves or their region. Others, however, have been pleased to think otherwise, and among them Jerome, who thinks they were a people beyond India, whose region, according to the same writer, also had as queen the Sheba who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (1 Kings 10), from whom he also thinks that frankincense is still brought to us.

units.la: †) Vel. Pagn. In manu. *) Aqu. Sym. †) Theod. statuit. At notatur censoria virgula a Drufio, qui mendum in eo esse arbitratur, inde inprimis ortum, quod non accurate distinxisset inter שבא Sheba cum schin sch. & סבא Sabah cum Samech, S. quæ sunt diversa nomina personarum diversarum (quæ diversarum gentium possunt esse genitores) & regionum (unde fortean personæ nomen sortitæ sunt, ut Psal. 72, 10. מלכי שבא וסבא reges Sheba & Seba) Ubicunque vero Seba fit sita, sive in Æthiopia, sive in Arabia Chusæa; de Sheba quam maxime est probabile & plerisque concessum, eam sitam esse in Arabia felice, nec est, qui dubitet, inde advehi thus; quin & hoc a vero non admodum dissimile, ex ea venïsse ostm reginam Sheba, quam Salvator noster Matth. 12, 42. & Luc. 11, 31. vocat reginam Austri, quo videtur vocem yaman interpretari, adjiciens, eam venïsse ab ultimis partibus terræ, unde regio eorum, cum esset sita in extremis Arabiæ littoribus, non secus atque incolæ hoc loco possint vocari gens x) longinqua, quippe hæc pars Arabiæ si in ea sit sita, tam longe dissidet a Tyro & Sidone & terminis Palestinæ, ut jure merito sic dici possit. Interim diffiteri non possumus, aliam restare verborum interpretationem, qua circa hanc rem omnis difficultas tollitur. Ea autem est, quod eos sint vendituri Sabæis, qui y) eos abducerent & venderent gentibus remotis & procul dissitis; verum res tam plana est, ut istiusmodi minus indigeat. Hucusque quæ spectant literalem interpretationem verborum quinque præcedentibus versibus comprehensorum, in quibus enucleandis non est, quod de difficultate queramur; majoris certe momenti est ac ardui sane laboris opus ulterius in ea inquirere ac definire, quomodo & quando his prædictis verbis eventus responderit, quibus adhuc subjicitur, quia Dominus hoc locutus est, i. e. certo z) determinavit. Non est ullum dubium, quin justo tempore justaque ratione ea certe essent futura; verum cum vetera monumenta, prorsus sileant, quando & quomodo ea facta sint, in varias itum est interpretibus sententiás, aliis literali sensui adhærentibus, alius ad figuratum confugientibus,
units.tr: †) Vel. Pagn. in the hand. *) Aquila, Symmachus. †) Theodotion: "decided." But a censorious mark is placed against this by Drusius, who thinks there is an error here, arising chiefly from the fact that he had not carefully distinguished between שבא Sheba with shin (sch) and סבא Sabah with samech (S). These are different names of different persons (who may be the ancestors of different nations) and of regions (from which perhaps the persons received their names, as in Psal. 72, 10.: "the kings of Sheba and Seba" [מלכי שבא וסבא]). Wherever Seba is located, whether in Ethiopia or in Arabia Chusaea, it is very probable, and granted by most, that Sheba lies in Arabia Felix, and no one doubts that frankincense is brought from there. Nor is it far from the truth that the queen of Sheba came from there to hear the wisdom of Solomon, whom our Saviour calls "the queen of the south" in Matth. 12, 42. & Luc. 11, 31., which seems to be how the word yaman is to be understood. He adds that she came "from the ends of the earth," and since their region lay on the furthest shores of Arabia, the inhabitants here may likewise be called "a distant nation" (gens x) longinqua), for that part of Arabia, if it is located there, lies so far from Tyre and Sidon and the borders of Palestine that it may rightly be called so. Meanwhile we cannot deny that there remains another interpretation of the words, by which every difficulty in this matter is removed. It is that they are to be sold to the Sabeans, who y) would carry them off and sell them to remote and far-off nations. But the matter is so plain that such an explanation hardly needs it. So far, these things concern the literal interpretation of the words contained in the five preceding verses, and in explaining them there is no reason to complain of difficulty. But it is certainly a matter of greater importance and truly a work of arduous labour to inquire further into and determine how and when the events answered to these foretold words, to which is added, "for the Lord has spoken it," that is, z) he has determined it with certainty. There is no doubt that at the right time and for a just reason these things would certainly come about; but since ancient records are entirely silent as to when and how they were done, interpreters have taken varied views, some clinging to the literal sense, others fleeing to the figurative,

units.la: u) Secus videtur sentire Mercerus. y) Kimchi de iis dicit, Sebaim sunt filii Seba & sunt Orientales ac Austrini terræ Israel ac Tyro, Sidoni & Palestinæ. x) Vid. Jerem. 6, 20. y) Drufius. z) Abarbinel. bus,quo nimium quantum verba videntur propendere, ita ut Calvinus dicat: Stultum esset ac puerile, nimis insistere in ipsa litera. Qui quamvis non exprelle dicat Prophetam allegorice loqui, sibique omnem allegoriarum spem praecidat, quae nihil habeat firmi ac solidi; attamen inquit, aliquam figuram subesse in his verbis, quibus Tyrii & Sidones dicuntur vendendi ac amovendi in terras procul distitas: Idque fiet in gratiam electi populi & Ecclesiae, ac si Judaei ipsi essent venditores. Hinc fortean etiam fit, ut de hujusmodi ambiguitate ac sensu mystico, quem in verbo putat latere, Ribera notet de praedictionum harum eventu verba faciens, quod divinent expositores & multa dicant, sed quae nequeant comprobare. At non omnem allegoriam in eo absolvit, quod sub Judaeis electum populum DEI praefiguratum esse statuat; sed ulterius procedit ac per Tyrum & Sidonem & terminos a) Palestinae intelligit omnes eas gentes, quae accolae olim erant Christianis, a quibus etiam gravi afficiebantur damno; tempus autem, quo retributionem sint laturi praedictam, statuit diem extremi judicii, quo Sanctos illos suos sit excitaturus, quos vendiderant in mancipia, & qui mortem oppetierant in peregrinis regionibus, ut vita rursus donati judicio huic possint adesse ac videre, quo supplicii genere hostes suos velit afficere. Cumque ipsi hostes dicantur vendendi, id ita intelligit, quod illi tradendi sint sanctis, qui insidentes cum Deo thronis ad judicandum impios, eos sint tradituri in aeternam captivitatem. Sub Sabaeis, quibus dicitur eos esse vendituros, innui censet diabolos, quibus erunt tradendi in saevissimos durissimosque cruciatus. Eandem rationem exponendi sequuntur etiam alii & qui ejus aetatem longe b) praecedunt, & qui sequuntur, pedibusque in ejus sententiam eunt. At quemadmodum non infici as ire possum, verba ita explicari posse; ita difficile probatu esse autumo, eum esse solum ac primarium sensum verborum a Prophetis prolatorum, temporisque ac circumstantiarum omnem exhaurire rationem. Quare satius multo existimo arctius paulo ac magis literali sensui inhaerere, licet arduum sit, uti diximus, modum ac tempus præstitucre, quo facta sint aut futura ob historiarum in sacris literis dilucide traditarum inopiam.
units.tr: u) Mercerus seems to think otherwise. y) Kimchi says of them: the Sebaim are the sons of Seba, and they are Easterners and Southerners of the land of Israel, of Tyre, Sidon and Palestine. x) See Jer. 6, 20. y) Drusius. z) Abarbanel. The words seem to lean much too far in one direction, so that Calvin says: "It would be foolish and childish to insist too much on the letter itself." Although he does not expressly say that the Prophet speaks allegorically, and cuts off all hope of allegories as having nothing firm or solid in them, yet he says that "some figure lies beneath these words," by which Tyrians and Sidonians are said to be sold and carried off into distant lands: "And this will happen for the sake of the elect people and the Church, as if the Jews themselves were the sellers." Hence perhaps it comes about that Ribera, speaking of the fulfilment of these predictions and of the mystical sense which he thinks lies hidden in the words, notes that "the expositors guess and say many things, but cannot prove them." But he does not confine every allegory to the point that under the Jews the elect people of God is prefigured; he goes further and by Tyre and Sidon and the borders of Palestine understands all those nations which were once neighbours to Christians and by which they were also gravely harmed. He holds that the time when they will pay the foretold retribution is the day of the last judgment, when he will raise up those saints of his whom they had sold into slavery and who died in foreign lands, so that, restored to life, they may be present at that judgment and see what kind of punishment he wills to inflict on their enemies. And since the enemies themselves are said to be sold, he understands it thus: that they are to be handed over to the saints, who, sitting with God on thrones to judge the wicked, will deliver them into eternal captivity. He thinks that under the Sabeans, to whom they are said to be sold, the devils are meant, to whom they will be delivered for the most savage and harshest torments. Other interpreters also follow the same method of explanation, both those who far precede his time and those who come after and walk in his footsteps. But just as I cannot deny that the words can be explained in this way, so I think it hard to prove that this is the sole and primary sense of the words uttered by the Prophets, and that it exhausts the whole account of times and circumstances. Therefore I think it much better to adhere somewhat more closely to the literal sense, even though, as we have said, it is difficult to fix the manner and time in which the things were or will be done, because of the lack of clearly transmitted histories in the sacred letters.

units.la: Inter Judæos juxta literam ea videtur intelligere Kimchi, cui tamen, cum tempus assignare conetur, quo rerum prædictarum eventus sit futurus, aqua hæret, ambiguus est ac dubius, ut in cæteris, ita & hic; nihilque revera dicit. Quando dicitur: Ecce ego suscitabo eos de loco quo vendidistis eos, expositionis loco adjicit כי ער ישובו לארצם &c. Adhuc enim redibunt in terram suam. Etiamsi locus captivitatis eorum remotus sit, redibunt in terram suam הם או בניהם vel ipsi vel eorum filii vel גם הם גם בניהם tam ipsi, quam eorum filii ההם ipsi in suscitatione mortuorum, & filii eorum שיהיו בזמן הישועה qui erunt tempore salutis. Ex quibus verbis apparet, ejus opinionem non aliam esse, quam quæ ad literam hic sunt prædicta, habitura esse suum eventum, nondum autem habuisse, nec prius habitura, quam instante resurrectione mortuorum & temporibus Messiæ sive Christi, qui salutem allaturus est Judæis, at nondum venit. Quam bene ipsi conveniat cum cæteris Judæis, jam non est officii nostri scrupulose indagare; id unum quod observatione dignum duco, hoc est, ejus sententiam non congruere veritati religionis Christianæ, qua sat superque persuasi sumus Christum jam venille populoque suo salutem attulisse, ejusque secundum adventum, quo mortui refurgent, ac sententiam sunt audituri tam vivi quam mortui, non fore illud tempus, quo hæc prædicta peragat, illosque emat ab una vendatque alteri genti ac humanis rebus sese immisceat, mercaturamque exerceat, quando d) terra, & quæ sunt in ea, conflagrabunt, & impii abibunt in pœnam sempiternam, Matth. 25, 46. Ita ut ad literam intelligi nequeat, si adhuc futurum est, quod hic prædicitur. Facilius concipi potest, quod notat Abarbinel, qui cum ex iis quoque sit qui literæ adhærent, hoc factum esse putat tempore templi secundi, quo Alexander Magnus hæc loca Tyrum & Sidonem vastabat. Nec desunt ex e) Christianis qui ejus vestigiis insistunt. Verba enim, quibus Deus prædicatur filios Judæ & Hierosolymæ, quos vendiderant Græcis &c. suscitaturus ex loco, quo eos vendiderant, impietas fuisse censet Gro-
units.tr: Among the Jews, Kimchi seems to understand these things according to the letter; yet, when he tries to assign the time when the events of the foretold things will happen, he sticks fast, and is ambiguous and doubtful, as elsewhere, so also here; and he really says nothing. When it is said, "Behold, I will raise them up out of the place where you sold them," he adds by way of explanation: "for still they will return to their land" [כי ער ישובו לארצם], etc. "For they will yet return to their own land. Even if the place of their captivity is remote, they will return to their land," [הם או בניהם] "either they themselves or their sons," [גם הם גם בניהם] "both they and their sons," [ההם] "they themselves in the resurrection of the dead, and their sons" [שיהיו בזמן הישועה] "who will be in the time of salvation." From these words it appears that his opinion is none other than that what is foretold here is to be fulfilled literally, but not yet fulfilled, and that it will not be fulfilled before the resurrection of the dead and the times of the Messiah or Christ, who is to bring salvation to the Jews, but who has not yet come. How well he agrees with the other Jews is not now our business to examine scrupulously; the one thing I think worth noting is that his opinion does not agree with the truth of the Christian religion, of which we are fully persuaded that Christ has already come and brought salvation to his people, and that at his second coming, when the dead will rise and both the living and the dead will hear the sentence, that will not be the time when these predictions are fulfilled, when he buys these people from one nation and sells them to another, and mingles in human affairs and carries on trade, "when the earth and the things in it will be burned up, and the wicked will go away into everlasting punishment," Matth. 25, 46. So that, taken literally, it cannot be understood, if what is foretold here is still to come. What Abarbanel notes is easier to grasp, for although he too is among those who cling to the letter, he thinks this was done in the time of the second temple, when Alexander the Great was laying waste these places, Tyre and Sidon. Nor are there lacking among the e) Christians those who follow in his footsteps. For he thinks it an impiety to take the words in which God is proclaimed as going to raise up the "sons of Judah and Jerusalem, whom they had sold to the Greeks," etc., "out of the place where they had sold them." Grotius

units.la: {c} Chr. a Castro. Sa. Menoch. {d} 2. Pet. 3,10. {e} Grotius, Brennius. Grotius per Alexandrum & ejus successores, qui in gratiam Judaicæ gentis multos Judæos in Græcia servientes libertati reddiderint. Quod autem prædicitur Tyro & Sidoni, quod vendere velit filios eorum ac filias in manum filiorum Judæ, qui eos venderent Sabæis, idem evenisse statuit, cum Alexander caperet Gazam, Sidonem & Tyrum. Alii fortem harum prædictionum impletam esse volunt tempore f) Cyri & g) Maccabæorum. Alii omnia ad literam fine dubio esse facta contendunt, quantumvis nulla extet historia, quæ accurate horum eventum describat, quia DEus dixit ea ita fore. Atqui hæc juxta literam ista verba interpretandi ratio omnium videtur planissima rectissimaque. Quodsi quid omni ex parte non possit dici effectum, ad diem judicii id (non autem totum negotium ut quibusdam perplacet) referri posse arbitramur, quo loca hic dicta cum cæteris omnibus vocabuntur ad ulteriorem rationem reddendam de iis, quæ ullo unquam tempore in mundo commiserant. A quo quod non sint eximenda, ex Salvatore nostro discimus prædicente Chorazin & Bethsaidæ, mitius actum iri in die judicii cum Tyro & Sidone, quam cum his, Matth. 11, 22.
units.tr: {c} Chr. a Castro. Sa. Menoch. {d} 2. Pet. 3,10. {e} Grotius, Brennius. Grotius refers this to Alexander and his successors, who, out of favour to the Jewish nation, restored liberty to many Jews enslaved in Greece. He holds that what is foretold to Tyre and Sidon, that God would sell their sons and daughters into the hand of the sons of Judah, who would sell them to the Sabaeans, came to pass when Alexander took Gaza, Sidon and Tyre. Others wish the fulfilment of these predictions to have occurred in the time of f) Cyrus and g) the Maccabees. Others insist that everything was undoubtedly fulfilled literally, although no history survives that accurately describes how these things turned out, because God said that they would be so. Yet this way of interpreting these words according to the letter seems to everyone the plainest and most correct. If anything cannot be said to have been fulfilled in every respect, we think it can be referred to the day of judgement (not, however, the whole matter, as some are quite pleased to hold), when the places mentioned here, together with all the others, will be summoned to give a further account of whatever they ever committed in the world. That they are not to be exempted from this, we learn from our Saviour, who foretold that it would go more gently for Chorazin and Bethsaida in the day of judgement than for Tyre and Sidon, rather than for them, Matth. 11, 22.

units.la: Quod ex hoc loco juxta expositiones traditas necessario fit inferendum, eo redit, Deum quidem interdum permittere, ut populus suus proculcetur, contemtim habeatur ac omni injuria afficiatur a suis & ipsius hostibus; at suo tempore eum liberare velle ex manibus hostium suorum, iisque justam reddere retributionem injuriæ respondentem, qua affecerunt populum suum. Quod DEus hic pollicetur facturum Judæis, qui tunc temporis populus ejus erant, ad omnem ejus populum spectare omni tempore hanc boni eventus promissionem in oppressionibus certum habemus. Rursus ex eo sibi legant suam sententiam hostes ecclesiæ ac populi DEI, quod prædictum est Tyro & Sidoni &c. Peculiare est hoc exemplum ac fpeciminis loco in his atque similibus casibus, de quo certe possumus esse persuasi, quia Dominus locutus est, cujus veritas non est limitata vel alligata huic vel alteri personæ aut loco, sed in omnibus hisce ad eundem modum agit. Varie præterea hæc verba a h) quibusdam explican-
units.tr: What must necessarily be inferred from this passage, according to the explanations handed down, comes to this: God indeed sometimes permits his people to be trampled down, despised and subjected to every kind of injury by their own people and by his enemies; but in his own time he wishes to deliver them from the hands of their enemies, and to render a just retribution answering to the injury they inflicted on his people. What God promises here he will do for the Jews, who were then his people; we hold it as certain that this promise of a good outcome applies to his whole people and holds good at all times in oppressions. Again, let the enemies of the Church and of the people of God take to heart what is foretold for Tyre and Sidon, and so on. This is a notable example, and a sample for such and similar cases, of which we can certainly be persuaded, because the Lord has spoken, whose truth is not limited or bound to this or that person or place, but acts in the same way in all these cases. Moreover, these words are explained in various ways by h) some

units.la: f) Pet. a Fig. g) Trem. h) Vid. Pelic, Mercer. Tarnov. ex V Vinckelm. plicantur,ac si hoc dicto, vendam filios Tyriorum &c. Judæis & illi vendent eos Sabæis, respiciatur ad Apostolos,quatenus eos,qui Christo erant initiati, in remotissimos ablegabant locos,ut alios ad eum converterent Evangelium promulgando,vel hoc genus alia. Verum id verbis tam exacte non congruit, in quibus manifeste conspicuæ sunt malorum minæ,non autem bonorum promissiones,quales sententia illorum exigit.
units.tr: f) Pet. a Fig. g) Trem. h) See Pelic, Mercer, Tarnov., from V. Vinckelm., are explained as if by this saying, "I will sell the sons of the Tyrians" etc. to the Jews, and they will sell them to the Sabaeans, it refers to the Apostles, in so far as they sent those who had been initiated into Christ into the most remote regions, so that by proclaiming the Gospel they might convert others to him; or some other interpretation of this kind. But this does not agree so exactly with the words, in which threats of evils are plainly visible, and not promises of good things, such as their view requires.

units.la: 9. Proclamate hoc inter Gentes, præparate bellum, suscitate fortes, accedant omnes viri bellatores, ascendant.
units.tr: 9. Proclaim this among the nations: prepare war, stir up the mighty men, let all the men of war draw near, let them come up.

units.la: 10. Concidite ligones vestros in gladios & falces vestras in lanceas ; dicat debilis,fortis sum.
units.tr: 10. Beat your ploughshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears; let the weak say, I am strong.

units.la: 11. Congregate vos & venite omnes gentes,& congregate vos de circuitu, eo fac descendere fortes tuos, Domine.
units.tr: 11. Assemble yourselves and come, all you nations, and gather yourselves together round about; there cause your mighty ones to come down, O Lord.

units.la: Sermone finito,quem ab initio v. 4. habuerat hucusque ad quasdam peculiares gentes, videlicet ad Tyrum & Sidonem &c. jam iterum ad illud reverti videtur, quod i) ad omnes gentes pertinet,de quibus locutus erat v. 2. mandato dato, ut animum ad id advertant, quasi a caduceatore,vel alio quodam huic negotio præfecto, esset omnibus proclamatum. Jubentur autem hic præparare bellum, conscribere militem,adornare omnia pro virili,junctisque ac extremis uti viribus, quicunque hostili arderent odio in Deum & ecclesiam ejus gentilium nomine notati, ut obniterentur potentiæ ejus, quæ jam inflicturus est iis, quæ constituto tempore facere constituerat. Quo mandato ita agendi, ac præparandi se ad ei hac ratione resistendum,certo prædicere videtur,etsi jam victoriam videantur reportare de Ecclesia ejus, nemine eorum resistente aut ad resistendum capace,fore tamen aliquando tempus, quo impetum ac sævitiam eorum esset coerciturus, quantus etiam sit eorum furor,quantaque demum nube confluant-
units.tr: Having finished the discourse which from the beginning, v. 4, he had addressed up to this point to certain particular nations, namely Tyre and Sidon and so on, he now seems to return to that which concerns i) all the nations, of whom he spoke in v. 2, a command having been given that they should give heed to it, as if it had been proclaimed to all by a herald, or by some other official appointed for this business. They are commanded here to prepare war, to enlist soldiers, to equip everything to the best of their power, and to use all their strength and resources, all those who burn with hostile hatred against God and his Church, branded with the name of gentiles, so that they may resist his power, which is about to inflict on them what he has determined to do at the appointed time. By this command to act and prepare themselves for resisting him in this way, he seems to foretell with certainty that, although they may now seem to be winning the victory over his Church, with no one of them resisting or able to resist, there will nonetheless come a time when he will restrain their onslaught and fury, however great their rage and however great the cloud in which they gather

units.la: i) Livel. ant adversus eum & electos suos. Quid enim aliud sibi vult hoc jussum præparandi bellum & adornandi, quæ ad id suscipiendum opus effent, quam fe ipsum constituisse,adversus eos apparare bellum illudque illis indicere? Idque ipsum est quod continent verba simpliciter sumta. Quodsi autem ironice accipiantur, (ut quibusdam accipere ea visum est) id innui eis in aprico est,omnes eorum conatus ac molimina,postquam adhibuerint omni nisu ac opera,prout jubentur,in vanum fore ac irrita; non fore ipsos resistendo, nec perferendo ea judicia quæ adversus eos fit exerciturus.Ad quod temporis intervallum hoc respiciat,& quando harum rerũ eventus fit futurus,uti &per quos & in quos; cum hoc loco non fit expresse traditum, neque Sacræ literæ eorum alibi exsertam faciant mentionē, factum esse constat,ut sensus verborum admodum fit ambiguus,atq; in quo interpretibus parum conveniat. Sunt qui ad res gestas Nebuchadnezaris spectari putant: k) Alii autem præcipue ad prælium ad Arbela (inter Alexandrum & Darium.) l) Alii ad ea,quæ futura sunt sub Antichristo circa finem mundi. m) Alii ita accipiunt, ac fi Deus gentes alias contra alias suscitare velit,quæ odio haberent populum suum,ut itafe invicem diriperent. At non est eorum quispiam, qui, quod statuit, comprobatum det. Itaque cum Doctissimo D. Livel. sentirerectius mihi videtur, qui ultimum DEI judicium hic exhiberi autumat, similitudine sumta a bello, quo potentissimi imperatores sitos hostes proterunt & consumunt. Atque ita pro hostibus habet hos prædictos gentiles, de quibus DEus vindictam fumere cupit, quosqueidcirco jubet cogere atque facere,quod mandat. Hanc esse opinionem Judæorum tradit Hieronymus, cui ipse etiam calculum adjicit. Eidem quoque favere R. Salomonem, manifesto apparet ex eo,quod enucleet hæc verba præparate bellum, אכנ תוכלן להלחם כנגרי fi possitis pugnare adversus me. In contrarium aliquatenus eunt,qui eos significari hic censent,quibus provinciam daturus est ultionemfumendi de hostibus suis & populi fui. Cujus sententiæ fautores suo tempore fuisse notat Hieronymus, qui statuebant, hac sanctis gentibus prædicari ut præparentur ad bellum & pro populo Dei dimicent. Qq 3 Eadem k) Tirin. Grot. l) Lyra. Pet. a Fig. m) Calv.
units.tr: i) Livel. against him and his elect. For what else does this command to prepare war and to equip whatever is needed for undertaking it mean, than that he himself has resolved to prepare war against them and to declare it on them? And this is what the words, taken simply, contain. But if they are taken ironically (as it has seemed to some that they should be taken), it is obvious that it is hinted to them that all their endeavours and efforts, however much they exert themselves with every effort and labour, as they are commanded, will come to nothing and be in vain; that they will be unable to resist, nor endure the judgements which he is about to execute against them. As to what interval of time this refers, and when the outcome of these things is to be, and through whom and upon whom, since this place does not expressly state it, and the Sacred Letters do not make any clear mention of them elsewhere, it is evident that the sense of the words is very ambiguous, and interpreters agree little on it. Some think it refers to the deeds of Nebuchadnezzar. k) Others refer it especially to the battle at Arbela (between Alexander and Darius). l) Others to those things that will happen under the Antichrist near the end of the world. m) Others understand it as if God wished to stir up one nation against another, nations that hated his people, so that they might tear each other apart. But there is none of them who gives proof of what he has determined. Therefore, with the most learned D. Livel., I think it more correct to hold that the last judgement of God is set forth here, the comparison being taken from war, in which the most powerful commanders crush and destroy their enemies. And so he regards as enemies these foretold gentiles, against whom God desires to take vengeance, and whom he therefore commands to be gathered and to do what he orders. Jerome reports that this is the opinion of the Jews, and he adds his own vote to it. It is also plainly evident that R. Solomon favours it, from the fact that he explains these words, prepare war, as if you are able to fight against me [אכנ תוכלן להלחם כנגרי]. Some go somewhat in the opposite direction, who think that those are meant here to whom he will give the task of taking vengeance on his enemies and the enemies of his people. Jerome notes that in his time there were supporters of this view, who held that this is announced to the holy nations, that they may prepare themselves for war and fight for the people of God. Tirin., Grot. l) Lyra, Pet. a Fig. m) Calv.

units.la: Eadem videtur olim fuisse mens Cyrillo, qui hæc verba dirigi putat ἐπὶ τὰς ἰδίας προσωνυμίας, ad proprios suos adoratores, ut certos eos reddat ὅτι καὶ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἀμείνοι ἔσονταί αὐτὸ περιασπίζοντes, ipsos fore potiores hostibus suis, se protegente. Nec ab ea sententia admodum abhorrent quidam recentiores interpretes, qui his verbis idem indicari volunt, ac si DEus velit n) colligere suos exercitus, & instruere suas copias, ut pœnas sumat de hostibus ecclesiæ suæ, ac ostendat, o) quantæ vires, qualis exercitus & quanta potentia sibi sint in promtu, quas in auxilium Ecclesiæ vocet ejusque inimicos destruat eo ipso tempore, quo sibi complacitum sit. De tempore autem non inveni-nio ab illis in specie quid esse notatum.
units.tr: The same view seems once to have been held by Cyril, who thinks these words are directed to their own worshippers [ἐπὶ τὰς ἰδίας προσωνυμίας], so as to assure them that they shall be better than their enemies, he protecting them [ὅτι καὶ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ἀμείνονες ἔσονται αὐτὸ περιασπίζοντες]. Nor do certain more recent interpreters differ much from that view, who want the same thing to be indicated by these words, as if God wished n) to gather his armies and marshal his forces, so as to exact punishment from the enemies of his Church, and to show o) what great strength, what kind of army, and what great power he has at hand, which he may call on to help the Church and destroy its enemies at whatever time it pleases him. But I have not found anything specifically noted by them about the time.

units.la: Hanc duplicem explicandi viam cum monstret S. Hieronymus, in eo totus est, ut præferat priorem, qua in re etiam multi p) alii cum eo faciunt, nec est, mea ipsius sententia, improbanda, quippe satis concinna videtur verbisque insigniter respondens. Ea erat etiam, eodem observante, sententia Judæorum suo tempore, vel ante ejus ætatem, quos inter etiam recensendus est aliquatenus Abarbinel, quamvis quoad totum horum verborum sensum singularem videatur tueri sententiam, quam ut nemo unquam, quod sciam, probavit aut secutus est, ita nulla est ratio in ea sita, quare nos in opinionem suam adducat. Quæ cum ita sit, operæ pretium fore arbitror, eam rudi quasi penicillo adumbrare, ut integrum sit penes lectorem de ea judicium. Concedit quidem, hæc verba exponi posse de bello, ad quod suscipiendum DEus suscitabit animos filiorum Edomus & Ismaelis, (qui ex mente & lingua ejus sunt Christiani & Mahumedani) ut intrent vel invadant terram sanctam, ibique alii in alios irruant, donec se ipsos destruxerint omnes; verum extra dubitationis aleam esse putat, Prophetam hic notare resurrectionem mortuorum dicendo י׳ ρ. העורו הגבורים suscitate fortes, & ν. 12. יעורו ויעלו הגוים excitentur gentes & ascendant; usurpando vocem excitare, & verf. 14. המנים בעמק החרוץ multitudines in valle decisionis. Ex his loquendi
units.tr: Although St Jerome sets out this twofold way of explaining the passage, he is wholly intent on preferring the first, and in this many others agree with him. Nor, in my own view, is it to be rejected, since it seems rather neat and answers the words remarkably well. This was also, with the same observance, the opinion of the Jews in his own time or before his age, and among them Abarbanel must be counted to some extent. Yet as to the whole sense of these words he seems to defend a peculiar opinion, which, so far as I know, no one has ever approved or followed, and there is no reason set down in it that should lead us into his view. This being so, I think it worth the effort to sketch it with a rough brush, so that the judgment on it remains with the reader. He does concede that these words may be explained of a war, for the undertaking of which God will stir up the spirits of the sons of Edom and of Ishmael (who in mind and language are, respectively, Christians and Mahometans), so that they enter or invade the holy land and there fall upon one another until they have all destroyed themselves. But he thinks it beyond all doubt that the prophet here signifies the resurrection of the dead, by saying in v. 9, "Rouse up the mighty men," and in v. 12, "Let the nations be stirred up and come up," using the word "stir up" and, in v. 14, "multitudes in the valley of decision." From these ways of speaking

units.la: n) Calvin. o) Danæus. p) Mercer. Riber. Pet. a Fig. Christ. a Castro. Jun. Tremell. Piscator, &c. di formulis concludit,mentem Prophetæ esse hanc,quod qui in terra dormiunt, sint excitandi & resurrecturi ex mortuis,atque eorum quidam inprimis tum ex filiis Israelis, ut interitum ac cladem eorum videant,qui eos persecuti erant; tum ex aliis gentibus, v. g. Sennacherib, Nebucadnezar, Titus, aliisque horum similes hostes, ut una plectantur cum femine suo ac videant ruinam ac cladem regionum suarum, id quod his verbis significari arbitratur: Proclamate hoc inter gentes, præparate bellum &c. non autem, ut R. Salomo explicat τὸ præparate bellum,quod juxta eum valet,si possitis pugnare adversus me. Neque eorum sententiæ locum dat,qui de illis exponunt,qui adversus Jehosaphat pugnabant, prout eam citat Aben-Ezra ex quodam R. Mosf. Mordecai, sed ad illud bellum refert, quod futurum est באחרית הימים ultimis diebus, de quo loquitur dicens: Proclamate hoc inter gentes & omnes sese præparent ad bellum. Quamvis enim hoc inter gentes fuerit notissimum; tamen effugiendi ejus nullus erit locus, quippe certa sunt ac vera nullo non tempore,quæ DEus locutus est. Quando quidem etiam multi Reges ac Principes,qui gravissime Israelem afflixerant in eorum destructione & exilio,magna auctoritate & honore summo adhuc constituti decesserant, ad illos pertinere autumat quod dicitur: suscitate fortes, quasi dicat, expergiscimini, expergiscimini ex somno mortis, accedite & ascendite. Congregabuntur enim ibi omnis generis gentes ad bellum gerendum atq; cum cæteris etiam, qui habitant in pulvere terræ,eo reducentur. Quod autem non omnes in vitam sint reducendi,sed reges duntaxat & terræ dominatores, viri fortes, qui olim contra Israelem pugnabant,ex his verbis apparere asserit: אנשי מלחמה anshe milchamah,viri bellatores, i. e. qui bellum gerebant cum DEO & populo suo,eodem modo quo populus ferox vocatur Anshe milchamah (Deut. 2,14.) quia adversus DEum bellum gerebat verboque ejus fidem nullam habebat. Eos vero, qui ex mortuis resurgent & in vallem Jehosaphat venient (v. 12.) statuit resurrecturos & venturos לא לחרוב non ad pugnandum, sed ad videndum quomodo DEus sedeat ad judicandum gentes de circuitu, & ad spectandum judicium & vindictam,quam hic de iis fit sumturus. Quod ut aliquatenus daret comprobatum, duas juxta quosdam ex sapientibus illorum statuit resurrectiones ex mortuis, quarum prior spectabit reliquum illud quod DEus vocabit (c.2,32.) tempore redemtionis, nimirum ex יחירים מבני ישראל electione peculiares filiorum Israelis, uti & peculiares ex gentilibus, qui gravibus afflixerunt Israelem malis, quorum resurrectio praecedet, ut videant tunc temporis suam ruinam, quae resurrectio non nisi in terra sancta futura fit atque in valle Iehosaphat, de quibus Prophetiam edere putat Iesaiam c.66,24. his verbis: Et egressi videbunt cadavera hominum illorum qui defecerunt a me. Alteram existimant hanc esse secuturam eamque fore magis generalem omnium justorum Israelitarum, qui omni aevo fuerunt, ut & multarum aliarum gentium, quae erant ingenui fideles, quos resurrecturos esse putat in omnibus habitabilibus mundi partibus, ejusque diversis regionibus, ut veritatem DEI & legis in orbe promulgent omnesque homines eo usque disponant, ut uno ore invocent nomen DEI ac unanimi consensu eum colant. Atque haec est sententia, quam in verbis Prophetae latitare sperio sibi persuadet, quam recensendo tot fanaticis ac pertricosis rebus ex suo cerebro enatis conspurcat, ut haud immerito suspicer numerum assentientium ei in hac re fore admodum exiguum. Id quod ipse aliquatenus sensisse dicendus est, cum, si cui haec verba de resurrectione accipere non allubeat, velit, ut excitationis loco ea habeat ad ascendendum ad hoc bellum gerendum quod tunc fiet. At non est corripiendus eo quod ad resurrectionis tempus ex mortuis careferat, sed propter sensum, quem illis affingit. Quod si in idem tempus incidant cum judicio extremo, uti nos ea accipimus, vero simillima mihi videtur diversarum opinionum, quas adduximus, interpretatio, quam praefert doctissimus Livel. quippe quae omnium maxime exprimit confusionem, cui eo tempore omnes gentes erunt nimium quantum implicitae.
units.tr: n) Calvin. o) Danaeus. p) Mercer, Ribera, Pet. a Fig., Christ. a Castro, Junius, Tremellius, Piscator, etc. he concludes that the prophet's meaning is this: that those who sleep in the earth are to be roused and to rise again from the dead, and especially some of them, both from the sons of Israel, so that they may see the destruction and ruin of those who had persecuted them, and also from other nations, for example Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, Titus, and other enemies like these, so that together with their offspring they may be punished and see the ruin and destruction of their lands. He thinks this is what is signified by the words, "Proclaim this among the nations, prepare war," etc. He does not, however, accept that the phrase "prepare war" means, as R. Solomon explains it, "if you are able to fight against me." Nor does he admit the view of those who explain it of the men who fought against Jehoshaphat, as Aben Ezra cites it from a certain R. Moses Mordecai. He refers it rather to that war which is going to happen "in the latter days" [באחרית הימים], of which he speaks, saying: "Proclaim this among the nations, and let them all make ready for war." For although this was very well known among the nations, there will nevertheless be no place for escaping it, since what God has spoken is certain and true at every time. Since indeed many kings and princes, who had most grievously afflicted Israel in their destruction and exile, have died while still holding great authority and the highest honour, he claims that what is said, "rouse up the mighty men," refers to them, as if he were saying: "Wake up, wake up from the sleep of death, approach and come up." For there all kinds of nations will gather to wage war, and together with the rest who dwell in the dust of the earth they will be brought back there. That not all are to be brought back to life, but only the kings and rulers of the lands, the mighty men who once fought against Israel, he asserts appears from these words: "men of war" [anshe milchamah], that is, those who waged war against God and his people, in the same way that a fierce people is called "anshe milchamah" (Deut. 2:14), because it waged war against God and had no faith in his word. But those who rise from the dead and come into the valley of Jehoshaphat (v. 12) he holds will rise and come, not "to fight" [lo lecharov], but to see how God sits to judge the nations round about, and to witness the judgment and vengeance which he will then take upon them. So that he might establish this to some extent, he posits, following certain of their wise men, two resurrections from the dead. The first will look to "that remainder which God will call" (2:32) at the time of redemption, namely the chosen ones [yechidim] of the sons of Israel, and likewise the particular ones of the Gentiles who afflicted Israel with grievous evils; their resurrection will precede, so that they may then see their own ruin. This resurrection will take place only in the holy land and in the valley of Jehoshaphat, and to these he thinks Isaiah 66:24 refers, in these words: "And they shall go out and see the corpses of those men who have rebelled against me." The other, they think, will follow, and will be more general, of all the righteous Israelites who have existed in every age, as well as of many other nations who were free-born believers, whom he thinks will rise in all the inhabited parts of the world and in its various regions, so that they may proclaim the truth of God and of the law throughout the earth, and dispose all men until they call upon the name of God with one mouth and worship him with united consent. This is the opinion which he persuades himself lies hidden in the words of the prophet. By reciting it he defiles it with so many fanatical and most tiresome notions born from his own brain, that I suspect not unreasonably the number of those who agree with him in this will be very small. This he seems in some measure to have perceived himself, since he says that if anyone is not pleased to take these words as referring to the resurrection, he may wish to take them as a rousing to go up to the war that will then be waged. Yet he should not be blamed for referring the words to the time of the resurrection of the dead, but for the sense which he attaches to them. But if these events fall at the same time as the last judgment, as we understand them, the interpretation of the various opinions which we have brought forward that is preferred by the most learned Livelius seems to me most like the truth, since it most of all expresses the confusion in which all nations will then be inextricably entangled.

units.la: Hisce discrepantibus interpretum opinionibus quoad scopum horum verborum in genere praemissis, id operis mihi cumprimis restare video, ut quorundam in specie tradam literalem sensum, quo magis magisque obviam fiat benigno lectori, quomodo huic vel alteri allatarum sententiarum possint applicari. Præparate bellum] Ita nostrates in Textu; at in margine , innuentes eam verbum hebraicum t) קדשו Kaddeschu proprie habere significationem. Quod ut inficias ire nemo potest; ita non minus verum est, illud interdum vsurpari pro, se præparare solenni ratione ad aliquid, quod, cum homines ad id faciendum summa religione sint obligati, nequaquam negligi aut violari potest; hinc præparandi voce satis apte reddi & hic & alibi non tantum Judæi, sed Christiani quoque censuere. Quocirca Chaldæus זמינו עברי קרבא præparate bellatores, & Aben-Ezra הזמינו Kimchi הזמינו præparate. MS. Arab. præparate vos ipsos, vel estote præparati, sive accincti ad bellum, ut & R. Tanchum, qui reddit אערו אלחרב præparate bellum (vel ad bellum) & exponit estote parati, vel præparate vos ipsos ad illud. Unde facile colligendum est, quid sibi velint & LXX. (& quæ eos sequitur Arabica impressa) & Syrus & Vulgatus cum quibusdam recentioribus, quando interpretantur, sanctificate bellum, videlicet, ut omnibus viribus & tanquam fœdere sanctissimo obstricti in id incumberent, vel propterea se præpararent, tanquam sacram rem celebraturi, quæ solemnem u) requirit ϖαρασκευήν. Hunc in finem inquit, suscitate fortes viros &c. העיר Hairu, suscitate (a radice עור Ur, suscitavit). Eadem vox extat v. 7. alio tamen tempore מעירם Meiram, nostratibus reddita, suscitabo eos. Manifestum est, hac conjugatione significare aliquem excitare vel ex somno vel ex mortuis; vel concitare ad aliquid strenue obcundum; qua vero notione hic sit accipiendum, ex sequentium verborum argumento videre licet, quibus est conjuncta, & ex sensu loci, quo hæc referuntur. Etenim qui per viros fortes vel viros belli intelligunt eos, qui aliquando vixerunt, mortui autem in terra quiescunt, id putant referendum ad resurrectionem eorum ex somno mortis ad vitam, quæ est sententia x) Abarbinelis. Qui vero per eos intelligunt, qui tunc temporis adhuc in vivis erunt, eosdem hic censent incitari ad prosequendum animo forti ac strenuo, quod hic illis, Rr . ad
units.tr: With these differing opinions of the interpreters about the general aim of these words set out in advance, I see that what remains for me in this work is chiefly to give, in particular, the literal sense of certain of them, so that it may be more and more evident to the kindly reader how each of the opinions brought forward can be applied to this or that passage. "Prepare war": thus our people render it in the text, but in the margin they indicate that the Hebrew word [קדשו, Kaddeschu] properly has the meaning of "sanctify." No one can deny this; yet it is no less true that it is sometimes used for "to prepare oneself in a solemn manner for something," which, since men are bound to do this with the utmost reverence, can by no means be neglected or violated. Hence the word "prepare" is quite aptly rendered here and elsewhere, and this has been judged so not only by the Jews but also by Christians. Accordingly, the Chaldee has "prepare the warriors" [זמינו עברי קרבא], and Aben Ezra and Kimchi have "prepare" [הזמינו]. The Arabic manuscript has "prepare yourselves," or "be ready, or girded, for war," as also R. Tanchum, who renders it "prepare yourselves for the sword" [אערו אלחרב], "prepare war" (or "for war"), and explains it as "be ready," or "prepare yourselves for it." From this it is easy to gather what the Seventy (and the printed Arabic that follows them), the Syriac, and the Vulgate, with certain more recent writers, mean when they translate it "sanctify war," namely, that being bound by all their strength and as if by the most holy covenant, they should apply themselves to it, or else prepare themselves as if about to celebrate a sacred rite, which requires a solemn preparation [παρασκευήν]. To this end he says, "rouse up the mighty men," etc. [העיר, Hairu], "rouse up" (from the root עור [Ur], to rouse). The same word occurs in v. 7, though at another time as [מעירם, Meiram], rendered by our people as "I will raise them up." It is clear that in this conjugation it signifies to rouse someone either from sleep or from the dead, or to stir someone up to carry out something vigorously. In which sense it is to be taken here may be seen from the subject matter of the words that follow, to which it is joined, and from the sense of the place where these things are related. For those who understand by "mighty men" or "men of war" those who once lived but now rest dead in the earth, think that this is to be referred to their resurrection from the sleep of death to life, which is the opinion of Abarbanel. But those who understand by them those who will still be alive at that time think that here they are urged on to pursue the matter with a brave and vigorous spirit, which here is enjoined on them, namely the business of preparing for war, of going down and going up, that is, of presenting themselves together in the sight of

units.la: t) Did. c. 1. 14. u) Grot. x) Qui proprie hoc verbum videtur intelligere de resurrectione mortuorum ad vitam, ut & Ribera. ad quoscunque demum referas, injungitur negotium scilicet apparandi belli, descendendi ac ascendendi, i. e. simul comparendi in conspectu Dei eo loco, qui ad id ab eo est constitutus. Chaldaus suscitare hic tantundem valere arbitratur atque palam venire, cum reddat יתן בני yetun bigli, veniant publice, quo pacto etiam interpretatur הנני מעורם v. 7. Ecce ego adducam eos publice. Sunt qui x) per יעלו y.aalu, ascendant, alludi volunt ad situationem Judæ vel Hierosolymæ, quo illi jubentur ascendere; quippe altioris habentur situs cæteris extra eam regionibus. Verum equidem est verbum יעלו (ab עלה) proprie denotare ascendere; at ut tam stricte semper sumatur, ut altitudo istius loci, quo vocantur, denotetur, necessarium haudquaquam duco. Forsan hujusmodi y) altitudinis locus, quorsum jubentur ascendere, hic innuitur, quamvis non præcise sit Judæa vel Hierosolyma. Verum necesse non est, ut vi hujus verbi tale quid eliciatur, cum largiori sensu venire videatur, eodemque, quo præcedens verbum ישׁנ, descendant, nempe z) veniant, ut nonnullis placet, quæ notio confirmari ac illustrari potest ex simili usu cujusdam vocis, quæ eandem habet significationem in lingua Arabica. Ea autem est ʿala (ab ʿala) quæ quidem significationis vi, qua pollet ejus radix, proprie denotat, ascendere, atque revera idem notat; communi tamen usu amplius nihil significat, quam a) Adesdum, nulla vel altitudinis vel demissionis loci, unde vel quo quis vocatur, habita ratione. Clarum igitur est, his verbis populum incitari, ut omni, quapotis est, ope se præparet ad bellum, quod jubetur suscipere, id quod etiam emphaticis fit atque continuatur expressionibus in verbis sequentibus, veluti ɉ. 10. Concidite ligones vestros in gladios & falces vestras in lanceas; dicat debilis, fortis sum. Quasi omnia, quorum curam gerebant, eo dirigi deberent rerumque nullarum satagerent amplius, neque earum, quæ spectarent ad usum vitæ necessarium, ut sunt agri, vini, arborumque fructiferarum cultura (quod non obscure innuitur hoc mandato, quo jubentur ligones & falces, quæ necessaria ad
units.tr: t) Didymus, c. 1.14. u) Grotius. x) He seems to understand this word properly of the resurrection of the dead to life, as Ribera also does. Whichever of these you refer it to, the task laid on them is to prepare for war, to go down and to go up, that is, to present themselves at once before the sight of God in the place he has appointed for this. The Chaldee suscitare thinks this word means much the same as to come openly, since he renders yetun bigli, let them come openly, and in the same way he translates הנני מעורם in v. 7 as Behold, I will bring them out openly (Hebrew: הנני מעורם). Some wish y.aalu, let them go up, to allude to the situation of Judah or Jerusalem, to which they are bidden to go up, since it was regarded as a higher site than the regions outside it. Indeed the verb יעלו (from עלה) properly means to go up, but I do not think it necessary that it should always be taken so strictly as to denote the height of the place to which they are summoned. Perhaps a place of such height, to which they are bidden to go up, is hinted at here, although it is not precisely Judah or Jerusalem. But it is not necessary that such a thing be drawn out by the force of this word, since it seems to mean to come in a looser sense, and in the same sense as the preceding verb ישנ, let them go down, namely let them come, as some like to hold. This meaning can be confirmed and illustrated by the similar use of a word which has the same sense in the Arabic language. That word is ʿala (from ʿala), which by the force of its root properly denotes to go up, and really means this; yet in common use it signifies nothing more than come on, without regard to any height or depth of the place from which or to which someone is summoned. It is clear, then, that by these words the people are urged to prepare themselves for the war they are bidden to undertake by every means possible. This is also done and continued with emphatic expressions in the following words, as in v. 10: Beat your ploughshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears; let the weak say, I am strong. It is as if everything they were attending to ought to be directed to this, and they should be concerned no longer with things of no account, nor with those that pertain to the necessary use of life, such as the cultivation of fields, vines and fruit trees. This is clearly hinted at by the command to beat into swords and spears the mattocks and sickles, which are the tools needed for those things;

units.la: x) Jun. Trem. y) Ut sunt nubes, vel aer, si accipiatur de resurrectione vel die judicii, uti 1. Thess. 4, 17. z) Drus. Cast. proficiscatur. a) Vers. u. redditur vox בא in MS. Arab. ad ea sunt instrumenta, concidere in gladios & lanceas) imo ne illarum quidem, quæ ad corporis salutem pertinerent, aut quibus infirmitatibus suis consulerent, non obstante imbecillitate, cui esset obnoxii. Atque his manifesto declarat illius temporis extraordinarium tumultum belliquæ magnitudinem ac gravitatem, qua non licitum foret ea curare, quibus homines plerumque subsistunt, quæque idcirco omnium curantur ac habentur primo loco. Quorum verborum hanc esse mentem, ex contraria loquendi forma dilucide patet, qua pacis atque securitatis notantur tempora: Concident suos gladios in ligones & falces in lanceas, Esa. 2, 4. & Mich. 4, 3. quam descriptionem habet pacis b) Kimchi, quæ bellum, de quo hic sermo est, sequetur. Quod ad reliqua verba, dicat debilis, fortis sum, id est, in prima acie eum statuite nulla ejus imbecillitatis ac impotentiæ ratione habita, eodem tendere patet; quandoquidem usu compertum est, infirmos imbecillibus suis corporibus parcere, nec se ipsos temere ingerere rebus periculo plenis, ut sunt bella & hujus generis alia. Unde non est, ut excusationis loco hoc putemus adjici, sed fortes se gerere debebant, omnesque nervos intendere, ad rite obeundum, quod hic illis injungitur, negotium. Distrahuntur hic quoque interpretes in verbis quibusdam vertendis, quorum, insuper habitis cæteris minoris momenti, hoc unum notatu dignum censemus, quod אתים ittim (in אתיכם ittechem) a quibusdam reddatur c) aratra, ab aliis vomeres (veluti a Syro ܐܬܝܟܡ) ab aliis d) ligones, ab aliis e) Bidentes, vel alia voce denotante hujusmodi instrumentum ferreum f) שחיפרים כהם quibus terram effodiunt. Pari ratione redditur מזמרותיכם Mizmoretechem, a nostr. in textu alia voce; alia in margine. Quarum utraque falcem significante, in eundem conspirare finem, apparet, quippe nihil aliud illis innuitur, quam tantam ferri vim opus fore ad cudenda arma bellica, ut quæ antea hujus metalli in alium usum cesserant, ad hunc necessario jam forent convertenda.
units.tr: x) Jun. Trem. y) As clouds, or air, if taken of the resurrection or the day of judgment, as in 1 Thess. 4, 17. z) Drus. Cast. proceeds. a) The word בא [ba] is rendered in the Arabic manuscript version. "To those are the instruments, to beat into swords and spears." Nay, not even those which pertain to the health of the body, or by which they might attend to their infirmities, notwithstanding the weakness to which they were subject. By these words he plainly declares the extraordinary tumult of that time and the greatness and seriousness of the war, in which it would not be lawful to attend to those things by which men for the most part sustain themselves, and which for this reason are by everyone attended to and held first. That this is the meaning of these words is clear from the opposite form of expression, by which times of peace and security are marked: They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks, Esa. 2, 4. & Mich. 4, 3. This is the description of peace which b) Kimchi, gives, and which the war here spoken of will follow. As for the remaining words, "let the weak say, I am strong," that is, place him in the front line with no regard to his weakness and impotence, it is plain that they tend to the same end, since experience has shown that the sick spare their feeble bodies and do not rashly thrust themselves into perilous affairs such as war and others of this kind. Hence we should not think this is added by way of excuse, but that they ought to act as strong men and strain every nerve to discharge properly the task enjoined on them here. Here too the interpreters are divided over the rendering of certain words. Setting aside the others, which are of lesser importance, we think this one alone worth noting: that the word אתים [ittim] (in אתיכם [ittechem]) is rendered by some as ploughs, by others as plowshares (as by the Syriac), by others as mattocks, by others as two-pronged hoes, or by another word denoting an iron instrument of this kind, by which they dig up the earth [שחיפרים כהם]. In the same way מזמרותיכם [mizmoretechem] is rendered by our translators with one word in the text and another in the margin. Since both of these mean a pruning hook, it is plain that they tend to the same end, for nothing else is hinted at than that so great a quantity of iron will be needed to forge weapons of war that what had previously been turned to other uses of this metal must now of necessity be converted to this one.

units.la: v. 11. Congregate vos ipsos & venite omnes gentes &c.) עושו, congregate
units.tr: v. 11. Gather yourselves together and come, all nations, etc.) [עושו] gather

units.la: b) Quem Drusius in eo sequitur. c) LXX. Vulg. d) Interlin. e) Pagn. f) Kimchi. gate vos. Vox est אסף ἅπαξ λεγόμενον, nullibi in S. literis usitata eoque intelligenda, (ut R. Tanchum ait) ᵴᵃ prout conveniens erit textui, vel connexioni verborum, quibus in sententia est juncta, quare juxta g) hanc regulam denotare eam censet الاجتماع والالتئام congregari & colligi. Qua notione a h) nonnullis interpretibus & veteribus & recentioribus accipitur, quos nostrates etiam in eo sequuntur. Ex ejus deflexione descendit juxta Aben-Ezra & Kimchi aliosque nomen septem stellarum ψιαish, five Arcturus Job. 31, 32. quatenus simul apparent quasi nodatæ. Alii, inquit, i) eandem arbitrantur esse vocem cum חושׁ, quæ notat, fefinare (mutatis invicem literis gutturalibus ח & ע) qua ratione eam sumit R. Salomo, k) nonnullis ex Christianis approbantibus. Vulgatus habet, erumpite, quod primam videtur includere significationem. Ribera exponit illud in hunc modum: Prodite magno cum impetu ex omnibus urbibus vestris & congregamini. Hinc non est, ut, omnibus fere consentientibus ab expositione recedamus, qua noftrat. reddunt, congregate vos. Quæ sequuntur frequentiora sunt, significationisque magis tritæ noftratibus reddita: Et venite omnes gentes & congregate vos de circuitu. Qui textum hebraicum intuiti fuerint accuratius, dubio procul observaturi sunt, verbum נקבצו, Nikbatzu congregamini ipsi, l) formæ esse juxta Grammaticam minus usitatæ, quippe sensu exigente imperativo modo deberet esse, qui juxta m) formam regularem foret הקבצו Hikkabetzu, uti non uno in loco occurrit; Quod quidem exemplum solum hic extare autumat R. Tanchum; verum n) ab aliis huc quoque refertur נלוו Nilvu, Jer. 50,5. pro Nillavu, conjungimini, quanquam secus videtur quibusdam, qui præterito tempore ac propria sumunt forma, quemadmodum & noftrates locum Jeremiæ ita exponunt, etsi imperativo modo reddunt, ut ex eo apparet, quod in prima persona nume-
units.tr: b) Whom Drusius follows in this. c) LXX. Vulg. d) Interlin. e) Pagn. f) Kimchi. Gather yourselves. The word is אסף [asaf], a hapax legomenon (ἅπαξ λεγόμενον), not used anywhere else in Holy Scripture, and so is to be understood (as Rabbi Tanchum says) as suits the text or the connection of the words with which it is joined in the sentence. Therefore, according to this rule, he thinks it denotes [al-ijtima wa-l-iltiam], to be congregated and gathered together. In this sense it is taken by some interpreters, both ancient and modern, whom our people also follow in this. From its derivation, according to Aben-Ezra, Kimchi and others, comes the name of the seven stars, ish, or Arcturus, Job 31, 32, inasmuch as they appear together, as if knotted together. Others, he says, think it is the same word as חושׁ [chush], which means to hasten (the gutturals ח and ע being exchanged), in which sense Rabbi Solomon takes it, with some Christians approving. The Vulgate has "break forth," which seems to include the first meaning. Ribera explains it in this way: "Come forth with great impetus from all your cities and gather yourselves together." Hence we need not depart, with almost everyone agreeing, from the rendering which our translators give, "gather yourselves." What follows is more common, and is rendered by our people in the more familiar sense: "And come, all you nations, and gather yourselves together from round about." Those who look more carefully at the Hebrew text will doubtless observe that the word נקבצו [nikbatzu], "gather yourselves," is a form less usual in grammar, for the sense requires the imperative, which by the regular form would be הקבצו [hikkabetzu], as occurs in more than one place. Rabbi Tanchum thinks this is the only example of it here; but others also refer here to נלוו [nilvu], Jer. 50, 5, for nillavu, "join yourselves," though it seems otherwise to some who take it as a past tense in its proper form, just as our translators also explain the passage in Jeremiah in this way, although they render it in the imperative mood, as appears from the fact that in the first person plural

units.la: g) MS. Arab. habet אתלמץ (quod fortasse debet esse אלתמץ.) h) Chald. LXX. Syr. Arab. impgeff. i) Vid. notas in MS. Arab. Verf. k) Tig. Livel. l) Vid. Tanch. m) In Niph, a קבץ Kabats. n) Vid. Buxtorf. Gram. l.1.c. 14.&c. c. 50. in notis ad Imperativ. numeri pluralis ponant. Verba hujus versus videntur complecti o) partem ejus,quod DEus jubet proclamari inter Gentes, licet a p) quibusdam habeantur pro verbis Prophetæ; verum planiora multo videntur ratione prædicta sumta, quibus q) Prophetæ verba subjunguntur optantis,vel desiderantis id ipsum,quod DEus fieri volebat,nimirum ut congregarentur vel ut faceret congregari omnes gentes atque inde hæc tantum ejus censeri possunt, quæ sequuntur: Eo fac descendere tuos fortes, Domine. In quibus reddendis ac exponendis multum rursus diffident interse Interpretes. Optima vero interpretandi ratio eaque omnium planissima mihi videtur, quam nostrat. sequuntur in textu,quo הנחרת Hancbeth,habent pro imperativo conjugationis Hiphil, a נחרת Nachath, r) descendit, quod notat lingua hebraica interdum, at sæpius multo Chaldaica. Hac notione usurpant illud MS. Arab. Aben-Ezra & Kimchi, nec non recentiorum quidam. Aliis eadem forma eademque radice significat confringere: quam significationem & antiquus Grammaticus Abu-Walid & R. Tanchum, qui habet frangere (ad imitationem Paraphrastæ Chaldæi) præferre videtur, mentionem faciendo prioris, præterquam quod eam improbet. R. Salomo adeo indifferentem eam habet, ut nesciat, quam cui præferat. Etenim multi sunt revera iique viri auctoritatis haud contemnendæ, qui pro posteriori militant,interque eos Chaldæus Paraphrastes & Syrus, quorum uterque reddit per הבר quæ significat confringere. Quo referenda est etiam versio Vulgati Lat. occumbere faciet, Duacensi interpretantibus, there will the Lord make all thy strong ones to be slaine: Quod tamen ad alteram significationem etiam referri poterit. Præter differentiam,quam notavimus in significatione hujus verbi, aliaadhuc est, qua diffident,quanam forma hic præcipue sit sumendum, cum illud non reddant per secundam personam imperativi modi, sed per tertiam futuri temporis indicativi: Dominus confringet &c. Videntur illud accepisse pro s) infinitivo, qui deinde futuri loco habetur, quam construendi rationem verbis insigniter respondere nostrates innuunt,cum in margine scribant, sive, Dominus descendet: Et Anglicana ex Genevensi con-
units.tr: g) The Arabic manuscript has אתלמץ (which perhaps should be אלתמץ). h) Chaldee, Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic: impelled. i) See the notes on the Arabic manuscript version. k) Tigurinus, Livelius. l) See Tanchum. m) In Niphal, from קבץ Kabats. n) See Buxtorf, Grammar, bk. 1, ch. 14, etc., ch. 50, in the notes on the imperative of the plural number. The words of this verse seem to contain a part of what God bids to be proclaimed among the Gentiles, although by some they are held to be the words of the Prophet. But they seem much plainer when taken in the sense given above, where the words of the Prophet are subjoined as those of one wishing or desiring the very thing God wished to be done, namely that all nations should be gathered, or that he should cause them to be gathered; and from this only those things that follow can be considered his: Cause thy mighty ones to come down there, O Lord. In rendering and explaining these, the interpreters again differ much among themselves. But the best way of interpreting, and to me the plainest of all, is the one our people follow in the text, taking הנחרת Hancbeth as the imperative of the conjugation Hiphil, from נחרת Nachath, to go down, which the Hebrew language sometimes means, but much more often Chaldee. In this sense the Arabic manuscript, Aben Ezra and Kimchi, and some of the more recent writers, use it. To others, the same form and the same root means to break. This meaning the ancient grammarian Abu Walid and R. Tanchum seem to prefer, the latter having to break (in imitation of the Chaldee paraphrast), mentioning the former only to reject it. R. Solomon is so indifferent that he does not know which to prefer. Indeed there are many men of no small authority who support the latter, among them the Chaldee paraphrast and the Syriac, each of whom renders it by הבר, which means to break in pieces. To this too belongs the Latin version of the Vulgate, will cause to fall. Yet this too could be referred to the other meaning. Besides the difference we have noted in the meaning of this verb, there is another, over which they differ as to which form should chiefly be taken here, since they do not render it by the second person of the imperative but by the third person of the indicative future: The Lord shall break, etc. They seem to have taken it for an infinitive, which is then held to stand for the future, a construction that our people clearly indicate, since in the margin they write or, The Lord shall go down; and the older English Bible, put together from the Geneva version,

units.la: o) Vide sis Pisc at. p) Druf. ad.sin. v, 10. q) Aben-Ezra. r) Kimchi. s) Merc. Glass. Gram. p. 361. concinnata, then shall the Lord cast down the mighty men; atque in eundem modum nostra Biblia Anglicana antiquiora. Quod ad nomen attinet, quod ab hoc verbo regitur, sicut pro notione sua diversa diverso sensu sumitur, ita & diversa ratione elicitur, quid intelligendum sit per גבורים nostrat. fortes tuos. In quæstionem equidem non venit, quod vox גבורים significet fortes sive potentes; at in eo cardo quæstionis vertitur, quinam per eos sint intelligendi in diversum abeuntibus, quotquot verbo vel hanc vel illam affricant notionem. Qui verbum exponunt per saccere descendere, sanctos angelos Dei autumant innui per fortes, ut volunt Aben-Ezra & Kimchi: הגבורים sunt Angeli. Quam in sententiam etiam Abu Walid & R. Tanchum ait, si verbum accipiatur notione faciendi descendere, per גבורים Gibboreca tuos fortes intelligendi sunt Angeli, qui hoc titulo insigniuntur Psal. 103, 20. quod sint גבורי כח Gibbore Coach, potentes fortitudine: Ita ut verborum sensus atque Prophetæ desiderium eo redeat: t) ... u) o Deus, fac descendere eo (i. e. in eum locum, quo congregabuntur gentes) Angelos tuos & fortes tuos in nostrum subsidium & auxilium; quibus nos adjicere possemus, ut destruant hostes illos qui illuc jubentur congregari; quippe ad utrumque sunt a DEO constituti hi fortes, & ad populum ejus defendendum, & ad inimicos illorum destruendos. Populi sui curam demandat Angelis suis in omnibus eorum viis, Psal. 91, 11. Quo pacto autem illorum ministerio utatur ad hostes illorum destruendum, ex eo apparet, quod extat 2. Reg. 19, 13. ubi Angelus Domini exibat ac percutiebat in castris Assyriorum centum & octoginta quinque millia. Itaque multi etiam sunt interpretum w) Christianorum, qui cum Judæis prædictis hanc vocem ita exponunt, ut concordet cum notione faciendi descendere, quam tribuerunt verbo. At si altera significatione frangendi vel confringendi vel dejiciendi sumatur, non quadrabit huic loco hæc notio nominis; sed tales tunc sunt per fortes intelligendi,
units.tr: o) See Piscator. p) Drusius, ad Sophon. v. 10. q) Aben-Ezra. r) Kimchi. s) Mercerus, Gram. Glass., p. 361. "then shall the Lord cast down the mighty men," as the Geneva version has it; and our older English Bibles read the same way. As for the noun governed by this verb, it is taken in different senses according to the different meanings the verb is given, and so it is explained in different ways: what is to be understood by [גבורים], which our translation renders thy mighty ones. That the word means mighty or powerful is not in doubt at all. The point of the question turns on who is meant by them, among those who take the verb one way or another. Those who explain the verb as to cause to descend think that the holy angels of God are meant by the mighty ones, as Aben-Ezra and Kimchi hold: "the mighty ones are angels." To this opinion Abu Walid and R. Tanchum also say that, if the verb is taken in the sense of making to descend, then by [גבורים] Gibboreca tuos fortes, your mighty ones, the angels are to be understood, who are given this title in Psal. 103, 20., being [גבורי כח] Gibbore Coach, mighty in strength. So the sense of the words and the Prophet's desire come to this: t) ... u) O God, cause your (i.e. to that place, where the nations will be gathered) angels and your mighty ones to come down to our aid and help; to which we could add, that they may destroy those enemies who are ordered to gather there. For these mighty ones are appointed by God for both purposes: to defend his people and to destroy their enemies. He commits the care of his people to his angels in all their ways, Psal. 91, 11. But how he uses their ministry to destroy his enemies appears from 2. Reg. 19, 13., where the Angel of the Lord went out and struck in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand. Accordingly there are also many w) Christian interpreters who, along with the Jews just mentioned, explain this word in such a way that it agrees with the sense of causing to descend, which they gave to the verb. But if the other meaning, of breaking, crushing or casting down, is taken, this sense of the noun will not fit this place; in that case such people must be understood by the mighty ones,

units.la: t) Abu V Valid in נחרת. u) Vel ut R. Tanch. tuos fortes angelos. w) Merc. Tarnov.
