[Diodat.] gendi, qui elate sentientes de potentia ac fortitudine sua, superbe ac arroganter se efferunt atque Deo & populo ejus sese opponunt: hinc R. Tanchum hæc ita exponit intelligit per Gibboreca fortes & potentes tuos, eos qui arroganter se ipsos efferunt adversus te, (illos, qui vocantur tui, i. e. DEI, non quod essent pro, sed contra eum). Quo sensu manifestum etiam est accipere Chaldæum, tum quod verbum reddat significatione confringendi, tum quod personam mutet in affixum sive pronomen reddendo, robur fortium eorum, i. e. hostium congregatorum: nec latum unguem necesse est ab ea sententia discedant, x) quotquot hoc vel simili sensu accipiunt verbum. Atque tunc particula Shammah non est reddenda eo; sed, y) ibi vel z) tunc. Quæ expositiones, quamvis inter se nimium quantum videantur diversæ, tamen tam egregie conveniunt verbis usitatis significationibus acceptis, ut & eruditissimis videamus interpretibus aquam hærere, quam earum inprimis eligant, &, si verum fateri volumus, non potest alia adstrui, quin altera subintelligatur. Si statuatur, Deum esse missurum vel facturum, ut eo descendant ejus fortes, i. e. Angeli ejus, necessario subintelligendum esse nemini non patet, ut confringant robur vel supprimant fortes inimicos ibi vel tum congregatos adversus populum ejus. Rursus si statuatur, Deum velle confringere hostes eorum fortes, facillimo negotio intelligi potest, se id facturum esse opera instrumentorum suorum virtute multo præstantiorum, i. e. Angelorum suorum, qui uti in his, ita & in aliis ejus voluntatem faciunt. Adeo ut utrobique nihil sit, quod non conciliari possit sive inter se, sive cum textu Originali, cujus hæ sunt interpretationes verumque ejus sensum tenentur exprimere, qui verbis respondeat, quibus continetur. Verum si oculos nostros convertamus ad LXX, nec cum harum alterutra, quas inspeximus, nec cum Textu Originali convenire eos reperimus, quippe qui reddunt πραὺς ἔσω μαχατῆς (vel uti alia exemplaria, πολεμιστής) mitis sit pugnator sive bellator; quod cum nequaquam textui hebraico congruat, in opinionem adduxit a) quosdam eos olim aliter legisse,
units.tr: t) Abu Walid, under [נחרת]. u) Or as R. Tanchum has it, your mighty angels. w) Mercerus, Tarnovius [Diodati]. who, proud of their own power and strength, exalt themselves arrogantly and set themselves against God and his people. Hence R. Tanchum explains this thus: he understands by Gibboreca, your mighty and powerful ones, those who arrogantly exalt themselves against you (those who are called yours, i.e. God's, not because they were for him but against him). In this sense it is also clear that the Chaldee paraphrast takes it: he renders the verb in the sense of breaking, and he changes the person into a suffix by rendering the strength of their mighty ones, i.e. of the enemies gathered together. Those who take the verb in this or a similar sense need not depart a hair's breadth from that view. Shammah then is not to be rendered there, but x) y) there or z) then. These explanations, though they seem very different from one another, nevertheless agree so well with the verbs in their usual meanings that even the most learned interpreters are at a loss which of them to choose first; and, if we are to speak the truth, one cannot be affirmed without the other being implicitly understood. If it is held that God will send or cause his mighty ones, that is his angels, to come down there, it is plain to everyone that it must be understood that they will break the strength, or subdue the mighty enemies gathered there or then against his people. Again, if it is held that God wishes to break their mighty enemies, it can very easily be understood that he will do this by the agency of his instruments, far more powerful, that is his angels, who carry out his will in these and other matters. So that on either view there is nothing that cannot be reconciled, either with each other or with the original text, whose interpretations these are and which they are held to express, in a sense that corresponds to the words in which it is contained. But if we turn our eyes to the Septuagint, we find that they agree neither with either of the explanations we have examined nor with the original text: they render [πραὺς ἔσω μαχατῆς] (or, as other copies have it, [πολεμιστής]), let the fighter be gentle, or a warrior. Since this by no means agrees with the Hebrew text, it has led a) some to suppose that they once read it differently from what we read today,

units.la: x) Hieron, Munst, Castal, &c. y) Munst. Tig. z) Drus. Tarnov. a) Drus. Cap. 18. gisse, quam hodie, nempe הנחרת יהיר גבור Hannachat yihyeh gibbor, loco Jehovah, Gibboreca, atque accepisse hann.achat (significatione נוח Nuach vel Nach, requievit, immutata lectione vocis secundae ac praetermissa in ultima tum numeri pluralis nota, tum pronomine affixo: At perquam difficile est captu, tantam legendi diversitatem in textu Hebraico locum habere. Illorum versio videtur magis esse repetita explicatio ultimi hemistichii praecedentis versus, dicat debilis, fortis sum, quam propriae translationis horum verborum. Sequitur eos rursus Arabica impressa الوجع يكون ... qui mansuetus est, bellator esto. Nec satis liquet, cur adeo diverse legerint Graeci interpretes. Id tamen certum habemus, nihil quicquam exinde posse colligi contra Hebraicae lectionis & antiquitatem & veritatem, cum omnia exemplaria insigniter concordent. Quare si suspicioni ullus detur locus, ratio differentiae potius quaerenda est in diversis exemplaribus versionis illorum, si inveniri possint.
units.tr: x) Jerome, Munster, Castalio, etc. y) Munster, Tigurinus. z) Drusius, Tarnovius. a) Drusius, ch. 18. namely [הנחרת יהיר גבור] Hannachat yihyeh gibbor, instead of Jehovah, Gibboreca, and that they took hann.achat (in the sense of [נוח] Nuach or Nach, rested), with the second word read differently, and with the sign of the plural in the last word dropped, and with a pronominal suffix. But it is very hard to grasp that so great a variation in reading could exist in the Hebrew text. Their version seems rather to be a repeated explanation of the last half-verse of the preceding verse, let the weak say, I am strong, than a proper translation of these words. The printed Arabic, al-wajaʿ yakūn ... whoever is meek, let him be a warrior, also follows them. Nor is it sufficiently clear why the Greek interpreters read so differently. This much, however, we hold to be certain: nothing can be inferred from this against the antiquity and truth of the Hebrew reading, since all the copies agree remarkably. Therefore, if any room is given to suspicion, the cause of the difference should rather be sought in differing copies of their version, if these can be found.

units.la: 12. Excitentur Gentes & ascendant ad vallem Josa- phat: Nam ibi sedebo ad judicandum omnes Gentes de circuitu.
units.tr: 12. Let the nations be stirred up and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about.

units.la: Videntur haec verba responsionis loco iis subjungi, quae Propheta petierat vel desideraverat in verbis praecedentibus, quibus declarat se certissime in effectum esse deducturum, quod antea jusserat proclamari, quodque tanto desiderio a Propheta exigebatur, addendo, quo modo & quo loco id fit futurum, nimirum, curando ut congregarentur omnes gentes in eum locum, quem constituisset, ad eas judicandum. יעורו yauru, Excitentur. Eandem vocem, quamvis ablimili forma, habuimus v. 7. ubi inquit הנני מעירם Hinneni meiram, nostratibus, Ecce ego suscitabo eos, ut & v. 9. העירו הגבורים Hairu hagibborim, suscitate fortes, ad quae loca tantum notavimus, quantum judicavimus opus. Jubet ibi, ut excitent alios; hoc loco autem ut se ipsos excitent ac surgant. Verba haec imperativo modo reddita, Excitentur, ascendant, futuri temporis sunt, eoque non minus apte reddi possunt, quam imperativo, b) Excitabuntur, ascendent, sensusque etiam magis erit obvius atque præcedentibus egregie respondens, ubi DEUS in mandatis dat legatis suis, ut proclament bellum, ac porro agant, quæ illis agenda imponuntur, Prophetaque flagitat, ut ea velit esse futura; quali his affirmare velit se id certissime daturum esse effectum. Gentes (sive nationes) suscitabuntur. Verbum יעירו jauru, poterit applicari iis, qui vel ex somno evigilant, vel ex mortuis resurgunt, vel alio modo se suscitant & suscitantur. Hinc futuro tempore c) nonnulli hæc verba interpretantur, excitabuntur, & ascendent: quamvis generalior est eorum interpretatio, qui imperativo ea reddunt veluti nostrates, Excitentur &c. Pari modo leguntur etiam futuro tempore apud d) Chaldæum יתין בגלי Venient aperte &c. quare ex LXX & Vulgato Latino infert Ribera reddens ea imperativo modo, imperatiuum pro futuro poni; at nullius momenti est hæc annotatio, cum Chaldæus cum cæteris Orientalibus, Syris & Arab. alio modo imperativi tertiam personam exprimere nequeant quam futuro tempore non secus atque Hebræi, ita ut ex sensu ac scopo hujus loci judicandum sit, qua forma & a quibusnam hæc verba optime reddantur. Eodem autem redibit, utro hic exprimantur modo. Ubi enim Deus, cujus propositum inhiberi ac eludi nequit, aliquid fieri jubet aut futurum dicit, id solum certissimum est indicium, certissime ita esse futurum. Et ascendant (vel, ascendent ad vallem Josaphat) v. 2. dixerat, & faciam eos descendere in vallem Josaphat, quia magis proprie dicitur descendere, eo quod potius in vallem homines descendant, quam ascendant. Quod quidam ita solvunt, ut respectum haberi dicant ad situationem altiorem Hierosolymæ vel regionis, quo descendentes ibant per hanc vallem sive e) versus eam: At non video huic opinioni aliquid certi inesse, plus veritatis habere arbitramur, quod ante notavimus ad v. 9. de voce יעלו yaulu, eam quidem stricte ac proprie denotare ascendere, nonnunquam tamen nihilominus sumi pro aliquo venire, quo quis est vocatus respectu nullo habito situationis loci, sive fit altior, sive depressior, ita ut neSs quaquam b) Excitabunt & ascendent, Druf. c) Jun. Trem. Pisc. d) Ut & apud Syr. & Arab. e) Druf.
units.tr: These words seem to be added as an answer to what the Prophet had asked or desired in the preceding verses. There he declares that he will most certainly bring to effect what he had earlier ordered to be proclaimed, and what the Prophet had demanded with such longing, adding how and where this will happen: namely, by taking care that all the nations are gathered into the place he has appointed, to be judged there. yauru [יעורו], Let them be roused. We had the same word, though in a different form, at v. 7, where he says hinneni meiram [הנני מעירם], in our idiom, Behold, I will raise them up, and at v. 9, hairu hagibborim [העירו הגבורים], Stir up the mighty men. We have noted these passages only as far as we judged necessary. There he bids others to be roused; here he bids them rouse themselves and rise. These words, rendered in the imperative, Let them be roused, let them ascend, are in the future tense, and they can be rendered no less aptly in the future, b) They shall be roused, they shall ascend. The sense will also be more obvious and will answer the preceding verses admirably, where God in his commands gives his messengers the charge to proclaim war and then to do what is laid upon them to be done, and the Prophet asks that these things should come to pass. In this way God affirms that he will most certainly bring it about. The nations (or peoples) shall be roused. The verb יעירו jauru can be applied to those who either wake from sleep, rise from the dead, or otherwise rouse themselves or are roused. Hence some interpreters render these words in the future tense, they shall be roused, and they shall ascend, c) although the more general interpretation is that of those who render them in the imperative, as our people do, Let them be roused, and so on. Likewise the Chaldee paraphrast also reads them in the future tense, d) They shall come openly, etc. Therefore Ribera, following the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate, infers from this and renders them in the imperative, the imperative is put for the future. But this observation is of no weight, since the Chaldee, together with the other Orientals, the Syriac and Arabic, cannot express the third person of the imperative in any other way than by the future tense, just as the Hebrews do. So it must be judged from the sense and purpose of this passage which form, and by whom, these words are best rendered. Yet it comes to the same thing in which mode they are expressed here. For when God, whose purpose cannot be hindered or mocked, orders something to be done or says that it will be, this is the one sure sign that it will most certainly be so. And they shall ascend (or, they shall ascend to the valley of Jehoshaphat): at v. 2 he had said, and I will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, because it is more properly said to go down, since men go down into a valley rather than up. Some resolve this by saying that regard is had to the higher situation of Jerusalem or of the region, from which those who went down went through this valley, or e) toward it. But I do not see that there is anything certain in this opinion. We judge that there is more truth in what we noted before at v. 9 concerning the word יעלו yaulu: strictly and properly it means to ascend, yet it is nonetheless sometimes taken to mean to come to some place to which one has been summoned, with no regard to whether the place is higher or lower. There is therefore by no means any need to save the stricter meaning by referring these words, with Grotius, to those who are held in underground prisons. [b) They shall be roused and shall ascend, Drusius. c) Junius, Tremellius, Piscator. d) So also the Syriac and Arabic. e) Drusius.]

units.la: quaquam opus fit salvandæ significationi ftrictiori hæc ad eos (cum Grotio) referre, qui in subterraneis carceribus tenentur; qui hic vocantur gentes, vel nationes indefinite atque ita in genere. Unde, præterquam quod effent venturi in conspectum altissimi DEI, optime dici possint ascensuri, quo demum cunque loco id fiet. Locus, quo jubentur ascendere, vocatur vallis Jofaphat, ut & supra v. 2. nec alio alicubi venit nomine in Sacris literis. Quid interpretibus de ea videatur, quamque variæ eorum & discrepantes sint sententiæ, ad illum versum notavimus, quod sufficiens fore remur. Illud tantum addendum hic vel potius repetendum est, vallem Josaphat quidem primo plerisque adstipulantibus esse nomen proprium, eum inprimis denotans locum, ubi DEus gravissima sua exercebat judicia in hostes Juda tempore Josaphat (qui DEum precabatur ut eos judicaret, quia & in se & in populo suo nullam animadvertebat vim eis obstiendi, quod cum audiret DEus eorumque hostes destrueret, locum illum, ubi id factum erat, vocabat vallem Beracha, quia benedicebant ibi Domino) ob exertum autem DEI judicium, ut ait Mercerus, in eo loco, in generale evasisse vocabulum g) cuique loco commune, ubi pari modo potentiam suam exserturus est ad Ecclesiam suam atque populum vindicandum in suos atque illorum hostes, in mentem illis hisce revocans illud, quod tunc temporis actum est, atque certos reddens, se adhuc posse ac velle eodem modo pro illis agere necessitate id exigente. Atque ex eo fit, ut ab aliis, quod supra diximus, & ad locum & ad tempus relatum fit, ubi & quando Deus exercuit vel exercebit ullum grave judicium in hostes ecclesiæ suæ in conspectu, juxta ac in gratiam ejus. Grotius id applicat ad destructionem Persarum per Græcos, quos horum judiciorum statuit executo-
units.tr: Here the nations, or peoples, are called in an indefinite way, and so in general. Hence, apart from the fact that they were going to appear before the face of the Most High God, they can well be said to be going up, wherever the place may finally be. The place to which they are ordered to ascend is called the valley of Jehoshaphat, as also above at v. 2; nor does it go by any other name anywhere in the Sacred Letters. What the interpreters think of it, and how various and conflicting their opinions are, we have noted at that verse, which we judge will be sufficient. This only is to be added here, or rather repeated: the valley of Jehoshaphat is first, as most agree, a proper name, denoting especially that place where God executed his most severe judgments upon the enemies of Judah in the time of Jehoshaphat. (Jehoshaphat prayed that God would judge them, since he saw in himself and in his people no power to resist them. When God heard this and destroyed their enemies, he called that place where it happened the valley of Berachah, because they blessed the Lord there.) But because of the judgment of God thus displayed, as Mercerus says, in that place the name became a general word, common to every place where God in the same way is going to put forth his power to vindicate his Church and people against their enemies and his own. It recalls to their minds what was done at that time, and it makes them certain that he can still and will still act in the same way for them, as the need requires. And from this it comes about that, as we said above, it is applied by others to the place and time at which God has executed, or will execute, any grievous judgment upon the enemies of his Church, in the sight of all and for the sake of his own. Grotius applies it to the destruction of the Persians by the Greeks, whom he holds to have been the executors of these judgments.

units.la: f) 2. Paral. 20, 12. g) Verf. MS. Arabica a Judæo quodam concinnata reddit hoc loco vallis vocandi ad judicium, licet v. 2. proprium nomen retineat. vallis Jehosaphat eoque loco notet hanc vallem diversis insigniri nominibus, utpote quæ diceretur 1. עמק הארץ 2. עמק 3. עמק חמלך 4. גיא הרגה 5. גיא בן הנם.
units.tr: f) 2 Chron. 20:12. g) The Arabic version, put together by a certain Jew, renders at this place "the valley of calling to judgment", although at v. 2 it keeps the proper name. The valley of Jehoshaphat, in that place, notes that this valley is marked with various names, for it is called 1. the valley of the land, 2. the valley, 3. the valley of the king, 4. the valley of slaughter, 5. the valley of the son of Hinnom.

units.la: 1. Vallis decisionis. 2. Vallis Rephaim five Gigantum. 3. Vallis Regis (Gen. 14,17.) 4. Vallis cædis. 5. Vallis filii Hinnom, Jer. 19,6. cutores. Potest quidem pariter referri ad eum locum, ubi DEus colliget omnes die extremi generalis judicii,quo non pauci in specie respici putant; verum non est, ut exinde cum quibusdam colligamus,vallem Josiphat proprie ita dictam,specialem illum locum esse futurum,ubi congregabuntur in universum omnes gentes illo die,ex rationibus supra memoratis; sed potius eos certos DEum reddere voluerit, se tempore constituto effectum daturum, ut omnes ascendant ad id,quod ab eo,quod ibi futurum fit,hoc nomine vocari possit. Ad judicium enim DEI hæc respici, ex eo apparet quod adjicitur: Nam ibi sedebo ad judicandum omnes gentes de circuitu. Nisi id, quocunq; etiam futurum fit loco,eo nomine antea esset insignitum, certe ob hunc DEI actum, ex illo jam merito sibi nomen accerseret. Is autem est, quod ibi velit sedere לשפט lishpot ad judicandum. Sedebo, inquit, non quod DEO proprie possit attribui sedendi vel standi actio,sed de se ipso loquitur b) humano more, vel ea loquendi ratione,qua exprimitur,quod inter eos maxime in usu est, ubi sedere solet judex causam cognoscens ac sententiam cuique ferens. Chaldæus reddit איתגלי ithgele manifestabo me ipsum לשפט lishpot ad judicandum, quæ vox, cujus prior pars ex parte composita est, præfert atque comprehendit in se nomen DEI. Eadem extat supra ꝟ. 2. alia forma נשפטו nishphatti, nostrat. disceptabo cum eis. Complectitur ea dubio procul ejus examen,causæ cognitionem atque juxta eam sententiæ lationem contra personas citatas & ad judicium vocatas pro suis meritis. Personæ vocantur hic מסביב הגוים Omnes gentes (sive nationes) de circuitu, quod pro diversa expositione vallis Josaphat diversimode accipitur, a Grotio, juxta rationem, quam vidimus, pro i) omni vi sive populo Asiæ, ab aliis aliter. Exactissima omnium videtur explicatio,qua id intelligitur de iis,qui colligentur k) ex cunctis terræ partibus, vel omnibus l) nationibus congregatis ut judicentur.
units.tr: It may indeed be referred in the same way to the place where God will gather all the nations on the day of the final general judgment, as some think many are particularly inclined to do. But it does not follow, as some conclude, that the valley of Jehoshaphat, properly so called, will be that special place where all the nations will be gathered together on that day, for the reasons mentioned above. Rather, God wished to assure them that at the appointed time he would bring it about that all should come up to that place, which could be called by this name from what would happen there. For that this refers to the judgment of God appears from what is added: For there I will sit to judge all the nations round about. Unless the place, wherever it may be, had already been marked by this name, it would surely have deserved to take the name from this act of God. What he means is that he will sit there lishpot, to judge. I will sit, he says. This does not mean that sitting or standing can properly be attributed to God, but he speaks of himself after the human manner, or in that mode of speech by which is expressed what is most common among men, when a judge sits to hear a case and to pronounce sentence on each person. The Chaldee renders it ithgele [איתגלי], I will manifest myself, lishpot [לשפט], to judge. This word, whose first part is partly compounded, carries and includes within itself the name of God. The same word occurs above at verse 2 in another form, nishphatti [נשפטו], which our people render I will plead with them. Without doubt it includes the examination of the case, the hearing of it, and the pronouncing of sentence in accordance with it against the persons summoned and called to judgment, according to their deserts. The persons here are called all the nations (or peoples) round about, hamisabib hagoyim [מסביב הגוים]. Their meaning is taken differently according to the different interpretation of the valley of Jehoshaphat. Grotius takes it, in line with the reasoning we have seen, to mean i) all the force or people of Asia, and others differently. The most exact of all interpretations seems to be that by which it is understood of those who will be gathered k) from all parts of the earth, or from all the l) nations brought together to be judged.

units.la: Quodsi hæc verba non primario dicta sint de extremo generali judicio; exprimendi tamen formulæ tales sunt, ut in mentem id iis Ss 2 addu-
units.tr: But even if these words were not primarily spoken of the last general judgment, the forms of expression are nevertheless such that they bring that judgment to the minds of those who read them,

units.la: b) Drus. & vid. Grot. in v. 2. i) Grot. k) Calv. l) Pet. a Fig. m) Quod quibusdam videtur nimis coactè Calv. in v. 12. adducere possent, expectandumque esse tempore a DEO constituto, certo sibi persuaderent. Idem faciunt sequentia verba proximi versus, quibus judicium, quod exerciturusest,jubet exequi per illos, quibus ad ministerium suum constituit, uti
units.tr: b) Drusius, and see Grotius on verse 2. i) Grotius. k) Calvin. l) Pet. a Fig. m) Some think this is too forced, as Calvin says on verse 12, and they could be brought to be certain that they must wait for the time appointed by God. The following words of the next verse do the same, in which he orders that the judgment he is going to execute be carried out by those whom he has appointed to his ministry, as

units.la: 13. Immittite falcem, quia maturuit messis, venite, descendite, quia plenum est torcular, exuberant dolia, nam multa est malitia eorum.
units.tr: 13. Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe; come, go down, for the winepress is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.

units.la: Si quis quaerat, quinam sint ii,qui hic notantur,responsum habeat, eosdem esse,qui paulo ante vocabantur fortes DEI, secundum versionem verborum v. 11. Eo fac descendere tuos fortes. Quod hic jubentur agere ad illud judicium exequendum, quod contra gentes exercebit,metaphoricis continetur terminis ex eo desumtis, quod solent agere agricolæ cum frumento; in quod falcem immittunt maturitatem adeptum; & cum vino, cujus uvas decerpunt ac torcularibus inferras premunt atque calcant,id quod ad homines & hostes relatum nihil aliud denotat,quam eorum ruinam ac plenam destructionem. Quod hic exstat, similibus expressionibus illustrari potest,quas non difficile reperire est alibi in Scriptura Sacra. Quod ad primum hujus versus membrum attinet,pari ferme modo legimus apud Matth. 13,39. Christum sermone habito de tempore,quo eradicandi sint impii cum zizaniis ab eo sub tritico collati in agro mundi, dixisse:Messis est consummatio mundi & messores sunt Angeli, quos Filius hominis mittet, & colligent e regno illius omnia scandala & omnes facientes iniquitatem, & conjicient illos in fornacem ignis, v. 41. & 42. Ita & Apoc. 14,15. ubi juxta priushujus versiculi membrum Angelus magna voce ad eum clamabat,qui insidebat nubi: Immitte salcem tuam & mete, quia venit tibi tempus metendi; nam aruit messis terræ. Et juxta alterum v. 18. ubi itidem Angelus dicitur clamasse ad eum,qui habebat falcem acutam, dicens: Mitte falcem tuam acutam & vindemia botros vini terræ: nam maturæ sunt ejus uvæ. Et (pergit) Angelus misit falcem suam in terram,& conjecit id in magnum torcular excandescentiæ DEI. Ex quibus locis manifestum evadit,demetere id מא שאנה אן יחכר ma shanaho an yohfad, cujus proprii sive conditio est demeti sive defecari,ut interpretatur R. Tanchum vocem קציר Katzeir,noftrat.messis,vel ut habet M.S.Arab. אלמסתחצר quod aptum est defecari vel meti; & calcare sive premere uvas decerptas & torcularibus sive doliis injectas, ut calcentur & premantur, aptè admodum usurpari ad exprimendum & describendum executionem judiciorum Dei in impios suos inimicos, quibus succidentur atque subigentur justo suo tempore. Quodsi hoc applicatur, quo non pauci speciliter spectare id putant,ad magnum & ultimum diem generalis judicii, quod Dominus per ministros suos Angelos sanctos executuros est, non parum id confirmari liquet a Salvatore, cum apud Matthaum expresse dicat: Messis est consummatio Mundi, & messores sunt Angeli. At cum non expresse determinetur temporis spatium, quo DEus sedebit ad judicandum omnes gentes de circuitu, & messis, alii potius id referunt, uti diximus,ad quandam aliam cladem, quam alio quocunque tempore accepturi sint hostes Dei & ecclesiæ ad internecionem usque, iis administrantibus, quibus hoc onus imponet, quando ei tempestivum videbitur, id quod his verbis innuit: Quia maturuit messis, torcular est plenum, quibus indicat, quod planius exprimit verbis sequentibus, multam esse malitiam eorum, i. e. eam eo usque se extendere atque in tantam mensuram excrescere, ut non amplius eam possit ferre; atque adeo maturos esse satis,qui destruantur,quod jam certissime sit futurum,&quod sequens versus complectitur,dies Domini prope sit. Quænam temporis periodus per hunc diem Domini & messem maturam intelligenda sit, cum expresse non habeatur, æqua est omnibus libertas id ad insigne quoddam judicium vel destructionem applicandi, quod Deus jam jam exercuit contra quandam gentem sive populos, qui se hostes præbuerunt populo ipsius atque eum persecuti sunt, vel aliquando exercitturus est ante finem hujus mundi; verum non possunt aliquo commodius trahi quam ad n) ultimum diem generalis judicii, quippe tunc latissime exactif-
units.tr: If anyone asks who these are who are meant here, let him take the answer that they are the same ones who were called a little earlier "the mighty ones of God", according to the rendering of verse 11: "Bring down your mighty ones there." That they are commanded here to carry out that judgment, which he will exercise against the nations, is conveyed in metaphorical terms taken from what farmers customarily do with grain, into which they put the sickle when it has reached ripeness, and with wine, whose grapes they pick and carry to the presses, pressing and treading them. When this is applied to men and enemies, it signifies nothing other than their ruin and complete destruction. What is said here can be illustrated by similar expressions, which are not hard to find elsewhere in Holy Scripture. As for the first part of this verse, we read in much the same way in Matthew 13:39, where Christ, speaking of the time when the wicked, gathered with the tares sown among the wheat in the field of the world, are to be uprooted, said: "The harvest is the end of the world, and the reapers are the angels," whom the Son of Man will send, and they will gather out of his kingdom all offences and all who work iniquity, and cast them into the furnace of fire, vv. 41 and 42. So too in Revelation 14:15, where, according to the first part of this verse, "an angel cried with a loud voice to him who sat on the cloud: Put in your sickle and reap, for the time to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is dried up." And according to the second part, v. 18, where likewise an angel is said to have called to him who had the sharp sickle, saying: "Put in your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, for its grapes are ripe." And (it goes on) "the angel thrust his sickle into the earth and cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God." From these passages it is clear that to reap is ma shanaho an yohfad, whose proper sense or condition is to be cut down or harvested, as R. Tanchum interprets the word qatzir [קציר], our "harvest"; or, as the Arabic manuscript has it, almustahsar, which fits being cut down or reaped; and to tread or press grapes that have been picked and thrown into the presses or vats, so that they are trodden and pressed. This is quite fittingly used to express and describe the execution of God's judgments against his impious enemies, who will be cut down and subdued at his appointed time. If this is applied, as not a few specifically think it should be, to the great and last day of the general judgment, which the Lord is to carry out through his holy angels as ministers, it is clearly not a little confirmed by the Saviour, since in Matthew he expressly says: "The harvest is the end of the world, and the reapers are the angels." But since the span of time in which God will sit to judge all nations round about is not expressly determined, others refer the harvest and the winepress, as we have said, to some other destruction, which the enemies of God and of the Church will suffer, to utter extermination at whatever time, by those whom he will charge with this burden when it seems fitting to him. This he hints at with the words: "For the harvest is ripe, the winepress is full," by which he indicates what he expresses more plainly in the following words, "for their wickedness is great", that is, that it extends so far and grows to such a measure that it can no longer bear it; and therefore those who are to be destroyed are ripe enough, which will most certainly come to pass, and which the next verse embraces: "the day of the Lord is near." As to what period of time is to be understood by this day of the Lord and the ripe harvest, since it is not expressly stated, all are free to apply it to some notable judgment or destruction, which God has already just now executed against some nation or peoples who showed themselves enemies to his people and persecuted them, or which he will at some time execute before the end of this world; but they cannot be drawn more fittingly to anything than to n) the last day of the general judgment, since then it will be most fully carried out.

units.la: n) Vide fis Diodat. in v.1. & Livel. in v. 9.
units.tr: n) See also Diodati on verse 1 and Livelly on verse 9.

units.la: exactissimeque fiet, quicquid haec verba comprehendere putaveris. Nec quicquam huic rei obstat, quod prope dicatur hic dies, cum adesse ea dicuntur, quae a Deo sunt determinata, utpote quae tam certo sunt futura, ac si jam essent facta. Hominibus quidem id temporis longum videtur; at secus se res habet in Deo, quippe apud eum unus annus est instar mille annorum, & mille anni instar unius diei (2. Pet. 3, 8.) & quod procul abest, ei est in promptu, quoque futurum, haud secus, ac si praesens esset. Porro his verbis, messis est matura, etiam innuit, Deum quidem tardum esse in exigendis rationibus, nec eo ipso momento exsequi judicium adversus suos ac ecclesiae suae hostes, quod videntur mereri; verum non esse segnem veluti homines, aut earum rerum socordem, quae in terris contingunt, sed constituisse certum quoddam temporis spatium omnibus judicandis, prout poenam vel mercedem meriti fuerint, quo adventante ita se geret, ut utrumque omni luce futurum sit clarius illustriusve. Devoverat Deus Emorraeos & incolas Canaan, quos exitio traderet propter iniquitatem eorum magnam, Abrahamoque & ejus semini promiserat eorum regionem in possessionem; attamen multos annos distulit hoc judicium in eos ad quartam usque generationem, idque ob hanc cumprimis rationem; Quia nondum completa est iniquitas Emorraeorum, Gen. 15, 16. Nimirum eo usque illis volebat parcere atque respiscentiae tempus largiri; verum cum perseverantes in eadem cordis pertinacia ad mensuram illam pervenissent, nihil certius suturum erat, quam ut eam coerceret, illosque summo traderet exitio. Eodem modo eum egisse olim cum antiquo mundo Noachi tempore res manifesta est, cui non obstante hominum impietate, ob quam spiritus ejus non semper cum illis disceptare constituerat, centum adhuc & viginti annos concedebat, ut mensuram peccatorum suorum implerent, Gen. 6, 3. At cum omnem carnem videret corrupisse viam suam super terram, finis, inquit, universae carnis adventat coram me, quia plena est terra violentia ab ipsis; & ecce ego perditurus sum ipsos cum terra, v. 12, 13. Pari hic eum processurum ratione, cum illis, quos dicit se esse judicaturum, sat superque quae que ipse declarat hujusmodi exprimendi formis, quæ non obscure innuunt, se eo usque indulsisse peccatis eorum, donec ad maturitatem pervenissent, quaad messem forent apti atque impietatis succo infarcti, haud secus ac maturæ uvæ, quæ liquorem attrahere succo,quo turgent, abundantes desinunt & presse dolia implent. Nec dubium est, quin talis maturitas & impietatis excessus in iis, de quibus hic sermo est, notetur hujusmodi verbis, messis maturuit, plenum est torcular, exuberant dolia. Quippe id planum fit ex sequentibus, quæ omnibus perspicuum reddunt sensum, nam multa est malitia eorum, adeo ut jam essent parati ac maturi, qui perderentur, non aliter ac messis matura, quæ meteretur, vel uvæ liquore plenæ, quæ in torcular conjicerentur atque presse doliis inderentur, quæ præ nimia ejus liquoris abundantia exundant. Quod attinet ad sensum literalem & significationem horum verborum, non est hic iterum eadem mens interpretibus. Verbum ירד Redu, a nostratibus redditum est, descendite (quo ipsis convenit fere cum plerisque aliis) ac si esset a ירד yarad, quod significat descendere. Secus autem sentit R. Salomo Jarchi, qui id deducit a radice ירד radah dominari, & exponit hic לשון כבישורת וירידי significatione subjectionis & dominationis, quo sensu usurpatur Gen. 1, 28. וירדו בדגת הים Et dominamini piscibus maris. Chaldæus habet רשישו conculcare (verbo præcedenti בא venite reddito per היתו (hutu, descendite) quod non procul abest a significatione hac dominationis, quamvis magis videatur congruere calcandi significatio, qua etiam gaudet in lingua Arabica ꞓ Rada, quod notat calcationem duram, veluti o) calcavit terram ungulis suis equus &c. Quod idem, sive a ירד yarad, sive a ירה rada deducatur (ab horum autem alterutro deducendum est) in hebraica lingua eandem habere significationem, haud temere conjiciendum est ex interpretatione Græca καταῖτε, Syriaca &c. Arab. impress. quibus omnibus est, calcate, vox, quæ propria est loquentibus de uvis in torcularibus, cujus quoque usus alibi in scriptura est, etsi id alio verbo tunc hebraice invenimus expressum. Adeo ut, si descen-
units.tr: Nor does anything stand in the way of this, that this day is said to be near, since things determined by God are said to be at hand, inasmuch as they are as certain to come as if they were already done. To men, indeed, that time seems long; but it is otherwise with God, for with him one year is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8), and what is far off to him is at hand, and what is future is just as present as if it were now. Moreover, by these words, the harvest is ripe, he also indicates that God is indeed slow in calling men to account and does not carry out judgment against his enemies and the enemies of his Church at that very moment, though they seem to deserve it; yet he is not idle, as men are, or careless of the things that happen on earth, but has appointed a certain fixed span of time for judging all, according to the punishment or reward each has deserved, and when it arrives he will so conduct himself that both will be clearer and more illustrious than the light. God had devoted the Emorites and the inhabitants of Canaan to destruction, because of their great iniquity, and had promised their land in possession to Abraham and his seed; yet he deferred this judgment upon them for many years, down to the fourth generation, and that chiefly for this reason: "Because the iniquity of the Emorites is not yet full" (Gen. 15:16). Clearly he wished to spare them until then and to grant them time for repentance; but when they, persisting in the same obstinacy of heart, had reached that measure, nothing was more certain than that he would restrain them and deliver them to utter destruction. That he dealt in the same way with the old world in the time of Noah is also plain. Notwithstanding the impiety of men, for which his Spirit had resolved not always to contend with them, he still allowed them a hundred and twenty years, so that they might fill up the measure of their sins (Gen. 6:3). But when he saw that all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, "the end of all flesh," he said, "has come before me, for the earth is full of violence through them; and behold, I will destroy them with the earth" (vv. 12, 13). He will proceed in the same way here with those whom he says he will judge; and what he himself declares by such forms of expression, which obscurely hint that he has indulged their sins until they came to maturity and were fit for the harvest and stuffed with the juice of impiety, just as ripe grapes, which draw in the liquid by which they swell, end up abundant and fill the vats when pressed. Nor is there any doubt that such ripeness and excess of impiety in those of whom he speaks is marked by these words: "the harvest is ripe," "the winepress is full," "the vats overflow." Indeed, this becomes plain from what follows, which makes the sense clear to everyone: "for their wickedness is great," so that those who were to be destroyed were already prepared and ripe, just as a ripe harvest is to be reaped, or grapes full of juice are to be thrown into the winepress and pressed into vats, which overflow from the excess of their juice. As for the literal sense and meaning of these words, the interpreters are again not of one mind. The verb ירד [Redu], rendered by our people go down (in which most others agree with them), is taken as if it were from yarad, which means to go down. But R. Solomon Jarchi thinks otherwise. He derives it from the root radah, to rule, and explains here that it is used in the sense of subjection and dominion, in which sense it is used in Genesis 1:28: ורדו בדגת הים [veradu bidgat hayam], "and have dominion over the fish of the sea." The Chaldee has rishu, to tread down, rendering the preceding word "come" by hutu ("go down"), which is not far from this sense of dominion, though the sense of treading seems more fitting, and this sense also belongs to the Arabic word Rada, which signifies a hard treading, as when a horse has trodden the ground with its hoofs, and so on. That this same word, whether derived from yarad or from rada (one of which must be the derivation), has the same meaning in Hebrew, may reasonably be conjectured from the Greek rendering katēte [καταπατεῖτε], and from the Syriac and the printed Arabic, all of which have the word tread, a word proper to those speaking of grapes in winepresses, the use of which also occurs elsewhere in Scripture, although there we find it expressed in Hebrew by another word. So that, if go down is taken in the sense of descending, as most do, it at the same time designates the task they are to undertake by descending, namely, to tread the ripe grapes that are ready to be thrown in, or already thrown into the winepresses, by which they would then overflow and be filled with so much juice.

units.la: o) Kamus Gol. descendendi notione sumatur, ut fit a plerisque, una etiam designet, cui rei operam sint daturi descendendo, nimirum, ut calcarent maturas uvas, quæ forent paratæ, ut injicerentur, vel injectæ jam essent torcularibus, quibus adeo abundarent atque succi tantam suppeditarent copiam, ut dolia sint impleturi ad inundationem usque. Ita enim inquit השיקו היקביכם Exuberant dolia. Eadem sunt verba (quamvis alio sensu, tempore scil. futuro) quæ habemus cap. 2,24. ישיקו jafhiku exuberabunt, ubi ample satis tum de derivatione, tum de significatione hujus verbi locuti sumus, ita ut ulteriori opera jam non egeamus. Quod autem ex prædictis hoc loco repetitione fit dignum, eo tendit, hoc verbum vi notionis, quam diversimode obtinet, significare abundantiam & ingentem mensuram rei subjectæ, sicuti eo loco & hic magnam copiam liquoris vel succi uvarum, atque exinde etiam ejus rei abundantiam, quæ cum hujusmodi uvis comparatur, quod ex sequentibus verbis, multa est malitia eorum, apparet, malitiam talem esse intelligendam, quæ sit magna mensura & abundans, qua mente etiam a p) plerisque accipitur, eos scilicet tam plenos esse malitia quam uvas succo. Alii tamen id maluunt explicare de magna sanguinis effusione earum scelestarum gentium, quæ hic memorantur, quæ ita destruendæ sunt hoc bello, prout DEus, qui satis diu illis pepercerat, constituto tempore decreverat. Sic Kimchi היא משיר לשפיכות הדם Metaphora est de effusione sanguinis, cum earum venerit tempus ut interficiantur: quia multa est earum malitia, quam fecerunt Israelitis, ipsi & patres eorum. Pariter & Grotius, Exuberent dolia i. e. multus fundatur sanguis, qui cum vino comparari solet. Sanguine hic intelligit exercituum magnorum ex omni Asia campos impletum iri, quos putat comparari cum torculari uvarum pleno: verbaque, nam multa est malitia illorum, subdere rationem, quare jubeat cruentam hanc cædem atque destructionem eorum exequi, nimirum; ita merucre illæ gentes. Verum antiquior multo est hæc expositio, quippe jam olim a Paraphraste Chaldæo in hanc mentem hæc verba explanata sunt: Emittite in eos gladium; etenim p) Calov. Livel. etenim pervenit tempus finis eorum, descendite, conculcate interfectos fortes eorum, sicut quod calcari solet in torculari: fundite sanguinem eorum, quia multiplicata est eorum malignitas. Nec dicereri possumus, quod alterutri harum comparationum haec verba applicari queant, sive ut nequitia illorum ingens conferatur cum abundanti liquore in uvis maturissimis; sive cum vino magna copia elicito ex talibus uvis effusio multi sanguinis, prout conditio illorum exiget, quos quilibet hic censuerit intelligendos. Si quis putet sermonem hic esse de tali quorundam hostium ecclesiae vel populi sui destructione, quam DEUS illis aliquando illaturus est hac rerum humanarum facie adhuc existente, comparatio succi uvarum cum sanguine propria erit ad id rite praefigurandum, altera alterius abundantem effusionem denotante, (licet nec altera adeo impropria dicenda sit, qua malitiae magnitudo cum liquoris uvarum plenitudine & redundantia doliorum comparatur) atque tum omnino rationem his ultimis verbis subesse dicendum est, cur tanta copia sanguis effundendus sit, sicut vinum ex uvis in torculari excalcatum & doliis reconditum, videlicet, quia magna est illorum malitia.
units.tr: o) Kamus Gol. If the word is taken in the sense of descending, as most do, it also indicates the task for which they would be descending, namely to tread the ripe grapes, which had been gathered so that they could be put into the winepresses, or had already been put in, so that they would abound and yield such a great quantity of juice that they would fill the casks to overflowing. For it says השיקו היקביכם [jafhiku hayekebim] The vats overflow. These are the same words (though in a different sense, namely in the future tense) that we have in ch. 2:24, ישיקו [jafhiku], they shall overflow, where we have spoken amply enough both about the derivation and the meaning of this verb, so that we need no further labour here. What is worth repeating from what has been said, however, is this: the verb, by the force of the meaning it carries in its various uses, signifies abundance and a very great measure of the thing it governs; here, as in that passage, it signifies a great quantity of the liquid or juice of the grapes, and so also an abundance of that thing which is compared with such grapes. This is clear from the following words, their wickedness is great. The wickedness is to be understood as something of great and overflowing measure, and in this sense many take it as well, namely that they are as full of wickedness as the grapes are of juice. Others, however, prefer to explain it of the great shedding of blood of those wicked nations mentioned here, who are to be destroyed in this war, as God, who had spared them for a long time, had decreed at the appointed time. So Kimchi: היא משיר לשפיכות הדם [hi meshal lishfekhot hadam], It is a metaphor for the shedding of blood, when the time has come for them to be slain, because their wickedness is great, the wickedness they committed against the Israelites, they and their fathers. Likewise Grotius: the vats overflow, that is, much blood is poured out, which is usually compared with wine. By blood he understands that the plains will be filled with great armies from all Asia, which he thinks are compared to a winepress full of grapes; and the words for their wickedness is great give the reason why he bids them carry out this bloody slaughter and destruction, namely: for those nations have deserved it. But this explanation is much older, for already long ago the Chaldee paraphrast explained these words in this sense: "Send the sword against them; for the time of their end has come. Go down, tread their mighty dead, as is trodden in the winepress; pour out their blood, because their wickedness has been multiplied." Nor can we deny that these words may be applied to either of these comparisons: whether their great wickedness is compared with the abundant juice in very ripe grapes, or with the wine drawn in great quantity from such grapes, and the outpouring of much blood, as their condition shall require, which anyone may judge to be meant here. If someone thinks that the discourse here is about the destruction of certain enemies of the Church or of his people, which God will at some time inflict upon them while this face of human affairs still remains, then the comparison of the juice of the grapes with blood will be fitting to prefigure this properly, the one denoting the abundant outpouring of the other (although the one is not to be called so improper either, in which the greatness of wickedness is compared with the fullness of the grape juice and the overflowing of the casks). And then it must be said that the reason for these last words lies entirely in why such a quantity of blood is to be poured out, just as wine is trodden from the grapes in the winepress and stored in casks, namely: because their wickedness is great.

units.la: Quod si autem ad gravissimum illud judicium referantur, quo omnes impios peccatores DEUS judicaturus est in fine mundi, rationis loco hic erit impietatis hominum in hoc mundo gravitas cum torcularibus plenis & doliis exundantibus collata, (simul cum hac praecedenti expressione, quoniam messis maturuit) quare DEUS jam velit sedere ad eos judicandum. Atque ita subjecta dici possunt, ut antea notavimus, haec ultima verba: malitia eorum est magna, ut planius exprimant, quod antea erat indicatum verbis figuratis, DEO scilicet negotium fore cum hostibus suis & ecclesiae suae, malitia eorum ad summum apicem provecta, quam DEUS haud ulterius ferre constituerit. Hinc sententia ac decreto lato, ut vindictam de iis sumat, ac demetat eos, ut frumentum messi aptum, & calcet in torculari vindictae suae, veluti uvae maturae ac succo plenae premuntur & calcantur, nulla iis erit evadendi via, nec extricabunt se vel sua potentia, vel multitudine, qua haftenus alios antecesserant, & adhuc antecessuros sibi persuadent, ex manibus fortium illorum, quos jam missurus erit judicia sua exsecutum. Quanta etiam polleant potestate, quanto excedant demum numero, cuncti tamen congregabuntur in eo loco, ubi sententiam suam adversus eos latam exsecuturus est, id quod sequentia verba expresse docent.
units.tr: But if these words are referred to that most weighty judgment by which God will judge all wicked sinners at the end of the world, then the gravity of human impiety in this world, compared with full winepresses and overflowing casks, will here serve as the reason (together with the preceding expression, for the harvest is ripe) why God now wishes to sit down to judge them. And so these last words, as we noted before, can be taken as the subject, so that they express more plainly what was indicated before in figurative words: that God will have a matter with his enemies and with his Church, their wickedness having risen to its highest peak, which God has determined he will bear no longer. Hence, once the sentence has been pronounced and the decree issued that he will take vengeance on them and reap them, as ripe grain for the harvest, and tread them in the winepress of his vengeance, just as ripe grapes full of juice are pressed and trodden, there will be no way of escape for them, nor will they extricate themselves either by their power or by their multitude, by which they have hitherto surpassed others and still persuade themselves they will surpass them, from the hands of those mighty ones whom he will send to carry out his judgments. However much they may prevail in power, and however greatly they may at last exceed in number, they will all nevertheless be gathered together in that place where he is about to execute the sentence pronounced against them, as the following words expressly teach.

units.la: 14. Multitudines, multitudines in valle concisionis: quia propinquus est dies Domini in valle deci- sionis.
units.tr: 14. Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.

units.la: Magnum, ac fere infinitum eorum, de quibus hic sermo est, hic exprimit numerum, repetendo multitudinis nomen pluralinumero, juxta regulam q) Grammaticorum Hebraeorum multis confirmatam exemplis. Cum vero duo nomina hic conjungantur sine ullo verbo vel particula, quae ad constructionem ducat vel innuat, quid sit intelligendum, vel quibus aut de quibus hoc dictum sit, vel quid agant aut acturi sint aut effectum jam reddiderint, indicio est hunc sermonem esse defectivum, necessarioque esse supplendum particulam quadam, qua regatur & ad sensum pateat aditus. Atque in eo magnopere discrepant interpretes, aliis hoc, aliis alio casu hoc nomen vertentibus. Quidam pro nominativo illud habent supplendo r) cadent, s) concidentur; alii t) erunt; alii u) congregati sunt. Alii pro vocativo habent supplendo w) adeste, alii x) ite. Quo modo accipit Anglicana nostra antiqua: O people, people, come into, O populé, popule, adeste. Et quae ex Genev. est concinnata: O multitudo, multitudo adeste &c. Alii nullum omnino censent addendum esse verbum; sed potius legendum nomen exclamandi forma, subintelligendo duntaxat exclamationis particulam, ac si oculis sibi jam subjiceret, quod certo aliquando futurum est, & prae admiratione magna ita exclamaret: O quantam conspicio multitudinem congregatam! vel o quanta multitudo ibi congregabitur, y) quantum turbae, quantum tumultus! Quem sensum insigniter ferent & verba textus originalis, & interpretatio Vulgati, populi, populi: & nostratium (ut & aliorum
units.tr: Here the prophet expresses the great, almost endless, number of those of whom he speaks, by repeating the word multitude in the plural, following the rule of the Hebrew grammarians, which many examples confirm. But since the two nouns are joined here without any verb or particle to govern the construction or show what is meant, or who or what they refer to, or what they are doing or are about to do, or what they have already brought about, this is a sign that the sentence is incomplete and that some particle must be supplied, so that the sense may be reached. On this point the interpreters differ widely, some rendering the noun in one case and some in another. Some take it as a nominative and supply shall fall, shall be cut down; others shall be; others are gathered together. Others take it as a vocative and supply come, others go. Our old English version reads it this way: O people, people, come in! O populé, popule, adeste. And the Geneva version, put together from it: O multitude, multitude, be present, etc. Others think no verb at all should be added, but that the noun should be read as an exclamation, understanding only the interjection, as if the prophet were already setting before his eyes what will certainly happen at some time, and in great amazement cried out: O what a great multitude I see gathered! or, O how great a multitude will gather there, how much uproar, how much tumult! The original Hebrew words and the Vulgate's rendering, people, people, bring out this sense strongly, as do some of our own writers and others, multitudes, multitudes, except that something is added to them.

units.la: q) Buxt. Thef. l. 1. c. 2. p. 351. Glaff. Gram. l. 3. r) Aben-Ezra. s) Vid. Drus. t) Jun. Trem. Pisc. u) Pet. a Fig. ss) Vid. Drus. Merc. x) Grot. y) Tig. & Vatab. in 4to & 8vo. rum nonnullorum) multitudines, praeterquam quod aliquid iis subjungatur. Sic & paraphrasi haec verba enucleantur a quibusdam Theologis nostris Anglicanis,uti ab R. Episcopo Hallio: Quot multitudines, quam infinitae multitudines improborum tum ibi judicabuntur! &c. & a D. Stokio: O multitudinem haereticorum, schismaticorum, impiorum atque profanorum! O ingens consortium Atheorum, Idololatrarum, Tyrannorum & aliorum malignorum hostium professionis verae & cultus Dei, quos mihi videor intueri in hac valle comparentes &c. Pro eo autem, quod noftrates & multi alii reddunt multitudines, multitudines (vel aliis verbis aequipollentibus) Graeci habent ἠχοι ἐχήχησαν sonitus personuerunt (vel ut quaedam exemplaria z) ἠκούσησαν, auditi sunt) quos Arabica impressa secuta est [Arabic text] concentus personuerunt. Eodem facit Syriaca [Syriac text] quod latine redditur, sensus tumultus. Barbahlul id in Lexico suo interpretatur voce Arabica [Arabic text] five potius [Arabic text] quae significat [Arabic text] clamorem vel mixtos hominum sonos. Quod tamen a priori nihil quicquam differt, quippe clamor tumultuosus arguit magnam populorum nubem confluxisse. Cum vero differant in literali sensu, id tantum ex diversa oriri videtur notione vocis הָמוֹן Hamon, quae notat & magnum strepitum & multitudinem populi, quarum hanc alii, alii illam malunt. Causa repetitionis hujus vocis haec est, uti diximus, ut gravitas earum rerum appareat, quas hic designare constituit. Aliam hujus rei causam reddit Abarbinel, nimirum propter diversa illorum genera, qui has multitudines conficerent, hoc fieri autumat, quorum quidam resurrecturi essent ex mortuis, alii adhuc in vivis forent inprimis Edomitarum (qui juxta eum sunt Christiani) & Ifmaelitarum (qui sunt Mahumedani) qui, ut ejus opinio habet, quam tradidimus ad v. 9. &c. fe congregaturi sunt resurrectionis die ex mortuis, ad quod temporis spatium hoc spectare, atque ideo per [Hebrew text] bamonim, bamonim, multitudines, multitudines, intelligi putat [Hebrew text] z) Vid. Druf. & Bibl. Graeca Francof. in variantibus lectionibus. a) Kam. הַחַיִּים והמתים multitudinem vivorum & multitudinem mor-tuorum. Quæ opinio non adeo absurda est, quin facili negotio, si necessitas urgeret, cum eorum mente posset reconciliari, qui hæc dicta ad diem generalis judicii spectare volunt, quo & vivi & mortui, atque adeo totus orbis hominum, qui usquam fuere, congregandi sunt coram divino tribunali, ut se sistant. Minus tamen accedet eis, qui non ad hunc diem ea referunt, sed ad quosvis tales, quibus DEUS est congregaturus ingentes exercitus (ut MS. Arabicum vocem hic exprimit per ﻋﺴﻜﺮ) qui injuria eum affecerunt ecclesiam & populum ejus male excipientes, atque hostilia iis inferentes, ut eos exscindat atque protinus destruat. Quod idem etiam affirmat Abarbinel, si de vivis hæc verba accipiantur, repetitionem eorum nihil aliud denotare, quam הֲמוֹנִים רַבִּים hamonim rabbim, ingentes multitudines. Quod ad locum attinet, ubi congregantur vel quo citantur a b) Propheta, qui de certo futuris haud aliter ac de præsentibus loquitur, is vocatur עֵמֶק הַחָרוּץ Emek hacharuts, vallis decisionis, ut textus postremæ nostræ interpretationis habet; in margine autem duæ aliæ voces positæ sunt, concisionis & trituratonis; unde liquet hanc vocem eas omnes significationes ferre, earumque quamvis infigniter huic loco quadrare, ita ut lector sibi eligere possit, quæ genio suo quam maxime accedat. Cum autem in textu malint decisionis, denominationis hujus hanc subesse nobis suggerunt causam, quod DEUS ibi decisurus sit omnes eorum causas, qui coram eo congregabuntur atque sententias laturus, prout quisque fecerit vel meritus fuerit, quam ob causam antea vocabatur Vallis Jehosaphat, ut vidimus; & Chaldæus Paraphrastes utroque loco interpretatur פלוג דינא vallis divisionis judicii vel ferendæ sententiæ singulis pro suis meritis. LXX. itidem ἐν τῇ κοιλάδι τῆς δίκης, in valle judicii, quibuscum facit Arabica impressa ﻭﺍﺩﻱ ﺍﻟﺨﺼﻮﻣﺔ; Syrus quoque habet ܒܩܥܬܐ ܕܕܝܢܐ in valle decisionum. Eadem id ratione etiam acceperunt c) auctores versionis nostræ b) Vid. Cyrill. Gvalt. c) Nec non Diodati. nostræ Anglicanæ antiquioris reddendo the valley of final judgment, vallis extremi judicii. Nec abludit R. Salomo, qui expositionis loco addit שששם חרץ המשפט אמת ubi decidetur judicium veritatis, cujus etiam mentionem facit Kimchi, veluti significationis, quæ egregie voci congruat una cum altera, qua redditur concisionis, quæ, uti a nostratibus ad marginem notatur tanquam secundaria, ita ab aliis in textum refertur, quemadmodum etiam revera sibi priores vendicare partes videtur, cum altera non nisi d) metaphorice hinc deduci possit. Hinc a Vulgato Latino versum est, in valle concisionis, quod imitantur non pauci recentiores, ut Piscator, Junius & Tremellius; Kimchi quoque ex eis est, uti notavimus, qui huic significationi priores concedit ratione hujus denominationis addita כי שם יהיה הגויים חרוציים ותוכיים quia ibi erunt gentes concisæ & comminutæ. Sensum hujus loci atque rationem denominationis Abarbinel putat extare Jes. 10, 23. לפי שכלה ונחרצה תהיה בהם שהורה quia confummationem ibi facturus est in omni terra, quam decrevit. MS. Arabicum habet מרג אלקטע ... الـــقطع pratum (vel vallis plana) scissionis vel præcisionis, (quamvis etiam intelligi potest de decisione) R. Tanchum ait hoc exponendum esse خندق الوادي fossam (sive vallem) destructionis, atque ita vocari يا بقع فيه مرج الـــــــــــــــ والـــــــــ ني نلكك الـــــوفـــــت a cæde & strage, quæ in ea futura est eo tempore, quam significationem etiam Abu Walid (ante eum) cæteris aliis, quas hoc loco ei tribuunt, e) præfert, eandem, inquiens, esse hanc vallem, quæ antea vocabatur vallis Jehosaphat, de qua dicit: f) ibi sedebo ad judicandum omnes gentes de circuitu. Atque hanc vocis notionem, quam putant hunc locum requirere, deducunt a significatione scissionis. Hinc est quod R. Tanchum in g) Dictionario suo dicat, quandocunque חרץ Charats (verbum) vel חריץ Charits vel חרוץ Charuts nomina verbalia occurrant ... sensum eorum includere.
units.tr: See Buxtorf, Thesaurus, bk. 1, ch. 2, p. 351; Glassius, Grammar, bk. 3. Ibn Ezra. See Drusius. Jun., Tremellius, Piscator. Pet. a Figueroa. See Drusius and Mercer. Grotius. Tigurinus and Vatablus, in the quarto and octavo editions. Thus some of our English theologians also paraphrase these words, as Bishop Hall does: How many multitudes, how countless the multitudes of the wicked who will then be judged there! etc. And Dr. Stock: O the multitude of heretics, schismatics, impious and profane persons! O vast company of atheists, idolaters, tyrants and other malicious enemies of the true profession and worship of God, whom I seem to see gathering in this valley, etc. In place of what our writers and many others render multitudes, multitudes (or with other equivalent words), the Greeks have echoes resounded [ἠχοι ἐχήχησαν], sounds rang out (or, as some manuscripts have, ἠκούσησαν, were heard), which the printed Arabic follows with a word meaning harmonies resounded. The Syriac agrees, which is rendered in Latin as the sense of tumult. Bar Bahlul explains it in his lexicon by an Arabic word, or rather a related one, meaning a shout or confused human sounds. This, however, differs little from the former reading, since a tumultuous shout shows that a great cloud of people has come together. But since the readings differ in the literal sense, this seems to arise only from the different meanings of the word הָמוֹן hamon, which means both a great noise and a multitude of people, and some prefer one of these and some the other. The reason for repeating this word is, as we have said, to make clear the seriousness of the things the prophet means to describe. Abarbanel gives another reason: because of the different kinds of people who would make up these multitudes, he holds that this is done, some of them being those who would rise from the dead, and others who would still be alive, especially of the Edomites (who by his account are Christians) and the Ishmaelites (who are Muslims), who, according to his opinion, which we have set out at v. 9 etc., will gather themselves from the dead on the day of resurrection; he thinks the prophet refers to that period of time, and therefore understands by bamonim, bamonim, multitudes, multitudes [בהמונים בהמונים] ... the multitude of the living and the multitude of the dead [הַחַיִּים והמתים]. This opinion is not so absurd that, if necessity pressed, it could not with little trouble be reconciled with the mind of those who refer these words to the day of general judgment, when both the living and the dead, and indeed the whole race of men who have ever existed, are to be gathered before the divine tribunal to stand before it. Less agreeable to them, however, are those who refer these words not to that day but to any such people whom God will gather into great armies (the Arabic manuscript renders the word here by army) who have wronged him, the Church and his people, and have treated them badly, inflicting hostilities upon them, so that he may root them out and destroy them at once. Abarbanel also affirms this, if these words are taken of the living: that their repetition signifies nothing other than many multitudes [הֲמוֹנִים רַבִּים], great crowds. As for the place where the prophet, who speaks of future events as surely as of present ones, gathers or summons them, it is called עֵמֶק הַחָרוּץ Emek hacharuts, the valley of decision, as the text of our latest translation has it; but in the margin two other words are given, cutting and threshing. From this it is clear that the word bears all these meanings, and that each of them fits this place remarkably well, so that the reader may choose whichever suits his own disposition most. But since they prefer decision in the text, they suggest to us this reason for the name: that God will there decide the cases of all who are gathered before him and pronounce sentence, according to what each has done or deserved; for which reason it was formerly called the Valley of Jehoshaphat, as we have seen. The Chaldee paraphrast in both places renders it the valley of the division of judgment, or of pronouncing sentence on each according to his merits. The Seventy likewise have in the valley of judgment (ἐν τῇ κοιλάδι τῆς δίκης), with which the printed Arabic agrees, the valley of decisions; the Syriac also has in the valley of decisions. The authors of our older English version took it in the same way, rendering it the valley of final judgment. Solomon the Rabbi does not differ, adding by way of explanation where judgment of truth shall be decided, a meaning Kimchi also mentions, as fitting the word well along with the other sense, cutting, which our writers note in the margin as secondary, while others put it into the text; indeed the first sense seems rightly to claim the first place, since the other can only be derived from it metaphorically. Hence the Latin Vulgate has in the valley of cutting, which many more recent writers imitate, such as Piscator, Junius and Tremellius. Kimchi is also among them, as we noted, though he gives the former sense priority, adding the reason for the name: because there the nations will be cut in pieces and broken small. Abarbanel thinks the sense of this place, and the reason for the name, is found in Isaiah 10:23: for a complete destruction will be made in them, which he has decreed. The Arabic manuscript has a word meaning meadow (or level valley) of cutting or cleaving (though it may also be understood as decision). Rabbi Tanchum says it is to be explained as the ditch (or valley) of destruction, and so called from the slaughter and carnage that will be there at that time; Abu Walid, before him, prefers this meaning to the others they assign to this place, saying that this is the same valley that was formerly called the valley of Jehoshaphat, of which it is said: there I will sit to judge all the nations round about. They derive this meaning of the word, which they think this place requires, from the sense of cutting or dividing. Hence Rabbi Tanchum says in his dictionary, whenever the verb חרץ charats or the nouns חריץ charits or חרוץ charuts occur ... their sense includes cutting or dividing.

units.la: d) Livel. e) هذا عندي اولي ما يعتقد فيه. f) Vers. 12. g) Quod inscribitur Morshed. re significationem fciffionis vel divisionis. Quo pacto cum acceperit Munsterus (quamvis nomen cum aliis videatur participii loco habere) interpretatur, in valle intercisa: obscure admodum, ni fallor; attamen ita, ut non obscure pateat, eum ad significationem scissionis hanc vocem retulisse. Tertia significatio, cujus nostrates nobis dant electionem, est triturationis, quo sensu etiam a nonnullis redditur. Sic legit nostra Anglicana ex Genev. concinnata, in the valley of h) threshing, in valle triturationis; cui accedit interpretatio Piscatoris, qui hanc maxime putat appositam in valle triturationis. Hebraice, adjicit ille, sonat ac si esset, in valle tribula; quam vocem etiam admodum convenientem putat huic loco Calvinus, adhibitis in praecedentibus hujusmodi loquendi formis, quae agricolis sunt familiares & ad ea pertinent, quibus plerumque sunt occupati, quibus hoc insigniter congruit; quippe malitiae eorum gravitatem exponit, de quibus loquitur, atque eorundem maturitatem ad judicium, dicendo, messis maturuit, torcular est plenum, atque operarios falcem immittere jubet; quae omnia proprie sequetur. triturutio frumenti depositi, & locus ubi id fieri debet, adeo ut judicium, cui subeundo satis maturi sunt, recte dici possit valles triturationis. Verum ut recto tunc stet talo hujus loci sensus, necesse erit inquirere, quid intelligendum sit triturationis voce, ut egregie respondeat hebraico verbo Charuts, quae a praedictis latine exprimitur tribula. Nimirum non intelligitur talis triturario, quam plerumque sic nuncupamus, quae contusione tribulae peragitur ad exterendum gramina; sed quae fiebat ope cujusdam instrumenti, quod stramen atq; glumas frangebat & secabat, atq; ita grana extrudebat, ubi scindendi notio adhuc locum habebit. Duo vero hodie adhuc sunt horum instrumentorum genera, quorum unum conficitur ex gravissimis ligneis asseribus, quibus infiguntur cuspidatissimi lapides aut silices, qui a jumentis tracti per frumenta ordine digesta una vice (uti diximus) exterunt grana, glumas frangunt, stramenque secant vel confringunt in minutissima fruftula ad instar palae, quae in jumentorum postea cedat alimentum.
units.tr: d) Livelius. e) Hadha 'indi awwal ma yu'taqad fihi: this, in my judgment, is the first thing to be held about it. f) Ver. 12. g) The work entitled Morshed, on the meaning of cutting or division. Munster, though the word seems to have the force of a participle along with the others, renders it "in the cut-off valley." This is very obscure, unless I am mistaken, yet it plainly enough shows that he referred the word to the sense of cutting. The third meaning, which our countrymen offer us as an alternative, is "threshing," and in this sense some also render it. Thus our English version, drawn up from the Geneva Bible, reads "in the valley of threshing," and to this agrees the interpretation of Piscator, who thinks it most suitable: "in the valley of threshing." In Hebrew, he adds, it sounds as if it were "in the valley of the threshing-sledge." Calvin also thinks this word very fitting for the place, given the forms of speech used in the preceding verses, which are familiar to farmers and belong to the things with which they are usually occupied, and with which this agrees remarkably. For he sets out the gravity of the wickedness of those he is speaking of, and their ripeness for judgment, saying "the harvest is ripe, the winepress is full," and he bids the workers put in the sickle. All these things properly follow the threshing of gathered grain and the place where it must be done, so that men ripe enough to undergo judgment may rightly be called "the valley of threshing." But for the true sense of this place to stand firm, it will be necessary to inquire what is to be understood by the word "threshing," so that it answers well to the Hebrew word Charuts, which above is expressed in Latin by tribula. Clearly it is not meant that kind of threshing which we commonly call by that name, performed by beating with a flail to tread out the grain. It is rather the threshing done by means of a certain instrument, which broke and cut the straw and husks and so pushed out the grains, where the notion of cutting still has its place. Two kinds of these instruments are still in use today. One is made of very heavy wooden boards, into which the sharpest stones or flints are fixed; drawn by draught animals over the grain laid out in order, it threshes out the grains at one pass (as we said), breaks the husks, and cuts or crushes the straw into very small pieces like chaff, which then serves as fodder for the beasts.

units.la: b) Cui concinit versio Tigur. Excussionis. tum. Notum illud instrumentum probe describit Kimchi in dictionario radicum hebraicarum, ubi ab usu, quem praestat, id putat vocari Charuts (a radice Charats) scindendi significatione, idemque vocari i) מורג Moreg. Quod etiam affirmat Abu W'alid, verum adjicit, dum explanat vocem Moreg, nil quicquam differre a נורג Naurage Arabico, quod instrumentum notat يَوْرَجٌ, quo conculcatur frumentum, sive fit ferreum, sive ligneum, quae eadem fere est ejus descriptio, quam in Arabico dictionario tradit naurage, qua voce hanc interpretatur. Atque ex eo apparet, aliud etiam hujus instrumenti genus in usu esse praeter illud ligneum, quod ex ferro conficitur (cujus adhuc usus in illis regionibus viget); illud autem consistit, nisi memoria me fallat, ex duabus ferreis rotis crenarum incisione notatis, dentibus acutissimis ferrae instar praeditis, quae inter fe connectuntur axe ligneo, quod cum per frumenta in area trahitur, idem efficit in conterendis granis & frangendis fcindendisque glumis & stramine, atque id, quod priori loco descriptum est. Ad quem modum exterendi frumenta alterutro horum inftrumentorum alluditur Jef. 28, 27. 28. Hinc alio prorsus veniat necesse est eoque multo largiore fignificatu vox triturationis, si ita fit vertenda, quam nobis plerumque venit, quibus forsitan nullum aliud triturandi instrumentum est cognitum, quam tribula vel flagellum. Quo sensu, si verba accipiantur, captu perquam facile est, verba, in valle triturationis, nihil aliud significare, quam Deum exequi velle in impios illuc congregandos hujusmodi judicia, quae comparari possint cum tali agendi modo, quo agricolae utuntur in maturis frumentis in areas collectis. Quod autem judiciorum gravium executio talibus exprimendi formis innuatur, haud obscure liquet ex Proverb. 20, 26. Ventilat improbos rex sapiens, postquam convertit in eos rotam. Et Amos. 1, 3. dicuntur Damasceni triturasse Giliadem בחרצות הברזל bacharut foth habarzel, instrumentis triturandi ferris. Fieri autem potest, ut ad literam haec loca sumenda
units.tr: b) The Zurich version agrees with this, rendering it of shaking out. Kimchi describes that instrument well in his dictionary of Hebrew roots. From its use, he thinks it is called Charuts (from the root Charats) in the sense of cutting, and that it is also called Moreg. [מורג] Abu W'alid also affirms this, but adds, in explaining the word Moreg, that it differs in nothing from the Arabic naurage [נורג], which denotes the instrument by which grain is trampled, whether it is made of iron or of wood. His description is almost the same as the one he gives of naurage in the Arabic dictionary, by which he explains this word (the Arabic is yawraj). From this it appears that there is also another kind of this instrument in use, besides the wooden one: the one made of iron, whose use still flourishes in those regions. Unless my memory fails me, that one consists of two iron wheels marked with notches, equipped with very sharp teeth like a saw, which are joined to each other by a wooden axle. When this is dragged through the grain on the threshing floor, it does the same things: it crushes the grain, breaks and cuts the husks and straw, just as the first one described does. The verse Isa. 28, 27. 28. alludes to threshing by one or other of these instruments. Hence the word "threshing", if it is to be rendered so, must necessarily take on a quite different and much broader meaning than it commonly has for us, to whom perhaps no other threshing instrument is known except the threshing sledge or the flail. In that sense, if the words are taken as they stand, it is quite easy to grasp that the words in valle triturationis ("in the valley of threshing") signify nothing other than that God wishes to carry out, on the impious gathered there, such judgments as can be compared with the way farmers deal with ripe grain gathered onto the threshing floors. That the execution of heavy judgments is indicated by such figurative forms is clear enough from Proverb. 20, 26. The wise king winnows the wicked, after he has turned the wheel upon them. And Amos. 1, 3. says that the Damascenes threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron, בחרצות הברזל [bacharuts habarzel]. It is possible, however, that these passages must be taken literally, with regard to carrying out such judgments with instruments of this kind, as David did to the inhabitants of Rabbah of the Ammonites, 2 Sam. 12, 31, to which here only an allusion is made.

units.la: i) Conjunctas invenias: Ef. 41, 15. menda sint de executione suscipienda hujusmodi instrumentis, ficuti David fecerat incolis Rabbam Hammonitarum 2. Sam. 12,31. quo hic duntaxat alluditur.
units.tr: i) You will find them joined: Isa. 41, 15. ...and the threshing is to be undertaken by instruments of this kind, as David had done to the inhabitants of Rabbah of the Ammonites, 2 Sam. 12, 31., to which this place merely alludes.

units.la: Est & alia significatio vocis חרוּץ Charuts, qua notat aurum. Hujus mentionem injicit Hieronymus, ac fi loci nomen, auctoribus quibusdam Judæis, uti ait, spectaret Vallem judicii (quam putant esse orcum) in qua excoctis sordibus peccatorum, purum aurum remaneat, i. e. electi soli relinquantur, ut ejus mentem explanat Mercerus.
units.tr: There is also another meaning of the word חרוּץ Charuts, in which it denotes gold. Jerome mentions this, as if the name of the place, according to some Jews, as he says, pointed to the "valley of judgment" (which they think is hell), in which, when the dross of sins has been burnt away, pure gold remains, that is, only the elect are left behind. Mercer explains his meaning in this way.

units.la: Eodem autem ferme redit hæc expositio, quo præcedens, ac fi nomen sortiretur hic locus a judiciorum executione, quam Deus suscepturus est adversus hostes suos. Quamvis altera vocem Charuts ad impios referat, qui evertendi ac destruendi sunt; hæc autem ad pios, qui liberandi sunt ac salvandi; eodem nempe loco, eodemque judiciorum tempore in utrosque sententia lata. Quæcunque præterea interpretibus de literali sensu hujus vocis intendatur lis, quamque demum huic loco optime arbitrentur congruere, id adfirmare habeo, omnes qua sensum egregie sibi ipsis respondere, quem haud inconvenienter exprimit Caftalio, reddendo, in valle severitatis. Omnes enim in severum Dei processum unanimi consensu conspirant, quo causas decisurus est amicorum æque, ac inimicorum, idque in mercedem unius atque in pœnam alterius consortii eodem & tempore & loco ab eo determinato. Quod cum tam certe ei fit constitutum, illos hic etiam Propheta sistit, quasi jam jam congregatos, vel citat eos, ut ipsi illuc congregarentur, causa hujus rei luculenta annexa; quia propinquus est dies Domini in valle decisionis. Dies Domini ] Dies, quo certo judicium executurus, vel vindictam sumturus est de inimicis suis, propinquus est. Adeo certo est hoc tempus ab eo huic rei destinatum, cui omnia sunt præfentia, & k) mille anni instar unius diei, ut jure meritoque dici possit propinquum, licet res fe aliter habeat respectu hominum. Cujus differentiæ rationem habet S. Paulus ad Phil. 4,5. Dominus propinquus est. Cum rursus dicat:
units.tr: This explanation, however, comes to much the same as the preceding one, as if this place received its name from the execution of judgments which God is about to undertake against his enemies. Although the one word Charuts refers the one sense to the wicked, who are to be overthrown and destroyed, this other refers to the godly, who are to be freed and saved; namely, sentence is pronounced upon both in the same place and at the same time of judgment. Moreover, whatever dispute is raised among the interpreters about the literal sense of this word, and whichever they finally think agrees best with this place, I must affirm that they all agree in the sense which Castalio expresses not inappropriately, rendering it "in the valley of severity." For all agree in unanimous consent upon God's severe proceeding, by which he is about to decide the causes of friends and enemies alike, and that for the reward of the one company and the punishment of the other, at the time and place appointed by him. Since this is so certainly established by him, the prophet here sets these people before us as though they were already gathered, or summons them to be gathered there, with a clear reason annexed: "For the day of the Lord is near in the valley of decision."
