"The day of the Lord": the day on which he will surely execute judgment, or take vengeance on his enemies, is near. So certainly is this time appointed for this matter by him, to whom all things are present, and k) "a thousand years are as one day," that it may justly and rightly be called near, although with respect to men the matter stands otherwise. St. Paul gives the reason for this difference at Phil. 4, 5. "The Lord is near." Again he says:

units.la: k) 2. Petr. 3, 8. cat: ne cito mente dimoveamini, neque conturbemini, quasi dies Domini esset propinquus, 2. Thess. 2,2. Ita Johannes, quae futura vel in eo erant, ut fierent, eadem ratione, quod suo tempore certo futura sint, dicit fore ἐν τάχει, cito, Apocal. 1,1. Adeo ut huc faciant verba Prophetae Habacuk ad visionem ejus pertinentia: Si cunctabitur, expecta eam; nam omnino eventura est, & non tardabit, Hab. 2,3. Adhuc enim pusillum tempus est, & qui venturus est, veniet neque tardabit, Hebr. 10,37. Hinc ad omnes hoc aeque spectare manifestum est, ut se praeparent obviam ituri Domino eo die, quasi in praesentiarum ad id obeundum citarentur. Nec quicquam contra hanc veritatem excipi potest, sive ad peculiare quoddam Dei judicium in gentem hanc vel alteram exsequendum, sive ad ultimum generalis judicii diem trahatur, prout ad hoc aliis, aliis ad illud referre visum est, uti diximus. Idem dicendum est de loco, qui hic sub nomine vallis Charuts designatur, de quo non minus disceptant quam de tempore. Quicquid autem id nominis significet juxta opiniones diversas, quas retulimus; in eo tamen universi conveniunt, eundem esse hic, qui supra vocatur v. 2. & 12. Vallis Jehosaphat, quocirca nihil amplius hic addendum esse reor ad quendam fixum constituendum locum, quam quod ibi jam jam sat superque tradidimus. Grotius ex opinione, qua in specie haec verba statuit spectare ad destructionem Persarum a Graecis, Alexandro rerum potiente, illatam, intelligit hic vallem vel planitiem apud Gaugamela, ubi praelium ultimum est commissum cum Dario; at singularis est haec expositio ejusque peculiaris. Mercerus huic loco convenire ratus diversa haec nomina vallis Jehosaphat & vallis Charuts, argui iis censet non certo loco n) conclusam vallem, sed esse eam, ubicunque Dominus de impiis Ecclesiae persecutoribus poenas sumit & eas concidit, vel in eos certam ac definitam sententiam fert. Atque certum habeo, si hoc nomen, & quod futurum hic dicitur, tali applicari potest loco, tanto magis etiam spectare ad magnum generale judicium atque illum locum, quo omnes gentes citabuntur, ut
units.tr: k) 2 Pet. 3, 8. ...that you be not quickly shaken in mind, nor troubled, "as though the day of the Lord were at hand," 2 Thess. 2, 2. So John, speaking of things that were to come, and were to happen in their time, by the same reasoning, because they will certainly be future in their time, says they will happen ἐν τάχει [en tachei], "quickly," Rev. 1, 1. So also the words of the prophet Habakkuk, pertaining to his vision, are to the point: "Though it tarry, wait for it; for it will surely come, and will not delay," Hab. 2, 3. "For yet a very little while, and he that shall come will come, and will not tarry," Heb. 10, 37. Hence it is plain that this applies equally to all, so that they may prepare themselves to meet the Lord on that day, as though they were summoned to meet him at the present time. Nor can anything be objected against this truth, whether it is referred to some particular judgment of God to be executed upon this or that nation, or to the last day of the general judgment; as it has seemed right to some to refer it to the one, and to others to the other, as we have said. The same must be said of the place which here is designated under the name valley of Charuts, about which men dispute no less than about the time. Yet whatever that name signifies according to the various opinions which we have related, all agree in this, that it is the same place which above is called the valley of Jehoshaphat (v. 2 and 12). Wherefore I think nothing more needs to be added here to fix the place, than what we have already said quite enough about there. Grotius, from the opinion that these words in particular refer to the destruction of the Persians by the Greeks, under Alexander's rule, understands by this the valley or plain near Gaugamela, where the last battle was fought with Darius; but this exposition is peculiar and singular. Mercer, thinking these different names, the valley of Jehoshaphat and the valley of Charuts, fit this place, argues from them that it is not a valley shut in at a certain place, but is wherever the Lord takes vengeance on the wicked persecutors of the Church and cuts them down, or pronounces a certain and definite sentence against them. And I am certain that if this name, and what is said here about the future, can be applied to such a place, it applies all the more to the great general judgment, and to that place where all nations will be summoned, so that…

units.la: l) Cap. 1,15. cap. 2, 11. & 31. & hoc cap. v. 9. m) Arian. de expeditione Alexand. n) Consule Danaeum in h. l.
units.tr: l) Chap. 1.15; chap. 2.11 and 31; and v. 9 of this chapter. m) Arrian, on the expedition of Alexander. n) Consult Danaeus on this passage.

units.la: ut pro meritis suis judicentur, quo haud fine gravi causa id multi præcipue referunt eo sensu, quem apte fatis expressit prædictus R. Episcopus D. Hall hujusmodi paraphrasi: Nam magnus ille dies Domini propinquus est, cujus terror ineffabilis erit, in terribili loco judicii. Non habetur in textu epitheton magni (uti quidem alibi c. 2. v. 11. & 31.) verum necesse est, ut fubintelligatur, utpote Domini diei optime conveniens. Quin & terroris eum fore diem ex nomine constat, quo insignitur harum rerum, quæ futuræ sunt, locus, scilicet vallis Charuts, quacunque etiam significationum supra memoratarum eam fumas, five decisionis, five concisionis, five triturationis denotatione. Verum multo prolixius exponitur tum gravitas, tum terror ejus per insolitas ac terribiles rerum naturalium mutationes, quibus manifestatio ejus diei erit stipata, verbis quæ sequuntur:
units.tr: so that they may be judged according to their deeds. Many writers refer this, and not without good reason, especially in the sense which the aforesaid reverend Bishop Hall has aptly expressed in this paraphrase: For that great day of the Lord is near, whose terror will be unspeakable, in the dreadful place of judgment. The epithet "great" is not in the text (as it is elsewhere, at chap. 2 vv. 11 and 31), but it must be understood, since it suits the day of the Lord perfectly. Indeed, that the day will be terrible is clear from the name of the place where these future things are to happen, namely the valley of Charuts, whichever of the meanings mentioned above you take it to have, whether "decision", "cutting up" or "threshing". But its gravity and terror are set out at much greater length, through the unusual and dreadful changes in natural things with which the manifestation of that day will be accompanied, in the words that follow:

units.la: v. 15. Sol & luna obtenebrabuntur, & stellæ retrahent splendorem suum.
units.tr: v. 15. The sun and moon will be darkened, and the stars will withdraw their brightness.

units.la: Verba קדרו Kadaru, noftratibus futuro tempore, obtenebrabuntur, &ΝΣΟΝ Asephu, retrahent, sunt lingua Originali præteriti temporis, ut & Chaldæo, Syro & M. S. Arab. Vulgato Lat. quoque; Sol & luna obtenebrati sunt, & stellæ retraxerunt splendorem suum. Quem sequuntur etiam Duac. & o) alii nonnulli. At alii quidam, quibuscum faciunt noftrates, malunt ea futuro reddi, quod fit futurum, non quod peractum fit aut præfens, denotantia. Et hoc recte; id quod hinc saltem apparet, quod verba a Propheta prolata respiciant ea, quæ futura sunt, non quæ facta erant aut præfentia, Prophetisque q) frequenti usu veniat, ut quæ a Deo sunt determinata, recenseant tanquam præterita vel præsentia, ad significandum, tam certo ea esse futura, acsi jam actu effent vel fuiffent, sicut notavimus ad cap. 2. v. 10. ubi eadem extant verba eademque ratione & constructione, quo etiam lectorem remittimus earum expositionum, quas dederunt interpretes, cupidum. Primo statim
units.tr: The Hebrew verbs kadaru, rendered by our people in the future tense as "will be darkened", and asephu, "will withdraw", are in the original language in the past tense, as also in the Chaldee, the Syriac, the Arabic manuscript and the Latin Vulgate: "The sun and moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness." The Douay and some others follow this. But others, with whom our people agree, prefer to render them in the future, as denoting what will be, not what has been done or is present. And this is right, at least as is clear from the fact that the words spoken by the Prophet refer to what is to come, not to what has happened or is happening. It is also a frequent practice of the Prophets to recount, as past or present, things that have been determined by God, to signify that they will be as certain as if they already were or had been, as we noted at chap. 2 v. 10, where the same words occur with the same reasoning and construction. There we also refer the eager reader to the explanations given by the interpreters.

units.la: o) Trg. Pag. Jun. Trem. Caftalio. q) Ar. Mont. statim intuitu, atque ad literam magna ac terribilia hæc verba præ se ferunt, digna certe, quæ comitentur hunc diem, qui κυριακὴν ἡμέραν dicit posset, dies Domini, non dies vulgaris. Verum enim vero, sintne tali sensu hic accipienda, an alio, strenue inter interpretes disceptatur, prout eo loco vidimus. Hac obscuratione luminarium cœlestium Grotius autumat innui, eorum lumen hominibus obscuratum iri a spissitudine aeris, quam magnus ille fumus coegit, ascendens ex incensa civitate Persepoli, omnia hæc adhuc referens, ut vidimus, ad cladem, quam Alexander Magnus intulit Persis atque eorum regioni. At figurate tunc hæc verba intelligenda sunt, non ad literam, diesque ille, atque ostenta, quibus ille illustris foret, diu jam exitum habuissent, quem prædixerat Propheta. Sunt qui etiam hæc verba figurate accipiunt, sed diversa plane ratione & differentia inter se ipsos haud vulgari, tum quoad diem constituendum, tum quoad signorum naturam, quibus illustris redditur & ab aliis vulgaribus diebus distinguitur. Quidam eorum per solem, lunam & stellas intelligunt magnas mundi potestates, & calsitudines & per obscurationem cœlestium horum corporum & splendoris retractionem conditionis ) illustrissimæ eorum privationem maximamque confusionem, cui erunt subjectæ. Hinc verba ita D. Stokius: Instante illo horrendo die mundus videbitur totus confusus: Qui erunt lumina ac gloria istius temporis atque tam conspicui in sphæra regiminis ut sol, luna & stellæ in firmamento cœli, subito obscurabuntur atque splendorem suum perdent. Quo terribili die intelligere videtur cumprimis ultimum judicii diem; cum alio modo, atque hic, cum referat Danæus ad quodlibet tempus, sive præteritum sive futurum, quo Deus exercuit vel exercebit judicia sua in gentes earumque præstantissimas ad finem mundi, quo temporis spatio, quod hic designatur cœlestium corporum obtenebratione, eventum habuit vel habiturum est, prout hæ figuratæ expressiones exigunt. Nec antiquorum Judæorum suffragiis destituta est hæc sententia. Meminit ejus Abarbinel, quasi Mosi Maimonidi probatæ, quam nec ipse videtur aversari לפרש השמש והירח.
units.tr: o) Targum, Pagninus, Junius, Tremellius, Castalio. q) Arias Montanus. At first sight these words, taken literally, carry a great and terrible sense, certainly worthy to accompany this day, which could be called the Lord's day (Greek kyriakē hēmera), not an ordinary day. But whether they are to be understood in this sense here, or in another, is vigorously debated among the interpreters, as we saw in that place. Grotius thinks that by this darkening of the heavenly lights is meant that their light will be obscured for men by the thickness of the air, which that great smoke raised by the burning of the city of Persepolis produced, all these things still referring, as we saw, to the ruin which Alexander the Great brought upon the Persians and their country. But in that case these words must be understood figuratively, not literally, and that day and the portents by which it was to be made illustrious would long since have had the outcome the Prophet foretold. Some also take these words figuratively, but in a quite different way, and with no little difference among themselves, both as to the day to be fixed and as to the nature of the signs by which it is made illustrious and distinguished from other ordinary days. Some of them understand by the sun, moon and stars the great powers of the world and its rulers, and by the darkening of these heavenly bodies and the withdrawal of their brightness, the utter deprivation and great confusion of their most illustrious condition, to which they will be subjected. Hence D. Stoke says: When that dreadful day is at hand, the whole world will seem confused. Those who are the lights and glory of that time, and as conspicuous in the sphere of government as the sun, moon and stars in the firmament of heaven, will suddenly be darkened and lose their splendour. He seems to understand by that terrible day chiefly the last day of judgment. But Danaeus refers it otherwise, to any time, past or future, in which God has exercised or will exercise his judgments upon the nations and their most eminent men before the end of the world. According to the figurative expressions, the period designated here by the darkening of the heavenly bodies has come or will come to pass. Nor is this view without support from the ancient Jews. Abarbanel records it, as approved by Maimonides, and he himself does not seem to reject it: לפרש השמש והירח

units.la: r) Danæus, Stokius.
units.tr: r) Danaeus, Stokius.

units.la: והירח והכוכבים ער מלכי האוםות per solem, lunam & stellas intelligendos esse reges gentium, hominesque magna dignitate ac potentia praestantes. Aliam etiam adjicere non dubitat, scilicet obscurationem solis & lunae, stellarumque splendoris retractionem ita fumi posse, ac si horum coelestium corporum influxus, qui gentibus videbatur prosperrimus, ab iis foret retrahendus. Quod non procul abit ab ea quorundam & Judaeorum & Christianorum opinione, qua hac expressione de obscuratione solis & lunae putant innui magnas f) calamitates & consternationem, qua obruendi erunt homines propter horrenda illa judicia Dei, ubi hominibus omnia videbuntur merae tenebrae, imo ipse sol non videbitur lucere, vel lumine suo ullum solatium praebere. S. Hieronymus autem eo inclinat, quod & haec coelestia corpora ex terrore sibi sint retractura suam praesentiam, utpote quae non poterunt intueri moestum hunc judiciorum divinorum diem, tormentaque crudelissima, quibus afficientur perituri. Quo ad diem ultimi judicii terribilem haec videtur referre, in quo multos habet assectas alios, quamvis rationem hujus obscurationis luminarium reddant diversam, videlicet, t) quod splendorem suum amissura sint ob gloriosissimum splendorem Christi, qui tum apparebit in gloriae splendore, qui ita obscurabit solem, ut splendor solis obscurat lunae & stellarum splendorem naturali die, non quidem privando lumen quod iis inest, sed extinguendo & longe excedendo. At est alia horum verborum explicatio, quae ut multo est planior, ita literae etiam propius accedit, qua arbitrantur notari u) hujusmodi prodigia, quae vel antecedent vel conjuncta erunt cum ultimo hoc horrendo die, veramque alterationem splendoris solis, lunae & stellarum, cum non figuratae sint hoc loco, ut saepius alibi, hae expressiones, sed denotent, quid revera futurum. Atque haec est quam maxime puto approbandam, licet conjectura duntaxat assequi possimus, quo modo & quibus mediis hae mutationes illis diebus futurae sint, nec certi
units.tr: [והירח והכוכבים ער מלכי האומות] "the moon and the stars, the kings of the nations", and so on; the sun, moon and stars are to be understood as the kings of the nations and men of great dignity and power. He does not hesitate to add another view as well, namely that the darkening of the sun and moon and the withdrawal of the stars' brightness may be taken as if the influence of these heavenly bodies, which seemed most prosperous to the nations, were to be withdrawn from them. This is not far from the opinion of some Jews and Christians, who think that by the darkening of the sun and moon are meant great calamities and consternation, by which men will be overwhelmed on account of those dreadful judgments of God, when all things will seem to men sheer darkness, indeed the sun itself will not seem to shine or to offer any comfort by its light. St. Jerome, however, inclines to the view that these heavenly bodies too will withdraw their presence out of terror, since they will not be able to look upon this sorrowful day of divine judgments and the most cruel torments with which the perishing will be afflicted. He seems to refer this to the terrible day of the last judgment, and has many followers in this, although they give a different reason for the darkening of the lights, namely that they will lose their brightness because of the most glorious brightness of Christ, who will then appear in the splendour of his glory, which will so obscure the sun that the sun's brightness obscures the light of the moon and stars by day, not indeed depriving them of the light that is in them, but extinguishing it and far surpassing it. But there is another explanation of these words, which is much plainer and also comes closer to the letter, by which it is thought that these portents are signified, which will either precede or accompany this dreadful last day, and a real change in the splendour of the sun, moon and stars; since these expressions are not figurative here, as they often are elsewhere, but denote what will truly happen. This I think is by far the most to be approved, although we can only conjecture how and by what means these changes will come about on those days, and nothing certain can be determined, until the day itself brings the truth to light with its signs and wonders.

units.la: f) Kimchi in c. 2. v. 10. & v. 31. Merc. Sa. Menoch. Tirin. & in eandem sententiam Cyrillus t) Lyra & vide Chr. a Castro. u) Pet. a Figuer. Ribera, Diodati. certi quid statuendum sit, donec veritatem produxerit ipse dies cum signis ac prodigiis. Interim persuasi sumus omnino, DEum certo certius esse facturum, quod dixit & suo tempore, & juxta arbitrium & potentia & eo modo & iis instrumentis, quibus ad hoc opus peragendum uti constituit.
units.tr: f) Kimchi on chap. 2 vv. 10 and 31; Mercerus, Sa(lmeron?), Menochius, Tirinus; and to the same effect Cyril. t) Lyra; and see Christopher a Castro. u) Pedro a Figueroa, Ribera, Diodati. Meanwhile we are fully persuaded that God will most certainly do what he has said, both at his appointed time, and according to his will and power, and in the manner and by the instruments which he has determined to use for accomplishing this work.

units.la: 16. Dominus etiam rugiet ex Sione, & dabit vocem suam ex Hierosolyma, & contremiscent cœli & terra: Dominus autem erit spes populi sui & forti- tudo filiorum Israelis.
units.tr: 16. The Lord also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth shall shake: but the Lord will be the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel.

units.la: Hæc verba habentur a nonnullis pro ulteriori descriptione hujusmodi rerum, quibus Dominus se ipse manifestabit die judicii. Dominus יהוה Jehovah. Sunt w) qui observant Christum hic vocari nomine Jehovah, quod soli DEO proprium est, & verbis, dabit vocem suam, respici ad terribilem illam vocem, quam uti viventes, ita & omnes in sepulchris audient expergefactique ad judicium venient (Joh. 5, 28. 29.) ut & horrendam sententiam, qua inimicos suos in æternum condemnabit ignem, Matth. 25, 41. Sionis autem & Hierosolyma nomine, unde dicitur rugitum atque vocem edere, egregie juxta eos intelligitur cœlum. Ita in paraphrasi Reverend. Episcopus Hall. Laturus est Dominus, Jesus horrendam sententiam ex cœlis adversus impios; & Diodatus in notis ad hunc locum: nimirum ex solio gloriæ, quod cumprimis adumbrabatur per sanctuarium, Hebr. 12, 22. ac in eandem mentem alii: e medio sanctorum & Angelorum, quorum sancta societas Zion & Hierosolyma vocari potest. Quæ interpretatio figurata tutior mihi videtur expeditiorve, quam propria illa, qua thronum, cui insessurus est Christus severissimas sententias pronuntiaturus, vel super vel prope Sionem & Hierosolymam fore y) nonnulli statuunt. Præterea non est, qui, autore Christophoro a Castro, hæc non trahat ad horrendam judicii sententiam, quam tunc temporis eoque loci Christus laturus est. Quod de omnibus quidem in genere affirmat;
units.tr: Some take these words as a further description of those things by which the Lord will reveal himself on the day of judgment. The Lord Jehovah [יהוה]. Some observe that Christ is here called by the name Jehovah, which belongs to God alone, and that the words he will utter his voice refer to that terrible voice which will be heard by the living and by all in their graves, and by which they will rise for judgment (John 5:28, 29), and also to the dreadful sentence by which he will condemn his enemies to the fire of eternity (Matt. 25:41). By the names Zion and Jerusalem, from which he is said to roar and to utter his voice, they understand, quite fittingly, heaven. So the Reverend Bishop Hall in his paraphrase: The Lord, Jesus, will pronounce a dreadful sentence from heaven against the wicked; and Diodati in his notes on this passage: namely, from the throne of glory, which was especially foreshadowed by the sanctuary (Heb. 12:22); and others to the same effect: from the midst of the saints and angels, whose holy company may be called Zion and Jerusalem. This figurative interpretation seems to me safer and more straightforward than the literal one, which some hold, that the throne on which Christ is to sit, when he pronounces his most severe sentences, will be upon or near Zion and Jerusalem. Moreover, following Christopher a Castro, there is no one who does not apply these words to the dreadful sentence of judgment which Christ will then and there pronounce. This he affirms of all in general;

units.la: w) Vat. 40. 8vo. y) Vatab. in 4to & 8vo. Christ. a Castro. Menoch. Tirin. Vide supra de hac opinione in v. 2. & 12. mat; verum salva ejus auctoritate dicendum est, omnes non eodem modo agere, neque de hoc loco neque de hac sententia æque exponere. Etenim non desunt, qui per Sionem & Hierosolymam intelligunt DEI z) ecclesiam in his terris, quæ loca olim peculiaris ejus erant sedes, ubi cultus ei exhibebatur verus; at postea quam omnibus nationibus lætum nuncium est prædicatum, latius hæc nomina patent, ecclesiasque quasvis ubique locorum in toto terrarum orbe denotant. Quocirca hæc verba, rugiet ex Sione & dabit vocem suam ex Hierosolyma, aliud nihil complecti dicendum foret, quam judicia ac signa indignationis terribilia, quæ exhibiturus est a) suo tempore adversus ecclesiæ ac fidelium hostes, quamvis aliquantisper ferat, ut persecutione premantur ab adversariis suis, atque ita sese gerat, quasi nullam eorum haberet curam. Grotius hæc refert ad victorias Judæorum de Antiochi ducibus, super cujus agmina DEUS dicitur pluisse ignem ac lapides, uti ipse citat locum Ezech. 38,22. quæ ejus peculiaris est opinio, nihil autem prorsus habet, quo in castra sua nos trahi posset. Porro omnes hi eandem constructionem sequuntur, quam nostrates, ex Sione & ex Hierosolyma, qua ratione מציון Mitzion & מירושלים Mirushalim optime reddi possunt. Alio autem modo redduntur ab aliis, scilicet pro Sione & pro Hierosolyma. Sic R. Salomo Jarchi מִמֶּרְחָק שֶׁעָשׂוּ לְצִיּוֹן propter id quod fecerunt ipsi Sion: & Abarbinel expresse dicit præfixam præpositionem מ mi esse מִסִּבַּת מְחָמַת הַסִּבָּה membahaibbab, mem causale; ac si diceret שֶׁעָשׂוּ לְצִיּוֹן propter id, quod fecerunt Sioni & Hierosolymæ, DEUS rugiet ut leo, & vocem suam dabit; id quod nec latini quidem b) interpretes aversantur; at multo planior est prior reddendi ratio. Alii non adeo differunt a prioribus in reddenda verborum constructione, quam in eorum quorundam sensu, cum per vocem DEI, quam ex Hierosolyma dabit, c) intelligant dulcia illa verba, quæ fidelibus suis judicii die dicet: Venite benedicti Patris mei &c. vel ut d) aliis placet, ministerium Evangelii. Quos contra cumprimis excipiendum est, hic non nisi de *) talibus rebus sermonem esse, quæ terrorem injiciunt.
units.tr: w) Vat. 40. 8vo. y) Vatab. in 4to & 8vo. Christ. a Castro. Menoch. Tirin. See above on this opinion at vv. 2 and 12. But, with due respect to his authority, it must be said that not all deal with this passage in the same way, nor expound this view equally. For there are some who understand by Zion and Jerusalem the church of God on this earth, since those places were once his special seat, where true worship was offered to him; but after the glad tidings were preached to all nations, these names extend more widely and denote the churches anywhere in the whole world. Hence, if these words, he will roar out of Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem, are taken this way, they must be said to contain nothing other than the terrible judgments and signs of wrath which he will display in due time against the enemies of the church and of the faithful, although for a while he allows them to be oppressed by their adversaries, and conducts himself as though he had no care for them. Grotius refers these words to the victories of the Jews over the generals of Antiochus, upon whose army God is said to have rained fire and stones, as he himself cites Ezek. 38:22. This is his own peculiar opinion, but it has absolutely nothing by which we could be drawn into his camp. Moreover, all these follow the same construction as our people, out of Zion and out of Jerusalem, by which the Hebrew [מציון Mitzion] and [מירושלים Mirushalim] can best be rendered. Others, however, render it in another way, namely for Zion and for Jerusalem. Thus R. Solomon Jarchi renders [מִמֶּרְחָק שֶׁעָשׂוּ לְצִיּוֹן] on account of what they did to Zion; and Abarbanel expressly says that the prefixed preposition [מ mi] is [מִסִּבַּת מְחָמַת הַסִּבָּה membahaibbab], a causal mem; as if he were saying [שֶׁעָשׂוּ לְצִיּוֹן] on account of what they did to Zion and Jerusalem, God will roar like a lion and will utter his voice. Even the Latin interpreters do not reject this; yet the former way of rendering it is far plainer. Others do not differ so much from the earlier ones in the construction of the words as in the sense of some of them, since by the voice of God, which he will utter from Jerusalem, they understand those sweet words which he will speak to his faithful on the day of judgment: Come, you blessed of my Father, etc. Or, as others prefer, the ministry of the Gospel. Against these, above all, it must be objected that here the discourse concerns only such things as strike terror.

units.la: z) Merc. Tarnov. D. Stokius. a) Calv. b) Ar. Mont. c) Lyra. d) Vid. Merc. & Bochart. de Animal. *) Pet. a Fig. ciunt.Quo præcipue spectat verbum שאג yshag rugiet, quod proprium est leonis, præ cæteris animantibus maxime terribilis; Leone rugiente quis non timeat? Amos.3,8. cui e) subjungitur alterum: dabit vocem suam; quo idem vel repetitur, vel priori quid additur. Quamvis enim hoc verbum latioris sit significationis parumque aut nihil huiusmodi duritiei habeat; attamen terribile non nihil hic videtur postulare haud secus ac præcedens, idque juxta f) quosdam, tonitrua, quibus DEI vox alibi non minus exprimitur, quam leonum rugitu, quasi idem utraque voce innueretur, quod dicitur rugitus vocis ejus, & sonus ex ore ejus exiens, Job.37,2. & v.4. ejusdem rei hæc est descriptio: Vox rugiens tonat voce excellentia sua, & v.5. DEUS tonat mirabiliter voce sua. Bochartus, a quo hæc verba expositia sunt de prædicatione Evangelii, quod & ab aliis factum notavimus, commode ei congruere putat, quod habetur: rugiet & dabit vocem suam, quatenus hæc vox tam clara & sonora, ut per totum orbem audita fuerit, nec solum aures, sed etiam auditorum animos vi sua perculerit & sollicitos reddiderit de salute sua cum metu & tremore procurandâ. Sed vocis descriptio non adeo hic videtur significare sonum ac efficaciam ejus, quæ optime convenit Evangelio, quippe g) sonus ejus exivit in universam terram & verba ejus ad ultima orbis terrarum, quant horrorem atque trepidationem, quæ magis videntur apta in horrendis judiciis prædicendis. Unde autem tantus terror fit oriundus, partim patet ex ea, quæ jam tradita est ejus descriptio, partim ex essectis, quæ ita traduntur in verbis sequentibus: Et cœli & terra contremiscent. Quomodocunque hæc verba sumantur, sive proprie, sive figurate, utique magnum eorum notant terrorem, coram quibus hæc prodigiosa effecta, quæ his expressionibus necessario continentur, producenda sunt, Cæli & terra contremiscent. Ingentem hæc verba præ se ferunt communis naturæ cursus immutationem, si ad literam ea sumseris, quæ vi vocis divinæ, cui nil omnino ἀδύνατον, facili negotio effici potest, quo tempore quave occasione hoc ipsi collibitum fuerit, adeo ut ad literam si intelligatur (ut quidam faciunt) nihil sit, quod in oppositum urgeat. At neque hic consentiunt interpretes.
units.tr: z) Merc. Tarnov. D. Stokius. a) Calv. b) Ar. Mont. c) Lyra. d) See Merc. and Bochart, de Animal. *) Pet. a Fig. ... To this especially refers the verb [שאג yshag], he will roar, which is proper to the lion, the most terrifying of all animals: When the lion roars, who will not fear? (Amos 3:8). To this is added the second phrase, he will utter his voice, by which the same idea is either repeated or something is added to the first. For although this verb has a wider meaning and possesses little or nothing of such harshness, nevertheless here it seems to demand something terrible, no less than the preceding verb. And according to some, this means thunders, by which the voice of God is elsewhere expressed no less than by the roar of lions, as if the same thing were signified by both voices. So it is said: the rumbling of his voice, and the sound that goes out of his mouth (Job 37:2); and in verse 4 the same thing is described thus: the roaring voice thunders with the voice of his majesty, and in verse 5: God thunders marvellously with his voice. Bochart, by whom these words are expounded of the preaching of the Gospel, as we have noted was also done by others, thinks it fits well with what is said: he will roar and utter his voice, inasmuch as this voice is so clear and resonant that it is heard through the whole world, and strikes with its force not only the ears but also the minds of the hearers, and makes them anxious to secure their salvation with fear and trembling. But the description of the voice does not seem here to signify its sound and its efficacy so much, which agrees excellently with the Gospel, since their sound has gone out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Rom. 10:18); rather it signifies the horror and trembling which seem more fitting when dreadful judgments are foretold. Where such great terror arises is partly clear from the description already given, and partly from the effects which are stated in the following words: And the heavens and the earth shall tremble. However these words are taken, whether literally or figuratively, they certainly denote great terror in the presence of which these prodigious effects, necessarily contained in these expressions, are to be brought about: The heavens and the earth shall tremble. These words carry with them a vast change in the ordinary course of nature, if you take them literally, which by the power of the divine voice, to which nothing is impossible, can be brought about with ease, at whatever time or occasion it shall please him. So that, if understood literally (as some do), there is nothing that argues against it. But here too the interpreters do not agree.

units.la: e) Mercer. f) Drus. g) Rom. 10,18. terpretes. Sunt qui extraordinarios intelligunt motus ac tremores, qui in terra fiunt terrae motibus, &(ut hominibus h) videtur) in coelis tonitru. Ut terra terrae motu, ita coelum tonitru concuti & tremere dicitur, inquit D. Livel. Atque id tantum quoad tonitrua & terrae motus, quae fiunt juxta communem cursum naturae; quanto verius hoc erit,si de hujusmodi accipiatur effectis,quae naturam longe sunt transgressura,qualia futura sunt,quando DEUS rugiente sua voce terrorem incutiet die judicii, quod tam prodigiosis signis erit conjunctum, quam i) praedictum est, quorum efficacia coeli & tota naturae forma contremiscet? Quod cum ita applicatur, a literali sensu haud abitur, ita ut, quod Hieronymus ait, coelorum cardines & terrarum fundamenta quatiantur. Alienum quippe id esse non potest, cum S. Petrus de terribili hoc die verba faciens, k) dicat: coeli cum stridore peribunt, elementa aestuantia solventur, terraque & quae in ea sunt opera exurentur. Alii haec verba non sumunt tam stricte de forma horum corporum,coelorum & terrae, quam quidem de incolis eorum ,angelorum pariter & hominum,(ut l) quidam ajunt) qui non parum movebuntur eo horrendo die,quo Dominus apparebit: vel (ut alii) de civibus tam m) coelestibus quam terrenis,pios atque impios innuendo; vel ut Lyra interpretatur, quorum alii cum recipientur in coelum,coeli,alii cum servandi sunt in terra,terra movebuntur, quippe orcus locus dicitur sub terra. R. Salomo Jarchi idem arbitratur haec verba,coeli & terra contremiscent,valere ac ידרע משרים שני n) ultionem fumet de Principibus supernis, de principibus gentium ואחר כך מן האימורים & postea de gentibus. Quam sententiam videtur approbare Abarbinel non abhorrentem ab carum quadam, (dixerat enim etiam literaliter ea posse exponi) quam attulerat,per coelum & terram intelligi posse המשפעים העליונים corpora superiora quae influxum dant, & inferiora quae influxum recipiunt, quae tum reddentur inefficacia, priora quidem influxum dandi,posteriora recipiendi.
units.tr: e) Mercer. f) Drus. g) Rom. 10:18. Some understand extraordinary motions and tremors, such as occur on the earth in earthquakes, and (as seems to men) in the heavens in thunder. As the earth is said to be shaken and tremble by an earthquake, so the heavens by thunder, says D. Livel. And this only as regards thunder and earthquakes, which happen according to the common course of nature. How much truer will this be if it is taken of such effects as will far exceed nature, such as will come to pass when God, roaring with his voice, strikes terror on the day of judgment, which will be joined with such prodigious signs as have been foretold, by whose power the heavens and the whole form of nature will tremble? When it is applied in this way, one does not depart from the literal sense, so that what Jerome says holds: the hinges of the heavens and the foundations of the earth are shaken. For this cannot be foreign to the matter, since St. Peter, speaking of this dreadful day, k) says: The heavens will pass away with a great noise, the elements will melt with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up. Others do not take these words so strictly of the form of these bodies, the heavens and the earth, as of their inhabitants, the angels as well as men (as l) some say), who will be greatly moved on that dreadful day when the Lord shall appear; or (as others say) of the citizens of both the heavenly and the earthly realms, signifying both the pious and the impious; or, as Lyra explains, some of whom, when they are received into heaven, the heavens will be moved, and others, when they are to be kept on earth, the earth will be moved, since the underworld is said to be beneath the earth. R. Solomon Jarchi thinks these words, the heavens and the earth shall tremble, mean [ידרע משרים שני] he will take vengeance on the princes above, on the princes of the nations, [ואחר כך מן האימורים] and afterwards on the nations. This opinion Abarbanel seems to approve, not far from a certain view which he had set forth (for he had said that these words too may be explained literally), namely that by heaven and earth can be understood [המשפעים העליונים] the higher bodies, which give influence, and the lower, which receive influence, which then will be rendered ineffective, the former in giving influence, the latter in receiving it.

units.la: Quibus expositionibus neminem Christianorum reperio suffragari, nisi eas complectantur sub generali incolarum aut civium o) coelestium & terrenorum nomine, ut dictum est antea. Alii p) hyperbolice haec dicta volunt, ac si tam terribilem vocem DEUS exserturus sit, quae vel ad totam mundi formam tremefaciendam sufficiat; quanto magis ad homines fragiles & imbecilles? q) Alii hoc sensu, quod, etsi omnia terrena imo ipsi coeli & terra sese opponerent conatibus suis, nihil tamen valerent ad resistendum, sed omnia voce ejus terribili audita contremiscerent, ipseque superior evasurus sit. Quo vero cunque haec verba referant, sive ad diem ultimi judicii, sive ad aliam temporis periodum, qua DEUS peculiari ratione vel destruxit vel destruet inimicos suos atque ecclesiae, id inprimis liquet, DEUM quidem conatus hostium ad tempus ferre ac fortunare; constituisse tamen justo tempore ultionem de iis sumere, iisque tanta potentia ac terrore contra ire, ut resistendo nequaquam sint, etiamsi totus mundus a parte illorum staret; sed ita succumbant ac tremiscant, ut, quo se vertant, vel quem effugiendi quaerant locum, prorsus nesciant.
units.tr: I find no Christian who supports these explanations, except those who include them under the general name of inhabitants or citizens of heaven and earth, as was said above. Others want these words to be hyperbole, as if God were about to utter a voice so terrible that it would suffice to make the whole frame of the world tremble, how much more then frail and feeble men? Others take it in this sense: that even if all earthly things, indeed heaven and earth themselves, opposed their efforts, they would still be worth nothing in resisting, but would all tremble at the hearing of his terrible voice, and he himself would emerge superior. But whatever these words refer to, whether to the day of the last judgment or to some other period of time in which God in a particular way has destroyed or will destroy his enemies and the Church, this above all is clear: God does indeed bear with and prosper the attempts of enemies for a time, but he has determined to take vengeance on them at the proper time, and to come against them with such power and terror that they will by no means be able to resist, even if the whole world stood on their side. Rather they will so collapse and tremble that they will utterly not know where to turn or what place of escape to seek.

units.la: Interim ingens quamvis sit futurus terror, quo adventus ejus erit conjunctus, omnes tamen non eodem modo eo afficientur, dispar quippe erit respectu hostium ejus atque insontium. Ad omnium quidem animos aeque penetrabit terroris gravitas, at qui in desperationem deducet hostes ejus atque in illorum exitium desinet; fideles vero tantum excitabit, ut propius ad eum accedendo nullibi refugium quaerant, quam apud ipsum atque arctius illi adhaereant & uniantur. Quod quomodo futurum sit eo magno terribili ac hostibus atro die, sequentia docent: Sed Dominus erit spes populi sui &c. r) Sed pro &, vel, quia Dominus vult esse, vel, erit; vel, ut s) alii, est. Varie enim redditur a quibusdam futuro, ab aliis praesenti tempore, quia hebraice non habetur. Nec multum hic refert, cum sermo sit de Domino, qui erat, est, & futurus est semper idem, uti in omnibus aliis rebus, ita & hic, ubi dicitur esse vel fore, etiam tum, cum aliis maxima sit metus atque terroris causa, spes populi sui &c. ita ut, quo tempore alii causa
units.tr: Meanwhile, however great the terror that will accompany his coming, it will not affect everyone in the same way, for it will be different for his enemies and for the innocent. The weight of terror will indeed penetrate the minds of all alike, but in the case of his enemies it will drive them to despair and end in their destruction; while for the faithful it will only rouse them, so that, drawing nearer to him, they will seek refuge nowhere but with him, and cling to him and be united with him more closely. How this will come about on that great day of terror, dark for his enemies, the following words teach: But the Lord will be the hope of his people, etc. But stands for "and", or "because the Lord wishes to be", or "he will be"; or, as others have it, "he is". For some render it in the future tense, others in the present, because it is not so in Hebrew. Nor does it matter much here, since the subject is the Lord, who was, is, and will be always the same. As in all other things, so here, where it is said that he will be, or is, even at the time when for others the greatest cause of fear and terror is present, the hope of his people, etc., so that at the time when others give up in despair, these may be able to look up and lift up their head, firmly persuaded that deliverance is near, the Saviour himself commanding it (Luke 21:28).

units.la: o) Grotius angelos intelligit per coelos. p) Merc. Menoch. q) Calv. r) Quarum significationum quavis sumitur copulativa, vel prout sensus postulat. s) Jun. Trem. desperata animum dimittant, hi possint aspicere & caput tollere, certo persuasi, liberationem appropinquare, ipso Salvatore jubente Luc. 21, 28. Pro eo, quod in textu est, pes, ultima nostra translatio in margine habet, Heb. (i. e. hebraice extat) locus refectionis vel hospitium. At idem est sensus, qua notione etiam reddideris, cum vox hebraea harum alterutra vel alia similis naturae reddi possit, quippe מחסה machaseh descendit a חסה chasah, quod notat frequentare, & se ipsum ad aliquid conferre, atque etiam sperare vel confidere. Quibus rebus factum est, ut in eandem sententiam a plerisque vertatur, t) spes, u) receptus, w) refugium. Sunt tamen ex veteribus qui longius recedere videntur, veluti LXX qui legunt, καὶ ὁ κύριος Φείσεται τᾶς λαῶ αὐτᾶς, καὶ ἐνισχύσῃ τᾶς ὑᾶς Ἰσραήλ, & Dominus parcebit suo populo & corroborabit filios Israelis. Gemina habet Arab. impressa, quae Graec. sequitur. Ut & Syrus ܐܬܪܚܡ ܘܐܬܩܝܡ, quod conjiciendi nobis praebet occasionem, verbum חסה chasah olim usitatum fuisse hebraeis non tantum praedicta notione se conserendi, sed & eadem, qua est חוס chus, parcendi sive propitium se gerendi, id quod haud improbabile est, quia Syriaca lingua, quae multum affinitatis habet cum Hebraea, utraque radix & ܚܣ sive ܚܣܐ, quae respondet Hebr. חסה chasah, & ܚܣ chas, quae respondet Hebr. חוס chus significat parcere, misericordiam ac propitium esse.
units.tr: o) Grotius understands angels by heavens. p) Merc. Menoch. q) Calv. r) Any one of these meanings may be taken as copulative, as the sense requires. s) Jun. Trem. Instead of what is in the text, pes (refuge), our latest translation has in the margin Heb. (that is, in Hebrew it stands) a place of refreshment or a lodging. But the sense is the same whichever notion you render, since the Hebrew word can be rendered by one of these or another of similar nature: machaseh [מחסה] comes from chasah [חסה], which means to resort to, and to betake oneself to something, and also to hope or to trust. For these reasons it has come about that most render it to the same sense as hope, shelter, or refuge. Yet some of the ancients seem to depart further, such as the Seventy, who read: "And the Lord will spare his people and strengthen the sons of Israel" [καὶ ὁ κύριος Φείσεται τᾶς λαῶ αὐτᾶς, καὶ ἐνισχύσῃ τᾶς ὑᾶς Ἰσραήλ], and the Lord will spare his people and strengthen the sons of Israel. The printed Arabic has a double reading, which the Greek follows; and so does the Syriac, etrachem wa-etqim, which gives us occasion to conjecture that the Hebrew verb chasah was once in use among the Hebrews not only in the aforesaid sense of betaking oneself, but also in the same sense as chus [חוס], that is, to spare or to show oneself favourable. This is not improbable, since the Syriac language, which has much affinity with Hebrew, uses for both roots, chas or chasa (corresponding to Hebrew chasah) and chas (corresponding to Hebrew chus), which mean to spare, to show mercy, and to be favourable.

units.la: Populus ejus est, cujus spes vult esse DEUS, & Filii Israelis, quorum robur se fore promisit, utraque voce easdem personas denotante, i. e. qui vere in eum credunt, veraque fide ei serviunt ac morem gerunt, illi sunt ejus populus, illi soli ejus Israel, non qui ex Israele ortum ducunt secundum carnem. Ita hunc titulum docemur intelligere, quotiescunque populo DEI tribuitur. Hinc Apostolus dicit Rom. 9,7. Non omnes sunt Israel, qui ex Israele sunt; neque omnes filii, quia sunt semen Abrahami. Sed quotquot incedunt juxta regulam Israelis, vera fide & sincera obedientia, DEOque arcte adhaerent, licet ex semine Israelis non sint, Israel Dei sunt (Gal. 6,16). Ad eos solos ac pro-
units.tr: His people are those whose hope God wishes to be, and the sons of Israel, whose strength he has promised to be, both words denoting the same persons, that is, those who truly believe in him, and serve and obey him with genuine faith: they are his people, they alone are his Israel, not those who derive their origin from Israel according to the flesh. We are taught to understand this title in this way whenever it is given to the people of God. Hence the Apostle says: Romans 9:7. Not all are Israel who are of Israel; neither are all children [the seed of Abraham] simply because they are the seed of Abraham. But as many as walk according to the rule of Israel, with true faith and sincere obedience, and cling closely to God, even though they are not of the seed of Israel, are the Israel of God (Gal. 6:16). This promise applies properly to them alone, and to the people of God made here and elsewhere under the name of Israel (or sons of God).

units.la: t) Vulg. u) Jun. w) Tig. Chald. חסן fulcrum. proprie spectat hæc promissio, hic & alibi populo DEI sub nomine Israelis (sive filiorum Dei facta. Hoc illis x) peculiare est, quod in DEO sint inventuri suam spem & robur, sive certum refugium, quando durissimo terrore concutientur ejus ac illorum inimici, quantumvis antea omni fortean viderentur spe & auxilio privati. Quem autem effectum habitura sit in eis hæc DEI gratiosa in eos voluntas, verba sequentis versus præclare docent.
units.tr: t) Vulgate. u) Junius. w) Tigurine. Chaldee [חסן], a support. This promise is made properly here and elsewhere to the people of God under the name of Israel (or sons of God). It is peculiar to them x) that they will find in God their hope and strength, or a sure refuge, when both his enemies and theirs are shaken by the most severe terror, however much they may have seemed before to be deprived of all hope and help. What effect this gracious will of God towards them will have in them, the words of the following verse clearly teach.

units.la: 17 Ita scietis, me esse Dominum DEum vestrum, ha- bitantem in Sione sancto meo monte: Tum erit Hierosolyma sancta, & alieni non transibunt am- plius per eam.
units.tr: 17 So you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain: then Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through it.

units.la: Ex eo, quod jam in effectum deduci vident, ejus rei jam habent argumentum certissimum experientia haud unquam mendaci probatum, cujus antea tantum fidem ac spem conceperant, DEUM scilicet revera esse Dominum eorum DEum, cui cordi essent, eumque peculiarem eorum gerere curam omniaque ita ordinare, ut in bonum eorum nihil non cedere eventus probet, quomodo etiam cunque hoc iu mundo cum illis ageretur, imo etiamsi a DEO plane viderentur deserti atque ad eum nihil prorsus pertinere. Quod ipsum hæc verba inferre videntur, quibus ea exprimitur relatio, qua DEUS sibi eos adhuc asserit, dicendo, se esse Dominum illorum Deum habitantem in Sione sancto suo monte. Nimirum illi scient, ipsum Dominum DEUM totius terrarum orbis, atque omnis carnis esse iis, non tantum eo modo, quo omnibus incolis mundi est, sed peculiari jure ac relatione illorum DEum habitantem ac degentem inter eos ratione longe præstantissima, in Sione, tanquam in proprio suo habitaculo ac loco sibi præ cæteris dicato ac sacrato, unde majora etiam necessario ipsis erant privilegia & præsentiæ ejus favorisque signa, quam exaliis quibuscunque. Videnda sunt præterea quæ notavimus ad hanc exprimendi formam, qua se DEum illorum vocat, ad caput 2. v. 27. quid autem intelligendum per Sionem ad v. 32. Probe cognitum est, quænam
units.tr: From what they now see brought into effect, they already have the most certain proof of this thing, proved by an experience that never deceives, of what before they had only conceived as faith and hope: namely that God is truly the Lord their God, who is dear to them, who takes a special care of them and arranges all things so that the outcome proves that nothing turns out other than for their good, however things go with them in the world, indeed even if they seemed utterly abandoned by God and in no way related to him. These very words seem to imply this, in which that relation is expressed by which God still claims them for himself, saying that he is the Lord their God, dwelling in his holy mountain Zion. Assuredly they will know that the Lord God himself, the God of the whole circle of the earth and of all flesh, is theirs, not merely in the way he is to all inhabitants of the world, but by a special right and relation as their God, dwelling and living among them in a manner far more excellent, in Zion, as in his own dwelling and place dedicated and consecrated to himself above others. Hence greater privileges and signs of his presence and favour necessarily came to them than to any others. Moreover, what we noted at this form of expression, by which he calls himself their God, at chapter 2, verse 27, should be looked at, and also what is to be understood by Zion at verse 32. It is well known what

units.la: x) Pet. a Fig. nam præsentiæ suæ signa peculiaria olim ad tempora Christi usque exhibuerit eo in loco, qui proprie sic vocatur, quodque ea tantum de causa dicatur habitare in eo templo ibi extructo; verum largiori id postea sumtum est sensu, adeo ut non eum tantum designet locum, sed & ecclesiam, eamque non solum militantem his in terris, quocunque in loco; verum etiam triumphantem in cœlis, quo modo etiam ab interpretibus accipitur, *) aliis hoc, y), aliis alio respectu. Equidem inficias iri non potest DEUM utrobique habitare vel signa exhibere curæ, quam eorum gerit, ac præsentiæ suæ, qua ipsis adest, illustrissima. Quid sibi velint hæc verba, ita scient, sic exponit Abarbinel, quod, cum filii Israelis viderint vindictam illam ingentem, quam DEUS sumturus sit ab hostibus eorum, & inprimis mortuos ex terra resurgere, revera tum scient ac credent, Dominum esse illorum DEUM, qui perpetuo eorum curam gerat, mundumque haudquaquam regi natura sive casu, sed omnia negotia אימחנו nostræ gentis, inquit ille, providentia ejus gubernari, quod indicant verba, & scietis me esse Dominum DEum vestrum. Cum vero dicatur, benedictum, quem scient, habitare in Sione monte suo sancto, idem significare putat, ac ejus præsentiam & sanctitatem majori ibi fore mensura, quam prioribus temporibus &c. Hanc in opinionem omnes conspirant Judæorum interpretes, qui sibi peculiarem afferunt DEUM ejusque specialem curam & providentiam, ecclesiamque, cujus sedes olim erat eorum mons Sion, ad suam tantum nationem referunt. Nec contrarient iis quicquam interpretes illi prisci, modo talia ecclesiæ membra admitterent, quæ evangelica doctrina imbuta sunt & a Christianis hic intelligantur, qui hæc verba exponunt de magna DEI benignitate & indiciis favoris ejus illustribus, quæ benignitate & indiciis favoris ejus illustribus, quæ in ecclesia sua ejusque in gratiam tum maxime exhibebit, quando resurrectione facta eam triumphantem reddiderit in cœlis, omnesque sancti, qui ejus sunt membra, perenni ejus fruituri sint gloria ac gratiosa præsentia, omnibusque inimicorum insultibus suerint omnino erepti. Beneficia utiq; Dei ingentia, signaque ejus gratiæ, qua complectitur ecclesiā, non nisi tunc temporis omni ex parte explebun-
units.tr: x) Pet. a Fig. for the particular signs of his presence he displayed formerly, up to the time of Christ, in that place which is properly so called, and that he is said to dwell in that temple built there for this reason alone. But later this was taken in a broader sense, so that it designates not only that place but also the church, and not only the church militant on this earth, wherever it is, but also the church triumphant in heaven, as it is also understood by the commentators, *) some in one respect, others in another y). Indeed it cannot be denied that God in both cases dwells there, or displays signs of the care he has for them and of his presence, by which he is most illustriously with them. Abarbanel explains thus what these words, so you shall know, mean: when the children of Israel see that great vengeance which God will take on their enemies, and especially the dead rising from the earth, then truly they will know and believe that the Lord is their God, who continually takes care of them, and that the world is not governed by nature or chance, but that all the affairs of our nation [אומתנו], he says, are governed by his providence, as the words indicate: you shall know that I am the Lord your God. But since it is said that he whom they will know dwells in his holy mountain Zion, he thinks it means that his presence and holiness will there be in greater measure than in former times, and so on. All the Jewish commentators agree with this opinion. They claim for themselves God in a special way, with his particular care and providence, and refer the church, whose seat once was their mountain Zion, to their own nation alone. Nor do those early interpreters contradict them in anything, provided they admitted such members of the church as are imbued with evangelical doctrine and are understood here by Christians. These explain the words of the great goodness of God and the illustrious tokens of his favour, which he will then especially display in his church and for its sake, when, after the resurrection, he has made it triumphant in heaven, and all the saints who are its members shall enjoy his eternal glory and gracious presence, and shall be wholly delivered from all the insults of their enemies. Indeed the great benefits of God and the signs of his grace, by which he embraces the church, will not be fulfilled in every respect except at that time

units.la: *) Merc. y) Pet. a Fig. plebuntur;quamvis negari non possit,ea omni tempore a Christo tali mensura conferri etiam in militante Ecclesiam hac in terra,ut merito ad eam ( quod alii faciunt ) hæc verba applicari queant, quæ Dei præsentia & providentiæ protectionisque signis tam peculiari ratione gaudet, qua nullum aliud hominum genus aut secta unquam gavisa est, cujusque z) defectus , sicubi ea non in omnibus clare pateant, fide ac certissima spe compensatur. Unde etiam facillimo negotio capi potest, quomodo accipienda sint verba sequentia: Tunc Hierosolyma sanƈta erit &c. Ubi eodem modo Hierosolyma accipi potest, & a multis, imo aplerisque, recte quidem accipitur, quo Sion, non quidem pro civitate, quæ proprie ita nuncupatur, sed pro eo, cujus hæc erat typus, videlicet, ecclesia Dei, sive ea sit militans, sive triumphans, prout a a) quibusdam exponitur de ecclesia in terris, ab aliis, iisque admodum multis, de triumphante in‑ cœlis, quæ vocatur sanƈta Hierosolyma descendens ex cœlis a Deo, Apoc. 21,10. Utri autem harum nos rectius obstringamus, optime judicari poterit, cum inspexerimus, quid in se habeant hæc verba, tunc erit sanƈta &c. Tunc ( vel &) Hierosolyma, locus hoc nomine insignitus erit sanctus, קדש Kodesh, sanƈtitas, hebraice, uti nostrates ad marginem notant, quia substantivum est & in abstracto, non in concreto,vel adjectivum, quo quidem innuitur superlativus gradus, majorq; sanctitas, quam vocabulum præ se fert, quando in‑ concreto quid simpliciter sanƈtum dicitur, ac si tam sanctum sit, quam sanctitas ipsa, locusque hic sanctus dicatur superlativo gradu super omne id, quod ejus nominis eo tempore erat. Quæ tunc erat Hierosolyma, vocatur civitas sancta, ut Nehem. 11, 1. & 18. Esa. 52,1. Matth.4,5. & 27,53. & alibi. Quam cum dicit fore sanƈtitatem, id innuere videtur, vel quod major futura sit ejus sanctitas, vel quod alia notetur Hierosolyma, præter eam, quæ olim erat. Alludi hic arbitratur Abarbinel ad diversos sanctitatis gradus, qua diversa loca Hierosolyma præstabant, cum adhuc integro esset statu. Verba ejus, quæ citata jam sequuntur, eo redeunt, quod, cum tem-
units.tr: *) Merc. y) Pet. a Fig. will be fulfilled; although it cannot be denied that at all times Christ bestows these in such measure also upon the church militant on this earth, so that these words can rightly be applied to it (as others do), since it enjoys the presence of God and the signs of his providence and protection in such a peculiar way as no other kind of men or sect has ever enjoyed; and wherever these are not clearly evident in every respect, the defect is made up for by faith and most certain hope. Hence it can also be very easily grasped how the following words are to be taken: Then Jerusalem will be holy, etc. Here Jerusalem can be taken in the same way, and by many, indeed by most, it is rightly so taken, so that Zion is understood not indeed as the city properly so called, but as that of which it was the type, namely the church of God, whether militant or triumphant. Some explain it of the church on earth, others, and very many, of the triumphant church in heaven, which is called the holy Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, Rev. 21:10. Which of these we should rather adhere to can best be judged when we have looked at what these words, then it will be holy, etc., contain. Then (or and) Jerusalem, a place marked by this name, will be holy: kodesh [קדש], holiness, in Hebrew, as our countrymen note in the margin, because it is a substantive in the abstract, not in the concrete, or an adjective, by which indeed the superlative degree is implied, and a greater holiness than the word itself conveys, when something in the concrete is simply called holy, as if it were as holy as holiness itself, and this holy place is said in the superlative degree above everything of that name which existed at that time. Jerusalem, as it then was, is called the holy city, as in Neh. 11:1, 18; Isa. 52:1; Matt. 4:5; 27:53, and elsewhere. When it says it will be holiness, it seems to suggest either that its holiness will be greater, or that another Jerusalem is noted, besides the one that formerly existed. Abarbanel thinks an allusion is made here to the various degrees of holiness which the various places of Jerusalem possessed while it was still in its entire state. His words, which follow as already cited, come to this: that, since
