units.la: z) Quæ enim ipsa habet in re, hæc latet in spe. Pet. a Fig. a) Mercer. hoc de ecclesia in terris intelligo. „pore prioris templi domus Dei sancta effet, neminique intrare—„ permissum in הובר Hecal, corpus templi, praeterquam sacer„dotibus Domini, multoque minus in sanctum sanctorum, quo „nemo ingrediebatur, quam solus pontifex semel quotannis, e „contrario לעתיד לבוא tempore futuro, tota civitas Hierosolyma—„fimilis futura fit domui Domini sanctæ & templo Dei, ita utin„circumcisus vel profanus non illud fit intraturus, propter præfen„tiam majestatis ejus, quam in medio ejus est manifestaturus. Atque hinc est, quod dicat,Hierosolyma erit sancta (vel sanctitas) & alieni non transibunt amplius per eam לקרשתה propter sanctitatem ejus. Alii, inquit, aliter hæc explicant,ac fi hoc, alieni non transibunt amplius per eam, idem effet dictum, atque, non amplius transibunt perHierofolymam ad bellum adversus eam gerendum, ruinam magnam intuentes, in quam ex gentes sunt irruturæ, quæ id contra eam— suscipere contendunt; quam expositionem fatis putat commodam. Eodem fere modo, quo utraque hæc interpretatio concinnata,longo ante eum intervallo exposuit hæc R. Kimchi huncce in modum „scribens: Et erit Jerusalem sanctitas, i. e. velut sanctum quod „prohibitum est externis (vel nefas peregrinis id contrectare) & a„lieni non transibunt per eam, i.e. ut amplius malefaciant illis, uti fecerunt usque in hodiernum diem. Id, inquit, ita intelligi potest, ne ingrediantur externi Hierosolymam, quia magna erit fanctitas ejus לעתיד leatid in futurum: Ita ut, quemadmodum vetitum erat (olim) templum ingredi, etiam Israeli; sic tota civitas sancta futura fit, adeo ut non ingredianturin eam externi ex populis mundi. Duo inprimis his in explicationibus sunt obfervatu digna: primo, quod per Hierosolymam proprie & ad literam hanc civitatem intelligant: Secundo quod magnum hoc privilegium— de sanctitate extraordinaria hic promissa pertineat לעתיד לבוא ad tempus futurum, de quo in specie Abarbinel declarat fe intelligere illud, quod post b) mortuorum resurrectionem futurum est. Kimchi quidem tempus non exprimit; verum conjectu difficile non est, quo respiciat. c) Somniant enim, ut non nemo recte notat, illam terre-
units.tr: z) For what it has in fact, this lies hidden in hope. Pet. a Fig. a) Mercer: I understand this of the Church on earth. "In the time of the former temple the house of God was holy, and no one was permitted to enter the hekhal [היכל], the body of the temple, except the priests of the Lord, and much less into the Holy of Holies, which no one entered except the high priest alone, once a year. On the contrary, in the time to come [לעתיד לבוא] the whole city of Jerusalem will be like the holy house of the Lord and the temple of God, so that no circumcised or profane person will enter it, because of the presence of his majesty, which he will manifest in its midst. And hence he says, Jerusalem will be holy (or holiness), and strangers will no longer pass through her [לקדשתה] because of her holiness. Others, he says, explain these words differently, as if this, strangers will no longer pass through her, meant the same as: they will no longer pass through Jerusalem to wage war against her, looking on the great ruin into which the nations are about to rush, which they undertake against her; this explanation he thinks quite suitable." Almost in the same way as both of these interpretations were devised, R. Kimchi explained these things long before him, writing thus: "And Jerusalem will be holiness, that is, like something holy which is forbidden to foreigners (or wrong for strangers to touch), and strangers will no longer pass through her, that is, so that they no longer do evil to them as they have done until this day. This, he says, can be understood in this way: that foreigners may not enter Jerusalem, because her holiness will be great in the future [לעתיד]; so that, just as it was once forbidden even to Israel to enter the temple, so the whole city will be made holy, so that foreigners from the peoples of the world will not enter it." Two things in particular in these explanations are worth noting: first, that by Jerusalem they properly and literally understand this city; second, that this great privilege of extraordinary holiness promised here pertains to the time to come [לעתיד לבוא], the future time, of which Abarbanel in particular declares that he understands it to be what is to come after b) the resurrection of the dead. Kimchi indeed does not state the time; but it is not difficult to conjecture to what he refers. For c) they dream, as not a few rightly observe, of that earthly

units.la: b) Duplicem enim resurrectionem fore arbitratur. c) Pet, a Fig. terrenam Jerusalem, quam expectant, per Messiam ædificandam. Verum quicquid concipiant de gloriosa quadam Hierosolyma futura in terris, quam his promissis privilegiis gavisuram esse sibi persuadent, in eorum numero a nobis necessario censetur, quæ vane ac fine ullo fundamento futura expectant inter se & in gratiam suæ gentis, haud secus atque ea opinio, qua Messiam adhuc putant venturum. Quod ad interpretes Christianos attinet, qui norunt eum venisse, necesse est, qui hic capiunt Hierosolymam pro ea urbe, quæ proprie ita nominatur, ut ea jam eventum suum habuisse dicant cum adhuc esset in flore; verum in assignando tempore, quo hæc impleta fuerint, non arbitror ullum nobis esse facturum satis; Unde est, quod Cyrillus & Theodoretus hæc promissa non habeant absoluta, sed conditionata, ita ut felici hac conditione usuri sint, si civitatis hujus incolæ se ipsos purgarent ob omni iniquitate & cultu idololatrico, atque ea, qua par est, Deum colerent puritate ac sinceritate: si adversa uterentur fortuna, quod id unum attribuendum esset, juxta Theodoretum, rebus suis improbe gestis, quippe promissa divina requirunt, ut a parte ipsorum prius peragantur probeque observentur, quæ postulantur. Idem confirmat Aben Ezra ex Judæis, qui subaudiendum putat &c. Si custodierint legem Domini, uti hoc expressum est Zach. qui postquam multa bona promiserat, uti quod in medio illorum vellet habitare cap. 2, 10. postea addit c. 6, 15. Hoc totum tum implebitur, si diligenter observaveritis vocem Domini Dei vestri.
units.tr: b) For he thinks there will be a twofold resurrection. c) Pet. a Fig. earthly Jerusalem, which they expect to be built by the Messiah. But whatever they imagine about some glorious Jerusalem to come on earth, which they persuade themselves will enjoy these promised privileges, we must necessarily count among those things which they vainly and without any foundation expect, for themselves and for the sake of their nation, no less than that opinion by which they still think the Messiah is yet to come. As for Christian interpreters, who know that he has come, those who here take Hierosolymam for the city that is properly so called must say that these things were already fulfilled when it was still in its prime; but I do not think any of them will give us a satisfactory account of the time when these things were fulfilled. Hence it is that Cyril and Theodoret do not regard these promises as absolute but as conditional, so that they will enjoy them on this happy condition, if the inhabitants of this city purified themselves from all iniquity and idolatrous worship, and worshipped God with the purity and sincerity that is fitting; if they met with adversity, that is to be attributed, according to Theodoret, solely to their own wicked conduct, since the divine promises require that what is demanded of them be first carried out and duly observed on their part. Aben Ezra among the Jews confirms the same, thinking that one must supply: If they keep the law of the Lord, as this is expressed in Zach., who, after promising many good things, such as that he would dwell in the midst of them (2:10), afterwards adds (6:15): All this will then be fulfilled, if you diligently obey the voice of the Lord your God.

units.la: Grotius nihil notat ad hunc versum, præterquam quod verbis, externi non transfibunt per eam, adjiciat, bellili exercitu, nulla alicujus temporis mentione addita. At ex præcedenti versu palam fit, eum hæc referre ad tempora, quæ post cladem Antiochi fluxere. Quoscunque autem Christianorum interpretum mihi videre contigit, illis fere omnibus sentio minus probatam esse sententiam de terrena Sione vel Hierosolyma secura reddenda hisce verbis a Prophetis prolatis. Quocirca figurate hæc nomina sunt (ut alibi non uno loco sunt sumenda) pro ecclesia Dei, eaque vel militante in
units.tr: Grotius makes no note on this verse, except that to the words strangers will not pass through her he adds with an army of war, with no mention of any time. But from the preceding verse it is plain that he refers these things to the times that followed the defeat of Antiochus. Among the Christian interpreters I have happened to see, almost all of them, I feel, judge less favourably the opinion that these words of the prophets are to be applied to an earthly Zion or Jerusalem made secure. Therefore these names are figurative (as they are to be taken in many places elsewhere) for the Church of God, and that either militant on this earth or triumphant in heaven.

units.la: hac terra, vel triumphante in cœlis, quippe alterutri harum congruit & ab aliis huic, ab aliis alteri applicatur. Ad utramque harum dico, hæc verba possunt referri & applicari; verum extra dubium est, in militante Ecclesia eorum eventum esse multo evidentiorem juxta ea, quæ verba complectuntur, quam in triumphante. Unde ad militantem ecclesiam, si hæc referantur, quamvis ea dici possit sancta, sive sanctitas, imputata justitia sponsi sui d) vestita, e) sanctificata per fidem in eo,f) qui se ipsum exposuit pro ea, ut eam sanctificaret & purificaret lavacro aquæ per verbum, ut sisteret eam sibi gloriosam non habentem maculam aut rugam &c. in quam nihil ingredietur alienum & adversus quam nec ipsæ portæ inferni prævalebunt ipso Salvatore dicente Matth. 16, 18. id tamen contra hanc opinionem excipi posse videtur, quod nunquam adeo pura ac sancta sit visibilis ecclesia, quin multi in ea sint, qui impure secus, quam oportet, se gerunt, qui vera nihilominus ejus membra esse sibi persuasum habent; cui annexum est, quod, qui sanctissima purissimaque ecclesiæ sunt membra, ab inimicis ejus fuerint oppressi & omne persecutionis genus passi. Quam objectionem ita quidam expediunt, ut dicant, membra hæc impura quidem immixta esse veris ac ingenuis ecclesiæ membris, ut lolium tritico; ea tamen non esse ecclesiæ membra, eoque impuram eam non reddere posse. Quantumvis enim hominibus offendiculo esse queant, qui alios ab aliis secernere nesciunt; oculos tamen Dei non effugiunt, qui probe eos novit & non nisi eos ecclesiam suam ejusque membra habet, qui puro sinceroque sunt animo atque pro virili sanctitatem sectantur, licet infirmitatibus multis sint obnoxii. g) In vera enim Ecclesia, quæ Dei sponsa est sine ruga & macula, impiis, etiam in hoc seculo, locus non est &c. Utcunque consortii hujus participes esse contendant hominibusque imponant, Deo tamen imponere non possunt, qui illos ex Ecclesiæ suæ numero non habet, vel ex incolis sanctæ Hierosolymæ, quæ, quoad ingenua sua membra, est sanctificata, purgata & reddita, vocataque sanctitas, nec in vanum abire potest, quod ei fecit promissum. Hinc, quod porro objicitur, eam quam sæpissime subire
units.tr: Each of these, I say, these words can be referred and applied to; yet it is beyond doubt that their fulfilment is far more evident in the militant Church, according to what the words embrace, than in the triumphant. Hence, if these are referred to the militant Church, although she may be called holy, or holiness, clothed with the imputed righteousness of her Bridegroom, sanctified through faith in him who gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her and cleanse her by the washing of water through the word, that he might present her to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle, etc., into which nothing unclean will enter and against which not even the gates of hell will prevail, the Saviour himself saying (Matt. 16:18); yet it seems this can be objected against this opinion: that the visible Church is never so pure and holy that there are not many in her who conduct themselves impurely, otherwise than they ought, yet who are persuaded that they are true members of her; and to this is joined the fact that those who are the most holy and purest members of the Church have been oppressed by her enemies and have suffered every kind of persecution. Some resolve this objection by saying that these impure members are indeed mixed in with the true and genuine members of the Church, as darnel is with wheat; yet they are not members of the Church, and so cannot make her impure. For however much they may be a stumbling block to men, who do not know how to separate some from others, they do not escape the eyes of God, who knows them well and has as his Church and her members only those who are of a pure and sincere mind and pursue holiness as far as they can, although they are subject to many infirmities. For in the true Church, which is God's bride without wrinkle or spot, there is no place for the impious, even in this age, etc. However much they contend that they share in this fellowship and deceive men, they cannot deceive God, who does not count them in the number of his Church, or among the inhabitants of holy Jerusalem, which, as to her genuine members, is sanctified, purged and made, and is called holiness, nor can what he promised her come to nothing. Hence, what is further objected, that she very often has to undergo

units.la: d) Taraov. e) Act. 26, 18. f) Eph. 5, 25. 26. 27. Tit. 2, 14. g) Vid. Merc. subire hostium crudelem oppressionem, tali expeditur b) responso, quod istud non oriatur ex promissionis divinæ implendæ fideique, persolvendæ defectu, sed ex sua ipsius culpa, qua non exsolvit, quod ex sua parte exigitur, officiū sancte ac immaculate fe fe gerendi, cujus perficiendi auxiliatrices porrigit manus, manumq; ei, ut admoveant, præstolatur. Hoc debet imputari peccatis nostris; nos enim facimus ruptaras, per quas irrumpunt hostes ecclesiæ, eamque conculcant, inquit Calvinus. i) Quoties illud fit, hoc nostro vitio fieri certum est, inquit alius, qui in his verbis etiam conditionem ex illorum parte contineri vult, ut fe tales gerant, quales Deus efficere velle promittit, fi in effectum deduci optarent, quod DEus præterea pollicitus suerat de iis defendendis ab inimicis irrumpentibus. Quod refponsum non procul abit ab opinione Theodoreti, quam antea vidimus, quamvis alio fortean fignificatu hic accipit Hierosolymā, quam cæteri. Quibus adjungi potest, quod k) alibi refponfionis loco reperimus, scilicet, promissis a Deo hic factis nullo modo contrariari afflictiones ac persecutiones, quibus premitur Ecclesia, extraneorumque ac profanorum vim, qua videntur præpollere. Non transibunt hi, nocendi scilicet causa. Deus enim nequaquam feret, quamvis auxiliis faciant frequentes, ut ea illis protinus succumbat & in poteftatem illorum veniat; habet adhuc, quo fe suffulciat ac soletur in suis afflictionibus, adeo ut nihil damni exinde ferat, sed magis magisque ad studium ac viam sanctitatis iis incitetur & in ea confirmetur. Atque hæc sufficiant ad probandum, fi per Hierosolymam intelligatur ecclesia militans in terris, ad eandem quoque spectare, hæc promissa, omnique tempore esse completa. Sunt nihilominus quibus ea planiore expeditioreque ratione ad ecclesiam triumphantem in cœlis referre placet, cui verba fignificatu absolutissimo applicari possunt. Sancta erit. (Sanctitas Domino) omni ratione ac respectu, quem hoc epitheton inferre possit. (1) Sancta, i. e. l) pura ab omni labe culpæ, cujus membra erunt pura & ab omni macula & inquinatione peccati purgata. (2) Sancta, i. e. m) sacra, Deo tota con-
units.tr: d) Taraov. e) Act. 26, 18. f) Eph. 5, 25. 26. 27. Tit. 2, 14. g) See Mercer. the cruel oppression of enemies, is resolved by such a b) response: that it does not arise from any failure in fulfilling the divine promise or keeping faith, but from her own fault, by which she does not discharge what is required of her part, namely the duty of conducting herself holily and blamelessly, toward accomplishing which God stretches out helping hands and waits for her to put her own hands to them. This ought to be imputed to our sins; for we make the breaches through which the enemies of the Church rush in and trample her underfoot, says Calvin. i) Whenever that happens, it is certain it happens through our fault, says another, who wants a condition on their part to be contained in these words too, namely that they should behave as God promises to make them, if they wished to bring to effect what God had further promised about defending them against the enemies who break in. This answer is not far from the opinion of Theodoret which we saw earlier, although he takes Jerusalem in a different sense, perhaps, from the others. To this can be added what k) elsewhere we find as a response, namely that the afflictions and persecutions by which the Church is pressed in no way contradict the promises made here by God, nor does the force of strangers and profane people, by which they seem to prevail. These will not pass through, that is, for the purpose of harming. For God will by no means allow, although they make frequent attacks, that she immediately succumb to them and come into their power; she still has something by which she may support and comfort herself in her afflictions, so that she suffers no loss from them, but is rather stirred more and more to zeal and the way of holiness, and confirmed in it. These considerations are enough to prove that if by Jerusalem is understood the Church militant on earth, these promises also refer to her and have been fulfilled at all times. Nevertheless there are some who prefer to refer them, by a plainer and more direct reasoning, to the Church triumphant in heaven, to which the words can be applied in their fullest sense. Holy she will be (Holiness to the Lord) in every respect and regard that this epithet can bear. (1) Holy, that is, i.e. l) pure from every stain of guilt, whose members will be pure and cleansed from every spot and defilement of sin. (2) Holy, that is, i.e. m) sacred, wholly consecrated to God

units.la: b) Calv. Gvalt. i) Gvalter. k) Apud Merc. l) Ribera. m) Pet. a Fig. consecrata ac peculiaris, atque ita n) chara Deo & sub ejus cura, favore ac tutela tuta ac immunis a dominatione, praeda & possessione populorum profanorum, a quibus contaminari ac profanari possit.(3) Sancta, i.e. quae non admittit aut novit ullum membrum profanum.
units.tr: b) Calv. Gvalt. i) Gvalter. k) Apud Merc. l) Ribera. m) Pet. a Fig. Consecrated and set apart, and thus n) dear to God and under his care, favour and protection, safe and free from the lordship, plunder and possession of profane peoples, by whom it could be defiled and profaned. (3) Holy, that is, one that admits or knows no profane member.

units.la: Non enim intrabit quicquam in eam, quod inquinat, aut abominandum quippiam patrat, vel mendacium facit, Apoc. 21, 27. quod idem exprimitur his verbis: Et alieni non transfibunt amplius per eam. Alieni nulli fine Christo, o) alieni a conversatione Israelis & extranei pactis promissionis; ubi non quidem ita accipienda vox, ut nationum ferat distinctionem, & alii aliis hoc respectu sint peregrini. Etenim in Christo & in Ecclesia ejus talis distinctio locum non habet, neque ulla differentia est inter p) Graecum & Judaeum, circumcisionem & praeputium, barbarum & Scytham, servum & liberum, ut quis idcirco posset censeri peregrinus Ecclesiae, q) omnes sunt unus in eo, omnes r) Israel Dei, s) concives sanctorum & domestici Dei. Sed peregrini sunt Ecclesiae ejus, qui peregrini sunt respectu Dei & veritatis, peregrini t) a fide, infideles, profani & impii, hostesque Ecclesiae. De his dicitur, non esse transituros per sanctam ejus Hierosolymam, ecclesiam ejus, vel nocendi, vel profanandi causa, aut si mavis, nullum iis intercessurum esse commercium cum ea. Syrus hoc loco (iis exemplaribus quae habemus) habet lo yaamerun, non inhabitabunt. Recte quoad sensum; quippe sub hebraico verbo id etiam latet, si ad literam sumatur, uti faciunt fere omnes interpretes; at subdubito, num initio auctor hujus versionis ita reddiderit, & non potius lo necberun, quod & radicalibus literis Hebraico congruit, & significatione, qua alii id accipiunt, quae multo est largior, quam habitandi, quae videtur fixam in loco innuere sedem, cum altera notet, eos omnino non esse venturos ac commercium in ea habituros. Quae quod sit vera alienorum ac profanorum conditio, respectu coelestis Hierosolymae Ecclesiae triumphantis, quo referunt, qui opinioni recens allatae addicti sunt, hanc
units.tr: For there shall in no wise enter into it anything that defileth, or worketh abomination, or maketh a lie, Rev. 21:27. The same is expressed in these words: And strangers shall no more pass through it. Strangers means none apart from Christ, o) strangers from the commonwealth of Israel and aliens from the covenants of promise. Here the word is not to be taken as bearing a distinction of nations, so that one people is a stranger to another in this respect. For in Christ and in his Church no such distinction has any place, nor is there any difference between p) Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond and free, so that anyone could on that account be counted a stranger to the Church; q) they are all one in him, all r) the Israel of God, s) fellow citizens of the saints and of the household of God. But those are strangers to his Church who are strangers with respect to God and the truth, strangers t) to the faith, unbelievers, profane and impious men, and enemies of the Church. Of these it is said that they shall not pass through his holy Jerusalem, his Church, either to harm or to profane it; or, if you prefer, that they shall have no intercourse with it. The Syriac in this place (in the copies we have) reads lo yaamerun, they shall not dwell. This is right in sense, for under the Hebrew verb too this meaning lies hidden, if it is taken literally, as nearly all the interpreters do. But I doubt whether the author of this version at first rendered it so, and did not rather write lo necberun, which agrees with the Hebrew in its radical letters and in the meaning which others give it, a meaning much broader than to dwell; for dwelling seems to suggest a fixed seat in a place, whereas the other word means that they will not come at all and will have no intercourse in it. That this is indeed the condition of aliens and profane persons with respect to the heavenly Jerusalem, the triumphant Church, to which those refer who hold the opinion just stated, this

units.tr: v. 18. And it shall come to pass in that day, that the mountains shall drop down new wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the rivers of Judah shall flow with waters, and a fountain shall come forth of the house of the LORD, and shall water the valley of Shittim.

units.la: Exposita praecedenti versu immunitate, quae futura erat in sancta Hierosolyma ipsis, ab omni quorumcunque hostium impietate & violentia, ulterius hic describere pergit ingentem incolarum ejus felicitatem, exhibendo eam omnium bonorum copiam, quae ad illam pertinet, quibusque tunc temporis erant fruituri. Verba, quibus haec continentur, Montes stillabunt musto, & colles fluent lacte & c. primo intuitu, R. Tanchum auctore, prae se ferre videntur [Arabic] metaphoricum figuratumque sermonem, denotantem abundantiam plenitudinis ac benedictionum. Montes, inquit, stillabunt [Hebrew] afis, musto, ut noftrat. cum aliis non paucis habent. Non enim sibi constant interpretes in hac voce vertenda tum hoc loco, tum alibi, ubi occurrit, ut [Hebrew] praeter alia supra cap. 1, 5. & Amos. 9, 13. ubi eadem fere habentur verba, quae hic sunt, eaque vox [Hebrew] afis a noftrat. redditur vinum dulce, x) in margine autem, musum, quod hic in textu habent. Chaldaeus omnibus his in locis habet [Hebrew] chamar merat, vinum merum (quod quidam vertunt y) vinum inebrians, vinum admodum forte). LXX. hic & apud Amos. 9, 13. [Greek] Vulgatus, dulcedinem. Tigur. hic & supra cap. 1. succum expressum, & apud Amos. succum dulcem. Caftalio hoc & aliis duobus locis, laticem, fine ullo addito epitheto. Perquam exigua est haec diversitas, nec multum nos morari debet, quia ex notatis ad c. 1, 5. apparet hanc vocem deduci a radice [Hebrew] afas, quae cum significet expressit, calcavit, proprie talem denotat succum vel liquorem, qui exprimendo vel calcando ex quodam fructu aut aliis rebus elicitur, nulla ratione habita ejus qualitatis, sitne dulcis an acida &c. Quandoquidem autem hocce modo vinum paratur caeterorumque liquorum hoc proprium habet, uti notum est, de eo cum primis accipi potest, si locus, ubi occurrit, id patitur; quod hoc loco quam plurimi faciunt, eoque, cum id recens plerumque sit dulce, haud temere pro vino dulci aut musto sumunt; LXX. vero & Vulgatus in abstracto pro dulcedine, qua tamen intellexisse dicenti sunt vinum, quod dulcedine abundat, ad substantiam ejus verius spectantibus, quam ad qualitatem. Atque hac ratione facillimo negotio conciliari possunt discrepantes interpretationes, omni-
units.tr: Having set out in the preceding verse the immunity that was to be given to the holy Jerusalem and its inhabitants from every impiety and violence of any enemies, the prophet goes on here to describe at greater length the great happiness of its inhabitants, by setting out the abundance of all the good things that belong to it and that they were then to enjoy. The words in which these things are contained, The mountains shall drop down sweet wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, etc., at first sight, according to R. Tanchum, seem to present a metaphorical and figurative manner of speaking, denoting an abundance of fullness and blessings. The mountains, he says, will drip afis, that is, new wine, as our translators render it with many others. For the interpreters do not agree about how this word should be rendered, either in this place or elsewhere where it occurs, as in addition to what is said above at chapter 1, verse 5, and at Amos 9, 13, where almost the same words occur as here. Our translators render the word afis there as sweet wine x), but in the margin as must, which is what they have here in the text. The Chaldee has in all these places chamar merat, pure wine (which some render y) intoxicating wine, very strong wine). The Seventy here and at Amos 9, 13 have sweetness. The Zurich Bible here and above at chapter 1 has expressed juice, and at Amos sweet juice. Castalio, in this and two other places, has liquor, without any added epithet. This difference is very slight, and we need not dwell on it long, because from the notes on chapter 1, verse 5, it appears that this word is derived from the root afas, which means to press out, to tread, and properly denotes a juice or liquid that is drawn out of some fruit or other things by pressing or treading, without regard to its quality, whether it is sweet or sour, and so on. Since wine is prepared in this way, and as is well known this property belongs to other liquids too, it can be understood especially of wine, if the place where the word occurs allows it. This is what very many do in this place, and because it is usually sweet while fresh, they readily take it to mean sweet wine or must. But the Seventy and the Vulgate take it in the abstract as sweetness, though these translators seem to have understood wine that abounds in sweetness, looking more to its substance than to its quality. And in this way the differing interpretations can be reconciled with the greatest ease, since all

units.la: {ff} Esa. 49, 26. Cant. 8, 2. x) Ut & in eo loco Esaias. y) Bibl. Polyg. omnibus intelligentibus dulcem ac suavem liquorem, qualis in deliciis habebatur ac communiter in usu erat, quod vinum fuisse uvarum haud vero absimile est, quanquam R. Tanchum ad hunc locum notat illud quibusdam inprimis denotare ﺷﺮﺍﺏ vinum ex malis punicis (qua ratione accipi posse arbitror Cant. 8, 2.) licet in Rabbinico Dictionario suo, quod vocat Morshed, dicat, non posse ibi de succo malorum punicorum sumi, sed de vino rubro, quod colore referat mala punica (vel grana malorum punicorum). Quibus verbis ita intellectis de quodam pretioso liquore, manifestum evadit, verba reliqua, montes stillabunt, non posse accipi ad literam, sed metaphorice (uti diximus) & hyperbolice, ut innuant ingentem hujus liquoris copiam, qualis nullo negotio ex uvis aut similibus fructibus erat proventurus, quae tanta abundantia in montibus protuberaturae erant, ac si ipsi montes stillarent, atque ex iis multum exiliret, non quod revera id facturos esse montes sibi quisquam persuadeat. Res quippe esset nunquam hucusque visa, nec ullo tempore expectanda, utpote quae e diametro creationis naturae contrariatur. Pari modo & sequentia verba intelligenda sunt, Et colles fluent lacte, id est, tanta lactis copia ibi colligetur ex pecudibus pabulum his in collibus quaerentibus, ut ipsi colles videantur fontes ac rivos lactis effundere, vel ipsi in lac resoluti, quod inde defluteret. Ita enim proprie sonant verba תלכנרי חלב telacnah chalab, defluet vel decurret lac, quibus, ut ait Kimchi, actionem eundi f. fluendi, quae lactis est, ipsis tribuit collibus ad innuendum mirandam ejus plenitudinem, שיוצא מהמרעי quod procedit a pascuis (vel a pecudibus pascuis fruentibus) quae in iis erunt, ut explanat Abarbinel. Necessarium igitur est, ut magna earum rerum intelligatur copia, quae hic describuntur, aut earum nominibus comprehenduntur. Nam antequam inquiramus, an proprie sint intelligenda, vel secus, oportet ad literam etiam examinemus verba quae sequuntur, Et omnes rivi Judae fluent (vel ibunt, in margine) aquis, de quibus idem observat hic Kimchi, quod de prioribus, actum nimirum fluendi vel eundi, qui aquarum est, tribui loco ubi fluit. Vox enim אפיקי Aphike, quam nostrat interpre-
units.tr: {ff} Isa. 49, 26. Cant. 8, 2. x) As also in that place in Isaiah. y) Polyglot Bible: all who understand it agree that it is a sweet and pleasant liquor, such as was held in delight and commonly in use; that this was the juice of grapes is not very unlikely. Yet R. Tanchum notes on this place that it especially denotes to some sharab, wine made from pomegranates (in which sense I think it can be taken at Cant. 8, 2.), although in his Rabbinic Dictionary, which he calls Morshed, he says that it cannot be taken there as the juice of pomegranates, but as red wine, which resembles pomegranates in colour (or the seeds of pomegranates). When these words are understood in this way, as referring to some precious liquor, it becomes clear that the remaining words, the mountains shall drop, cannot be taken literally, but metaphorically (as we said) and hyperbolically, to suggest the great abundance of this liquor, such as would easily have come from grapes or similar fruits, which were to grow on the mountains in such plenty that it would seem as if the mountains themselves dripped and that much flowed out of them; not that anyone should suppose the mountains would really do this. For such a thing would be unlike anything seen until now, and not to be expected at any time, since it runs directly counter to the nature of creation. In the same way the following words must be understood, And the hills shall flow with milk, that is, so great an abundance of milk will be gathered there from the flocks seeking pasture on these hills, that the hills themselves seem to pour out springs and streams of milk, or to be turned into milk that flows down from them. For this is the proper sense of the words telacnah chalab, the milk shall flow down or run down, by which, as Kimchi says, the action of going or flowing, which belongs to milk, is attributed to the hills themselves, to suggest its marvellous fullness; that which comes forth from the pastures (or from the flocks feeding in them), which will be in them, as Abarbanel explains. It is therefore necessary that a great quantity of those things described here be understood, or be comprehended under their names. For before we inquire whether they are to be understood properly or otherwise, we must also examine the following words literally: And all the brooks of Judah shall flow (or shall go, in the margin) with water. On this Kimchi makes the same observation as on the earlier words, namely that the action of flowing or going, which belongs to water, is attributed to the place where it flows. For the word aphike, which our translators render brooks, seems rather to mean valleys than the waters that flow in them. As for the sense, nothing else is noted here again than their great abundance, which here

units.la: * Hebrew word and Greek/Hebrew glosses in the printed text as above. terpretantur rivi, ipsi videtur magis significare z) valles, quam aquas quæ in eis fluunt. Quoad sensum autem, nihil aliud hic iterum notatur, quam eorum magna abundantia, quæ hic nominantur. Quod etiam locum habet in sequentibus, Et fons e domo Domini egredietur, & irrigabit (fons qui tantam præbebit aquarum copiam, ut irrigaturus etiam fit) vallem Shittim. שִׁטִּים Shittim nostrat. est proprium nomen loci, qua ratione & Chaldæo (qui scribit Sittin) & Syro, (qui habet ܣܘܛܝܢ Sotim) aliisque non paucis recentioribus interpretibus accipitur. Eodem occurrit etiam sensu aliis in locis Scripturæ, veluti Num. 25, 1. ubi Israel dicitur mansisse in Shittim, ibique commisisse scortationem cum filiabus Moabitarum. Rursus dicitur Jos. 2,1. & 3,1. ut & Mich. 6,5. fuisse in terra Moabitarum trans Jordanem, non procul ab eo, ita ut pro Jordane ipso eum accipiat R. Saadias a Kimchi & Abarbinel citatus, adversus quod a) nonnemo excipit, quod arida loca dicantur irriganda, non rivi. Verum non videtur vero absimile, illum forte intellexisse per Jordanem regionem ad Jordanem. Quod dicitur, illum irrigatum iri, argumento est, locum per se esse siccum atque procul ab Hierosolyma remotum, ut fons ex domo Domini egrediens necessario rivus debeat esse magnus, qui tantum aquarum atq; eousque se effundat, solumque aridum ibi irriget. Pro nomine loci proprio etiam habet eam R. Salomo, cujus mentio fit Num. 25,1. juxta quem verba ad literam sonant, irrigabit planum (sive vallem Shittim) sensu autem allegorico, expiabit pro iniquitate Peor.
units.tr: * Hebrew word and Greek/Hebrew glosses in the printed text as above. Our translators render it streams, but the word itself seems to signify valleys rather than the waters that flow in them. As to the sense, nothing else is noted here than the great abundance of water they name. This also holds for what follows: And a fountain shall come forth from the house of the Lord, and shall water (a fountain that will supply such a copious abundance of waters that it will even be about to water) the valley of Shittim. שִׁטִּים Shittim [Shittim] in our translation is the proper name of a place, and in this sense it is taken by the Chaldee paraphrast (who writes Sittin), by the Syriac (who has Sotim), and by not a few other more recent interpreters. It occurs in the same sense elsewhere in Scripture, as in Num. 25:1, where Israel is said to have stayed in Shittim and there to have committed fornication with the daughters of Moab. Again, it is said in Josh. 2:1 and 3:1, as also in Mic. 6:5, that they were in the land of Moab beyond the Jordan, not far from it, so that R. Saadias, cited by Kimchi and Abarbanel, takes it as the Jordan itself. Against this someone objects that dry places are said to be watered, not streams. But it does not seem far from the truth that he perhaps understood by the Jordan the region near the Jordan. That it is said to be watered is evidence that the place is in itself dry and far from Jerusalem, so that the fountain coming out of the house of the Lord must necessarily be a great river, which pours out so much water and so far, and waters that dry ground there. R. Solomon also takes it as a proper name, mentioned in Num. 25:1; according to him the words literally sound, it will water the plain (or the valley of Shittim), but in an allegorical sense, it will make atonement for the iniquity of Peor.

units.la: Verum ex interpretibus priscis sunt, qui pro nomine proprio id non accipiunt, sed pro appellativo, quod etiam interpretantur, idque non una ratione. Agmen hic ducunt LXX, qui quamvis aliis in locis, uti Num. 25,1. &c. pro loci nomine habeant atque reddant σατ]ειμ, Satteim, vel σατ]ειν, Sattein, ut Jos. 2,1. vel σατ]ειν, Jos. 3,1. tamen hic illud interpretantur τὸν χειμάρρων τῶν ξοινῶν (vel ut alii legunt ξοινίων) quod idem valet ac, torrentem funiculorum. Quo Hieronymus indicari putat certum mensurandi genus, quod in usu est Ægyptiis, qui numerant per funiculorum longitudinem. At alii intelligunt juncos, vel quoddam genus juncorum, quod vox etiam denotat,
units.tr: But among the ancient interpreters there are some who do not take it as a proper name but as a common noun, and they translate it too, and not for one reason. The Septuagint lead the way here: although in other places, as Num. 25:1 and elsewhere, they take it as a place name and render it Σατ[τ]ειμ (Satteim) or Σατ[τ]ειν (Sattein), as in Josh. 2:1, or Σατ[τ]ειν in Josh. 3:1, here they translate it τὸν χειμάρρων τῶν σχοινῶν [ton cheimarrōn tōn schoinōn] (or, as others read, σχοινίων), which means the same as the torrent of ropes. Jerome thinks this indicates a certain measure of length used by the Egyptians, who count by the length of ropes. But others understand reeds, or a certain kind of reed, which the word also denotes.

units.la: z) Kimchi. a) Pet. a Fig. tat, uti in quarta Oratione Nazianzeni, & in commentario ad hunc locum b) Nicetas, cui torrens vel vallis hic nominatus, est locus non procul ab Hierosolyma, aqua carens & juncos proferens. Pari ratione id accipit etiam Cyrillus pro denominatione χειμάῤῥα τινός, cujusdam torrentis vel rivuli, in quo crescunt juncι, quem eundem hic innui putat, qui vocatur rivulus Cedron (vel a Cedais) Job. 18,1.
units.tr: a) Peter a Figueiredo, as in the fourth Oration of Nazianzen and in his commentary on this passage; b) Nicetas, for whom the torrent or valley named here is a place not far from Jerusalem, lacking water and producing reeds. Cyril also takes it in the same way, as a name derived from χειμάῤῥα τινός [cheimarra tinos], some torrent or stream in which reeds grow, which he thinks is the same one referred to here, which is called the brook Kidron (or Cedron) in John 18:1.

units.la: Has interpretationes autem quamvis nemo diffiteri potest esse sono admodum discrepantes, attamen quam facillime inter se conciliari possunt. Ambæ enim eundem locum notare dicendi sunt, quatenus vox σχοῖνος significat & juncum & funiculum ex juncís nexum, adeo ut eodem recidat, sive dicamus rivum funiculorum ex juncis nexorum, sive juncorum, ex quibus hujusmodi funiculi sunt nexi. Eadem funiculorum notione hoc loco id reddit. Græcorum Latinus interpres, quamvis ambigue eandem reddat Mich. 6,5. ubi eadem occurrit, per Schœnis (quod quidem non nisi pro loci nomine habendum) quo in loco manifestus est error Arabicæ impressæ (quæ ex Græca in libris Prophetarum videtur concinnata) ubi habetur Men gebal, a montibus, diverse admodum a Græca; cum hic convenienter satis redditum sit Men Hebal, a funiculis; quod facile fieri potuit transmutatis literis ז & ז, quarum differentia tantum in addito vel omisso puncto sita est. Quo in loco juxta Hieronymum & in Græca error est; quodsi verum, idem dicendum est de hoc loco. Nimirum loco σχοῖνῳ, quod ibi a Latino redditur Schœnis, hic funiculorum, antea scriptum & lectum putat σχίνῳ, quod notat lentiscum vel mastichen, atque librariorum incuria conversum in σχοίνων, funiculorum. Quo etiam facit interpretatio Vulgati latini, qui utroque loco id habet pro arboris nomine diversi licet generis. Qui etiamsi vocem apud Micham pro nomine proprio accipiat, reddendo de Setim; tamen hic interpretatur נחל הששטים nachal hashittim, torrentem spinarum, quasi tantundem valeret Shittim ac spinas. Arboris autem nomen esse Shittim, comprobatum redditur ex Esa. 41,19. & ex aliis locis, ubi mentio fit ligni
units.tr: No one can deny that these interpretations differ considerably in sound, yet they can very easily be reconciled with one another. For both are to be said to indicate the same place, inasmuch as the word σχοῖνος [schoinos] signifies both a reed and a rope woven from reeds, so that it comes to the same thing whether we say a stream of ropes woven from reeds or of reeds from which such ropes are woven. With this sense of ropes the Latin translator of the Greek renders it here. Although he renders the same word ambiguously in Mic. 6:5, where it occurs again, as Schœnis (which is to be taken only as a place name), the error in the printed Arabic (which seems to have been put together from the Greek in the books of the Prophets) is manifest there, where it reads Men gebal, from the mountains, quite different from the Greek; whereas here it is rendered fairly well as Men Hebal, from the ropes. This could easily have happened by the interchange of the letters ז and ז, whose difference lies only in the adding or omitting of a point. In that passage the error is in Jerome and in the Greek too; if that is true, the same must be said of this passage. Indeed, in place of σχοῖνῳ [schoinō], which the Latin there renders Schœnis, here of ropes, one may suppose it was earlier written and read as σχίνῳ [schinō], which means mastic tree or lentisk, and through the carelessness of copyists was changed into σχοίνων [schoinōn], of ropes. The Vulgate Latin also agrees with this, for in both places it has the word as the name of a tree, though of a different kind. Although in Micah it takes the word as a proper name, rendering it de Setim, here it translates נחל הששטים [nachal hashittim] as the torrent of thorns, as if Shittim meant the same as thorns. But that Shittim is the name of a tree is shown from Isa. 41:19 and from other places where mention is made of wood of Shittim.

units.la: b) p. 1067. gni Shittim tanquam peculiaris notæ, atque inter præcipua censetur, quæ tabernaculo constituto in oblationem adferre jubentur Israelitæ Exod. 25,5. & ex quo res maximi momenti erant confectæ, ut arca, v. 10. vectes, v.13. mensa, v.23. ut & cap.26. afferes, v.15. vectes, v.26. columnæ, v.32. & altare suffitus cap. 30,1. Sic rursus in oblationibus, quæ a populo erant offerendæ, numeratur lignum Shittim Exod.35,7. & 24. & Deut.10, 3. dicitur Moses curasse arcam fieri ex ligno Shittim, cui imponebat duas tabulas legis. His omnibus in prædictis locis retinetur vox hebræa in latina versione Shittim, ut hujus arboris cognita denominatio, hoc loco tantum & primo, qui est apud Esaiam, excepto, ubi redditur pinus; Verum ex ipso hujus ligni usu constat, communem spinam nequaquam innui; quare & c) Hieronymus enodatius adjicit se non intelligere proprie spinam, sed arborem quæ similis sit spinæ albæ colore & foliis, non magnitudine; quippe tantæ est magnitudinis, ut perlati exinde parentur afferes, lignumque ejus robustum fit atque leve & pulchrum, quod cæteroquin non putrefit & corrumpitur, eoque a LXX. loco ex lege citato, redditur ἄσηπτα imputribilia, quæ arbor, inquit, non crescit ullo in loco exculto, aut in territoriis Romanis, sed in deserto Arabiæ. Quæ omnia ita profert ac si eorum oculatus fuisset testis, cui etiam hac in re fidem esse habendam censet M. Fullerus; d) Kimchi vero ait esse genus optimarum Cedrorum, hinc etiam Junius & Tremellius, vallem Cedrorum lectissimarum; qua ratione etiam Esa. 41,19. reddunt שטים lectissimam Cedrum, (ubi nostr. arborem Shittah) distinguentes eam ab אררז Arctz cognita ac communi cedro, cujus ibidem fit mentio, quod idem faciunt in cæteris Exodi & Deuteronomii locis, quæ ante adduximus, reddentes ligna cedrorum lectissimarum. Has inter differentes acceptiones vocis שטים Shittim nostrat, eos inprimis sequuntur, qui eam pro loci proprio habent, qui eam ob causam fortean ita vocabatur, quod multæ in eo vel e) circa eum hujusmodi crescebant arbores, quamvis f) aliis magis placeat, arbores ibi crescentes atque lignum inde delatum nomen accepisse a nomine vallis, in qua magna copia crescebant, g) non vallem ab arbore z) Vide fis eum in h. l. & in Esa. 41,19. d) In Rad. e) Schindl, Ribera. f) Ferrar. in Diction. Syriac. in ..., g) Ch. a Castro. bore illa, sed vel ab oppido vel alia ratione ita dictam. Vox נחל Nachal, quam alii interpretantur Torrentem, alii vallem, utriusque, quod ex diversis exemplis manifeste patet, significationis capax est. Nimirum depressum notat locum, in quo aqua fluere ac recipi potest בין יש בור מים בין אין בור מים five in eo fit aqua, five non fit, ut hoc explanat R. b) Kimchi, adeo ut commode alterutra harum significationum reddi possit, prout locus, ubi occurrit, postulat, atque congruenter id fieri in aprico est. Quod ad hunc locum, ab aliis hac, ab aliis alia factum esse ratione diximus, illi tamen quam maxime hujus loci rationem videntur habuisse, qui interpretantur per vallem. Sunt qui Vulgat. sequuntur, & cum eo reddunt torrentem, quo quidem non stricte ac propria sua significatione sumunt torrentis vocem, sed tam late, ut etiam denotet i) vallem vel planitiem, quibus plerumque manant torrentes vel rivi, quamvis hoc non fit omni tempore. Qua notione eadem vox, uti observatum est, in latina versione etiam alibi usurpatur, ut Gen. 26, 19. ubi de servis Isaaci dicitur, foderunt in torrente, sicuti a Duacenf. est redditum & in margine notatum, i. e. in rivo, ubi interdum vehemens volvitur fluentum, interdum nihil ejus omnino. Sic & 1. Sam. 15, 5. Tetendit Saul insidias suas in torrente, id quod nullo alio modo intelligi potest, quam ut ab aliis est expressum, in valle, & sic, inquit Pet. a Figuiero in praesenti loco, quem in Dictionario etiam suo citat Kimchi exempli loco, quo probat נחל Nachal denotare vallem aqua & scatentem & carentem. Quodsi enim aquis abundet, ut irrigetur k), opus non est.
units.tr: b) p. 1067. wood of Shittim, as of a peculiar and well-known kind, and it is counted among the principal things which the Israelites were commanded to bring as an offering when the tabernacle was set up (Exod. 25:5), and from which things of the greatest importance were made: the ark (v. 10), the poles (v. 13), the table (v. 23), and likewise in chapter 26 the boards (v. 15), the bars (v. 26), the pillars (v. 32), and the altar of incense (chap. 30:1). So again, among the offerings which were to be brought by the people, wood of Shittim is listed (Exod. 35:7, 24), and in Deut. 10:3 it is said that Moses had the ark made of wood of Shittim, on which he placed the two tables of the law. In all these passages the Hebrew word is kept in the Latin version as Shittim, as the known name of this tree, except in the only other place, which is in Isaiah, where it is rendered pine. But from the very use of this wood it is clear that the common thorn is by no means meant. Hence Jerome also adds more fully that he does not understand a thorn properly, but a tree which is like the white thorn in colour and leaves, though not in size; for it is of such size that boards of it can be cut from the trunk, and its wood is strong, light, and beautiful, and does not otherwise rot or decay; therefore the Seventy, in the passage cited from the law, render it ἄσηπτα [asepta], incorruptible. This tree, he says, does not grow in any cultivated place or in Roman territories, but in the desert of Arabia. He sets all this forth as if he had been an eyewitness of it, and M. Fuller judges that he is to be believed in this matter too. Kimchi, however, says it is a kind of the best cedars; hence also Junius and Tremellius render it a valley of the choicest cedars, and in the same way in Isa. 41:19 they render שטים [shittah] as the choicest cedar (where our translation has shittah tree), distinguishing it from אררז [arez], the known and common cedar mentioned in the same place. They do the same in the other passages of Exodus and Deuteronomy cited above, rendering wood of the choicest cedars. Among these differing senses of the Hebrew word שטים [Shittim] in our translation, those who take it as the proper name of a place follow in particular, and perhaps for this reason the place was so called because many trees of this kind grew in it or e) around it; yet others prefer that the trees growing there and the wood brought from them took their name from the name of the valley in which they grew in great abundance, not that the valley was named from that tree, but so named from the town or some other cause. e) Schindler, Ribera. f) Ferrar, in his Syriac dictionary, under ... g) Christopher a Castro. The word נחל [nachal], which some translate torrent and others valley, is capable of both meanings, as is plain from the various examples. It denotes a depressed place in which water can flow and be collected, בין יש בור מים בין אין בור מים [bein yesh bor mayim bein ein bor mayim], whether or not there is water in it, as R. Kimchi explains. So either of these meanings can suitably be given, according as the place where the word occurs requires, and in this it is clearly agreeable. As for this passage, some have rendered it one way and some another, but those who translate it valley seem to have taken most account of the sense of the passage. Some follow the Vulgate and with it render torrent, though they do not take the word torrent in its strict and proper sense, but so broadly that it also denotes i) a valley or plain, into which torrents or streams usually flow, though this is not always the case. In this sense the same word, as has been observed, is used elsewhere in the Latin version, as in Gen. 26:19, where it is said of Isaac's servants that they dug in the torrent, as the Douai version renders it and notes in the margin, that is, in a stream where sometimes a violent flood rolls, sometimes none at all. So also in 1 Sam. 15:5: Saul laid his ambush in the torrent, which can be understood in no other way than as others have expressed it, in the valley. And so, says Peter a Figueiredo on this passage, whom Kimchi also cites in his Dictionary as an example to prove that נחל [nachal] denotes a valley that is either full of water or lacks it. For if it abounds in waters, so that it may be watered, there is no need [of more].

units.la: Quod autem dicitur, fons egredietur ex domo Domini & irrigabit vallem, non parum convenientiae habere videtur cum eo, quod extat de sacris aquis Ez. 47, 1. &c. & vivis illis aquis, quae dicuntur egressurae ex Hierosolyma Zach. 14, 8. Hinc observatum est de hoc loco R. Tanch. הרא ממא ינאסב קיר זכריה Hoc convenit cum eo quod dicitur apud Zachariam, viva aqua egredientur ex Hierosolyma; quo etiam spectat fluvius, cujus mentio fit apud Ezechiel. & ad horum verborum genuinum sensum eruendum Clarist. Libel. censet illarum cum his fieri oportere comparationem.
units.tr: As for the words, "a fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD and shall water the valley," they seem to have no small agreement with what is said about the holy waters in Ezek. 47:1 etc., and with the living waters said to flow out from Jerusalem in Zech. 14:8. Hence R. Tanchum observed on this passage: "This agrees with what is said in Zechariah, that living water shall flow out from Jerusalem." To the same passage belongs the river mentioned in Ezekiel. The Clarissimus Libellus holds that to draw out the genuine sense of these words, they must be compared with those passages.

units.la: Hisce de verborum significatione traditis, reliquum est, ut inquiramus,
units.tr: Having set out these matters concerning the meaning of the words, it remains for us to inquire:

units.tr: (b) Likewise in Rad., and R. Tanchum. (i) Pet. a Fig. (k) Id. at what time and in what manner the things promised here were accomplished, and whether these sayings are to be taken literally or figuratively. Abarbinel notes that Aben-Ezra (alone) (l) says these words are spoken "parabolically" or by way of comparison, while on the contrary R. Solomon says that what is said is to be taken "simply and literally." Kimchi likewise says that it is to be understood "as it sounds," though none of them goes on to explain what he thinks is to be understood. Abarbinel works out a sense of his own, which comes very close to each of these opinions. According to those who take these words literally, he thinks a miracle is promised here, by which, since there had formerly been great scarcity of water at Jerusalem, so that water collected in pits and cisterns had to be used (as found in Isaiah: "to the conduit of the upper pool," Isa. 7:3, and 36:2), at the time of deliverance to which these things refer there would flow an abundance of all things, and God, creating anew (m), there would be no lack of anything. So a fountain of living waters would arise in that place, coming forth from the house of the LORD, whereby it would be easy for all the inhabitants of the world to grasp and understand that the condition of this region had at once been changed, and that a rock, very hard and dry, had been turned by God into a fountain of waters, and this solely for the sake of Jerusalem. He says there is nothing wonderful in this promise, since the Prophet here sets forth far greater things. He thinks this sense holds if the words are taken literally. But if the expressions in which this promise is contained are figurative and metaphorical, which, he says, in my opinion is "more solid and more fitting," then the reference is to what the Prophet Isaiah (n) declared: that in the last times "the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established on the top of the mountains, and many peoples shall go up, receiving the law, and saying: Out of Zion shall go forth the teaching, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem." For since the divine law and teaching are compared to water because of the likeness they bear to one another, the Prophet here promises that divine truth (or the true knowledge of God) will go forth from Jerusalem, from the house of the LORD, into the whole world, saying: "a fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD and shall water the

units.la: l) Ita certe dicit initio versus. m) Vel novum quid condente Num. 16,30. n) Esa. 2,2. irrigabit vallem Shittim, ac si diceret, totum irrigabit mundum, qui est vallis, in qua oberrant & declinant, qui dictis Domini non sunt obedientes. Quo etiam faciunt verba Zacharia c.14,8. Erit die illo, prodeuntibus aquis vivis ex Hierosolyma parte sui ad mare Orientale & parte sui ad mare posterum, quod æstate & hyeme futurum est. Quod idem subjungitur (uti hoc loco) prædictioni ingentis belli, quod ultimis temporibus futurum est, cui postea subjicitur: Et Dominus erit rex super totam terram, & illo die erit unus Dominus & unum ejus nomen. Atque huc in finem mentio facta est fontis, qui huic rei præfigurandæ valde accommodus est. Comparatio enim revera sublimis est atque mirandum in modum insigniterque, eo, quod dicitur, ex Hierosolyma (quæ erat terra arida aquis destituta) prodibit aqua viva, quæ ad mare usque se effundet, exprimens; ex Hierosolyma, quæ o) tributaria erat atque igne p) deleta & eversa, prodituram esse legem, doctrinam & veram fidem ad omnes incolas mundi. Has expositiones Abarbinelis paulo largius apponere visum fuit, quæ alibi in Judaicis interpretibus tam diserte non habentur, ut conferri queant cum illis, quas præbent Christiani, quos non minus invenimus alios magis adhærentes literæ, alios sensui figurato. Prioribus annumerandus est Grotius, qui ita exponit hæc verba: omnes rivi Judæ fluent aquis, ac si populus ab hoste liber & in magno otio oblitatas fossas detergeret, ut liberæ ac impræpeditæ fluerent. Fontem autem, qui egredietur ex domo Domini & vallem Shittim rigabit, putat aquæ ductum eundem fore, qui describitur ab q) Ezechiele, quod a templo ad mare mortuum usque exæstuaturus sit. At vulgare quid juxta hanc expositionem in his verbis tunc latere manifestum est, cum tamen, quod Abarbinel notat, insoliti ac mirandi nonnihil complectantur, quod expectare jubentur. Quare rectius ab aliis figurate accipi videntur, quibus in genere magis declaratur, quænam bona Deus collaturus sit in membra Ecclesiæ. Per fontem inde proditurum r) quidam sacrum illud baptismi lavacrum, quod est fons apertus domui Davidis & habitatoribus Hierosolymorum in s) expiationem peccati, & pro separatione ex immunditia, Ezech. 13,11. t); Alii fontem Verbi Domini intelligunt. Quod utrumque quidem ita non incongrue sumi
units.tr: (l) He certainly says this at the beginning of the verse. (m) Or creating something new, Num. 16:30. (n) Isa. 2:2. Shittim valley," as if he said: it will water the whole world, which is the valley in which those wander and go astray who are not obedient to the words of the LORD. To this also the words of Zech. 14:8 tend: "In that day, living waters shall go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the western sea; it shall be in summer and in winter." The same is added (as in this place) to the prediction of a great war which is to come in the last times, to which is subjoined: "And the LORD shall be king over all the earth; in that day the LORD shall be one, and his name one." And to this end the mention of the fountain has been made, which is very suitable for prefiguring this matter. For the comparison is indeed sublime and wonderfully and remarkably expressive: that from Jerusalem (which was a dry land destitute of waters) "living water shall go forth," which shall pour itself out even to the sea; signifying that from Jerusalem, which was (o) tributary and was destroyed and overthrown by fire (p), the law, teaching and true faith would go forth to all the inhabitants of the world. I have thought it fitting to set out Abarbinel's explanations somewhat more fully, since they are not found in other Jewish interpreters so expressly, so that they may be compared with those given by Christians, whom we find no less some adhering more closely to the letter, others to the figurative sense. Among the former must be counted Grotius, who explains these words thus: "all the streams of Judah shall flow with waters," as if the people, freed from the enemy and at great leisure, were clearing out the neglected ditches so that they might flow free and unhindered. He thinks the fountain which "shall come forth from the house of the LORD and water the valley of Shittim" will be the same aqueduct which Ezekiel (q) describes, which is to flow from the temple down to the Dead Sea. But it is clear that according to this explanation nothing common lies hidden in these words, whereas (as Abarbinel notes) they contain something somewhat unusual and wonderful, which they are bidden to expect. Therefore others seem to take them more rightly figuratively, by which it is declared more generally what good things God will bestow on the members of the Church. Some understand by the fountain that proceeds from there the holy laver of baptism, which is "a fountain opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for the cleansing of sin and for separation from uncleanness" (Zech. 13:1) (r) (s) (t). Others understand the fountain of the Word of the LORD. Each of these may indeed be taken not inappropriately,

units.la: o) למס. p) Psal. 80,16. q) Cap. 47. r) Vid. Merc. & Tarn. s) Jun. Trem. t) Merc. fumi potest, verum talis praeterea mihi videtur haec vox naturae, ut caetera etiam omnia complectatur beneficia in membra ecclesiae a Deo collata Hinc accommode satis ipse ) Christus intelligendus per sontem, atque per aquas ab eo fonte defluentes, tum sacra Dei decreta & ordinationes, tum omnia Spiritus ejus Sancti dona & beneficia ad eorum salutem spectantia & ad gratiam gloriamque a Christo derivatam pertinentia, ab eoque & per eum in illos benigne collata, ita ut ad statum ecclesiae Christianae militantis aeque ac triumphantis universum haec promissio pertinere statuatur, qua illos certos reddat de omnium bonorum ad veram utriusque status felicitatem spectantium abundanti suppeditatione. Quando dicitur, fontem irrigaturum vallem Shittim locum procul distantem ab Hierosolyma, ubi domus erat Domini, ex qua dicitur egressurus, notari hic cum quibusdam observare juvat, benignitatis divinae atque favoris largam extensionem, w) Dei scilicet benedictionem longe lateque diffusum in, ita ut universam Ecclesiam perfundat, atque adeo non fore circumscriptam arctis Hierosolymae vel terrae sanctae limitibus, sed dilatatam ad remotissimas incultismasque gentes evangelii praedicatione, cujus x) sonus in omnem debeat exire terram & verba ejus ad ultima orbis terrarum.
units.tr: (o) Lit. "to be tributary." (p) Ps. 80:16. (q) Ch. 47. (r) See Mercer and Tremellius. (s) Junius, Tremellius. (t) Mercer. but in addition this expression seems to me of such a nature that it embraces all the other benefits which God bestows on the members of the Church. Hence Christ himself may fittingly be understood as the fountain, and by the waters flowing from that fountain, both the sacred decrees and ordinances of God, and all the gifts and benefits of his Holy Spirit which concern their salvation and pertain to the grace and glory derived from Christ, and which are bestowed graciously on them by him and through him. So this whole promise is held to pertain equally to the state of the Church militant and of the Church triumphant, assuring them of the abundant supply of all good things which concern the true happiness of both states. When it is said that the fountain will water the valley of Shittim, a place far distant from Jerusalem, where the house of the LORD was, from which it is said to come forth, it is helpful to observe here with some others the large extent of divine kindness and favour: the blessing of God is spread far and wide, so that it bathes the whole Church. Thus it will not be confined within the narrow limits of Jerusalem or the holy land, but will be extended to the most remote and uncultivated nations by the preaching of the gospel, whose "sound must go out into all the earth and its words to the ends of the world."

units.la: 2. Quod si hunc locum (vallem Shittim) consideremus tanquam locum siccum ac sterilem, nullius rei praeterquam spinarum ac juncorum feracem, per fontem, qui irrigaturus ac proditurus est ex domo Domini, efficaciam gratiae divinae per evangelium collatae intelligere possumus, qua, qui natura sunt steriles ac fructuum bonorum expertes, idonei redduntur, ut ferant bonos fructus. Hanc ejus efficaciam quidam his verbis putant innui, quamvis alia ratione ea vertant, uti Junius & Tremellius, qui interpretantur, irrigabit vallem cedrorum lectissimarum; ad vallem autem notant, eam esse ecclesiam, in qua justi plantati crescunt ut Cedri lectissimae, juxta comparationem quae est Psal. 92,12. Justus ut palma germinabit, ut cedrus in Libano crescet.
units.tr: 2. If we consider this place (the valley of Shittim) as a dry and barren place, bearing nothing but thorns and rushes, then through the fountain which is to water and come forth from the house of the LORD we can understand the efficacy of divine grace conferred through the gospel, by which those who are by nature barren and destitute of good fruits are made fit to bear good fruit. Some think this efficacy is hinted at in these words, although they render them in another way, as Junius and Tremellius do, who translate: "he shall water the valley of the choicest cedars." By the valley they note that it is the Church, "in which the righteous, planted, grow like choice cedars," according to the comparison in Ps. 92:12: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon."

units.la: 3. Quod si ad beneficia & benedictiones divinas attendamus, quatenus comparantur rivis aquarum perpetuo fluentium, quid aliud hocce
units.tr: 3. If we consider the divine benefits and blessings, as they are compared to streams of water flowing perpetually, what else can we say this signifies than the abundant and constant supply with which God will provide for his servants?

units.la: *) Cyrill. ¶¶) Livel. x) Rom. 10,18. hocce significari dixeris,quam eorundem & abundantem communicationem & perpetuam continuationem, quibus servos suos Deus instruet. Quæ ex fonte continuo profluunt aquæ,non tam facile deficiunt, quam aliæ, quibus hujusmodi adminiculi nihil est. y) Quodsi alii fontes aliquando arucrint, hic nunquam arescet, qui a domo Domini egreditur. Quocirca merito dicendum, hisce expressam esse persectissimam felicitatem & lætitæ abundantiam, qua in vita futura continuo ac indesinenter fruituri sunt in conspectu Dei sancti bibentes ex torrente z) deliciarum ejus & ab a) agno ducti ad vivos fontes aquarum. Atque hunc felicem statum b) quidam hic egregie depingi censent,licet non minus apte etiam benedictiones eæ innuantur, quibus membra ecclesiæ hujus militantis hac in vita adhuc fruuntur.
units.tr: *) Cyrill. ¶¶) Livel. x) Rom. 10,18. Waters that flow from a continuous spring do not fail as easily as others that have no such supply. y) If other springs have sometimes dried up, this one, which flows out of the house of the Lord, will never dry up. Therefore it is rightly said that this expresses the most perfect happiness and the abundance of joy with which those who drink from the torrent of his delights, and are led by the Lamb to the living fountains of waters, will enjoy in the sight of the holy God continually and without ceasing in the future life. Some think that this happy state is splendidly portrayed here, although those blessings, by which the members of this militant Church are still enriched in this life, are also indicated no less fittingly.

units.la: Quascunque vero adduximus hactenus opiniones considerationesque,certum est,eas ab his verbis nobis suggeri & in eis esse comprehensas. Manifestum enim est, quamcunque demum harum quis prætulerit,ea continere magnorum ac eximiorû privilegiorum promissiones populo Dei factas,quibus ejus ac illorum hostes nunquam sunt gavisuri. Dilucide enim tradit in sequentibus, quam diversa e orum futura fit conditio.
units.tr: Now, of all the opinions and considerations we have adduced so far, it is certain that they are suggested to us by these words and contained in them. For it is clear that whichever of these one prefers, they contain promises of great and excellent privileges made to the people of God, which their enemies will never enjoy. For the prophet clearly states in what follows how different their future condition will be.

units.la: v. 19. Ægyptus in desolationem erit, & Edom in defertum desolatum propter injuriam filiorum Juda,quia effuderunt innocentem sanguinem in terra eorum.
units.tr: v. 19. Egypt shall be a desolation, and Edom a desolate wilderness, for the violence done to the children of Judah, because they have shed innocent blood in their land.

units.la: Quinam intelligendi sint per gentes hic dictas, non una est interpretum tum Judæorum tum Christianorum expositio. Quidam easdem hic spectari putant,quæ nominatenus sunt descriptæ; alii laxius ea nomina sumunt, ut sub iis etiam comprehendant alios, qui in iis, ob quæ hic reprehenduntur ac minis impetuntur, se illis similes reddiderunt. units.tr: There is no single interpretation, among both Jewish and Christian interpreters, of who is to be understood by the nations mentioned here. Some think that those are meant who are named by name; others take those names more loosely, so as to include under them others who have made themselves like those for whose deeds they are rebuked and threatened. Among the Jews, R. Solomon seems to take these words in their proper and literal sense, except that he adds something further in explanation of the matter, where he says that Edom was not left surviving without Egypt, and therefore these nations are also joined together in the vengeance that is to be taken on them. Abn Ezra takes them in the same way, when

units.la: y) Ribera z) Psal. 36, 6. a) Apoc. 7, 17. b) Ribera.Ch. a Castro c) 1. Reg. 11, 17. &c. cum dicit, eas fuisse desolatas tempore Nabuchodonozoris (atque ita hæc prophetia tunc temporis eventum suum habuit;) quod si autem objiciatur Ægyptum superstitem mansisse, resolutionem ejus addere videtur dicendo, Ægyptum (sive primariam ejus civitatem, uti mihi sentire videtur) non fuisse priscam illam Ægyptum (vel civitatem.) At non probat hanc opinionem Abarbinel hoc argumento impulsus, quod, incolis licet ac fœmine metropoleos mutato, nequaquā sit mutata, sed eadem adhuc gens, populus atque posteri veterum Ægyptiorum permanserint, ex quo patere vult prophetiæ eventū suo tempore adhuc esse expectandum. Alia hic procedit via R. David Kimchi, quippe non proprie his nominibus arbitratur harum regionū incolas designari, sed Ismaelitas (vel Mahumedanos) & Romanos. Hæ enim, inquit, nationes duæ sunt, quæ prævalent his jam multis annis, eruntque prævalituræ usque ad tempus redemtionis. Ismaelitas putat denotari Ægypti nomine, quia uxor Ismaelis Ægyptia fuit; Regnum Romanum nomine Edom, quia magna ex parte, sua quidem opinione, continet Idumæos. Et quamvis inter illos permixti sint alii populi, uti permixti sunt etiam in Regno Ismaelitarum, appellari tamen ab eo, quod est præcipuum. Cæsar, inquit porro, (primum intelligat necesse est) Idumæus fuit; sic quoque omnes imperatores post eum, qui Romæ fuerunt. Atque hæ duæ nationes, pergit, male egerunt tribui Judæ & Benjamin, quæ exules agebant inter illas, & sanguinem eorum fuderunt ut aquam in terra sua. Et Edom, quod est regnum Romanum, erat, quod vastabat domum secundam per Titum, & sanguinem eorum fuderunt, & captivos abduxerunt inter gentes. Et de hoc exilio, ait, dictus est hic versiculus; quapropter non nisi Judæ fit mentio, quia decem tribus, quas in exilium abduxit Rex Assyriorum, nec usque in hodiernum diem sunt reversæ, non fuerunt sub ditione harum duarum gentium. Hæc est sententia Kimchi, quam fuse hic subjicere libuit. Videtur ei succinere Abarbinel, licet in quibusdam ab eo discedat, e. g. quod proprie hic sermonem esse velit de populo Ægyptio, quem hic nominari putat, quia ingentis illius belli, quod supra memoratum est, æstus primus ad eum penetrabit, quatenus Christiani in potestatem suam redigere cupientes terram Israelis destructuri sunt Ægyptum ac ad ad internecionem deleturi, terramque Judæ ac Hierosolymæ, quibus tunc dominabitur Ægyptus, in ditionem suam recepturi. Quo fiet ut populi Orientis ac Septentrionis vindictam sumturi propter fusos Ægyptios fratres, ac recuperaturi sanctam terram a possessione Christianorum, resurgant ac bellum cum Christianis suscipiant, quo tempore tanta erit ruina regni Edom, ut, quod unquam in aliis gentibus factum non legimus, nemo incolarum ejus superstes relinquatur &c. Frivolæ sunt ac nulla firma ratione stant hæ expositiones Kimchi & Abarbinel, quod rationibus d) non unis probari posset; verum cæteris posthabitis una nobis sufficit ad eas rejiciendas, quod nitantur hoc principio falso, Messiam nondum venisse, cujus adventum hæc putant præcessura, viamque paratura ad ejus regnum, quo Judæi in felicissimam super omnes gentes conditionem & statum sunt evehendi. Quod omnino consentaneum non est uti Veteris, ita nec Novi Testamenti scriptis, quibus persuasi sumus eum jamdiu venisse. Adeo ut alibi nobis quærendum sit, si genuinum velimus horum verborum sensum percipere, ubi non in dubium vocatur præcipuum hoc fidei nostræ caput. Quare ad Christianos ut deflectamus eorumque hic opiniones scrutemur, tempus ac locus quam maxime monet. Horum non infimus est Grotius, qui proprie hic accipit nomina Ægypti & Edom, quodque Ægypto hic videmus prædictum, impletum fuisse autumat diripiente eam e) Antiocho; quod autem Idumæis, vastantibus eam f) Maccabæis. Verum alii tam præcise non restringunt hæc verba ad eas gentes hoc nomine designatas, sed ad omnes alias laxiore significationem trahunt, quæ sunt hostes ecclesiæ ac populi Dei quocunque tempore, uti Ægyptii, & Idumæi fuere Judæorum, qui tum temporis Dei erant peculium. Cum vero dicuntur in desolationem traditi, id ita sumunt, quod contraria sit futura eorum conditio felicissimæ illi, quæ in præcedentibus verbis populi Dei describitur. Cum populo Dei hic promissio sit ingentium beneficiorum ac benedictionum hujusmodi exprimendi formulis, quod montes mustoslillabunt, colles lacte diffluent,

Ch. a Castro c) 1 Kings 11:17, etc. he says that they were laid waste at the time of Nebuchadnezzar (and so this prophecy had its fulfilment at that time). But if it is objected that Egypt remained surviving, he seems to add a solution by saying that Egypt (or its chief city, as he seems to me to mean) was not that ancient Egypt (or city). Abarbanel, however, does not prove this opinion, being moved by the argument that, although the inhabitants and the head of the metropolis have changed, the land has by no means changed, but the same nation, people and descendants of the ancient Egyptians have remained, from which he wishes to show that the fulfilment of the prophecy is still to be awaited in its time. R. David Kimchi proceeds by another path, for he thinks that these names properly designate not the inhabitants of these regions but the Ishmaelites (or Muslims) and the Romans. For, he says, these are the two nations that have prevailed for many years now, and will continue to prevail until the time of redemption. He thinks Egypt is the name for the Ishmaelites because Ishmael's wife was an Egyptian; he takes Edom to be the Roman kingdom, because, in his opinion, it contains for the most part the Idumaeans. And although other peoples are mixed among them, just as they are also mixed in the kingdom of the Ishmaelites, they are nevertheless named from what is chief. Caesar, he goes on, (one must first understand this) was an Idumaean; so too were all the emperors after him who were at Rome. And these two nations, he continues, have treated badly the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, who lived as exiles among them, and have shed their blood like water in their land. And Edom, which is the Roman kingdom, was the one that laid waste the second house through Titus, and they shed their blood and led the captives away among the nations. And, he says, this little verse was spoken about this exile; therefore only Judah is mentioned, because the ten tribes, whom the king of the Assyrians led into exile, have not returned even to this day, and were not under the rule of these two nations. This is Kimchi's opinion, which I have been pleased to set out here at length. Abarbanel seems to agree with him, although he departs from him in some points, e.g. in wishing that the discourse here is properly about the Egyptian people, whom he thinks are named here, because the first heat of that great war, mentioned above, will penetrate to them, insofar as Christians, desiring to bring the land of Israel under their power, will destroy Egypt and utterly exterminate it, and will take into their own control the land of Judah and Jerusalem, over which Egypt will then rule. The result will be that the peoples of the East and North, intending to take vengeance for their Egyptian brethren who were slain, and to recover the holy land from the possession of the Christians, will rise up and undertake war against the Christians; at that time the ruin of the kingdom of Edom will be so great that, as we do not read has ever happened among other nations, none of its inhabitants will be left surviving, etc. These expositions of Kimchi and Abarbanel are trivial and stand on no firm reason, which could be proved by more than one argument; but, setting the others aside, one is enough for us to reject them: they rest on the false principle that the Messiah has not yet come, whose coming they think will precede this and prepare the way for his kingdom, in which the Jews are to be raised to the most happy condition and state above all nations. This is wholly inconsistent with the writings of both the Old and the New Testament, by which we are persuaded that he came long ago. So much so that, if we wish to grasp the genuine sense of these words, we must seek it elsewhere, where this chief article of our faith is not called into doubt. Therefore the time and place very strongly urge us to turn to the Christians and examine their opinions here. Among them Grotius is no minor figure, who takes the names Egypt and Edom properly, and claims that what we see here foretold for Egypt was fulfilled when Antiochus plundered it; and that what was foretold for the Idumaeans, who laid it waste, was fulfilled by the Maccabees. Others, however, do not restrict these words so precisely to the nations designated by these names, but draw them with a looser meaning to all others who are enemies of the Church and of the people of God at any time, just as the Egyptians and Idumaeans were enemies of the Jews, who at that time were God's peculiar people. When they are said to be given over to desolation, they understand this to mean that their future condition will be the opposite of that most happy condition of the people of God described in the preceding words. For the promise to the people of God here is of great benefits and blessings, expressed in formulas such as: the mountains shall drip with sweet wine, the hills shall flow with milk,

units.la: d) Inspice Petri a Fig. censuram Kimchi. e) Huncin finem citat Dan. 11, 40. &c. cujus annotationes vide. f) Quod probare conatur ex Joseph. XII, 11, 12 & Esa. 63. & omnes rivi fluent aquis, & quod irrigabuntur continuo a fonte, qui egredietur e domo Domini, hostibus Dei e contrario praedicitur, ipsos eorum nunquam fore participes, nec eorum quicquam adepturos, quibus illi fruuntur, sed dum videantur florere ac prospere agere; eorum conditionem futuram esse in desolationem & in desertum desolatū; quod idem & alibi illis praedicitur. Qui oderunt justitiam, disperdentur, Psal. 34, 21. Quibus nihil aliud intelligendum in promtu est, quam omnibus bonis eos fore destitutos & omnibus malis excruciandos. Non parum jam in his terris diversus filiorum Dei ac ejus illorumque hostium conditio apparet, unde conjiciendum, quanta illa futura sit in futuro seculo, quo quidem in specie hæc referenda esse nonnulli judicant. Asseritur hujus promissionis veritas etiam in hoc seculo, quando Christus in medio inimicorum suorum dominatur, suosque inter quotidianas afflictiones protegit, & exempla in hostes suos horrenda edit, plene tamen praestabitur in caelis, quando omni metu ac periculo exemti in aeternum cum Christo regnabunt, eorum autem hostes in perpetuum disperdentur ac destruentur. Alius censet in desolationem esse, idem valere ac, aeterna damnationi esse addicendos. Erunt, inquit non nemo, in deserto perditionis, sc. infernalis. Cur autem tam horrenda illos maneant, ex sequentibus videre est: Propter injurium filiorum Judæ, quia fuderunt innocentem sanguinem in terra eorum. Propter injuriam filiorum Judæ; ita enim ad literam sonant verba hebraica מחמס בני יהודה Mechamas bene Jehudah. Similem habemus constructionem apud Obad. v. 10. מחמס אחיך יעקב mechamas achica yaacob, propter injuriam fratris tui Jacobi, vel ut nostrat. recte vertunt, propter injuriam adversus fratrem tuum Jacobum. LXX. ut & Syrus & Arabs in versionibus suis fixius adhaerent literæ (veluti, ἐξ ἀδικῶν υἱῶν Ἰούδα ex iniquitatibus filiorum Judæ) obscuritate involventes verba, quamvis sensus necessario sit idem. Nec eadem hic iterum interpretum est mens, quinam per filios Judæ sint intelligendi.
