Qui juxta literam sumunt Ægyptum & Edom pro populis suis proprie dictis, per filios Judæ quoque non denotari volunt, nisi incolas regionis hoc nomine cognitæ; Qui vero sub his nominibus omnes ecclesiæ Dei comprehendunt
units.tr: d) See the criticism of Kimchi by Peter a Fig. e) He cites Dan. 11:40 etc. as the end of this, see his notes. f) He tries to prove this from Joseph. 12:11, 12 and Isa. 63. And all the streams shall flow with water, and they shall be watered continually from the fountain which shall come out of the house of the Lord: on the contrary, it is foretold to God's enemies that they will never share in these things, nor obtain anything of what those others enjoy; but while they seem to flourish and prosper, their future condition will be desolation and a desert laid waste. The same is foretold to them elsewhere: those who hate righteousness shall be destroyed, Ps. 34:21. What is readily understood by this is that they will be deprived of all good things and tormented by every evil. The difference between the condition of the sons of God and that of their enemies already appears plainly in this earthly life, so it may be conjectured how great it will be in the future age, to which some judge that this should in particular be referred. The truth of this promise is asserted even in this age, when Christ rules in the midst of his enemies, protects his own amid daily afflictions, and displays dreadful examples against his foes; but it will be fully fulfilled in heaven, when, freed from all fear and danger, they will reign with Christ forever, while their enemies will be destroyed and ruined in perpetuity. Another thinks that desolation means the same as to be consigned to eternal damnation. They will be, says someone, in the desert of perdition, namely of hell. Why they will remain under such dreadful things can be seen from what follows: on account of the violence against the sons of Judah, because they shed innocent blood in their land. On account of the violence against the sons of Judah; for so the Hebrew words מחמס בני יהודה [mechamas bene Jehudah] sound word for word. We have a similar construction in Obad. v. 10: מחמס אחיך יעקב [mechamas achika Yaacob], on account of the violence against your brother Jacob, or as our translators rightly render it, on account of the violence against your brother Jacob. The Septuagint, and likewise the Syriac and Arabic versions, cling more closely to the letter (as ἐξ ἀδικῶν υἱῶν Ἰούδα [ex adikōn huiōn Ioudas], from the iniquities of the sons of Judah), obscuring the words, although the sense is necessarily the same. Nor is the opinion of the interpreters the same again here as to who are to be understood by the sons of Judah. Those who take Egypt and Edom literally for their proper peoples want the sons of Judah to denote only the inhabitants of the region known by this name; but those who include all the Churches of God under these names

units.la: g) Vid. Lyram. h) Gvalt. i) Vide Veil. k) Lyra. dunt hostes,per filios Jude inprimis intelligunt l) ecclesiam Dei ejusque membra.Adversus quam,qua ratione etiam fumas,injuriæ ab hoftibus admissæ gravitas ac magnitudo ulterius exprimitur his verbis; quia innocentem sanguinem fuderunt in eorum terra ; Non bonis suis tantum spoliaverant eos, quod m) quidam in prioribus verbis per injuriam volunt denotatum; sed eo usque etiam processerant,ut innocentem etiam profudissent sanguinem in terra eorum ; illorum sanguinem qui innocentes respectu quodam erant, atque tam funesta_ & crudelia non commeriti fuerant. Differunt hic aliquatenus in his verbis reddendis interpretes quamvis sensui nil differentiæ inferant. Quidam cum noftrat. reddunt, quia &c. n) Alii & quod &c. o) Alii ,qui insontem sanguinem in terra sua fuderint. Vulgat Lat. & effuderunt &c. p) Alii ,in quorum terra effuderunt sanguinem innocentem. q) Alii ,quorum &c. At, ut diximus, non quicquam mutant sensum hæ differentes interpretationes. Majoris momenti erit ratio affixi in verbis postremis in terra eorum, ad quam nam regionem id sit applicandum, num ad terram Ægypti & Edom, an filiorum Jude, quod adeo ambiguum videtur Kimchi, ut ad utramlibet referri posse tantum dicat, nihil autem quicquam in aliquam partem determinet. Ad utramque hoc referri posse censet etiam Calvinus, si ad priorem,tunc innui putat,eos trucidasse injuste illos,qui in fidem eorum se receperant in regione refugium sibi quæritantes; si ad posteriorem, crimen illorum aggravari autumat,quatenus regionem,quam impollutam ac sacram sibi reddiderat Deus, injustis polluebant homicidiis. At ea ratione hæc verba inprimis videntur respicere ad incolas terræ Jude, atque non omnia Ecclesiæ membra sua cujusvis in regione, quæcunque sit, quo a quibusdam latissime referuntur, complecti, quod quidem ingentis ac immanis crudelitatis adhuc indicium. Verum ad quem demum cunque hoc retuleris locum, id extra omnem controversiam est, innocentis sanguinis fusionem esse tam detestandum peccatum, ut certissime graviter in eos Deus sit animadversurus qui ejus censeri possunt rei. Quod verbis minacibus hic prædicitur, quæ tamen
units.tr: g) See Lyra. h) Gvalt. i) See Veil. k) Lyra. enemies: by the sons of Judah they understand first of all the Church of God and its members. Against whom, by which reasoning you also gather smoke, the gravity and magnitude of the injury inflicted by the enemies is further expressed in these words: because they have shed innocent blood in their land. They had not only plundered them of their goods, which m) some want to be denoted by injury in the preceding words; but they had proceeded so far as to shed innocent blood in their land, the blood of those who were in a certain respect innocent and had not deserved such deadly and cruel treatment. The interpreters differ somewhat here in rendering these words, though they make no difference to the sense. Some with our translators render it because etc. n) Others and that etc. o) Others who have shed innocent blood in their land. The Vulgate Latin has they have shed etc. p) Others in whose land they have shed innocent blood. q) Others whose etc. But, as we have said, these differing renderings do not change the sense at all. More important will be the question of how the attached phrase in their land is to be applied: to the land of Egypt and Edom, or to the land of the sons of Judah? Kimchi finds this so ambiguous that he says it can be referred to either, and determines nothing in either direction. Calvin also thinks it can be referred to both: if to the former, he supposes it hints that they unjustly slew those who had taken refuge with them, seeking a refuge for themselves in their region; if to the latter, he thinks their crime is made heavier, inasmuch as they polluted with unjust murders the region which God had made pure and holy for himself. But on that reasoning these words seem chiefly to look to the inhabitants of the land of Judah, and not to embrace all the members of the Church wherever they might be, as some extend them very widely; which is indeed a sign of huge and monstrous cruelty. But to whichever place you refer it, it is beyond all controversy that the shedding of innocent blood is so detestable a sin that God will most certainly punish severely those who can be counted guilty of it. This is foretold here in threatening words, which nevertheless

units.la: t) In Ecclesiam, Merc. in pios quosdis, Tarnov. m) Pet. a Fig. n) Fagn. Munst LXX. Sa. o) Chald. Castal. p) Jun. Trem. vide MS. Arab. q) Vatab. in 4to & 8vo. men etiam admonitionem ac solatium complectuntur ratione perfonarum habita, ad quas sunt directa. Minæ hic sunt factæ hostibus populi Dei, quod apertum est, qui pro sua crudelitate ac violentia in eum admissa, non obstante præsente felici statu, quo gaudeant ac prævaleant, tandem aliquando certissime castigabuntur ac funditus & ad internecionem usque evertentur. Nec solatio sunt destituta, quod non minus manifestum est, quo frui potest ejus populus, quatenus calamitates, quibus vexatur ob cultum divinum, non argumento sunt, eum a Deo esse relictum, sed pretiosum esse ejus sanguinem in conspectu Dei & tempore suo vindicatam esse sumendam de illis, qui eum suderunt atque ei violentiam intulerunt, quod etiam simul necessario includit restitutis promissum, quo Deus repetere velit mala, quæ tam injuriose passi sunt, & in sempiterna recipere habitacula pro momentaneis ac caducis rebus, quibus hic caruerunt, quod hic tantum ὡς ἐν παροδῷ suggeritur, cum verba in specie spectent hostium supplicia, verum uberius nos eam rem docebunt verba sequentia.
units.tr: t) Into the Church, Merc. into certain pious people, Tarnov. m) Pet. a Fig. n) Fagn. Munst LXX. Sa. o) Chald. Castal. p) Jun. Trem. see MS. Arab. q) Vatab. in 4to & 8vo. also contain an admonition and a consolation, having regard to the persons to whom they are addressed. Threats are here made against the enemies of God's people, which is plain: those who, for their cruelty and violence against him, are to be punished with certainty at some time, despite their present happy state in which they rejoice and prevail, and will be utterly overthrown and destroyed to the point of annihilation. Nor are they without consolation, which is no less clear: his people can enjoy it, inasmuch as the calamities by which they are harassed on account of divine worship are no proof that God has forsaken him, but that his blood is precious in the sight of God, and that in his time vengeance will be taken on those who shed it and inflicted violence on him. This also necessarily includes the promise of restitution, by which God will wish to restore the evils which they suffered so unjustly, and to receive in eternal dwellings in place of the transitory and perishable things of which they have been deprived here. This is only hinted at here as in passing [ὡς ἐν παροδῷ], since the words look specifically at the punishments of the enemies; but the following words will teach us this matter more fully.

units.la: v. 20. Sed Juda in æternum habitabit, & Hierosolyma a generatione in generationem.
units.tr: v. 20. But Judah shall dwell for ever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.

units.la: Recensitis eorum suppliciis in præcedenti versu, qui sub nomine Ægypti & Edom innuuntur, promissa jam e contrario facit illis, qui Judæ ac Hierosolymæ notatione veniunt. Quinam sint intelligendi per illos priores juxta interpretum diversas opiniones, sat superq; ea verba enucleantes vidimus; quare ut & in hos inquiramus, qui hic nominantur, æquum esse censemus. Ubi in easdem iterum videmus distrahi diversas sententias eosdem interpretes, aliis ad literam ea, quæ hic nominantur loca intelligentibus, aliis ad figuram confugientibus, qua tam late accipiunt verba, ut non dictos præcise spectent, sed omnes illos, qui hoc respectu non secus atque Israel vetus, possent dici ad Deum peculiari modo pertinere, atque ab eo præter cætera loca ac personas quasvis tantopere diligi, ut iis accommodari posset quod hic promissum est; in æternum habitabit & a generatione in generationem. Antequam vero illis examinandis plus operæ collocemus, ordine prius suo & ad literam inspicienda esse hæc verba necessarium duximus. Juda habitabit in aeternum &c Juda vox nota est ac ex usu, quo alibi in sacris literis venit, populum vel tribum illam notat, quæ originem suam debet Patriarchæ Judæ, cujus nomen incolæ istius regionis, vel partis, quam inhabitabant ac possidebant, gerunt atque ab eo Judæ vocantur. Pari modo & per Hierosolymam vel ipsa urbs, quæ hoc nomine nemini non cognita est, vel hujus urbis incolæ denotantur, quod ut ex quibusdæaliis scripturæ locis apparet, ita fatis obvium est ex eo quod dicitur Matth. 3,5. Tunc exivit ad eum tota Hierosolyma & tota Judæa. De his dicitur hic תשב Teshceb, quod verbum fi ita reddatur, quomodo a noftrat. Redditum est, habitabit, ad populum vel incolas r) videtur referendum; sin, permanebit, ut nonnullis perplacet, ad utrosque five ad populum five ad locum referri posse patet. Ad locum id refert Vulgatus Latinus, Juda mutata in Judæa, & verbo in passivum converfo, habitabitur, quod etiam LXX. faciunt. Idem tamen fine sensus ulla immutatione hic innui liquet, quamcunque illarum interpretationem secutus fueris, nimirum hæc loca perpetuo (id enim inferunt voces in aeternum, a generatione in generationem) permansura esse habitabilia, progeniemque incolarum antiquorum in eis habitaturam. Ita ad literam sonant hæc verba; quo sensu retento etiam Judæi statum hic felicem prædici volunt, quo Juda & Hierosolyma, quæ jam desolatæ sunt, postea restaurabuntur ac perpetuo colentur, ביומרת חכשיח temporibus Meffiæ, quibus שכינה Shechinah, vel præfentia majeftatis eo redierit, ut ad versum sequentem notat Kimchi; vel promissionem esse spectantem לעתיד לבוא ad tempus futurum, qua DEUS populum Ifraeliticum certum reddit, fore שלא תשוב עוד לכסלה ואא תגלה עוד בגלות אחר ut non amplius postĥac sint in contumacia, nec in ullam abducantur captivitatem (uti in hæc verba Abarbinel) sed ut regnum Juda & domus Davidis, quæ dominabitur Israeli & Hierosolymæ, quo nomine comprehenduntur omnes civitates Israelis, permaneat in aeternum בשובה ונחה וברבקות האלהי s) in reversione & in tranquillitate & fiducia in Deum.
units.tr: Having reviewed their punishments in the preceding verse, those who are indicated under the names of Egypt and Edom, he now makes promises in contrast to those who are signified by the name of Judah and Jerusalem. We have seen quite enough, explaining those words, who are to be understood by the former according to the differing opinions of the interpreters; therefore we think it fair to inquire also into those who are named here. Here again we see the same interpreters divided into different opinions: some understand the places named here literally, others take refuge in a figure, and take the words so broadly that they refer not precisely to the named persons but to all those who, in this respect no less than old Israel, could be said to belong to God in a peculiar way, and to be loved by him above all other places and persons, so that what is promised here could be applied to them: he will dwell for ever and from generation to generation. But before we spend more effort examining these, we have thought it necessary first to look at these words in their proper order and literally. Judah will dwell for ever etc. The word Judah is well known and in its usual sense, as it occurs elsewhere in Holy Scripture, denotes that people or tribe which owes its origin to the Patriarch Judah, whose name the inhabitants of that region, or part, which they inhabited and possessed, bear, and from him are called Judah. In the same way, by Jerusalem either the city itself is denoted, which is known to everyone by this name, or the inhabitants of this city; as appears from some other places of Scripture, so it is obvious enough from what is said in Matth. 3,5: "Then went out to him all Jerusalem and all Judaea." Of these it says here teshceb, which word, if it is rendered as our translators have rendered it, will dwell, seems to refer to the people or inhabitants; but if will remain, as is quite pleasing to some, it is clear that it can be referred to both, to the people or to the place. The Vulgate Latin refers it to the place, changing Judah into Judaea, and turning the verb into the passive, will be inhabited, which the Seventy also do. Yet it is clear that the same sense is implied here without any change, whichever interpretation you follow: namely, that these places will remain habitable forever (for the words for ever, from generation to generation imply this), and the posterity of the ancient inhabitants will dwell in them. The words sound this way literally; and retaining this sense, the Jews also want a happy state to be predicted here, in which Judah and Jerusalem, which are now desolate, will afterwards be restored and inhabited perpetually, in the days of the Messiah (bimot ha-mashiach), in which the Shechinah, or presence of majesty, will have returned, as Kimchi notes on the following verse; or they say the promise regards the future time (leatid lavo), by which God makes the Israelite people certain that they will no longer be in rebellion, nor led away into any captivity again (as Abarbanel says on these words), but that the kingdom of Judah and the house of David, which will rule over Israel and Jerusalem, a name which comprehends all the cities of Israel, will remain for ever in return, and in rest, and in trust in God s) [Isa. 30:15].

units.la: Sed falsis eorum opinio nititur principiis falsaque hypothesi, Meffiam nondum venifie, venturumque erecturum esse regnum terrenum
units.tr: But their opinion rests on false principles and a false hypothesis, namely that the Messiah has not yet come, and that when he comes he will set up an earthly kingdom

units.la: r) Ita in MS. Arabic. ... & ... s) Esa. 30, 15. rium omni felicitate affluens. Quod quam parum congruat veritati, cuivis obvium erit, qui non gravabitur prophetias de eo ac regno ejus historiamque veteris ac eventum in Novo Testamento inspicere atque comparare. Quorum alterum nobis exhibet, quid de eo suturum esset, alterum quantum & quatenus id sit impletum, quid adhuc superest & quomodo id quoque sit implendum. Adeo ut manifestum sit, eum & jam venisse & jam dudum esse praestitum, quod ab eo expectabatur, idque ea, qua fas erat, ratione, quod autem nondum completum esse animadvertimus, id pertinere leatid lebo (ut nostras faciamus illorum loquendi formas) ad futurum i. e. ad mundū futurum. Quocirca alio nos conferamus necesse est, si verum horum verborum sensum velimus, nihil hic inventuri quo acquiescamus.
units.tr: r) So in the Arabic manuscript ... & ... s) Isa. 30:15. abounding in every happiness. How little this agrees with the truth will be obvious to anyone who is not reluctant to look at and compare the prophecies about him and his kingdom, and the history of the Old Testament and its fulfilment in the New Testament. The one sets before us what was to become of him, the other how far and in what way it has been fulfilled, what still remains and how that too is to be fulfilled. So that it is clear that he has both already come and long since accomplished what was expected of him, and that in the proper manner; but as to what we notice has not yet been completed, it pertains (to use their own forms of speech) leatid lebo, that is, to the future, that is, to the future world. Therefore, if we wish to have the true sense of these words, we must necessarily turn elsewhere, since here we will find nothing in which to rest.

units.la: Ex Christianis ad eum statum Judaeorum haec referre videtur Grotius, quo erant in regione sua deletis hostibus Aegypti & Edom eoque pacato rerum statu haec putat esse impleta, quo non paucos annos frueb antur tempore, quod elapsum est inter reditum ex captivitate Babylonica & destructionem Romanorum. Ne autem quis ei opponeret, quod habituri sint vel permansuri in aeternum & a generatione in generationem, ita has expressiones explicat; per longum tempus in pace erit, & per aliquot hominum aetates. At id nimis longe videtur abesse ab eo, quod hic dicitur & haec loquendi formula plerumque significari solet. Hinc t) aliorum magis fixum sedet animo, haec nondum evenisse, nec Juda terrestri esse praestita, nec a Juda & Hierosolyma proprie & ad literam esse expectanda, sed melius applicanda ad ecclesiam Dei, quae eorum locorum gestat nomina, ubi olim propria ac peculiaris erat sedes, promissionemque hic factam insignicer convenire ecclesiae militanti atque (verius etiam) triumphanti.
units.tr: Grotius seems to refer this to the state of the Jews among Christians, when, with their enemies Aegypti & Edom destroyed, their land was at peace. He thinks these things were fulfilled in the time that passed between the return from the Babylonian captivity and the destruction by the Romans, a period of not a few years. To meet the objection that the people are to have or remain for ever and from generation to generation, he explains these expressions thus: In peace for a long time, and for several generations of men. But this seems much too far removed from what is said here, and from the usual meaning of this form of expression. Hence t) the view of others is more firmly settled in my mind: that these things have not yet happened, nor were they promised to the land of Judah, nor are they to be expected literally of Judah and Jerusalem, but are better applied to the Church of God, which bears the names of those places where once was her proper and peculiar seat, and that the promise made here fits the militant Church and (more truly still) the triumphant Church.

units.la: Ne autem lectorem fatigemus enumerandis diversis in eundem scopum collineantibus sententiis, omnium loco tanquam in compendio apponere lubet, quod egregie commentatus est Gvalterus tum ad ea quae praedicta sunt supplicia Dei hostibus sub nomine Aegypti & Edom, tum ad ea, quae promissa sunt ejus populo sub nomine Juda & Hierosolyma, hisce verbis: u) Asseritur hujus promissionis veritas etiam in
units.tr: So that we do not weary the reader by listing the various opinions that aim at the same goal, it pleases me to set down, as if in summary, what Gvalterus has admirably commented, both on the punishments of God foretold for his enemies under the names Aegypti & Edom, and on the things promised to his people under the names Juda & Hierosolyma, in these words: u) The truth of this promise is asserted also in

units.la: t) Vid. Chr. a Castro u) Huc adjunge Danaeum in hoc seculo, quando Christus in medio inimicorum suorum dominatur, suosque inter quotidianas afflictiones protegit, & exempla in⁂ hostes suos horrenda edit: plene tamen præstabitur in cœlis quando extra omnem teli jactum constituti, cum Christo æternum regnabimus. Ipsa perpetuitas, inquit, quæ hic promittitur, argumento est dilucido, hinc locum non accipiendum esse de carnali Juda, sed de spirituali, i.e. Ecclesia, gente judaica (carnali Juda) dudum terra promissa expulsa, regimineque tum ecclesiastico tum politico amisso. Quod vero ad ecclesiam (militantem hisin terris) ejusque durationem in⁂ omne ævum attinet, id ipse Salvator, cum adhuc visibili esset in terra forma, hinc ascensurus in cœlum, ipsi fecit promissum: Vobiscum sum usque ad finem mundi Matth. 28, 20. Quodque nunquam sit desitura, ex eo liquet quod, cum Christus secunda vice in fine mundi venerit, superfuturi sint eorum nonnulli, qui in cœlestem Hierosolymam, triumphantem illam ecclesiam in cœlum transferentur, ubi in æternum cum eo regnabunt, uti & ex Matth. 24, 31. ubi dicitur se missurum esse Angelos suos, & congregaturum electos suos a quatuor ventis, ab uno extremo cœlorum ad alterum; & ex S. Paulo 1. Cor. 15, 51. qui non omnes dicit esse obdormituros sed omnes immutatum⁂ iri, & 1. Thess. 4, 15. & 17. de membris ecclesiæ Christi ait, sore, ut vtri qui reliqui erunt in adventu Domini, rapiantur simul cum eis, qui obdormierint, in nubes in occursum Domini in aera & ita semper cum Domino sint. Ita ut omni ex parte, literaque & sensu horum verborum, in æternum & a generatione in generationem, stricte observato, quatenus denotant perpetuitatem & æternitatem, ecclesiæ Christi, non alii Judæ & Hierosolymæ, conveniat.
units.tr: t) See Chr. a Castro. u) Add here Danaeus: in this age, when Christ rules in the midst of his enemies, and protects his people amid their daily afflictions, and displays terrible examples against his enemies; but it will be fully performed in heaven, when we are placed beyond every dart's reach and shall reign eternally with Christ. The very perpetuity, he says, which is promised here is a clear proof that the place is not to be taken of the carnal Judah, but of the spiritual, that is, the Church. The Jewish nation (the carnal Judah) was long ago driven from the promised land and lost both its ecclesiastical and its political government. But as for the Church (militant here on earth) and its continuance for all ages, the Saviour himself, while he still had a visible form on earth and was about to ascend into heaven, made this promise to her: I am with you always, even to the end of the world, Matth. 28, 20. And that she will never cease is clear from this: when Christ comes a second time at the end of the world, some of those who belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, that triumphant Church, will remain alive and will be carried up into heaven, where they will reign with him forever. This is also shown by Matth. 24, 31., where he says he will send his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other; and by St Paul, 1 Cor. 15, 51., who says not all will fall asleep but all will be changed; and 1 Thess. 4, 15 & 17., where he speaks of the members of Christ's Church: that those of us who are left alive at the coming of the Lord shall be caught up together with those who have fallen asleep, in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord. Thus, in every respect, both in the letter and the sense of these words, for ever and from generation to generation, strictly observed, insofar as they denote the perpetuity and eternity of the Church of Christ, fit not some other Judah and Jerusalem.

units.la: Huc iv) ejus redit expositio, quam tam fuse hic adducere allubuit, quia complectitur quicquid ab aliis Christianis in explicationem hujus loci fere adducitur, cujus sensus etiam breviter ac perspicue exprimitur a Reverend. Episcop. Hall, qui hæc verba ita παρεφράζει: At electi Dei habitabunt in æternum in ejus sanctò habitaculo, & postquam ex ecclesia militante in terris translati fuerint, regnabunt in gloria cœlorum sine sine.
units.tr: To this comes the exposition of his, which I have been pleased to cite here so fully, because it includes nearly everything that other Christians bring forward to explain this place. Its sense is also briefly and clearly expressed by the Reverend Bishop Hall, who paraphrases these words thus: iv) paraphrazei [παρεφράζει]: But the elect of God shall dwell for ever in his holy habitation, and after they are translated out of the militant Church on earth, they shall reign without end in the glory of heaven.

units.la: §§) Quæ cum etiam comparari potest expositio Danæi. Qua ratione autem favorem suum ac curam, quam eorum, praeter perpetuam conservationem, gerit, fit declaraturus, fit palam ex eis, quæ ultimo hocce versu exhibentur.
units.tr: The exposition of Danaeus can also be compared with this. But in what way he will show his favour and care, which he bears toward them besides their perpetual preservation, is made plain from what is set out in the last verse here.

units.la: 21. Nam purgabo eorum sanguinem, quem non purga- vi, Dominus enim habitat in Sione.
units.tr: 21. For I will cleanse their blood, which I have not cleansed; for the Lord dwells in Zion.

units.la: Tanta in hoc versu est eorum varietas, qui genuinum ejus scrutantur sensum, quanta non est in ullo alio hujus prophetiæ, ne dicam, totius S. Scripturæ, adeo ut non videa qua ratione lectori possit fieri satis, nisi earum, quas reperio præcipuas opiniones, seriem pertexere, aggrediar. Verba hebraica ita habent ונקיתי דם לא נקיתי venikketi damam lo nikketi, quæ ad literam sonant: & mundabo sanguinem eorum, non mundavi, quæ uti varie possunt distingui ac construi, varieque ab interpretibus juxta varias, quas habent, significationes, redduntur atque supplentur, ita variæ etiam eorum ortæ sunt opiniones, quarum epitomen hic subjicere visum est. Initium facimus a Judæis, quos inter R. Tanchum inprimis quatuor recenset, quas hæc verba interpretationes ferre possunt.
units.tr: There is so much variety among those who seek the genuine sense of this verse, greater than in any other verse of this prophecy, not to say of all Holy Scripture, that I do not see how the reader can be satisfied unless I set out in order the chief opinions I find. The Hebrew reads ונקיתי דם לא נקיתי venikketi damam lo nikketi [ונקיתי דם לא נקיתי], which word for word sounds: and I will cleanse their blood, I have not cleansed. This can be divided and construed in various ways, and rendered and supplied variously by the interpreters according to the various meanings they find; and so various opinions have arisen, whose summary I have thought fit to add here. We begin with the Jews, among whom R. Tanchum especially lists four interpretations these words can bear.

units.la: 1. Ut affixum in voce דם damam, sanguinem eorum, usitata sanguinis significatione retenta, referatur ad Israelitas, ac si ita haberent verba ואם נקיתי דם לא נקיתי, i.e. &, vel sed si purgabo, non purgabo ab eorum sanguine, i.e. etsi purgaturus (vel absoluturus) sim eorum hostes ab omnibus aliis peccatis, attamen non absolvam eos ab eorum sanguine, videlicet Edumæos & Ægyptios antea dictos, sed exigam ab eis, vel vindicabo sanguinem Israelitarum ab eis fusum, & nunquam hoc illis condonabo.
units.tr: 1. Let the suffix in the word דם damam, their blood be taken in its usual sense of blood and referred to the Israelites, as if the words read ואם נקיתי דם לא נקיתי [and if I cleanse blood, I have not cleansed], that is, and or but if I cleanse, I will not cleanse from their blood: that is, although I shall cleanse (or acquit) my enemies of all their other sins, yet I will not acquit them of their blood, namely of that of Edomites and Egyptians mentioned before; rather I will exact it from them, or I will avenge the blood of the Israelites shed by them, and never forgive them this.

units.la: 2. Ut ad eosdem quidem Israelitas referatur affixum, sed sanguis eorum accipiatur pro peccatis eorum, qua ratione sumtum arbitratur Hos.12,14. Atque verbum bis repetitum נקיתי nikketi, quod nostrat interpretantur notione purgandi; priore quidem loco accipiendum ait, significatione purgandi, uti in his verbis נקתה ונזרעה זרע quæ nostrates reddunt, libera erit & consequetur semen, Num.5,28, quasi esset; reddam eos puros vel insontes eorum peccatorum; posteriore autem loco significatione [illegible, ~5 letters] prorsus tollendi vel immunem reddendi, quo pacto accipi illud sibi persuadet, Jer. 30, 11. ונקה לא אנקך venakkeh lo anakkecah, ex interpretatione nostratium, & non relinquam te prorsus immunem; cum Chaldaeus reddat ותשיצאה לא אשיצך & perdendo te non perdam; & Pagn. & succidendo non succidam te; & in eandem sententiam quidam alii: atque idcirco idem hoc valere vult atque, ego repurgabo eorum peccata & non (rigide) puniam eos ad extremam eorum destructionem; ita ut aliud affixum ultima vox requirat ac si haberet, ונקיתי דם ולא אנקם Purgabo (vel tollam) eorum sanguinem, i. e. eorum peccata, & non prorsus tollam vel protinus destruam eos.
units.tr: 2. Let the suffix again refer to the Israelites, but let their blood be taken for their sins, as he thinks Hos. 12, 14 takes it. And the word נקיתי nikketi, repeated twice, which our people translate in the sense of cleansing: in the first place, he says, it is to be taken in the sense of cleansing, as in these words נקתה ונזרעה זרע, which our people render she shall be free and shall conceive seed, Num. 5, 28, as if to say: I will make them clean, or free of their sins. In the second place, however, it is to be taken in the sense of utterly removing or making quit, in which way he persuades himself that the passage in Jer. 30, 11, ונקה לא אנקך [venakkeh lo anakkecah], is to be understood, according to our people's translation, and I will not leave you utterly unpunished; whereas the Chaldee renders it ותשיצאה לא אשיצך, and in destroying you I will not destroy you; and Pagninus and in cutting down I will not cut you down; and certain others to the same effect. Therefore he wants this to mean the same as: I will purge away their sins, and I will not (rigorously) punish them to their final destruction. So the final word requires a different suffix, as if the text had ונקיתי דם ולא אנקם: I will cleanse (or take away) their blood, that is, their sins, and I will not utterly take away or at once destroy them.

units.la: 3. Ut vox דם damam, sanguis eorum, iterum sumatur notione דנבהון danbahoni, eorum peccatum, atque affixum ם, m, illorum, referatur ad hostes, verbumque נקיתי priore loco accipitur significatu radicitus evertendi, vel exigendi ad ultimum supplicium, posteriore autem (ubi iterum repetendum affixum, & נקיתי pro אנקם) sensu purgandi vel purum & innocentem reddendi, ita ut sensus hunc in modum fluat Exigam eos ad extremum supplicium propter eorum peccata, & numquam eos criminc eximam (vel insontes reputabo).
units.tr: 3. Let the word דם damam, their blood, again be taken in the sense of דנבהון danbahoni, their sin, and let the suffix ם, m, of them, be referred to the enemies. The verb נקיתי is taken in the first place in the sense of utterly overthrowing, or exacting to the last punishment, but in the second place (where the suffix must again be supplied and נקיתי stands for אנקם) in the sense of cleansing, or making pure and innocent. So the sense flows in this manner: I will exact the extreme punishment from them for their sins, and I will never acquit them of guilt (or I will count them innocent).

units.la: 4. Denique aliam adducit expositionem, quae ipsi magis videtur accommodata atque congrua verbis, quam ulla caeterarum, qua tantum supplet vocem אשר asher, qui, quae, quod, quae quam saepissime brevitatis causa omittitur, quasi dictum esset ונקיתי דם אשר לא נקיתי ubi, cum ipsi verbum נקיתי nikketi utrobique denotet radicitus vel penitus destruere) & affixum ab eo referatur ad Judam & Hierosolymam, quarum in praecedenti versu facta erat mentio, eaque vox דם ei significet diyatahom, pretium sanguinis eorum, vel multam pro eorum sanguine fuso, quo sensu accipi contendit verba Exod. 22,2. y) אין לו דמים Ein lo damim, pretium sanguinis pro eo ne exgitor, & v. 3. דמים לו Damim lo, sanguinis (caedis) reus efso; Sic demum sensus enascitur ... Wa-talba diyatahom allati lam eslha.
units.tr: 4. Finally he offers another explanation, which seems to me better suited to the words than any of the others. It supplies only the word אשר asher, who, which, that, which is very often omitted for brevity, as if it had been said ונקיתי דם אשר לא נקיתי [and I will cleanse the blood that I have not cleansed]. Here the verb נקיתי nikketi in both places means to destroy utterly or root out, and the suffix is referred to Judah and Jerusalem, mentioned in the preceding verse. He takes the word דם as the price of their blood, that is, a fine paid for the blood shed. He argues that the words of Exod. 22:2 y) אין לו דמים [Ein lo damim], let him not be exacted the price of blood for him, and v. 3, דמים לו [Damim lo], he shall be guilty of bloodshed (murder), must be understood in this sense. So the meaning finally emerges as: ... Wa-talba diyatahom allati lam eslha [wa-talaba diyatahum allati lam uslih, "and I will demand their blood-price, which I have not yet fully exacted"].

units.la: x) Quae vox a radix significat vel radicitus evellere, protinus delere, vel ad ipsam radicem usque penetrare, sive omnem operam in aliquid collocare. y) Sic Abu VValid in דם. felba ela dhaleca alwakt, Et ad extremum progrediar exigendo pretium (vel vindictam) pro sanguine eorum, quod hucusque non plene exegeram.
units.tr: x) This verb means either to tear up by the root, to destroy at once, or to penetrate right down to the root, or to devote all one's effort to something. y) So Abu Walid under דם: felba ela dhaleca alwakt [fa-latiba ila dhalika al-waqt], and at last I will proceed to exact the price (or vengeance) for their blood, which until now I have not fully exacted.

units.la: Has quatuor horum verborum sententias, quas suo tempore perspectas habebat, literis consignavit, quarum ipse, meo quidem judicio, recte, ob constructionis facilitatem ac perfectionem praetulit ultimam. Primam autem caeteri, qui ad notitiam nostram pervenerunt Judaicae gentis interpretes, uti R. Salomo Jarchi, Aben-Ezra & David Kimchi, unanimi quasi consensu sequuntur, praeterquam quod aliarum injiciant mentionem, rejiciendo vocem eorum sanguinem, ad comma posterius, ut verba ita distincta in hunc sensum fluant; quantumvis purgem (vel absolvam) has nationes ab aliis peccatis admissis, tamen eas non purgabo vel absolvam a sanguine Israelitarum. Fuse praeterea haec verba explicat David Kimchi hoc modo: Ab argento & auro eorum, quod acceperunt, purgabo vel absolvam eas; quia etiam Israelitae talia ab illis tanquam in spolia accipient in futurum; At a sanguine eorum, quem fuderunt, non mundabo eas, sed anima pro anima (vita pro vita) sive anima vel vita fundentium sanguinem, sive filiorum illorum post illos. Nam si omne argentum & aurum, quod in orbe est, darent pro pretio animarum eorum, non erunt mundi ab eorum sanguine (quem fuderunt.) Cum vero eorum sanguinem ad posteriora verba referat cum duobus aliis, qui ante eum floruerunt, observatione tamen haud indignum putat adjicere, quod ad verbum praecedens venikketi & purgabo, id referat Chaldaeus reddens, id est, Et quorum ultus sum sanguinem a gentibus adhuc sum vindicaturus. Nil tamen ulterius addit quod vel ad explicationem vel ad censuram horum verborum quicquam facere queat. Mirari interim subit, quod non attenderit ad particulam lo non, quam plane omisit. Id quod z) nonnullos in opinionem adduxit, ejus interpretationem haud convenire textui hebraico, quo cum mihi tamen facile videtur posse conciliari, quippe quae ab eo affirmative sunt reddita, sensu negativam includunt, quamvis verbis non apponatur. Eodem enim redit,
units.tr: He recorded these four senses of the words in writing, having them in view at the time. Of these, in my judgment rightly, he preferred the last, because it makes the construction easier and more complete. The first sense is followed almost unanimously by the other Jewish interpreters known to us, such as R. Solomon Jarchi, Aben Ezra and David Kimchi, except that they omit mention of the others. They reject the words their blood as belonging to the later clause, so that the words, thus divided, run in this sense: however much I cleanse (or acquit) these nations from their other sins, yet I will not cleanse or acquit them from the blood of the Israelites. David Kimchi also explains these words at length in this way: I will cleanse or acquit them from the silver and gold which they have received; for the Israelites too will in future receive such things from them as spoils. But from the blood which they have shed I will not cleanse them, but soul for soul (life for life), that is, the soul or life of those shedding blood, or of their sons after them. For if they gave all the silver and gold that is in the world as the price of their souls, they would not be cleansed from the blood (which they have shed). Yet since he refers their blood to the latter words, along with two others who flourished before him, he thinks it worth adding this observation: the Chaldee paraphrast, rendering the preceding word venikketi ("and I will cleanse"), says that is, And whose blood I have avenged from the nations, I shall yet avenge. He adds nothing further that could help the explanation or the criticism of these words. It is strange, however, that he did not notice the particle lo, "not", which he has plainly omitted. This omission led some to think that his interpretation does not agree with the Hebrew text; but it seems to me that it can easily be reconciled with it, since what he has rendered affirmatively contains a negative sense, though the word is not added in the words. For it comes to the same thing,

units.la: z) Merc. Pet. a Fig. redit,iterum eos ulturus sum; atque,nondum eos eo ultus sum modo, quo ulcisci constitui.
units.tr: z) Mercerus, Pet. a Fig. comes to the same: I will avenge them again; and also: I have not yet avenged them in the way I had determined to avenge them.

units.la: His quoque accensendus, qui vocem רמם damum ad praecedens verbum venikketi refert, Arabicae versionis autor Judaeus, qui haec verba ita transfert وأري مب مطالبة بماهم الذي الي الان لم اجر Et purgatus ero, vel purgabo me a requirendo eorum sanguinem, a quo hucusque nondum sum purgatus; cujus mea sententia hic est sensus, quod omni ex parte ac plene se velit purgare, eorum sanguinem omnino exigendo vel ulciscendo quod hactenus non fecerat. Aliam tamen, recitata antea ea, quam Kimchi & alii sequntur, praefert Abarbinel, qua Damam, eorum sanguinem ad praecedens quidem refert verbum, alio tamen prorsus sensu, quam alii fecisse vidimus, quandoquidem verba priora interrogandi forma legit atque totum comma ita explicat האם נקיתי אני ארת האומרת מרם ישראל אשר שלכו הארץ באמרת לא נקיתי ולכן אפרע בהם i. e. An absolvi (vel purgavi) gentes a sanguine Israelis, quem fuderunt in terra? Certe ego nondum absolvi (eos) sed (vel atque ideo) ulturus sum eas. Quae distinguendi ac construendi ratio, qua רמם eorum sanguis, regitur a praecedenti verbo, omnium, quas habemus est antiquissima, nec auctoritate caret, quod diversa significatione accipiendum sit verbum utroq; membro expressum, quippe ex antiquissima LXX versione id luculenter apparet, qui ita haec verba interpretantur, a) καὶ ἐκζητήσω τὸ αἷμα αὐτῶν, καὶ ὁ μὴ ἀθωώσω, Et exigam vel ulciscar eorum sanguinem, multumque esse non patiar.
units.tr: This interpreter should also be counted among those who refer the word damum [דָּמָם, "their blood"] to the preceding verb venikketi [וְנִקֵּיתִי, "and I shall be acquitted"]. The Jewish author of the Arabic version translates these words thus: wa-ara mub muṭālabat bi-mā-hum alladhī ilā al-ān lam ajri, "And I shall be purged, or I shall purge myself, from demanding their blood, from which I have not hitherto been purged." In my view the sense is that he wishes to cleanse himself completely and fully, by exacting or avenging their blood altogether, which he had not done until now. Abarbanel, however, prefers another reading, recited above and followed by Kimchi and others, in which he also refers damum, their blood, to the preceding verb, but in a quite different sense from those we have seen. For he reads the earlier words as a question and explains the whole clause thus: הַאִם נִקֵּיתִי אֲנִי אֶת־הַגּוֹיִם מִדַּם יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר שָׁפְכוּ הָאָרֶץ? בְּאָמְרָהּ לֹא נִקֵּיתִי וְלָכֵן אֶפְרַע בָּהֶם. Have I acquitted the nations of the blood of Israel which they shed in the land? Certainly I have not yet acquitted them, and therefore I shall avenge them. This way of distinguishing and construing, in which דָּמָם, "their blood," is governed by the preceding verb, is of all the readings we have the most ancient, and it has authority, since the verb expressed in each member must be taken in a different sense. This clearly appears from the most ancient version, that of the Seventy, which renders these words: a) καὶ ἐκζητήσω τὸ αἷμα αὐτῶν, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀθωώσω [and I will require their blood, and I will not acquit them], And I shall exact or avenge their blood, and I shall not suffer it to go unpunished.

units.la: Hactenus, quod attinet ad Judaeorum de hoc loco sententias tum recentiorum tum priscorum. Quodsi jam Christianorum opiniones lubeat inspicere, sive interpretum, sive Commentatorum, multo inveniemus plures, quibusdam cum horum nonnullis, quos vidimus, conspirantibus, aliis in contrarium plane abeuntibus. Ex interpretibus quidam, isque non b) mediocris auctoritatis, quamvis recentioris aevi, facit cum Kimchi caeterisque Judaeis, quos cum eo conspirare vidimus, eodem modo verba distinguens ac construens, cum reddat: mundabo qui-
units.tr: So far as concerns the opinions of the Jews on this passage, both recent and ancient. If we now care to examine the opinions of Christians, whether of translators or of commentators, we shall find many more, some agreeing with some of those we have seen, others going quite in the opposite direction. Among the translators, one of no small authority, though of recent date, agrees with Kimchi and the other Jews whom we have seen agreeing with him, dividing and construing the words in the same way, since he renders: I will cleanse those

units.la: a) Vel ut alii Codic. ἐκδικήσω. b) Pagnin. quidem,sed sanguinem eorum non mundabo. Alii nostri æque ac priscorum temporum planiorem ducunt construendi rationem,quam secundo loco adduximus,qua ad prius membrum referunt nomé quod regitur, licet nec illis ipsis bene conveniat,qui ita accipiunt,quisnam eorum genuinus sit sensus.Ita ea reddit Syrus [Syriac text] Et ulcisfcar eorum sanguinem & non parcam. Et in eandem mentem Arabica impressa Græcos etiam imitans [Arabic text] Et Vulgatus Latinus,& mundabo sanguinem eorum, quem non mundaveram. Quo cum videmus nostrates facere, excepto,quod conjunctionem ve reddant,nam, quam ille ex significatione ejus usitata, reddidit & ; quod idem etiam facit in Italica versione sua Diodati,ut & Tigur Lat. præterquam quod loco quem,habeat quos,ad personas referens,quod ille refert ad sanguinem.
units.tr: a) Or, as other codices have, ἐκδικήσω [ekdikēsō, "I will avenge"]. b) Pagninus. indeed, but I will not cleanse their blood. Others of our people, as well as of earlier times, follow a plainer way of construing, the second one we have mentioned, in which the governed noun is referred to the first member, although even those who take it so do not agree well among themselves about what its true sense is. So the Syriac renders it [Syriac text]: And I will avenge their blood and not spare. And in the same sense the printed Arabic, also imitating the Greek: [Arabic text] And the Latin Vulgate: and I will cleanse their blood, which I had not cleansed. We see our own people doing the same, except that they render the conjunction ve as for, which the other, from its usual meaning, rendered as and. Diodati does the same in his Italian version, as does the Tigurine Latin, except that instead of quem ("which") it has quos ("whom"), referring to persons, which the other refers to the blood.

units.la: Nihil autem horum exprimitur in textu hebraico,hinc plane id videmus quibusdam prætermissum in versionibus suis,reddendo duntaxat,mundabo sanguinem eorum,non mundavi. Cum vero ad sensum exprimendum se accingant,alterutrum horum necessario subintelligendum est, vel quorum sanguinem vel quem sanguinem,vel quos, uti habet Castalio : eorumque sanguinem expiabo,quos non expiavero, verum nil quicquam,officere potest sensui,quicquid eorum suppleveris. At longe major hic est differentia inter commentatores,quæ tamen aliunde originem trahit. Nimirum non eodem omnes modo intelligunt voces,sanguinem &purgare,nec de iisdem subjectis. Atque hinc est,quod tam discrepantes eorum nascantur opiniones,quarum peculiares sunt hæ sequentes.Primo sunt,quibus verbum [Hebrew] nikkeb accipitur,ut plerumque solet,pro absolvere vel purgare, & sanguis laxiore significatione pro detestandis peccatis (quæ sanguinis instar pollunt vel mortem merentur, vel propter quæ sanguis fundetur peccatoris) ut sensus sit,Deum promittere ecclesiam suam atque electos suos purgare a pollutione eorum peccatorum, quibus hactenus fuere inquinati.Ita qui verterunt Anglicanam ex Geneν. quibus recentiores hoc in loco accedunt,in notis suis explicandi gratia addunt; Hactenus in impuritate ecclesiam suam Deus tulit,jam vero promittit eam mundare sibique
units.tr: None of this, however, is expressed in the Hebrew text, and so we see that some have plainly passed it over in their versions, rendering only I will cleanse their blood, I have not cleansed. When they set themselves to express the sense, one of these must necessarily be understood, either whose blood, or which blood, or whom, as Castalio has it: and I will atone for their blood, whom I have not atoned for. Yet whatever you supply can do no harm to the sense. But the difference among the commentators is far greater, and it arises from other sources: not all understand the words blood and to cleanse in the same way, nor do they take the same subjects. Hence arise such divergent opinions, of which the following are the chief. First are those who take the verb [Hebrew] nikkeb, as it usually is, to mean to absolve or to cleanse, and blood in a looser sense for detestable sins (which are like blood, and deserve death, or on account of which the sinner's blood is shed), so that the sense is that God promises to cleanse his Church and his elect from the pollution of those sins by which they have hitherto been defiled. So those who translated the English version from the Geneva Bible, and more recent writers on this passage, add in their notes, by way of explanation: Hitherto God has borne with his Church in its impurity, but now he promises to cleanse it and make it pure for himself.

units.la: c) Munst. Calv. sibique puram reddere. His quoque concinit Reverend.Episcop.Hallius in paraphrasi sua: Nam ego abluam vel purgabo peccata horum electorum meorum, quae antea non ablui, atque cooptatos liberabo a gentibus, quarum iniquitatibus erant polluti. Consimiliter Diodati in versione sua Italica hunc sensum exprimit: Ecclesiam meam ab omnibus imperfectionibus & maculis peccati, quae in hoc mundo in ipsa adhuc remanserant perfecte sanctificabo. Eodem collineant non pauci alii Auctores latini, quamvis non eadem omnes sentiant de tempore, quo haec sint futura, cum quidam ad evangelii praedicationem haec traducant, quo Deus purgare volebat in Evangelio, quos in lege peccantes immundos reliquerat, ut ait Hieronymus; quando, ut fusius haec exsequuntur d) alii purgabit gentes in Ecclesiam cooptatas, quae prius erant e) mortuae in offensis & peccatis suis, absque Christo, alienae a republica Israelis, extraneae a pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, & Dei expertes in mundo, reddens eas vicinas ac propiores per sanguinem Christi, qui purgat ab omnibus peccatis; fideque illarum corda purgans, Act. 15,9. Imo & Judaeos, ut addunt f) alii, quos lex omnibus suis ceremoniis & abluendi ritibus adeo non purgare poterat, quin adhuc essent g) conclusi sub peccatum, ut promissio ex fide Jesu Christi daretur credentibus, qua fide sola illis pariter ac gentibus, h) fons apertus est propeccato & separatione ex immunditie, i. e. ad purgandum eos a peccatis suis. Quo cum utrisque aeque sit opus, in Christo solo is est apertus atque ejus vis non efficax redditur nisi per fidem in eum etiam in hac vita. Quia tamen non omni ex parte hic purgantur, alii sunt una cum his, quos jam adduximus, qui id potius suturum ducunt omnibus credentibus in altera vita, quando mortalitate depolita cum omni ejus fragilitate & corruptione recipientur in coelestem Hierosolymam, in quam i) nihil quod pollutum est, nihil quod non purgatum est a peccatis, intrabit.
units.tr: c) Munster, Calvin: and make it pure for himself. The Reverend Bishop Hall agrees with this in his paraphrase: For I will wash away or cleanse the sins of these my elect, which I did not wash away before, and I will free those chosen from the nations, by whose iniquities they were polluted. Diodati in his Italian version likewise expresses this sense: I will perfectly sanctify my Church from all the imperfections and stains of sin which had remained in it in this world. Not a few other Latin authors aim at the same thing, although they do not all agree about the time when these things will happen. Some refer them to the preaching of the gospel, in which God wished to cleanse those whom he had left unclean while they sinned under the law, as Jerome says. Others, explaining this more fully, d) say that he will cleanse the Gentiles gathered into the Church, who once were e) dead in their offences and sins, without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world, making them near and close through the blood of Christ, who cleanses from all sins, cleansing their hearts by faith, Acts 15:9. Indeed, as others add f), he will cleanse also the Jews, whom the law with all its ceremonies and rites of washing could not so cleanse that they were not still g) shut up under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. By this faith alone, equally for them and for the Gentiles, h) a fountain is opened for sin and for uncleanness, that is, to cleanse them from their sins. Since both need this, it is opened in Christ alone, and its power is not effective unless one believes in him, even in this life. Yet because they are not cleansed in every respect here, others, together with those already cited, think this will happen rather to all believers in the next life, when, laying aside mortality with all its frailty and corruption, they are received into the heavenly Jerusalem, into which i) nothing that is defiled, nothing not cleansed from sins, will enter.

units.la: Quodsi hac ratione haec verba sint sumenda, ut purgare eorum sanguinem, tantundem sit, ac illos puros reddere a peccatis suis, utramque hic innui puritatem mihi persuadeo, & eam, quam illis adhuc praebet in hac vita, & qua in futura eos perficiet. Utraque enim ejus donum est,
units.tr: If these words are to be taken in this way, so that to cleanse their blood is the same as to make them pure of their sins, then I am persuaded that both purities are meant here: the one which he still gives them in this life, and the one by which he will perfect them in the future. For each is his gift, and they can be made capable of receiving it only through faith in Christ.

units.la: d) Jun. Trem. e) Eph. 2,12. f) Tarn. Ribera. Danaeus. g) Gal. 3,22. h) Zach. 13,1. i) Apoc. 21,27. est, cui recipiendo non nisi per fidem in Christum reddi possunt capaces, k) Prima autem consistit in condonandis peccatis, quando illorum eos poenitet; altera in iisdem penitus abolendis, ac ab eis illos plane immunes reddendo, quod, cum in hac vita eos non prorsus purget a peccatis, quamvis ea illis remittat, futuro tempore plene ac summa mensura facturus est eosque perfecte purgaturus cum condonando maxima illa peccata, quae ob gravitatem immanitatemque sanguini comparantur, atque omnino remitti non posse videntur (uti/) quidam addunt) tum etiam eos sanctificando, ut nullum amplius peccatum admittant, sed ab omnibus repurgati innocentem vivant vitam. Hanc exponendi rationem ipsa verba nobis suggerunt, si verbum accipitur significatione purgandi, idque communi notione, atque sanguinis nomen pro detestandis quibusdam peccatis. Nec longe ab hac interpretatione verborum abire videtur Petrus a Figuero, cum lectoris judicio subjiciat atque in deliberationem ut cadat, moneat, num hoc loco videatur Judaeis dari promissum, fore, ut ultimis diebus resipiscentes ac ad Christum se convertentes a reatu sanguinis purgentur, quem in se derivabant dicendo, sanguis ejus sit super nos &c. cuique adhuc sunt obnoxii atque postea futuri sunt, donec eorum superstites ad eum se recipientes ab eo purgabuntur. Quandoquidem autem aliis alio sensu sumitur verbum, videlicet ulciscendi significatione atque sanguinis denominatio proprie & magis stricte, unde necessario alia enascitur sententia, hanc inprimis iis tunc subesse is putat sensum, quod scilicet Deus m) innocentem populi electi sanguinem, quem ab hostibus suis fusum nondum ultus erat, constituto tempore ulturus sit. Quo certe etiam ducimur, a Graecis, Syro & Arabe, uti vidimus. Grotius censet ΠΡΣ nikke hoc loco esse ulcisci, sensumque pulchre esse expressum a Chaldaeo, qui paraphrasi haec verba ita enucleat, si quis adhuc esset Judaeorum sanguis effusus; quem ultus nondum fuero, etiam hunc ulcisci. Hanc esse mentem Chaldaei equidem infinitas iri vix potest, verba autem ubi huncce in modum legerit vel quo exemplari usus fuerit, non liquet, quippe nullibi haec verba ita inventa sed ea ratione, qua antea nos ea citavimus. Idque vult in Annotationibus k) Vid. Piscat. l) Munst. & vide sis Chr. a Castro. m) Christ. a Castro. nitis & Moabitis revera fuisse completum. Verum nimis anguste hae expositione verba videtur limitare ac restringere ad sanguinem tantum Judæorum & ad Ammonitas & Moabitas, de quibus ultionem erat sumturus. Satius igitur nostra sententia erit, si hac ratione sint explicanda, ut sanguis intelligatur populi Dei injuria fusus atque vindicandus propter hanc fusionem, ab omnibus infensissimis hostibus & persecutoribus ecclesiæ Dei: quæ interpretatio fulcimentum haud mediocre sibi petit ex versu præcedenti, ubi Ægyptus & Edom in desolationem fore dicuntur ob violentiam filiorum Juda, & quia effuderant innocentem sanguinem in terra eorum, quod illustrandum ex Apoc. 6, 9. 10. ubi occisorum animæ propter verbum Dei & propter testimonium, quod tuebantur, magna voce dicuntur clamasse; usque quo Domine, qui sanctus es & verax, non ulciscerisanguinem nostrum ab iis qui habitant in terra? Alia tamen nihilominus præfertur sententia ab iis, qui etsi dubio procul hanc noverint, tamen purgare hic malunt idem esse ac manifestare, reddere, & declarare purum, eoque redire sensum quod ultimo judicio, quo omnium rerum veritas manifestabitur, declaraturus sit, ad se pertinere hujus populi sanguinem in hoc mundo fusum, eumque (quamvis hostes sibi persuadeant jure merito id factum ac si optime id meriti suissent) revera fuisse innocentem, quatenus hos ab æterno supplicio immunes reddet, quo in eos animadvertit, quibus eum fundere volupe fuit. Atque has præcipuas remur horum verborum expositiones; quarum ultimæ duæ verbis ac loco egregie videntur convenire, quæ quamvis verbis quam maxime discrepent, re tamen videntur nequaquam differre, sed se mutuo inferre, quippe cum Deus ulturus sit sanctorum suorum sanguinem, manifestum est, id fieri non posse quin eosdem etiam declaret puros atque innocentes, cui rei declarandæ nulla via est commodior, quam qua justa in fundentes sanguinem propter peccata sua edet supplicia. In eo conveniunt cuncti, esse hic solatii loco fido Dei populo promissum, ea certo esse futura, si non hic in præsenti seculo, attamen instante ultimo judicio, cui etiam sequentia suffragantur: Nam, inquit, Dominus habitat in Sione, habitatio ejus est Sion. i. e. ecclesia ejus, & electi, qui commode hoc nomine
units.tr: d) Junius, Tremellius. e) Eph. 2:12. f) Tarrantius, Ribera, Danaeus. g) Gal. 3:22. h) Zech. 13:1. i) Rev. 21:27. It is ... k) The first consists in the forgiveness of sins, when they repent of them; the second in utterly abolishing them and rendering them wholly free from them. Since in this life he does not altogether cleanse them from sins, though he remits them, he will do this at a future time fully and to the highest degree, perfectly cleansing them: both by pardoning those very great sins which are compared to blood because of their gravity and enormity, and which seem altogether unable to be remitted (as some add), and then also by sanctifying them so that they admit no further sin, but, purged of everything, live an innocent life. The words themselves suggest this way of explaining them, if the word is taken in its common sense of cleansing, and the name blood is taken for certain detestable sins. Petrus a Figuero seems not far from this interpretation of the words, when he submits the matter to the reader's judgment and urges him to consider whether a promise seems to be given here to the Jews, that in the last days, repenting and turning to Christ, they will be cleansed from the guilt of the blood which they brought upon themselves when they said his blood be upon us, etc., a guilt to which they are still liable and will be afterwards, until those of them who survive, turning to him, are cleansed by him. Since, however, others take the word in another sense, namely that of avenging, and blood in its proper and stricter sense, from which another meaning necessarily arises, they think this is the sense chiefly underlying the words: that God will at the appointed time avenge the innocent blood of his chosen people, which he had not yet avenged, shed by their enemies. To this we are certainly also led by the Greeks, the Syriac and the Arabic, as we have seen. Grotius thinks that the Hebrew word nikke here means to avenge, and that the sense is beautifully expressed by the Chaldee, who in his paraphrase unfolds these words thus: if any blood of the Jews was shed which I have not yet avenged, I will avenge this too. That this was the Chaldee's meaning can scarcely be doubted, but it is not clear from what text, or in what manner, he read the words, since these words are found nowhere in this form, but in the way we cited them before. And Grotius wishes this to have been truly fulfilled in the Ammonites and Moabites. But this exposition seems to limit and restrict the words too narrowly, to the blood of the Jews alone and to the Ammonites and Moabites, on whom he was about to take vengeance. Our view, therefore, will be more satisfactory if the words are explained in this way: that blood is understood as the blood of the people of God, shed by injury and to be avenged for that shedding, by all the most hostile enemies and persecutors of the Church of God. This interpretation finds no small support in the preceding verse, where Egypt and Edom are said to become a desolation because of the violence done to the sons of Judah, and because they shed innocent blood in their land. This is illustrated from Rev. 6:9, 10, where the souls of those slain for the word of God and the testimony they kept are said to have cried out with a loud voice: How long, Lord, who art holy and true, dost thou not avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? Nevertheless another view is preferred by those who, though without doubt they know this, prefer here that to cleanse means the same as to make manifest, to render and declare pure, and so the sense returns that at the last judgment, in which the truth of all things will be made manifest, he will declare that the blood of this people shed in this world belongs to him, and that it was truly innocent (although their enemies persuade themselves that it was done justly and deservedly, as if they had best merited it), since he will render them free from eternal punishment, while he punishes those who were pleased to shed it. We judge these to be the chief explanations of these words. The last two seem remarkably to suit both the words and the place, and though they differ greatly in wording, they seem in substance not to differ at all, but to imply one another. For since God will avenge the blood of his saints, it is manifest that this cannot happen without his also declaring them pure and innocent; and for declaring this there is no more fitting way than that by which he inflicts just punishments on those who shed their blood for their sins. All agree that here a promise is given to the faithful people of God, as a comfort, that these things will certainly come to pass, if not in the present age, yet at the coming last judgment, to which the following words also lend support: For, it says, the Lord dwells in Sion, his dwelling is Sion, that is, his Church and the elect, who may conveniently be understood by this name,

units.la: *) Lyra, Merc. Drus. Livel. mine possunt intelligi, ut exponit etiam hæc R. Tanchum [?] continuatio providentiæ ejus super ea atque manifestatio augustæ ejus præsentiæ in ea. Quæ ubi sunt, certum est, nihil quicquam nocere posse ulli superstiti, atque nihil etiam ad felicitatem & bonum statum inhabitantium conducere his deficientibus. Præsentia ejus omnia necessario dispelluntur mala, omniaque e contrario suppeditantur bona. Noštrates interpretantur hic particulam וve per nam, ac si fiduciam velit facere illis, quod certo eventura sint, quæ hic promittuntur, quo mihi videntur genuinum ac verum verborum promere sensum, quamvis, quoad videre potui, foli sint qui ita faciunt. Adjiciunt equidem aliam interpretationem, at ea a priore non adeo discrepat sensu, quam verbis; ita enim habet: Etiam ego Dominus qui habitat in Zione; quid enim emphaseos aliud hacet ꞔ etiam ego, quam id, quod certo dicitur futurum, fore; quia, vel nam, qui dicit, Dominus est, qui habitat in Zione.
units.tr: *) Lyra, Merc. Drus. Livel. may be understood in this sense, as R. Tanchum also explains it: a continuation of his providence over them and a manifestation of his august presence among them. Where this presence is, it is certain that nothing can harm any survivor, and nothing contributes to the happiness and good state of the inhabitants when these things are lacking. His presence necessarily drives out all evils, and on the contrary supplies all goods. The Hebrews interpret the particle [ו] ve here as nam (for), as if he wished to give them confidence that the things promised here will certainly come to pass. This seems to me to bring out the genuine and true sense of the words, although, as far as I have been able to see, they are the only ones who do so. They do add another interpretation, but it does not differ so much in sense from the first as in wording; it reads: Also I, the Lord who dwells in Zion. For what other emphasis does also I have than this, that what is said will certainly come to pass, because, or for, he who says it is the Lord who dwells in Zion.

units.la: Aliis plerumque vertitur per &c, quæ est vocis Hebrææ cognita significatio, verum uti sæpissime eadem usurpatur pro nam; ita & eodem sensu usu venire particulam &, non possum quin mihi persuadeam, adeo ut & hoc loco non mera sit copulativa, quæ tantum connectat præcedentia cum consequentibus, sed rationem reddens ejus rei veritatis ac certitudinis, quæ hic promittitur. Quicopulativam eam reputant, nemo est præterquam Junius & Tremellius in versione sua; ubi tamen ad plenum sensum reddendum supplent ante eam Ego o) interpretando, ego & Jehovah habitans Tzijone. Hinc ego ipsis notat, Deum Patrem, & Jehovah, Deum Filium, ut explanatum hoc dant in peculiari quadam p) nota. Quod verum esse, si rei attendamus, atque promissorum veritatem afferere nemo non videt, verum hac additione vim fieri verbis haud obscure liquet, quocirca interpretatio altera literalis planior videtur simpliciorque. Quamque nostrat, nobis suggerunt in textu, ad cæterarum omnium nos deducere posset sensum, ea, quam primo loco adduximus, ratione, qua ejus rei hic certos fieri dicendum, cujus in præcedentibus erat illis facta promissio. Quo pacto etiam ea videtur accipi a Chaldæo hæc particula, quia loco ןֹאָמ amar, ait, reddit, inquit Dominus, qui locavit majestatem suam in Zion. Quod ille, qui q) Jehovah est, Dominus potentia infinitus ac æternus omniaque sua decreta ac promissa suo tempore
units.tr: Others for the most part translate it by etc., which is the known meaning of the Hebrew word; but just as it is very often used in the sense of nam (for), so I cannot but be persuaded that the conjunction [&] here also has the same sense, and is not a mere copulative that only joins what precedes to what follows, but gives the reason for the truth and certainty of what is promised here. Those who take it as a mere copulative are none but Junius and Tremellius in their version; yet to bring out the full sense they supply I before it in their rendering, I and Jehovah dwelling in Zion. Hence by I they mean God the Father and Jehovah, God the Son, as they explain in a special note p). That this is true, if we consider the matter and no one fails to see that it affirms the truth of the promises, is clear enough, but this addition plainly does violence to the words; therefore the other, more literal interpretation seems plainer and simpler. The one we have put first, by which the text suggests to us the things said to be made certain, can lead us to the sense of all the others, in that the matter of which a promise had been made in the preceding verses is here declared certain. In this way the Chaldee paraphrast also seems to take this particle, for instead of amar (he said) he renders it: says the Lord who placed his majesty in Zion. He who is q) Jehovah, the Lord infinite and eternal in power, who in his own time necessarily performs all his decrees and promises,

units.la: o) Quos interpretando sequitur Tarnovius p) Hæc autem ita habet: Verba sunt Dei Patris loquentis Dei filio, Jehova qui manet in nobis & nos in illo, & in quo Pater nos purgat ut feramus fructum. q) De hoc nomine vide in Hos. p. 650. tempore necessario præstans, illis promisit quos sibi in peculium suum ascivit, quibusque peculiaria ostendit suæ præsentiæ ac favoris indicia, non potest non certissime fieri ac in eventum deduci, atque hoc ipsum est, quod volunt hæc verba, Deum scilicet qui peculiari modo Majestatis suæ habitaculum fixit in Sion, Membra ac inhabitatores ejus loci ea de re certos reddere. Quorum in gratiam sicut se ubique præsentem atque majestatem suam dicit implere cœlum & terram, ita peculiari ratione eos dignatur sua habitatione vocans se ipsum שכן בציון inhabitatorem Sionis. Gemina his verbis occurrunt v. 17. ubi de iis sic egimus ut & ad hunc locum possint referri dicta; quod superest eo redit, verbum שכן Shochen esse participium proprieque denotare habitans, quod ad omnia tempora trahi potest, ut significet vel, qui habitat, vel qui habitavit, vel qui habitabit, atque ideo ab aliis r) præsenti, ab aliis f) futuro tempore redditur. Discrepantia autem quæ inter eos tunc existit, non nisi in loco est, quem utriq; intelligunt diversum, in quo dicitur habitare vel habitaturus. Is enim locus, qui dicitur Sion, dupliciter, uti notum est, sumitur, vel pro eo loco, qui proprie ita vocatur, atque ubi olim templi erat sedes, vel pro ecclesia Dei eaque iterum vel militante vel triumphante; ad quam hæc nonnulli referunt ad hanc quidem alii, alii ad illam. Inter eos qui proprie id intelligunt de eo loco ad literam, est Kimchi, & cum illo, quod credo, omnes Judæi, qui hisverbis innui vult, Deum non tantum ibi habitasse eo tempore, cum hæc verba a Propheta pronunciabantur, sed & iterum ibi habitaturum, quando reversi erunt & huic loco desolationis tempore elapso suus iterum constabit honos ac gloria. Ita enim ejus verba habent. Et Dominus habitans in Sion (שכן בציון Shoken Betzion) etiam sic in æternum: nam in omnem æternitatem erit שכינתו commoratio ejus in Sion שם שתשוב אחר פוסלquam eo redierit temporibus Messiæ. Ad futurum tempus id quoque revocat R. Tanchum, supplendumque putat verbo ויהיה & erit, ac si scriptum esset שכן ויו בציון & Dominus erit inhabitans (vel habitabit) in Sione. Satius tamen censet Abarbinel ad præteritum referri ac notari, quod antea erat factum, quare paulusum ab aliis discrepat, dum his non vult contineri earum rerum promissionem, quas Deus postea facturus erat; sed earum recensionem, quæ jamjam fecerat, quibus rationem putat dare, quare ulcisci vellet eorum inimicos, nempe quia sanctū illum locū, in quo erat sibi sedes ac habitaculū, destruerent ac incendio delerent. ●
units.tr: o) Those whom Tarnovius follows in interpreting it. p) Now this note reads: These are the words of God the Father speaking to God the Son: Jehovah who abides in us and we in him, and in whom the Father cleanses us that we may bear fruit. q) On this name see on Hos., p. 650. has promised, at the necessary time, to those whom he has taken to himself as his own peculiar people, and to whom he shows the particular tokens of his presence and favour; this cannot but be most certainly fulfilled and brought to pass, and this is just what these words mean: that God, who in a peculiar manner has fixed the dwelling place of his majesty in Zion, makes certain the members and inhabitants of that place concerning this matter. For their sake, just as he says that he is present everywhere and fills heaven and earth with his majesty, so in a special way he deigns to call them his dwelling, calling himself the inhabitant of Zion [שכן בציון]. Twice these words occur in v. 17, where we treated them in such a way that what was said may also be referred to this passage. What remains comes to this: the word [שכן] Shochen is a participle and properly denotes dwelling, which can be applied to all tenses, so as to mean either who dwells, or who dwelt, or who will dwell; therefore some render it in the present tense r), others in the future f). The disagreement that exists between them is only about the place they understand differently as the place where he dwells or will dwell. For the place called Zion is taken, as is well known, in two senses: either for the place that is properly so called, where the temple once stood, or for the Church of God, and that again either militant or triumphant. Some refer these words to the one, others to the other. Among those who understand it properly of that place according to the letter is Kimchi, and with him all the Jews, I believe, who wish that this statement means that God not only dwelt there at the time when these words were spoken by the prophet, but would dwell there again when they had returned and, after the time of desolation had passed, honour and glory would again be established in that place. For his words read: And the Lord dwelling in Zion [שכן בציון Shoken Betzion] also thus forever; for throughout eternity his Shekhinah [שכינתו] will dwell in Zion [שם שתשוב אחר פוסל], to which it would return after the disqualification of [the place], in the time of the Messiah. R. Tanchum also refers this to the future tense, and thinks the verb and it shall be [ויהיה] must be supplied, as if it were written the Lord shall be dwelling (or shall dwell) in Zion. Yet Abarbanel thinks it better to refer it to the past and to note what had happened before; in this he differs somewhat from the others, since he does not want these words to contain a promise of things that God would afterwards do, but a recounting of what he had already done, by which he thinks a reason is given why he would wish to avenge himself on their enemies, namely because they had destroyed and burned that holy place in which he had his seat and dwelling. ●

units.la: Ad Sionem proprie ita dictam hæc etiam refert ex Christianis Grotius, cum verborum hanc dat explicationem; cultus Dei manebit Hierosolymis. Verum id diutius durare non potuit, quam ipsa Hierosolyma, atque templum, in quo habitabat illustri præsentiæ suæ manifestatione, & ad quod cultus tunc temporis erat adstrictus. Et ipse Salvator noster dicit mulieri Samaritanæ Joh. 4,21. Hora venit, qua non etiam Hierosolymis adorabitis Patrem, imo v. 23. quod tunc hora esset.
units.tr: Among Christians, Grotius also refers these words to Zion properly so called, when he gives this explanation of the words: the worship of God will remain in Jerusalem. But this could not last longer than Jerusalem itself and the temple, in which he dwelt with the illustrious manifestation of his presence, and to which worship was then tied. And our Saviour himself says to the Samaritan woman, John 4,21. The hour comes when you will worship the Father not even at Jerusalem; indeed, in v. 23, that hour is now.

units.la: Pariter
units.tr: Likewise

units.la: r) Pag.Tig.Munst.&c. s) LXX. Arab. impref. Pifc. Diodati & Castel. Pariter ea accipere videtur de terrena Sione Calvinus, quibus gratia divina in mentem revocatur Judæis juxta fœdus, quod erat sancitum, quo inter eos sibi habitaculum elegerat Sionem (habitaculum proprium in monte Sione). Verum longe excellentior est assertio, qua Deus hic dicitur inter eos, de quibus hic sermo est, co in loco, qui Sion vocatur perpetuo habitaturus; quod cum de monte Sione Hierosolymæ affirmari non possit, de ecclesia necessario intelligitur, cui hoc nomen alibi quam sæpissime tribuitur, t) ut Heb. 12, 22. Apoc. 14, 1. quæ cum in militantem his in terris ac triumphantem in cœlis dispescatur, ad harum utramque hæc verba accommodari possunt, quia de utraque vere dici potest, Dominum in ea habitare idque in perpetuum. De priore id liquet ex eo, quod Christus ipse dicit: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi. Matth. 28, 20. & ex descriptione eorum, qui eam constituunt, de quibus Paulus ait, quod sint domestici Dei Eph. 2, 19. templum sanctum in Domino, in quo ædificati sunt, ut sint domicilium Dei per Spiritum. verf. 21, 22. De altera nemini dubium est, quin in ea habitet, & habitaturus sit, gloriosamque præsentiam in æternum manifestaturus. Qua re nonnulli sunt adducti, ut in specie ad hanc ipsam hic respici arbitrentur, in quibus etiam est Reverend. Episcop. Hallius qui hæc verba ita παραΦράζει: Numeroque electorum completo, Dominus in æternum cum iis habitabit in cœlesti sua Zione. Utrique ea accommodari posse censet D. Strokius, cum ita hæc verba deducat: Atque ita Deus semper cum sua ecclesia vult esse atque servos suos maximis etiam in periculis servare, aut eo remunerari, quod præsentem hanc liberationem longe excedit, & virtutis ac innocentiæ illorum sufficiens est præmium. Hac ratione, utramvis etiam elegeris, si verba accipiantur, manifestum est, uti non una vice diximus, iis certo asseverari, quod promissum est ecclesiæ & membris ejus veris, & quicquid ad eorum salutem facere queat, id certo certius esse futurum, quod partim patet ex denominatione promittentis, qui est יהוה Jehovah, quod nomen soli Deo (Patri, Filio & Spiritui Sancto) competit, neminique præter eum communicatur, & uti x) denotat essentiam ejus in se ipso, ita & necessitatem verba ac promissa sua præstandi; partim ex ea relatione, qua sibi ipsi eos asserit dicendo, se habitare (vel habitaturum) in Sione. Quo perpetua ejus innuitur præsentia, qua adesse vult inhabitatoribus ac membris ejus, quod idem valet ac si plenam æternamque illis promisisset salutem. Namin conspectu ejus est satietas gaudiorum & a dextra ejus delicia in æternum, Psal. 16, 12. Ad quem amœnissimum ejus conspectum infinita sua gratia nos velit præparare atque ejus aliquando participes reddere per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, cui cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto tribus personis ac uni Domino sit honos & gloria nunc & in omnem æternitatem,
units.tr: r) Pag., Tig., Munst., etc. s) LXX, Arab. impref., Pisc., Diodati and Castal. Likewise Calvin seems to understand it of the earthly Zion, by which the divine grace is recalled to the Jews according to the covenant that had been sanctioned, by which he had chosen Zion for himself as a dwelling (a dwelling of his own on mount Zion). But the assertion by which God is said to dwell among those of whom this speaks, in that place which is called Zion, forever, is far more excellent; and since this cannot be affirmed of mount Zion at Jerusalem, it must necessarily be understood of the Church, to which this name is attributed very often elsewhere, t) as in Heb. 12, 22. Rev. 14, 1. Since this is divided into the militant on earth and the triumphant in heaven, these words can be applied to each of these, because of each it can truly be said that the Lord dwells in it, and that forever. Of the former this is clear from what Christ himself says: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age. Matt. 28, 20. and from the description of those who make it up, of whom Paul says that they are the household of God, Eph. 2, 19, a holy temple in the Lord, in whom they are built, to be a dwelling place of God through the Spirit, vers. 21, 22. Of the latter there is no doubt that he dwells in it, and will dwell in it, and will manifest his glorious presence forever. For this reason some have been led to think that this very thing is especially looked to here; among them is the Reverend Bishop Hall, who paraphrases these words thus [παραφράζει]: When the number of the elect is complete, the Lord will dwell with them forever in his heavenly Zion. Dr. Strock thinks they can be applied to both, for he draws out the words thus: And thus God always wills to be with his Church and to keep his servants safe even in the greatest dangers, or to reward them with something that far exceeds this present deliverance and is a sufficient reward for their virtue and innocence. In this way, whichever of these you choose, if the words are taken as they stand, it is manifest, as we have said more than once, that by them is certainly affirmed what is promised to the Church and to its true members, and whatever can serve their salvation will be more certainly fulfilled. This is clear partly from the name of the one who promises, who is יהוה Jehovah, a name which belongs to God alone (Father, Son and Holy Spirit) and is communicated to no one but him, and which, as x) it denotes his essence in himself, so also the necessity of performing his words and promises; partly from the relation by which he claims them for himself, saying that he dwells (or will dwell) in Zion. By this his perpetual presence is implied, by which he wishes to be present with the inhabitants and members of it, which amounts to the same as if he had promised them full and everlasting salvation. For in his presence is fullness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures forever, Ps. 16, 12. May he, by his infinite grace, wish to prepare us for that most pleasant sight of him, and at some time make us partakers of it through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, three persons and one Lord, be honour and glory now and forever,
